# MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE

->By JAMES MOONEY<-

## I—INTRODUCTION

The myths presented in this paper are part of a large collection of material gathered from the Cherokee, primarily during consecutive field seasons from 1887 to 1890, inclusive. This collection includes more or less extensive notes, along with original Cherokee manuscripts, relating to the history, archaeology, geographic naming, personal names, botany, medicine, arts, home life, religion, songs, ceremonies, and language of the tribe. It is intended that this material will appear from time to time in a series of papers which, when finally brought together, will constitute a monograph on the Cherokee Indians. This paper may be considered the first of the series; everything that has appeared until now is a short paper on the sacred formulas of the tribe, published in the Seventh Annual Report of the Bureau in 1891. That earlier work contained a synopsis of the Cherokee medico-religious theory, with twenty-eight examples selected from a collection of about six hundred ritual formulas written in the Cherokee language and alphabet by former doctors of the tribe. These constitute, altogether, the largest body of Indigenous American literature in existence.

Although the Cherokee are probably the largest and most important tribe in the United States—having their own national government and numbering between 20,000 and 25,000 people at any point in their history—almost nothing has yet been written about their history or general ethnology compared to the literature of northern tribes such as the Delawares, the Iroquois, or the Ojibwa. The difference is due to historical reasons that do not need to be discussed here.

It might seem at first thought that the Cherokee—with their civilized code of laws, their national press, and their schools and seminaries—are so far advanced along the "white man’s road" as to offer little incentive for ethnological study. This is largely true of those in the Indian Territory, for whom the forced deportation from their familiar landscapes and surroundings two generations ago did more at a single stroke to wipe out Indian ideas than could have been accomplished

<summary>James Mooney introduces his extensive research on the Cherokee, noting that this paper on myths is the first in a planned series of monographs. He highlights the lack of existing literature on the Cherokee compared to other tribes and discusses the impact of forced deportation on their traditional culture.</summary>

<keywords>Cherokee, James Mooney, ethnology, ritual formulas, Delawares, Iroquois, Ojibwa, Indian Territory, deportation, Indigenous literature</keywords>

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues James Mooney’s introduction, focusing on the Eastern Band of Cherokee in North Carolina as the primary source of preserved traditions and explaining the scope and comparative method of his study.</meta>

# MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19]

...by fifty years of slow development. However, a significant group remained behind in the heart of the Carolina mountains, currently outnumbering such well-known western tribes as the Omaha, Pawnee, Comanche, and Kiowa. It is among these—the traditional Kitu'hwa element—that ancient traditions have been preserved. Mountaineers guard the past well, and in the secluded forests of Nantahala and Oconaluftee, far from the main-traveled roads of modern progress, the Cherokee priest still treasures the legends and repeats the mystic rituals handed down from his ancestors. Though there is indeed a change in dress and outward appearance, the heart of the Indian is still his own.

For this and other reasons, much of the material contained here was obtained among the Eastern Cherokee living on the Qualla reservation in western North Carolina and in various isolated settlements between the reservation and the Tennessee border. This has been supplemented with information obtained from the Cherokee Nation in Indian Territory, primarily from elderly men and women who had emigrated from what is now Tennessee and Georgia. Consequently, they had better local knowledge of these areas, as well as the history of the Western Nation, than is possessed by their relatives in Carolina. The historical data and the parallels are, of course, compiled mainly from printed sources, but the myths themselves are, with few exceptions, the result of original research.

The historical sketch must be understood expressly as a sketch, not a detailed narrative, for which there is not enough space in this paper. The Cherokee have made a deep impression on the history of the Southern states, and I have attempted nothing more here than to provide the leading facts in a logical sequence. Since the history of the Nation after the removal to the West and the reorganization in Indian Territory offers few points of ethnologic interest, it has been treated briefly. On the other hand, the affairs of the Eastern Band have been discussed at some length, because so little regarding this remnant of the tribe is to be found in print.

One of the primary goals of ethnologic study is to trace the development of human thought under varying conditions of race and environment; the results show consistently that primitive man is essentially the same in every part of the world. With this goal in mind, considerable space has been devoted to parallels drawn almost entirely from Indian tribes of the United States and British America <note>Canada</note>. For the southern countries, there is little reliable material, and to expand the inquiry to the Eastern Hemisphere and the islands of the sea would be an endless task.

The author wishes to express gratitude for many favors from the Library of Congress, the Geological Survey, and the Smithsonian Institution, and for much polite assistance and friendly suggestion from the officers and staff of the Bureau of American Ethnology; and

<summary>Mooney explains that his research relies heavily on the Eastern Cherokee in North Carolina, who have preserved ancient rituals more effectively than the Western Nation. He also defines his work as a historical sketch and an ethnologic study comparing North American tribal myths.</summary>

# II—HISTORICAL SKETCH OF THE CHEROKEE

## THE TRADITIONARY PERIOD

The Cherokee were the mountain people of the South, occupying the entire Allegheny region from the connected headwaters of the Kanawha and the Tennessee rivers southward almost to the site of Atlanta. Their territory stretched from the Blue Ridge in the east to the Cumberland range in the west, comprising an area of about 40,000 square miles that is now part of Virginia, Tennessee, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and Alabama. Their principal towns were located at the headwaters of the Savannah, Hiwassee, and Tuckasegee rivers, and along the entire length of the Little Tennessee to its junction with the main river. Itsâtĭ, or Echota, on the south bank of the Little Tennessee—a few miles above the mouth of the Tellico River in Tennessee—was generally considered the capital of the Nation. As white settlers advanced and pressed upon them from the east and northeast, the more exposed towns were destroyed or abandoned, and new settlements were formed further down the Tennessee River and on the upper branches of the Chattahoochee and the Coosa.

As is always the case with tribal geography, there were no fixed boundaries, and the Cherokee frontiers were contested on every side by rival claimants. In Virginia, there is reason to believe the tribe was held in check in the early days by the Powhatan and the Monacan. To the east and southeast, the Tuscarora and Catawba were their constant enemies, with hardly even a momentary truce within the historic period; evidence also indicates that the Sara, or Cheraw, were just as hostile. To the south, there was a hereditary war with the Creeks, who claimed nearly the whole of upper Georgia as theirs by original possession. However, the Creeks were gradually pressed down toward the Gulf until a treaty was finally made through the mediation of the United States, fixing the boundary between the two tribes along a line running nearly due west from the mouth of the Broad River on the Savannah. To the west, the Chickasaw on the lower Tennessee and the Shawano on the Cumberland repeatedly turned back the tide of Cherokee invasion from the rich central valleys. Meanwhile, the powerful Iroquois in the far north maintained an almost unchallenged claim of supreme lordship from the Ottawa River in Canada southward at least to the Kentucky River.

<summary>This page describes the original 40,000-square-mile territory of the Cherokee in the southern Allegheny region and identifies their traditional capital as Echota. It also details the tribal conflicts and shifting boundaries the Cherokee maintained with neighboring nations like the Creeks, Iroquois, and Chickasaw.</summary>

# MOONEY] TRIBAL NAMES

On the other hand, by their defeat of the Creeks and the expulsion of the Shawano, the Cherokee secured the claim they asserted to all the lands from upper Georgia to the Ohio River, including the rich hunting grounds of Kentucky. Occupying the great mountain barrier between the English settlements on the coast and the French or Spanish garrisons along the Mississippi and the Ohio, their geographic position, as well as their superior numbers, would have given them the balance of power in the South if not for a looseness of tribal organization. This was in striking contrast to the compactness of the Iroquois league, which held French power in check in the north for more than a century. The English, indeed, found it convenient to recognize certain chiefs as supreme in the tribe, but the only real attempt to unite the whole Cherokee Nation into a political unit was made by the French agent, Priber, around 1736; this attempt failed because it was discovered prematurely by the English. We frequently find their kingdom divided against itself; their very numbers prevented unity of action, while still giving them an importance greater than that of neighboring tribes.

The proper name by which the Cherokee call themselves (1)¹ is <term>Yûñ'wiyă'</term>, or <term>Ani'-Yûñ'wiyă'</term> in the third person, signifying "real people" or "principal people"—a word closely related to <term>Oñwe-hoñwe</term>, the name by which the related Iroquois know themselves. The word properly denotes "Indians" as distinguished from people of other races, but in usage, it is restricted to members of the Cherokee tribe. People of other tribes are designated as Creek, Catawba, etc., as the case may be. On ceremonial occasions, they frequently speak of themselves as <term>Ani'-Kitu'hwagĭ</term>, or "people of <term>Kitu'hwa</term>," an ancient settlement on the Tuckasegee River and apparently the original nucleus of the tribe. Among the western Cherokee, this name has been adopted by a secret society recruited from the full-blood population and pledged to resist the advances of the white man's civilization. Under various forms such as <term>Cuttawa</term>, <term>Gattochwa</term>, <term>Kittuwa</term>, etc., as spelled by different authors, it was also used by several northern Algonquian tribes as a synonym for Cherokee.

Cherokee, the name by which they are commonly known, has no meaning in their own language and seems to be of foreign origin. As used among themselves, the form is <term>Tsa'lăgĭ'</term> or <term>Tsa'răgĭ'</term>. It first appears as <term>Chalaque</term> in the Portuguese narrative of De Soto's expedition, originally published in 1557, while we find <term>Cheraqui</term> in a French document from 1699, and Cherokee as an English form at least as early as 1708. The name thus has an authentic history of 360 years. There is evidence that it is derived from the Choctaw word *choluk* or *chiluk*, signifying a pit or cave, and comes to us through the so-called Mobilian trade language, a corrupted Choctaw jargon formerly used as the

<header>MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19</header>
<page-num>16</page-num>

medium of communication among all the tribes of the Gulf states, as far north as the mouth of the Ohio (2). Within this area, many of the tribes were commonly known by Choctaw names, even if they belonged to widely different linguistic groups. If such a name existed for the Cherokee, it would undoubtedly have been shared with the first Spanish explorers by De Soto’s interpreters. This theory is supported by their Iroquois (Mohawk) name, <term>Oyata’ge’ronoñ’</term>, as recorded by Hewitt, meaning “inhabitants of the cave country.” The Allegheny region is uniquely a cave country, where “rock shelters” containing many traces of Indian occupancy are common. Their Catawba name as well, <term>Mañterañ</term>, as recorded by Gatschet, meaning “coming out of the ground,” seems to contain the same reference. Adair’s attempt to connect the name Cherokee with their word for fire, *atsila*, is an error based on an imperfect knowledge of the language.

Among other synonyms for the tribe are <term>Rickahockan</term>, or <term>Recnahecrian</term> (the ancient Powhatan name), and <term>Tallige’</term>, or <term>Tallige’wi</term> (the ancient name used in the *Walam Olum* chronicle of the Lenape). There has been much dispute regarding both the application and the origin of this last name, but there seems to be no reasonable doubt as to the identity of the people.

Linguistically, the Cherokee belong to the <term>Iroquoian</term> stock. This relationship was suspected by Barton over a century ago, and by Gallatin and Hale at a later period, and was definitely established by Hewitt in 1887.<note>1 Barton, Benj. S., *New Views on the Origin of the Tribes and Nations of America*, page xlv, throughout; Philadelphia, 1797; Gallatin, Albert, *Synopsis of Indian Tribes, Transactions of the American Antiquarian Society*, II, page 91; Cambridge, 1836; Hewitt, J. N. B., *The Cherokee an Iroquoian Language*, Washington, 1887 (Manuscript in the archives of the Bureau of American Ethnology).</note> While there is now no question of the connection, the significant differences in vocabulary and grammar indicate that the separation must have happened very early. As is usually the case with a large tribe occupying a vast territory, the language is spoken in several dialects. For want of other names, the principal ones may be conveniently labeled as the Eastern, Middle, and Western. Adair’s classification into “Ayrate” (<term>eladĭ</term>), or low, and “Ottare” (<term>â'talĭ</term>), or mountainous, must be rejected as imperfect.

The Eastern dialect, formerly often called the Lower Cherokee dialect, was originally spoken in all the towns along the waters of the Keowee and Tugaloo—the head-streams of the Savannah River in South Carolina and the adjacent part of Georgia. Its chief peculiarity is a rolling *r*, which takes the place of the *l* used in the other dialects. In this dialect, the tribal name is <term>Tsa’rǎgi’</term>, which the English settlers of Carolina corrupted to Cherokee. Meanwhile, the Spaniards, advancing from the south, became more familiar with the other form, which they wrote as <term>Chalaque</term>. Due to their exposed frontier position next to the white settlements of Carolina, the Cherokee of this division

<header>MOONEY] DIALECTS—RELATED TRIBES</header>
<page-num>17</page-num>

were the first to feel the shock of war in the campaigns of 1760 and 1776, with the result that before the end of the Revolution, they had been completely removed from their original territory and scattered as refugees among the more western towns of the tribe. The consequence was that they lost their distinctive dialect, which is now almost extinct. In 1888, it was spoken by only one man on the reservation in North Carolina.

The Middle dialect, which might properly be called the Kituhwa dialect, was originally spoken in the towns on the Tuckasegee and the headwaters of the Little Tennessee, in the very heart of the Cherokee country, and is still spoken by the great majority of those now living on the Qualla reservation. In some of its phonetic forms, it agrees with the Eastern dialect, but resembles the Western in having the *l* sound.

The Western dialect was spoken in most of the towns of east Tennessee and upper Georgia and on the Hiwassee and Cheowa rivers in North Carolina. It is the softest and most musical of all the dialects of this musical language, having a frequent liquid *l* and dropping many of the harsher consonants found in the other forms. It is also the literary dialect and is spoken by most of those now making up the Cherokee Nation in the West.

Scattered among the other Cherokee are individuals whose pronunciation and occasional unique terms for familiar objects indicate a fourth and perhaps a fifth dialect, which cannot now be localized. It is possible that these differences may come from foreign mixing, such as Natchez, Taskigi, or Shawano blood. There is some reason for believing that the people living on the Nantahala River differed in dialect from their neighbors on either side (3).

The Iroquoian stock, to which the Cherokee belong, had its main home in the north, its tribes occupying a compact territory which comprised parts of Ontario, New York, Ohio, and Pennsylvania, and extended down the Susquehanna and Chesapeake Bay almost to the latitude of Washington. Another group, including the Tuscarora, Nottoway, and perhaps also the Meherrin, occupied territory in northeastern North Carolina and the adjacent part of Virginia. The Cherokee themselves formed the third and southernmost group. It is evident that tribes of a common stock must at one time have occupied adjacent territories, and we find that to be the case in this instance. The Tuscarora and Meherrin, and presumably also the Nottoway, are known to have come from the north, while traditional and historical evidence agree in assigning the region around the headwaters of the Ohio as the Cherokee's early home, immediately to the south of their kinsmen, but bitter enemies, the Iroquois. The theory which brings the Cherokee from northern Iowa and the Iroquois from Manitoba is not worth serious consideration. (4)

<header>MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19</header>
<page-num>18</page-num>

the Delaware tradition of the expulsion of the Talligewi from the north, as first noted by the missionary Heckewelder in 1819, and published more fully by Brinton in the *Walam Olum* in 1885. According to the first account, the Delawares, advancing from the west, found their further progress opposed by a powerful people called Alligewi or Talligewi, occupying the country upon a river which Heckewelder thinks is identical with the Mississippi, but which the sequel shows was more probably the upper Ohio. They were said to have regularly built earthen fortifications, in which they defended themselves so well that at last the Delawares were obliged to seek the assistance of the “Mengwe,” or Iroquois. This resulted in a warfare extending over many years, after which the Alligewi finally received a crushing defeat. The survivors fled down the river and abandoned the country to the invaders, who then parceled it out among themselves. The “Mengwe” chose the portion about the Great Lakes, while the Delawares took possession of the land to the south and east. The missionary adds that the Allegheny (and Ohio) river was still called by the Delawares the Alligewi Sipu, or river of the Alligewi. This would seem to indicate it as the true river of the tradition. He also speaks of remarkable earthworks seen by him in 1789 in the neighborhood of Lake Erie, which were said by the Indians to have been built by the exterminated tribe as defensive fortifications during this war. Near two of these, in the vicinity of Sandusky, he was shown mounds under which it was said some hundreds of the slain Talligewi were buried. <note>Heckewelder, John, Indian Nations of Pennsylvania, pp. 47-49, 1876 edition.</note> As is usual in such traditions, the Alligewi were said to have been of giant stature, far exceeding their conquerors in size.

In the *Walam Olum*, which is asserted to be a metrical translation of an ancient hieroglyphic bark record discovered in 1820, the main tradition is given in practically the same way, with an appendix which follows the fortunes of the defeated tribe up to the beginning of the historic period, thus completing the chain of evidence. (5)

In the *Walam Olum* we also find the Delawares advancing from the west or northwest until they come to “Fish river”—the same which Heckewelder identifies as the Mississippi (6). On the other side, we are told, “The Talligewi possessed the East.” The Delaware chief “desired the eastern land,” and some of his people go on, but are killed by the Talligewi. The Delawares decide upon war and call in the help of their northern friends, the “Talamatan,” meaning the Wyandot and other allied Iroquoian tribes. A war ensues which continues through the terms of four successive chiefs, until victory is declared for the invaders, and “all the Talega go south.” The country is then divided, with the Talamatan taking the northern portion, while the Delawares “stay south of the lakes.” The chronicle proceeds to tell how, after eleven more chiefs have ruled, the Nanticoke and Shawano separate from the main body.

### MOONEY] DELAWARE TRADITIONS—THE NAME TALLIGEWI

...parent tribe and moved south. Six other chiefs followed in succession until we reach the seventh, who “went to the <term>Talega</term> mountains.” By this time, the <term>Delawares</term> had reached the ocean. Other chiefs succeeded, after whom “the Easterners and the Wolves”—probably the <term>Mahican</term> or <term>Wappinger</term> and the <term>Munsee</term>—moved off to the northeast. At last, after six more chiefs, “the whites came on the eastern sea,” which likely refers to the landing of the Dutch on Manhattan in 1609 (7). We may consider this a marker date, approximating the beginning of the seventeenth century. Two more chiefs ruled, and of the second, we are told that “He fought in the south; he fought in the land of the <term>Talega</term> and <term>Koweta</term>,” and again the fourth chief after the coming of the whites “went to the <term>Talega</term>.” We thus have a traditional record of a war of conquest carried out against the <term>Talligewi</term> by four successive chiefs, and a succession of about twenty-five chiefs between the final expulsion of that tribe and the appearance of the whites. During this interval, the <term>Nanticoke</term>, <term>Shawano</term>, <term>Mahican</term>, and <term>Munsee</term> branched off from the main <term>Lenape'</term> stem. Without attempting to entangle ourselves in the complex maze of Indian chronology, it is enough to note that all this implies a very long period of time—so long, in fact, that during it, several new tribes, each of which eventually developed a distinct dialect, branched off from the main <term>Lenape'</term> stem. It is clearly stated that all the <term>Talega</term> went south after their final defeat; from later references, we find that they took refuge in the mountain country near the <term>Koweta</term> (the <term>Creeks</term>), and that <term>Delaware</term> war parties were still raiding both these tribes long after the first appearance of the whites.

Although at first glance it might be thought that the name <term>Talligewi</term> is only a corruption of <term>Tsalagi</term>, a closer study suggests that it is a genuine <term>Delaware</term> word, most likely connected with <term>*waloh*</term> or <term>*walok*</term>, meaning a cave or hole (Zeisberger). This explains why we find the word <term>*oligonunk*</term> in the <term>Walam Olum</term> translated as “at the place of caves.” It would thus be an exact <term>Delaware</term> translation of the same name, “people of the cave country,” by which, as we have seen, the <term>Cherokee</term> were commonly known among the tribes. Whatever the origin of the name itself, there can be no reasonable doubt about its application. “Name, location, and legends combine to identify the <term>Cherokees</term> or <term>Tsalaki</term> with the <term>Tallike</term>; and this is as much evidence as we can expect to produce in such research.” <note>Brinton, D. G., *Walam Olum*, p. 231; Philadelphia, 1885.</note>

The <term>Wyandot</term> confirm the <term>Delaware</term> story and establish the identity of the expelled tribe. According to their tradition, as told in 1802, the ancient fortifications in the <term>Ohio Valley</term> were built during a long war between themselves and the <term>Cherokee</term>, which finally resulted in the defeat of the latter. <note>Schoolcraft, H. R., *Notes on the Iroquois*, p. 162; Albany, 1847.</note>

# MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19
## 20

...supplement and corroborate those of the northern tribes, thus bringing the story down to their final settlement upon the headwaters of the Tennessee in the rich valleys of the southern Alleghenies. Due to the Cherokee preference for new gods—which contrasted strongly with the conservatism of the Iroquois—their ritual forms and national epics had fallen into decay even before the Revolution, as we learn from Adair. Some remains of their migration legend still existed in Haywood’s time, but it is now completely forgotten both in the East and in the West.

According to Haywood, who wrote in 1823 using information obtained directly from leading members of the tribe long before the Removal, the Cherokee formerly had a long migration legend. This legend was already lost, but within the memory of the mother of one informant—around 1750—it was still recited by chosen orators on the occasion of the annual green-corn dance. This migration legend appears to have resembled those of the Delawares and the Creeks by beginning with genesis and the period of animal monsters, and then following the shifting fortunes of the chosen band to the historic period. The tradition recited that they had originated in a land toward the rising sun, where they had been placed by the command of “the four councils sent from above.” In this original home were great snakes and water monsters; for this reason, it was supposed to have been near the seacoast, although this assumption is not a necessary conclusion, as these are a feature of the mythology of all the eastern tribes. After this genesis period, a slow migration began, during which “towns of people moved in many nights’ encampment,” but no details are given. From Heckewelder, it appears that the expression “a night’s encampment,” which also occurs in the Delaware migration legend, is a Native American figure of speech for staying in one place for a year.¹

In another place, Haywood says, although apparently confusing the chronological order of events: “One tradition they have among them says they came from the west and exterminated the former inhabitants; it then says they came from the upper parts of the Ohio, where they built the mounds on Grave Creek, and that they moved there from the region where Monticello (near Charlottesville, Virginia) is situated.”² The first reference is to the famous mounds on the Ohio near Moundsville, below Wheeling, West Virginia. The other undoubtedly refers to a well-known burial mound described by Jefferson in 1781 as then existing near his home, on the low grounds of the Rivanna River opposite the site of an ancient Indian town. He had opened it himself and found it to contain perhaps a thousand disjointed skeletons of both adults and children; the bones were piled in successive layers, with those near the top being the least decayed. They showed no signs

of violence, but were clearly the accumulation of many years from the nearby Indian town. The distinguished writer adds:

> “But regardless of the occasion on which they may have been made, they are very well known among the Indians. About thirty years ago <note>i.e., about 1750</note>, a party passing through the part of the country where this burial mound is located went directly through the woods to it without any instructions or inquiry. After staying there for some time, with expressions interpreted as those of sorrow, they returned to the high road—which they had left about six miles earlier to make this visit—and continued their journey.”¹

Although the tribe is not named, the Indians were probably Cherokee, as no other Southern Indians were then accustomed to travel in that section. Supporting this opinion is the statement of a prominent Cherokee chief, given to Schoolcraft in 1846, that according to their tradition, his people had formerly lived at the Peaks of Otter in Virginia—a well-known landmark of the Blue Ridge, near the point where the Staunton River breaks through the mountains.²

From a careful examination of the evidence, Haywood concludes that the creators of the most ancient remains in Tennessee had spread over that region from the south and southwest at a very early period. However, he believes the later occupants, the Cherokee, entered the area from the north and northeast in relatively recent times, overrunning and exterminating the original inhabitants. He declares that the historical fact seems to be established that the Cherokee entered the country from Virginia, making temporary settlements on the New River and the upper Holston. They remained there until, under continued hostile pressure from the north, they were again forced to move further south, settling on the Little Tennessee River in what later became known as the Middle Towns. A leading person of mixed heritage within the tribe informed him that they had made their first settlements within their modern home territory on the Nolichucky River. Having lived there for a long time, they could give no clear account of an earlier location. Echota, their capital and peace town, “claimed to be the eldest brother in the nation,” and this claim was generally acknowledged.³ Confirming the statement about an early occupation of the upper Holston region, it should be noted that “Watauga Old Fields” (now Elizabethton) were so named because when the first white settlement in the present state of Tennessee began there as early as 1769, the bottomlands were found to contain graves and numerous other ancient remains of a former Indian town. Tradition attributed these remains to the Cherokee, even though their nearest settlements at that time were many miles to the south.

While the Cherokee claimed to have built the mounds on the upper

Ohio, they still, according to Haywood, explicitly denied being the authors of the numerous mounds and rock carvings (petroglyphs) in the territory they later occupied, asserting that these ancient works looked the same when they themselves had first moved into the region.¹ This matches Bartram's statement that the Cherokee—although they sometimes used the mounds as sites for their own town houses—were as ignorant as the white settlers about their origin or purpose, having only a general tradition that their ancestors had found them in much the same condition when they first arrived in the country.²

Although, as previously noted, Haywood expresses the opinion that the invading Cherokee had overwhelmed and wiped out the earlier inhabitants, he states elsewhere—based on the authority of a person of mixed ancestry—that the newcomers found no Indians along the waters of the Tennessee, with the exception of some Creeks living on that river near the mouth of the Hiwassee; the main body of that tribe was established on and claimed all the streams to the south.³ There is significant evidence that the Creeks arrived before the Cherokee, and within the last century, they still claimed the Tennessee River, or at least the Tennessee watershed, as their northern boundary.

There is a faint but persistent tradition of a strange white race that lived there before the Cherokee. Some of the stories even go so far as to locate their former settlements and identify them as the creators of the ancient works found in the region. The earliest reference seems to be from Barton in 1797, based on a statement from a gentleman whom he quotes as a valuable authority on the southern tribes. "The Cherokee tell us that when they first arrived in the country they now inhabit, they found it occupied by certain 'moon-eyed people' who could not see during the day. They drove these unfortunates out." He seems to consider them an albino race.⁴ Twenty-six years later, Haywood says that the invading Cherokee found "white people" near the headwaters of the Little Tennessee, with forts extending from there down the Tennessee as far as Chickamauga Creek. He provides the locations of three of these forts. The Cherokee waged war against them and drove them to the mouth of Big Chickamauga Creek, where they entered into a treaty and agreed to relocate if they were allowed to depart in peace. Once permission was granted, they abandoned the region. Elsewhere, he mentions that this exterminated white race had also spread into Kentucky and likely into western Tennessee, according to the matching traditions of various tribes. He describes their houses—though he does not state his source—as having been small, circular structures

Harry Smith, a man of mixed ancestry born about 1815 and the father of the late chief of the Eastern Cherokee, informed the author that as a boy, he had been told by an old woman a tradition of a race of very small, perfectly white people. These people once came and lived for some time on the site of the ancient mound on the northern side of Hiwassee, at the mouth of Peachtree Creek, a few miles above the present Murphy, North Carolina. They afterward moved to the West. Colonel Thomas, the white chief of the Eastern Cherokee born about the beginning of the century, had also heard a tradition of another race of people who lived on the Hiwassee, opposite the present-day Murphy. They warned the Cherokee that they must not attempt to cross over to the south side of the river, or the great leech in the water would swallow them.<note>See the story, "The Great Leech of Tlanusi'yĭ," p. 328.</note> They finally went west, "long before the whites came." The two stories are plainly the same, although told independently and many miles apart.

### THE PERIOD OF SPANISH EXPLORATION—1540–?

The definite history of the Cherokee begins with the year 1540. At this date, we find them already established in the mountains of Carolina and Georgia, where they were always afterward known to reside. The earliest Spanish adventurers failed to penetrate so far into the interior, and the first entry into their country was made by De Soto, who was advancing up the Savannah River on his fruitless quest for gold in May of that year.

While at Cofitachiqui, an important Indian town on the lower Savannah governed by a "queen," the Spaniards had found hatchets and other objects made of copper. Some of this copper was of a finer color and appeared to be mixed with gold, although they had no means of testing it.<note>Garcilaso de la Vega, The Florida of the Inca, pp. 129, 133–134; Madrid, 1723.</note> On inquiry, they were told that the metal had come from an interior mountain province called Chisca, but the country was represented as thinly peopled and the way as impassable for horses. Some time before, while advancing through eastern Georgia, they had also heard of a rich and plentiful province called Coça toward the northwest. The people of Cofitachiqui now told them that Chiaha, the nearest town of the Coça province, was twelve days inland. As both men and animals were already nearly exhausted from hunger and hard travel, and the Indians either could not or would not furnish sufficient provisions for their needs, De Soto determined not to attempt the passage of the mountains then. Instead, he decided to push on at once to Coça to rest and recuperate before undertaking further exploration. In the mean—

At that time, he also hoped to obtain more definite information about the mines. Since the primary goal of the expedition was the discovery of these mines, many of the officers regarded this change of plans as a mistake. They favored staying where they were until the new crop had ripened, then heading directly into the mountains; however, because the general was "a stern man and of few words," no one ventured to oppose his decision.1 The province of Coça was the territory of the Creek Indians, whom the Cherokee called Ani'-Kusa, named after Kusa, or Coosa, their ancient capital. Chiaha was identical to Chehaw, one of the principal Creek towns on the Chattahoochee River. Cofitachiqui may have been the capital of the Uchee Indians.

The Spaniards' outrageous conduct had so angered the Indian queen that she now refused to provide guides and porters. Consequently, De Soto took her prisoner, intending to force her to act as a guide herself and to use her as a hostage to ensure the obedience of her subjects. However, instead of leading the Spaniards along the direct trail toward the west, she led them far off their course until she finally managed to escape, leaving them to find their own way out of the mountains as best they could.

Departing from Cofitachiqui, they turned first toward the north, passing through several towns subject to the queen. Even though she was a prisoner, the Indians everywhere showed her great respect and obedience, providing whatever assistance the Spaniards forced her to demand for their own purposes. In a few days, they came to "a province called Chalaque," the territory of the Cherokee Indians, likely located on the waters of the Keowee River, the eastern head-stream of the Savannah. It is described as the poorest country for corn they had yet seen; the inhabitants lived on wild roots, herbs, and game which they killed with bows and arrows. They were naked, thin, and not inclined toward war. The country was full of wild turkeys ("*gallinas*"), which the people gave very freely to the strangers—one town presented them with seven hundred. A chief also gave De Soto two deerskins as a significant gift.2 Garcilaso, writing on the authority of an old soldier nearly fifty years later, says that the "*Chalaques*" abandoned their towns as the white men approached and fled to the mountains, leaving behind only the elderly and those who were nearly blind.3 Although it was too early for the new harvest, the poverty of the people may have been more apparent than real, caused by their unwillingness to give any part of their stored provisions to the unwelcome strangers. As the Spaniards were greatly in need of corn for themselves and their horses, they did not stay long but hurried on. In a few days, they arrived

at Guaquili, which is mentioned only by Ranjel, who does not specify whether it was a town or a province—that is, a tribal territory. It was probably a small town. Here they were welcomed in a friendly manner; the Indians gave them a little corn and many wild turkeys, along with some dogs of a peculiar small species that were bred for eating and did not bark.1 They were also supplied with men to help carry the baggage. The name Guaquili has a Cherokee sound and may be connected with *wa' guli'*, "whippoorwill," *uwâ'gi'li*, "foam," or *gi'li*, "dog."

Traveling still toward the north, they arrived a day or two later in the province of Xuala, in which we recognize the territory of the Suwali, Sara, or Cheraw Indians, in the piedmont region near the head of the Broad River in North Carolina. Garcilaso, who did not see it, describes it as a rich country, while the Elvas narrative and Biedma agree that it was a rough, broken country, thinly inhabited and poor in provisions. According to Garcilaso, it was under the rule of the queen of Cofitachiqui, although a distinct province in itself.2 The principal town was beside a small rapid stream, close under a mountain. The chief received them in a friendly fashion, giving them corn, dogs of the small breed already mentioned, carrying baskets, and burden bearers. The surrounding country showed greater indications of gold mines than any they had yet seen.1

Here De Soto turned to the west, crossing a very high mountain range which appears to have been the Blue Ridge, and descending on the other side to a stream flowing in the opposite direction, which was probably one of the upper tributaries of the French Broad River.3 Although it was late in May, they found it very cold in the mountains.4 After several days of such travel they arrived, about the end of the month, at the town of Guasili, or Guaxule. The chief and principal men came out some distance to welcome them, dressed in fine robes of skins with feather head-dresses, after the fashion of the country. Before reaching this point, the queen had managed to make her escape, along with three slaves of the Spaniards, and the last that was heard of her was that she was on her way back to her own country with one of the runaways as her husband. What grieved De Soto most in the matter was that she took with her a small box of pearls, which he had intended to take from her before releasing her, but had left with her for the present in order "not to displease her entirely."5

Guaxule is described as a very large town surrounded by a number of small mountain streams which united to form the large river down which the Spaniards proceeded after leaving the place.6 Here, as

elsewhere, the Indians received the white men with kindness and hospitality—so much so that the name of Guaxule became a synonym for good fortune to the army.<note>1</note> Among other things, they gave the Spaniards 300 dogs for food, although, according to the Elvas narrative, the Indians themselves did not eat them.<note>2</note> The principal officers of the expedition were lodged in the “chief’s house,” which we are to understand as the townhouse, located on a high hill with a roadway to the top.<note>3</note> From a close study of the narrative, it appears that this “hill” was none other than the great Nacoochee mound, in White county, Georgia, a few miles northwest of the present Clarkesville.<note>4</note> It was within the Cherokee territory, and the town was probably a settlement of that tribe. From here De Soto sent runners ahead to notify the chief of Chiaha of his approach, so that sufficient corn might be ready upon his arrival.

Leaving Guaxule, they proceeded down the river, which we identify with the Chattahoochee, and in two days arrived at Canasoga, or Canasagua, a frontier town of the Cherokee. As they neared the town, they were met by the Indians, who were carrying baskets of “mulberries,”<note>5</note> more probably the delicious service-berry of the southern mountains, which ripens in early summer, while the mulberry matures later.

From here they continued down the river, which grew constantly larger, through an uninhabited country which formed the disputed territory between the Cherokee and the Creeks. About five days after leaving Canasagua, they were met by messengers who escorted them to Chiaha, the first town of the province of Coça. De Soto had crossed the state of Georgia, leaving the Cherokee country behind him, and was now among the Lower Creeks, in the neighborhood of the present Columbus, Georgia.<note>6</note> We need not concern ourselves with his subsequent wanderings after crossing the Chattahoochee into Alabama and beyond (8).

While resting at Chiaha, De Soto met with a chief who confirmed what the Spaniards had heard before concerning mines in the province of Chisca, saying that there was a “melting of copper” there and of another metal of about the same color, but softer, and therefore not used as much.<note>7</note> The province was northward from Chiaha, somewhere in upper Georgia or the adjacent part of Alabama or Tennessee, through all of which mountain region native copper is found. The other mineral, which the Spaniards understood to be gold, may have been iron pyrites, although there is some evidence that the Indians occasionally found and shaped gold nuggets.<note>6</note>

Accordingly, two soldiers were sent on foot with Indian guides to find <term>Chisca</term> and learn the truth of the stories. They rejoined the army some time after the march had been resumed and reported, according to the Elvas chronicler, that their guides had taken them through a country so poor in corn, so rough, and over such high mountains that it would be impossible for the army to follow. For this reason, as the journey became long and slow, they turned back after reaching a small, poor town where they saw nothing of value. They brought back with them a dressed buffalo skin that the Indians there had given them—the first ever obtained by white men—which was described in the quaint old chronicle as “an ox hide as thin as a calf’s skin, with hair like soft wool, somewhere between the coarse and fine wool of sheep.”<note>Elvas, Hakluyt Society, IX, p. 66, 1851.</note>

Garcilaso’s glowing narrative gives a somewhat different impression. According to this author, the scouts returned full of enthusiasm for the fertility of the country and reported that the mines contained a fine species of copper, with indications of gold and silver as well, while their progress from one town to another had been a continual series of feasts and Indian hospitality.<note>Garcilaso, La Florida del Inca, p. 141, ed. 1723.</note> However that may have been, De Soto made no further effort to reach the <term>Cherokee</term> mines but continued his course westward through the <term>Creek</term> country, having spent a total of one month in the mountain region.

There is no record of any second attempt to enter the <term>Cherokee</term> country for twenty-six years (9). In 1561, the Spaniards took formal possession of the bay of <term>Santa Elena</term> (now Saint Helena, near Port Royal, on the coast of South Carolina). The next year, the French made an unsuccessful attempt at settlement at the same place, and in 1566, <term>Menendez</term> secured Spanish control by establishing a fort there called <term>San Felipe</term>.<note>Shea, J. G., in Winsor, Justin, Narrative and Critical History of America, II, pp. 260, 278; Boston, 1886.</note> In November of that year, Captain <term>Juan Pardo</term> was sent with a party from the fort to explore the interior. Accompanied by the chief of “<term>Juada</term>” (which, from <term>Vandera</term>’s narrative, we find should be “<term>Joara</term>”—the <term>Sara Indians</term> already mentioned in the De Soto chronicle), he proceeded as far as the territory of that tribe, where he built a fort. However, because of the snow in the mountains, he did not think it wise to go further and returned, leaving a sergeant with thirty soldiers to garrison the post. Soon after his return, he received a letter from the sergeant stating that the chief of <term>Chisca</term>—the rich mining country De Soto had heard of—was very hostile to the Spaniards, and that in a recent battle the Spaniards had killed a thousand of his Indians and burned fifty houses with almost no damage to themselves. Either the sergeant or his chronicler must have been an outrageous liar, as it was claimed that all this was done with only fifteen men. Immediately afterward, according to the same story, the sergeant marched with twenty men about a day’s

After a hard fight, he and his men stormed and burned the town, killing fifteen hundred Indians without losing a single man themselves. Under instructions from his superior officer, the sergeant and his small party then proceeded to explore the area beyond. Taking a road that they were told led to the territory of a great chief, they arrived after four days of hard marching at his town, called Chiaha (mistakenly written as Chicha in the manuscript translation), the same place where De Soto had rested. At this time, it is described as palisaded and strongly fortified, with a deep river on each side, and defended by over three thousand fighting men, with no women or children among them. It is possible that, given their previous experience with the Spaniards, the Indians had sent their families away from the town; at the same time, they may have summoned warriors from the neighboring <term>Creek</term> towns in order to be prepared for any emergency. However, as before, they received the white men with the greatest kindness, and the Spaniards continued for twelve days through the territories of the same tribe until they arrived at the principal town (possibly <term>Kusa</term>?). There, at the invitation of the chief, they built a small fort and awaited the arrival of Pardo, who was expected to follow with a larger force from Santa Elena. Pardo did so in the summer of 1567 and was met upon his arrival with every show of hospitality from the <term>Creek</term> chiefs. This second fort was said to be one hundred and forty leagues distant from the one in the <term>Sara</term> country, which itself was said to be one hundred and twenty leagues from Santa Elena.<note>Narrative of Pardo’s expedition by Martinez, about 1568, Brooks manuscripts.</note>

In the summer of 1567, according to a previous agreement, Captain Pardo left the fort at Santa Elena with a small detachment of troops. After a week’s travel, sleeping each night at a different Indian town, he arrived at “Canos, which the Indians call Canosi, and by another name, Cofetacque” (the <term>Cofitachiqui</term> of the De Soto chronicle). This location is described as favorable for a large city and was fifty leagues from Santa Elena; the easiest road to it was by a river (the Savannah) which flowed by the town, or by another river they had passed ten leagues earlier. Proceeding onward, they passed Jagaya, Gueza, and Arauchi, and arrived at Otariyatiqui, or Otari, in which we find perhaps the <term>Cherokee</term> *â’tărĭ* or *â’tălĭ*, meaning “mountain.” It may have been a frontier <term>Cherokee</term> settlement, and, according to the old chronicler, its chief and language ruled over much good land. From here, a trail went northward to Guatari, Sauxpa, and Usi—that is, the Wateree, Waxhaw (or perhaps Sissipahaw?), and Ushery or <term>Catawba</term>.

This, as previously noted, was the Xuala mentioned in the De Soto chronicle—the territory of the Sara Indians in the foothills of the Blue Ridge, southeast of present-day Asheville, North Carolina. The difference is not significant, as both figures were merely estimates. From there, they traveled "along the mountains" to Tocax (possibly Toxaway?), Cauchi (possibly Nacoochee?), and Tanasqui—apparently Cherokee towns, although the names cannot be positively identified—and after resting for three days at the last location, they continued "to Solameco, also known as Chiaha," where the sergeant met them. The combined forces then continued through Cossa (<term>Kusa</term>), Tasquiqui (<term>Taskigi</term>), and other <term>Creek</term> towns as far as Tascaluza in the Alabama region, and from there returned to Santa Elena, having apparently been received kindly everywhere along the route. From Cofitachiqui to Tascaluza, they traveled roughly the same route taken by De Soto in 1540.<sup>1</sup>

We now come to a significant gap of nearly a century. Shea mentions a Spanish mission established among the Cherokee in 1643 that was supposedly still flourishing when an English traveler visited ten years later;<sup>2</sup> however, since his information comes entirely from the fraudulent work of Davies, and because Barcia mentions no such mission during those years, we may consider the story false (10). The first actual mission work among the tribe appears to have been that of Priber, nearly a hundred years later. However, long before the end of the sixteenth century, the existence of gold mines and other metal deposits in Cherokee territory was common knowledge among the Spaniards at St. Augustine and Santa Elena, and several expeditions had been organized to explore the interior.<sup>3</sup> Numerous traces of ancient mining operations—including remains of old shafts and fortifications clearly of European origin—show that these discoveries were pursued, even though Spanish policy kept these facts hidden from the rest of the world. It is impossible to estimate how much of a lasting impression this early Spanish contact made on the Cherokee, but it must have been significant (11).

### THE COLONIAL AND REVOLUTIONARY PERIOD—1654-1784

It was not until 1654 that the English first encountered the Cherokee, who were called "Rechahecrians" in the records of that period—a corruption of "Rickahockan," which was apparently the name the Powhatan tribes used for them. In that year, the Virginia colony—which had only recently ended a long and devastating war with the Powhatan—was alarmed by news that a large group of

Six or seven hundred Rechahecrian Indians—which probably refers to that number of warriors—from the mountains had invaded the lower country and established themselves at the falls of the James River, where the city of Richmond now stands. The assembly at once passed resolutions "that these newly arrived Indians should by no means be allowed to settle there, or in any place near us, as it has cost so much blood to expel and eliminate those treacherous and deceitful Indians who were there previously." It was therefore ordered that a force of at least 100 white men be sent against them immediately, to be joined by the warriors of all the neighboring subject tribes, according to treaty obligations. The Pamunkey chief, with a hundred of his men, responded to the summons, and the combined force marched against the invaders. The result was a bloody battle with a disastrous outcome for the Virginians; the Pamunkey chief and most of his men were killed, while the whites were forced to make such peace terms with the Rechahecrians that the assembly dismissed the commander of the expedition and compelled him to pay the entire cost of the treaty from his own fortune. <gloss>1</gloss>

Due to the gaps in the Virginia records, we have no way of knowing the causes of the sudden invasion or how long the invaders held their position at the falls. In all probability, it was only the last of a long series of otherwise unrecorded raids by the mountain people on the more peaceful dwellers in the lowlands. From a remark by Lederer, it is likely that the Cherokee were also assisted by some of the Piedmont tribes who were hostile to the Powhatan. The Peaks of Otter, near which the Cherokee claim to have once lived (as previously noted), are only about one hundred miles in a straight line from Richmond, while the burial mound and town site near Charlottesville mentioned by Jefferson are only half that distance away.

In 1655, a Virginia expedition sent out from the falls of the James River (Richmond) crossed over the mountains to the large streams flowing into the Mississippi. No details are given and the route is uncertain, but whether or not they met Indians, they must have passed through Cherokee territory. <gloss>2</gloss>

In 1670, the German traveler John Lederer went from the falls of the James River to the Catawba country in South Carolina, following for most of the distance the path used by the Virginia traders, who already had regular dealings with the southern tribes, including probably the Cherokee. He speaks in several places of the Rickahockan, which seems to be a more correct form than Rechahecrian, and his narrative and the accompanying map place them in the mountains of North Carolina, behind the Catawba and the Sara and south of the headwaters of the Roanoke River. They were apparently on hostile terms with the tribes to the east, and while the traveler was stopping at an Indian

Upon reaching the Catawba country, he heard of white men to the south and incidentally mentions that the neighboring mountains were called the Suala Mountains by the Spaniards.¹ In the next year, 1671, a party from Virginia under Thomas Batts explored the northern branch of the Roanoke River and crossed over the Blue Ridge to the headwaters of the New River, where they found traces of occupation, but no Indians. By this time, all the tribes of this section, east of the mountains, were in possession of firearms.²

The first permanent English settlement in South Carolina was established in 1670. In 1690, James Moore, secretary of the colony, led an exploratory expedition into the mountains and reached a point at which, according to his Indian guides, he was within twenty miles of where the Spaniards were engaged in mining and smelting with bellows and furnaces. However, because of some misunderstanding, he returned without visiting the place, although he obtained specimens of ores which he sent to England for assay.³ This may have been in the neighborhood of present-day Lincolnton, North Carolina, where a dam of cut stone and other remains of former civilized occupation have recently been discovered (11). In this year, also, Cornelius Dougherty, an Irishman from Virginia, established himself as the first trader among the Cherokee, with whom he spent the rest of his life.⁴ Some of his descendants still occupy honored positions in the tribe.

Among the manuscript archives of South Carolina, it was said some fifty years ago that there was a treaty or agreement made with the government of that colony by the Cherokee in 1684. It was signed with the hieroglyphic marks of eight chiefs of the lower towns, namely: Corani, the Raven (Kâ'lanû); Sinnawa, the Hawk (Tlǎ'nuwǎ); Nellawgitehi, Gorhaleke, and Owasta, all of Toxawa; and Canacaught, the great Conjurer, Gohoma, and Caunasaita, of Keowa. If still in existence, this is probably the oldest Cherokee treaty on record.⁵

What seems to be the next mention of the Cherokee in the South Carolina records occurs in 1691, when we find an inquiry ordered regarding a report that some of the colonists “have, without any proclamation of war, fallen upon and murdered” several members of that tribe.⁶

By this course, it was asserted, he had "already almost utterly ruined the trade for skins and furs, through which we held our chief correspondence with England, and turned it into a trade of Indians or slave making, by which the Indians to the south and west of us are already involved in blood and confusion." The formal accusation concludes with a warning that such conditions would in all probability draw down upon the colony an Indian war with all its dreadful consequences.² In view of what happened a few years later, this reads like a prophecy.

<margin>✓</margin>About the year 1700, the first guns were introduced among the Cherokee, the event being traditionally established as having occurred during the girlhood of an old woman of the tribe who died about 1775.³ In 1708, we find them described as a numerous people, living in the mountains northwest from the Charleston settlements and having sixty towns, but of small importance in the Indian trade, being "but ordinary hunters and lesser warriors."⁴

In the war with the Tuscarora in 1711–1713, which resulted in the expulsion of that tribe from North Carolina, more than a thousand southern Indians reinforced the South Carolina volunteers; among them were over two hundred Cherokee, hereditary enemies of the Tuscarora. Although these Indian allies did their work well in the actual encounters, their assistance was of doubtful advantage, as they helped themselves freely to whatever they wanted along the way, so that the settlers had reason to fear them almost as much as the hostile Tuscarora. After torturing a large number of their prisoners in the usual savage fashion, they returned with the remainder, whom they afterward sold as slaves to South Carolina.⁵

The war opened with a terrible massacre by the Yamassee in April 1715, followed by assaults along the whole frontier, until for a time it was seriously feared that the colony of South Carolina would be wiped out of existence. In a contest between what was then termed savagery and civilization, however, the final result is inevitable. The settlers at last rallied their whole force under Governor Craven and administered such a crushing blow to the Yamassee that the remnants abandoned their country and took refuge with the Spaniards in Florida or among the Lower Creeks. The English then made short work of the smaller tribes along the coast, while those in the interior were soon glad to sue for peace.^1

After a number of Cherokee chiefs came down to Charleston in the company of a trader to express their desire for peace, a force of several hundred white troops and a number of negroes under Colonel Maurice Moore went up the Savannah River in the winter of 1715-16 and established headquarters among the Lower Cherokee. There they were met by the chiefs of the Lower and some of the western towns, who reaffirmed their desire for a lasting peace with the English but refused to fight against the Yamassee, although they were willing to proceed against some other tribes. They laid the blame for most of the trouble upon the traders, who "had been very abusive to them lately."

<margin>✓</margin>
A detachment under Colonel George Chicken, sent to the Upper Cherokee, penetrated to "Quoneashee" (<term>Tlanusi'yĭ</term>, on the Hiwassee, near present-day Murphy) where they found the chiefs more defiant. They were resolved to continue the war against the Creeks, with whom the English were then trying to make peace, and they demanded large supplies of guns and ammunition. They argued that if they made peace with the other tribes, they would have no means of capturing slaves with which to buy ammunition for themselves. At this time they claimed 2,370 warriors, of whom half were believed to have guns. As the strength of the whole Nation was much greater, this estimate may have been for the Upper and Middle Cherokee only. After "much persuasion" by the officers, they finally "told us they would trust us once more," and an arrangement was made to furnish them two hundred guns with a supply of ammunition, together with fifty white soldiers to assist them against the tribes with which the English were still at war. In March 1716, this force was increased by one hundred men. The detachment under Colonel George Chicken returned by way of the towns on the upper part of the Little Tennessee, thus penetrating the heart of the Cherokee country.^2

Steps were now taken to secure peace by establishing a satisfactory trade system. For this purpose, a large quantity of suitable goods was purchased at the public expense of South Carolina, and a correspondingly large party was equipped for the initial trip.<note>Journal of the South Carolina Assembly, in North Carolina Colonial Records, ii, pp. 225-227, 1886.</note> In 1721, in order to further systematize Indian affairs, Governor Nicholson of South Carolina invited the chiefs of the Cherokee to a conference, at which thirty-seven towns were represented. A treaty was made by which trading methods were regulated, a boundary line between their territory and the English settlements was agreed upon, and an agent was appointed to superintend their affairs. At the governor's suggestion, one chief, called Wrosetasatow (?) <note>For information, see the glossary.</note> was formally commissioned as supreme head of the Nation, with authority to punish all offenses, including murder, and to represent all Cherokee claims to the colonial government. Thus were the Cherokee reduced from their former condition of a free people, traveling where they pleased, to that of dependent subjects with boundaries fixed by a colonial governor. The negotiations were accompanied by a cession of land, the first in the history of the tribe. In little more than a century thereafter, they had signed away their entire original territory.<note>Hewat, South Carolina and Georgia, i, pp. 297-298, 1778; Royce, Cherokee Nation, in the Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, p. 144 and map, 1888.</note>

The document of 1716 already quoted puts the strength of the Cherokee at that time at 2,370 warriors, but in this estimate, the Lower Cherokee seem not to have been included. In 1715, according to a trade census compiled by Governor Johnson of South Carolina, the tribe had thirty towns, with 4,000 warriors and a total population of 11,210.<note>Royce, as cited above, p. 142.</note> Another census in 1721 gives them fifty-three towns with 3,510 warriors and a total population of 10,379,<note>Document of 1724, in Fernow, Berthold, Ohio Valley in Colonial Days, pp. 273-275; Albany, 1890.</note> while the report of the board of trade for the same year gives them 3,800 warriors,<note>Report of the Board of Trade, 1721, in North Carolina Colonial Records, ii, p. 422, 1886.</note> equivalent, by the same proportion, to nearly 12,000 total. Adair, a good authority on such matters, estimates, about the year 1735, when the country was better known, that they had "sixty-four towns and villages, populous and full of children," with more than 6,000 fighting men,<note>Adair, James, American Indians, p. 227; London, 1775.</note> equivalent on the same basis of computation to between 16,000 and 17,000 souls. From what we know of them in later times, it is probable that this last estimate is very nearly correct.

For reasons of their own, the Chickasaw, whose territory lay within the recognized limits of Louisiana, soon became the uncompromising enemies of the French, and as their position enabled them to somewhat control the approach from the Mississippi, the Carolina government saw to it that they were kept well-supplied with guns and ammunition. British traders were in all their towns, and on one occasion, a French force advancing against a Chickasaw fortified village found it garrisoned by Englishmen flying the British flag.<note>Pickett, H. In 1730, to further secure the Cherokee in the English interest, Sir Alexander Cuming was dispatched on a secret mission to 그hat tribe, which was again suffering under grievances and almost ready to join with the Creeks in an alliance with the French. Seven chiefs were selected to visit England, where, in the palace at Whitehall, they solemnly renewed the treaty, acknowledging the sovereignty of England and binding themselves to have no trade or alliance with any other nation, not to allow any other white people to settle among them, and to deliver up any fugitive slaves who might seek refuge with them. To confirm their words, they delivered a "crown," five eagle-tails, and four scalps, which they had brought with them. In return, they received the usual glittering promises of love and perpetual friendship, together with a substantial quantity of guns, ammunition, and red paint. They took ship for Carolina, where they arrived, as we are told by the governor, “in good health and very well satisfied with His Majesty’s bounty to them.”¹

In the following year, some action was taken to use the Cherokee and Catawba to subdue the stubborn remnant of the Tuscarora in North Carolina; however, when it was found that this was likely to bring down the wrath of the Iroquois upon the Carolina settlements, more peaceful methods were used instead.²

<margin>✓</margin>
In 1738 or 1739, smallpox—brought to Carolina by slave ships—broke out among the Cherokee with such terrible effect that, according to Adair, nearly half the tribe was swept away within a year. The awful mortality was due largely to the fact that, as it was a new and strange disease to the Indians, they had no proper remedies against it. Therefore, they resorted to the universal Indian cure-all for “strong” sickness of almost any kind: namely, cold plunge baths in the running stream, which was the worst treatment that could possibly be devised. As the pestilence spread unchecked from town to town, despair fell upon the nation. The priests, believing the visitation was a penalty for violating ancient laws, threw away their sacred items as things which had lost their protecting power. Hundreds of warriors committed suicide upon seeing their frightful disfigurement. “Some shot themselves, others cut their throats, some stabbed themselves with knives and others with sharp-pointed canes; many threw themselves with sullen madness into the fire and there slowly expired, as if they had been completely stripped of the natural ability to feel pain.”³ Another authority estimates their loss at a thousand warriors, partly from smallpox and partly from rum brought in by the traders.⁴

About the year 1740, a trading path for horsemen was marked out by the Cherokee from the new settlement of Augusta, Georgia, to their towns on the headwaters of the Savannah River and from there to the west. This road, which went up the south side of the river, soon became frequently used.⁴ Before this time, most trade goods had been transported on the backs of Indians. In the same year, a party of Cherokee under the war chief Kâ'lanû, “The Raven,” took part in Oglethorpe’s expedition against the Spaniards of Saint Augustine.⁵

In 1736, Christian Priber, said to be a Jesuit acting in the French interest, had come among the Cherokee. Through the ease with which he learned the language and adapted himself to the native dress and

### MOONEY] PRIBER’S WORK—1736-41

way of life, he had quickly acquired a leading influence among them. He drafted a plan of government for them to adopt, modeled after the European system, with the capital at Great Tellico in Tennessee. The principal medicine man was to serve as emperor, and Priber himself as the emperor’s secretary. Under this title, he corresponded with the South Carolina government until they began to fear that he would eventually win the entire tribe over to the French side. A commissioner was sent to arrest him, but the Cherokee refused to surrender him, and the deputy was forced to return under the protection of an escort provided by Priber. However, five years after starting his work, he was captured by some English traders while on his way to Fort Toulouse. He was taken as a prisoner to Frederica, Georgia, where he died shortly afterward while in confinement. Although his enemies had portrayed him as a monster who incited the Indians to the crudest immoralities, he proved to be a gentleman of refined manners, extensive learning, and rare courage—as was shown later during an explosion in the barracks' ammunition store. Besides Greek, Latin, French, German, Spanish, and fluent English, he also spoke Cherokee. Among his seized papers was a manuscript dictionary of the language which he had prepared for publication; this was the first, and perhaps still the most important, study of the language ever made. Adair says:

> “Since he was learned and possessed a very wise and penetrating judgment, and had every qualification required for his bold and difficult enterprise, there was no doubt that, as he wrote a Cherokee dictionary intended to be published at Paris, he also recorded a great deal that would have been very welcome to the curious and useful to the representatives of South Carolina and Georgia. These works may easily be found in Frederica, if the manuscripts have had the good fortune to escape the destructive hands of military power.”

He claimed to be a Jesuit acting under the orders of his superior to introduce habits of steady industry, civilized arts, and a regular form of government among the southern tribes, with the goal of eventually founding an independent Indian state. From everything that can be learned about him, even though it comes from his enemies, there can be little doubt that he was a worthy member of that illustrious order whose name has been a synonym for scholarship, devotion, and courage from the days of Jogues and Marquette down to De Smet and Mengarini. <note>¹ Adair, American Indians, pp. 240–243, 1775; Stevens, W. B., History of Georgia, Vol. I, pp. 104–107; Philadelphia, 1847.</note>

Up to this time, no civilizing or missionary work had been undertaken by either of the Carolina governments among any of the tribes within their borders. As one writer of the period curiously puts it, “The spirit of the gospel has not yet risen so gloriously as to seek them more than their possessions,” while another affirms in stronger terms, “To the shame of

<meta>This page continues the historical narrative of the Cherokee during the 18th century, transitioning from the failed missionary efforts of the English to a detailed account of the tribe's frequent intertribal conflicts with the Tuscarora, Shawnee, Chickasaw, Iroquois, and Creeks.</meta>

<header>MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19</header>

...the Christian name, no effort has ever been taken to convert them to Christianity; on the contrary, their morals are perverted and corrupted by the sad example they daily see from those depraved practitioners of it living in their towns.”<note>Anonymous writer in Carroll, Historical Collections of South Carolina, volume 2, pages 97-98, 517, 1836.</note> Readers of Lawson and other narratives of the period will feel the force of this rebuke.

Throughout the eighteenth century, the Cherokee were engaged in chronic warfare with their Indian neighbors. As these quarrels concerned the whites very little, however significant they may have been to the participants, we have few details. The war with the Tuscarora continued until that tribe's uprising against Carolina in 1711 gave the Cherokee an opportunity to cooperate in striking the blow that drove the Tuscarora from their ancient homes to seek refuge in the north. The Cherokee then turned their attention to the Shawano on the Cumberland River, and with the help of the Chickasaw, finally expelled them from that region around the year 1715. Raids against the Catawba were probably continued until the latter had been so reduced by war and disease that they became mere dependent pensioners of the whites. The former friendship with the Chickasaw was eventually broken by the overbearing conduct of the Cherokee, and a war followed—of which we find incidental notice in 1757<note>Buckle, Journal, 1757, in Rivers, South Carolina, page 57, 1856.</note>—that ended in a decisive victory for the Chickasaw around 1768. The bitter war with the Iroquois of the far north continued, despite all the efforts of the colonial governments, until a formal peace treaty was achieved through the efforts of Sir William Johnson (12) in the same year.

The hereditary war with the Creeks for possession of upper Georgia continued, with brief intervals of peace or even alliance, until the United States finally intervened as a mediator between the rival claimants. In 1718, we find notice of a large Cherokee war party moving against the Creek town of Coweta, on the lower Chattahoochee River, but they dispersed upon learning that French and Spanish officers, as well as English traders, were present there, all intent on arranging an alliance with the Creeks. The Creeks themselves had declared their willingness to be at peace with the English, while remaining determined to keep the "bloody hatchet" raised against the Cherokee.<note>Barcia, A. G., Chronological Essay for the General History of Florida, pages 335, 336, Madrid, 1723.</note> The most important incident in the struggle between the two tribes was probably the battle of Tali’wa around the year 1755.<note>For more regarding these intertribal wars, see the historical traditions.</note>

By this time, the weaker coastal tribes had become practically extinct, and the more powerful tribes of the interior were beginning to grow alarmed as they saw restless frontier settlers pushing further into Indian territory every year. <header>MOONEY] FRENCH AND INDIAN WAR—1754-61 39</header>

mountains to the southwest, discovering and naming the celebrated Cumberland Gap and passing on to the headwaters of the Cumberland River. Two years later, he made a second exploration and reached the Kentucky River, but on account of the Indian troubles, no permanent settlement was attempted at that time.<note>Walker, Thomas, *Journal of an Exploration, etc.*, pages 8, 35-37; Boston, 1888; Monette (*Valley of the Mississippi* I, page 317; New York, 1848) erroneously makes the second date 1758.</note> This invasion of their territory awakened a natural resentment in the native owners, and we also find proof in the Virginia records that the irresponsible frontiersmen seldom let pass an opportunity to kill and plunder any stray Indian found in their neighborhood.

In 1755, the Cherokee were officially reported to number 2,590 warriors, as against probably twice that number previous to the great smallpox epidemic sixteen years before. Their neighbors and ancient enemies, the Catawba, had dwindled to 240 men.<note>Letter of Governor Dobbs, 1755, in *North Carolina Colonial Records*, volume 5, pages 320, 321, 1887.</note>

Although war was not formally declared by England until 1756, hostilities in the seven years' struggle between France and England—commonly known in America as the “French and Indian War”—began in April 1754, when the French seized a small post which the English had begun at the present site of Pittsburgh, and which was afterward finished by the French under the name of Fort Duquesne. Strenuous efforts were made by the English to secure the Cherokee to their interest against the French and their Indian allies, and treaties were negotiated by which they promised assistance.<note>Ramsey, *Tennessee*, pages 50-52, 1853; Royce, *Cherokee Nation*, in *Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology*, page 145, 1888.</note> As these treaties, however, carried the usual surrenders of territory and stipulated for the building of several forts in the heart of the Cherokee country, it is to be feared that the Indians were not duly impressed by the disinterested character of the proceeding. Their preference for the French was but thinly veiled, and only immediate policy prevented them from throwing their whole force into the scale on that side. The reasons for this preference are given by Timberlake, the young Virginian officer who visited the tribe on an embassy of conciliation a few years later:

> I found the nation much attached to the French, who have the wisdom—by familiar politeness, which costs but little and often does a great deal, and by conforming themselves to their ways and temper—to win the favor of almost all the Indians they are acquainted with, while the pride of our officers often disgusts them. Indeed, they did not hesitate to admit to me that it was the trade alone that induced them to make peace with us, and not any preference for us over the French, whom they loved a great deal better. . . . The English are now so near, and encroached daily so far upon them, that they not only felt the bad effects of it in their hunting grounds, which were ruined, but had every reason in the world to fear being swallowed up by such powerful neighbors or driven from the country inhabited by their fathers, in which they were born and brought up—in short, their native soil, for which all men have a particular tenderness and affection.
