He adds that only dire necessity had forced them to make peace with the English in 1761.<note>Timberlake, Henry, *Memoirs*, pages 73, 74; London, 1765.</note>

In accordance with the treaty terms, Fort Prince George was built in 1756 next to the important Cherokee town of Keowee, on the headwaters of the Savannah River, and Fort Loudon was built near the junction of the Tellico River with the Little Tennessee River, in the center of the Cherokee towns beyond the mountains.<note>Ramsey, *Tennessee*, page 51, 1853; Royce, *Cherokee Nation*, in *Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology*, page 145, 1888.</note> By a special arrangement with the influential chief, Ata-kullakulla (Ătă′-gûl′kălû′),<note>For more information, see Ătă′-gûl′kălû′ in the glossary.</note> Fort Dobbs was also built in the same year about 20 miles west of present-day Salisbury, North Carolina.<note>Ramsey, in the work previously cited, page 50.</note>

The Cherokee had agreed to provide four hundred warriors to cooperate against the French in the north, but before Fort Loudon was completed, it was very clear that they had regretted their promise; their great council at Echota ordered the work to stop and the garrison on its way to turn back, plainly telling the officer in charge that they did not want so many white people among them. Ata-kullakulla, previously supposed to be one of the staunchest friends of the English, was now one of the most determined in his opposition. There was also evidence that they were in constant communication with the French. Through much tact and argument, their objections were finally overcome for a time, and they very unwillingly began raising the promised force of warriors. Major Andrew Lewis, who supervised the building of the fort, became convinced that the Cherokee were actually friendly to the French and that all their claims of friendship and assistance were “only to put a gloss on their knavery.” The fort was finally completed and, at his suggestion, was garrisoned with a strong force of two hundred men under Captain Demeré.<note>Letters of Major Andrew Lewis and Governor Dinwiddie, 1756, in *North Carolina Colonial Records*, volume 5, pages 585, 612-614, 635, 637, 1887; Ramsey, in the work previously cited, pages 51, 52.</note> There was strong reason to believe that some raids committed about this time at the headwaters of the Catawba and Broad rivers in North Carolina were the joint work of the Cherokee and northern Indians.<note>Letter of Governor Dobbs, 1756, in *North Carolina Colonial Records*, volume 5, page 604, 1887.</note> Despite all this, a considerable body of Cherokee joined the British forces on the Virginia frontier.<note>Dinwiddie letter, 1757, in the same source, page 765.</note>

Fort Duquesne was taken by the American provincial troops under Washington on November 25, 1758. Quebec was taken on September 13, 1759, and by the final peace treaty in 1763, the war ended with the transfer of Canada and the Ohio Valley to the British Crown. Louisiana had already been ceded by France to Spain.

<meta>This page continues the account of rising tensions between the English and the Cherokee, focusing on the specific events in 1756 that shifted the tribe from allies to enemies during the French and Indian War.</meta>

<page-num>41</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] LEWIS' EXPEDITION—1756</header>

The Indians themselves were not ready to accept the settlement. In the north, the confederated tribes under Pontiac continued to war on their own account until 1765. In the South, the very Cherokee who had acted as allies of the British against Fort Du Quesne, and had voluntarily offered to guard the frontier south of the Potomac, returned to rouse their tribe to resistance.

The immediate triggering cause of the trouble was an unfortunate expedition undertaken against the hostile Shawano in February 1756 by Major Andrew Lewis (the same who had built Fort Loudon) with some two hundred Virginia troops assisted by about one hundred Cherokee. After six weeks of unproductive trekking through the woods, with the ground covered with snow and the streams so swollen by rains that they lost their provisions and ammunition while crossing, they were forced to return to the settlements in a starving condition, having killed their horses for food on the way. From the start, the Indian contingent had been disgusted by the contempt and neglect they experienced from those they had come to assist. The Tuscarora and others had already gone home, and the Cherokee now started to return on foot to their own country. Finding some horses running loose on the range, they took them, reasoning that since they had lost their own animals—not to mention having risked their lives—in the service of the colonists, it was only a fair exchange. The frontiersmen took another view of the matter, however; they attacked the returning Cherokee and killed a number of them (the number is variously stated as being between twelve and forty), including several of their prominent men. According to Adair, they also scalped and mutilated the bodies in the savage fashion to which they had become accustomed during the border wars, and brought the scalps into the settlements; there, the scalps were represented as belonging to French-allied Indians and sold at the regular price then established by law. The young warriors immediately prepared to take revenge, but they were restrained by the chiefs until satisfaction could be demanded in the ordinary way, according to the treaties arranged with the colonial governments. Petitions for redress were made in turn to Virginia, North Carolina, and South Carolina, but without success. While the women were still wailing night and morning for their slain kindred, and the Creeks were taunting the warriors for their cowardice in so quietly submitting to the injury, some lawless officers of Fort Prince George committed an unpardonable outrage at the neighboring Indian town while most of the men were away hunting.<note>Adair, *American Indians*, 245-246, 1775; *North Carolina Colonial Records*, volume 5, page xlviii, 1887; Hewat, quoted in Ramsey, *Tennessee*, page 54, 1853.</note> The warriors could no longer be restrained. Soon there was news of attacks upon the frontier settlements of Carolina, while on the other side of the mountains, two soldiers of the Fort Loudon garrison were killed. War seemed at hand.

<summary>A failed military expedition against the Shawano in 1756 led to Cherokee warriors being murdered and scalped by the very frontiersmen they had served. This betrayal, combined with a lack of legal redress and further outrages by British officers, pushed the Cherokee toward open war.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the account of rising tensions between the English and the Cherokee, focusing on the specific events in the late 1750s that shifted the tribe from allies to enemies during the colonial period.</meta>

<page-num>42</page-num>
<header>MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19]</header>

At this juncture, in November 1758, a party of influential chiefs—having first ordered back a war party that was just about to set out from the western towns against the Carolina settlements—came down to Charleston and succeeded in arranging the difficulty on a friendly basis. The assembly had officially declared peace with the Cherokee when, in May 1759, Governor Lyttleton unexpectedly came forward with a demand for the surrender and execution of every Indian who had killed a white man in the recent skirmishes, among these being the chiefs of Citico and Tellico. At the same time, the commander at Fort Loudon, forgetful of the fact that he had only a small garrison in the midst of several thousand restless savages, made a demand for twenty-four other chiefs whom he suspected of unfriendly action. To compel their surrender, orders were given to stop all trading supplies intended for the upper Cherokee.

This roused the whole Nation, and a delegation representing every town came down to Charleston, protesting the desire of the Indians for peace and friendship, but declaring their inability to surrender their own chiefs. The governor replied by declaring war in November 1759, at once calling out troops and sending messengers to secure the aid of all the surrounding tribes against the Cherokee. In the meantime, a second delegation of thirty-two of the most prominent men, led by the young war chief Oconostota (Âgăn-stâta),<sup>1</sup> arrived to make a further effort for peace, but the governor, refusing to listen to them, seized the whole party and confined them as prisoners at Fort Prince George, in a room large enough for only six soldiers, while at the same time he set fourteen hundred troops in motion to invade the Cherokee country. On further representation by Ata-kullakulla (Ătă'-gûl'kălû'), the civil chief of the Nation and well known as a friend of the English, the governor released Oconostota and two others after compelling some half-dozen of the delegation to sign a paper by which they pretended to agree for their tribe to kill or seize any Frenchmen entering their country, and consented to the imprisonment of the party until all the warriors demanded had been surrendered for execution or otherwise. At this stage of affairs, smallpox broke out in the Cherokee towns, making a further stay in their neighborhood unsafe, and thinking the whole matter now settled on his own terms, Lyttleton returned to Charleston.

The event soon proved how little he knew of Indian temperament. Oconostota at once laid siege to Fort Prince George, completely cutting off communication at a time when, as it was now winter, no help could well be expected from below. In February 1760, after having kept the fort thus closely besieged for some weeks, he sent word one day by an Indian woman that he wished to speak to the commander, Lieutenant Coytmore. The soldiers immediately rushed into the room where the hostages were kept—each of whom was a prominent chief in the tribe—and slaughtered every last one of them.

It was now war to the end. Led by Oconostota, the Cherokee attacked the frontier settlements of Carolina, while the warriors from across the mountains closely besieged Fort Loudon. In June 1760, a strong force of over 1,600 men under Colonel Montgomery set out to subdue the Cherokee towns and rescue the trapped garrison. After crossing the Indian frontier, Montgomery quickly drove the enemy away from around Fort Prince George. Then, advancing rapidly, he took Little Keowee by surprise, killing every one of the defenders, and systematically destroyed all of the Lower Cherokee towns. He burned them to the ground, destroyed the cornfields and orchards, killed or captured more than a hundred of their men, and drove the entire population into the mountains ahead of him. His own losses were very light. He then sent messengers to the Middle and Upper towns, summoning them to surrender under threat of a similar fate. However, receiving no reply, he led his men across the divide to the headwaters of the Little Tennessee River and continued down that stream without opposition until he reached the vicinity of *Echoee* (Itse’yĭ), a few miles above the sacred town of *Nĭkwăsĭ’*, the present-day Franklin, North Carolina. Here, the Cherokee had gathered their full force to resist his progress, and the result was a fierce battle on June 27, 1760, from which Montgomery was forced to retreat to Fort Prince George after losing nearly one hundred men in killed and wounded. The Indian losses are unknown.

His retreat sealed the fate of Fort Loudon. Although the garrison was hard-pressed and forced to eat horses and dogs, they had been able to hold out through the kindness of the Indian women. Many of these women had found sweethearts among the soldiers and brought them supplies of food daily. When threatened by the chiefs, the women boldly replied that the soldiers were their husbands and it was their duty to help them; they claimed that if any harm came to them for their devotion, their English relatives would avenge them.<note>Timberlake, Memoirs, page 65, 1765.</note> The end was only postponed, however, and on August 8, 1760, the garrison of about two hundred men under Captain Demeré surrendered to Oconostota. This was on the promise that they should be allowed to retreat unharmed with their weapons and enough ammunition for the march, on the condition that they deliver up all remaining military supplies.

Shortly after, the chief took him into the woods, supposedly on a hunting trip, and guided him for nine days through the wilderness until he delivered him safely to friends in Virginia. The chief's kindness was well rewarded, and it was largely through his influence that peace was finally achieved.

It was now too late, and the settlements were too exhausted for another expedition, so the English spent the fall and winter preparing for a massive campaign the following year to crush all resistance. In June 1761, Colonel Grant set out from Fort Prince George with an army of 2,600 men, including a number of Chickasaw and almost every remaining warrior of the Catawba.1 Rejecting a request from Ata-kullakulla for a peaceful settlement, he crossed Rabun Gap and advanced rapidly down the Little Tennessee along the same trail taken by the previous year's expedition. On June 10, when within two miles of Montgomery's battlefield, he encountered the Cherokee. He defeated them after a stubborn battle lasting several hours, though he suffered significant losses himself. Having repulsed the Indians, he continued on his way, sending out detachments to the outlying settlements. Within a month, he had destroyed every one of the Middle Towns—15 in all—along with all their granaries and cornfields, driving the inhabitants into the mountains and "pushing the frontier seventy miles farther to the west."

<margin>✓</margin>
The Cherokee were now reduced to the most desperate state. With some of their best towns in ashes, their fields and orchards laid waste for two consecutive years, their ammunition nearly exhausted, and many of their bravest warriors dead; with their people as fugitives in the mountains, hiding in caves and living like animals on roots or killing their horses for food; with the terrible scourge of smallpox adding to the miseries of starvation; and furthermore torn by factional differences which had existed from the very beginning of the war—it was impossible for even brave men to resist any longer. In September, Ata-kullakulla, who had consistently done everything in his power to stop the hostility, went down to Charleston. A treaty of peace was made, and the...

<meta>This page continues the history of the Cherokee War’s conclusion, picking up after the military campaigns to describe the peace treaties, the reduction of the Cherokee population, and the subsequent wave of white settlement leading up to the American Revolution.</meta>

<page-num>45</page-num>
# MOONEY] AUGUSTA TREATY—ADVANCE OF SETTLEMENTS

The war ended. From an estimated population of at least 5,000 warriors some years before, the Cherokee had now been reduced to about 2,300 men.<sup>1</sup>

Meanwhile, a force of Virginians under Colonel Stephen had advanced as far as the Great Island of the Holston—now Kingsport, Tennessee—where they were met by a large delegation of Cherokee who asked for peace. This peace was concluded with them by Colonel Stephen on November 19, 1761, independently of what was being done in South Carolina. At the urgent request of the chief that an officer might visit their people for a short time to strengthen the new friendship, Lieutenant Henry Timberlake—a young Virginian who had already distinguished himself in active service—volunteered to return with them to their towns, where he spent several months. He afterward led a delegation of chiefs to England; however, because they had come without authority from the Government, they met such an unpleasant reception that they returned home disgusted.<sup>2</sup>

Upon the conclusion of peace between England and France in 1763, by which the entire western territory was ceded to England, a great council was held at Augusta. This council was attended by the chiefs and principal men of all the southern Indians. There, Captain John Stuart, the superintendent for the southern tribes, together with the colonial governors of Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia, explained the new state of affairs fully to the Indians, and a treaty of mutual peace and friendship was concluded on November 10 of that year.<sup>3</sup>

<margin>✓</margin>
Under several leaders, such as Walker, Wallen, Smith, and Boon, the tide of emigration now surged across the mountains despite every effort to restrain it.<sup>4</sup> The period between the end of the Cherokee War and the start of the Revolution is primarily notable for a number of treaty cessions by the Indians, each a failed attempt to establish a permanent barrier between themselves and the advancing wave of white settlement. Chief among these was the famous Henderson purchase in 1775, which included the entire tract between the Kentucky and Cumberland rivers, covering the greater part of the present state of Kentucky. Through these treaties, the Cherokee were stripped of practically all their ancient territorial claims north of the present Tennessee line and east of the Blue Ridge and the Savannah River, including much of their best hunting range; however, their home settlements were still left in their possession.<sup>5</sup>

--- Page 60 ---
<meta>This page continues the historical account of the Cherokee following the war of 1761, focusing on the series of treaties and land cessions that rapidly diminished their territory in the years leading up to the American Revolution.</meta>

<page-num>46</page-num>
<header>MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19]</header>

As one result of the recent Cherokee War, a royal proclamation was issued in 1763 with the goal of stopping future trespassing by white settlers. This proclamation prohibited any private land purchases from the Indians and forbade the granting of land warrants west of the headwaters of the streams flowing into the Atlantic.¹ In 1768, at the request of the Indians themselves, the British superintendent for the southern tribes, Captain John Stuart, negotiated a treaty at Hard Labor in South Carolina. By this agreement, the Kanawha and New rivers, along their entire course downstream from the North Carolina line, were established as the boundary between the Cherokee and the white settlers in that direction. Within two years, however, so many frontiersmen had crossed into the Indian country—where they clearly intended to stay—that it was necessary to replace it with another treaty. By this new agreement, the line was made to run due south from the mouth of the Kanawha to the Holston, thereby removing from the Cherokee nearly all of their hunting grounds in Virginia and West Virginia. Two years later, in 1772, the Virginians demanded a further surrender of land, by which everything east of the Kentucky River was given up; and finally, on March 17, 1775, the great Henderson Purchase was completed, including the entire tract between the Kentucky and Cumberland rivers. <margin>✓</margin>By this final surrender of land, the Cherokee were at last cut off from the Ohio River and all of their rich Kentucky hunting grounds.²

While these transactions were called treaties, they were actually forced upon the Native owners, who resisted each one in turn and eventually signed only under protest and with the most solemn promises that no further demands would be made. <margin>✓</margin>Even before the purchases were made, large numbers of intruders had settled on each of the areas in question. They refused to withdraw behind the boundaries now established, but stayed on one excuse or another to wait for a new agreement. This was particularly the case on the Watauga and upper Holston rivers in northeastern Tennessee, where the settlers, finding themselves still within the Indian boundary and being determined to stay, negotiated a temporary lease from the Cherokee in 1772. As was expected and intended, the lease became a permanent occupation, forming the core settlement of the future State of Tennessee.³

Just before the start of the Revolutionary War, the botanist William Bartram went on an extensive tour of the Cherokee country and left behind a pleasant account of the Indians' hospitality and friendly nature at that time. He provides a list of forty-three towns then inhabited by the tribe.⁴

The start of the great Revolutionary War in 1776 found almost every Indian tribe siding with the British against the

<header>MOONEY] BEGINNING OF THE REVOLUTION</header>

Americans. There was a good reason for this. Since the fall of French power, the British government had stood to them as the sole representative of authority, and the guardian and protector of their rights against constant encroachments by the American borderers. Licensed British traders resided in every tribe, and many had intermarried and raised families among them, while the frontiersman looked upon the Indian only as an obstacle on the earth. They knew the British superintendents—Sir William Johnson in the north and Captain John Stuart in the south—as generous friends, while hardly any warrior among them was without some old reason for resentment against their backwoods neighbors. They felt that the only barrier between themselves and national extinction lay in the strength of the British government, and when the final separation came, they threw their whole power onto the British side. They were encouraged in this decision by gifts of clothing and other goods, along with promises of plunder from the settlements and hopes of recovering a portion of their lost territories. Having determined as early as June 1775 to call upon the Indians to fight against the Americans, the British government issued supplies of hatchets, guns, and ammunition to the warriors of all the tribes from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico, and bounties were offered for American scalps brought to the commanding officer at Detroit or Oswego.<note>1 Ramsey, Tennessee, pp. 143–150, 1853; Monette, Valley of the Mississippi, I, pp. 400, 401, 431, 432, and II, pp. 33, 34, 1846; Roosevelt, Winning of the West, I, pp. 276–281, and II, pp. 1–6, 1889.</note> Even the Six Nations, who had agreed in a solemn treaty to remain neutral, were won over by these persuasions. In August 1775, an Indian “talk” was intercepted in which the Cherokee assured Cameron, the resident agent, that their warriors, enlisted in the service of the king, were ready at a signal to attack the frontier settlements of Carolina and Georgia.<note>2 Ramsey, work cited above, p. 143.</note> Circular letters were sent out to all those persons in the back country supposed to have Loyalist sympathies, directing them to go to Cameron’s headquarters in the Cherokee country to join the Indians in the invasion of the settlements.<note>3 Quoted from Stedman, in Ramsey, work cited above, p. 162.</note>

In June 1776, a British fleet under the command of Sir Peter Parker, with a large naval and military force, attacked Charleston, South Carolina, by both land and sea. Simultaneously, a body of Cherokee, led by Tories in Indian disguise, came down from the mountains and ravaged the exposed frontier of South Carolina, killing and burning as they went. After a gallant defense by the garrison at Charleston, the British were repulsed, after which their Indian and Tory allies withdrew.<note>4 Ramsey, work cited above, p. 162.</note>

About the same time, a warning came from Nancy Ward (14), a noted friendly Indian woman of great authority in the Cherokee Nation, that seven hundred Cherokee warriors were advancing in two divisions against the Watauga and Holston settlements, with the design of

They met and defeated them with significant loss after a hard-fought battle near the Long Island in the Holston (Kingsport, Tennessee) on August 20. The next day, the second division of the Cherokee attacked the fort at Watauga, which was garrisoned by only forty men under Captain James Robertson (15), but they were repelled without any loss to the defenders; the Indians withdrew upon news of the outcome at Long Island. A Mrs. Bean and a boy named Moore were captured on this occasion and taken to one of the Cherokee towns near Tellico. There, the boy was burned, but the woman—after she had been condemned to death and everything was ready for the tragedy—was rescued by the intervention of Nancy Ward. Two other Cherokee detachments moved against the upper settlements at the same time. One of these, finding all the inhabitants safely locked in forts, returned without doing much damage. The other ravaged the country on the Clinch River almost to its head, and killed a man and wounded others at Black's station, now Abingdon, Virginia.¹

At the same time that one part of the Cherokee were raiding the Tennessee settlements, others came down upon the frontiers of Carolina and Georgia. On the upper Catawba, they killed many people, but the whites took refuge in the stockade stations, where they defended themselves until General Rutherford (16) came to their relief. In Georgia, an attempt had been made by a small party of Americans to seize Cameron, who lived in one of the Cherokee towns with his Indian wife; but, as was to be expected, the Indians intervened, killing several of the party and capturing others, who were afterward tortured to death. The Cherokee of the Upper and Middle towns, along with some Creeks and Tories of the vicinity, led by Cameron himself, immediately began ravaging the South Carolina border. They burned houses, drove off cattle, and killed men, women, and children without distinction, until the whole country was in a wild panic, with the people abandoning their farms to seek safety in the garrisoned forts. On one occasion, an attack by two hundred of the enemy—half of them being Tories, stripped and painted like Indians—was repulsed by the timely arrival of a body of Americans, who succeeded in capturing thirteen of the Tories. The invasion extended into Georgia, where property was also destroyed and the inhabitants were driven from their homes.²

<header>MOONEY] RUTHERFORD AND WILLIAMSON EXPEDITIONS—1776</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

In the summer of 1776, four expeditions were equipped from Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia to enter the Cherokee territory simultaneously from four different directions.

In August of that year, the army of North Carolina, 2,400 strong, under General Griffith Rutherford, crossed the Blue Ridge at Swannanoa Gap. Following the main trail almost along the present line of the railroad, they struck the first Indian town, Stikâ'yĭ, or Stecoee, on the Tuckasegee near present-day Whittier. Since the inhabitants had fled, the soldiers burned the town, along with an unfinished townhouse ready for its roof, cut down the standing corn, killed one or two straggling Indians, and then proceeded on their mission of destruction. Every town upon the Oconaluftee, Tuckasegee, and the upper part of the Little Tennessee, and on the Hiwassee to below the junction of the Valley River—thirty-six towns in all—were destroyed in turn. The corn was cut down or trampled under the hooves of the livestock driven into the fields for that purpose, and the livestock itself was killed or carried off. Before such an overwhelming force, supplemented as it was by three others simultaneously advancing from other directions, the Cherokee offered only weak resistance and fled with their women and children into the strongholds of the Great Smoky Mountains, leaving their devastated fields and smoking towns behind them. As was usual in Indian wars, the actual number killed or captured was small, but the destruction of property was beyond calculation. At Sugartown (Kûlsetsi'yĭ, east of present-day Franklin), one detachment sent to destroy it was surprised and escaped only through the aid of another force sent to its rescue. Rutherford himself, while proceeding to the destruction of the Hiwassee towns, encountered the Indians drawn up to oppose his progress in the Waya Gap of the Nantahala Mountains. One of the hardest fights of the campaign resulted, with the soldiers losing over forty killed and wounded, although the Cherokee were finally repulsed (17). One of the Indians killed on this occasion was later discovered to be a woman, painted and armed like a warrior.<note>See no. 110, "Incidents of Personal Heroism." For Rutherford's expedition, see Moore, *Rutherford's Expedition*, in North Carolina University Magazine, February 1888; Swain, *Sketch of the Indian War in 1776*, ibid., May 1852, reprinted in *Historical Magazine*, November 1867; Ramsey, *Tennessee*, p. 164, 1853; Roosevelt, *Winning of the West*, I, pp. 294-302, 1889, etc.</note>

On September 26, the South Carolina army, 1,860 strong, under Colonel Andrew Williamson and including a number of Catawba Indians, joined Rutherford's forces on the Hiwassee River near present-day Murphy, North Carolina. It had been expected that Williamson would join the northern army at Cowee, on the Little Tennessee, where they would proceed together against the western towns, but he had been delayed, and the work of destruction in that direction was already completed. Therefore, after a short rest, each army returned home along the route by which it had come.

The Virginia army, about two thousand strong under Colonel William Christian (18), assembled in August at the Long Island of the Holston, the regular gathering place on the Tennessee side of the mountains. Among them were several hundred men from North Carolina, along with all who could be spared from the garrisons on the Tennessee side. Paying very little attention to small bodies of Indians who tried to divert their attention or delay their progress with attacks on their sides, they advanced steadily but cautiously along the great Indian war-path (19) toward the crossing of the French Broad River, where a large force of Cherokee was reported to be waiting to challenge their passage. Knowing that his own strength was overwhelming, Christian allowed the envoy to go through the whole camp and then sent him back with the message that there could be no terms until the Cherokee towns had been destroyed. Arriving at the river crossing, he lit fires and made all preparations as if he intended to camp there for several days. As soon as night fell, however, he secretly withdrew half his force and crossed the river further downstream to attack the Indians from behind. This was a difficult task, as the water was so deep that it reached almost to the men's shoulders, while the current was so rapid that they were forced to support each other four abreast to keep from being swept off their feet. However, they kept their guns and powder dry. On reaching the other side, they were surprised to find no enemy. Disheartened by the strength of the invasion, the Indians had fled without any sign of resistance. It is likely that nearly all their men and resources had been pulled away to oppose the Carolina forces on their eastern border, and the few who remained felt they were no match for the conflict.

Advancing without opposition, Christian reached the towns on the Little Tennessee early in November. Finding them deserted, he proceeded to destroy them one after another, along with their outlying fields. The few remaining warriors who were discovered were all killed. In the meantime, messages had been sent out to the more distant towns. In response, several of their leaders came into Christian's camp to negotiate for peace. Upon their agreement to surrender all the prisoners and captured livestock in their possession, and to give up all the disputed territory occupied by the Tennessee settlements to the whites as soon as representatives of the whole tribe could be assembled in the spring, Christian consented to stop the fighting and withdraw without doing further damage. An exception was made against Tuskegee and another town, which had been involved in the burning of the boy taken from Watauga, as previously mentioned; these two towns were burned to the ground. The sacred "peace town" of Echota (20) was not attacked. Most of the troops were disbanded upon their return to the Long Island, but some remained and built Fort Patrick Henry, where they stayed in winter quarters.<note>1. For the Virginia-Tennessee expedition, see Roosevelt, *Winning of the West*, I, pp. 303-305, 1889; Ramsey, *Tennessee*, pp. 165-170, 1853.</note>

From brief mentions in narratives written by some of the participants, we obtain interesting insights into the merciless character of this old border warfare. In addition to the usual destruction of war—the burning of towns, the ruining of productive fields, and the killing of defenders—we find that every Indian warrior killed was scalped whenever the opportunity allowed. In a personal encounter, "a stout Indian engaged a sturdy young white man, who was a good fighter and expert at gouging. After breaking their guns on each other, they grabbed hold of one another, and the 'cracker' instantly had his thumbs in the man's eyes, who roared and cried 'canaly'—'enough,' in English. 'Damn you,' says the white man, 'you can never have enough while you are alive.' He then threw him down, set his foot upon his head, and scalped him alive; then he took up one of the broken guns and knocked out his brains. After getting what information she could give them through a mixed-race interpreter, "the informant being unable to travel, some of our men favored her so much that they killed her there to put her out of her pain." A few days later, "a party of Colonel Thomas's regiment, being on a hunt for plunder or something similar, found an Indian woman and took her prisoner; since she was lame, she was unable to go with her friends. She was so sullen that she would, as the old saying goes, neither lead nor be driven, and by their account she died in their hands; but I suppose they helped her to her end." Continuing to another town, "we engaged in our former labor, that is, cutting and destroying all things that might be of advantage to our enemies. Finding here curious buildings, large apple trees, and improvements like those of white men, we destroyed these."¹

At the Wolf Hills settlement, now Abingdon, Virginia, a party sent out from the fort returned with the scalps of eleven warriors. Having recovered the books which their minister had left behind in his cabin, they held a prayer service for their success, after which the fresh scalps were hung upon a pole above the gate of the fort. The brutal custom of scalping, to which the frontiersmen had become accustomed in the earlier wars, was practiced at every opportunity—at least upon the bodies of warriors—and the South Carolina legislature offered a bounty of seventy-five pounds for every warrior’s scalp; however, a higher reward was offered for prisoners. <note>Roosevelt, Winning of the West, I, pp. 285, 290, 303, 1889.</note> Despite all the bitterness the war aroused, there seems to be no record of Americans scalping Tories or other whites (21).

The effect of this invasion of more than six thousand armed enemies into Cherokee territory was almost paralyzing. More than fifty of their towns had been burned, their orchards cut down, their fields destroyed, their cattle and horses killed or driven off, and their stores of buckskin and other personal property plundered. Hundreds of their people had been killed or had died of starvation and exposure, others were prisoners in the hands of the Americans, and some had been sold into slavery. Those who had escaped were fugitives in the mountains, living on acorns, chestnuts, and wild game, or were refugees with the British. <note>Approximately five hundred sought refuge with Stuart, the British Indian superintendent in Florida, where they were fed for some time at the expense of the British government (Jones, Georgia, II, p. 246, 1883).</note> From the Virginia line to the Chattahoochee, the chain of destruction was complete. For the time being, any further resistance was hopeless, and they were compelled to sue for peace.

By a treaty concluded at De Witts Corners in South Carolina on May 20, 1777—the first ever made with the new states—the Lower Cherokee surrendered to the victors all of their remaining territory in South Carolina, except for a narrow strip along the western boundary. Just two months later, on July 20, by a treaty at Long Island (as had been arranged by Christian in the previous fall), the Middle and Upper Cherokee ceded everything east of the Blue Ridge, together with all the disputed territory on the Watauga, Nolichucky, upper Holston, and New rivers. By this second treaty, Captain James Robertson was also appointed agent for the Cherokee, to reside at Echota to watch their movements, recover any captured property, and prevent their correspondence with persons unfriendly to the American cause. As the Federal government was not yet fully operational, these treaties

were negotiated by commissioners from the four states bordering the Cherokee country, with the newly acquired territory being divided among South Carolina, North Carolina, and Tennessee. <note>Royce, Cherokee Nation, in Fifth Ann. Rep. Bureau of Ethnology, p. 150 and map, 1888; Ramsey, Tennessee, pp. 172-174, 1853; Stevens, Georgia, II, p. 144, 1859; Roosevelt, Winning of the West, I, p. 306, 1889.</note>

While the Cherokee Nation had thus been forced into a peace treaty, a very significant portion of the tribe remained irreconcilably hostile to the Americans and refused to participate in the recent land cessions, especially on the Tennessee side. Although Ata-kullakulla sent word that he was ready with five hundred young warriors to fight for the Americans against British or Indian enemies whenever called upon, Dragging-canoe (Tsiyu-gûnsi'nĭ), who had led the opposition against the Watauga settlements, declared that he would hold fast to Cameron’s word and continue to wage war upon those who had taken his hunting grounds. Under his leadership, several hundred of the most warlike and relentless warriors of the tribe, along with their families, withdrew from the Upper and Middle towns and moved far down the Tennessee River. There, they established new settlements on Chickamauga Creek, near present-day Chattanooga. The area seems to have already been a gathering place for a kind of Indian banditry, who sometimes plundered boats that were disabled in the rapids at this point while descending the river. Under the name “Chickamaugas,” they soon became famous for their uncompromising and never-ceasing hostility. In 1782, following the destruction of their towns by Sevier and Campbell, they abandoned this location and moved further down the river. There, they built what were afterwards known as the “five lower towns”: Running Water, Nickajack, Long Island, Crow Town, and Lookout Mountain Town. These were all on the extreme western Cherokee frontier, near where the Tennessee River crosses the state line. The first three were within the present limits of Tennessee, while Lookout Mountain Town and Crow Town were located in the adjacent corners of Georgia and Alabama, respectively. Their population was increased by Creeks, Shawano, and white Tories, until they were estimated at a thousand warriors. They remained here, a constant thorn in the side of Tennessee, until their towns were destroyed in 1794. <note>Ramsey, op. cit., pp. 171-177, 185-186, 610 et passim; Royce, op. cit., p. 150; Campbell letter, 1782, and other documents in Virginia State Papers, III, pp. 271, 571, 599, 1883, and IV, pp. 118, 286, 1884; Blount letter, January 14, 1793, American State Papers: Indian Affairs, I, p. 431, 1832. Campbell says they abandoned their first location because of the invasion from Tennessee. Governor Blount says they left because of witches.</note>

The displaced Lower Cherokee also moved to the farthest western border of their tribal territory, where they hoped to be secure from encroachment for at least a while, and built new towns for themselves on the upper waters of the Coosa River. Twenty years after—

In April 1777, the legislature of North Carolina (of which Tennessee was still a part) authorized land bounties in the new territory for all able-bodied men who volunteered against the remaining hostile Cherokee. Under this act, companies of rangers were stationed along the exposed border to intercept raiding parties of Indians and to protect the steady advance of the pioneers. As a result, the Tennessee settlements enjoyed a brief respite and were even able to send some assistance to their brethren in Kentucky, who were sorely pressed by the Shawnee and other northern tribes. <note>² Ramsey, Tennessee, pp. 174–178, 1853.</note>

The war between England and the colonies still continued, however, and the British government was tireless in its effort to secure the active assistance of the Indians. With the Creeks raiding the Georgia and South Carolina frontiers, and with a British agent, Colonel Brown, and a number of Tory refugees regularly living at Chickamauga, <note>³ Campbell letter, 1782, Virginia State Papers, III, p. 271, 1883.</note> it was impossible for the Cherokee to remain quiet for long. In the spring of 1779, a warning came from Robertson, stationed at Echota, that three hundred warriors from Chickamauga had started against the frontier settlements of North Carolina. Without a day’s delay, the states of North Carolina (including Tennessee) and Virginia united to send a strong force of volunteers against them under the command of Colonels Shelby and Montgomery. Descending the Holston in April in a fleet of canoes built for the occasion, they took the Chickamauga towns so completely by surprise that the few remaining warriors fled to the mountains without attempting to battle. Several were killed, Chickamauga and the outlying villages were burned, twenty thousand bushels of corn were destroyed, and large numbers of horses and cattle were captured, along with a great quantity of goods sent by the British Governor Hamilton at Detroit for distribution to the Indians. The success of this expedition frustrated Hamilton's plan to unite all the northern and southern Indians, assisted by British regulars, in a concerted attack along the entire American frontier. Upon learning through runners of the disaster that had befallen them, the Chickamauga warriors abandoned all ideas of invading the settlements and returned to their ruined villages. <note>⁴ Ramsey, op. cit., pp. 186–188; Roosevelt, Winning of the West, II, pp. 236–238, 1889. Ramsey’s statements, based primarily on Haywood’s authority regarding the strength of the expedition and the number of warriors killed, are so clearly exaggerated that they are omitted here.</note> They, as well as the Creeks, however, kept in constant communication with

<summary>In 1779, a joint force from North Carolina and Virginia led by Colonels Shelby and Montgomery destroyed the Chickamauga Cherokee towns and their supplies. This preemptive strike successfully dismantled a British-backed plan for a unified Indian assault on the American frontier.</summary>

In the early spring of 1780, a large company of emigrants under Colonel John Donelson traveled down the Holston and Tennessee rivers to the Ohio. From there, they ascended the Cumberland River and joined another party under Captain James Robertson, which had just arrived by a difficult overland route. Together, they established the first settlement at the present site of Nashville. While passing the Chickamauga towns, they had to run the gauntlet of the hostile Cherokee, who pursued them for a considerable distance past the whirlpool known as "The Suck," where the river breaks through the mountain. Because the family of a man named Stuart was infected with smallpox, his boat fell behind. All twenty-eight people on board were either killed or captured by the Indians; their cries were clearly heard by their friends ahead, who were unable to help them. Another boat ran onto the rocks, and the three women in it—one of whom had become a mother the night before—threw the cargo into the river. They then jumped into the water and managed to push the boat into the current while the husband of one of the women held the Indians at bay with his rifle. The infant was killed during the chaos. Three cowards attempted to escape without any thought for their companions. One drowned in the river; the other two were captured and taken to Chickamauga, where one was burned and the other was ransomed by a trader. The rest of the party continued on their way to found the capital of a new commonwealth. <note>² Donelson’s Journal, etc., in Ramsey, Tennessee, pp. 197–203, 1853; Roosevelt, Winning of the West, II, pp. 324–340, 1889.</note> As if by a form of retributive justice, smallpox broke out among the Chickamauga band as a result of the capture of Stuart’s family, causing a great many deaths. <note>³ Ibid., II, p. 337.</note>

After the British had reconquered Georgia and South Carolina and destroyed all resistance in the south, Cornwallis—along with his subordinates, Ferguson and the ruthless Tarleton—prepared in early 1780 to invade North Carolina and sweep through the country northward to Virginia. The Creeks under McGillivray (23) and a number of the Cherokee under various local chiefs, along with the Tories, immediately joined his cause.

While the Tennessee frontiersmen were gathered at a barbecue to compete for a shooting prize, a paroled prisoner brought a demand from Ferguson for their submission. Ferguson threatened that if they refused, he would cross the mountains, hang their leaders, kill every man found carrying a weapon, and burn every settlement. Until this time, the mountain men had limited their efforts to keeping the Indian enemy in check, but now, with the fate of the Revolution at stake, they felt

# MOONEY] THE BORDER FIGHTERS

That the time for wider action had come. They decided not to wait for the attack but to anticipate it. Without orders or authority from Congress, without tents, provisions, or supplies, the Indian fighters of Virginia, North Carolina, and Tennessee quickly assembled at the Sycamore Shoals of the Watauga, totaling about one thousand men under Campbell of Virginia, Sevier and Shelby of Tennessee, and McDowell of North Carolina. Crossing the mountains, they met Ferguson at Kings Mountain in South Carolina on October 7, 1780, and won the decisive victory that turned the tide of the Revolution in the South. <note>¹ Roosevelt, *Winning of the West*, Vol. II, pp. 241-294, 1889; Ramsey, *Tennessee*, pp. 208-249, 1853.</note>

It is appropriate here to quote a description of these men in buckskin—white by blood and tradition, but half-Indian in habit and instinct—who, in half a century of continuous conflict, drove back the Creeks, Cherokee, and Shawano, and with one hand on the plow and the other on the rifle, reclaimed a wilderness and carried civilization and free government to the banks of the Mississippi.

> “They were led by leaders they trusted, they were accustomed to Indian warfare, they were skilled as horsemen and marksmen, and they knew how to face every kind of danger, hardship, and privation. Their fringed and tasseled hunting shirts were secured by bead-worked belts, and the trappings of their horses were stained red and yellow. On their heads, they wore caps of raccoon skin or mink skin with the tails hanging down, or else felt hats, in each of which was tucked a buck tail or a sprig of evergreen. Every man carried a small-bore rifle, a tomahawk, and a scalping knife. A very few of the officers had swords, and there was not a bayonet nor a tent in the army.” <note>² Roosevelt, op. cit., p. 256.</note>

To strike the blow at Kings Mountain, the frontiersmen had been forced to leave their own homes unprotected. Even before they could cross the mountains on their return, news arrived that the Cherokee were out in force again to destroy the upper settlements, and their numerous small bands were killing, burning, and plundering in the usual Indian fashion. Without losing time, the Holston settlements of Virginia and Tennessee immediately raised seven hundred mounted riflemen to march against the enemy, with the command assigned to Colonel Arthur Campbell of Virginia and Colonel John Sevier of Tennessee.

Sevier set out first with nearly three hundred men, heading south along the great Indian war trail and driving small parties of the Cherokee before him, until he crossed the French Broad and encountered seventy of them at Boyd's Creek, not far from present-day Sevierville, on December 16, 1780. Ordering his men to spread out into a half-circle, he sent scouts ahead who, by attacking and then feigning a retreat, managed to draw the Indians into the trap they had prepared,

There is a great discrepancy in the various accounts of this fight, arising from the attempts of biased historians to exaggerate the scale of the victory. One writer claims the Indians had 1,000 warriors. Here, as elsewhere, Roosevelt is a more reliable guide, as his statements are usually drawn from official documents.</note>

A few days later, Sevier was joined by Campbell with the rest of the force. Advancing to the Little Tennessee with only slight resistance, they crossed three miles below Echota while the Indians were watching for them at the ford above. Then, dividing into two groups, they proceeded to destroy the towns along the river. The chiefs sent peace messages through Nancy Ward, the Cherokee woman who had so greatly befriended the whites in 1776, but Campbell returned an evasive answer to these proposals until he could first destroy the towns on the lower Hiwassee, whose warriors had been particularly hostile. Continuing southward, the troops destroyed these towns, Hiwassee and Chestuee, along with all their stores of provisions, finishing the work on the last day of the year. The Indians had fled before them, keeping spies out to watch their movements. One of these, while giving signals from a ridge by beating a drum, was shot by the whites. The soldiers lost only one man, who was buried in an Indian cabin that was then burned down to hide any trace of the burial.

<margin>✓</margin>The return march began on New Year’s Day. Ten principal towns, including Echota, the capital, had been destroyed, along with several smaller villages, containing a total of over one thousand houses and no less than fifty thousand bushels of corn and large stores of other provisions. Everything not needed for the return march was set on fire or otherwise destroyed. Of all the towns west of the mountains, only Talassee and one or two near Chickamauga or on the headwaters of the Coosa escaped. The whites had lost only one man killed and two wounded. Before the return, a proclamation was sent to the Cherokee chiefs, warning them to make peace or face the penalty of an even worse invasion. <note>² Roosevelt, *op. cit.*, pp. 300–304; Ramsey, *op. cit.*, pp. 265–268; Campbell, report, January 15, 1781, in Virginia State Papers, I, p. 436. Haywood and others who followed him claim the expedition went as far as Chickamauga and the Coosa River, but Campbell’s report explicitly denies this.</note>

Some Cherokee who met them at Echota during the return march to discuss peace brought in and surrendered several white prisoners. <note>³ Ramsey, *op. cit.*, p. 266.</note> One reason for the slight resistance offered by the Indians was likely the fact that at the very time of the invasion, many of their warriors were away raiding on the Upper Holston and in the neighborhood of Cumberland Gap. <note>⁴ Roosevelt, *op. cit.*, p. 302.</note>

Although the Upper or Overhill Cherokee were thus humbled, those of the middle towns on the headwaters of the Little Tennessee still continued to send out parties against the frontier settlements. Sevier

<header>MOONEY] TREATY OF LONG ISLAND—1781</header>

He determined to make a sudden strike against them, and early in March of the same year, 1781, with 150 selected horsemen, he started to cross the Great Smoky Mountains over trails never before attempted by white men. These trails were so rough in places that it was barely possible to lead horses. Attacking Tuckasegee unexpectedly, near the present-day Webster, North Carolina, he took the town completely by surprise, killing several warriors and capturing a number of women and children. Two other principal towns and three smaller settlements were taken in the same way, along with a quantity of provisions and about 200 horses. The Indians were entirely off their guard and unprepared to make any effective resistance. After spreading destruction through the middle towns, with the loss of only one man killed and another wounded, he left as suddenly as he had come, moving so rapidly that he was well on his way home before the Cherokee could gather for pursuit.<gloss>1</gloss> At the same time, a smaller Tennessee expedition set out to scatter the Indians who had been making their headquarters in the mountains around Cumberland Gap and harassing travelers along the road to Kentucky.<gloss>2</gloss> Numerous signs of Indians were found, but none were met, although the country was searched for a considerable distance.<gloss>3</gloss> In the summer, the Cherokee made another raid, this time upon the new settlements on the French Broad River, near the present-day Newport, Tennessee. With a hundred horsemen, Sevier fell suddenly upon their camp on Indian Creek, killed a dozen warriors, and scattered the rest.<gloss>4</gloss> By these successive blows, the Cherokee were so exhausted and discouraged that they were forced to ask for peace, and in the mid-summer of 1781, a treaty of peace—doubtful though it might be—was negotiated at Long Island of the Holston.<gloss>5</gloss> The relief came just in time to allow the Tennesseeans to send a detachment against Cornwallis.

Although there was a truce in Tennessee, there was none in the South. In November of this year, the Cherokee made a sudden raid upon the Georgia settlements, destroying everything in their path. In response, a force under General Pickens marched into their country, destroying their towns as far as the Valley River. Finding further progress blocked by heavy snows and learning through a prisoner that the Indians, who had retreated before him, were gathering to oppose him in the mountains, he withdrew, as he stated, “out of absolute necessity,” having accomplished very little of the expected result. Shortly afterward, the Cherokee, together with some Creeks, again invaded Georgia,

The Overhill Cherokee, on the lower Little Tennessee, seem to have been trying in good faith to uphold the peace established at Long Island. In early 1781, the government land office had been closed to further entries, not to be reopened until peace had been declared with England; however, the border settlers paid little attention to the law in such matters, and the mania for speculating in Tennessee lands grew stronger daily.<note>2</note> In the fall of 1782, the chief, Old Tassel of Echota, on behalf of all the friendly chiefs and towns, sent a moving message to the governors of Virginia and North Carolina, complaining that despite all their efforts to remain peaceful, the settlers were constantly encroaching upon them and had built houses within a day's walk of the Cherokee towns. <margin>✓</margin> They requested that all the whites who had settled beyond the recently established boundary should be removed.<note>3</note> As was to be expected, this was never done.

The Chickamauga band, however, and those farther to the south, were still intent on war, being actively encouraged in that inclination by British agents and refugee loyalists living among them. They continued to raid both north and south, and in September 1782, Sevier, with 200 mounted men, again led an attack on their towns, destroying several of their settlements around Chickamauga Creek and penetrating as far as the important town of Ustana'li, on the headwaters of the Coosa River, near present-day Calhoun, Georgia. This he also destroyed. Every warrior found was killed, along with a white man found in one of the towns, whose papers showed that he had been active in inciting the Indians to war. On the return journey, the expedition halted at Echota, where new assurances were received from the friendly faction.<note>4</note> In the meantime, a Georgia expedition of over 400 men under General Pickens had been ravaging the Cherokee towns in the same area, with such effectiveness that the Cherokee were forced to buy peace by a further surrender of territory at the head of the Broad River in Georgia.<note>5</note> This land cession was finalized at a peace treaty held with the Georgia commissioners at Augusta in the following year and was later confirmed by the Creeks, who claimed an interest in the same lands; however, it was never accepted by either tribe as the voluntary act of their nation as a whole.<note>6</note>

<header>MOONEY] TREATY OF HOPEWELL—1785</header>

Continuing the contest alone, they began to sue for peace. Through seven years of constant warfare, they had been reduced to the lowest depths of misery, almost indeed to the verge of extinction. Over and over again, their towns had been burned to the ground and their fields destroyed. Their best warriors had been killed, and their women and children had fallen ill and starved in the mountains. Their great war chief, Oconostota, who had led them to victory in 1780, was now a broken old man, and in this year, at Echota, he formally resigned his office in favor of his son, The Terrapin. To complete their overflowing cup of misery, smallpox broke out among them again in 1783.<note>1</note> Deprived of the assistance of their former white allies, they were left to their own cruel fate; the last feeble resistance of the mountain warriors to the advancing tide of settlement came to an end with the burning of Cowee town,<note>2</note> and the way was left open for an agreement. In the same year, the North Carolina legislature appointed an agent for the Cherokee and made regulations for the government of traders among them.<note>3</note>

# RELATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES

## FROM THE FIRST TREATY TO THE REMOVAL—1785-1838

<margin>✓</margin>
Passing over several unsatisfactory and generally failed negotiations conducted by the various state governments in 1783–84, including the treaty of Augusta already noted,<note>4</note> we come to the turning point in the history of the Cherokee: their first treaty for peace and boundary definition with the new government of the United States, concluded at Hopewell (25) in South Carolina on November 28, 1785. Nearly one thousand Cherokee attended; the commissioners for the United States were Colonel Benjamin Hawkins (26) of North Carolina, General Andrew Pickens of South Carolina, Cherokee Agent Joseph Martin of Tennessee, and Colonel Lachlan McIntosh of Georgia. The document was signed by thirty-seven chiefs and principal men, representing nearly as many different towns. The negotiations occupied ten days, being complicated by a protest from North Carolina and Georgia against the action of the government commissioners in confirming to the Indians some lands which had already been designated as bounty lands for state troops without the consent of the Cherokee. On the other hand, the Cherokee complained that 3,000 white settlers were at that moment occupying unceded land between the Holston and the French Broad rivers. Despite their protest, these intruders were allowed to remain, although the territory was not acquired by treaty until some years later. As finally arranged, the treaty left the Middle and Upper towns, and those in the vicinity

While the Hopewell treaty defined the relations of the Cherokee to the general government and provided a safe basis for future negotiation, it still failed to bring complete peace and security. Thousands of intruders were still settled on Indian lands, and minor aggressions and retaliations were continually occurring. The Creeks and the northern tribes were still hostile and remained so for several years, and their warriors, cooperating with those of the relentless Chickamauga towns, continued to harass the exposed settlements, particularly on the Cumberland. The British had withdrawn from the South, but the Spaniards and French, who claimed the lower Mississippi and the Gulf region and had their trading posts in west Tennessee, took every opportunity to encourage the spirit of hostility toward the Americans.<note>2. Ramsey, in the work cited, pages 459–461; Agent Martin and Hopewell commissioners, in the same place, pages 318–336; Bledsoe and Robertson letter, in the same place, page 465; Roosevelt, *Winning of the West*, volume II, page 368, 1899.</note> But the spirit of the Cherokee nation was broken, and the Holston settlements were now too firmly established to be destroyed.

The Cumberland settlements founded by Robertson and Donelson in the winter of 1779–80 had had only a short relief. Early in the spring, the Indians—Cherokee, Creeks, Chickasaw, and northern Indians—had begun a series of attacks with the intent of driving these intruders from their lands, and from then on for years, no man’s life was safe outside the stockade. The long list of settlers shot down while working or hunting in the woods, of livestock stolen and property destroyed, while of sorrowful interest to those most directly affected, is too lengthy to recount here, and only the leading events need to be recorded. Detailed accounts may be found in the works of local historians.

The attacks continued throughout this and the next year to such an extent that it seemed at one time as if the Cumberland settlements must be abandoned, but in June 1783, commissioners from Virginia and North Carolina arranged a treaty near Nashville (Nashborough) with chiefs of the Chickasaw, Cherokee, and Creeks. Thereafter the Chickasaw remained friendly, and only the Cherokee and Creeks continued to make trouble.<note>3. Ibid., pp. 358–366, 1889.</note>

The valley towns on Hiwassee, as well as those of Chickamauga, seem to have continued hostile. In 1786 a large body of their warriors, led by the mixed-blood chief, John Watts, raided the new settlements in the vicinity of the present Knoxville, Tennessee. called, concluded a negotiation, locally known as the “treaty of Coyatee,” with the chiefs of the Overhill towns. In spite of references to peace, love, and brotherly friendship, it is very doubtful if the era of goodwill was in any way hastened by the so-called treaty, as the Tennesseeans—who had just burned another Indian town in retaliation for the killing of a white man—announced, without mincing words, that they had been given the whole country north of the Tennessee River as far west as the Cumberland Mountain by North Carolina (against which state, by the way, they were then in organized rebellion), and that they intended to take it “by the sword, which is the best right to all countries.” As the whole of this country was within the limits of the territory solemnly guaranteed to the Cherokee by the Hopewell treaty only the year before, the chiefs simply replied that Congress had said nothing to them on the subject, and so the matter rested.<note>1 Reports of Tennessee commissioners and replies by Cherokee chiefs, etc., 1786, in Ramsey, *Tennessee*, pp. 343–346, 1853.</note> The theory of states' rights was too complicated for the Indian understanding.

While this conflict between state and federal authority continued, with the Cherokee lands as the prize, there could be no peace. In March 1787, a letter from Echota, apparently written by Agent Martin, speaks of a recent expedition against the Cherokee towns, and the confusion and alarm among them as a result of the daily encroachments of the “Franklinites” or Tennesseeans. These settlers had proceeded to make good their promise by opening a land office for the sale of all the lands southward to the Tennessee River, including even a part of the beloved town of Echota. At the same time, messengers were coming to the Cherokee from traders representing foreign interests, telling them that England, France, and Spain had combined against the Americans and urging them, with promises of guns and ammunition, to join in the war.<note>2 Martin (?) letter of March 25, 1787, *ibid.*, p. 359.</note> As a result, each further advance of the Tennessee settlements, which was in defiance of any recognized treaty, was stubbornly contested by the Indian owners of the land. The record of these encounters, extending over a period of several years, is too tedious for recital. “If a diagram could be drawn, accurately marking every spot signalized by an Indian massacre, surprise, or raid, or courageous attack, defense, pursuit, or victory by the whites, or station or fort or battlefield, or personal encounter, the whole of that section of country would be studded over with descriptions of such incidents. Every spring, every ford, every path, every farm, every trail, and nearly every house, in its first settlement, was once the scene of danger, exposure, attack, exploit, achievement, or death.”<note>3 *Ibid.*, p. 370.</note> The end result was the winning of Tennessee.

<header>MOONEY] DEFEAT OF GENERAL MARTIN—1788</header>
<sig>19 ETH—01—5</sig>

The allies on the Georgia frontier and the Cumberland settlements around Nashville became so threatening that plans were made for a joint campaign by the combined forces of Georgia and Tennessee (then called "Franklin"). The mission failed because of the intervention of the federal government.<note>1 Ramsey, Tennessee, pp. 393-399, 1853.</note> Throughout the year 1788, there were reports of attacks and retaliatory raids along the Tennessee border, even though the agent for the Cherokee stated in his official report that, with the exception of the Chickamauga band, the Indians wanted peace if the whites would leave them alone. In March, two expeditions under Sevier and Kennedy set out against the towns in the direction of the French Broad River. In May, several members of a family named Kirk were murdered a few miles south of Knoxville. In revenge, Sevier raised a large party and marched against a town on the Hiwassee River—one of those that had been destroyed some years earlier and rebuilt—and burned it, killing a number of the residents in the river while they were trying to escape. He then turned and, proceeding to the towns on the Little Tennessee River, burned several of them as well, killing a number of Indians. Here, a small party of Indians, including Abraham and Tassel—two well-known friendly chiefs—was brutally murdered by one of the Kirks while no one intervened, even though they had come in voluntarily at the request of one of the officers. This occurred while Sevier was temporarily away. Another expedition under Captain Fayne was caught in an ambush at Citico town and lost several men, both killed and wounded. The Indians chased the survivors almost to Knoxville, attacking a small station near present-day Maryville along the way. They were driven off by Sevier and others, who in turn invaded the Indian settlements, crossing the mountains and reaching as far as the valley towns on the Hiwassee; they retreated quickly when they found the Indians gathering to face them.<note>2 Ibid., pp. 417-423, 1853.</note> That same summer, another expedition was organized against the Chickamauga towns. General Martin was given the main command; he left White's Fort (now Knoxville) with four hundred and fifty men and made a rapid march to the area of present-day Chattanooga, where the main force camped on the site of an old Indian settlement. A detachment sent ahead to surprise a town a few miles further down the river was fired upon and driven back. A general battle took place in the narrow pass between the bluff and the river, with such disastrous results that three captains were killed. The men were so demoralized that they refused to move forward. Martin was forced to turn back after burying the dead officers in a large town house, which was then burned down to hide the grave.<note>3 Ibid., pp. 517-519, and Brown's narrative, ibid., p. 515.</note>

In October, a large party of Cherokee and Creeks attacked Gillespie's Station, south of present-day Knoxville. The small garrison was

The Indians left behind a letter signed by four chiefs, including John Watts, expressing regret for what they called the accidental killing of the women and children. They reminded the whites of their own treachery in killing Abraham and Old Tassel, and defiantly concluded, “When you move off the land, then we will make peace.” Other exposed settlements were attacked until, at last, Sevier again gathered a force, cleared the enemy from the frontier, and pursued the Indians as far as their towns on the headwaters of the Coosa River. He did this in such a vigorous fashion that they were forced to ask for peace terms and agree to a surrender of prisoners. This was accomplished at Coosawatee town, in upper Georgia, the following April.<note>1 Ramsey, Tennessee, pp. 515, 519.</note>

Among the captives thus returned to their friends were Joseph Brown, a boy of sixteen, and his two younger sisters. They, along with several others, had been captured at Nickajack town while traveling down the Tennessee River in a flatboat nearly a year before. His father and the other men of the party—about ten in all—had been killed at the time, while the mother and several other children were carried to various Indian towns. Some of them went to the Creeks, who had aided the Cherokee in the capture. Young Brown, whose short and simple narrative is of vivid interest, was at first sentenced to death, but was rescued by a white man living in the town and was afterward adopted into the family of the chief. This happened despite the warning of an old Indian woman that, if allowed to live, he would one day lead an army to destroy them. The warning was strangely prophetic, for it was Brown himself who guided the expedition that finally destroyed the Chickamauga towns a few years later. When rescued at Coosawatee, he was in Indian costume, wearing a shirt, breechcloth, and scalp lock, and had holes bored in his ears. His little sister, five years old, had become so attached to the Indian woman who had adopted her that she refused to go to her own mother and had to be pulled along by force.<note>2 Brown's narrative, etc., ibid., pp. 508-516.</note> The mother and another daughter, who had been taken by the Creeks, were afterward ransomed by McGillivray, head chief of the Creek Nation, who returned them to their friends, generously refusing any payment for his kindness.

An arrangement had been made with the Chickasaw in 1783 by which they surrendered to the Cumberland settlement their own claim to the lands from the Cumberland River south to the ridge of Duck River.<note>3 Ibid., pp. 459, 489.</note> However, it was not until the Treaty of Hopewell, two years later, that the Cherokee surrendered their claim to the same region. <page-num>67</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] DESTRUCTION OF COLDWATER—1787</header>

The hostile Creeks and Shawano refused to acknowledge the land cession and continued their attacks with the stated purpose of destroying the new settlements. Until the final survey of the boundary line in 1797, Spain claimed all the territory west of the mountains and south of the Cumberland River, and her agents were accused of inciting the Indians against the Americans, even to the point of offering rewards for American scalps.<note>1 Bledsoe and Robertson letter of June 12, 1787, in Ramsey, *Tennessee*, p. 465, 1853.</note>

One of these raiding parties, which had killed the brother of Captain Robertson, was tracked to Coldwater, a small mixed town of Cherokee and Creeks on the south side of the Tennessee River, near present-day Tuscumbia, Alabama. Robertson determined to destroy it, and taking a force of volunteers with a couple of Chickasaw guides, he crossed the Tennessee without being discovered and surprised and burned the town. The Indians, who numbered fewer than fifty men, attempted to escape to the river but were surrounded, and over twenty of them were killed, with the loss of only one man to the Tennesseans. Several French traders were also found in the town. Three of these, who refused to surrender, were killed, together with a white woman who was accidentally shot in one of the boats. The others were afterward released, their large stock of trading goods having been taken and sold for the benefit of the troops. The incident took place around the end of June 1787. Through this action, and an effort made by Robertson about the same time to come to an understanding with the Chickamauga band, there was a temporary halt to hostile raids upon the Cumberland; however, long before the end of the year, the attacks were renewed to such an extent that it was found necessary to keep a force of rangers active with orders to scour the country and kill every Indian found east of the Chickasaw boundary.<note>2 Ibid., with Robertson letter, pp. 465-476.</note>

Since the Creeks now seemed to be nearly as much involved in these raids as the Cherokee, a protest was addressed to McGillivray, their principal chief. He replied that, although the Creeks, like the other southern tribes, had supported the British interest during the Revolution, they had accepted proposals of friendship; however, while negotiations were pending, six of their people had been killed in the affair at Coldwater, which had led to a renewal of hostile feelings. He promised, however, to use his best efforts to bring about peace, and seems to have kept his word, although the raids continued through this and the next year, with the usual cycle of pursuit and retaliation. In one of these skirmishes, a company under Captain Murray followed some Indian raiders from near Nashville to their camp on the Tennessee River and succeeded in killing the entire party of eleven warriors.<note>3 Ibid., pp. 479-486.</note> A treaty of peace was signed with the Creeks in 1790, but, owing to the intrigues of the Spaniards, it had little practical effect,<note>4 Monette, *Valley of the Mississippi*, I, p. 505, 1846.</note> and not

Until Wayne’s decisive victory over the confederated northern tribes in 1794 and the final destruction of the Nickajack towns in the same year, real peace did not come to the frontier.

By a deed of cession on February 25, 1790, Tennessee ceased to be a part of North Carolina and was organized under federal laws as “The Territory of the United States south of the Ohio River,” preliminary to taking full rank as a state six years later. William Blount (27) was appointed the first territorial governor and also the superintendent for the southern Indians, with a deputy residing with each of the four principal tribes.<note>1 Ramsey, Tennessee, pp. 522, 541, 561, 1853.</note> Pensacola, Mobile, St. Louis, and other southern posts were still held by the Spaniards, who claimed the entire country south of the Cumberland, while the British garrisons had not yet been withdrawn from the north. The resentment of the Indians at the occupation of their reserved and guaranteed lands by the whites was diligently encouraged from both quarters, and raids along the Tennessee frontier were of common occurrence. At this time, according to the official report of President Washington, over five hundred families of intruders were settled upon lands belonging rightfully to the Cherokee, in addition to those between the French Broad and the Holston rivers.<note>2 Washington to the Senate, August 11, 1790, American State Papers: Indian Affairs, I, p. 83, 1832.</note> More than a year earlier, the Secretary of War had stated that “the disgraceful violation of the Treaty of Hopewell with the Cherokee requires the serious consideration of Congress. If such direct and manifest contempt for the authority of the United States is permitted with impunity, it will be futile to attempt to extend the arm of government to the frontiers. The Indian tribes can have no faith in such weak promises, and the lawless whites will ridicule a government which only on paper makes Indian treaties and regulates Indian boundaries.”<note>3 Secretary Knox to President Washington, July 7, 1789, ibid., p. 53.</note> To prevent any increase of the dissatisfaction, the general government issued a proclamation forbidding any further encroachment upon the Indian lands on the Tennessee River; notwithstanding this, early in 1791, a party of men descended the river in boats and, landing on an island at the Muscle Shoals, near the present Tuscumbia, Alabama, erected a blockhouse and other defensive works. Immediately afterward the Cherokee chief, Glass, with about sixty warriors, appeared and quietly informed them that if they did not at once withdraw he would kill them. After some discussion the intruders retired to their boats, at which point the Indians set fire to the buildings and reduced them to ashes.<note>4 Ramsey, op. cit., pp. 550, 551.</note>
