<header>MOONEY] TREATY OF HOLSTON—1791</header>

ville, Tennessee, in the summer of 1791. With much difficulty, the Cherokee were finally brought to consent to a cession of a triangular section in Tennessee and North Carolina, extending from the Clinch River almost to the Blue Ridge and including nearly the whole of the French Broad and the lower Holston, along with the sites of present-day Knoxville, Greenville, and Asheville. The whole of this area, with a considerable amount of adjacent territory, was already fully occupied by white settlers. Permission was also given for a road from the eastern settlements to those on the Cumberland, along with the free navigation of the Tennessee River. Prisoners on both sides were to be restored, and perpetual peace was guaranteed. In consideration of the lands surrendered, the Cherokee were to receive an annuity of one thousand dollars, along with some extra goods and some assistance on the road to civilization. A treaty was signed by forty-one principal men of the tribe and was concluded July 2, 1791. It is officially described as being held “on the bank of the Holston, near the mouth of the French Broad,” and is commonly spoken of as the “Treaty of Holston.”

The Cherokee, however, were dissatisfied with the arrangement, and before the end of the year, a delegation of six principal chiefs appeared at Philadelphia—then the seat of government—without any previous announcement of their coming. They declared that when they had been summoned by Governor Blount to a conference, they were not aware that it was to persuade them to sell lands; they stated that they had resisted the proposition for days and only yielded when compelled by the persistent and threatening demands of the governor; they argued that the payment was entirely too small and that they had no faith that the whites would respect the new boundary, as they were, in fact, already settling beyond it. Finally, as the treaty had been signed, they asked that these intruders be removed. As their presentation of the case seemed just and it was desirable that they should carry home with them a favorable impression of the government’s attitude toward them, a supplementary article was added, increasing the annuity to eight thousand five hundred dollars. On account of renewed Indian hostilities in the Ohio Valley and the desire of the government to keep the goodwill of the Cherokee long enough to obtain their help against the northern tribes, the new line was not surveyed until 1797.<note>1</note>

The treaty seems to have had little effect in preventing Indian hostilities, probably because the intruders still remained upon the Indian lands, and raiding still continued. The Creeks were known to be responsible for some of the mischief, and the hostile Chickamaugas were supposed to be the chief authors of the rest.<note>1</note> Even while the Cherokee delegates were negotiating the treaty in Philadelphia, a boat which had accidentally run aground on the Muscle Shoals was attacked by a party of Indians under the pretense of offering assistance, one man being killed and another severely wounded with a hatchet.<note>2</note>

While these negotiations had been pending at Philadelphia, a young man named Leonard D. The journey, which then seemed so long, was to be made by wagons from Philadelphia to the head of navigation on the Holston River, and then by boat to the Cherokee towns. Shaw seems to have taken up his residence at Ustanali, which had replaced Echota as the Cherokee capital. We hear of him being present at a council there in June of the same year, with no evidence of hostility toward his presence.<note>2 Estanaula conference report, June 26, 1792, ibid., p. 271; Deraque, deposition, September 15, 1792, ibid., p. 292; Pickens, letter, September 12, 1792, ibid., p. 317.</note> This friendly feeling lasted only a short time, however, for a few months later we find him writing from Ustanali to Governor Blount that because of the aggressive hostility of the Creeks, whose stated intention was to kill every white man they met, he was not safe even fifty yards from the house. Soon afterward, the Chickamauga towns declared war again. Because of this, along with renewed threats by the Creeks, the Cherokee advised him to leave Ustanali, which he did early in September 1792, traveling to the home of General Pickens near Seneca, South Carolina, escorted by a guard of friendly Cherokee. During the following winter, he was dismissed from service on serious charges, and his mission appears to have been a failure.<note>3 See letters of Shaw, Casey, Pickens, and Blount, 1792-93, ibid., pp. 277, 278, 317, 436, 437, 440.</note>

To prevent an alliance of the Cherokee, Creeks, and other southern Indians with the confederated hostile northern tribes, the government had tried to persuade the southern tribes to provide a group of warriors to serve with the army against the northern Indians, and special instructions had been given to Shaw to use his influence to achieve this result. Nothing, however, came of the attempt. St. Clair’s defeat turned the tide against the United States, and in September 1792, the Chickamauga towns formally declared war.<note>4 Knox, instructions to Shaw, February 17, 1792, ibid., p. 247; Blount, letter, March 20, 1792, ibid., p. 263; Knox, letters, October 9, 1792, ibid., pp. 261, 262.</note>

In November of this year, the governor of Georgia officially reported that a group of lawless Georgians had entered the Cherokee Nation, burned a town, and brutally killed three Indians; around the same time, two other Cherokee were killed within the settlements. Fearing retaliation, the governor ordered a patrol of troops to guard the frontier in that direction and sent a conciliatory letter to the chiefs, expressing his regret for what had happened. No answer was returned to the message, but a few days later an entire family was found murdered—four women, three children, and a young man—all scalped and mutilated, with arrows sticking in their bodies. Early in 1792, a messenger who had been sent on business for Governor Blount to the Chickamauga towns returned with the report that a party had just arrived with prisoners and some fresh scalps, over which the chiefs and warriors of two towns were then dancing. He reported that the Shawano were urging the Cherokee to join them against the Americans; that a strong body of Creeks was on its way against the Cumberland settlements; and that the Creek chief, McGillivray, was trying to form a general confederacy of all the Indian tribes against the whites. To understand this properly, it must be remembered that at this time all the tribes northwest of the Ohio and as far as the headwaters of the Mississippi were joined together in a grand alliance, headed by the warlike Shawano, for the purpose of holding the Ohio River as the Indian boundary against the advancing tide of white settlement. They had just destroyed one of the finest armies ever sent into the West, under the veteran General St. Clair (28), and it seemed for the moment as if the American advance would be driven back behind the Alleghenies.

In the emergency, the Secretary of War directed Governor Blount to hold a conference with the chiefs of the Chickasaw, Choctaw, and Cherokee at Nashville in June to enlist their warriors, if possible, in active service against the northern tribes. The conference was held as proposed, in August, but nothing seems to have come of it, although the chiefs seemed to be sincere in their assurances of friendship. Very few of the Choctaw or Cherokee were in attendance. At the distribution of the Cherokee annuity shortly before, the chiefs had also been generous in their declarations of their desire for peace.² Notwithstanding all this, the attacks along the Tennessee frontier continued to such an extent that the blockhouses were again prepared and garrisoned. Soon afterward, the governor reported to the Secretary of War that the five lower Cherokee towns on the Tennessee (the Chickamauga), led by John Watts, had finally declared war against the United States, and that between three and six hundred warriors, including a hundred Creeks, had started against the settlements. The militia was at once called out, both in eastern Tennessee and on the Cumberland. On the Cumberland side, it was ordered that no pursuit should be continued beyond the Cherokee boundary, the ridge between the waters of the Cumberland and Duck rivers. The order issued by Colonel White, of Knox County, to each of his captains shows how great the alarm was:

<header>MOONEY] ATTACK ON BUCHANAN'S STATION—1792</header>

->KNOXVILLE, *September 11, 1792.*<-

> SIR: You are hereby commanded to go with your company to Knoxville, equipped to protect the frontiers; there is imminent danger. Bring with you two days' provisions, if possible; but you are not to delay an hour on that account.
> ->I am, sir, yours,<-
> ->JAMES WHITE.<gloss>1</gloss><-

About midnight on the 30th of September, 1792, the Indian force, consisting of several hundred Chickamaugas and other Cherokee, Creeks, and Shawano, attacked Buchanan’s station, a few miles south of Nashville. Although numbers of families had collected inside the stockade for safety, there were fewer than twenty able-bodied men among them. The approach of the enemy alarmed the cattle, by which the garrison had warning just in time to close the gate when the Indians were already within a few yards of the entrance. The assault was furious and determined, with the Indians rushing up to the stockade, attempting to set fire to it, and aiming their guns through the portholes. One Indian succeeded in climbing upon the roof with a lighted torch, but was shot and fell to the ground, holding his torch against the logs as he drew his last breath. It was learned afterward that he was a half-blood, the stepson of the old white trader who had once rescued the boy Joseph Brown at Nickajack. He was a desperate warrior and, when only twenty-two years of age, had already taken six white scalps. The attack was repulsed at every point, and the assailants finally drew off with considerable loss, carrying their dead and wounded with them and leaving a number of hatchets, pipes, and other spoils upon the ground. Among the wounded was the chief John Watts. Not one of those in the fort was injured. It was well said that the defense of Buchanan’s station by such a handful of men against an attacking force estimated anywhere from three to seven hundred Indians is a feat of bravery which has scarcely been surpassed in the annals of border warfare. The effect upon the Indians must have been thoroughly disheartening.<gloss>2</gloss>

In the same month, arrangements were made for protecting the frontier along the French Broad by means of a series of garrisoned blockhouses, with scouts to patrol regularly from one to another, while North Carolina cooperated on her side of the line. The hostile raids still continued in this section, with the Creeks acting alongside the hostile Cherokee. One raiding party of Creeks having been traced toward Chilhowee town on the Little Tennessee, the whites were about to burn that and a neighboring Cherokee town when Sevier interposed and prevented it.<gloss>3</gloss> There is no reason to suppose that the people of these towns were directly concerned in the raids along the frontier at this period,

Toward the end of this year, 1792, Captain Samuel Handley, while leading a small party of men to reinforce the Cumberland settlement, was attacked by a mixed force of Cherokee, Creeks, and Shawnee near the Crab Orchard, west of present-day Kingston, Tennessee. Becoming separated from his men, he encountered a warrior who had lifted his hatchet to strike; Handley seized the weapon, crying out “Canaly” (for *higĭna'liĭ*), “friend,” to which the Cherokee responded with the same word, at once lowering his arm. Handley was carried to Willstown, in Alabama, where he was adopted into the Wolf clan <note>29</note> and remained until the next spring. After having made use of his services in writing a peace letter to Governor Blount, the Cherokee finally sent him home in safety to his friends under a protecting escort of eight warriors, without any demand for ransom. He afterward resided near Tellico blockhouse, near Loudon, where, after the wars were over, his Indian friends frequently came to visit and stay with him.^1

The year 1793 began with a series of attacks all along the Tennessee frontier. As before, most of the raiding was by Chickamaugas and Creeks, with some stray Shawnee from the north. The Cherokee from the towns on the Little Tennessee remained peaceable, but their temper was sorely tried by a regrettable circumstance which occurred in June. While a number of friendly chiefs were assembled for a conference at Echota, at the express request of the President, a party of men under the command of a Captain John Beard suddenly attacked them, killing about fifteen Indians, including several chiefs and two women. One of those killed was the wife of Hanging-maw (Ushwâ'li-gûtă), the principal chief of the nation, who was himself wounded. The murderers then fled, leaving others to suffer the consequences. Two hundred warriors at once took up arms to avenge their loss, and only the most earnest appeal from the deputy governor could restrain them from swift retaliation. While the chief, whose wife was thus murdered and who was himself wounded, refrained from taking revenge in order not to bring war upon his people, the Secretary of War was obliged to report, “to my great distress, I find that to punish Beard by law just now is out of the question.” Beard was in fact arrested, but the trial was a farce and he was acquitted.^2

Believing that the Cherokee Nation, with the exception of the Chickamaugas, was honestly trying to preserve peace, the territorial government, while making provision for the safety of the exposed settlements, had strictly prohibited any invasion of the Indian country. The frontier people were of a different opinion, and in spite of the prohibition, a company of nearly two hundred mounted men under

# MOONEY] MASSACRE AT CAVITTS STATION—1793

Colonels Doherty and McFarland crossed over the mountains in the summer of this year and destroyed six of the middle towns, returning with fifteen scalps and as many prisoners. <note>Ramsey, Tennessee, p. 579.</note>

Late in September, a strong force estimated at one thousand warriors—seven hundred Creeks and three hundred Cherokee—under John Watts and Doublehead, crossed the Tennessee River and advanced toward Knoxville, where public supplies were then stored. In their eagerness to reach Knoxville, they passed quietly by one or two smaller settlements until they were near the town. At daybreak on the 25th, they heard the garrison fire the sunrise gun and imagined that they had been discovered. Disagreements had already broken out among the leaders; without venturing to advance further, they contented themselves with an attack on a small blockhouse a few miles to the west, known as Cavitt's Station, which at the time held only three men and thirteen women and children. After defending themselves bravely for some time, they surrendered on the promise that they would be held for prisoner exchange. However, as soon as they came out, Doublehead's warriors fell upon them and killed them all, except for a boy who was saved by John Watts. This bloody deed was entirely the work of Doublehead, as the other chiefs had done their best to prevent it. <note>Ramsey, Tennessee, pp. 580-583, 1853; Smith, letter, September 27, 1793, American State Papers: Indian Affairs, I, p. 468, 1832. Ramsey estimates the Indian force at 1,000 warriors; Smith says that in many places they marched in files 28 abreast, with each file supposed to number 40 men.</note>

A force of seven hundred men under General Sevier was immediately sent after them, with orders this time to pursue them into the heart of the Indian nation. Crossing the Little Tennessee and Hiwassee rivers, they reached Ustanali town, near present-day Calhoun, Georgia. Finding it deserted, though well-stocked with provisions, they rested there for a few days. During this time, the Indians attempted a night attack without success. After burning the town, Sevier continued down the river to Etowah town, near the present site of Rome. Here the Indians—Cherokee and Creeks—had dug entrenchments and prepared to make a stand, but being outflanked, they were defeated with losses and forced to retreat. This town, along with several others in the neighborhood belonging to both Cherokee and Creeks, was destroyed, including all the Indians' provisions and three hundred cattle. Afterward, the army began the march home. The Americans had lost only three men. This was the last military service of Sevier. <note>Ramsey, Tennessee, pp. 584-588.</note>

During the absence of Sevier's force in the south, the Indians made a sudden raid on the French Broad, near present-day Dandridge, killing and scalping a woman and a boy. While their friends were escorting the remains to a nearby burial ground, two men who had incautiously gone ahead were fired upon. One

One of them escaped, but the other was found killed and scalped when the rest of the company arrived, and was buried with the first victims. Sevier’s success brought a temporary respite to the Cumberland settlements. During the early part of the year, Indian attacks by small raiding parties had been so frequent and annoying that a force of men had been kept on patrol service under officers who adopted, with some success, the policy of hunting the Indians in their camping places in the thickets rather than waiting for them to come into the settlements. <note>Ramsey, Tennessee, pp. 590, 602–605, 1853.</note>

In February 1794, the Territorial assembly of Tennessee met at Knoxville and, among other business transacted, addressed a strong memorial to Congress calling for more efficient protection for the frontier and demanding a declaration of war against the Creeks and Cherokee. The memorial states that since the Treaty of Holston (July 1791), these two tribes had killed more than two hundred citizens of Tennessee of both sexes in a most barbarous and inhuman manner, had carried others into captivity, destroyed their livestock, burned their houses, and laid waste their plantations. They had robbed the citizens of their slaves and stolen at least two thousand horses. Special attention was directed to the two great invasions in September 1792 and September 1793, and the memorialists declare that there was scarcely a man in the assembly who could not tell of “a dear wife or child, an aged parent or near relation, besides friends, massacred by the hands of these bloodthirsty nations in their houses or fields.” <note>Haywood, Civil and Political History of Tennessee, pp. 300–302; Knoxville, 1823.</note>

In the meantime, the raids continued and every scattered cabin was a target for attack. In April, a party of twenty warriors surrounded the house of a man named Casteel on the French Broad River, about nine miles above Knoxville, and massacred the father, mother, and four children in a most brutal fashion. Only one child was left alive, a girl of ten years, who was found scalped and bleeding from six tomahawk gashes, yet survived. The others were buried in one grave. The massacre roused such a storm of excitement that it required all the effort of the governor and the local officials to prevent an invasion in force of the Indian country. It was learned that Doublehead, of the Chickamauga towns, was trying to get the support of the valley towns, which, however, continued to maintain an attitude of peace. The friendly Cherokee also declared that the Spaniards were constantly instigating the lower towns to hostilities, although John Watts, one of their principal chiefs, advocated peace. <note>Ibid., pp. 303–308, 1823; Ramsey, op. cit., pp. 591–594. Haywood’s history of this period is little more than a continuous record of killings and petty encounters.</note>

On June 26, 1794, another treaty, intended to be supplementary to the Treaty of Holston in 1791, was negotiated at Philadelphia. It was signed by the Secretary of War and thirteen principal men of the Cherokee. An arrangement was made for the proper marking of the boundary established at that time, and the annual payment was increased to five thousand dollars, with a condition that fifty dollars were to be deducted for every horse stolen by the Cherokee and not returned within three months.<note>*Indian Treaties*, pp. 39, 40, 1837; Royce, *Cherokee Nation*, *Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology*, pp. 171, 172, 1888; *Documents of 1797-98*, *American State Papers: Indian Affairs*, I, pp. 628-631, 1832. This treaty is not mentioned by Tennessee historians.</note>

In July, a man named John Ish was shot down while plowing in his field eighteen miles south of Knoxville. By order of Hanging-maw, the friendly chief of Echota, a party of Cherokee took to the trail and captured the murderer. He proved to be a Creek, and they brought him to the agent at the Tellico blockhouse, where he was formally tried and hanged. When asked the usual question, he said that his people were at war with the whites, that he had left home to kill or be killed, that he had killed the white man and would have escaped if not for the Cherokee, and that there were enough of his nation to avenge his death. A few days later, a party of one hundred Creek warriors crossed the Tennessee River to attack the settlements. The alarm was given by Hanging-maw, and fifty-three Cherokee, along with a few Federal troops, started in pursuit. On the 10th of August, they caught up with the Creeks, killing one and wounding another; one Cherokee was slightly wounded. The Creeks retreated and the victors returned to the Cherokee towns, where their arrival was announced by the death song and the firing of guns. "The night was spent in dancing the scalp dance, according to the custom of warriors after a victory over their enemies, in which the white and Native people heartily joined. The Upper Cherokee had now stepped too far to go back, and their professions of friendship were now no longer to be questioned." In the meantime, Governor Blount was trying to negotiate peace with the entire Cherokee Nation, but with little success. The Cherokee claimed to be anxious for permanent peace, but they said it was impossible to restore the property they had taken, as it had been captured in war, and they themselves had lost just as much to the whites. They also said they could not prevent hostile Creeks from passing through their territory. Around the end of July, it was learned that a strong force of Creeks had started north against the settlements. The militia was at once ordered out along the Tennessee frontier, and the friendly Cherokees offered their services, while measures were taken to protect their women and children from the enemy. The Creeks advanced as far as Willstown, but when news arrived of the complete defeat of the allied northern tribes by General Wayne (30), they feared the same fate for themselves, turned back, and scattered to their towns.<note>Haywood, *op. cit.*, pp. 314-316; Ramsey, *op. cit.*, p. 596.</note>

The Tennesseans, especially those on the Cumberland, had long ago concluded that peace could be achieved only through the destruction of the Chickamauga towns. Anticipating an action of this kind—which the general government did not think necessary or advisable—the Secretary of War had issued orders to Governor Blount against any such attempt. The frontier people went about their preparations, however, and it is evident from the result that the local military authorities were secretly cooperating with the undertaking. General Robertson was the chief organizer of the volunteers around Nashville, who were reinforced by a company of Kentuckians under Colonel Whitley. Major Ore had been sent by Governor Blount with a detachment of troops to protect the Cumberland settlements, and upon arriving at Nashville, he entered into the project as heartily as if no counter-orders had ever been issued. He was given chief command of the expedition, which for this reason is commonly known as “Ore’s expedition.”

On September 7, 1794, the army of five hundred and fifty mounted men left Nashville, and five days later crossed the Tennessee River near the mouth of the Sequatchee River. Their guide was the same Joseph Brown of whom the old Indian woman had said would one day bring the soldiers to destroy them. Having left their horses on the other side of the river, they moved up along the south bank just after daybreak on the 13th and surprised the town of Nickajack, killing several warriors and taking a number of prisoners. <header>MOONEY] END OF CHEROKEE WAR—1794</header>

People in Running Water town, four miles above, heard the firing and came at once to the assistance of their friends, but they were driven back after attempting to hold their ground, and the second town shared the fate of the first. More than fifty Indians had been killed, a number were taken prisoner, and both towns and all their contents had been destroyed, with a loss to the attackers of only three wounded men. The Breath, the chief of Running Water, was among those killed. Two fresh scalps, along with a large quantity of stolen goods from the settlements, were found in the towns, together with a supply of ammunition said to have been provided by the Spaniards.<note>Haywood, *Political and Civil History of Tennessee*, pp. 392–396, 1823; Ramsey, *Tennessee* (with Major Ore's report), pp. 608–618, 1853; Royce, *Cherokee Nation*, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, p. 171, 1888; Ore, Robertson, and Blount, reports, *American State Papers: Indian Affairs, I*, pp. 632–634, 1832.</note>

Soon after the expedition returned, Robertson sent a message to John Watts, the principal leader of the hostile Cherokee, threatening a second attack if the Indians did not very soon surrender their prisoners and give assurances of peace.<note>Ramsey, *op. cit.*, p. 618.</note> The destruction of their towns on the Tennessee and Coosa rivers and the total defeat of the northern allies had now broken the spirit of the Cherokee. At their own request, Governor Blount held a conference with them at the Tellico blockhouse on November 7 and 8, 1794, which was attended by Hanging-maw, head chief of the Nation, and Colonel John Watt, the principal chief of the hostile towns, along with about four hundred of their warriors. The result was satisfactory; all differences were settled on a friendly basis and the long Cherokee war came to an end.<note>Tellico conference, November 7-8, 1794, *American State Papers: Indian Affairs, I*, pp. 536–538, 1832, Royce, *op. cit.*, p. 173; Ramsey, *op. cit.*, p. 596.</note>

Due to the continued destruction of their towns during the Revolutionary struggle, a number of Cherokee, mainly from the Chickamauga band, had moved across the Ohio River around 1782 and settled on Paint Creek, a branch of the Scioto River, near their friends and allies, the Shawano. In 1787, they were reported to number about seventy warriors. They took an active part in the hostilities along the Ohio frontier and were present at the great battle at the Maumee Rapids, which effectively broke the power of the confederated northern tribes. Since they had failed to attend the treaty conference held at Greenville in August 1795, General Wayne sent them a special message through their chief, Long-hair, stating that if they refused to come in and agree to terms as the others had done, they would be considered outside the protection of the government. Upon this, some of them came in and promised that as soon as they could harvest their crops, the entire band would leave Ohio forever and return to their people in the south.<note>Beaver's talk, 1784, *Virginia State Papers, III*, p. 571, 1883; McDowell, report, 1786, *ibid., IV*, p. 118, 1884; McDowell, report, 1787, *ibid.*, p. 286; Todd, letter, 1787, *ibid.*, p. 277; Tellico conference, November 7, 1794, *American State Papers: Indian Affairs, I*, p. 538, 1832; Greenville treaty conference, August, 1795, *ibid.*, pp. 582-583.</note>

<summary>Following the destruction of Running Water town and the death of Chief The Breath, the Cherokee leaders met with Governor Blount at the Tellico blockhouse to finalize a peace treaty. This agreement, combined with the return of Cherokee bands from the Ohio territory, marked the official end of the Cherokee war in 1794.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the historical account of the late 1790s, detailing the diplomatic tensions between the United States government, white settlers in Tennessee, and the Cherokee Nation regarding land rights and border security.</meta>

<header>MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19</header>

The Creeks were still hostile and continued their raids upon the western settlements. Early in January 1795, Governor Blount held another conference with the Cherokee and tried to persuade them to organize a company of their young men to patrol the frontier against the Creeks, but the chiefs refused to consent to this proposal.<note>Royce, *Cherokee Nation*, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, p. 173, 1888.</note>

In the next year, it was discovered that a movement was underway to take possession of certain Indian lands south of the Cumberland River under the pretext of authority formerly granted by North Carolina for the relief of Revolutionary War soldiers. As such action would almost certainly have resulted in another Indian war, Congress intervened, at the recommendation of President Washington, with an act for the regulation of interaction between citizens of the United States and the various Indian tribes. Its main purpose was to prevent intrusion upon lands to which the Indian title had not been extinguished by treaty with the federal government, and under its provisions, a number of squatters were evicted from the Indian country and removed across the boundary. The pressure of border sentiment, however, was constantly pushing to extend the area of white settlement, and the result was an immediate agitation to obtain another treaty cession.<note>Ibid., pp. 174, 175; Ramsey, *Tennessee*, pp. 679–685, 1853.</note>

In consequence of urgent requests from the people of Tennessee, Congress took steps in 1797 to obtain a new treaty with the Cherokee by which the evicted settlers might be reinstated and the boundaries of the new state extended so as to bring about closer communication between the eastern settlements and those on the Cumberland. The Revolutionary warfare had forced the Cherokee west and south, and their capital and central gathering place was now Ustanali town, near present-day Calhoun, Georgia, while Echota, their ancient capital and beloved peace town, was almost on the edge of the white settlements. The commissioners wished to have the proceedings conducted at Echota, while the Cherokee favored Ustanali. After some debate, a choice was made of a convenient place near the Tellico blockhouse, where the conference opened in July, but it was brought to an abrupt close by the firm refusal of the Cherokee to sell any lands or to permit the return of the evicted settlers.

The rest of the summer was spent in negotiation along the lines already proposed, and on October 2, 1798, a treaty, commonly known as the "first treaty of Tellico," was concluded at the same place, and was signed by thirty-nine chiefs on behalf of the Cherokee. By this treaty, the Indians ceded a tract between the Clinch River and the Cumberland ridge, another along the northern bank of the Little Tennessee extending up to Chilhowee Mountain, and a third in North Carolina on the headwaters of the French Broad and Pigeon rivers and including the sites

of present-day Waynesville and Hendersonville. These cessions included most or all of the lands from which settlers had been evicted. Permission was also given to lay out the "Cumberland Road," connecting the East Tennessee settlements with those around Nashville. In exchange for the surrendered lands and rights, the United States agreed to provide the Cherokee with five thousand dollars in goods, to increase their existing annual payment by one thousand dollars, and, as was customary, to "continue to guarantee the remainder of their country forever."<note>Indian Treaties, pp. 78-82, 1837; Ramsey, *Tennessee*, pp. 692-697, 1853; Royce, *Cherokee Nation* (including map and detailed discussion), *Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology*, pp. 174-183, 1888.</note>

General Wayne's victory over the northern tribes at the Battle of the Maumee Rapids completely broke their power and forced them to accept the peace terms dictated at the Treaty of Greenville in the summer of 1795. The immediate result was that the Indians surrendered the Ohio River boundary and the British withdrew their garrisons from the interior posts, which they had continued to occupy until this time despite the treaty made at the end of the Revolutionary War. By the treaty signed in Madrid in October 1795, Spain relinquished all claims on the eastern side of the Mississippi River north of the thirty-first parallel. However, using various excuses, the formal transfer of posts was delayed, and a Spanish garrison continued to occupy San Fernando de Barrancas (at present-day Memphis, Tennessee) until the fall of 1797, while the post at Natchez, Mississippi, was not surrendered until March 1798. The Creeks, seeing the direction of events, made peace at Colerain, Georgia, in June 1796. With hostile European influence eliminated—at least for the time—and with the warlike tribes to the north and south crushed and discouraged and the Chickamauga towns destroyed, the Cherokee realized they had to accept the situation. After nearly twenty years of constant warfare, they laid aside the tomahawk to pursue the arts of peace and civilization.

The close of the century found them still a unified people (as the westward movement had hardly begun), numbering approximately 20,000 individuals. After repeatedly ceding large tracts of land—some of which they had only questionable claims to—they remained in recognized possession of nearly 43,000 square miles of territory, an area roughly equal in size to Ohio, Virginia, or Tennessee. About half of this territory lay within the borders of Tennessee; the remainder was divided almost equally between Georgia and Alabama, with a small area in the extreme southwestern corner of North Carolina.<note>See the table in Royce, *op. cit.*, p. 378.</note> The old Lower Towns on the Savannah River had been disbanded for twenty years, and white settlers had encroached so far upon the Upper Towns that the nation's capital and council fire had been moved from the ancient peace town of Echota to Ustanali, Georgia. The

towns on the Coosa River and in Alabama were almost all established recently, populated by refugees from the east and north. The Middle towns, in North Carolina, were still surrounded by Indian country.

Firearms had been introduced to the tribe about one hundred years earlier, and the Cherokee had learned their use well. Civilized goods such as hatchets, knives, clothes, and trinkets had become so common before the first Cherokee war that they could no longer live without the traders. Horses and other domestic animals had been introduced early in the century, and at the start of the war of 1760, according to Adair, the Cherokee had “a prodigious number of excellent horses.” Although hunger had compelled them to eat a great many of these during that period, they still had, in 1775, from two to a dozen each, and seemed likely to soon have plenty of the best kind; according to the same authority, they were skillful jockeys and precise in their choices. Some of them had grown fond of cattle, and they also had an abundance of hogs and poultry. Indian pork was considered better than that raised in the white settlements because of the chestnut diet.<note>Adair, *American Indians*, pp. 230, 231, 1775.</note> In Sevier’s expedition against the towns on the Coosa River in 1793, the army killed three hundred cattle at Etowah and left their carcasses rotting on the ground. While crossing the Cherokee country in 1796, Hawkins met an Indian woman on horseback driving ten very fat cattle to the settlements to be sold. Peach trees and potatoes, as well as the native corn and beans, were abundant in their fields, and some had bees and honey and conducted a considerable trade in beeswax. They seem to have quickly recovered from the repeated ravages of war, and there was a general air of prosperity throughout the nation. The native arts of pottery and basketmaking were still the primary employment of the women, and the warriors hunted with such success that a party of traders brought down thirty wagonloads of skins on a single trip.<note>See Hawkins, MS journal from South Carolina to the Creeks, 1796, in the library of the Georgia Historical Society.</note> In dress and housebuilding, the Indian style remained practically unchanged.

In pursuit of a civilizing policy, the government had agreed, by the treaty of 1791, to provide the Cherokee with free farming tools and similar assistance. This policy was continued and expanded to such an extent that in 1801, Hawkins reports that “in the Cherokee agency, the spinning wheel, the loom, and the plow are in fairly general use; farming, manufacturing, and stock raising are the topics of conversation among the men and women.” At a conference held this year, we find the chiefs of the mountain towns complaining that the people of the more western and southwestern settlements had received more than their share of spinning wheels and cards, and were consequently more advanced in making their own clothing as well as in farming, to which

<header>MOONEY] INTERMARRIAGE WITH WHITES</header>

<margin>pencil bracket and cross mark in right margin</margin>
The others responded that these opportunities had been offered to everyone at the same time, but while the lowland people had been quick to accept them, the mountaineers had held back. "Those who complain arrived late. We have a head start on them, which we are determined to keep." The progressives, under John Watts, Doublehead, and Will, threatened to secede from the rest and leave those east of Chilhowee mountain to fend for themselves.<note>Hawkins, Treaty Commission, 1801, manuscript No. 5, in the library of the Georgia Historical Society.</note> We see here the source of the dissatisfaction which led ultimately to the emigration of the western band. Along with other aspects of civilization, Negro slavery had been introduced and several of the leading men were now slaveholders (31).

Much of the progress in civilization had been due to the intermarriage within the tribe of white men—chiefly traders from the pre-Revolutionary period—along with a few Americans from the backcountry settlements. The families that have shaped Cherokee history were nearly all of this mixed descent. The Doughertys, Galpins, and Adairs were from Ireland; the Rosses, Vanns, and McIntoshes, like the McGillivrays and Graysons among the Creeks, were of Scottish origin; the Waffords and others were Americans from Carolina or Georgia, and the father of Sequoya was a German (possibly from Pennsylvania). Most of this white lineage was of good stock, very different from the "squaw man" element found among the western tribes. Those of mixed heritage who could afford it usually sent their children away to be educated, while some built schoolhouses on their own property and brought in private teachers from the outside. By the beginning of the nineteenth century, we find influential people of mixed heritage in almost every town, and the idea of civilization dominated even the national councils. The Middle towns, isolated from the outside world by high mountains, remained a stronghold of Cherokee conservatism.

With the exception of Priber, there seems to be no authentic record of any missionary worker among the Cherokee before 1800. There is, indeed, an incidental mention of a Presbyterian minister from North Carolina being on his way to the tribe in 1758, but nothing seems to have come of it, and we find him soon after in South Carolina, separated from his original jurisdiction.<note>Foote (?), in *North Carolina Colonial Records*, volume 5, page 1226, 1887.</note> The first permanent mission was established by the Moravians, those peaceful German immigrants whose teachings were so well demonstrated in the lives of Zeisberger and Heckewelder. As early as 1734, while temporarily settled in Georgia, they had tried to bring some knowledge of the Christian religion to the Indians immediately around Savannah, including perhaps some scattered Cherokee. Later on, they established missions among the Delawares in Ohio, where their first Cherokee convert was received in 1773; he was a man who had been captured by the Delawares as a boy and had grown up and married within the tribe. In 1752, they had formed a settlement on the upper Yadkin, near present-day Salem,

Another visit was made the following summer, and a council was held at the Tellico agency. After a debate in which the Indians showed a considerable difference of opinion, it was decided to open a mission. Having obtained permission from the government, the work was begun in April 1801, by the Rev. Abraham Steiner and Rev. Gottlieb Byhan at the residence of David Vann, a prominent mixed-blood chief. He housed them in his own home and gave them every assistance in building the mission, which they later called Spring Place; this is now the village of the same name in Murray County, northwestern Georgia. They were also greatly assisted by the agent, Colonel Return J. Meigs (32). It was soon apparent that the Cherokee wanted educators for their children and not new theologies. When they found that a school could not be opened immediately, the great council at Ustanali sent orders to the missionaries to organize a school within six months or leave the nation. With Vann’s help, the matter was arranged and a school was opened, with several sons of prominent chiefs among the pupils. Another Moravian mission was established by Reverend J. Gambold at Oothcaloga, in the same county, in 1821. Both were in a flourishing condition when they were shut down, along with other Cherokee missions, by the State of Georgia in 1834. In 1804, the Reverend Gideon Blackburn, a Presbyterian minister from Tennessee, opened a school among the Cherokee, which continued for several years until it was abandoned for lack of funds.<note>Morse, *American Geography*, volume I, page 577, 1819.</note>

Despite the promise made to the Cherokee in the treaty of 1798 that the Government would “continue the guarantee of the remainder of their country forever,” measures were started almost immediately to obtain another large surrender of land and road privileges. In spite of the strong objections of the Cherokee, who sent a delegation of prominent chiefs to Washington to protest against any further sales, such pressure was applied—chiefly through the efforts of the agent, Colonel Meigs—that the Government’s objective was accomplished. In 1804 and 1805, three treaties were negotiated at the Tellico agency, by which the Cherokee were stripped of more than eight thousand square miles of their remaining territory.

In compensation, the Cherokee were to receive an immediate payment of five thousand dollars in goods or cash, with an additional annual payment of one thousand dollars. By the other treaties—October 25 and 27, 1805—a large tract of land was obtained in central Tennessee and Kentucky, extending between the Cumberland range and the western line of the Hopewell treaty, and from the Cumberland River southwest to the Duck River. One section was also secured at Southwest Point (now Kingston, Tennessee) with the intention of establishing the state capital there; however, it was located at Nashville instead seven years later. Permission was also obtained for two mail roads through the Cherokee country into Georgia and Alabama. In consideration of the land surrendered by these two treaties, the United States agreed to pay fifteen thousand six hundred dollars in tools, goods, or cash, with an additional annual payment of three thousand dollars. To secure the consent of some of the leading chiefs, the treaty commissioners resorted to the disgraceful practice of secret articles. Through these, several valuable small tracts of land were reserved for Doublehead and Tollunteeskee; this agreement was recorded as part of the treaty but was not included in the copy sent to the Senate for confirmation.<note>Indian treaties, pages 108, 121, 125, 1837; Royce, Cherokee Nation, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, pages 183-193, 1888 (map and full discussion).</note> Because of the continued abuse of his official position for selfish ends, Doublehead was killed soon afterward according to a decree from the chiefs of the Nation, with Major Ridge being selected as the executioner.<note>McKenney and Hall, Indian Tribes, volume II, page 92, 1858.</note>

Through the treaty of October 25, 1805, the settlements in eastern Tennessee were connected with those around Nashville on the Cumberland, and the state finally took on a compact form. The entire southern portion of the state, as defined in its charter, was still Indian country, and there was strong and constant pressure to open it. The prevailing sentiment favored making the Tennessee River the boundary between the two races. New immigrants were constantly crowding in from the east, and, as Royce says, "the desire to settle on Indian land was as powerful and insatiable with the average border settler then as it is now." Barely two months after the last treaties, another one was concluded at Washington on January 7, 1806. By this treaty, the Cherokee surrendered their claim to a large tract of land between the Duck River and the Tennessee River, encompassing nearly seven thousand square miles in Tennessee and Alabama, along with Long Island (Great Island) in the Holston River, which they had claimed as theirs until this time. In exchange, they were promised ten thousand dollars in five cash installments, a grist mill, a cotton gin, and a life annuity

In 1807, Colonel Elias Earle, with the consent of the government, obtained a concession from the Cherokee for the establishment of iron works at the mouth of Chickamauga Creek, on the south side of the Tennessee River, to be supplied from ores mined in the Cherokee country. It was hoped that this would be a significant step toward the civilization of the Indians, while also enabling the government to obtain its supplies of manufactured iron at a cheaper rate; however, after a long effort, the project was finally abandoned because the state of Tennessee refused to approve the grant.<note>See treaty, December 2, 1807, and Jefferson's message, with enclosures, March 10, 1808, American State Papers: Indian Affairs, I, pages 752–754, 1832; Royce, op. cit., pages 199–201.</note> In the same year, by arrangement with the federal government, the legislature of Tennessee attempted to negotiate with the Cherokee for that part of their unsurrendered lands lying within the state limits, but without success, due to the unwillingness of the Indians to part with any more territory and their special dislike for the people of Tennessee.<note>Ibid., pages 201, 202.</note>

In 1810, the Cherokee national council registered a further advance in civilization by formally abolishing the custom of clan revenge, which had been universal among the tribes until then. The law bears the signatures of Black-fox (Ina'lĭ), principal chief, and seven others, and reads as follows:

->IN COUNCIL, OOSTINALEH, *April 18, 1810.*<-

> 1. Let it be known today that the various clans or tribes which compose the Cherokee nation have unanimously passed an act of oblivion for all lives for which they may have been indebted to one another, and have mutually agreed that after this evening the aforementioned act shall become binding upon every clan or tribe within it.
> 2. The aforementioned clans or tribes have also agreed that if, in the future, any life should be lost without intended malice, the innocent aggressor shall not be held guilty;

Under an agreement with the Cherokee in 1813, a company composed of representatives of Tennessee, Georgia, and the Cherokee nation was organized to lay out a free public road from the Tennessee River to the head of navigation on the Tugaloo branch of the Savannah River, with provisions for convenient stopping places along the line. The road was completed within the next three years and became the great highway from the coast to the Tennessee settlements. Beginning on the Tugaloo or Savannah a short distance below the entrance of Toccoa Creek, it crossed the upper Chattahoochee, passing through Clarkesville, Nacoochee Valley, the Unicoi Gap, and Hiwassee in Georgia; then entering North Carolina, it descended the Hiwassee, passing through Hayesville and Murphy and over the Great Smoky range into Tennessee, until it reached the terminus at the Cherokee capital, Echota, on the Little Tennessee. It was officially styled the Unicoi Turnpike,<note>See contract appended to Washington treaty, 1819, Indian Treaties, pp. 269-271, 1837; Royce map, Fifth Ann. Rep. Bureau of Ethnology, 1888.</note> but was commonly known in North Carolina as the Wachesa Trail, from Watsi'sa or Wachesa, a prominent Indian who lived near the crossing-place on Beaverdam Creek, below Murphy; this portion of the road was laid out along the old Indian trail which already bore that name.<note>Author's personal information.</note>

Passing over for the present some negotiations aimed at the removal of the Cherokee to the West, we arrive at the period of the Creek War.

Ever since the Treaty of Greenville, it had been the dream of Tecumtha, the great Shawano chief (33), to weld together again the confederacy of the northern tribes as a barrier against the further aggressions of the white man. His own burning eloquence was ably seconded by the subtler persuasion of his brother, who assumed the role of a prophet with a new revelation. The core of this message was that the Indians must return to their traditional Indian way of life if they wished to preserve their national existence. The new doctrine spread among all the northern tribes and at last reached those of the south, where Tecumtha himself had gone to enlist the warriors in the great Indian confederacy. The prophets of the Upper Creeks eagerly accepted the doctrine, and in a short time their warriors were dancing the "dance of the Indians of the lakes." In

In anticipation of an expected war with the United States, the British agents in Canada had been encouraging hostile feelings toward the Americans through talks and presents of goods and ammunition, while the Spaniards also secretly fanned the flames of discontent.<note>Mooney, *Ghost-dance Religion*, Fourteenth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, p. 670 and following, 1896; contemporary documents in *American State Papers: Indian Affairs*, I, pp. 798-801, 845-850, 1832.</note> At the height of the unrest, war was declared between this country and England on June 28, 1812. Tecumtha, at the head of fifteen hundred warriors, immediately entered the British service with a commission as a general, while the Creeks began murdering and burning along the southern frontier, after having unsuccessfully attempted to secure the cooperation of the Cherokee.

From the Creeks, the new revelation was brought to the Cherokee, whose priests immediately began to dream dreams and to preach a return to the old life as the only hope for the Indian race. A great medicine dance was scheduled at Ustanali, the national capital, where, after the dance was over, the doctrine was publicly announced and explained by a Cherokee prophet introduced by a delegation from Coosawatee. He began by saying that some of the mountain towns had abused him and refused to receive his message, but nevertheless, he must continue to testify to his mission whatever might happen. The Cherokee had broken the path which had been given to their ancestors at the beginning of the world. They had taken the white man's clothes and trinkets; they had beds and tables and mills; some even had books and cats. All this was bad, and because of it, their gods were angry and the wild animals were leaving their country. If they would live and be happy as before, they must cast aside the white man's dress, throw away his mills and looms, kill their cats, put on paint and buckskin, and be Indians again; otherwise, swift destruction would come upon them.

His speech appealed strongly to the people, who cried out in great excitement that his talk was good. Of all those present, only Major Ridge, a principal chief, had the courage to stand up and oppose it, warning his listeners that such talk would inevitably lead to war with the United States, which would end in their own destruction. The maddened followers of the prophet sprang upon Ridge and would have killed him if not for the intervention of friends. As it was, he was thrown down and narrowly escaped with his life, while one of his defenders was stabbed by his side.

The prophet had threatened that after a certain time, he would summon a terrible storm, which would destroy everyone but the true believers, who were urged to gather for safety on one of the high peaks of the Great Smoky mountains. In full faith, they abandoned their bees, their orchards, their slaves, and everything that had come to them from the white man, and began their difficult march to the high mountains. There they waited until the appointed day had come and passed, show-

Among the Creeks, where other hostile influences were at work, the excitement culminated in the Creek War. Several murders and outrages had already been committed, but it was not until the terrible massacre at Fort Mims <note>34</note> on August 30, 1813, that the entire American nation was aroused. Through the influence of Ridge and other prominent chiefs, the Cherokee had refused to join the hostile Creeks; on the contrary, they had promised to assist the whites and the friendly towns. <note>Letters of Hawkins, Pinckney, and Cussetah King, July 1813, *American State Papers: Indian Affairs*, II, pp. 847–849, 1832.</note> More than a year earlier, the council had sent a friendly letter to the Creeks warning them against taking the British side in the approaching war, while several prominent chiefs had proposed to enlist a Cherokee force for the service of the United States. <note>Meigs, letter, May 8, 1812, and Hawkins, letter, May 11, 1812, ibid., p. 809.</note> Finding that no help was to be expected from the Cherokee, the Creeks took the opportunity to kill a Cherokee woman near the town of Etowah, in Georgia. With the help of a conjurer, the murderers were trailed, overtaken, and killed on the evening of the second day in a thicket where they had hidden themselves. After this, there could be no alliance between the two tribes. <note>Author’s information from James D. Wafford.</note>

At the time of the Fort Mims massacre, McIntosh <note>35</note>, the chief of the friendly Lower Creeks, was visiting the Cherokee, among whom he had relatives. By order of the Cherokee council, he was escorted home by a delegation under the leadership of Ridge. On his return, Ridge brought with him a request from the Lower Creeks that the Cherokee would join with them and the Americans in putting down the war. Ridge himself strongly urged the proposal, declaring that if the prophets were allowed to have their way, the work of civilization would be destroyed. The council, however, decided not to interfere in the affairs of other tribes, whereupon Ridge called for volunteers; the result was that so many warriors responded that the council reversed its decision and declared war against the Creeks. <note>McKenney and Hall, *Indian Tribes*, II, pp. 96–97, 1858.</note> For a proper understanding of the situation, it is necessary to state that the hostile feeling was confined almost entirely to the Upper Creek towns on the Tallapoosa, where the prophets of the new religion lived. The mixed-blood chief, Weatherford <note>36</note>, was the leader of the war party. The Lower Creek towns on the Chattahoo-

It is not our purpose to give a history of the Creek War, but only to note the role that the Cherokee played in it. The friendly Lower Creeks, under McIntosh, along with a few refugees from the Upper towns, operated mainly with the army under General Floyd, which invaded the southern part of the Creek country from Georgia. Some friendly Choctaw and Chickasaw also provided assistance in this direction. The Cherokee, along with some friendly Creeks of the Upper towns, served with the armies under Generals White and Jackson, which entered the Creek country from the Tennessee side. While some hundreds of their warriors were thus fighting in the field, the Cherokee at home were busily collecting supplies for the American troops.

As Jackson approached from the north around the end of October 1813, he was met by messengers asking him to come to the aid of Path-killer, a Cherokee chief. Path-killer was in danger of being cut off by hostile forces at his village of Turkeytown, on the upper Coosa River, near present-day Center, Alabama. A new detachment on its way from east Tennessee, under General White, was ordered by Jackson to relieve the town and successfully performed this task. White's force consisted of one thousand men, including four hundred Cherokee under Colonel Gideon Morgan and John Lowrey. <note>Drake, *Indians*, pp. 395-396, 1880; Pickett, *Alabama*, p. 556, reprint of 1896.</note>

As the army advanced down the Coosa, the Creeks retired to Tallasee-hatchee, on the creek of the same name, near present-day Jacksonville, Calhoun County, Alabama. One thousand men under General Coffee, together with a company of Cherokee under Captain Richard Brown and a few Creeks, were sent against them. The Indian allies wore headdresses of white feathers and deer tails. The attack was made at daybreak on November 3, 1813, and the town was taken after a desperate resistance from which not one of the defenders escaped alive, as the Creeks had been completely surrounded on all sides. Coffee said in his official report:

> They offered all the resistance that an overpowered soldier could do—they fought as long as one existed, but their destruction was very soon completed. Our men rushed up to the doors of the houses and in a few minutes killed the last warrior among them. The enemy fought with fierce fury and met death with all its horrors, without shrinking or complaining—not one asked to be spared, but they fought as long as they could stand or sit.

The Creeks proved themselves to be made of such fighting spirit against overwhelming numbers throughout the war. The bodies of nearly two hundred dead warriors were counted on the field, and the general repeated that "not one of the warriors escaped." A number of women and children were taken prisoner. Nearly every Creek man had a bow with a bundle of arrows, which he used after the

### MOONEY] BATTLES OF TALLADEGA AND HILLABEE—1813

White’s advance guard, consisting chiefly of the four hundred other Cherokee under Morgan and Lowrey, reached Tallaseehatchee the same evening, only to find it already destroyed. They picked up twenty wounded Creeks, whom they brought with them to Turkeytown. <note>Ibid., p. 556.</note>

The next great battle was at Talladega, on the site of the present town of the same name in Talladega County, Alabama, on November 9, 1813. Jackson commanded in person with two thousand infantry and cavalry. Although the Cherokee are not specifically mentioned, they were a part of the army and must have taken part in the engagement. The town itself was occupied by friendly Creeks, who were besieged by the hostile forces, estimated at over one thousand warriors on the outside. Here again, the battle was simply a slaughter, as the odds were two to one and the Creeks were also without cover, although they fought so desperately that at one time the militia was driven back. They left two hundred and ninety-nine dead bodies on the field, which, according to their own statement afterward, was only a part of their total loss. The Americans lost fifteen killed and eighty-five wounded. <note>Drake, *Indians*, p. 396, 1880; Pickett, cited above, pp. 554, 555.</note>

A day or two later, the people of Hillabee town, located near the site of the present village of that name in Clay County, Alabama, sent messengers to Jackson’s camp to ask for peace, which that commander immediately granted. In the meantime, even while the peace messengers were on their way home with the good news, an army of one thousand men from east Tennessee under General White—who claimed to be independent of Jackson’s authority—together with four hundred Cherokee under Colonel Gideon Morgan and John Lowrey, surrounded the town on November 18, 1813. They took the town by surprise, as the inhabitants had trusted so confidently in the success of their peace embassy that they had made no preparations for defense. Sixty warriors were killed and over two hundred and fifty prisoners were taken, with no loss to the Americans, as there was practically no resistance. In White’s official report of the affair, he states that he had sent ahead a part of his force, together with the Cherokee under Morgan, to surround the town, and adds that “Colonel Morgan and the Cherokees under his command gave undeniable evidence that they merit the employment of their government.” <note>White’s report, etc., in Fay and Davison, *Sketches of the War*, pp. 240, 241; Rutland, Vermont, 1815; Low, John, *Impartial History of the War*, p. 199; New York, 1815; Drake, cited above, p. 397; Pickett, cited above, p. 557; Lossing, cited above, p. 767. Low states that White had about 1,100 mounted men, “including upward of 300 Cherokee Indians.” Pickett gives White 400 Cherokee.</note> Not knowing that the attack had been made without Jackson’s sanction or knowledge, the Creeks naturally con-

concluded that peace overtures were of no use, and from then on until the end of the war, there was no talk of surrender.

On November 29, 1813, the Georgia army under General Floyd—consisting of nine hundred and fifty American troops and four hundred friendly Indians, mainly Lower Creeks under McIntosh—captured and destroyed the town of Autossee on the Tallapoosa River, west of present-day Tuskegee. They killed about two hundred warriors and burned four hundred well-built houses. On December 23, the Creeks were defeated again by General Claiborne, assisted by some friendly Choctaws, at Ecanachaca (also known as the Holy Ground) on the Alabama River, near present-day Benton in Lowndes County. This town and another a few miles away were also destroyed, along with a large quantity of supplies and other property. <note>Drake, *Indians*, pp. 391, 398, 1880; Pickett, *Alabama*, pp. 557-559, 572-576, 1896 reprint.</note> It is doubtful whether any Cherokee were involved in either battle.

Before the end of the year, Jackson’s forces in northern Alabama had been so greatly reduced by mutinies and the expiration of service terms that he had only one hundred soldiers left. He was forced to employ the Cherokee to garrison Fort Armstrong on the upper Coosa River and to protect his supply depot. <note>Ibid., p. 579; Lossing, *Field Book of the War of 1812*, p. 773.</note> At the beginning of the new year, 1814, after receiving reinforcements from Tennessee along with about two hundred friendly Creeks and sixty-five more Cherokee, he left his camp on the Coosa and advanced against the towns on the Tallapoosa. Upon arriving near the river and learning that he was within a few miles of the main body of the enemy, he halted for a reconnaissance and camped in battle formation on Emukfaw Creek, on the northern bank of the Tallapoosa, just a short distance from the famous Horseshoe Bend. There, on the morning of January 22, 1814, he was suddenly attacked by the enemy with such fury that, even though the troops charged with bayonets, the Creeks returned to the fight. They were finally broken only with the help of the friendly Indians, who attacked them from the rear. Even so, Jackson's force was so badly damaged that he retreated to Fort Strother on the Coosa, carrying his wounded—including General Coffee—on horse-hide litters. The Creeks pursued and attacked him again as he was crossing Enotochopco Creek on January 24, but after a severe fight, they were driven back by discharges of grapeshot from a six-pounder cannon at close range. The army then continued its retreat to Fort Strother. The American loss in these two battles was about one hundred killed and wounded. The loss of the Creeks was much greater, but they had forced a superior force, armed with bayonets and artillery, to retreat. Without the aid of the friendly Indians, it is doubtful whether Jackson could have saved his army from total collapse. The Creeks themselves claimed a victory and later boasted that they had “whipped Jackson and run him to the Coosa River.”

# MOONEY] BATTLE OF HORSESHOE BEND—1814

Pickett states, on what seems to be good authority, that the Creeks involved numbered no more than five hundred warriors. Jackson probably had at least one thousand two hundred men, including Indians.<note>Fay and Davison, *Sketches of the War*, pp. 247-250, 1815; Pickett, *Alabama*, pp. 579-584, 1896 reprint; Drake, *Indians*, pp. 398-400, 1880. Pickett says Jackson had "767 men, with 200 friendly Indians"; Drake says he started with 930 men and was joined at Talladega by 200 friendly Indians; Jackson himself, as quoted in Fay and Davison, says that he started with 930 men, excluding Indians, and was joined at Talladega "by between 200 and 300 friendly Indians," 65 being Cherokee, the rest Creeks. The inference is that he already had a number of Indians with him at the start—probably the Cherokee who had been performing garrison duty.</note>

While these events were taking place in the north, General Floyd advanced again from Georgia with a force of about one thousand three hundred Americans and four hundred friendly Indians. However, he was surprised at Caleebee Creek, near present-day Tuskegee, Alabama, on the morning of January 27, 1814, and forced to retreat, leaving the enemy in possession of the field.<note>Pickett, *op. cit.*, pp. 584-586.</note>

We come now to the final event of the Creek War, the terrible Battle of Horseshoe Bend. Having received large reinforcements from Tennessee, Jackson left a garrison at Fort Strother, and, around the middle of March, traveled down the Coosa River to the mouth of Cedar Creek, southeast of present-day Columbiana, where he built Fort Williams. Leaving his supplies here with a garrison to protect them, he began his march toward the Horseshoe Bend of the Tallapoosa River, where the hostiles were reported to have gathered in great numbers. At this place, known to the Creeks as To-hopki or Tohopeka, the Tallapoosa made a bend that enclosed some eighty or a hundred acres in a narrow peninsula opening to the north. On the lower side was an island in the river, and about a mile below was Emukfaw Creek, entering from the north, where Jackson had been driven back two months earlier. Both locations were in what is now Tallapoosa County, Alabama, within two miles of the current post village of Tohopeka. Across the neck of the peninsula, the Creeks had built a strong breastwork of logs, behind which were their houses; behind these were a number of canoes moored to the bank to be used if retreat became necessary. The fort was defended by a thousand warriors, accompanied by about three hundred women and children. Jackson's force numbered about two thousand men, including, according to his own statement, five hundred Cherokee. He also had two small cannons. The account of the battle—or rather, massacre—which occurred on the morning of March 27, 1814, is best summarized from the official reports of the primary commanders.

Having arrived in the vicinity of the fort, Jackson positioned his men for the attack by sending General Coffee with the mounted men and nearly the entire Indian force to cross the river at a ford about three miles below and surround the bend so that none could escape in that direction. He himself, with the rest of his force, advanced to the front of the breastwork and positioned his can-

He was now upon a slight rise within eighty yards of the fortification. He then directed a heavy cannonade upon the center of the breastwork, while the rifles and muskets kept up an intense fire upon the defenders whenever they showed themselves behind the logs. The breastwork was very strongly and compactly built, from five to eight feet high, with a double row of portholes, and so planned that no enemy could approach without being exposed to a crossfire from those on the inside. After about two hours of cannonading and rifle fire to no great purpose, "Captain Russell's company of spies and a party of the Cherokee force, headed by their gallant chieftain, Colonel Richard Brown, and conducted by the brave Colonel Morgan, crossed over to the peninsula in canoes and set fire to a few of their buildings situated there. They then advanced with great bravery toward the breastwork and commenced firing upon the enemy, who lay behind it. Finding that this force, notwithstanding the determination they displayed, was wholly insufficient to dislodge the enemy, and that General Coffee had secured the opposite banks of the river, I then determined to take possession of their works by storm."<note>Jackson's report to Governor Blount, March 31, 1814, in Fay and Davison, *Sketches of the War*, pp. 253, 254, 1815.</note>

Coffee's official report to his commanding officer states that he had taken seven hundred mounted troops and about six hundred Indians, of whom five hundred were Cherokee and the rest friendly Creeks, and had come in from behind, having directed the Indians to take positions secretly along the bank of the river to prevent the enemy from crossing, as already noted. This was done, but with fighting going on so near at hand, the Indians could not remain silent spectators. Continuing, Coffee says:

> The firing of your cannon and small arms in a short time became general and heavy, which encouraged our Indians; and seeing about one hundred of the warriors and all the women and children of the enemy running about among the huts of the village, which was in our plain view, they could no longer remain silent spectators. While some kept up a fire across the river to prevent the enemy's approach to the bank, others plunged into the water and swam across the river for canoes that lay at the other shore in considerable numbers and brought them over. A number of them embarked in these crafts and landed on the bend with the enemy. Colonel Gideon Morgan, who commanded the Cherokees, Captain Kerr, and Captain William Russell, with a part of his company of spies, were among the first who crossed the river. They advanced into the village and very soon drove the enemy from the huts up the riverbank to the fortified works from which they were fighting you. They pursued and continued to harass them during your entire action. This movement of my Indian forces left the river bank unguarded and made it necessary that I should send a part of my line to take possession of the river bank.<note>General Coffee's report to General Jackson, April 1, 1814, *ibid.*, p. 257.</note>

so that no part was left unoccupied, and the few fugitives who attempted to escape from the fort by water “fell as easy prey to their vengeance.” Finally, seeing that the cannonade had no more effect upon the breastwork than boring holes in the logs, some of the Cherokee plunged into the river, and swimming over to the town, brought back a number of canoes. A portion of them crossed in these, under cover of the guns of their companions, and sheltered themselves under the bank while the canoes were sent back for reinforcements. In this way they all crossed over and then advanced up the bank, where they were immediately and fiercely attacked from every side except the rear, which they kept open only by hard fighting.¹

The Creeks had been fighting the Americans in front of them at such close quarters that their bullets flattened upon the bayonets thrust through the portholes. This attack from the rear by five hundred Cherokee diverted their attention and gave an opportunity to the Tennesseans—Sam Houston among them, cheering them on—to swarm over the breastwork. With death from the bullet, the bayonet, and the hatchet all around them, and the smoke of their blazing homes in their eyes, not a single warrior begged for his life. When more than half their number lay dead upon the ground, the rest turned and plunged into the river, only to find the banks on the opposite side lined with enemies and escape cut off in every direction. General Coffee says:

> Attempts to cross the river at all points of the bend were made by the enemy, but not one ever escaped. Very few ever reached the bank, and those few were killed the instant they landed. From the report of my officers, as well as from my own observation, I feel warranted in saying that from two hundred and fifty to three hundred of the enemy were buried underwater and were not numbered with the dead that were found.

Some swam for the island below the bend, but a detachment had been posted here as well and “not one ever landed. They were sunk by Lieutenant Bean’s command before they reached the bank.”²

Quoting again from Jackson—

> The enemy, although many of them fought to the last with that kind of bravery which desperation inspires, were at last entirely routed and cut to pieces. The battle may be said to have continued with severity for about five hours, but the firing and slaughter continued until it was suspended by the darkness of night. The next morning it was resumed and sixteen of the enemy were killed who had concealed themselves under the banks.³

three hundred were shot in the water. How many more there may have been cannot be known, but Jackson himself states that not more than twenty could have escaped. There is no mention of any wounded. About three hundred prisoners were taken, of whom only three were men. The defenders of the Horseshoe had been exterminated.<sup>1</sup>

On the other side, the loss was 26 Americans killed and 107 wounded, 18 Cherokee killed and 36 wounded, and 5 friendly Creeks killed and 11 wounded. It should be noted that the loss of the Cherokee was out of all proportion to their numbers, as their fighting consisted of hand-to-hand combat without protecting cover. Given that Jackson had been compelled to retreat before this same enemy only a few weeks earlier, and that two hours of artillery and rifle fire had produced no result until the Cherokee attacked the enemy's rear by their daring crossing of the river, there is considerable truth in the Cherokee boast that they saved the day for Jackson at Horseshoe Bend. In terms of the number of men actually engaged and the high proportion of those killed, this ranks as the greatest Indian battle in the history of the United States, with the possible exception of the Battle of Mauvila, fought by the same Indians in De Soto’s time. The result was decisive. Two weeks later, Weatherford came in and surrendered, and the Creek War was at an end.

As is usual when Indians have acted as auxiliaries to white troops, it is difficult to obtain an accurate statement of the number of Cherokee engaged in this war or to distribute credit among the various leaders. Coffee’s official report states that five hundred Cherokee were engaged in the last great battle, and from incidental hints, it seems probable that others were employed elsewhere, on garrison duty or otherwise, at the same time. McKenney and Hall state that Ridge recruited eight hundred warriors for Jackson,<sup>2</sup> and this may be close to the truth, as the tribe then had at least six times as many fighting men. Because of the general loose nature of Indian organization, we commonly find credit claimed for whichever chief is best known to the historian. Thus, McKenney and Hall make Major Ridge the hero of the war, especially of the Horseshoe fight, although he is not mentioned in the official reports. Jackson speaks particularly of the Cherokee in that battle as being “headed by their gallant chieftain, Colonel Richard Brown, and conducted by the brave Colonel Morgan.” Coffee says that Colonel Gideon Morgan “commanded the Cherokees,” and it is Morgan who makes the official report of their part in the battle.
