# MOONEY] TREATIES OF WASHINGTON—1816

In the delegation of 1816, the six signers are mentioned as Colonel [John] Lowrey, Major [John] Walker, Major Ridge, Captain [Richard] Taylor, Adjutant [John] Ross, and Kunnesee (*Tsi'yu-gûnsi'nǐ*, *Cheucunsene*). They are described as men of cultivation, nearly all of whom had served as officers of the Cherokee forces under Jackson and distinguished themselves both by their bravery and by their attachment to the United States.<note>1. Drake, Indians, p. 401, 1880.</note> Among the East Cherokee in Carolina, the only name still remembered is that of their old chief, Junaluska (*Tsunu'lahuñ'skǐ*), who said afterward: "If I had known that Jackson would drive us from our homes, I would have killed him 그날 [that day] at the Horseshoe."

<margin>✓</margin>
The Cherokee returned to their homes to find them despoiled and ravaged in their absence by disorderly white troops. Two years later, by a treaty in Washington, the Government agreed to reimburse them for the damage. Interested parties denied that they had suffered any damage or provided any services, to which their agent indignantly replied: "The response could be that thousands witnessed both; that in nearly all the battles with the Creeks, the Cherokees provided the most effective service, and at the expense of the lives of many fine men, whose wives and children and brothers and sisters are mourning their fall."<note>2. Indian Treaties, p. 187, 1837; Meigs' letter to the Secretary of War, August 19, 1816, in American State Papers: Indian Affairs, II, pp. 113, 114, 1834.</note>

In the spring of 1816, a delegation of seven prominent leaders, accompanied by Agent Meigs, visited Washington. This resulted in the negotiation of two treaties there on the same date, March 22, 1816. By the first of these, the Cherokee ceded their last remaining territory in South Carolina—a small strip in the extreme northwestern corner, adjoining the Chattooga River—for five thousand dollars. By the second treaty, a boundary was established between the lands claimed by the Cherokee and Creeks in northern Alabama. This action was necessary to determine the boundaries of the great tract which the Creeks had been forced to surrender as punishment for their recent uprising. The line ran from a point on Little Bear Creek in northwestern Alabama directly to the Ten Islands of the Coosa at old Fort Strother, southeast of present-day Asheville. General Jackson protested strongly against this line, arguing that all the territory south of the Tennessee River and west of the Coosa belonged to the Creeks and was part of their cession. The Chickasaw also protested against considering this tract as Cherokee territory. The treaty also granted free and unrestricted road privileges throughout the Cherokee country, a concession that was the result of years of persistent effort by the Government; and an appropriation of twenty-five thousand five hundred dollars was made

# MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19

...for damages suffered by the Cherokee from the raids of the troops passing through their country during the Creek War.<note>1. Indian Treaties, pp. 185–187, 1837; Royce, Cherokee Nation, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, pp. 197–209, 1888.</note>

At the previous treaty, the Cherokee had resisted every effort to persuade them to give up more land on either side of the Tennessee River, as the government was particularly eager to end their claim north of that river within the borders of the state of Tennessee. Failing in this, pressure was immediately applied to bring about a land transfer in Alabama. As a result, on September 14 of that same year, a treaty was concluded at the Chickasaw council house and later ratified in a general council at Turkeytown on the Coosa River. By this treaty, the Cherokee gave up all their claims in that state south of the Tennessee River and west of an irregular line running from Chickasaw Island in that river—below the mouth of the Flint River—to the junction of Wills Creek with the Coosa, at what is now Gadsden. For this territory, covering an area of nearly three thousand five hundred square miles, they were to receive sixty thousand dollars in ten annual payments, along with five thousand dollars for the property improvements they abandoned.<note>2. Indian Treaties, pp. 199, 200, 1837; Royce, previously cited work, pp. 209–211.</note>

We now turn away from the direct narrative for a time to note the development of events that culminated in the forced exile of the Cherokee from their ancestral homes and their removal to the far western wilderness.

With a few notable exceptions, the relations between the French and Spanish colonists and the native tribes had been friendly and pleasant after the initial occupation of the country. Under French or Spanish rule, there was never a defined Indian boundary. Pioneer and Indian built their cabins and farmed their fields side by side, traveled the woods together, knelt before the same altar, and frequently married one another on equal terms, as far as race was concerned. The result is seen today in the mixed-blood communities of Canada and in Mexico, where a nation has been built upon an Indigenous foundation. Within the area of English colonization, it was different. From the first settlement to the recent start of the allotment system, it never occurred to those of Teutonic descent that they could have a neighbor who was not of their own heritage and color. While the English colonists recognized native ownership enough to make treaties with the Indians, it was mainly for the purpose of setting boundaries that the Indians should never cross once they had sold their title in exchange for goods and trinkets. In an early Virginia treaty, it was even required that friendly Indians crossing the line would be put to death. The Indian was viewed as an obstacle to be cleared away, like the trees and the wolves, before white men could live in the country. Intermarriages were practically

<header>MOONEY] EARLY WESTWARD EMIGRATION</header>

Under these circumstances, the tribes viewed the expansion of the English and their successors, the Americans, with deep distrust. As early as the end of the French and Indian War, we find some of them moving away from the neighborhood of the English settlements to seek safer shelter in the more remote territories still held by Spain. Shortly after the French withdrew from Fort Toulouse in 1763, a portion of the Alabama—a tribe within the Creek confederacy—left their villages on the Coosa River. After crossing the Mississippi and stopping for a time on its western bank, they settled on the Sabine River under Spanish protection.<note>1. Claiborne, letter to Jefferson, November 5, 1808, American State Papers, I, p. 755, 1832; Gatschet, Creek Migration Legend, I, p. 88, 1884.</note> They were followed some years later by a part of the Koasati from the same confederacy;<note>2. Hawkins, 1799, quoted in Gatschet, previously cited work, p. 89.</note> the two tribes eventually drifted into Texas, where they live today. The Hichitee and others of the Lower Creeks moved down into Spanish Florida, where Yamassee exiles from South Carolina had arrived long before. These two groups combined to form the modern Seminole tribe. When the American Revolution created a new line of division, the native tribes, almost without exception, sided with England against the Americans. As a result, about half of the Iroquois fled to Canada, where they still live on lands granted by the British government. A short time before General Wayne’s victory, a group of the Shawano and Delawares, exhausted by nearly twenty years of fighting the Americans, crossed the Mississippi. With the permission of the Spanish government, they settled on lands near Cape Girardeau, in what is now southeastern Missouri, for which they obtained a formal deed from that government in 1793.<note>3. See Treaty of St. Louis, 1825, and of Castor Hill, 1852, in Indian Treaties, pp. 388, 539, 1837.</note> Driven out by the Americans about twenty years later, they moved to Kansas and then to the Indian Territory, where they are now part of their old friends, the Cherokee.

It is impossible to say when the first Cherokee crossed the Mississippi, but there was likely never a time in the history of the tribe when their warriors and hunters were not accustomed to making trips beyond the great river. According to an old tradition, the earliest migration took place shortly after the first treaty with Carolina. At that time, a portion of the tribe, under the leadership of Yûnwĭ-usga’sĕ’tĭ (“Dangerous-man”)—who foresaw the inevitable outcome of yielding to the colonists’ demands—refused to have any dealings with the white man and began a long march toward the unknown West. They kept in contact with the main body of the tribe until after they crossed the Mississippi, at which point they were lost from sight and forgotten. Long years

Later, a rumor came from the west that they were still living near the base of the Rocky Mountains. <note>1. See story number 107, “The Lost Cherokee.”</note> In 1782, the Cherokee—who had fought faithfully on the British side throughout the long Revolutionary struggle—applied to the Spanish governor at New Orleans for permission to settle on the west side of the Mississippi, within Spanish territory. Permission was granted, and it is probable that some of them moved to the Arkansas country, although there seems to be no definite record of the matter. <note>2. See the letter from Governor Estevan Miro to Robertson, April 20, 1783, in Roosevelt, *Winning of the West*, volume II, page 407, 1889.</note> We learn incidentally, however, that around this period the hostile Cherokee, like the Shawano and other northern tribes, were in the habit of making friendly visits to the Spanish settlements in that region.

According to Reverend Cephas Washburn, the pioneer missionary of the western Cherokee, the first permanent Cherokee settlement beyond the Mississippi was the direct result of the massacre of the Scott party at Muscle Shoals on the Tennessee River in the summer of 1794, carried out by the hostile warriors of the Chickamauga towns. As told by the missionary, the story differs considerably from the account given by Haywood and other Tennessee historians, which is narrated elsewhere. <note>3. See pages 76–77.</note> According to Washburn, the white settlers were the aggressors, having first made the Indians drunk and then swindled them out of the annuity money they were just returning with from the agency at Tellico. When the Indians became sober enough to demand the return of their money, the white settlers attacked and killed two of them, after which the others boarded the boat and killed every white man. They spared the women and children, however, along with their Black slaves and all their personal belongings, and permitted them to continue on their way. The chief and his party personally escorted them down the Tennessee, Ohio, and Mississippi rivers as far as the mouth of the St. Francis River. From there, the emigrants traveled safely down to New Orleans, while their captors, under their chief, The Bowl, went up the St. Francis River—then a part of Spanish territory—to await the outcome of the event. As soon as the news reached the Cherokee Nation, the chiefs formally repudiated the actions of The Bowl's party and volunteered to assist in arresting those involved. The Bowl and his men were finally exonerated, but they had developed such bitterness toward the conduct of their former friends—and, moreover, found the soil so rich and the game so abundant where they were—that they refused to return to their tribe and decided to remain permanently in the West. Others joined them from time to time, attracted by the hunting prospects, until they were numerous enough to obtain recognition from the government. <note>4. Washburn, *Reminiscences*, pages 76–79, 1869; see also Royce, *Cherokee Nation*, in the Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, page 204, 1888.</note>

<header>MOONEY] THE BOWL EMIGRATION—1794</header>

While the missionary may be excused for presenting his friends in the best possible light, his statement contains several clear errors, and it is likely that Haywood's account is more accurate overall. Since the Cherokee annuity at that time amounted to only fifteen hundred dollars for the entire tribe—or just under ten cents per person—they could hardly have had enough money from that source to pay such excessive prices as sixteen dollars each for pocket mirrors, as it is claimed the boatmen received. Furthermore, because the Chickamauga warriors had refused to sign any treaties and were notoriously hostile, they were not yet entitled to receive payments. Haywood's claim that the party of emigrants was first attacked while passing the Chickamauga towns, then pursued to Muscle Shoals and massacred there, is probably close to the truth, though it is quite possible that the white settlers may have provoked the attack in some way, as the missionary suggests. Since Washburn received his account from one of the women in the party who lived in New Orleans long afterward, it is certain that at least some people were spared by the Indians; it is likely, as he states, that only the men were killed.

The migration led by The Bowl may not have been the first, or even the most significant move to the western country, as it was a period of general Indian unrest. Small groups were constantly crossing the Mississippi into Spanish territory to escape the advancing Americans, only to find themselves under American control again when the entire western territory was ceded to the United States in 1803. The settlers' relentless hunger for land could not be restrained or satisfied, and early that same year, President Jefferson suggested to Congress that it would be desirable to move all the tribes to the west of the Mississippi. The following year, 1804, funds were set aside to take the first steps toward that goal.<note>1. Royce, *Cherokee Nation*, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, pages 202, 203, 1888.</note> There were likely very few Cherokee on the Arkansas River at this time, as they are not mentioned in Sibley's 1805 list of tribes south of that river.

In the summer of 1808, as a Cherokee delegation prepared to visit Washington, their agent, Colonel Meigs, was instructed by the Secretary of War to do everything possible to get their consent to trade their lands for a tract west of the Mississippi. By this time, the government’s "civilizing" policy—implemented through the annual distribution of farm tools, spinning wheels, and looms—had created a significant difference in lifestyle and opinion between the northern and southern Cherokee. Those on the Little Tennessee and Hiwassee rivers were generally farmers and cattle ranchers, also producing a small amount of cotton which the women wove into cloth. Those further south in Georgia and Alabama, the formerly hostile group, still preferred a life of hunting and rejected all attempts at change, even though game had now become so scarce that it was clear a change must soon

# MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19

Jealousies had arisen as a result, and the delegates representing the progressive element now proposed to the government that a line be drawn through the nation to separate the two parties. This would allow those in the north to divide their lands in <term>severalty</term> and become citizens of the United States, while those in the south might continue to be hunters as long as the game should last. Taking advantage of this situation, the government authorities instructed the agent to submit a proposal to the conservatives for a <term>cession</term> of their share of the tribal territory in return for a tract west of the Mississippi large enough to enable them to continue their hunting life. The plan was approved by President Jefferson, and a sum was set aside to pay the expenses of a delegation to visit and inspect the lands on the Arkansas and White rivers, with a view toward removal. The visit was made in the summer of 1809, and the delegates brought back such a favorable report that a large number of Cherokee expressed their intention to remove at once. As no funds were then available for their removal, the matter was put on hold for several years. During this period, families and individuals moved to the western country at their own expense until, before the year 1817, they numbered in total two or three thousand people.¹ They became known as the Arkansas, or Western, Cherokee.

The emigrants soon became involved in difficulties with the native tribes; the Osage claimed all the lands north of the Arkansas river, while the Quapaw claimed those on the south. Upon complaining to the government, the emigrant Cherokee were told that they had originally been permitted to move only on the condition of a <term>cession</term> of a portion of their eastern territory, and that nothing could be done to protect them in their new western home until such a <term>cession</term> had been carried out. The main body of the Cherokee Nation, however, was strongly opposed to any such sale and proposed that the emigrants should be forced to return. After long negotiations, a treaty was concluded at the Cherokee agency (now Calhoun, Tennessee) on July 8, 1817, by which the Cherokee Nation ceded two large tracts—the first in Georgia, lying east of the Chattahoochee, and the other in Tennessee, between Walden's Ridge and the Little Sequatchee—as an equivalent for a tract to be assigned to those who had already moved, or intended to move, to Arkansas. Two smaller tracts on the north bank of the Tennessee, near the Muscle Shoals, were also ceded. In return for these cessions, the emigrant Cherokee were to receive a tract within the current limits of the state of Arkan-

sas, bounded on the north and south by the White River and Arkansas River, respectively; on the east by a line running between those streams roughly from present-day Batesville to Lewisburg; and on the west by a line to be determined later. As established afterward, this western line ran from the junction of the Little North Fork with the White River to just beyond the point where the current western Arkansas boundary meets the Arkansas River. Arrangements were made for taking a census of the entire Cherokee Nation, both east and west, in order to properly distribute <term>annuities</term> and other payments in the future, as the two bands were still to be considered as forming one people. The United States agreed to pay for any substantial improvements abandoned by those moving from the <term>ceded</term> lands. Each emigrant warrior who left no such valuable property behind was to be given, as full compensation for his abandoned field and cabin, a rifle and ammunition, a blanket, and either a kettle or a beaver trap. The government further agreed to provide boats and provisions for the journey. Provision was also made so that individuals living on the surrendered lands could keep their <term>allotments</term> and become citizens if they chose to do so; the size of these allotments would be subtracted from the total area given up.

The commissioners for the treaty were General Andrew Jackson, General David Meriwether, and Governor Joseph McMinn of Tennessee. On behalf of the Cherokee, it was signed by thirty-one principal men of the eastern Nation and fifteen of the western band, who signed by proxy. <note>1. Indian Treaties, pages 209-215, 1837; Royce, Cherokee Nation, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, pages 212-217, 1888; see also maps in Royce.</note>

The majority of the Cherokee were bitterly opposed to any land surrender or removal project. Before the treaty had been concluded, a memorial signed by sixty-seven chiefs and headmen of the nation was presented to the commissioners. This document stated that the delegates who had first brought up the subject in Washington some years earlier had acted without any authority from the nation. They declared that the great body of the Cherokee desired to remain in the land of their birth, where they were rapidly advancing in civilization, instead of being forced to return to their original primitive conditions and surroundings. They therefore prayed that the matter might not be pressed further, but that they might be allowed to remain in peaceful possession of the land of their fathers. No attention was paid to the memorial, and the treaty was carried through and ratified. Without waiting for the ratification, the authorities immediately took steps for the removal of those who wished to go to the West. Boats were provided at points between the Little Tennessee and Sequatchee rivers, and the emigrants were gathered under the direction of Governor McMinn. By the end of 1819, the number of emigrants was said to have increased to six thousand. The chiefs of the nation, however, claimed that the estimate was far greater than the truth.¹

> “There can be no question that a very large portion, and probably a majority, of the Cherokee nation residing east of the Mississippi had been and still continued to be bitterly opposed to the terms of the treaty of 1817. They viewed with jealous and aching hearts all attempts to drive them from the homes of their ancestors, for they could not help but consider the constant and urgent appeals of the federal authorities as an imperative demand for the surrender of more territory. They felt that they were, as a nation, being slowly but surely compressed within the contracting coils of the giant anaconda of civilization; yet they held to the vain hope that a spirit of justice and mercy would be born of their helpless condition which would finally prevail in their favor. Their traditions furnished them no guide by which to judge the results certain to follow such a conflict as that in which they were engaged. This difference of sentiment in the nation upon a subject so vital to their welfare produced much bitterness and violent animosity. Those who had favored the emigration scheme and had been induced, either through personal preference or by the bribing influences of government agents, to favor the conclusion of the treaty, became the objects of scorn and hatred to the rest of the nation. They were made the subjects of a persecution so relentless while they remained in the eastern country that it was never forgotten; and when, in the natural course of events, the rest of the nation was forced to remove to the Arkansas country and join the earlier emigrants, the old hatreds and dissensions broke out afresh, and to this day they still remain to some degree in the hearts of their descendants.”²

Two months after the signing of the treaty of July 8, 1817, and three months before its ratification, a council of the nation sent a delegation to Washington to recount in detail the improper methods and influences which had been used to carry it out, and to ask that it be set aside and another agreement substituted. The mission was without result.³

In 1817, the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions established its first station among the Cherokee at Brainerd, in Tennessee, on the west side of Chickamauga Creek, two miles from the Georgia line. The mission took its name from a distinguished pioneer worker among the northern tribes (37). The government aided in the construction of the buildings, which included a schoolhouse, gristmill, and workshops; in these, besides the ordinary school subjects, the boys were taught simple mechanical arts while the girls learned the use of the

The mission prospered, and the same board established others at Willstown, Hightower, and elsewhere; in these, two hundred pupils were receiving instruction in 1820.<note>Morse, Geography, I, p. 577, 1819; and p. 185, 1822.</note> Among the earliest and most notable workers at the Brainerd mission were Reverend D. Worcester, in particular, did much for the intellectual advancement of the Cherokee and suffered imprisonment more than once for his dedication to defending their cause. The missions flourished until they were broken up by the state of Georgia at the beginning of the removal troubles; they were later reopened in the western territory. Mission Ridge preserves the memory of the Brainerd establishment.

Early in 1818, a delegation of emigrant Cherokee visited Washington to secure a more satisfactory definition of the boundaries for their new lands in Arkansas. Measures were taken for that purpose shortly afterward. They also requested future recognition as a separate and distinct tribe, but no action was taken on the matter. To eliminate, if possible, the hostility between the emigrants and the native Osage—who viewed the newcomers as intruders—Governor William Clark, the superintendent of Indian affairs for Missouri, arranged a conference of the chiefs from both tribes in St. Louis in October of that year. After a long effort, he succeeded in establishing friendly relations between them. Around the same time, both the emigrant Cherokee and the government attempted to persuade the Shawnee and Delawares then living in Missouri, as well as the Oneida in New York, to join the western Cherokee, but nothing resulted from these negotiations.<note>Royce, Cherokee Nation, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, pages 221-222, 1888.</note> In 1825, a delegation of western Cherokee visited the Shawnee in Ohio for the same purpose, but without success. Their goal in inviting friendly Indians to join them was to strengthen themselves against the Osage and other local tribes.

Meanwhile, the government, through Governor McMinn, was exerting strong pressure on the eastern Cherokee to force their removal to the West. At a council he convened in November 1818, the governor told the chiefs that it was no longer possible to protect them from the encroachment of the surrounding white population. He argued that however much the government might wish to help them, their lands would be taken, their livestock stolen, their women corrupted, and their men made into drunkards unless they moved to the "western paradise." He concluded by proposing to pay them one hundred thousand dollars for their entire territory, along with the costs of relocation, if they would leave immediately. When they promptly and indignantly refused, he offered to double the amount, but with just as little success.

After every point of the negotiation had failed, another course was adopted, and a delegation was selected to visit Washington under the leadership of Agent Meigs. There, the effort was renewed until, worn down and discouraged by the persistent demands, the chiefs consented to a large land cession. This was represented as necessary to compensate in area for the land assigned to the emigrant Cherokee in Arkansas according to the previous treaty. This estimate was based on figures provided by Governor McMinn, who reported 5,291 Cherokee enrolled as emigrants, while the eastern Cherokee claimed that no more than 3,500 had moved and that those remaining numbered 12,544, or more than three-fourths of the whole nation. The governor, however, chose to consider one-half of the nation as being in favor of removal and one-third as having already moved. <note>Royce, Cherokee Nation, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, pages 222-228, 1888.</note>

The treaty, concluded at Washington on February 27, 1819, states that the greater part of the Cherokee nation, having expressed an earnest desire to remain in the East and being eager to begin the necessary measures for the civilization and preservation of their nation, and to settle the differences arising out of the treaty of 1817, have offered to cede to the United States a tract of country "at least as extensive" as that to which the Government is entitled under the previous treaty. The cession includes: (1) a tract in Alabama and Tennessee, between the Tennessee and Flint rivers; (2) a tract in Tennessee, between the Tennessee river and Walden’s Ridge; (3) a large, irregular tract in Tennessee, North Carolina, and Georgia, including in Tennessee nearly all the remaining Cherokee lands north of the Hiwassee river, and in North Carolina and Georgia nearly everything remaining to them east of the Nantahala mountains and the upper western branch of the Chattahoochee; and (4) six small pieces reserved by previous treaties. The entire cession totaled nearly six thousand square miles, or more than one-fourth of all the land then held by the nation. Individual reservations of one square mile each within the ceded area were allowed to a number of families who decided to remain among the whites and become citizens rather than abandon their homes. Payment was to be made for all substantial improvements that were abandoned, one-third of all tribal annuities were hereafter to be paid to the western band, and the treaty was declared to be a final adjustment of all claims and differences arising from the treaty of 1817. <note>Indian Treaties, pages 265-269, 1837; Royce, op. cit., pages 219-221 and table, page 378.</note>

MOONEY] CHEROKEE GOVERNMENT—MISSIONS

<meta>Small horizontal pencil mark in right margin next to "Calhoun, Georgia." line.</meta>

to send four representatives to the Cherokee national legislature, which met at <term>Newtown</term>, or <term>New Echota</term>, the capital, at the junction of the Conasauga and Coosawattee rivers, a few miles above present-day Calhoun, Georgia. The legislature consisted of an upper and a lower house, designated, respectively (in the Cherokee language), as the National Committee and National Council; the members were elected for limited terms by the voters of each district. The principal officer was titled President of the National Council; the distinguished John Ross was the first to hold this office. There was also a clerk of the committee and two principal members to express the will of the Council, or lower house. For each district, a council house was appointed for meetings twice a year, along with a judge and a marshal. Companies of "light horse" were organized to assist in the execution of the laws, with a "ranger" for each district to look after stray livestock. Each head of a family and each single man under the age of sixty was subject to a poll tax. Laws were passed for the collection of taxes and debts, for road repairs, for licenses for white persons engaged in farming or other business in the nation, for the support of schools, for the regulation of the liquor trade and the conduct of enslaved Black people, to punish horse stealing and theft, to compel all marriages between white men and Indian women to follow regular legal or church forms, and to discourage polygamy. By special decree, the right of blood revenge or capital punishment was taken from the seven clans and granted to the established authorities of the nation. It was made treason, punishable by death, for any individual to negotiate the sale of lands to white people without the consent of the National Council <note>39</note>. White men were not allowed to vote or to hold office in the nation. <note>Laws of the Cherokee Nation (several documents), 1820, American State Papers: Indian Affairs, II, pp. 279-283, 1834; letter quoted by McKenney, 1825, ibid., pp. 651, 652; Drake, Indians, pp. 437, 438, ed. 1880.</note> The system compared favorably with that of the Federal government or of any state government existing at that time.

At this time there were five principal missions, besides one or two small branch establishments in the nation, namely: <term>Spring Place</term>, the oldest, founded by the Moravians at Spring Place, Georgia, in 1801; <term>Oothcaloga</term>, Georgia, founded by the same denomination in 1821 on the creek of that name, near present-day Calhoun; <term>Brainerd</term>, Tennessee, founded by the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions in 1817; "<term>Valley-towns</term>," North Carolina, founded by the Baptists in 1820, on the site of the old Natchez town on the north side of the Hiwassee river, just above Peachtree creek; and <term>Coosawattee</term>, Georgia ("Tensawattee," by error in the State Papers), also founded by the Baptists in 1821, near the mouth of the river of that name. ...lack of accommodation. The superintendent reported that the children were quick to learn, willing to work, and easily followed discipline. He added that the Cherokee were rapidly advancing toward a civilized lifestyle and generally showed a strong desire for education. The Valley-towns mission, established at the request of Currahee Dick, a prominent local chief of mixed heritage, was led by the Reverend Evan Jones. Jones was known for translating the New Testament into the Cherokee language. His assistant was James D. Wafford, a student of mixed heritage who compiled a spelling book in the same language. Reverend S. A. Worcester, a productive translator and the compiler of the Cherokee almanac and other works, was stationed at Brainerd. He later moved to New Echota and then to the Cherokee Nation in the West.<note>List of missions and reports of missionaries, etc., American State Papers: Indian Affairs, II, pp. 277-279, 459, 1834; personal information from James D. Wafford concerning the Valley-towns mission. For notices of Worcester, Jones, and Wafford, see Pilling, Bibliography of the Iroquoian Languages, 1888.</note> Since 1817, the American Board had also supported an Indian school in Cornwall, Connecticut, where several young Cherokees were educated. Among them was Elias Boudinot, who later became the editor of the *Cherokee Phoenix*.

Around this time, an event occurred that immediately placed the Cherokee in the leading position among Native tribes and was destined to have a profound influence on their entire future history: the invention of the alphabet.

The inventor, appropriately called the Cadmus of his race, was a man of mixed heritage known among his own people as Sikwâ'yĭ (Sequoya) and among white people as George Gist, or less correctly as Guest or Guess. As is often the case with Native American biographies, much uncertainty exists regarding his parentage and early life. Authorities generally agree that his father was a white man who moved into the Cherokee Nation some years before the American Revolution and formed a temporary relationship with a Cherokee girl of mixed heritage, who became the mother of the future teacher. In 1828, a writer in the *Cherokee Phoenix* stated that only his paternal grandfather was a white man.<note>G. C., in *Cherokee Phoenix*; reprinted in *Christian Advocate and Journal*, New York, September 26, 1828.</note> McKenney and Hall say his father was a white man named Gist.<note>McKenney and Hall, Indian Tribes, I, p. 35, and throughout, 1858.</note> Phillips asserts that his father was George Gist, an unlicensed German trader from Georgia who entered the Cherokee Nation in 1768.<note>Phillips, Sequoyah, in *Harper's Magazine*, pp. 542-548, September, 1870.</note> A Kentucky family claims that Sequoya's father was Nathaniel Gist, the son of the scout who accompanied George Washington on his famous journey to the Ohio River. According to the story, Nathaniel Gist was captured by the Cherokee during Braddock's defeat (1755) and remained their prisoner for six years, during which time he became the father of Sequoya. Upon returning to civilization, he married a white woman in Virginia, with whom he had other children, and afterward

<header>MOONEY] SEQUOYA AND HIS ALPHABET</header>

...moved to Kentucky, where Sequoya, then a Baptist preacher, visited him often and was always recognized by the family as his son.¹

Besides the fact that the Cherokee served as allies to the English during the war in which Braddock was defeated, and that Sequoya, far from being a preacher, was not even a Christian, the story contains other unlikely elements and appears to be one of those genealogical myths built on a random similarity of names. On the other hand, it is certain that Sequoya was born before the date that Phillips suggests. On his mother’s side, he was from a prominent family in the tribe; his uncle was a chief in Echota.² According to personal information from James Wafford, who knew him well as his second cousin, Sequoya was probably born around the year 1760 and lived as a boy with his mother at Tuskegee town in Tennessee, just outside of old Fort Loudon. It is quite possible that his white father may have been a soldier in the garrison—one of those lovers for whom the Cherokee women risked their lives during the siege.³ What became of the father is not known, but the mother lived alone with her son.

The only story from his childhood that has been passed down to us is his presence at Echota during the visit of the Iroquois peace delegation, around the year 1770.⁴ His early years were spent amid the stormy alarms of the American Revolution, and as he grew to manhood, he developed considerable mechanical skill, especially in silver working. Like most of his tribe, he was also a hunter and fur trader. Having almost reached middle age before the first mission was established in the Cherokee Nation, he never attended school and throughout his life never learned to speak, read, or write the English language. He also never abandoned his native religion, although from frequent visits to the Moravian mission, he became inspired with a friendly feeling toward the new civilization. Of an essentially thoughtful nature, he was led by a chance conversation in 1809 to reflect on the ability of white men to communicate thoughts through writing, which resulted in him setting about creating a similar system for his own people. Due to a hunting accident that left him disabled for life, he was fortunately given more free time for study. The presence of his name, George Guess, added to a treaty in 1816, indicates that he was already a person of some importance in the Nation even before the completion of his great invention. After years of patient and tireless work in the face of ridicule, discouragement, and repeated failure, he finally developed the Cherokee syllabary and in 1821 submitted it to a public test by the leaders of the Nation. By this time, as a result of repeated land handovers, the Cherokee had been deprived of the country around Echota, and Sequoya was now living at Willstown,

...on an upper branch of the Coosa River in Alabama. The syllabary was soon recognized as an invaluable invention for the advancement of the tribe, and within a few months, thousands of previously illiterate Cherokee were able to read and write their own language, teaching each other in their homes and along the roadside. The following year, Sequoya visited the West to introduce the new system among those who had emigrated to the Arkansas region. In the next year, 1823, he again visited Arkansas and settled there permanently with the western band, never returning to his eastern relatives after that. In the autumn of the same year, the Cherokee national council publicly acknowledged his merit by sending him a silver medal through John Ross, then president of the national committee. The medal featured a commemorative inscription in both languages.¹ In 1828, he visited Washington as one of the delegates from the Arkansas band, attracting much attention; the treaty signed on that occasion contains a provision for a payment of five hundred dollars to him, "for the great benefits he has conferred upon the Cherokee people, in the beneficial results which they are now experiencing from the use of the alphabet discovered by him."² His later history belongs to the West and will be covered in another section (40).³

The invention of the alphabet had an immediate and wonderful effect on Cherokee progress. Because of the remarkable way the syllabary was adapted to the language, it was only necessary to learn the characters to be able to read immediately. No schoolhouses were built and no teachers were hired, yet the whole Nation became an academy for studying the system, until, "in the course of a few months, without schools or the expense of time or money, the Cherokee were able to read and write in their own language."⁴ An active correspondence began between the eastern and western divisions, and plans were made for a national press, along with a national library and museum to be established at the capital, New Echota.⁵ The missionaries, who had at first opposed the new alphabet because of its Indian origin, now saw the wisdom of using it to further their own work. In the fall of 1824, Atsĭ (or John Arch), a young native convert, made a manuscript translation of a portion of the Gospel of John in the syllabary; this was the first Bible translation ever given to the Cherokee. It was copied hundreds of times and was widely distributed through

<meta>This page continues the history of the Cherokee syllabary's adoption, following the account of Sequoya’s invention and its rapid spread among the Cherokee people. It specifically details the transition from manuscript to printed text and the founding of the first national newspaper.</meta>

<page-num>111</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] THE CHEROKEE PHOENIX</header>

...the Nation.<note>Foster, Sequoyah, pp. 120, 121, 1885.</note> In September 1825, David Brown, a prominent preacher of mixed heritage who had already made some attempt at translation using the Latin alphabet, completed a translation of the New Testament in the new syllabary. The work was circulated in manuscript, as no type had yet been cast in the Sequoya characters.<note>Pilling, Iroquoian Bibliography, p. 21, 1888.</note> In the same month, he forwarded a manuscript table of the characters with an explanation to Thomas McKenney, chief of the Bureau of Indian Affairs in Washington; this was likely its first introduction to official notice.<note>Unsigned Brown letter, in American State Papers: Indian Affairs, II, p. 652, 1834.</note>

In 1827, the Cherokee council formally resolved to establish a national newspaper in the Cherokee language and characters. Type for that purpose was cast in Boston under the supervision of the noted missionary, Samuel Worcester, of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. In December of that year, he contributed five verses of Genesis in the new syllabary to the *Missionary Herald*, which seems to be its first appearance in print. Early the next year, the press and type arrived at New Echota, and the first issue of the new paper, *Tsa'lăgĭ Tsu'lehisanun'hĭ* (the *Cherokee Phoenix*), printed in both languages, appeared on February 21, 1828. The first printers were two white men, Isaac N. Harris and John F. Wheeler, along with John Candy, an apprentice of mixed heritage. Elias Boudinot (*Gălagi'na*, "The Buck"), an educated Cherokee, was the editor, and Reverend S. A. Worcester was the guiding spirit who brought order out of chaos and set the work in motion. The office was a log house. After having been shipped by water from Boston, the hand press and type were transported two hundred miles by wagon from Augusta to their destination. The printing paper had been overlooked and had to be brought by the same tedious process from Knoxville. Cases and other equipment had to be designed and fashioned by the printers. Neither of them understood a word of Cherokee; they simply set the characters as they were handed to them in manuscript by Worcester and the editor. Such was the beginning of journalism in the Cherokee nation. After a precarious existence of about six years, the *Phoenix* was suspended due to the hostile action of the Georgia authorities, who went so far as to imprison Worcester and Wheeler. Its successor, after the removal of the Cherokee to the West, was the *Cherokee Advocate*, of which the first issue appeared at Tahlequah in 1844, with William P. Ross as editor. It is still continued under the auspices of the Nation, printed in both languages and distributed for free at the expense of the Nation to those unable to read English—an example without parallel in any other government.

What is perhaps strangest of all in this literary evolution is the fact that the same invention has been adopted by the priests and conjurers of the conservative party for the purpose of preserving for their successors the ancient rituals and secret knowledge of the tribe; the author obtained whole volumes of such occult literature in manuscript from them.<note>For an extensive account of Cherokee literature and authors, see numerous references in Pilling, *Bibliography of the Iroquoian Languages*, 1888; also Foster, *Sequoyah*, 1885, and *The Story of the Cherokee Bible*, 1899. In 1819, the entire Cherokee population was estimated at 15,000, one-third of whom lived west of the Mississippi. In 1825, a census of the eastern Nation showed: native Cherokee, 13,563; white men married into the Nation, 147; white women married into the Nation, 73; and negro slaves, 1,277. There were large herds of cattle, horses, hogs, and sheep, along with large crops of every staple, including cotton, tobacco, and wheat; some cotton was even exported by boat as far as New Orleans. Apple and peach orchards were numerous, butter and cheese were used to some extent, and both cotton and woolen cloths, especially blankets, were manufactured. Nearly all the merchants were native Cherokee. Mechanical industries flourished, the Nation was out of debt, and the population was increasing.<note>Unsigned Brown letter, September 2, 1825, *American State Papers: Indian Affairs*, II, pp. 651, 652, 1834.</note> Estimating one-third beyond the Mississippi, the total number of Cherokee, excluding adopted white citizens and negro slaves, must then have been about 20,000.

Simultaneously with the decrees establishing a national press, the Cherokee Nation, in a general convention of delegates held for that purpose at New Echota on July 26, 1827, adopted a national constitution based on the premise of a distinct and independent nationality. John Ross, who became so famous in connection with the history of his tribe, was president of the convention that framed the document. Charles R. Hicks, a Moravian convert of mixed heritage and the most influential man in the Nation at that time, was elected principal chief, with John

# MOONEY] WHITE-PATH'S REBELLION—1828
<sig>19 ETH—01—8</sig>

Ross as assistant chief.<gloss>1</gloss> With a constitution and a national press, a well-developed system of industries and home education, and a government run by educated Christian men, the Cherokee were now rightfully entitled to be considered a civilized people.

The idea of a civilized Indian government was not a new one. The first treaty ever negotiated by the United States with an Indian tribe, in 1778, held out to the Delawares the hope that through a confederation of friendly tribes they might be able "to form a state, of which the Delaware nation shall be the head and have a representative in Congress."<gloss>2</gloss> Priber, the Jesuit, had already introduced the Cherokee to the forms of civilized government before the middle of the eighteenth century. As the gap between the conservative and progressive groups widened after the Revolution, the idea grew until, in 1808, representatives of both parties visited Washington to propose an arrangement. Under this plan, those who clung to the old way of life might be allowed to move to the western hunting grounds, while the rest would remain to adopt civilization and "begin the establishment of fixed laws and a regular government." The project received the warm encouragement of President Jefferson, and it was with this understanding that the western migration was first officially recognized a few years later. Immediately upon the delegates' return from Washington, the Cherokee drew up their first brief written code of laws, modeled in accordance with the friendly suggestions of Jefferson.<gloss>3</gloss>

By this time, the rapid progress of civilization and Christianity had alarmed the conservative group, who saw in the new order of things only evidence of abandonment of faith and swift national decay. In 1828, White-path (*Nûñ'nâ-tsune'ga*), an influential full-blood and councilor living at Turniptown (*U'lûñ'yĭ*), near the present Ellijay in Gilmer County, Georgia, led a rebellion against the new code of laws and all that it implied. He soon had a large band of followers known to the whites as "Red-sticks," a title sometimes used by the more warlike group among the Creeks and other southern tribes. From the townhouse of Ellijay, he preached the rejection of the new constitution, the discarding of Christianity and the white man's ways, and a return to the old tribal law and custom—the same doctrine that had more than once been the core of Indian revelation in the past. However, it was now too late to turn back the wheel of progress, and under the leadership of men like Hicks and Ross, the conservative opposition gradually faded away. White-path was removed from his seat

# MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19

in council, but later submitted and was reinstated. He was afterward one of the detachment commanders during the Removal, but died while on the march.¹

In this year, also, John Ross became principal chief of the Nation, a position he held until his death in 1866, thirty-eight years later.² During this long period, which included the momentous episodes of the Removal and the War of the Rebellion, it may be truly said that his history is the history of the Nation.

And now, just when it seemed that civilization and enlightenment were about to accomplish their perfect work, the Cherokee began to hear the first low muttering of the coming storm that was soon to overturn their entire governmental structure and sweep them forever from the land of their birth.

By an agreement between the United States and the state of Georgia in 1802, the latter, for a valuable consideration, had ceded its claims west of the present state boundary to the general government. At the same time, the United States agreed to extinguish, at its own expense but for the benefit of the state, the Indian claims within the state limits, "as early as the same can be peaceably obtained on reasonable terms."³ In accordance with this agreement, several treaties had already been made with the Creeks and Cherokee, through which large tracts had been secured for Georgia at the expense of the general government. Despite this fact and the terms of the proviso, Georgia accused the government of bad faith for not taking immediate measures to compel the Indians to surrender all their remaining lands within the chartered state limits at once, joining the complaint with a threat to take the matter into her own hands. In 1820, Agent Meigs expressed the opinion that the Cherokee were now so far advanced that further government aid was unnecessary, and that their lands should be allotted and the surplus sold for their benefit, while they themselves would be granted full rights of citizenship in the several states where they resided. This suggestion was approved by President Monroe but met with the most determined opposition from the states concerned. Tennessee absolutely refused to recognize individual reservations made by previous treaties, while North Carolina and Georgia bought up all such reservations with money appropriated by Congress.⁴ No Indian was to be allowed to live within those states under any pretext whatsoever.

### MOONEY] PRESSURE FOR REMOVAL—1823-24

state. Every effort was met with a firm refusal, as the Indians declared that, having already made cession after cession from a territory that was once extensive, their remaining lands were no more than what were needed for themselves and their children—especially since experience had shown that each concession would be followed by a further demand. <margin>✓</margin> They concluded: “It is the fixed and unalterable determination of this nation never again to cede one foot more of land.” Soon afterward, they addressed a memorial of a similar tone to the President, to which Calhoun, as Secretary of War, returned an answer stating that because Georgia objected to their presence either as a tribe or as individual owners or citizens, they must prepare themselves for removal beyond the Mississippi.¹

<margin>✓</margin> In reply, the Cherokee, through their delegates—John Ross, George Lowrey, Major Ridge, and Elijah Hicks—sent a strong letter calling attention to the fact that, by the very wording of the 1802 agreement, the compact was a conditional one which could not be carried out without their own voluntary consent; they also suggested that Georgia might be satisfied with the adjoining government lands in Florida. Continuing, they reminded the Secretary that the Cherokee are not foreigners, but original inhabitants of America, inhabiting and standing now upon the soil of their own territory, with limits defined by treaties with the United States. They stated that, trusting in the good faith of the government to respect its treaty stipulations, they did not hesitate to say that their true interest, prosperity, and happiness demand their permanence where they are and the retention of their lands.²

A copy of this letter was sent by the Secretary to Governor Troup of Georgia, who returned a reply in which he blamed the missionaries for the Indians' refusal. He declared that the state would not permit them to become citizens, and that the Secretary must either assist the state in taking possession of the Cherokee lands or, by resisting that occupancy, make war upon and shed the blood of brothers and friends. The Georgia delegation in Congress addressed a similar letter to President Monroe, in which the government was criticized for having instructed the Indians in the arts of civilized life and having thereby inspired them with a desire to acquire property.³

For an answer, the President submitted a report by Secretary Calhoun showing that since the agreement had been made with Georgia in 1802, the government had, at its own expense, extinguished the Indian claim to 24,600 square miles within the limits of that state—or more than three-fifths of the whole Indian claim—and had paid nearly seven and a half million dollars on that and other accounts connected with the agreement.

### MOONEY] MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19

dollars, of which by far the greater part had gone to Georgia or its citizens. In regard to the other criticism, the report states that the policy of civilization was as old as the government itself, and that in performing these high duties of humanity toward the Indians, it had never been thought that the terms of the agreement were violated. In submitting the report, the President again called attention to the conditional nature of the agreement and declared his opinion that the Indians' title was not in the slightest degree affected by it, and that there was no obligation on the United States to remove them by force.¹

<margin>✓</margin>
Further efforts, even including the use of secret methods, were made in 1827 and 1828 to encourage a land surrender or relocation, but without success. On July 26, 1827, as already noted, the Cherokee adopted a constitution as a distinct and sovereign Nation. In response to this, the Georgia legislature passed resolutions affirming that the state "had the power and the right to take possession, by any means she might choose, of the lands in dispute, and to extend over them her authority and laws." The legislature recommended that this be done by the next session if the lands were not already acquired through successful negotiation by the federal government in the meantime. The government was warned that the lands belonged to Georgia, and that she must and would have them. It was suggested, however, that the United States might be permitted to grant a certain number of reservations to individual Indians.²

<margin>✓</margin>
Passing over for the present some important negotiations with the western Cherokee, we come to the events leading to the final act in the drama. Up to this time, the pressure had been for land only, but now a stronger motive was added. About the year 1815, a young Cherokee boy playing along the Chestatee River in upper Georgia brought a shining yellow pebble, hardly larger than the end of his thumb, to his mother. When it was washed, it proved to be a nugget of gold; on her next trip to the settlements, the woman carried it with her and sold it to a white man. The news spread, and although she probably concealed the knowledge of the exact spot where it was found, it was soon known that the golden dreams of De Soto had been realized in the Cherokee country of Georgia. Within four years, the entire territory east of the Chestatee had passed from the possession of the Cherokee. They still held the western bank, but the prospector was active in the mountains, and that would not last for long.³ Around 1828, gold was found on Ward's Creek, a western branch of the Chestatee near present-day Dahlonega,⁴ and the doom of the nation was sealed (41).

<header>MOONEY] EXTENSION OF GEORGIA LAWS—1830</header>
<page-num>117</page-num>

In November 1828, Andrew Jackson was elected to succeed John Quincy Adams as President. He was a frontiersman who was hostile toward Indians, and this change promised nothing good for the Cherokee. His position was well understood, and there is good reason to believe that the action immediately taken by Georgia was done at his own suggestion.<note>1 See the Butler letter, quoted in Royce, Cherokee Nation, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, p. 297, 1888; see also Everett's speech in the House of Representatives on May 31, 1838, pp. 16-17, 32-33, 1839.</note> On December 20, 1828, a month after his election, Georgia passed an act annexing that part of the Cherokee country within its chartered limits and extending its jurisdiction over it. All laws and customs established among the Cherokee were declared null and void. Furthermore, no person of Indian blood or descent living within the Indian country was from that time on allowed to be a witness or a party in any legal case where a white man was the defendant. The act was set to take effect on June 1, 1830 (42). Soon after, the entire territory was mapped out into counties and surveyed by state surveyors into “land lots” of 160 acres each and “gold lots” of 40 acres. These were put up and distributed among the white citizens of Georgia through a public lottery, with each white citizen receiving a ticket. 

Every Cherokee head of a family was indeed allowed a reservation of 160 acres, but no deed was granted, and their right to remain depended solely on the whim of the legislature. Provisions were made for the settlement of contested lottery claims among white citizens; however, through the most strict laws—in addition to the sweeping law that forbade anyone of Indian blood from bringing a lawsuit or testifying against a white man—it was made impossible for an Indian owner to defend his rights in any court or to resist the seizure of his homestead, or even his own house. Anyone who did resist was subject to imprisonment at the discretion of a Georgia court. Other laws aimed at the same goal quickly followed. One of these made any contract between a white man and an Indian invalid unless it was proven by the testimony of two white witnesses—effectively canceling all debts white men owed to Indians. Another law forced all white men living in the Cherokee country to take a special oath of allegiance to the state of Georgia, under penalty of four years’ imprisonment in the penitentiary. This act was intended to drive out all missionaries, teachers, and other educators who refused to support the plundering of the land. Around the same time, the Cherokee were forbidden from holding councils, assembling for any public purpose,<note>2 For extracts and summaries of these acts, see Royce, the work previously cited, pp. 259-264; Drake, Indians, pp. 438-456, 1880; Greeley, American Conflict, I, pp. 105, 106, 1864; Edward Everett, speech in the House of Representatives, February 14, 1831 (lottery law). The gold lottery is also mentioned incidentally by Lanman, Charles, Letters from the Alleghany Mountains, p. 10; New York, 1849, and by Nitze, in his report on the Georgia gold fields, in the Twentieth Annual Report of the United States Geological Survey, part 6 (Mineral Resources), p. 112, 1899. The author himself has seen in a mountain village in Georgia an old book titled “The Cherokee Land and Gold Lottery,” containing maps and charts covering the entire Cherokee country of Georgia, with each lot numbered and descriptions of the watercourses, soil, and suspected mineral veins.</note> or digging for gold on their own lands.

These repressive measures included targeting white missionaries who supported the Cherokee and forbidding the Cherokee from assembling or mining gold.</summary>

--- Page 136 ---
<meta>This page continues the historical account of the legislative actions taken by Georgia in 1830 to strip the Cherokee of their legal rights and protections, detailing the resulting lawlessness and violence.</meta>

<header>MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19]</header>
<page-num>118</page-num>

The purpose of this legislation was to make life in their own country intolerable for the Cherokee by stripping them of all legal protection and friendly counsel, and the effect was exactly as intended. In an eloquent address on the subject before the House of Representatives, the distinguished Edward Everett clearly pointed out the encouragement it gave to lawless men: “They only have to cross the Cherokee line; they only have to choose the time and place where no white man’s eye can see them, and they may burn the dwelling, waste the farm, plunder the property, assault the person, and murder the children of the Cherokee subject of Georgia. Although hundreds of the tribe may be watching, not one of them is permitted to testify against the plunderer.”¹ Senator Sprague of Maine said of the law that it surrendered the property of the Cherokee to the greed of their neighbors, leaving them exposed to every outrage lawless persons could inflict. Consequently, even robbery and murder could be committed with impunity in broad daylight, provided no white person was present who would testify against it.²

This prediction was fulfilled exactly. Bands of armed men invaded Cherokee country, forcibly seizing horses and cattle, taking possession of houses after throwing out the occupants, and assaulting owners who dared to resist.³ In one instance near present-day Dahlonega, two white men—who had been hospitably received and fed supper by an educated Cherokee citizen of nearly pure white blood—later that evening, during the parents' temporary absence, drove out the children and their nurse and deliberately set fire to the house. It was burned to the ground with all its contents. They were pursued and brought to trial, but the judge dismissed the case because no Indian could testify against a white man.⁴ Cherokee miners on their own land were arrested, fined, and imprisoned, and their tools and machinery were destroyed, while thousands of white intruders were allowed to dig in the same places without being disturbed.⁵ A Cherokee man on trial in his own nation for killing another Indian was seized by state authorities, tried, and condemned to death; since he did not understand English, he was unable to speak in his own defense. A United States court forbade the execution, but the judge who had conducted the trial defied the court order, went to the place of execution, and stood beside the sheriff while the Indian was hanged.⁶

<header>MOONEY] ARREST OF MISSIONARIES—1831</header>
<page-num>119</page-num>

Immediately after the passage of the first act, the Cherokee appealed to President Jackson, but they were told that no protection would be offered to them. Other efforts were then made—in 1829—to persuade them to relocate, or to secure another land transfer—this time for all their lands in North Carolina—but the Cherokee remained firm. The Georgia law was declared in force on June 3, 1830, after which the President directed that the annuity payment due to the Cherokee Nation under previous treaties should no longer be paid to their national treasurer, as had been done until then, but instead be distributed per capita by the agent. As a national fund, it had been used to maintain their schools and national press. As a per capita payment, it amounted to forty-two cents for each individual. Several years later, it still remained unpaid. Federal troops were also sent into the Cherokee country with orders to prevent all mining by either whites or Indians unless authorized by the state of Georgia. All these measures served only to make the Cherokee more bitter in their determination. In September 1830, another proposal was made for the removal of the tribe, but the national council emphatically refused to consider the subject. <note>Royce, Cherokee Nation, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, pages 261, 262, 1888.</note>

In January 1831, the Cherokee Nation, through John Ross as principal chief, brought a test suit for an injunction against Georgia in the United States Supreme Court. The majority of the court dismissed the suit on the grounds that the Cherokee were not a foreign nation within the meaning of the Constitution, with two justices dissenting from this opinion. <note>Ibid., page 262.</note>

Shortly afterward, under the law which forbade any white man to live in the Cherokee Nation without taking an oath of allegiance to Georgia, a number of arrests were made. These included Wheeler, the printer of the *Cherokee Phoenix*, and the missionaries Worcester, Butler, Thompson, and Proctor. Being there with the permission of the agent and feeling that plain American citizenship should be valid in any part of the United States, they refused to take the oath. Some of those arrested took the oath and were released, but Worcester and Butler, still refusing, were dressed in prison clothes and put to hard labor among felons. Worcester had pleaded in his defense that he was a citizen of Vermont and had entered the Cherokee country with the permission of the President of the United States and the approval of the Cherokee Nation. He argued that since the United States had acknowledged the Cherokee to be a nation with a guaranteed and definite territory through several treaties, the state had no right to interfere with him. He was sentenced to four years in the penitentiary. On March 3, 1832, the matter was appealed as a test case to the Supreme Court of the United States, which rendered a decision in favor of Worcester and the Cherokee Nation and ordered his release. Georgia, however, through her governor, had defied the summons with a threat of opposition, even to the

On July 19, 1832, a public fast was observed throughout the Cherokee Nation. In the proclamation recommending it, Chief Ross observes that:
> “Whereas the crisis in the affairs of the Nation presents a day of tribulation and sorrow, and the time appears to be quickly approaching when the destiny of this people must be sealed; whether it has been directed by the usual depravity and wickedness of man, or by the unsearchable and mysterious will of an all-wise Being, it equally becomes us, as a rational and Christian community, humbly to bow in humiliation,” etc. <note>Drake, Indians, page 458, 1880.</note>

Further attempts were made to persuade the Cherokee to move to the West, but they met the same firm refusal as before. It was learned that in view of the harassing conditions to which they were subjected, the Cherokee were now seriously considering the project of emigrating to the Pacific Coast, at the mouth of the Columbia River, a territory then claimed by England and held by the posts of the British Hudson Bay Company. The Secretary of War immediately took steps to discourage the movement. <note>Royce, in the same work, pages 262–264, 272, 273.</note> A suggestion from the Cherokee that the government satisfy those who had taken possession of Cherokee lands under the lottery drawing—by giving them instead an equivalent from the unoccupied government lands—was rejected by the President.

In the spring of 1834, the Cherokee submitted a memorial which, after asserting that they would never voluntarily consent to abandon their homes, proposed to satisfy Georgia by ceding to her a portion of their territory. They were to be protected in possession of the remainder until the end of a definite period to be fixed by the United States, at the end of which, after disposing of their surplus lands, they should become citizens of the various states within which they resided. They were told that their difficulties could be remedied only by their removal to the west of the Mississippi. In the meantime, a removal treaty was being negotiated with a self-styled committee of some fifteen or twenty Cherokee called together at the agency. It was carried through despite the protest of John Ross and the Cherokee Nation, as recorded in a paper said to contain the signatures of 13,000 Cherokee, but it failed to be ratified. <note>Ibid., pages 274, 275.</note>

In August of that year, another council was held at Red Clay, southeast from Chattanooga and just within the Georgia line, where the question of removal was again debated in what is officially described as a tumultuous and excited meeting. One of the principal advocates of the emigration plan, a prominent man of mixed ancestry named John Walker, Jr., was assassinated from ambush while returning from the council to his home a few miles north of the present Cleveland, Tennessee. On account of his superior education and influential connections—his wife being a niece of former agent Return J. Meigs—the affair created intense excitement at the time. The assassination has been considered the first in a long series of political murders growing out of the removal agitation, but, according to the testimony of elderly Cherokee familiar with the facts, the killing was due to a more personal motive. <note>Commissioner Elbert Herring, November 25, Report of the Indian Commissioner, page 240, 1834; author’s personal information from Major R. The Cherokee were now nearly worn out by constant battle against a fate from which they could see no escape. In February 1835, two rival delegations arrived in Washington. One, the national party, headed by John Ross, came prepared to still fight to the end for their home and national existence. The other, headed by Major John Ridge, a prominent sub-chief, losing hope of further successful resistance, was prepared to negotiate for removal. Reverend J. F. Schermerhorn was appointed commissioner to negotiate with the Ridge party for a treaty to be confirmed later by the Cherokee people in a general council. On this basis, a treaty was negotiated with the Ridge party by which the Cherokee were to cede their entire eastern territory and move to the West in exchange for the sum of $3,250,000, along with some additional acreage in the West and a small sum for damages committed against them by the whites. Finding that these negotiations were proceeding, the Ross party filed a counter-proposal for $20,000,000, which was rejected by the Senate as excessive. Once this was accomplished, Mr. Schermerhorn left for the Cherokee country, carrying an address from President Jackson in which the great benefits of removal were presented to the Cherokee. After spending the summer and fall in a fruitless effort to secure favorable action, the reverend gentleman notified the President, proposing either to obtain the signatures of the leading Cherokee by promising them payment for their improvements at their own valuation (if in any way reasonable) or to conclude a treaty with only a part of the Nation and force the rest to accept it. He was quickly informed by the Secretary of War, Lewis Cass, on behalf of the President, that if a treaty were concluded at all, it must be obtained on fair and open terms, with no specific promises to any individual, regardless of their rank, to gain their help or influence, and without sacrificing the interests of the whole to the greed of a few. He was also informed that, since it would likely be against his wishes, his letter would not be placed on the official record.1

In October 1835, the Ridge treaty was rejected by the Cherokee Nation in a full council at Red Clay; even its main supporters, Ridge himself and Elias Boudinot, joined the majority, which was quite unexpected to Schermerhorn. He reported the result, piously adding, "but the Lord is able to overrule all things for good." During the session of this council, notice was served to the Cherokee to meet with commissioners at New Echota the following December for the purpose of negotiating a treaty. The notice was also printed in the Cherokee language and circulated throughout the Nation, with a statement that those who failed to attend would be considered to have consented to any treaty that might be made.2

The council had authorized the official delegation, headed by John Ross, to conclude a treaty either there or at Washington, but, finding that Schermerhorn had no authority to negotiate on any basis other than the one rejected by the Nation, the delegates went to Washington.3 Before their departure, John Ross—who had moved to Tennessee to escape persecution in his own state—was arrested at his home by the Georgia Guard. All his private papers and the council's proceedings were seized at the same time and taken across the border into Georgia, where he was held for some time without any charges against him, and was finally released without an apology or explanation. <header>MOONEY] TREATY OF NEW ECHOTA—1835</header>

The national newspaper, the *Cherokee Phoenix*, had been suppressed and its printing equipment seized by the same guard a few days before.¹ Thus, in their greatest need, the Cherokee were deprived of the help and advice of their teachers, their national press, and their chief.

Although threats and incentives had been offered for two months to ensure a full attendance at the December conference at New Echota, only three hundred to five hundred men, women, and children were present when the proceedings opened—out of a population of over 17,000—according to the report of Schermerhorn himself. Despite the low attendance and the absence of the Nation's principal officers, a committee was appointed to arrange the details of a treaty, which was finally drafted and signed on December 29, 1835.²

Briefly stated, by this Treaty of New Echota, Georgia, the Cherokee Nation ceded its entire remaining territory east of the Mississippi to the United States for the sum of five million dollars and a joint interest in the territory already occupied by the Western Cherokee in what is now Indian Territory, along with an additional smaller tract adjoining it to the northeast in what is now Kansas. Property improvements were to be paid for, and the Indians were to be moved at the expense of the United States and supported at the government's expense for one year after their arrival in the new country. The removal was to take place within two years of the treaty's ratification.

At the strong insistence of the Cherokee signers, who likely would not have signed otherwise, it was agreed that a limited number of Cherokee who wished to stay behind in North Carolina, Tennessee, and Alabama and become citizens might do so—provided they were first judged "qualified or likely to become useful citizens"—along with a few who held individual reservations under previous treaties. This provision was allowed by the commissioners but was later removed when President Jackson announced his determination "not to allow any <term>preemptions</term> or reservations," as he desired "the entire Cherokee people to move together."

Provisions were also made for the payment of debts owed by the Indians from any money they were to receive under the treaty; for the reestablishment of missions in the West; for pensions to Cherokee wounded while serving the government in the War of 1812 and the Creek War; for permission to establish military posts and roads in the new country as the United States deemed necessary; and for settling Osage claims in the western territory and
