for bringing about a friendly understanding between the two tribes; and for the conversion of all annuities and other sums due from the United States into a permanent national fund. The interest was to be placed at the disposal of the officers of the Cherokee Nation and distributed by them, according to the will of their own people, for the care of schools and orphans, and for general national purposes.

The western territory assigned to the Cherokee under this treaty consisted of two adjoining tracts, namely: (1) a tract of seven million acres, together with a “perpetual outlet west,” already assigned to the western Cherokee under the treaty of 1833, as will be noted later,<sup>1</sup> being identical with the area currently occupied by the Cherokee Nation in Indian Territory, along with the former “Cherokee strip,” with the exception of a two-mile strip along the northern boundary, now included within the limits of Kansas; (2) a smaller additional tract of eight hundred thousand acres, running fifty miles north and south and twenty-five miles east and west, in what is now the southeastern corner of Kansas. For this second tract, the Cherokee themselves were to pay the United States five hundred thousand dollars.

The treaty of 1833, which assigned the first tract described to the western Cherokee, states that the United States agrees to “guarantee it to them forever, and that guarantee is hereby pledged.” By the same treaty, “in addition to the seven million acres of land thus provided for and bounded, the United States further guarantee to the Cherokee nation a perpetual outlet west and a free and undisturbed use of all the country lying west of the western boundary of said seven million acres, as far west as the sovereignty of the United States and their right to the soil extend . . . and <term>letters patent</term> shall be issued by the United States as soon as practicable for the land hereby guaranteed.” All of this was repeated by the present treaty, and made to include also the smaller (second) tract, in these words:

> ART. 3. The United States also agree that the lands ceded above by the treaty of February 14, 1833, including the outlet, and those ceded by this treaty, shall all be included in one patent, issued to the Cherokee nation of Indians by the President of the United States, according to the provisions of the act of May 28, 1830. . . .
> ART. 5. The United States hereby promise and agree that the lands ceded to the Cherokee nation in the previous article shall in no future time, without their consent, be included within the territorial limits or jurisdiction of any state or territory. But they shall secure to the Cherokee nation the right of their national councils to make and carry into effect all such laws as they may deem necessary for the government and protection of the persons and property within their own country belonging to their people or such persons as have joined them: Provided always, that they shall not be inconsistent with the Constitution of the United States and such acts of Congress as have been or may be passed regulating trade and communication with the Indians; and also that they shall not be considered as extending to such citizens and army of the United States as may travel or reside in the Indian

the country by permission, according to the laws and regulations established by its government. . . .

**ART. 6.** Perpetual peace and friendship shall exist between the citizens of the United States and the Cherokee Indians. The United States agrees to protect the Cherokee nation from domestic conflict and foreign enemies, and against internal wars between the various tribes. The Cherokees shall strive to preserve and maintain the peace of the country and not make war upon their neighbors; they shall also be protected against interference and trespassing by citizens of the United States who may attempt to settle in the country without their consent; and all such persons shall be removed from the area by order of the President of the United States. However, this is not intended to prevent useful farmers, mechanics, and teachers from living among them to instruct the Indians, according to the treaty agreements.

**ARTICLE 7.** Because the Cherokee nation has already made great progress in civilization, and considering it important that every proper and praiseworthy incentive should be offered to their people to improve their condition, as well as to guard and secure their guaranteed rights in the most effective manner, and with a goal to demonstrate the generous and broad policy of the United States government toward the Indians in their removal beyond the state borders, it is agreed that they shall be entitled to a Delegate in the House of Representatives of the United States whenever Congress makes provision for one.

The document was signed by Governor William Carroll of Tennessee and Reverend J. F. Schermerhorn as commissioners—though Carroll was unable to attend because of illness—and by twenty Cherokees. Among the most prominent signers were Major Ridge and Elias Boudinot, the former editor of the *Phoenix*. Neither John Ross nor any of the official officers of the Cherokee Nation were present or represented. After some changes by the Senate, the treaty was ratified on May 23, 1836. <note>See the New Echota treaty of 1835 and the Fort Gibson treaty of 1833 in Indian Treaties, pages 633–648 and 561–565, 1837; also, for a full discussion of both treaties, see Royce, Cherokee Nation, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, pages 249–298. For a summary of all the pressure tactics brought against the Cherokee up to the final removal, see also Everett's speech in the House of Representatives, May 31, 1838; the chapters on "Expatriation of the Cherokees" in Drake, Indians, 1880; and the chapter on "State Rights—Nullification" in Greeley, American Conflict, Volume I, 1864. The Georgia side of the controversy is presented in E. J. Harden's Life of Governor George M. Troup, 1849.</note>

Based on the Treaty of New Echota and the treaty previously made with the western Cherokee at Fort Gibson in 1833, the united Cherokee Nation established its claim to the territory currently held by the tribe in the Indian Territory, to the Cherokee outlet, and to national self-government with protection from outside interference.

An official census taken in 1835 showed the total number of Cherokees in Georgia, North Carolina, Alabama, and Tennessee to be 16,542. This number did not include 1,592 Black slaves and 201 white people married to Cherokees. The Cherokees were distributed as follows: Georgia, 8,946; North Carolina, 3,644; Tennessee, 2,528; and Alabama, 1,424. <note>Royce, cited work, page 289. The Indian total is also given in the Report of the Indian Commissioner, page 369, 1836.</note>

# MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19]

The treaty had been ratified by a majority of one vote more than the necessary number, and initial steps were immediately taken to carry it into execution. Councils were held in opposition throughout the Cherokee Nation, and resolutions denouncing the methods used and declaring the treaty absolutely null and void were drafted and submitted to General Wool, who was in command of the troops in the Cherokee country. He forwarded them to Washington. In reply, the President expressed his surprise that an army officer would have received or transmitted a paper so disrespectful to the Executive, the Senate, and the American people. He declared his firm determination that the treaty should be carried out without modification and with all consistent speed, and directed that after a copy of the letter had been delivered to Ross, no further communication, whether oral or written, should be held with him concerning the treaty. It was further ordered that no council should be permitted to assemble to discuss the treaty. Ross had already been informed that the President had stopped recognizing any existing government among the eastern Cherokee, and that any further effort by him to prevent the fulfillment of the treaty would be suppressed.<note>1</note>

Despite this suppression of opinion, the feeling of the Nation was soon made clear through other sources. Before the treaty was ratified, Major W. M. Davis had been appointed to enroll the Cherokee for removal and to appraise the value of their improvements. He soon learned the true state of affairs, and, although holding his office through the goodwill of President Jackson, he addressed a strong letter on the subject to the Secretary of War, from which the following extract is taken:

> I believe that my duty to the President, to yourself, and to my country reluctantly compels me to state the facts regarding a meeting of a small number of Cherokees at New Echota last December, who met with Mr. Schermerhorn, and articles of a general treaty were entered into between them for the whole Cherokee nation. . . . Sir, that paper, . . . called a treaty, is no treaty at all, because it was not sanctioned by the great body of the Cherokee and was made without their participation or consent. I solemnly declare to you that if it were referred to the Cherokee people, it would be instantly rejected by nine-tenths of them, and I believe by nineteen-twentieths of them. There were not more than one hundred Cherokee voters present at the conclusion of the treaty, and not more than three hundred people total, including women and children, although the weather was everything that could be desired. The Indians had long been notified of the meeting, and blankets were promised to all who would come and vote for the treaty. The most cunning and artful methods were used to hide the small number of people present at the treaty. Schermerhorn made no count of them. The business of making the treaty was transacted with a committee appointed by the Indians who were present, so as not to reveal their numbers. The power of attorney under which the committee acted was signed only by the president and secretary of the meeting, so as not to disclose their weakness. . . . Mr. Schermerhorn's apparent design was to hide the real number present and to deceive the public and the government on this point.

<header>MOONEY] GENERAL WOOL'S REPORTS—1837</header>

The delegation taken to Washington by Mr. Schermerhorn had no more authority to make a treaty than any other dozen Cherokee picked up at random for that purpose. I now warn you and the President that if this document of Schermerhorn's, which is called a treaty, is sent to the Senate and ratified, you will bring trouble upon the government and eventually destroy the Cherokee Nation. The Cherokee are a peaceful, harmless people, but you may drive them to desperation, and this treaty cannot be carried out except through the use of force.<sup>1</sup>

General Wool, who had been placed in command of the troops concentrated in the Cherokee country to prevent opposition to the enforcement of the treaty, reported on February 18, 1837, that he had called them together and delivered an address to them, but "it is, however, useless to talk to a people who are almost universally opposed to the treaty and who maintain that they never made such a treaty. They are so determined in their opposition that not one of all those who were present and voted at the council held just a day or two ago—no matter how poor or destitute—would receive either rations or clothing from the United States, for fear they might compromise themselves regarding the treaty. These same people, as well as those in the mountains of North Carolina, during the past summer, preferred living on the roots and sap of trees rather than receive provisions from the United States; and thousands, as I have been informed, had no other food for weeks. Many have said they will die before they will leave the country."<sup>2</sup>

Other letters from General Wool, written while he was engaged in the work of disarming and intimidating the Cherokee, show how very disagreeable that duty was to him and how strongly his sympathies lay with the Indians, who were practically unanimous in rejecting the treaty. In one letter he says:

<margin>L</margin>
> The whole scene since I have been in this country has been nothing but heart-rending, and it is a situation I would be glad to leave as soon as circumstances allow. Because I am firm and decisive, do not believe I would be unjust. If I could—and I could not do them a greater kindness—I would remove every Indian tomorrow beyond the reach of the white men, who, like vultures, are watching, ready to pounce upon their prey and strip them of everything they have or expect from the government of the United States. Yes, sir, nineteen out of twenty, if not ninety-nine out of every hundred, will go to the West penniless.<sup>3</sup>

How this was to be brought about is explained in part by a letter addressed to the President by Major Ridge himself, the primary signer of the treaty:

> We now come to address you regarding our griefs and suffering caused by the actions of the white people. They have taken our lands, and now they are preparing to swindle us out of the money resulting from the treaty. We found our plantations taken either entirely or in part by the Georgians—and lawsuits have been started against us for back rents on our own farms. These suits are begun in the lower courts, with the

Even the Georgia laws, which deny us our right to testify under oath, are being cast aside. Despite the cries of our people and our protestations of innocence and peace, the lowest classes of white people are flogging the Cherokees with cowhides, hickory sticks, and clubs. We are not safe in our houses—our people are attacked day and night by the rabble. Even justices of the peace and constables are involved in this business. This barbaric treatment is not limited to men, but women are also stripped and whipped without law or mercy. . . . Send regular troops to protect us from these lawless assaults, and to protect our people as they depart for the West. If this is not done, we shall carry away nothing but the scars of the whip on our backs, and our oppressors will get all the money. We speak plainly, as chiefs whose property and lives are in danger, and we appeal to you for protection. . . .¹

General Dunlap, in command of the Tennessee troops called out to prevent the alleged planned Cherokee uprising, having learned the true situation for himself, delivered an indignant address to his men. In it, he declared that he would never dishonor the Tennessee military by helping to carry out, at the point of a bayonet, a treaty made by a small minority against the will and authority of the Cherokee people. He stated further that he had given the Cherokee all the protection in his power, as the whites needed none.²

A confidential agent sent to report upon the situation wrote in September 1837 that opposition to the treaty was unanimous and irreconcilable. The Cherokee declared that it could not bind them because they did not make it, that it was the work of a few unauthorized individuals, and that the Nation was not a party to it. They had retained the forms of their government, although no election had been held since 1830, having continued the officers then in charge until their government could again be regularly reestablished. Under this arrangement, John Ross was the principal chief, with influence that was unbounded and unquestioned. “The entire Nation of eighteen thousand persons is with him; the few—about three hundred—who made the treaty have left the country, with the exception of a small number of prominent individuals—such as Ridge, Boudinot, and others—who remained to assist in carrying it out. It is evident, therefore, that Ross and his party are in fact the Cherokee Nation. . . . I believe that the mass of the Nation, particularly the mountain Indians, will stand or fall with Ross. . . .”³

Public feeling on the subject of this treaty was so intense that it became, to some extent, a party question, with the Democrats supporting President Jackson while the Whigs bitterly opposed him. Among

<header>MOONEY] ARRIVAL OF TROOPS</header>

Notable leaders of the opposition included Henry Clay, Daniel Webster, Edward Everett, Wise of Virginia, and David Crockett. The speeches in Congress on the subject “were characterized by a depth and bitterness of feeling that had never been exceeded, even on the slavery question.”¹ It was considered not merely an Indian question, but a conflict between state rights on one hand and federal jurisdiction and the Constitution on the other.

Despite threats of arrest and punishment, John Ross still continued his active efforts on behalf of his people. Again, in the spring of 1838, two months before the deadline fixed for the removal, he presented another protest and memorial to Congress, which—like the others—was tabled by the Senate. Martin Van Buren had now succeeded Andrew Jackson and was inclined to allow the Cherokee a longer time to prepare for migration. However, he was met by a declaration from Governor Gilmer of Georgia that any delay would be a violation of the rights of that state and in opposition to the rights of the *owners of the land*. Gilmer warned that if trouble arose from any protection provided by the government troops to the Cherokee, a direct confrontation must follow between the state authorities and the federal government.²

Until the very last moment, the Cherokee still believed that the treaty would not be carried out. Even with all the pressure brought to bear upon them, only about 2,000 of the 17,000 in the eastern Nation had moved by the deadline fixed for their departure, May 26, 1838. As it was clear that the removal could only be accomplished by force, General Winfield Scott was now appointed to that duty with instructions to start the Indians for the West at the earliest possible moment. For that purpose, he was ordered to take command of the troops already in the Cherokee country, along with additional reinforcements of infantry, cavalry, and artillery. He was authorized to call upon the governors of the neighboring states for as many as 4,000 militia and volunteers. The total force employed numbered about 7,000 men—regulars, militia, and volunteers.³ The Indians had already been disarmed by General Wool.

Upon arriving in the Cherokee country, Scott established headquarters at the capital, New Echota. From there, on May 10, he issued a proclamation to the Cherokee, warning them that the migration must begin in haste and that before another month had passed, every Cherokee man, woman, and child must be in motion to join their brothers in the far West, according to the decision of the President, which he, the general, had come to enforce. The proclamation concludes: “My troops already occupy many positions . . . . and

### THE REMOVAL—1838-39

The history of this Cherokee removal of 1838, as gathered by the author from the accounts of those who participated in the tragedy, may well exceed in the weight of grief and pathos any other event in American history. Even the famous exile of the Acadians falls far behind it in its total of death and misery. Under Scott's orders, the troops were positioned at various points throughout the Cherokee country, where stockade forts were built for gathering in and holding the Indians before their removal (43). From these, squads of troops were sent to search out with rifle and bayonet every small cabin hidden away in the valleys or by the sides of mountain streams, to seize and bring in as prisoners all the occupants, however or wherever they might be found.

Families at dinner were startled by the sudden gleam of bayonets in the doorway and rose up to be driven with blows and curses along the weary miles of trail that led to the stockade. Men were seized in their fields or while walking along the road, women were taken from their spinning wheels, and children from their play. In many cases, on turning for one last look as they crossed the ridge, they saw their homes in flames, set on fire by the lawless mob that followed on the heels of the soldiers to loot and pillage. So eager were these outlaws that in some instances they were driving off the cattle and other livestock of the Indians almost before the soldiers had even started the owners in the opposite direction. Systematic hunts were made by these same men for Indian graves, to rob them of the silver pendants and other valuables buried with the dead. A Georgia volunteer, who later became a colonel in the Confederate service, said: "I fought through the Civil War and have seen men shot to pieces and slaughtered by thousands, but the Cherokee removal was the cruelest work I ever knew."

To prevent escape, the soldiers had been ordered to approach and surround each house, as much as possible, so as to surprise the occupants without warning. One old patriarch, when thus surprised, calmly called his children and grandchildren around him and, kneeling down, told them to pray with him in their own language, while the astonished soldiers looked on in silence. Then rising, he led the way into

exile. A woman, finding her house surrounded, went to the door and called the chickens to be fed for the last time; then, taking her infant on her back and her two other children by the hand, she followed her husband and the soldiers.

Not everyone was so submissive. An old man named Tsalĭ, or “Charley,” was captured along with his wife, his brother, his three sons, and their families. Enraged by the brutality shown to his wife—who, unable to travel fast, was prodded with bayonets to hurry her along—he urged the other men to join him in a dash for freedom. Because he spoke in Cherokee, the soldiers heard him but understood nothing until each warrior suddenly lunged at the soldier nearest him and tried to wrestle his gun away. <insert>✓</insert> The attack was so sudden and unexpected that one soldier was killed and the rest fled, while the Indians escaped into the mountains. Hundreds of others, some from the various stockades, also managed to escape to the mountains from time to time. Those who did not die of starvation survived on roots and wild berries until the hunt was over. Finding it impossible to capture these fugitives, General Scott finally offered them a proposal through (Colonel) W. H. Thomas, their most trusted friend: if they would surrender Charley and his party for punishment, the rest would be allowed to remain until the government could settle their case. Upon hearing of the proposal, Charley came in voluntarily with his sons, offering himself as a sacrifice for his people. By command of General Scott, Charley, his brother, and his two eldest sons were shot near the mouth of the Tuckasegee River. A detachment of Cherokee prisoners was forced to perform the execution to impress upon the Indians the fact of their complete helplessness. <insert><u>From those fugitives who were permitted to remain, the present Eastern Band of Cherokee originated.<sup>1</sup></u></insert>

When nearly seventeen thousand Cherokee had been gathered into the various stockades, the work of removal began. Early in June, several groups, totaling about five thousand people, were brought by the troops to the old agency on the Hiwassee River, at present-day Calhoun, Tennessee, and to Ross’s Landing (now Chattanooga), and Gunter’s Landing (now Guntersville, Alabama), further down the Tennessee River. There, they were placed on steamboats and transported down the Tennessee and Ohio rivers to the far side of the Mississippi, where the journey continued by land to Indian Territory. This removal,

In the hottest part of the year, the removal was accompanied by such great sickness and mortality that, by resolution of the Cherokee National Council, Ross and the other chiefs submitted a proposal to General Scott that the Cherokee be allowed to move themselves in the fall, after the season of illness had ended. This was granted on the condition that everyone should have started by the 20th of October, except for the sick and elderly who might not be able to move so quickly. Accordingly, officers were appointed by the Cherokee council to take charge of the emigration; the Indians were organized into detachments averaging one thousand people each, with two leaders in charge of each detachment, and a sufficient number of wagons and horses for the purpose. In this way the remainder, recorded at about 13,000 (including Black slaves), started on the long march overland late in the fall (44).

Those who emigrated under the management of their own officers assembled at Rattlesnake Springs, about two miles south of the Hiwassee River, near present-day Charleston, Tennessee, where a final council was held. In this council, it was decided to continue their old constitution and laws in their new home. Then, in October 1838, the long procession of exiles was set in motion. A very few went by the river route; the rest, nearly all of the 13,000, went overland. Crossing to the north side of the Hiwassee at a ferry above Gunstocker Creek, they proceeded down along the river—the sick, the elderly, and the smaller children, with the blankets, cooking pots, and other belongings in wagons, and the rest on foot or on horses. The number of wagons was 645.

It was like the march of an army: regiment after regiment, the wagons in the center, the officers along the line, and the horsemen on the flanks and at the rear. The Tennessee River was crossed at Tucker’s <note>The text indicates uncertainty regarding this name</note> ferry, a short distance above Jolly’s Island, at the mouth of the Hiwassee. From there, the route lay south of Pikeville, through McMinnville, and on to Nashville, where the Cumberland River was crossed. Then they went on to Hopkinsville, Kentucky, where the noted chief White-Path, in charge of a detachment, became ill and died. His people buried him by the roadside, with a box over the grave and poles with streamers around it, so that the others coming behind might note the spot and remember him. Somewhere also along that march of death—for the exiles died by tens and twenties every day of the journey—the devoted wife of John Ross sank down, leaving him to go on with the bitter pain of loss added to heartbreak at the ruin of his nation. The Ohio River was crossed at a ferry near the mouth of the Cumberland, and the army passed on through southern Illinois until the great Mississippi was reached opposite Cape Girardeau, Missouri. It was now the middle of winter, with the river running full of ice, so that several detachments were obliged to wait some time on the eastern bank for the channel to become clear. In talking with old men

<header>MOONEY] ARRIVAL IN INDIAN TERRITORY—1839</header>

and women at Tahlequah, the author found that the passage of more than half a century had not been enough to erase the memory of the miseries of that stop beside the frozen river. There, hundreds of sick and dying people were crowded into wagons or stretched out on the ground, with only a blanket overhead to shield them from the January wind. The crossing was finally made in two divisions: one at Cape Girardeau and another at Green’s ferry, a short distance below. From there, the march continued through Missouri to Indian Territory. The later groups took a northern route through Springfield because those who had gone before had hunted all the game along the direct path. Finally, they reached their destination. They had started in October 1838, and it was now March 1839; the journey had taken nearly six months during the harshest part of the year. <note>1</note>

It is difficult to reach any accurate count of the number of Cherokee who died as a result of the Removal. According to official figures, those who moved under the direction of Ross lost over 1,600 people on the journey. <note>2</note> The death rate among those previously moved under military supervision was likely higher, as it was their suffering that led the Cherokee national officers to propose taking charge of the emigration themselves. Hundreds died in the stockades and the waiting camps, mainly because of the food provided; these rations of flour and other supplies were unfamiliar to them, and they did not know how to prepare them properly. Hundreds of others died soon after arriving in Indian Territory from illness and exposure suffered during the trip. In total, it is claimed—and likely with good reason—that more than 4,000 Cherokee died as a direct result of the removal.

Upon their arrival in Indian Territory, the emigrants immediately began building houses and planting crops, as the government had agreed under the treaty to provide them with rations for one year after their arrival. They were welcomed by their relatives, the “Arkansas Cherokee”—who would from then on be called the “Old Settlers” to distinguish them—who held the land under previous treaties from 1828 and 1833. However, because they were already organized under their own government and chiefs, they were not at all willing to be absorbed by the authority of the newcomers' government. Jealousies developed, in which the minority or “treaty party” of the emigrants, led by Ridge, sided with the Old Settlers against the Ross or “national party,” which outnumbered the other two groups combined by nearly three to one.

While these tensions were at their peak, the Nation was thrown into a state of intense excitement by the news that Major Ridge, his son John Ridge, and Elias Boudinot—all leaders of the treaty party—had been killed by followers of the national party, immediately after the end

The agent’s report to the Secretary of War, written two days later, says of the affair:

> The murder of Boudinot was treacherous and cruel. He was helping some workmen build a new house. Three men visited him and asked for medicine. He went with them toward the home of Wooster, the missionary, who kept medicine, about three hundred yards from Boudinot’s. When they were about halfway there, two of the men seized Boudinot and the third stabbed him, after which the three cut him to pieces with their knives and tomahawks. Because this murder took place within two miles of the residence of John Ross, his friends were worried it might be blamed on his involvement; and at this moment, as I am writing, there are six hundred armed Cherokee around Ross’s home, gathered for his protection. The murderers of the two Ridges and Boudinot are certainly from among the recent Cherokee migrants and are, of course, supporters of Ross; but I cannot yet believe that Ross encouraged the outrage. He has too much good sense to involve his nation in conflict at this critical time; and besides, his character, for the twenty-five years I have known him, has been peaceful. . . . Boudinot’s wife is a white woman, a native of New Jersey, as I understand. He has six children. The wife of John Ridge Jr. is a white woman, but I am not informed where she is from or what family she left behind. Boudinot had modest means. Both Ridges, father and son, were wealthy. . . . <note>1</note>

While all the evidence shows that Ross was in no way involved in the affair, there can be no question that the men were killed according to the law of the Nation—which had been written three times and was still in effect—that made it treason, punishable by death, to give away lands except by an act of the general council of the Nation. It was for violating a similar law among the Creeks that the chief, McIntosh, lost his life in 1825, and a party led by Major Ridge himself had killed Doublehead years before on suspicion of accepting a bribe for his part in a treaty.

Upon hearing of the deaths of the Ridges and Boudinot, several other signers of the rejected treaty—among whom were John Bell, Archilla Smith, and James Starr—fled for safety to the protection of the garrison at Fort Gibson. Boudinot’s brother, Stand Watie, swore revenge against Ross. Ross was urged to flee but refused, declaring his complete innocence. His friends gathered to support him, stationing a guard around his house until the initial excitement had subsided. About three weeks later, the national council passed decrees declaring that the men killed and their principal accomplices

<header>MOONEY] REUNION OF NATION—1839</header>

This was followed in August by another council decree declaring the New Echota treaty void and reasserting the Cherokee title to their old country. Three weeks later, another decree summoned the signers of the treaty to appear and answer for their conduct under the penalty of outlawry. At this point, the United States intervened by threatening to arrest Ross as an accessory to the killing of the Ridges.¹ Meanwhile, the National party and the Old Settlers had been coming together. A few of the latter, who had sided with the Ridge faction and tried to maintain a division in the Nation, were denounced in a council of the Old Settlers. This council declared that “by identifying themselves with those individuals known as the Ridge party—who by their conduct had made themselves hateful to the Cherokee people—they have acted in opposition to the known sentiments and feelings of that portion of this Nation known as Old Settlers, which have been frequently, variously, and publicly expressed.” The offending chiefs were at the same time removed from all authority. Among the names of over two hundred signers, the name of “George Guess” (Sequoya) appears second as vice-president.²

On July 12, 1839, a general convention of the Eastern and Western Cherokee, held at the Illinois camp ground in Indian Territory, passed an act of union, by which the two were declared “one body politic, under the name and title of the Cherokee Nation.” On behalf of the Eastern Cherokee, the document bears the signatures of John Ross, principal chief; George Lowrey, president of the council; and Goingsnake (I'nadû-na'ĭ), speaker of the council, with thirteen others. For the Western Cherokee, it was signed by John Looney, acting principal chief; George Guess (Sequoya), president of the council, and fifteen others. On September 6, 1839, a convention composed mainly of Eastern Cherokee assembled at Tahlequah, Indian Territory—which was then first officially adopted as the national capital—and adopted a new constitution. This constitution was accepted by a convention of the Old Settlers at Fort Gibson, Indian Territory, on June 26, 1840, an act which completed the reunion of the Nation.³

### THE ARKANSAS BAND—1817-1838

Having followed the fortunes of the main body of the Nation to their final destination in the West, we now turn to briefly review

the history of the earlier emigrants, the Arkansas or Old Settler Cherokee.

The events leading to the first westward migration and the subsequent negotiations which resulted in the assignment of a territory in Arkansas to the western Cherokee, by the treaty of 1817, have been already noted. The great majority of those who voluntarily removed belonged to the conservative hunter element, who desired to re-establish in the western wilderness the old Indian life from which—through the influence of schools and intelligent leadership—the main body of the Cherokee was rapidly drifting away. As the lands upon which the emigrants had settled belonged to the Osage, whose claim had not yet been extinguished by the United States, the Osage objected to their presence. The Cherokee were compelled to fight to maintain their own position, so that for the first twenty years or more, the history of the western band is a mere petty chronicle of Osage raids and Cherokee retaliations, emphasized from time to time by a massacre on a larger scale. By the treaty of 1817, the western Cherokee acquired title to a definite territory and official standing under Government protection and supervision; the lands assigned to them had been acquired by treaty from the Osage. The great body of the Cherokee in the East were strongly opposed to any recognition of the western band, seeing in such action only the beginning of an effort looking toward the ultimate removal of the whole tribe. The Government supported the scheme, however, and a steady emigration set in until, in 1819, the emigrants were said to number several thousand. Unsuccessful attempts were made to increase the number by inducing the Shawano and Delawares of Missouri and the Oneida of New York to join them.<note>See before, pp. 105–106; Nuttall, who was on the scene, gives them only 1,500.</note>

In 1818, Tollunteeskee (Ata'lûñti'skĭ), the principal chief of the Arkansas Cherokee, while on a visit to old friends in the East, became acquainted with one of the officers of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions and asked for the establishment of a mission among his people in the West. In response to the invitation, the Reverend Cephas Washburn and his assistant, Reverend Alfred Finney, set out the next year from the old Nation with their families. After a long and exhausting journey, they reached the Arkansas country where, in the spring of 1820, they established Dwight Mission. It was located next to the agency at the mouth of Illinois Creek, on the northern bank of the Arkansas River, in what is now Pope County, Arkansas. The name was bestowed in remembrance of Timothy Dwight, a Yale president and pioneer organizer of the American Board. Tollunteeskee, having died in the meantime, was succeeded as principal chief by his brother, John Jolly,<note>Washburn, Cephas, Reminiscences of the Indians, pp. 81, 103; Richmond, 1869.</note> the friend and adopted father of Samuel Houston.

<header>MOONEY] TROUBLES WITH OSAGE—1817-22</header>

had moved from his old home at the mouth of the Hiwassee in Tennessee in 1818.¹

In the spring of 1819, the naturalist Thomas Nuttall traveled up the Arkansas River, and he gives an interesting account of the Western Cherokee as he found them at that time. In traveling up the stream, 

> “as we proceeded, both banks of the river were lined with the houses and farms of the Cherokee. Although their clothing was a mixture of native and European styles, we observed a successful approach toward civilization in their houses, which were decently furnished, and in their farms, which were well-fenced and stocked with cattle. Their many families, also well-fed and well-clothed, suggest a favorable progress in their population. Their superior industry, either as hunters or farmers, proves the value of property among them, and they are no longer strangers to greed and the social distinctions created by wealth. Some of them possess property worth many thousands of dollars, have houses handsomely and conveniently furnished, and spread their tables with our dainties and luxuries.” 

He mentions a battle that occurred some time before between them and the Osage, in which the Cherokee had killed nearly one hundred of the Osage, in addition to taking a number of prisoners. He estimates their population at about fifteen hundred, which was about half the number estimated by the Eastern Nation to have emigrated to the West, and only one-fourth of the official estimate. A few Delawares were living with them.²

The Osage troubles continued despite a peace treaty between the two tribes made at a council held under the direction of Governor Clark at St. Louis in October 1818.³ Warriors from the Eastern Cherokee were accustomed to making the long journey to the Arkansas to assist their western brothers, and they returned with scalps and captives.⁴

In the summer of 1820, Governor Miller of the Arkansas territory made a second effort for peace. In reply to his address, the Osage complained that the Cherokee had failed to deliver their Osage captives as agreed upon in the previous agreement at St. Louis. It appears this was due in part to the fact that some of these captives had been taken to the Eastern Cherokee, and a messenger was accordingly sent to secure and bring them back. Another peace conference was held soon afterward at Fort Smith, but it achieved very little, as hostilities were soon resumed and continued until the United States actively intervened in the fall of 1822.⁵

Perhaps as a result of this encouragement, Sequoya moved permanently to the West in the following year and thereafter became a member of the Western Nation.¹

Like other Indians, the Western Cherokee held a firm belief in witchcraft, which led to frequent tragedies involving punishment or retaliation. In 1824, a step forward was marked by the passage of a law making it murder to kill anyone for witchcraft, and an offense punishable by whipping to accuse another of witchcraft.² This law may have been the result of the quiet influence of missionaries, supported by enlightened men like Sequoya.

The treaty that assigned the Arkansas lands to the Western Cherokee had stipulated that a census should be taken of the eastern and western divisions of the Nation separately, and a distribution of the national annuity immediately made on that basis. The western line of the Arkansas tract had also been left undecided until, according to another requirement of the same treaty, the total amount of land ceded to the United States by the Eastern Cherokee Nation could be determined, so that an equal quantity might be included within the boundaries of the western tract.³ These promises had not yet been fulfilled, partly because of the government's efforts to encourage more emigration or a further cession of land, partly due to delays in state surveys, and partly also because the Osage objected to the establishment of a boundary line that would make the Cherokee their next-door neighbors.⁴ With their boundaries undecided and their annuities withheld, distress and dissatisfaction overcame the Western Cherokee. Many of them, feeling free from territorial restrictions, spread over the country on the southern side of the Arkansas River,⁵ while others, led by a chief named The Bowl (Diwa’lĭ), crossed the Red River into Texas—then a part of Mexico—in a futile attempt to escape American jurisdiction.⁶

After a temporary western boundary was established, which proved unsatisfactory both to the Western Cherokee and to the people of Arkansas, an effort was made to resolve the difficulty by arranging an exchange of the Arkansas tract for a new territory west of the Arkansas line. However, the Western Cherokee were so strongly opposed to this project that their council, in 1825, passed a law—as the Eastern Cherokee and the Creeks had already done—establishing the death penalty

After a long series of negotiations, such pressure was brought to bear upon a delegation that visited Washington in 1828 that consent was finally obtained to exchange the Arkansas tract for another piece of seven million acres lying further west, together with "a perpetual outlet west" of the tract assigned, reaching as far west as the sovereignty of the United States might extend.<note>The same source, pages 247, 248.</note> The boundaries given for this seven-million-acre tract and the adjoining western outlet were modified by a treaty at Fort Gibson five years later so as to be practically equivalent to the present territory of the Cherokee Nation in Indian Territory, along with the Cherokee strip recently ceded.

The preamble of the Washington treaty of May 6, 1828, states that "Because it is the earnest desire of the United States government to secure a *permanent home* for the Cherokee Nation—including those currently living within the limits of the Arkansas territory as well as their friends and brothers who reside in states east of the Mississippi and who may wish to join their brothers of the West—this home shall, under the most solemn guarantee of the United States, be and remain theirs forever. This home shall never, in all future time, be hindered by having the lines of a territory or state extended around it, or by having the jurisdiction of a territory or state placed over it, nor shall it be encroached upon by the expansion in any way of the borders of any existing territory or state. Furthermore, as the current location of the Cherokees in Arkansas is unfavorable to their present peace and tends, as the past demonstrates, to their future degradation and misery, and as the Cherokees are anxious to avoid such consequences," etc.—therefore, they surrender everything confirmed to them in 1817.

Article 2 defines the boundaries of the new tract and the western outlet to be given in exchange, located immediately west of the current Arkansas line, while the next article provides for the removal of all white people and others residing within those boundaries, "so that no obstacles arising from the presence of a white population, or any population of any other sort, shall exist to disturb the Cherokees, and also to keep all such people from the west of said line in the future."

Other articles provide for payment for improvements left behind; for a cash sum of $50,000 to pay for the trouble and expense of removal and to compensate for the lower quality of the lands in the new tract; for $6,000 to pay for recovering livestock which may stray away "in search of the pastures from which they may be driven"; $8,760 for <term>spoliations</term> <note>Damages or losses resulting from robbery or destruction of property.</note> committed by the Osage and white settlers; $500 to George Guess (Sequoya)—who was himself one of the signers—in consideration of the beneficial results his tribe received from the alphabet he invented; $20,000 in ten annual payments for education; and $1,000 for a printing...

In article 6 "it is further agreed by the United States, whenever the Cherokee may desire it, to give them a set of simple laws, suited to their condition; also, when they wish to lay out their lands and own them individually, a surveyor shall be sent to conduct the surveys at the cost of the United States." This article was canceled in 1833 at the request of the Cherokee.

Article 9 provides for the Fort Gibson military reservation within the new tract, while article 7 requires the Cherokee to surrender and move from all their lands in Arkansas within fourteen months.

Article 8 shows that all this was intended to be only preliminary to the removal of the whole Cherokee Nation from the east of the Mississippi, a goal toward which the Jackson administration and the state of Georgia immediately began to focus every effort. It is as follows:

> ARTICLE 8. The Cherokee nation, west of the Mississippi, having by this agreement freed themselves from the harassing and ruinous effects resulting from living among a white population, and having secured to themselves and their descendants, under the solemn sanction of the guarantee of the United States as contained in this agreement, a large area of unobstructed country; and so that their brothers still remaining in the states may be encouraged to join them and enjoy the peace and blessings of such a state in the future, it is further agreed on the part of the United States that to each head of a Cherokee family now residing within the borders of Georgia, or of either of the states east of the Mississippi, who may desire to move west, shall be given, on enrolling himself for emigration, a good rifle, a blanket, a kettle, and five pounds of tobacco; (and to each member of his family one blanket), also a fair compensation for the property he may abandon, to be valued by persons to be appointed by the President of the United States. The cost of the emigration of all such people shall also be paid by the United States, and good and suitable routes opened and provided for their comfort, accommodation, and support along the way, and provisions for twelve months after their arrival at the agency; and to each person, or head of a family, if he takes four persons with him, shall be paid immediately on his arriving at the agency and reporting himself and his family or followers as emigrants or permanent settlers, in addition to the above, provided *he and they shall have emigrated from within the borders of the State of Georgia*, the sum of fifty dollars, and this sum in proportion to any greater or less number that may accompany him from within the aforementioned borders of the State of Georgia.

A Senate amendment, defining the limits of the western outlet, was afterward found to be impractical in its restrictions and was canceled by the treaty made at Fort Gibson in 1833.<note>Treaty of Washington, May 6, 1828, Indian Treaties, pages 423-428, 1837; treaty of Fort Gibson, 1833, ibid., pages 561-565; see also for a summary, Royce, Cherokee Nation, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, pages 229, 230, 1888.</note>

### MOONEY] EMIGRATION TO TEXAS—1828

...of the Western Cherokee made it a capital offense to negotiate any sale or exchange of land except by the authority of the council. Because the delegates had acted without such authority, they were so doubtful about what might happen upon their return that the Secretary of War sent a letter of explanation with them. He assured the Cherokee that their representatives had acted with integrity and earnest zeal for their people and had done the best that could be done regarding the treaty. Despite this, they found the entire tribe so strongly opposed to the treaty that their own lives and property were unsafe. The national council pronounced them guilty of fraud and deception and declared the treaty null and void, as it had been made without authority, and asked permission to send an authorized delegation to settle all differences.<note>¹ Royce, Cherokee Nation, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, p. 248, 1888.</note> In the meantime, however, the treaty had been ratified within three weeks of its conclusion. Thus, hardly ten years after they had cleared their fields on the Arkansas, the Western Cherokee were forced to abandon their cabins and plantations and move once more into the wilderness.

A considerable number, refusing to submit to the treaty or to trust guarantees and promises any longer, crossed the Red River into Texas and joined the Cherokee colony already established there by The Bowl under Mexican jurisdiction. Among those who relocated was the noted chief Tahchee (Tătsĭ') or “Dutch,” who had been one of the earliest emigrants to the Arkansas country. After several years in Texas, during which he led war parties against the wilder tribes, he recrossed the Red River and soon made himself so prominent in raids upon the Osage that General Arbuckle offered a reward of five hundred dollars for his capture. To show his defiance of the proclamation, he deliberately traveled to Fort Gibson, attacked a party of Osage at a nearby trading post, and scalped one of them within hearing of the fort's drums. With a rifle in one hand and the bleeding scalp in the other, he leaped off a precipice and made his escape, although a bullet grazed his cheek. On the promise of amnesty and the withdrawal of the reward, he later returned and settled with his followers on the Canadian River, southwest of Fort Gibson, establishing a reputation among army officers as a valuable scout and guide.<note>² For a sketch of Tahchee, with portraits, see McKenney and Hall, I, pp. 251–260, 1858; Catlin, North American Indians, II, pp. 121, 122, 144. Washburn also mentions the emigration to Texas following the treaty of 1828 (*Reminiscences*, p. 217, 1869).</note>

By treaties made in 1826 and 1827, the Creeks had ceded all their remaining lands in Georgia and agreed to move to Indian Territory. Some of these emigrants had settled along the northern bank of the Arkansas and on the Verdigris River, on lands later found to be within the limits of the territory assigned to the Western Cherokee by the treaty of 1828. This resulted in separate treaties being concluded with each on February 14, 1833, defining their respective boundaries to the satisfaction of all concerned. By the treaty made on this occasion with the Cherokee, the boundaries of the tract of seven million acres granted by the treaty of 1828 are defined so as to correspond with the present boundaries of the Cherokee country in Indian Territory, together with a strip two miles wide along the northern border, which was afterward annexed to the state of Kansas by the treaty of 1866. A tract in the northeastern corner, between the Neosho or Grand River and the Missouri line, was set apart for the use of the Seneca and several other remnants of tribes removed from their original territories. The western outlet established by the treaty of 1828 was re-established as a western extension from the seven-million-acre tract thus bounded, being what was afterward known as the Cherokee Strip or Outlet plus the two-mile strip extending westward along the southern line of Kansas.

After describing the boundaries of the main residential tract, the first article continues:

> In addition to the seven million acres of land thus provided for and bounded, the United States further guarantees to the Cherokee nation a perpetual outlet west and a free and undisturbed use of all the country lying west of the western boundary of the said seven million acres, as far west as the sovereignty of the United States and their <term>right of soil</term> extend—provided, however, that if the saline or salt plain on the great western prairie shall fall within the limits prescribed for the outlet, the right is reserved to the United States to permit other tribes of native people to obtain salt on that plain in common with the Cherokee—and <term>letters patent</term> shall be issued by the United States as soon as practicable for the lands hereby guaranteed.

The third article cancels, at the particular request of the Cherokee, that article of the treaty of 1828 by which the government was to give to the Cherokee a set of laws and a surveyor to survey lands for individuals, whenever so desired by the Cherokee.<note>² Treaty of 1833, *Indian Treaties*, pp. 561–565, 1837; Royce, *Cherokee Nation*, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, pp. 249–253, 1888; see also Treaty of New Echota, 1835, earlier in this volume, pp. 123–125.</note>

Their differences with the Creeks having been thus adjusted, the Arkansas Cherokee proceeded to occupy the territory guaranteed to them, where they were joined a few years later by their relocated kinsmen from the east. ### THE TEXAS BAND—1817–1900

As previously stated, a band of western <term>Cherokee</term> under <term>Chief Bowl</term>, dissatisfied with the delay in fulfilling the terms of the <term>treaty of 1817</term>, left <term>Arkansas</term> and crossed the <term>Red River</term> into <term>Texas</term>—which was then under <term>Mexican jurisdiction</term>. There, they were joined a few years later by <term>Tahchee</term> and others of the western band who were opposed to the <term>treaty of 1828</term>. Here they united with other refugee Indians from the United States, forming a loose confederacy known afterward as “the <term>Cherokee</term> and their associated bands.” This group consisted of <term>Cherokee</term>, <term>Shawano</term>, <term>Delaware</term>, <term>Kickapoo</term>, <term>Quapaw</term>, <term>Choctaw</term>, <term>Biloxi</term>, “Iawanie” (<term>Heyowani</term>, <term>Yowani</term>), “Unataqua” (<term>Nada'ko</term> or <term>Anadarko</term>, another <term>Caddo</term> subtribe), “Tahookatookie” (?), <term>Alabama</term> (a <term>Creek</term> subtribe), and “Cooshatta” (<term>Koasa'ti</term>, another <term>Creek</term> subtribe). Because the <term>Cherokee</term> were the largest and most important band, their chief, Bowl—known to the white settlers as <term>Colonel Bowles</term>—was regarded as the chief and principal leader of them all.

The refugees settled mainly along the <term>Angelina</term>, <term>Neches</term>, and <term>Trinity</term> rivers in eastern <term>Texas</term>, where Bowl attempted to obtain a land grant for their use from the <term>Mexican government</term>. According to Texan historians, they were tacitly permitted to occupy the country, and hopes were held out that a grant would be issued, but the legal papers had not been finalized when the <term>Texas Revolution</term> began.<sup>2</sup> According to the <term>Cherokee</term> account, the grant was actually issued, and the Spanish document, enclosed in a tin box, was on Bowl's person when he was killed.<sup>3</sup> In response to complaints from some of the American colonists in <term>Texas</term>, <term>President Jackson</term> issued a proclamation forbidding any Indians from crossing the <term>Sabine River</term> from the United States.<sup>4</sup>

In 1826–27, a dissatisfied American colony in eastern <term>Texas</term>, under the leadership of <term>Hayden Edwards</term>, organized what was known as the “<term>Fredonia Rebellion</term>” against the <term>Mexican government</term>. To secure an alliance with the <term>Cherokee</term> and their confederates, the Americans entered into a treaty by which the Indians were guaranteed the lands

In the fall of 1835 the <term>Texan revolution</term> began, resulting in the secession of <term>Texas</term> from <term>Mexico</term> and her establishment as an independent republic until she was annexed later to the <term>United States</term>. <term>General Samuel Houston</term>, a leading member of the revolutionary body, was an old friend of the <term>Cherokee</term>, and he presented the claims of the tribe and their confederates so strongly that the convention passed an act pledging to these tribes all the lands which they had held under the <term>Mexican government</term>. In accordance with this act, <term>General Houston</term> and <term>John Forbes</term> were appointed to hold a treaty with the <term>Cherokee</term> and their associated bands. They met the chiefs, including <term>Bowl</term> and <term>Big-mush</term> (<term>Gatûñ'wa'lĭ</term>, “<term>Hard-mush</term>”), of the <term>Cherokee</term>, at <term>Bowl</term>'s village on February 23, 1836, and concluded a formal treaty by which the <term>Cherokee</term> and their allies received a fee simple title to all the land lying “west of the San Antonio road and beginning on the west at a point where the said road crosses the <term>Angelina River</term>, and running up said river until it reaches the mouth of the first large creek below the great <term>Shawnee</term> village, emptying into the said river from the northeast, then running with said creek to its main source and from there a due north line to the <term>Sabine River</term> and with said river west. Then starting where the San Antonio road crosses the <term>Angelina</term> and with said road to where it crosses the <term>Neches River</term> and then running up the east side of said river in a northwest direction.” The historian remarks that the description is somewhat vague, but it is a literal transcription from the treaty.<note>Bonnell, Texas, pp. 142, 143, 1840.</note> The territory assigned in this way was approximately equivalent to the present <term>Cherokee County</term>, <term>Texas</term>.

The treaty provoked such general dissatisfaction among the <term>Texans</term> that it was not presented to the convention for ratification. <term>General Houston</term> became President of <term>Texas</term> in November, 1836, but notwithstanding all his efforts on behalf of the <term>Cherokee</term>, the treaty was rejected by the <term>Texas Senate</term> in a secret session on December 16, 1837.<note>Ibid., p. 143, 1840.</note>

<term>Texas</term>, having in the meantime achieved victorious independence, was now in a position to repudiate her engagements with the Indians; she did this not only with the <term>Cherokee</term>, but also with the <term>Comanche</term> and other wild tribes which had been induced to remain neutral during the struggle on the assurance of being secured in possession of their lands.

In the meantime <term>President Houston</term> was unremitting in his effort to secure the ratification of the <term>Cherokee</term> treaty, but without success. The first fight took place at a hill close to the main <term>Cherokee</term> village on the <term>Angelina</term>, where the Indians made a stand and defended their position well for some time. The second occurred at a ravine near the <term>Neches River</term>, where they were intercepted during their retreat. <term>Thrall</term> says, "After this fight, the Indians abandoned Texas, leaving their fine lands in the possession of the whites."<note>Bonnell, op. cit., pages 146–150; Thrall, op. cit., pages 118–120.</note>

By these two defeats, the forces of the <term>Cherokee</term> and their allies were completely broken up. ### THE CHEROKEE NATION IN THE WEST—1840-1900

With the final removal of the Cherokee from their native country and their reunion and reorganization under new conditions in Indian Territory in 1840, their indigenous period properly ends. The rest may be dismissed in a few paragraphs as being of interest more to the local historian than to the ethnologist. Having traced for three full centuries their gradual evolution from a nomadic tribe to a civilized Christian nation, with a national constitution and a national press printed in their own national alphabet, we can afford to leave the rest to others. The primary materials are readily accessible in the Cherokee national archives at Tahlequah, in the files of the *Cherokee Advocate* and other newspapers published in the Nation, and in the annual reports and other documents of the Indian Office.

For many years, the hunter and warrior had been giving way to the farmer and mechanic, and the forced exile made the change complete and final. Torn from their native streams and mountains, their council fires extinguished and their townhouses burned behind them, and transported bodily to a far distant country where everything was new and strange, they were forced by necessity to abandon the old life and adjust themselves to changed surroundings. The ball game was neglected and the green-corn dance prohibited, while the heroic traditions of former days became a fading memory or a tale to amuse a child. Instead of ceremonies and peace councils, we hear now of railroad deals and contracts with cattle syndicates; and instead of the old warrior chiefs who had made the Cherokee name a terror—Oconostota, Hanging-maw, Doublehead, and Pathkiller—we find the destinies of the

<summary>This page details the dispersal of the Texas Cherokee into Mexico and their reorganization in Indian Territory, marking their transition from a traditional tribe to a civilized nation with a formal government. This shift ended their indigenous era as they adapted to modern farming, politics, and a Westernized social structure.</summary>

<header>MOONEY] REORGANIZATION IN THE WEST—1840</header>
<page-num>147</page-num>

...a nation guided from then on by shrewd mixed-blood politicians, bearing white men's names and speaking the white man's language, and frequently with scarcely enough Indian ancestry to be visible in their features.

The change was not immediate, nor is it even yet complete; for although the trend is constantly away from the old ways, and although frequent intermarriage is rapidly lightening the complexion of the Indian skin, there are still several thousand full-blood Cherokee—enough to constitute a large tribe if set apart by themselves—who speak only their native language and in secret worship the nature gods of their ancestors. Here, as in other lands, the conservative members have found refuge in the mountain districts, while those of mixed-ancestry and the adopted white people are primarily located on the wealthier lowlands and in the railroad towns.

Upon the reorganization of the united Nation, the council grounds at Tahlequah were designated as the seat of government, and the current town was soon afterward laid out on that spot, taking its name from the old Cherokee town of Tălikwă', or Tellico, in Tennessee. The missions were re-established, the *Advocate* was revived, and the work of civilization was taken up again, though under great difficulties. Continued removals and persecutions, along with the awful suffering and death toll of the last great emigration, had impoverished and significantly reduced the population of the Nation and exhausted the courage of even the bravest. The bitterness caused by the New Echota treaty led to a series of murders, assassinations, and other acts of lawlessness, amounting almost to a civil war between the Ross and Ridge factions, until the Government was at last forced to interfere. The Old Settlers also had their grievances and complaints against the newcomers, so that the history of the Cherokee Nation for the next twenty years is largely a chronicle of factional disputes, during which civilization and all progress actually regressed to a state worse than that of a generation earlier.

Sequoya, who had occupied a prominent position in the affairs of the Old Settlers and assisted greatly in the reorganization of the Nation, became possessed by a desire to conduct linguistic investigations among the remote tribes, likely with the intention of creating a universal Indian alphabet. His mind also focused on the old tradition of a lost band of Cherokee living somewhere toward the western mountains. In 1841 and 1842, with a few Cherokee companions and with his provisions and papers loaded in an ox cart, he made several journeys into the West, received with kindness everywhere, even by the most remote tribes. Disappointed in his linguistic results, he started out in 1843 in search of the lost Cherokee, who were believed to be somewhere in northern Mexico; but, being now an old man and exhausted by hardship, he succumbed to the exertion and died—it is said, alone and unattended—near the

After rumors of his helpless condition reached them, a party was sent from the Nation to bring him back, but they arrived too late to find him alive. A pension of three hundred dollars, which had been previously granted to him by the Nation, was continued for his widow—the only literary pension in the United States. Besides his wife, he left two sons and a daughter.<sup>1</sup> Sequoyah district in the Cherokee Nation was named in his honor, and the great trees of California (*Sequoia gigantea*) also preserve his memory.

In 1846, a treaty was signed at Washington through which the conflicting claims of the "Old Settlers" and later emigrants were settled. It promised reimbursement for sums that were unfairly deducted from the five-million-dollar payment guaranteed under the treaty of 1835, and a general pardon was proclaimed for all past offenses within the Nation.<sup>2</sup> A final settlement of these treaty claims has not yet been reached, and the matter remains a subject of legal dispute, including all the treaties and agreements up to the present date.

In 1859, the devoted missionary Samuel Worcester—the author of numerous translations and the first organizer of the *Advocate*—died at the Park Hill mission in the Cherokee Nation. He passed away after spending thirty-five years in the service of the Cherokee, having suffered chains, imprisonment, and exile for their sake.<sup>3</sup>

The outbreak of the Civil War in 1861 found the Cherokee divided in their opinions. As slave owners, like the other Indians removed from the southern states, and surrounded by southern influences—with the agents in charge being southern sympathizers themselves—a considerable party in each of the tribes was inclined to take an active part with the Confederacy. The old Ridge party, led by Stand Watie and supported by the secret secessionist organization known as the Knights of the Golden Circle, declared for the Confederacy. The National party, led by John Ross and supported by the patriotic organization known as the Kitoowah society—whose members were later known as "Pin Indians"—declared for strict neutrality. At last, however, the pressure became too strong to resist, and on October 7, 1861, a treaty was concluded at Tahlequah with General Albert Pike, the commissioner for the Confederate states. By this treaty, the Cherokee Nation joined the Confederacy, as the Creeks, Choctaws, Chickasaws, Seminoles, Osages, Comanches, and several smaller tribes had already done.<sup>4</sup>

MOONEY] THE CIVIL WAR

Two Cherokee regiments were established for Confederate service, under the command of Stand Watie and Colonel Drew, respectively; the former was commissioned as a brigadier-general. They participated in several battles, the most significant among them being the Battle of Pea Ridge, Arkansas, on March 7, 1862. <note>In this battle, the Confederates were assisted by 4,000 to 5,000 Indians from the southern tribes, including the Cherokee, under the command of General Albert Pike.</note> In the following summer, the Union forces entered the Cherokee territory and sent a proposal to Ross, urging him to reject the treaty with the Confederate states, but the offer was indignantly refused. Shortly afterward, however, the men of Drew’s regiment, finding themselves unpaid and generally neglected by their allies, deserted almost as a group to the Union side. This forced Ross to reach an agreement with the Union commander, Colonel Weir. Leaving the Cherokee country, Ross retired to Philadelphia, from which he did not return until the end of the war. <note>Royce, Cherokee Nation, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, pages 329, 330, 1888.</note> In the meantime, Indian Territory was ravaged in turn by opposing factions and armed groups, and thousands of loyalist refugees were forced to seek safety in Kansas, where they were cared for by the government. Among these, at the end of 1862, were two thousand Cherokee. In the following spring, they were sent back to their homes under armed escort to give them an opportunity to plant a crop—seeds and tools being provided for that purpose—but they had hardly begun work when they were forced to retreat by the approach of Stand Watie and his regiment of Confederate Cherokee, estimated at seven hundred men. Stand Watie and his men, along with the Confederate Creeks and others, scoured the country at will, destroying or carrying off everything belonging to the loyalist Cherokee, who had now, to the number of nearly seven thousand, taken refuge at Fort Gibson. Refusing to take sides against a government which was still unable to protect them, they were forced to see all the prosperous results of twenty years of hard work swept away in this guerrilla warfare. In livestock alone, their losses were estimated at more than 300,000 head. <note>Same source, page 331.</note>

> “The events of the war brought more desolation and ruin to them than perhaps to any other community. Raided and looted in turn, not only by the Confederate and Union forces, but by the revengeful ferocity and hatred of their own divided factions, their country became a blackened and desolate waste. Driven from comfortable homes, exposed to want, misery, and the elements, they died like sheep in a snowstorm. Their houses, fences, and other improvements were burned, their orchards destroyed, their flocks and herds slaughtered or driven off, their schools broken up, their schoolhouses set on fire, and their churches and public buildings subjected to a similar fate; and that entire portion of their country which

<summary>During the Civil War, the Cherokee Nation was devastated by internal factional fighting and raids by both Confederate and Union forces, resulting in the displacement of thousands of refugees and the total destruction of their property and infrastructure. Chief John Ross eventually sided with the Union after Confederate neglect led to military desertions, while leaders like Stand Watie continued to fight for the Confederacy.</summary>

After five years of desolation, the Cherokee emerged from the war with their numbers reduced from 21,000 to 14,000,<sup>2</sup> and their whole country in ashes. On July 19, 1866, through a treaty concluded at Tahlequah, the nation was received back into the protection of the United States. A general amnesty was proclaimed, and all confiscations on account of the war were prohibited; slavery was abolished without compensation to former owners, and all Black people residing within the Nation were admitted to full Cherokee citizenship. By articles 15 and 16, permission was given to the United States to settle friendly Indians within the Cherokee home country or the Cherokee strip, provided there was consent from and purchase from the Nation. By article 17, the Cherokee sold the 800,000-acre tract in Kansas secured by the treaty of 1835, along with a two-mile strip running along the southern border of Kansas—which was thereafter to be included within the limits of that state—thus leaving the Cherokee country as it was before the recent surrender of the Cherokee strip. Payment was promised for damages from plundering by United States troops during the war; and $3,000 was to be paid out of the Cherokee funds to the Reverend Evan Jones, who was then disabled and in poverty, as a reward for forty years of faithful missionary labor. By article 26, "the United States guarantees to the Cherokees the quiet and peaceable possession of their country and protection against domestic feuds and insurrection, as well as hostilities from other tribes. They shall also be protected from intrusion by all unauthorized citizens of the United States attempting to settle on their lands or reside in their territory."<sup>3</sup>

The missionary, Reverend Evan Jones, who had followed the Cherokee into exile, and his son, John B. Jones, had been admitted to Cherokee citizenship the year before by a vote of the Nation. The act conferring this recognition states that "we do bear witness that they have done their work well."<sup>4</sup>

John Ross, now an old man, had been unable to attend this treaty, as he was in Washington at the time on business for his people. Before its ratification, he died in that city on August 1, 1866, at the age of seventy-seven. Fifty-seven of those years had been dedicated to the service of his Nation. No finer tribute was ever delivered than the memorial resolution passed by the Cherokee Nation upon learning of his death.<sup>5</sup> Despite repeated attempts to undermine his authority, his people had remained steadfast in their loyalty to him,

### MOONEY] FIRST RAILROAD—LITERARY REVIVAL—1870

And he died, as he had lived for nearly forty years, the officially recognized chief of the Nation. Despite repeated opportunities to enrich himself at the expense of his tribe, he died a poor man. His body was brought back and buried in the territory of the Nation. In remembrance of the great chief, one of the nine districts of the Cherokee Nation has been named by his Indian name, Cooweescoowee <note>46</note>.

Under the provisions of the recent treaty, the Delawares in Kansas, numbering 985, moved to Indian territory in 1867 and were incorporated as citizens of the Cherokee Nation. They were followed in 1870 by the Shawano, also chiefly from Kansas, numbering 770 <note>1 Royce, Cherokee Nation, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, pages 356-358, 1888; Constitution and Laws of the Cherokee Nation, pages 277-284; St. Louis, 1875.</note>. These immigrants settled mostly along the Verdigris River, in the northwestern part of the Nation. Under the same treaty, the Osage, Kaw, Pawnee, Ponca, Oto and Missouri, and Tonkawa were afterward settled on the western extension known then as the Cherokee strip. The captive Nez Percés of Joseph's band were also temporarily located there, but have since been moved to the states of Washington and Idaho.

In 1870, the Missouri, Kansas, and Texas railway, a branch of the Union Pacific system, was constructed through the lands of the Cherokee Nation under an agreement ratified by the Government; it was the first railroad to enter that country <note>2 Royce, op. cit., p. 367.</note>. Several others have since been constructed or planned.

The same year saw a Cherokee literary revival. The publication of the *Advocate*, which had been suspended since some years before the war, was resumed, and by authority of the Nation, John B. Jones began the preparation of a series of schoolbooks in the Cherokee language and alphabet for the benefit of those children who knew no English <note>3 Foster, Sequoyah, pages 147, 148, 1885; Pilling, Iroquoian Bibliography, 1888, articles "Cherokee Advocate" and "John B. Jones." The schoolbook series seems to have ended with the arithmetic—the cause, as the Cherokee national superintendent of schools explained to the author, was "too much white man."</note>.

In the spring of 1881, a delegation from the Cherokee Nation visited the East Cherokee still remaining in the mountains of North Carolina and extended to them a cordial and urgent invitation to move and incorporate upon equal terms with the Cherokee Nation in the Indian territory. In consequence, several parties of East Cherokee, numbering in all 161 persons, moved during the year to the western Nation, with the expense being paid by the Federal government. Others afterward applied for assistance to move, but as no further appropriation was made for the purpose, nothing more was done <note>4 Commissioner H. Price, Report of Indian Commissioner, page lxv, 1881, and page lxx, 1882; see also page 175.</note>. In 1883, the East Cherokee brought suit for a proportionate division of the Cherokee funds and other interests under previous treaties <note>5 Report of Indian Commissioner, page lxv, 1883.</note>, but their claim was
