In 1889, the Cherokee female seminary was completed at Tahlequah at a cost of over $60,000, supplementing the work of the male seminary, which had been built some years earlier at a cost of $90,000. The Cherokee Nation was now appropriating over $80,000 annually for school purposes; this included the support of the two seminaries, an orphan asylum, and over one hundred primary schools, besides which there were a number of mission schools. <note>Agent L. E. Bennett, in Report of Indian Commissioner, page 93, 1890.</note>

For a number of years, the pressure to open Indian Territory to white settlement had been growing in strength. Thousands of intruders had settled themselves upon the lands of each of the five civilized tribes, where they remained under various pretexts despite urgent and repeated appeals to the government by the Indians for their removal. Under treaties with the five civilized tribes, the right to decide citizenship or residence claims belonged to the tribes concerned. However, the intruders had at last become so numerous and strong that they had formed an organization among themselves to pass judgment upon their own claims, and others that might be submitted to them, with attorneys and ample funds to defend each claim in outside courts against the decision of the tribe. At the same time, the Government policy was moving steadily toward the reduction or complete breaking up of Indian reservations and the allotment of lands to the Indians in severalty, with a view to their final citizenship and the opening of the surplus lands to white settlement. As a part of this same policy, the jurisdiction of the United States courts was gradually being extended over the Indian country, taking notice of many things previously considered by the Indian courts under former treaties with the United States. Against all this, the Cherokee and other civilized tribes protested, but without avail. To add to the irritation, companies of armed "boomers" were organized for the express purpose of invading and seizing the Cherokee outlet and other unoccupied portions of the Indian territory—reserved by treaty for future Indian settlement—in defiance of the civil and military power of the Government.

We come now to what seems the beginning of the end of Indian autonomy. In 1889, a commission, afterward known as the Cherokee Commission, was appointed under an act of Congress to "negotiate with the Cherokee Indians, and with all other Indians owning or claiming lands lying west of the ninety-sixth degree of longitude in the Indian territory, for the cession to the United States of all their title, claim, or interest of every kind or character in and to said lands." In August of that year, the commission made a proposition to

# MOONEY] CESSION OF CHEROKEE STRIP—1892

Negotiations were held with Chief J. B. Mayes for the cession of all the Cherokee lands thus described, being that portion known as the Cherokee Outlet or Strip. The proposal was declined on the grounds that the Cherokee constitution forbade its consideration. <note>Report of the Indian Commissioner, page 22, 1889.</note> Other tribes were approached for a similar purpose, and the commission continued, with changing members from year to year, until agreements for cession and the taking of allotments had been made with nearly all the wilder tribes in what is now Oklahoma.

In the meantime, the Attorney General had rendered a decision denying the right of Indian tribes to lease their lands without the permission of the Government. At this time, the Cherokee were receiving an annual income of $150,000 from the lease of grazing privileges on the Strip; however, by a proclamation from President Harrison on February 17, 1890, ordering the cattlemen to vacate before the end of the year, this income was cut off and the Strip was rendered practically valueless to them. <note>See the proclamation by President Harrison and the order from the Indian Commissioner in the Report of the Indian Commissioner, pages lxxii-lxxiii, 421-422, 1890. The lease figures are from personal information.</note> The Cherokee were now forced to come to terms, and a second proposal for the <term>cession</term> of the Cherokee Strip was finally accepted by the National Council on January 4, 1892.

> “It was known to the Cherokee that for some time would-be settlers on the lands of the Outlet had been encamped in the southern end of Kansas, and by every influence at their command had been urging the Government to open the country to settlement and to negotiate with the Cherokee afterward, and that a bill for that purpose had been introduced in Congress.”

The payment was nearly $8,600,000, or about $1.25 per acre, for over 6,000,000 acres of land. One article of the agreement stipulates for

> “the reaffirmation to the Cherokee Nation of the right of local self-government.” <note>Commissioner T. J. Morgan, Report of the Indian Commissioner, pages 79-80, 1892.</note>

The agreement having been ratified by Congress, the Cherokee Strip was opened by Presidential proclamation on September 16, 1893. <note>Commissioner D. M. Browning, Report of the Indian Commissioner, pages 33-34, 1893.</note>

The movement for the abolition of the Indian governments and the allotment and opening of the Indian country had now gained such force that by an act of Congress approved March 3, 1893, the President was authorized to appoint a commission of three—known later as the Dawes Commission, after its distinguished chairman, Senator Henry L. Dawes of Massachusetts—to negotiate with the five civilized tribes of Indian Territory, namely, the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole, for

> “the <term>extinguishment</term> of tribal titles to any lands within that territory, now held by any and all of such nations and tribes, either by the <term>cession</term> of the same or some part of it to the United States, or by the allotment and division of the same in <term>severalty</term> among the Indians of such nations or tribes respectively as may be”

In September, the agent wrote: “The Indians now know that a survey of their lands is being made, and whether with or without their consent, the survey is going on. The meaning of such a survey is too plain to be disregarded, and it is justly considered as the initial step, solemn and authoritative, toward the overthrow of their present communal holdings. At this writing, surveying crews are at work in the <term>Creek</term>, <term>Choctaw</term>, and <term>Chickasaw</term> Nations, and therefore each one of these tribes has a visual demonstration of the actual intent and ultimate purpose of the government of the United States.” <note>Report of Agent D. M. Wisdom, Report of the Indian Commissioner for 1895, pages 159, 160, 1896.</note>

<page-num>155</page-num>
<header>->MOONEY] CONDITION IN 1895<-</header>

The general prosperity and advancement of the <term>Cherokee Nation</term> at this time can be judged from the report of the secretary of the Cherokee National Board of Education to Agent Wisdom. He reports 4,800 children attending two seminaries (male and female), two high schools, and one hundred primary schools; teachers were paid between $35 and $100 per month for nine months of the year. Fourteen primary schools were designated for the use of the Black citizens of the Nation; in addition, they had a fine high school, maintained, like all the others, at the expense of the Cherokee government. Besides the national schools, there were twelve mission schools providing excellent education for the children of both citizens and non-citizens. Children of non-citizens were not permitted to attend the Cherokee national schools, but instead had their own private subscription schools. The orphan asylum was ranked as a high school, where 150 orphans were housed and educated, with students graduating every year. It was a large three-story brick building, measuring 80 by 240 feet. The male seminary, which accommodated 200 pupils, and the female seminary, which accommodated 225 pupils, were also large three-story brick structures, measuring 150 by 240 feet. A board of education consisted of three members, all of whom were Cherokee by blood. The secretary added that the Cherokee are proud of their schools and educational institutions, and that no other country in the world is so blessed with general educational advantages.<note>Letter of A. E. Ivy, Secretary of the Board of Education, in the Report of the Indian Commissioner for 1895, page 161, 1896. The author can personally attest to the high quality of the seminary facilities.</note>

At this time, the Cherokee Nation numbered slightly over 25,000 Indian, white, and Black citizens. The total citizen population of the three races within the <term>Five Civilized Tribes</term> numbered about 70,000, while the number of non-citizens had increased to 250,000 and was rapidly growing.<note>Report of Agent Wisdom, in the same report, page 162.</note> Realizing that the swift and inevitable end would be the destruction of their national governments, the Cherokee began once more to consider moving away from the United States. This plan is outlined in a letter written by a brother of the <term>Principal Chief</term> of the Cherokee Nation, dated May 31, 1895, which we quote below.

After explaining that the United States government seems determined to dismantle the tribal independence of the Five Civilized Tribes and divide their lands—creating conditions under which the Cherokee could not survive—he continues:

> "Then, as a remedy that will lead us out of and away from this situation—one that promises to preserve us as a distinct people who can enjoy the social and political customs handed down to us from many generations past—my plan is for the Cherokee to sell all of their land holdings to the United States and divide the proceeds equally among the individuals. Then, those who wish to do so can unite to form an Indian colony and use their shared funds to collectively purchase land in Mexico"

. . . or South America a body of land sufficient for all their purposes, to be forever their joint home. . . I believe also that for those Indians who did not desire to join the colony and leave the country, provision should be made for them to buy back their old homes, or such other lands in the country here as they might desire; they could remain here and meet whatever fate awaits them. I believe this presents the most feasible and equitable solution to the questions that we must decide in the near future, and will prove absolutely just and fair to all classes and conditions of our citizens. I also believe that the same could be acted upon by any or all of the five civilized tribes. . . <note>1</note>

The final chapter is nearly written. By successive laws within the last ten years, the jurisdiction of the tribal courts has been steadily narrowed and the authority of the Federal courts proportionately extended. The right to determine Indian citizenship has been taken from the Indians and granted to a government commission. The lands of the five tribes have been surveyed and divided into sections by government surveyors; and by the sweeping provisions of the Curtis Act of June 28, 1898, "for the protection of the people of the Indian Territory," the entire control of tribal revenues is taken from the five Indian tribes and placed under a resident supervising inspector. Tribal courts are abolished, allotments are made compulsory, and authority is given to incorporate towns for white settlers within the Indian tribes. <note>2</note> By this act, the five civilized tribes are reduced to the status of ordinary reservation tribes under government agents, with white communities planted in their midst. In the meantime, the Dawes Commission, continued up to the present, has by constant effort broken down the opposition of the Choctaw and Chickasaw, who have consented to land allotment, while the Creeks and the Seminole are now wavering. <note>3</note> The Cherokee still hold out, the Ketoowah secret society (47) especially being strong in its resistance; when the end comes, it is possible that the protest will take the form of a mass emigration to Mexico. Late in 1897, the agent for the five tribes reports that "there seems to be a determined purpose on the part of many full-blood Indians . . . to emigrate to either Mexico or South America and there purchase new homes for themselves and families. Such individual action may grow to the size of a colony, and it is understood that generous grants of land can be obtained from the countries mentioned." <note>4</note> Mexican agents are now (1901) among the Cherokee advocating the scheme, which may develop to include a large proportion of the five civilized tribes. <note>5</note>

->MOONEY] U'TSĂLĂ AND CHARLEY<-

According to Wisdom, the Cherokee Nation numbered 34,461 people, categorized as follows: Cherokee by blood (including all degrees of mixed ancestry), 26,500; intermarried whites, 2,300; Black freedmen, 4,000; Delaware, 871; and Shawnee, 790. The total area of the Nation was 5,031,351 acres. If this land were divided per person under the provisions of the Curtis bill—after deducting 60,000 acres reserved for town-sites and other purposes—it would give each Cherokee citizen 144 acres. <note>1: Report of Agent D. M. Wisdom, Report of Indian Commissioner, p. 159, 1898.</note> It should be noted that the official rolls include a large number of people whose claims are disputed by the Cherokee authorities.

### THE EASTERN BAND

It remains to speak of the Eastern Band of Cherokee—the remnant that still clings to the woods and waters of their old homeland. As previously mentioned, a considerable number had eluded the troops during the general round-up of 1838 and had fled to the strongholds of the high mountains. Here they were joined by others who had managed to break through the guard at Calhoun and other collecting stations, until the total number of fugitives in hiding amounted to a thousand or more. These were principally the mountain Cherokee of North Carolina, the most conservative members of the Nation and those of the purest blood. About half of the refugee warriors had placed themselves under the command of a noted leader named U'tsălă ("Lichen"). He made his headquarters among the lofty peaks at the head of Oconaluftee. From this secure hiding place, although they were reduced to the extremes of suffering from starvation and exposure, they defied every effort to capture them.

The work of tracking down these fugitives proved to be such a difficult undertaking, and yielded so few results, that when Charley and his sons made their bold strike for freedom <note>2: See page 131.</note> General Scott eagerly seized the incident as an opportunity for compromise. To this end, he engaged the services of William H. Thomas, a trader who for more than twenty years had been closely identified with the mountain Cherokee and possessed their full confidence. Scott authorized him to submit a proposition to U'tsălă: if the chief would seize Charley and the others involved in the attack on the soldiers and surrender them for punishment, the pursuit of the other fugitives would be called off. They would then be allowed to stay unmolested until an effort could be made to secure permission from the federal government for them to remain.

Thomas accepted the assignment. Taking one or two Indians with him, he made his way over secret paths to U'tsălă's hiding place. He presented Scott’s proposition and explained to the chief that by helping to bring Charley’s party to justice according to the rules of war, he could secure a reprieve for his sorely pressed followers, with the ultimate hope that they might be allowed to remain in their

own country. Conversely, if he rejected the offer, the entire force of the seven thousand troops—who had now finished gathering and deporting the rest of the tribe—would be unleashed upon his own small band until the last refugee was either captured or killed.

U'tsǎlǎ considered the proposal long and seriously. His heart was bitter, for his wife and little son had starved to death on the mountainside, but he thought of the thousands who were already on their long march into exile, and then he looked around at his small band of followers. If only they might stay—even though a few must be sacrificed—it was better than for everyone to die, for they had sworn never to leave their country. He consented, and Thomas returned to report to General Scott.

Now a remarkable incident occurred which shows the character of Thomas and the masterful influence he already held over the Indians, although he was then hardly more than thirty years old. It was known that Charley and his party were hiding in a cave in the Great Smokies at the head of Deep Creek, but it was not thought likely that he could be captured without bloodshed and a further delay that might jeopardize the entire operation. Thomas decided to go to him and try to persuade him to come in and surrender. Declining Scott's offer of an escort, he went alone to the cave. Getting between the Indians and their guns while they were sitting around the fire near the entrance, he walked up to Charley and delivered his message. The old man listened in silence and then said simply, “I will come in. I do not want to be hunted down by my own people.” They came in voluntarily and were shot, as has already been narrated; only one, a mere boy, was spared because of his youth. This boy, now an old man, is still living: Wasitû'na, better known to the white people as Washington. <note>Charley's story as given here is from the author's personal information, derived chiefly from conversations with Colonel Thomas, Wasitû'na, and other old Indians. An ornate but somewhat inaccurate account is also given in Lanman's *Letters from the Alleghany Mountains*, written on the scene ten years after the events described. The leading facts are noted in General Scott's official dispatches.</note>

Having thus obtained a reprieve for the fugitives, Thomas next went to Washington to try to make some arrangement for their permanent settlement. Under the Treaty of New Echota in 1835, the Cherokee were entitled—besides the lump sum of five million dollars for the ceded lands—to additional compensation for the improvements they were forced to abandon and for property stolen by white citizens. This was in addition to a per-person allowance to cover the cost of removal and food for one year in the new country. The twelfth article had also provided that those Indians who chose to remain in the East and become citizens there might do so under certain conditions,

# MOONEY] PURCHASE OF QUALLA RESERVATION—1842

Each head of a family who remained was to be confirmed in a preemption right to 160 acres. Due to President Jackson’s fixed determination to deport every Indian, this permission was canceled and supplementary articles were substituted. By these articles, some additional compensation was allowed instead of the promised preemptions and all individual reservations granted under previous treaties.<note>1 See the New Echota treaty, December 29, 1835, and supplementary articles, March 1, 1836, in Indian Treaties, pages 633–648, 1837; also the full discussion of that same treaty in Royce, Cherokee Nation, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, 1888.</note> Every Cherokee was thus made a landless alien in his original country.

The last party of emigrant Cherokee had started for the West in December 1838. Nine months later, the refugees still scattered throughout the mountains of North Carolina and Tennessee were reported to number 1,046.<note>2 Royce, previously cited work, page 292.</note> Through persistent effort in Washington from 1836 to 1842, including one continuous stay of three years in the capital city, Thomas finally obtained government permission for these people to remain. Their share of the money due for confiscated improvements and reservations was placed at his disposal, as their agent and trustee, for the purpose of buying lands upon which they could be permanently settled. Under this authority, he bought several adjacent tracts of land for them at various times up to the year 1861, located on the Oconaluftee River and Soco Creek within the present Swain and Jackson counties of North Carolina, along with several detached tracts in the more western counties of the same state. The main body, located on the waters of the Oconaluftee—which was mostly within the limits of the cession of 1819—later became known as the Qualla Boundary, or Qualla Reservation, taking its name from Thomas's primary trading store and agency headquarters. The detached western tracts were within the final cession of 1835, but all alike were bought by Thomas from white owners. Since North Carolina refused to recognize Indians as landowners within the state, and persisted in this refusal until 1866,<note>3 Ibid., page 314.</note> Thomas, as their authorized agent under the Government, held the deeds in his own name. Before it was legally possible under the state laws to transfer the title to the Indians, his own affairs had become entangled and his health was impaired by age and the hardships of military service so that his mind failed. This left the entire question of the Indian title a subject of litigation until it was settled by the United States in 1875, supplemented by further decisions in 1894.

The Eastern Cherokee of today owe their existence as a people to Colonel William Holland Thomas, and for half a century he was as closely connected with their history as John Ross was with that of the main Cherokee Nation. Interestingly enough, their involvement in Cherokee affairs extended over nearly the same period, but while Ross participated in their national matters, Thomas dedicated his effort to

...a neglected band hardly known in the councils of the tribe. In his many-sided role, he strikingly resembles another white man prominent in Cherokee history, General Sam Houston.

Thomas was born in 1805 on Raccoon Creek, about two miles from Waynesville, North Carolina. His father, who was related to President Zachary Taylor, came from a Welsh family that had immigrated to Virginia early on, while on his mother’s side, he was descended from a Maryland family of Revolutionary War stock. He was an only child, born after his father had accidentally drowned a short time before the boy's birth. Being unusually bright for his age, he was hired when only twelve years old to work at an Indian trading store on Soco Creek, in what is now Jackson County. The store was owned by Felix Walker, the son of the Congressman of the same name who gained national fame for "talking for Buncombe." The store was on the south side of the creek, about a mile above the now-abandoned Macedonia mission within the current reservation; it was a branch of a larger business that Walker himself kept at Waynesville. The trade was mainly in skins and ginseng, or “sang.” The latter was shipped to China, where it was said to be worth its weight in silver. This trade was very profitable, as the price paid to the Indians was only ten cents per pound in merchandise for the green root, whereas it now brings seventy-five cents in cash on the reservation, with the supply steadily decreasing every year. The contract was for three years of service for a total payment of one hundred dollars plus expenses, but Walker focused so much of his attention on law studies that the Waynesville store was eventually closed due to debt. At the end of his contract term, young Thomas was forced to accept a collection of second-hand law books instead of other payment. How well he used them is clear from his later service in the state senate and other official positions.

Soon after starting his duties, he caught the attention of Yonaguska, or Drowning-bear (*Yâ’na-gûñ’skĭ*, “Bear-drowning-him”), the recognized chief of all the Cherokee then living along the Tuckasegee and Oconaluftee rivers—the old Kituhwa country. On learning that the boy had no father or brother, the old chief formally adopted him as his son. From then on, he was recognized by the tribe under the name *Wil-Usdi’*, or “Little Will,” as he was small in stature even as an adult. From his Indian friends, especially a boy of the same age who was his companion in the store, he learned the language as well as any white man ever has, so much so that in his later years, it remained in his memory more strongly than his native English. After the invention of the Cherokee alphabet, he also learned to read and write the language.

MOONEY] WILLIAM H. THOMAS

Indians, and Thomas's mother soon after moved from Waynesville to a farm which she purchased on the west bank of the Oconaluftee, opposite the mouth of Soco, where her son went to live with her, having now set up in business for himself at Qualla. Yonaguska and his immediate family continued to reside on a small reservation in the same neighborhood, while the rest of the Cherokee retired to the west of the Nantahala mountains, though they still visited and traded on Soco. After several moves, Thomas finally, soon after the removal in 1838, bought a farm on the northern bank of the Tuckasegee, just above the present town of Whittier in Swain county, and built a homestead there which he called Stekoa, after an Indian town destroyed by Rutherford which had occupied the same site. At the time of the removal, he was the proprietor of five trading stores in or adjoining the Cherokee country, namely: at Qualla town, near the mouth of Soco creek; on Scott's creek, near Webster; on Cheowa, near the present Robbinsville; at the junction of the Valley river and Hiwassee, now Murphy; and at the Cherokee agency at Calhoun (now Charleston), Tennessee. Besides carrying on a successful trading business, he was also studying law and taking an active interest in local politics.

In his capacity as agent for the eastern Cherokee, he laid out the lands purchased for them into five districts or "towns," which he named Bird town, Paint town, Wolf town, Yellow hill, and Big cove—the names which they still keep today—the first three being the names of Cherokee clans. <note>In the Cherokee language, *Tsiskwâ'hĭ* means "Bird place," *Ani'-Wâ'dihĭ* means "Paint place," *Wa'yâ'hĭ* means "Wolf place," *E'lawâ'di* means "Red earth" (now the Cherokee post-office and agency), and *Kâlânuñ'yĭ* means "Raven place." For a time, there was also a "Pretty-woman town" (*Ani'-Gilâ'hĭ*?).</note> He also drew up a simple form of government for them, the execution of which was in his own and Yonaguska's hands until the death of the latter; after that, the band knew no other chief than Thomas until his retirement from active life. In 1848, he was elected to the state senate and continued to serve in that capacity until the outbreak of the Civil War. As a state senator, he initiated a system of road improvements for western North Carolina and was also the founder of the Western North Carolina Railroad (now a part of the Southern system), originally projected to develop the copper mines of Ducktown, Tennessee.

With his colleagues in the state senate, he voted for secession in 1861 and at once resigned to recruit troops for the Confederacy, to which, until the close of the war, he gave his whole time, thought, and effort. In 1862, he organized the Thomas Legion, consisting of two regiments of infantry, a battalion of cavalry, a company of engineers, and a field battery, commanding it himself as colonel, although he was then nearly sixty years of age. Four companies were made up principally of his own Cherokee. The Thomas Legion operated chiefly as a frontier guard

After the close of the conflict, he returned to his home at Stekoa and again took charge, unofficially, of the affairs of the Cherokee. He cared for them during the smallpox epidemic of 1866 and assisted them through the unsettled conditions of the Reconstruction period. His own resources had been swept away by the war, and all his hopes had failed along with the lost cause. This, added to the effects of three years of hardship and anxiety in the field when he was already almost past the military age limit, soon after brought about a physical and mental collapse. He never afterward fully recovered except at intervals, when for a short time the old spirit would flash out in all its brightness. He died in 1893 at the advanced age of nearly ninety, retaining to the last the courteous manner of a gentleman by nature and training, with an exact memory and the clear-cut speech of a lawyer and man of affairs. To his work in the state senate, the people of western North Carolina owe more than to that of any other man, while among the older Cherokee the name of <term>*Wil-Usdi'*</term> is still revered as that of a father and a great chief.¹

Yonaguska, properly <term>*Yâ'nû-gûn'skĭ*</term>, the adoptive father of Thomas, is the most prominent chief in the history of the East Cherokee, although, strangely enough, his name does not occur in connection with any of the early wars or treaties. This is due partly to the fact that he was a peace chief and counselor rather than a war leader, and in part to the fact that the isolated position of the mountain Cherokee kept them mostly aloof from the tribal councils of those living to the west and south. In person he was strikingly handsome, being six feet three inches in height and strongly built, with a faint tinge of red—due to a slight strain of white blood on his father's side—relieving the brown of his cheek. In the power of oratory, he is said to have surpassed any other chief of his day. When the Cherokee lands on the Tuckasegee were sold by the treaty of 1819, Yonaguska continued to reside on a reservation of 640 acres in a bend of the river a short distance above the present Bryson City, on the site of the ancient <term>*Kituhwa*</term>. He afterward moved over to <term>*Oconaluftee*</term>, and finally, after the Removal, gathered his people about him and settled with them on <term>*Soco*</term> Creek on lands purchased for them by Thomas.

# MOONEY] YONAGUSKA

He was a prophet and reformer as well as a chief. When he was about sixty years old, he suffered a severe illness that ended in a trance, during which his people mourned him as if he were dead. After twenty-four hours, however, he regained consciousness and announced that he had been to the spirit world. There, he said he had spoken with friends who had died before him and with God, who had sent him back with a message for the Indians, promising to call for him again at a later time. From that day until his death, his words were listened to as those of someone inspired. He had previously been somewhat addicted to alcohol, but now, on the recommendation of Thomas, he not only quit drinking himself but also organized his tribe into a temperance society. To achieve this, he called his people together in a council. After clearly explaining the serious effects of drunkenness in an eloquent speech that moved some of his audience to tears, he declared that God had allowed him to return to earth specifically so he could warn his people and banish whiskey from among them. He then had Thomas write a pledge, which was signed first by the chief and then by every member of the council; from that time until after his death, whiskey was unknown among the Eastern Cherokee.

Although frequent pressure was applied to persuade him and his people to relocate to the West, he firmly resisted every attempt. He declared that the Indians were safer from aggression among their rocks and mountains than they could ever be in a land the white man found profitable, and that the Cherokee could only be happy in the country where nature had placed them. While advising peace and friendship with the white man, he always held to his Indian faith and was extremely suspicious of missionaries. On one occasion, after the Bible was first translated into the Cherokee language and alphabet, someone brought a copy of the Gospel of Matthew from New Echota. However, Yonaguska would not allow it to be read to his people until it had first been read to him. After listening to one or two chapters, the old chief dryly remarked, “Well, it seems to be a good book—strange that the white people are not better, after having had it so long.”

<margin><image-desc>A hand-drawn arrow in the left margin points to the following paragraph.</image-desc></margin>
He died at about eighty years of age in April 1839, within a year of the Removal. Shortly before his death, he had himself carried into the townhouse on Soco—the construction of which he had supervised—where, lying on a couch, he gave a final talk to his people. He recommended Thomas to them as their chief and again warned them earnestly never to leave their own country. Then, wrapping his blanket around himself, he quietly lay back and died. He was buried beside Soco, about a mile below the old Macedonia mission, with a simple mound of stones marking the spot. He left behind two wives and considerable property, including an elderly Black slave named Cudjo, who was devotedly attached to him. One of his daughters, Katâ’lsta, still sur-

The trance which, according to Thomas and Lanman, lasted about one day, is stretched by these later authors to fifteen days, with all 1,200 Indians marching and countermarching around the sleeping body!</note>

Yonaguska succeeded Yane'gwa (“Big-bear”) in authority. Yane'gwa appears to have been of considerable local prominence in his time, but even among the oldest members of the band, his name is now only a memory. He was one of the signers of the treaties of 1798 and 1805, and by the treaty of 1819, he was confirmed in a reservation of 640 acres. He was recognized as one of those living within the ceded territory who were “believed to be persons of industry and capable of managing their property with discretion,” and who had made significant improvements on their reserved tracts. This reservation, still known as the Big-bear farm, was on the western bank of the Oconaluftee River, a few miles above its mouth; it appears to have been the same land later occupied by Yonaguska.<note>The name in the treaties appears as Yonahequah (1798), Yohanaqua (1805), and Yonah (1819). — *Indian Treaties*, pages 82, 123, 268; Washington, 1837.</note>

Another of the old prominent figures among the East Cherokee was Tsunu'lăhûñ'skĭ, whose name was corrupted by the whites to Junaluska. He was a great warrior, and the ridge west of Waynesville is named after him. In his early life, he was known as Gûl'kăla'skĭ.<note>The name refers to something that habitually falls from a leaning position.</note> At the outbreak of the Creek War in 1813, he raised a party of warriors to go down and, as he boasted, “exterminate the Creeks.” When he did not meet with complete success, he announced the result—according to Cherokee custom—at the first dance after his return using a single word, *detsinu'lăhûñgû'*, “I tried, but could not.” This was given as a cue to the song leader, who immediately adopted it as the refrain of his song. From then on, the disappointed warrior was known as Tsunu'lăhûñ'skĭ, “One who tries, but fails.” He distinguished himself at the Horseshoe Bend, where the actions of the Cherokee decided the battle in favor of Jackson’s army. After the removal, he was often heard to say: “If I had known that Jackson would drive us from our homes, I would have killed him 그날 at the Horseshoe.” He accompanied the exiles in 1838 but later returned to his old home. He was allowed to stay, and in recognition of his services, the state legislature passed a special act in 1847 conferring citizenship upon him and granting him a tract of land in fee simple, though without the power to sell it.<note>Act quoted in the *Report of the Indian Commissioner for 1895*, page 636, 1896.</note> This reservation was in the Cheowa Indian settlement, near present-day Robbinsville in Graham County, where he died around the year 1858. His grave can still be seen just outside of Robbinsville.

As an illustration of his shrewdness, it is told that he once tracked a little Indian girl to Charleston, South Carolina, where she had been taken by kidnappers and sold as a slave. He regained her freedom by proving, through an expert microscopic examination, that her hair lacked any African characteristics. <note>The facts concerning Junaluska are based on information the author obtained from Colonel Thomas, Captain James Terrell, and Cherokee informants.</note>

Christianity was introduced among the Kituhwa Cherokee shortly before the Removal through Worcester and Boudinot’s translation of *Matthew*, which was first published at New Echota in 1829. In the absence of missionaries, the book was read by the Indians from house to house. After the Removal, a Methodist minister, Reverend Ulrich Keener, began visiting to preach at irregular intervals, and he was followed several years later by Baptist workers. <note>Information obtained by the author from Colonel Thomas.</note>

In the fall of 1839, the Commissioner of Indian Affairs reported that the East Cherokee had recently expressed a desire to join their brothers in the West, but they had been discouraged from doing so by the unsettled conditions in the Territory. He stated that “they have a right to remain or to go,” but since the interests of others are involved in their decision, they should decide without delay. <note>Commissioner Crawford, November 25, *Report of the Indian Commissioner*, page 333, 1839.</note>

In 1840, about one hundred Catawba—nearly all who remained of the tribe—became dissatisfied with their condition in South Carolina and moved as a group to take up residence with the Cherokee. However, latent tribal jealousies broke out, and at their own request, negotiations began in 1848, through Thomas and others, for their removal to Indian Territory. When the effort yielded no results, they soon began to drift back to their own homes, until, by 1852, only about a dozen remained among the Cherokee. By 1890, only one was left: an old woman who was the widow of a Cherokee husband. She and her daughter, both of whom spoke the language, were expert potters using the Catawba method, which differs significantly from that of the Cherokee. There are now two Catawba women, both married to Cherokee husbands, living with the tribe and practicing their native pottery art. While living among the Cherokee, the Catawba earned a reputation as doctors and leaders of dances. <note>Information obtained by the author from Colonel Thomas, Captain Terrell, and Indian sources; Commissioner W. Medill, *Report of the Indian Commissioner*, page 399, 1848; Commissioner Orlando Brown, *Report of the Indian Commissioner for 1849*, page 14, 1850.</note>

On August 6, 1846, a treaty was concluded in Washington with the representatives of the Western Cherokee Nation. By this treaty, the rights of the East Cherokee to participate in the benefits of the New Echota treaty of 1835 were clearly recognized, and provisions were made for a final settlement of all unpaid and pending claims due under that treaty. The benefits of the <term>New Echota treaty</term>, though not denied by the government, had been considered conditional upon their removal to the West. <note>Synopsis of the treaty, etc., in Royce, *Cherokee Nation*, Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, pages 300-313, 1888; see also earlier, page 148.</note>

In the spring of 1848, the author Lanman visited the East Cherokee and left an interesting account of their condition at the time, along with a description of their ball games, dances, and general customs. He had been the guest of <term>Colonel Thomas</term>, whom he describes as the guide, counselor, and friend of the Indians, as well as their business agent and chief, noting that the relationship was like that of a father and his children. He estimates the number of Indians at about 800 Cherokee and 100 <term>Catawba</term> on the "<term>Qualla town</term>" reservation—the name being in use even that early—with 200 more Indians residing in the more western portion of the state. Regarding their general condition, he says:

> About three-quarters of the entire population can read in their own language, and, though the majority of them understand English, a very few can speak the language. They practice the science of agriculture to a considerable extent and have acquired such a knowledge of the mechanical arts as meets all their ordinary needs; they manufacture their own clothing, their own plows and other farming tools, their own axes, and even their own guns. Their women are no longer treated as slaves, but as equals; the men labor in the fields and their wives are devoted entirely to household duties. They keep the same domestic animals as their white neighbors and cultivate all the common grains of the country. They are probably as temperate as any other class of people on the face of the earth, honest in their business dealings, moral in their thoughts, words, and deeds, and distinguished for their faithfulness in performing their religious duties. They are chiefly Methodists and Baptists and have regularly ordained ministers who preach to them every Sunday; they have also abandoned many of their merely senseless superstitions. They have their own court and try their criminals by a regular jury. Their judges and lawyers are chosen from among themselves. They maintain the public roads leading through their settlement. By a law of the state, they have a right to vote but seldom exercise that right, as they do not like the idea of being identified with any of the political parties. Except on festive days, they dress in the manner of the white man, but far more picturesquely. They live in small log houses of their own construction and have everything they need or desire in the way of food. They are, in fact, the happiest community that I have yet met with in this southern country. <note>Lanman, *Letters from the Alleghany Mountains*, pages 94-95, 1849.</note>

Among the other notable figures, Lanman speaks of <term>Salâ'lĭ</term> ("Squirrel"), a natural mechanic of the band who died only a few years ago:

> He is a fairly young man and has a remarkably thoughtful face. He is the blacksmith of his nation and, with some assistance, supplies all of <term>Qualla Town</term> with all their axes and plows. Even more impressively, he has manufactured a number of very superior rifles and pistols, including the stock, barrel, and lock, and he is also the builder of grist mills, which grind all the corn his people eat. A specimen of his workmanship in the form of a rifle may be seen at the Patent Office in Washington, where it was placed by Mr. Thomas; and I believe <term>Salola</term> is the first Indian who

On July 29, 1848, Congress approved an act to take a census of all those Cherokee who had remained in North Carolina after the Removal, and who still lived east of the Mississippi. This was done so that their share of the "removal and subsistence fund" under the <term>New Echota treaty</term> could be set aside for them. At the same time, a sum equal to $53.33⅓ was appropriated for each person, or their representative, to be used for covering the expenses of moving to the Cherokee Nation in the west and for living expenses there for one year whenever they should choose to move. Any surplus remaining after those expenses was to be paid to the individual in cash after their arrival in the west. The total amount spent this way was to be paid back to the Government from the general fund credited to the Cherokee Nation under the terms of the Treaty of New Echota. In the meantime, it was ordered that each eligible individual should be paid the interest accumulated on this per capita sum from the date the New Echota treaty was ratified (May 23, 1836), with annual interest payments at the same rate continuing after that.<note>See the act quoted in "The United States of America v. The others were payments of the annual interest upon the "removal and subsistence fund" set aside for their credit in 1848. To complete these payments, two other enrollments were conducted by D. W. In 1852, (Captain) James W. Terrell was hired by Thomas, who was then in the state senate, to take charge of his store at Qualla. He remained associated with Thomas and in close contact with the Indians from then until after the end of the war. During this time, he assisted as a special United States agent in the distribution of interest payments, and afterward served as a Confederate officer in the organization of the Indian companies, holding a commission as captain of Company A, Sixty-ninth North Carolina Confederate Infantry. Having an inquisitive nature, Captain Terrell was led to pay attention to the customs and mythology of the Cherokee, and to gather a wealth of information on the subject that was rarely possessed by a white man. He still lives at Webster, a few miles from the reservation, and is now seventy-one years of age.

In 1855, Congress ordered the per capita payment to the East Cherokee from the removal fund established for them in 1848, provided that North Carolina should first give assurance that they would be allowed to remain permanently in that state. This assurance, however, was not given until 1866, and the money was therefore not distributed but stayed in the treasury until 1875. At that time, it was used for the purchase of lands and the <term>quieting of titles</term> for the benefit of the Indians.<note>Royce, *as previously cited*, p. 314.</note>

From 1855 until after the Civil War, we find no official record of the East Cherokee, and our information must be obtained from other sources. It was, however, a most significant period in their history. At the outbreak of the war, Thomas was serving his seventh consecutive term in the state senate. As a passionate Confederate sympathizer, he was elected as a delegate to the convention that passed the secession ordinance. Immediately after voting in favor of that measure, he resigned from the senate in order to work for the Southern cause. Since he was already quite advanced in years, it is doubtful if his efforts would have gone beyond raising funds and other supplies if it were not for the fact that at this point, an effort was made by the Confederate General Kirby Smith to recruit the East Cherokee for active service.

[Morgan] had commanded the Cherokee at the Horseshoe Bend. Because of his Indian blood and historic ancestry, he was considered the most suitable emissary for the purpose. Early in 1862, he arrived among the Cherokee and, by appealing to old memories, so aroused their war spirit that a large number declared themselves ready to follow wherever he led. Believing that the issue at stake in the war did not concern the Indians, Thomas had discouraged their participation in it and advised them to remain at home in quiet neutrality. Now, however, knowing Morgan’s reputation for reckless daring, he became alarmed at the possible result of such leadership for them. Forced either to watch them leave his protection or to lead them himself, he chose the latter option and proposed that they enlist in the Confederate legion which he was about to organize. His goal, as he himself has stated, was to keep them out of danger as much as possible by using them as scouts and home guards throughout the mountains, away from the path of the large armies. Nothing of this was said to the Indians, who might not have been satisfied with such an arrangement. Morgan went back alone and the Cherokee enrolled under the command of their white chief.¹

The “Thomas Legion,” recruited in 1862 by William H. Thomas for the Confederate service and commanded by him as colonel, originally consisted of one infantry regiment of ten companies (Sixty-ninth North Carolina Infantry), one infantry battalion of six companies, one cavalry battalion of eight companies (First North Carolina Cavalry Battalion), one field battery (Light Battery) of 103 officers and men, and one company of engineers; in all about 2,800 men. Near the end of the war, the infantry battalion was expanded to a full regiment of ten companies. Companies A and B of the Sixty-ninth regiment and two other companies of the infantry regiment recruited later were composed almost entirely of East Cherokee Indians, with most of the commissioned officers being white men. The total number of Cherokee enlisted in this way was nearly four hundred, or about every able-bodied man in the tribe.²

The most important engagement in which they were involved occurred at Baptist Gap, Tennessee, on September 15, 1862, where Lieutenant Astu'gatâ'ga, "a splendid specimen of Indian manhood," was killed during a charge. The Indians were furious at his death, and before they could be restrained, they scalped one or two of the Federal dead. Ample apologies for this action were later given by their superior officers. The war, in fact, brought out all the latent Indian qualities in their nature. Before heading to the front, every man consulted an oracle stone to learn whether or not he might hope to return in safety. Their departure was celebrated with a grand, old-fashioned war dance at the townhouse on Soco, and the same dance was repeated at frequent intervals thereafter; the Indians were "painted and feathered in the good old style," and Thomas himself frequently assisted as the master of ceremonies. The ballplay, too, was not forgotten, and on one occasion, a detachment of Cherokee left to guard a bridge became so engrossed in the excitement of the game that they narrowly escaped capture during a sudden charge by the Federal forces. Due to Thomas's care for their welfare, they suffered only slightly in actual battle, although a number died of hardship and disease. When the Confederates evacuated eastern Tennessee in the winter of 1863–64, some of the white troops of the legion, along with one or two of the Cherokee companies, were transferred to western Virginia. By assignment to other regiments, a few of the Cherokee were present at the final siege and surrender of Richmond. The main body of the Indians, with the rest of the Thomas Legion, crossed over into North Carolina and served by protecting the western border until the close of the war, when they surrendered on parole at Waynesville, North Carolina, in May 1865; all those in the command were allowed to keep their guns. Their officers claim that they were the last of the Confederate forces to surrender. About fifty of the Cherokee veterans still survive; nearly half of them, led by Colonel Stringfield, attended the Confederate reunion at Louisville, Kentucky, in 1900, where they attracted a great deal of attention.¹

### MOONEY] CHEROKEE IN THE UNION ARMY

The payments established in 1848 had been paid annually up to and including the year 1859, at the rate of $3.20 per person, or a total (excluding the disbursing agent's commission) of $4,838.40 annually, based upon the original Mullay enumeration of 1,517 people.

Upon receipt of this report, it was enacted by the Confederate congress that the sum of $19,352.36 be paid to the East Cherokee to cover the interest for the four-year period from May 23, 1860, to May 23, 1864. In this connection, the Confederate commissioner suggested that the payment be made in provisions, which the Indians were then greatly in need of, and which they would be unable to purchase if the payment were made in cash due to the general scarcity. He adds that, according to his information, almost every Cherokee capable of bearing arms was then in the Confederate service. The roll provided by Captain Terrell is the original Mullay roll corrected to May 1860, with no reference being made to the later Mullay enumeration (2,133) already mentioned. There is no record to show that the payment authorized this way was ever made, and as the Confederate government was then in difficult straits, it is probable that nothing further was done in the matter.

In submitting his statement of previous payments, Colonel Thomas, their former agent, adds:

> As the North Carolina Cherokees have, like their brothers in the west, taken up arms against the Lincoln government, it is not probable that any further interest payments will be made by that government to any part of the Cherokee tribe. I also enclose a copy of the act of July 29, 1848, as far as it relates to the North Carolina Cherokees, and a printed explanation of their rights, prepared by me in 1851 and submitted to the attorney general, along with his opinion on it. These may not be entirely uninteresting to those who feel an interest in knowing something of the history of the Cherokee tribe of Indians, whose destiny is so closely identified with that of the Southern Confederacy.<note>Thomas-Terrell manuscript East Cherokee roll, with accompanying letters, 1864 (Bureau of American Ethnology archives).</note>

In a skirmish near Bryson City (then Charleston), Swain county, North Carolina, about a year after enlistment, a small party of Cherokee—perhaps a dozen in number—was captured by a detachment of Union troops and carried to Knoxville. Having become dissatisfied with their experience in the Confederate service, they were easily persuaded to switch to the Union side. Through the influence of their leader, Digăne'ski, several others were induced to desert to the Union army, making about thirty in all. As a part of the Third North Carolina Mounted Volunteer Infantry, they served with the Union forces in the same region until the close of the war. When they returned to their homes, they found their tribesmen so bitterly angry with them that for some time their lives were in danger. Eight of these individuals are still alive in 1900.<note>Personal information from Colonel W. H. Thomas, Captain J. W. Terrell, Chief N. J. Smith, and others; see also Carrington, *Eastern Band of Cherokees*, Extra Bulletin of Eleventh Census, page 21, 1892.</note>

smallpox from an infected camp near Knoxville. Shortly after his return, he became sick and soon died. As the characteristic pustules had not appeared—the disease seeming to work internally—the nature of his illness was not at first suspected, since smallpox had been an unknown disease among the Cherokee for nearly a century. Consequently, his funeral was largely attended. A week later, a number of those who had been present became sick, and Colonel Thomas recognized the disease as smallpox in all its virulence. It spread throughout the tribe during the early spring of 1866. In spite of all the efforts of Thomas, who brought a doctor from Tennessee to care for them, more than one hundred members of the small community died as a result. The fatal outcome was largely due to the Indians' lack of knowledge regarding the disease; finding their own remedies ineffective, they used the intense traditional treatment of plunging into the river and using cold-water douches, which resulted in death in almost every case. Thus the war brought its harvest of death, misery, and civil conflict to the East Cherokee.<note>Author's information from Colonel Thomas and others. Various informants have exaggerated the number of deaths to several hundred, but the estimate given here, obtained from Thomas, is probably more reliable.</note>

Shortly after this event, Colonel Thomas was forced by physical and mental illness to retire from further active participation in the affairs of the East Cherokee. This followed more than half a century spent in close connection with them, during most of which time he had been their most trusted friend and adviser. Their affairs immediately became a prey to confusion and internal conflict, which continued until the United States stepped in as an arbitrator.

In 1868, Congress ordered another census of the East Cherokee to serve as a guide for future payments. The roll was to include only those persons whose names had appeared on the Mullay roll of 1848 and their legal heirs and representatives. The work was completed in the following year by S. H. Sweatland, and a payment of interest then due under previous laws was made by him based on this list.<note>Royce, Cherokee Nation, Fifth Ann. Rep. Bureau of Ethnology, p. 314, 1888.</note> “In accordance with their earnestly expressed desire to be brought under the immediate charge of the government as its wards,” the Congress that ordered this last census directed that the Commissioner of Indian Affairs should assume the same responsibility over the East Cherokee as over other tribes. However, as no extra funds were made available for this purpose, the matter was put on hold.<note>Commissioner F. A. Walker, Report of Indian Commissioner, p. 25, 1872.</note> An unratified treaty made this year with the Cherokee Nation in the west contained a condition that any Cherokee east of the Mississippi who moved to the Cherokee Nation within three years should be entitled to full citizenship and privileges there; however, after that date, they could be admitted only by an act of the Cherokee national council.<note>Royce, op. cit., p. 353.</note>

### MOONEY] ADJUSTMENT OF TITLES 1873-76

Because of the need for governmental supervision, the tribe felt the necessity of some central authority. On December 9, 1868, a general council of the East Cherokee assembled at Cheowa, in Graham County, North Carolina, and took preliminary steps toward adopting a regular form of tribal government under a constitution. N. J. Smith, who later became the principal chief, served as the clerk of the council. The new government was formally inaugurated on December 1, 1870. It provided for a first and a second chief to serve for a term of two years, minor officers to serve for one year, and an annual council representing each Cherokee settlement within the state of North Carolina. Kâ'lahû', known as "All-bones" and commonly called Flying-squirrel or Sawnook (Sawănu'gĭ) by the whites, was elected chief. A new constitution was adopted five years later, which fixed the chief's term of office at four years.<sup>1</sup>

The status of the lands held by the Indians had now become a matter of serious concern. As previously stated, the deeds had been made out by Thomas in his own name, as state laws at that time forbade Indians from owning real estate. As a result of his losses during the war and his subsequent disability, the Thomas properties—of which the Cherokee lands were technically a part—had become legally entangled. The entire estate had passed into the hands of creditors. The most important of these, William Johnston, had obtained sheriff's deeds in 1869 for all of these Indian lands under three separate judgments against Thomas, totaling $33,887.11. To resolve the matter and secure title and possession for the Indians, Congress in 1870 authorized a lawsuit to be filed in their name to recover their interests. This suit began in May 1873 in the United States Circuit Court for western North Carolina. A year later, the matters in dispute were submitted by agreement to a board of arbitrators, whose award was confirmed by the court in November 1874.

The award found that Thomas had purchased, with Indian funds, a tract estimated to contain 50,000 acres on the Oconaluftee River and Soco Creek, known as the Qualla boundary, along with a number of individual tracts outside that boundary. It also found that the Indians were still indebted to Thomas for $18,250 toward the purchase of the Qualla boundary lands. From this amount, $6,500 (which they had paid to Johnston to release titles) was to be deducted, which, with interest to the date of the award, totaled $8,486. Additionally, a further sum of $2,478 had been entrusted to Terrell—the business clerk and assistant to Thomas—and turned over by him to Thomas as a creditor of the Indians under power of attorney. This latter sum, with interest to the date of the award, totaled $2,697.89. This left a balance of $7,066.11 due from the Indians to Thomas or his legal creditor, Johnston. The award declared that on account of the questionable manner in

To enable the Indians to clear off this lien on their lands and for other purposes, Congress in 1875 directed that whatever remained of the "removal and subsistence fund" set aside for their benefit in 1848 should be used "in perfecting the titles to the lands awarded to them, and to pay the costs, expenses, and liabilities attending their recent lawsuits; also to purchase and eliminate the titles of any white persons to lands within the general boundaries allotted to them by the court, and for the education, improvement, and civilization of their people." In accordance with this authority, the unpaid balance and interest owed to Johnston, totaling $7,242.76, was paid to him in the same year. Shortly afterward, approximately fifteen thousand additional acres were purchased on behalf of the Indians, with the Commissioner of Indian Affairs being appointed as trustee for the Indians. For the better protection of the Indians, the lands were made inalienable except by the consent of the council and upon the approval of the President of the United States. The deeds for the Qualla boundary and the 15,000-acre purchase were signed on October 9, 1876, and August 14, 1880, respectively.<note>See Royce, *above-cited work*, pages 315–318; Commissioner T. J. Morgan, *Report of Indian Commissioner*, page xxix, 1890. The final settlement, under the laws of North Carolina, was not completed until 1894.</note> As the boundaries of the various purchases were only vaguely defined, a new survey of the entire Qualla boundary and the adjoining tracts was authorized. The work was entrusted to M. S. Temple, a deputy United States surveyor, who completed it in 1876; his survey maps of the reservation were accepted as the official standard.<note>Royce, *above-cited work*, pages 315–318; Carrington, *Eastern Band of Cherokees*, with a map of the Temple survey, Extra Bulletin of the Eleventh Census, 1892.</note>

Once the titles and boundaries had been adjusted, the Indian Office assumed regular supervision of Eastern Cherokee affairs, and in June 1875, the first agent since the retirement of Thomas was sent out in the person of W. C. McCarthy. According to his report, he found the Indians destitute and discouraged, possessing almost no livestock or farming tools. There were no schools, and very few full-blooded Cherokee could speak English, although to their credit nearly all could read and write their own language, as parents taught the children. Under his authority, a distribution was made of livestock, seed wheat, and farming tools, and several schools were established. In the next year, however,

In the meantime, Kâʻlahûʻ had been succeeded as chief by Lloyd R. Welch (Daʻsiʻgiyaʻgi), an educated mixed-blood from Cheowa, who served for about five years, dying shortly after his reelection to a second term (48). He built a strong record through his efforts to reconcile the various factions that had formed after the withdrawal of Thomas’s guiding influence, and by defeating the schemes of fraudulent white claimants and troublemakers. Shortly before his death, the Government, through Special Agent John A. Sibbald, recognized his authority as principal chief, along with the constitution that had been adopted by the band under his leadership in 1875. N. J. Smith (Tsaʻlădihĭʻ), who had previously served as clerk of the council, was elected to fill his remaining term and continued to serve until the fall of 1890.²

There is no further official notice of the Eastern Cherokee until 1881, when Commissioner Price reported that they were still without an agent or superintendent. He stated that, as far as the Indian Office was concerned, their affairs were in an irregular and unsatisfactory condition, while internal feuds were increasing the difficulties and slowing the band’s progress. In the spring of that year, a visiting delegation from the Cherokee Nation in the west extended an urgent invitation to them to move to Indian Territory. The Indian Office encouraged the project, resulting in 161 members of the band moving to Indian Territory during that year, with the government covering the expenses. Others were reported to be willing to move, and the Commissioner recommended an appropriation for this purpose, but since Congress failed to act, the matter was dropped.³

The neglected condition of the Eastern Cherokee was brought to the attention of the Quakers—long-time friends of the Indians—through an appeal made on their behalf by members of that society living in North Carolina. The Western Yearly Meeting of Indiana volunteered to undertake the work of civilization and education. On May 31, 1881, representatives of the Friends entered into a contract with the Indians, subject to government approval, to establish and maintain an industrial school and other common schools among them for ten years. These were to be supported partly by the annual interest from the trust fund held by the government for the Eastern Cherokee, and partly by funds provided by the Friends themselves. Through the efforts of Barnabas C. Hobbs of the Western Yearly Meeting, a yearly contract to the same effect was established with the Commissioner—

The Commissioner of Indian Affairs later in the same year renewed the arrangement, and it was continued by various commissioners who followed to cover the ten-year period ending June 30, 1892. At that time, the contract system was terminated and the Government assumed direct control. Under this joint arrangement, with some initial aid from the North Carolina Meeting, work was begun in 1881 by Thomas Brown and several teachers sent by the Indiana Friends. They established a small training school at the agency headquarters in Cherokee, along with several day schools in the outlying settlements. He was succeeded three years later by H. W. Spray, an experienced educator. Along with a staff of efficient assistants and greatly improved facilities, Spray continued to work for the advancement of the Indians until the contract system ended eight years later. <note>See Commissioner T. J. Morgan, Report of Indian Commissioner, pp. 141-145, 1892; the author’s personal information from B. C. Hobbs, Chief N. J. Smith, and others. The Eastern Cherokee owe much of their current civilization and education to the work conducted under his leadership.

From some travelers who visited the reservation around this time, we have a pleasant account of a trip along Soco Creek and a day spent with Chief Smith at Yellow Hill. They describe the Indians as living so similarly to white people that a stranger could rarely distinguish an Indian's cabin or small mountain farm from that of a white man. Their principal crop was corn, which they ground themselves, and they also had plenty of apples, peaches, and plums, as well as a few small herds of ponies and cattle. Their needs were so few that they had little use for money. Their traditional clothing had long been out of use, and their dress was like that of white people, except that moccasins were worn instead of shoes. They manufactured their own clothing using spinning wheels and looms. They also produced finely carved pipes and well-made baskets, and the positive influence of the recently established schools was already evident in the children. <note>Zeigler and Grosscup, Heart of the Alleghanies, pp. 36-42, 1883.</note>

In 1882, the agency was reestablished and provisions were made to take a new census of all Cherokee living east of the Mississippi, with Joseph G. Hester appointed to the task. <note>Commissioner H. Price, Report of Indian Commissioner, pp. lxix-lxx, 1882.</note> The census was submitted as complete in June 1884. It contained the names of 1,881 persons in North Carolina, 758 in Georgia, 213 in Tennessee, 71 in Alabama, and 33 in other areas, totaling 2,956 people. <note>Report of Indian Commissioner, pp. li-lii, 1884.</note> Although this census received the approval and certification of the Eastern Cherokee council, a large portion of the band still refuses to recognize its authority, claiming that a large number of people enrolled in it have no Cherokee blood.

# MOONEY] SUIT AGAINST WESTERN CHEROKEE—1883–86

The Eastern Cherokee had never stopped fighting for a share in the rights and privileges given to the Western Nation under treaties with the Government. In 1882, a special agent was appointed to investigate their claims. The following year, under the authority of Congress, the Eastern Band of Cherokee brought a lawsuit in the Court of Claims against the United States and the Western Cherokee Nation to determine its rights to the permanent annuity fund and other trust funds held by the United States for the Cherokee Indians. <note>Commissioner H. Price, Report of Indian Commissioner, pp. lxix–lxxi, 1882, also "Indian legislation," ibid., p. 214; Commissioner H. Price, Report of Indian Commissioner, pp. lxv–lxvi, 1883.</note> The case was decided against the Eastern Band, first by the Court of Claims in 1885, <note>Commissioner J. D. C. Atkins, Report of Indian Commissioner, p. lxx, 1885.</note> and finally, on appeal, by the Supreme Court on March 1, 1886. In its decision, that court held that the Cherokee in North Carolina had dissolved their connection with the Cherokee Nation and ceased to be a part of it when they refused to accompany the main body during the Removal. The court ruled that if Indians in North Carolina or any state east of the Mississippi wished to enjoy the benefits of the common property of the Cherokee Nation in any form whatever, they must be readmitted to citizenship in the Cherokee Nation and comply with its constitution and laws.

In accordance with this decision, the agent in the Indian Territory was instructed to issue no more residence permits to claimants for Cherokee citizenship, and it was officially announced that all persons entering that country thereafter without the consent of the Cherokee authorities would be treated as intruders. <note>Same commissioner, Report of the Indian Commissioner, p. xlv, 1886; decision quoted by same commissioner, Report of Indian Commissioner, p. lxxvii, 1887.</note> This decision, cutting off the Eastern Cherokee from all hope of sharing in any of the treaty benefits enjoyed by their western relatives, was a bitter disappointment to them all—especially to Chief Smith, who had worked unceasingly on their behalf from the start of the legal proceedings. In view of the result, Commissioner Atkins strongly recommended a plan as the best method of settling them in permanent homes, secure from white intrusion and from anxiety caused by their uncertain tenure and legal status in North Carolina. He suggested that negotiations be opened through government channels for their readmission to citizenship in the Cherokee Nation, to be followed, if successful, by the sale of their lands in North Carolina and their removal to the Indian Territory. <note>Same commissioner, Report of the Indian Commissioner, p. li, 1886; reiterated by him in Report for 1887, p. lxxvii.</note>

In order to acquire a more definite legal status, the Cherokee residing in North Carolina—being practically all those of the Eastern Band having genuine Indian interests—became a corporate body under the laws of the state in 1889. The act, ratified on March 11, declares in its first section "That the North Carolina or Eastern Cherokee Indians, resident or domiciled in the counties of Jackson, Swain, Graham, and Cherokee, be and at the same time are hereby

...created and established as a legal and political entity under the name and title of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, with all the rights, franchises, privileges, and powers belonging to corporations under the laws of the state of North Carolina. <note>See the full act in the Report of the Indian Commissioner, vol. 1, pp. 680–681, 1891.</note>

On August 2, 1893, former Chief Smith died at Cherokee in his fifty-seventh year, having dedicated more than twenty years to the service of his people. Nimrod Jarrett Smith, known to the Cherokee as *Tsa'lădihi'*, was the son of a mixed-race father and an Indian mother. He was born near present-day Murphy in Cherokee County, North Carolina, on January 3, 1837. His earliest memories were of the suffering that accompanied the flight of the refugees into the mountains during the Removal period. Although his mother spoke very little English, his father was quite intelligent and had served as an interpreter and translator for Reverend Evan Jones at the old Valleytown mission. As the boy grew to manhood, he received a good education, which, combined with his commanding presence, made him an influential figure among his peers. At twenty-five years of age, he joined the Thomas Legion as a first sergeant in Company B of the Sixty-ninth North Carolina (Confederate) Infantry, serving in that role until the end of the war. He was the clerk of the council that wrote the first Eastern Cherokee constitution in 1868. Upon the death of Principal Chief Lloyd Welch in 1880, he was elected to fill the remaining term, continuing in office through successive re-elections until the end of 1891—a period of about twelve years, which was the longest term served by any chief up to that time. As principal chief, he signed the contract that established the school program in 1881. For several years afterward, his duties—especially regarding the lawsuit against the Western Cherokee—required him to spend much of his time in Washington. At home, his time was almost as constantly occupied with attending to the needs of a people who depended on him. Although the band’s constitution entitled him to a salary of five hundred dollars per year, no part of this salary was ever paid because of his people's limited resources. He was only partially reimbursed, shortly before his death, for the expenses he took on during official visits to Washington. Despite many opportunities to enrich himself at the expense of his people, he maintained his honor and died a poor man.

Physically, Chief Smith was an impressive man of great stature, standing six feet, four inches tall and well-proportioned. He had an upright figure, with long black hair curling down over his shoulders, a deep musical voice, and a kind spirit and natural dignity that never failed to impress strangers. He is survived by his widow, who is white, and several children. <note>From the author’s personal acquaintance; see also Zeigler and Grosscup, *Heart of the Alleghanies*, pp. 38–39, 1883; Agent J. L. Holmes, in the Report of the Indian Commissioner, p. 160, 1885; Commissioner T. J. Morgan, Report of the Indian Commissioner, p. 142, 1892; Moore, Roster of the North Carolina Troops, vol. IV, 1882.</note>

In 1894, the long-standing legal battle between the Eastern Cherokee and a number of creditors and claimants to Indian lands within and next to the Qualla boundary was finally settled by a compromise. By this agreement, the various white tenants and claimants within the boundary agreed to sign a <term>quitclaim</term> and move out upon payment of a total of $24,552. For another disputed adjacent tract of 33,000 acres, the United States agreed to pay $1.25 per acre on behalf of the Indians. Once the necessary Government approval was obtained, Congress appropriated a sufficient amount to carry out the agreement. This finally completed a perfect and unencumbered title to all the lands claimed by the Indians, with the exception of a few outlying tracts of minor importance.<note>Commissioner D. M. Browning, Report of the Indian Commissioner for 1894, pp. 81–82, 1895; also Agent T. W. Potter, same source, p. 398.</note>

In 1895, the Cherokee living in North Carolina on the reservation and in the outlying settlements were officially reported to number 1,479.<note>Agent T. W. Potter, Report of the Indian Commissioner for 1895, p. 387, 1896.</note> A year later, an epidemic of the flu spread through the band. As a result, the census of 1897 showed only 1,312 people.<note>Agent J. C. Hart, Report of the Indian Commissioner, p. 208, 1897.</note> Among those who died at this time were Big-witch (Tskĭl-e'gwa), the oldest man of the band, who clearly remembered the Creek War, and Wadi'yăhĭ, the last old woman who preserved the art of making double-walled baskets. In the next year, the population had recovered to 1,351. The description of the way of life then common to most of the Indians applies nearly as well today:

> While they are industrious, these people are not progressive farmers and have not learned modern methods. The same crops are grown continuously until the soil will no longer produce or is washed away, at which point new ground is cleared or plowed. The value of crop rotation and fertilizing has not yet been discovered or taught. . . .
> 
> That these people can live at all on the products of their small farms is due to the extreme simplicity of their food, clothing, and lifestyle. The typical house is made of logs, measuring about fourteen by sixteen feet, consisting of one room, just high enough for the residents to stand upright, perhaps with a small loft for extra storage. The roof is made of split shingles or <term>shakes</term>. There are no windows; the open door provides whatever light is required. At one end of the house is the fireplace, with an outside chimney made of stones or sticks sealed with clay. The furniture is simple and inexpensive. An iron pot, a baking kettle, a coffee pot and mill, a small table, and a few cups, knives, and spoons are all that is needed. These items, along with one or two homemade bedsteads, a few pillows and quilts, and feather mattresses for winter blankets as well as for their usual purpose, make up the main household possessions. For outdoor work, there is an ax, a hoe, and a shovel plow. A wagon or cart may be owned, but it is not essential. This setup is inexpensive and serves every purpose. The usual food is bean bread with coffee. In the fall, chestnut bread is also eaten. Beef is rarely eaten, but pork is highly valued, and many hogs are kept, running wild and untended during the summer.<note>Agent J. C. Hart, Report of the Indian Commissioner, pp. 218–219, 1898.</note>
