they are numbered 1,376 within the act of incorporation, of whom about 1,100 live on the reservation. The rest live farther to the west, on the Nantahala, Cheowa, and Hiwassee rivers. This does not include people of mixed ancestry in adjoining states and several hundred unrecognized claimants. Those listed own approximately 100,000 acres of land, of which 83,000 are included within the Qualla reservation and a connected tract in Jackson and Swain counties. They receive no rations or annuities and are entirely self-supporting; the annual interest on their trust fund established in 1848, which has decreased to about $23,000, is applied to the payment of taxes upon their unoccupied common lands. From time to time they have made leases for timber, gold-washing, and grazing privileges, but without any great profit to themselves. By special appropriation, the government supports an industrial training school at Cherokee, the agency headquarters, where 170 pupils are currently being boarded, clothed, and educated in the practical duties of life. This school, which in its operations is a model of its kind, owes much of its usefulness and high standing to the efficient management of Prof. H. W. Spray (Wilsǐnǐ'), already mentioned, who combines the duties of superintendent and agent for the band. His chief clerk, Mr. James Blythe (Diskwǎ'nǐ, “Chestnut-bread”), a Cherokee by blood, at one time served as agent, being perhaps the only Indian who has ever served in such a capacity.

The exact legal status of the Eastern Cherokee is still a matter of dispute, as they are simultaneously wards of the government, citizens of the United States, and (in North Carolina) a corporate body under state laws. They pay real estate taxes and perform road service, exercise the right to vote,<note>In the recent election of November 1900, they were prevented by the local polling officials from either registering or voting, and the matter is currently being contested.</note> and are subject to the local courts, but do not pay poll tax or receive any pauper assistance from the counties; neither can they make free contracts or <term>alienate</term> (transfer ownership of) their lands (49). Under their tribal constitution, they are governed by a principal and an assistant chief, elected for a term of four years, with an executive council appointed by the chief, and sixteen councilors elected by the various settlements for a term of two years. The annual council is held in October at Cherokee, on the reservation; the proceedings are conducted in the Cherokee language and recorded by their clerk in the Cherokee alphabet, as well as in English. The present chief is Jesse Reid (Tsě'si-Ska'tsǐ, “Scotch Jesse”), an intelligent man of mixed ancestry, who fills the office with dignity and ability. As a people, they are peaceable and law-abiding, kind and hospitable, providing for their simple needs by their own industry without asking or expecting outside assistance. Their fields, orchards, and fish traps, along with some few domestic animals and occasional hunting, supply them with food, while by the sale of

## MOONEY] PRESENT CONDITION

[By the sale of] ginseng and other medicinal plants gathered in the mountains, along with fruit and honey of their own raising, they obtain whatever additional supplies they need from the traders. The majority are fairly comfortable—faring far better than most Indian tribes and being little, if at all, behind their white neighbors. In literacy, they may even be said to surpass them; in addition to the results of nearly twenty years of schoolwork among the younger people, nearly all the men and some of the women can read and write their own language. All wear modern clothing, though an occasional pair of moccasins is seen, while the women find ways to satisfy their cultural love of color by wearing red bandanna kerchiefs instead of bonnets. The older people still cling to their ancient rites and sacred traditions, but the dances and the ballplay <note>Refers to the traditional Cherokee stickball game.</note> are fading, and the era of traditional Indian life is nearly over.

### III—NOTES TO THE HISTORICAL SKETCH

(1) TRIBAL SYNONYMY (page 15): Very few Indian tribes are known to us by the names they call themselves. One reason for this is that white settlers usually heard of a tribe from its neighbors, who spoke different languages, before they ever encountered the tribe itself. Many of the popular tribal names were originally nicknames given by neighboring tribes, often referring to some unique custom, and in many cases, these names would be strongly rejected by the people they describe. As a rule, each tribe had a different name in every surrounding Indian language, in addition to the names given by Spanish, French, Dutch, or English settlers.

*Yûñ'wiyă'*—This word is made up of *yûñwĭ* (person) and *yă* (real or principal). The assumption of superiority is clearly evident in Indian tribal names; for example, the Iroquois, Delawares, and Pawnee call themselves *Oñwe-hoñwe*, *Leni-lenape'*, and *Tsariksi-tsa'riks*, respectively. All of these may be translated as "men of men," "men who surpass other men," or "real men."

*Kitu'hwagĭ*—This word, which cannot be broken down into simpler parts, is derived from *Kitu'hwă*, the name of an ancient Cherokee settlement that was formerly located on the Tuckasegee River, just above the current Bryson City in Swain County, North Carolina. In 1730, it was noted as one of the "seven mother towns" of the tribe. Its inhabitants were called *Ani'-Kitu'hwagĭ* (people of Kituhwa) and seem to have had a dominant influence over all the towns along the Tuckasegee and the upper part of the Little Tennessee River; the entire group was often categorized together as *Ani'-Kitu'hwagĭ*. Linguistically, the dialect of these towns occupied a middle ground between the dialects spoken to the east (on the headwaters of the Savannah River) and to the west (on the Hiwassee and Cheowah Rivers, and the lower Little Tennessee). In various forms, the word was adopted by the Delaware, Shawnee, and other northern Algonquian tribes as a synonym for Cherokee, likely because the Kituhwa people guarded the northern Cherokee frontier. In the form *Cuttawa*, it appears on Vaugondy’s French map of 1755. Due to similar spelling, Schoolcraft incorrectly lists it as a synonym for Catawba, while Brinton wrongly claims it is an Algonquian term imaginatively translated as "inhabitants of the great wilderness." Among the western Cherokee, it is now the name of a powerful secret society that was founded shortly before the Civil War <note>The original text refers to this as the "War of the Rebellion."</note>.

*Cherokee*—This name appears in at least fifty different spellings. In its standard accepted form, which dates back to at least 1708, it has given its name to counties in North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and Alabama—all within the tribe's ancient territory—as well as to as many as twenty other geographic locations across the United States. In the Eastern or Lower dialect, with which English settlers first became familiar, the form is *Tsa'răgĭ'*, from which we get "Cherokee." In other dialects, the form is *Tsa'lăgĭ'*. It is clearly a foreign name to the tribe, as is often the case with tribal names, and it is most likely of Choctaw origin, having come north through the Mobilian trade jargon. It should be noted that De Soto, whose historians first used the word in the form *Chalaque*, obtained his interpreters from the Gulf Coast of Florida. Fontanedo, writing around 1575, mentions other inland tribes known to the natives of Florida by names which seem to be

MOONEY] TRIBAL SYNONYMY 183

The name is of Choctaw origin; for instance, the Canagacole is interpreted as “wicked people,” where the final part is apparently the Choctaw word *okla* or *ogula*, meaning “people.” This word also appears in names like Pascagoula, Bayou Goula, and Pensacola. Shetimasha, Atakapa, and probably Biloxi are also Choctaw names, even though the tribes themselves have other origins. Because the Choctaw controlled much of the Gulf coast and were the primary traders in that region, it was natural for explorers landing among them to adopt their names for more distant tribes.

The name seems to refer to the fact that the tribe occupied a region of caves. In the “Choctaw Lexicon” by Allen Wright (1880), page 87, we find *choluk*, a noun signifying a hole, cavity, pit, or chasm, and an adjective signifying hollow. In the manuscript Choctaw dictionary of Cyrus Byington, held in the library of the Bureau of American Ethnology, we find *chiluk*, a noun meaning a hole, cavity, hollow, or pit, with a note stating that in its usual application, it means a cavity or hollow rather than a hole passing through something. As an adjective, the same form is given as signifying hollow or having a hole, such as *iti chiluk* (a hollow tree), *aboha chiluk* (an empty house), or *chiluk chukoa* (to enter a hole). Other noun forms listed are *chuluk* and *achiluk* in the singular and *chilukoa* in the plural, all signifying a hole, pit, or cavity. Verb forms include *chilukikbi* (to make a hole) and *chilukba* (to open and form a fissure).

In accordance with the character of the Cherokee language, the root form of the tribal name takes noun or verb prefixes according to its connection with the rest of the sentence and is declined, or rather conjugated, as follows: SINGULAR—first person, *tsi-Tsa'lăgǐ*, I am a Cherokee; second person, *hi-Tsa'lăgǐ*, you are a Cherokee; third person, *a-Tsa'lăgǐ*, he is a Cherokee. DUAL—first person, *âsti-Tsa'lăgǐ*, we two are Cherokee; second person, *sti-Tsa'lăgǐ*, you two are Cherokee; third person, *ani'-Tsa'lăgǐ*, they two are Cherokee. PLURAL—first person, *atsi-Tsa'lăgǐ*, we (several) are Cherokee; second person, *hitsi-Tsa'lăgǐ*, you (several) are Cherokee; third person, *ani'-Tsa'lăgǐ*, they (several) are Cherokee. It should be noted that the third person dual and plural forms are identical.

*Oyata'ge'ronon'*, etc.—The Iroquois (Mohawk) form is provided by Hewitt as *O-yată'-ge'ronon'*, of which the root is *yată'* (cave), *o* is the assertive prefix, *ge* is the locative "at," and *ronon'* is the tribal suffix, equivalent to the English *-ites* or "people." The word, which has several dialect forms, signifies “inhabitants of the cave country” or “cave-country people,” rather than “people who dwell in caves,” as interpreted by Schoolcraft. The same root *yată'* also occurs in the Iroquois name for the opossum, which is a burrowing animal. As is well known, the Allegheny region is specifically a cave country; these caves were used by the Indians for burial and shelter, as proven by numerous remains found within them. It is likely that the Iroquois simply translated the name (*Chalaque*) current in the South, just as we see in the West, where the major plains tribes are known by translations of the same names in all the different languages. The Wyandot name for the Cherokee, *Wataiyo-ronon'*, and their Catawba name, *Mañteraⁿ'*, both seem to refer to emerging from the ground and may have been originally intended to convey the same idea of "cave people."

*Rickahockan*—This name was used by the German explorer Lederer in 1670 as the name of the people living in the mountains to the southwest of the Virginia settlements. On his map, he places them in the mountains on the southern headwaters of the Roanoke River in western North Carolina. He states that, according to his Indian informants, the Rickahockan lived beyond the mountains in a land of "great waves," which he interpreted to mean the seashore (!); however, it is more likely that the Indians were trying to convey, through sign language, the idea of a series of mountain ridges. The name likely had a Powhatan origin and is clearly identical to "Rechahecrian" from the Virginia chronicles of about the same period; the "r" in the latter spelling might be a misprint. It may be related to *Righkahauk*, shown on Smith's 1607 map of Virginia as the name of a town within the

We have too little material of the Powhatan language to risk an interpretation, but it may possibly contain the root of the word for sand, which appears as *lekawa, nikawa, negaw, rigawa, rekwa*, etc., in various eastern Algonquian dialects, from which come Rockaway (sand) and Recgawawank (sandy place). The Powhatan form, as given by Strachey, is *racawh* (sand). He also gives *rocoyhook* (otter), *reihcahahcoik* (hidden under a cloud, overcast), *rickahone* or *reihcoan* (a comb), and *rickewh* (to divide in halves).

**Talligewi**—As Brinton rightly says: “No name in the Lenape legends has caused more extensive discussion than this one.” On Colden’s map in his “History of the Five Nations” (1727), we find the “Alleghens” indicated on the Allegheny river. Heckewelder, who recorded the Delaware tradition in 1819, says: “Those people, as I was told, called themselves Talligeu or Talligewi. Colonel John Gibson, however, a gentleman who has a thorough knowledge of the Indians and speaks several of their languages, is of the opinion that they were not called Talligewi, but Alligewi; and it seems that he is right from the traces of their name which still remain in the country, the Allegheny river and mountains having undoubtedly been named after them. The Delawares still call the former Alligewi Sipu (the river of the Alligewi)”—*Indian Nations*, p. 48, 1876 edition. Loskiel, writing based on the authority of Zeisberger, says that the Delawares knew the entire country drained by the Ohio by the name Alligewinengk, meaning “the land in which they arrived from distant places,” basing his interpretation on an etymology compounded from *talli* or *alli* (there), *icku* (to that place), and *ewak* (they go), with a locative ending. Ettwein, another Moravian writer, says the Delawares called “the western country” Alligewenork, meaning a warpath, and called the river Alligewi Sipo. This definition would make the word come from *palliton* or *alliton* (to make war), *ewak* (they go), and a locative—essentially, “they go there to fight.” Trumbull, an authority on Algonquian languages, derives the river name from *wulik* (good, best), *hanne* (rapid stream), and *sipu* (river), of which its Iroquois name, *Ohio*, is nearly an equivalent. Rafinesque translates Talligewi as “found there,” from *talli* (there) and some other root not provided (Brinton, *Walam Olum*, pp. 229–230, 1885).

It must be noted that the names Ohio and Alligewi (or Allegheny) were not applied by the Indians, as we do, to different parts of the same river, but to the entire stream, or at least the majority of it from its head downward. Although Brinton sees no necessary connection between the river name and the traditional tribal name, the statement by Heckewelder, generally a reliable authority on Delaware matters, makes them identical.

In the traditional tribal name, Talligewi or Alligewi, *wi* is an assertive verbal suffix, so the form properly means “he is a Tallige,” or “they are Tallige.” This comes very close to *Tsa'lăgi'*, the name by which the Cherokee call themselves, and it may have been an early corruption of that name. In Zeisberger’s Delaware dictionary, however, we find *waloh* or *walok*, signifying a cave or hole, while in the “Walam Olum” we have *oligonunk* translated as “at the place of caves,” the region being further described as a buffalo land on a pleasant plain, where the Lenape, advancing seaward from a less productive northern region, at last found food (*Walam Olum*, pp. 194–195). Unfortunately, like other indigenous productions of its kind among the northern tribes, the Lenape chronicle is suggestive rather than complete and connected. With more light, it may be that seeming discrepancies would disappear and we would find at last that the Cherokee, in ancient times as in the historic period, were always the southern vanguard of the Iroquoian race, always primarily a mountain people, but with their flank resting upon the Ohio and its great tributaries, following the trend of the Blue Ridge and the Cumberland as they slowly gave way before the pressure from the north until they were finally cut off from the parent stock by the wedge of Algonquian invasion, but always, whether in the north

(2) MOBILIAN TRADE LANGUAGE (page 16): This trade jargon, based on Choctaw but also borrowing from all the neighboring dialects and even from the more northern Algonquian languages, was spoken and understood among all the tribes of the Gulf states. It likely extended as far west as Matagorda Bay and northward along both banks of the Mississippi to the Algonquian frontier near the entrance of the Ohio River. It was called *Mobilienne* by the French, named after Mobile, the great trading center of the Gulf region. Along the Mississippi, it was sometimes known also as the Chickasaw trade language, as Chickasaw is a dialect of the Choctaw language proper. Jeffreys, in 1761, compares the uses of this jargon to the <term>lingua franca</term> of the Levant. It was clearly through the aid of this intertribal medium that De Soto’s interpreter from Tampa Bay could converse with all the tribes they met until they reached the Mississippi. Some of the names used by Fontanedo about 1575 for the tribes northward from Appalachee Bay seem to be derived from this source, as were the names of other tribes of the Gulf region in later times. This occurred regardless of linguistic relationships and included, among others, the Taensa, Tunica, Atakapa, and Shetimasha, who represent as many different linguistic stocks. In his report on the southwestern tribes in 1805, Sibley says that “Mobilian” was spoken in addition to their native languages by all the Indians who had come from the east side of the Mississippi. Among those using it, he names the Alabama, Apalachi, Biloxi, Chactoo, Pacana, Pascagoula, Taensa, and Tunica. Woodward, writing from Louisiana more than fifty years later, says: 
> “There is still a language the Texas Indians call the Mobilian tongue, which has been the trading language of almost all the tribes that have inhabited the country. I know white men who speak it now. There is a man now living near me who is fifty years of age, raised in Texas, who speaks the language well. It is a mixture of Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Natchez <note>originally written Netches</note>, and Apalachi <note>originally written Apelash</note>”—Reminiscences, 79. 

For further information, see also Gatschet, Creek Migration Legend, and Sibley, Report.

The Mobilian trade jargon was not the only one of its kind. In America, as in other parts of the world, the common needs for communication have resulted in the formation of several such mixed dialects, which sometimes prevail over wide areas. In some cases, the language of a dominant tribe also serves as the common medium for all the tribes of a particular region. In South America, we find the <term>lingoa geral</term>, based on the <term>Tupi</term> language, which is understood for everyday purposes by all the tribes of the immense central region from Guiana to Paraguay, including almost the whole Amazon basin. On the northwest coast, we find the well-known “Chinook jargon,” which takes its name from a small tribe formerly residing at the mouth of the Columbia River and is in common use among all the tribes from California far up

(3) <term>DIALECTS</term> (page 17): The linguistic affinity of the Cherokee and northern Iroquoian dialects, although now well established, is not usually obvious on the surface, but requires a close analysis of words, with a knowledge of the laws of phonetic changes, to make it appear. The superficial agreement is perhaps most apparent between the Mohawk and the Eastern (Lower) Cherokee dialects, as both of these lack the labials entirely and use *r* instead of *l*. MOONEY] IROQUOIAN MIGRATIONS
189

It should be noted that the Eastern and Middle dialects are nearly the same, except for the change of *l* to *r* and the complete absence of the labial *m* from the Eastern dialect. Meanwhile, the Western dialect differs considerably from the others, particularly in the greater frequency of the liquid *l* and the softening of the guttural *g*; these changes tend to make it the most musical of all the Cherokee dialects. It is also the standard literary dialect. In addition to these three principal dialects, there are some peculiar forms and expressions used by a few individuals that indicate the former existence of one or more other dialects, which are now too extinct to be reconstructed. As with most other tribes, the ceremonial forms used by the priests are so filled with archaic and figurative expressions that they are almost unintelligible to the common people.

### (4) IROQUOIAN TRIBES AND MIGRATIONS (p. 17): 
The Iroquoian stock, named after the celebrated Iroquois Confederacy, formerly consisted of fifteen to twenty tribes who spoke nearly as many different dialects, including, among others, the following:

Wyandot, or Huron.
Tionontati, or Tobacco nation.
Attiwan'daron, or Neutral nation. } **Ontario, Canada.**
Tohotaenrat.
Wenrorono.

Mohawk.
Oneida.
Onondaga. } **Iroquois, or Five Nations, New York.**
Cayuga.
Seneca.

Erie. **Northern Ohio, etc.**
Conestoga, or Susquehanna. **Southern Pennsylvania and Maryland.**
Nottoway. } **Southern Virginia.**
Meherrin?. }
Tuscarora. **Eastern North Carolina.**
Cherokee. **Western Carolina, etc.**

Both tradition and history point to the St. Lawrence region as the early home of this stock. All authorities agree on this point. Hale says, in his paper on Indian Migrations (page 4):

> “The constant tradition of the Iroquois depicts their ancestors as emigrants from the region north of the Great Lakes, where they lived in early times with their Huron brothers. This tradition is recorded in great detail by Cadwallader Colden, the surveyor-general of New York, who in the early part of the last century wrote his well-known ‘History of the Five Nations.’ It is told in a slightly different form by David Cusick, the Tuscarora historian, in his ‘Sketches of Ancient History of the Six Nations,’ and it is repeated by Mr. L. H. Morgan in his now-classic work, ‘The League of the Iroquois,’ for which he gathered his information mainly from the Senecas. Finally, as we learn from the narrative of the Wyandot Indian Peter Clarke, in his book titled ‘Origin and Traditional History of the Wyandotts,’ the belief of the Hurons matches that of the Iroquois in this respect. Both point similarly to the country immediately north of the St. Lawrence, and especially to that portion of it lying east of Lake Ontario, as the early home of the Huron-Iroquois nations.”

Nothing is known of the traditions of the Conestoga or the Nottoway, but the Tuscarora tradition, as provided by Cusick and other authorities, describes them as a direct offshoot from the northern Iroquois, with whom they later reunited. The Cherokee traditions also, as we have seen, trace their origin to the north, thus completing the cycle. “The striking fact has become evident that the migration route of the Huron-Cherokee family has been from the northeast to the southwest—that is, from eastern Canada, on the Lower St. Lawrence, to the mountains of northern Alabama.”—Hale, Indian Migrations, page 11.

The retirement of the northern Iroquoian tribes from the St. Lawrence region was

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Iroquoian migrations, specifically focusing on the pressure from Algonquian tribes that displaced the Hurons and Iroquois, followed by notes on the Delaware "Walam Olum" and the identification of the "Fish River."</meta>

Due to the hostility of their Algonquian neighbors, who forced the Hurons and their allies to take refuge around Georgian Bay and the head of Lake Ontario, the Iroquois themselves retreated to central New York. In 1535, Cartier found the shores of the river from Quebec to Montreal occupied by an Iroquoian people, but upon the settlement of the country seventy years later, the same region was found in the possession of Algonquian tribes. The confederation of the five Iroquois nations, probably formed about the year 1540, enabled them to stop the Algonquian invasion and to take the offensive. Linguistic and other evidence shows that the separation of the Cherokee from the parent stock must have occurred long before this period.

(5) **WALAM OLUM** (p. 18): The name means “red score,” from the Delaware *walam*, “painted,” or more specifically “painted red,” and *olum*, “a score or tally mark.” The Walam Olum was first published in 1836 in a work titled “The American Nations,” by Constantine Samuel Rafinesque, a versatile and prolific, but very erratic, French scholar who spent the latter half of his life in this country, dying in Philadelphia in 1840. He asserted that it was a translation of a manuscript in the Delaware language, which was an interpretation of an ancient, sacred, metrical legend of the Delawares. This legend was recorded in pictographs cut into wood, which were obtained in 1820 by a medical friend of his among the Delawares then living in central Indiana. He says himself:

> “These actual *olum* were first obtained in 1820 as a reward for a medical cure; they were considered a curiosity and were inexplicable. In 1822, the songs attached to them in the original language were obtained from another individual, but I could find no one able to translate them. I therefore had to learn the language afterward, with the help of Zeisberger, Heckewelder, and a manuscript dictionary, specifically to translate them, which I only accomplished in 1833.”

On account of the unique character of the alleged Indian record and Rafinesque’s own lack of standing among his scientific contemporaries, little attention was paid to the discovery until Brinton took up the subject a few years ago. After a critical examination of the evidence from every point of view, he arrived at the conclusion that the work is a genuine native production, although the manuscript translation is faulty—partly due to the white scribe’s ignorance of the language and partly due to the Indian narrator’s ignorance of the meaning of the archaic forms. Brinton’s edition <note>quod vide; see the mentioned work</note>, published from Rafinesque’s manuscript, gives the legend in triplicate form—pictograph, Delaware, and English translation—with notes and a glossary, and a valuable ethnological introduction by Brinton himself.

It is not known whether any of the original woodcut pictographs of the Walam Olum still exist, although a statement by Rafinesque implies that he had seen them. As evidence of the truth of his statement, however, we have the fact that precisely similar pictographic series cut into birch bark—each pictograph representing a line or couplet of a sacred metrical recitation—are now known to be common among the Ojibwa, Menomini, and other northern tribes. In 1762, a Delaware prophet recorded his visions in hieroglyphics cut into a wooden stick, and about the year 1827, a Kickapoo reformer adopted the same method to spread a new religion among the tribes. One of these “prayer sticks” is now in the National Museum, being all that remains of a large basketful delivered to a missionary in Indiana by a party of Kickapoo Indians in 1830 (see the plate and description on pages 665, 697, and following in the author’s Ghost-dance Religion, Fourteenth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology).

(6) **FISH RIVER** (p. 18): Namæsi Sipu (Heckewelder, Indian Nations, 49), or Namassipi (Walam Olum, p. 198). Deceived by a slight similarity of sound, Heckewelder identifies this river with the Mississippi, but as Schoolcraft shows (Notes on Iroquois, p. 316), the true name of the Mississippi is simply Misi-sipi, “great river.” “Fish river” would be a most inappropriate name for such a turbulent current, where only the coarser species can live. The mere fact that there can be a question of identity among experts familiar with Indian nomenclature would indicate that it

(7) FIRST APPEARANCE OF WHITES (p. 19): It is possible that this may refer to one of the earlier adventurers who sailed along the North Atlantic coast in the first decades after the discovery of America. These included Sebastian Cabot in 1498, Verrazano in 1524, and Gomez in 1525. As these voyages were not followed by permanent occupation of the country, it is doubtful if they made any lasting impression on Indian tradition. The author has chosen to assume, along with Brinton and Rafinesque, that the *Walam Olum* reference is to the settlement of the Dutch at New York and the English in Virginia shortly after 1600.

(8) DE SOTO'S ROUTE (p. 26): On May 30, 1539, Hernando de Soto of Spain, with 600 armed men and 213 horses, landed at Tampa Bay on the west coast of Florida in search of gold. After more than four years of hardship and disappointed wandering from Florida to the great plains of the West and back again to the Mississippi—where De Soto died and his body was committed to the great river—311 men, all who remained of the expedition, finally arrived at Pánuco, Mexico, on September 10, 1543.

For the history of this expedition—the most important ever undertaken by Spain within the eastern United States—we have four original authorities. First is the very brief but evidently truthful Spanish report of Biedma, an officer of the expedition, presented to the King in 1544 immediately after the return to Spain. Next in order, but of primary importance for its detail and general reliability, is the narrative of an anonymous Portuguese cavalier of the expedition, commonly known as the Gentleman of Elvas, originally published in Portuguese in 1557. Next comes the Spanish narrative of Garcilaso, written in 1587 but not published until later. Unlike the others, the author was not an eyewitness to what he describes; instead, he compiled his account chiefly from the oral recollections of an old soldier of the expedition more than forty years after the event, supplemented by papers written by two other soldiers under De Soto. As might be expected, Garcilaso's narrative, though written in a flowery style, is full of exaggeration and trivial incidents. It compares unfavorably with the other accounts, though it probably provides more minor details. The fourth original account is an unfinished Spanish report by Ranjel, the secretary of the expedition, written soon after reaching Mexico and afterward incorporated—with considerable changes—by Oviedo into his "*Historia natural y general de las Indias*." As this fourth narrative remained unpublished until 1851 and has never been translated, it has been entirely overlooked by commentators until now, with the exception of Winsor, who mentions it incidentally. In general, it agrees well with the Elvas narrative and sheds valuable light on the history of the expedition.

The principal authorities, while maintaining a general unity in their narrative, differ greatly in detail—especially in estimates of numbers and distances—frequently to such an extent that it is useless to attempt to reconcile their conflicting statements. In general, the Gentleman of Elvas is the most moderate in his expressions, while Biedma takes a middle ground and Garcilaso exaggerates greatly. For example, the first named gives De Soto 600 men, Biedma says there were 620, while Garcilaso claims there were 1,000. At one stage of the journey, the Portuguese Gentleman gives De Soto 700 Indians as an escort, Biedma says 800, and Garcilaso claims 8,000. At the battle of Mavilla, the Elvas account reports 18 Spaniards and 2,500 Indians killed; Biedma says 20 Spaniards were killed without estimating the Indian casualties; while Garcilaso claims 82 Spaniards and over 11,000 Indians were killed. There is just as much discrepancy regarding distances. Biedma records the distance from Guaxule to Chiaha as four days, Garcilaso says it was six days, and Elvas says seven days. Regarding the length of an average day's march, we find it

estimated all the way from “four leagues, more or less” (Garcilaso) to “seven or eight leagues every day” (Elvas). In another place, the Elvas chronicler states that they usually covered five or six leagues a day through inhabited territories, but that in crossing uninhabited regions—such as that between Canasagua and Chiaha—they marched as far as possible every day for fear of running out of provisions. One of the most glaring discrepancies appears regarding the distance between Chiaha and Coste. Both the Portuguese writer and Garcilaso place Chiaha upon an island—a statement which in itself is at odds with any present conditions—but while the former makes the island a fraction over a league in length, the latter says that it was five leagues long. The next town was Coste, which Garcilaso places immediately at the lower end of the same island, while the Portuguese Gentleman represents it as being seven days away, even though he himself had given the island the shorter length.

Despite a deceptive appearance of exactness, especially in the Elvas and Ranjel narratives, which take the form of a daily journal, the conclusion is unavoidable that much of the record was written after dates had been forgotten and the sequence of events had become confused. Considering all the difficulties, dangers, and uncertainties that constantly beset the expedition, it would be too much to expect the precision of a ledger; it is more probable that the entries were made not from day to day, but at irregular intervals as opportunities arose at the various resting places. The story must be interpreted in the light of our later knowledge of the geography and ethnology of the country they traversed.

Each of the three principal narratives has passed through translations and later editions of more or less doubtful accuracy, with the English edition in some cases being itself a translation from an earlier French or Dutch translation. English-speaking historians of the expedition have usually drawn their material from one or another of these translations without knowledge of the original language, of the origins of the Indian names, the relations of the various tribes mentioned, or of the general system of Indian geographic naming. One of the greatest errors has been the attempt to assign a fixed local habitation to a name in every case, when in some instances it is not a proper name at all, and in others is merely a descriptive term or a duplicate name occurring at several places in the same tribal territory. Thus, *Tali* is simply the Creek word <term>talua</term>, meaning town, and not a definite place name as represented by a mistake natural when dealing through interpreters with an unknown Indian language. *Tallise* and *Tallimuchase* are respectively “Old Town” and “New Town” in Creek, and there can be no certainty that the same names were applied to the same places a century later. *Canasagua* is a corruption of a Cherokee name which occurs in at least three other places in the old Cherokee country in addition to the one mentioned in the narrative; almost every old Indian local name was thus repeated several times, just as common names like Short Creek, Whitewater, Richmond, or Lexington are among ourselves. The fact that only one name of the set has been retained on the map does not prove its identity with the town of the old chronicle. Again, such vague terms as “a large river” or “a beautiful valley” have been assumed to mean something more definitely localized than the wording warrants. The most common error in translation has been the rendering of the Spanish <term>despoblado</term> as “desert.” There are no deserts in the Gulf states, and the word means simply an uninhabited region, usually the disputed strip of land between two tribes.

There have been many attempts to trace De Soto’s route. As nearly every historian who has written of the Southern states has given attention to this subject, it is unnecessary to list them all. Of some thirty works consulted by the author, in addition to the original narratives already mentioned, no more than two or three can be considered as speaking with any authority, the rest simply copying from these without investigation. The first attempt to locate the route definitely was made by Meek (*Romantic Passages, etc.*) in 1839 (reprinted in 1857), his conclusions being

<header>MOONEY] DE SOTO’S ROUTE</header>

...based upon his general knowledge of the geography of the region. In 1851, Pickett tried to locate the route, chiefly—he asserts—from Indian tradition as related by people of mixed ancestry. It is unnecessary to say how much dependence can be placed upon Indian tradition interpreted in this way three centuries after the event. Both of these writers have tracked De Soto down the Coosa River, in which they have been followed without further investigation by Irving, Shea, and others; however, none of them were aware of the existence of a Suwali tribe or correctly acquainted with the Indian nomenclature of the upper country, or of the Creek country as so well summarized by Gatschet in his *Creek Migration Legend*. They are also mistaken in assuming that only De Soto passed through the country, whereas we now know that several Spanish explorers and numerous French adventurers traversed the same territory—the latest expeditions, of course, being the most recent in Indian memory. Jones, in his “De Soto’s March Through Georgia,” simply polishes the earlier statements into a more literary style, sometimes changing guesses into positive assertions without mentioning his sources. Maps of the supposed route, all bringing De Soto down the Coosa instead of the Chattahoochee, have been published in Irving’s *Conquest of Florida*, the Hakluyt Society’s edition of the Gentleman of Elvas’s account, and in Buckingham Smith’s translation of the same narrative, as well as in several other works. For the eastern portion, which we are dealing with, all of these are practically duplicates of one another. On several old Spanish and French maps, the names mentioned in the narrative seem to have been written down merely to fill space, without much reference to the text of the chronicle. For a list and notices of the principal writers who have touched upon this subject, see the appendix to Shea’s chapter on “Ancient Florida” in Winsor’s *Narrative and Critical History of America*, ii; Boston, 1886. We shall speak only of that part of the route that lay near the Cherokee mountains.

The first location that concerns us in the narrative is Cofitachiqui, the town from which De Soto set out for the Cherokee country. The name appears in various forms, such as Cofitachequi (Ranjel), Cofitachique (Biedma), Cofachiqui (Garcilaso), Cutifa-Chiqui (by transposition, Elvas), Cofetacque (Vandera), Catafachique (Williams), and Cosatachiqui (a misprint in the Brooks manuscripts), and the Spaniards first heard of the region as Yupaha from a tribe farther to the south. The correct form appears to be the one first given, which Gatschet—using later information than what he quoted in his *Creek Migration Legend*—identifies as a Hitchiti word roughly equivalent to “Dogwood Town,” from *cofi* (“dogwood”), *cofita* (“dogwood thicket”), and *chiki* (“house”), or collectively “town.” McCulloch places the town upon the headwaters of the Ocmulgee; Williams locates it on the Chattahoochee; Gallatin on the Oconee or the Savannah; Meek and Monette, following him, place it probably in the fork of the Savannah and the Broad Rivers; Pickett, with Jones and others following him, locate it at Silver Bluff on the east (north) bank of the Savannah, in Barnwell County, South Carolina, about 25 miles by water below present-day Augusta. It will thus be seen that at the very start of our inquiry, the commentators differ by a distance equal to more than half the width of the state of Georgia. It will suffice here to say, without entering into the full argument, that the author is inclined to believe the Indian town was on or near Silver Bluff, which was noted for its extensive ancient remains as far back as Bartram’s time (*Travels*, 313), and where the famous George Galphin established a trading post in 1736. The original site has since been almost entirely eroded by the river. According to the Indians of Cofitachiqui, the town—which was on the far (north) bank of the stream—was a two-days’ journey from the sea, probably by canoe, and the sailors with the expedition believed the river to be the same one that entered at St. Helena, which was a very close guess. The Spaniards were shown European articles here which they were told had been obtained from white men who had entered the river’s mouth many years before. These they conjectured to have been the men with Ayllon, who had landed on that coast in 1520 and again in 1524. The town was probably the ancient capital of the Uchee Indians, who, before their absorption by

the Creeks, held or claimed most of the territory on both banks of the Savannah River from the Cherokee border to within about forty miles of Savannah and westward to the Ogeechee and Cannouchee rivers (see Gatschet, *Creek Migration Legend*, I, 17–24). The country was already on the decline in 1540 from a recent fatal epidemic, but was still populous and wealthy, and was ruled by a female chief whose authority extended for a considerable distance. The town was visited also by Pardo in 1567 and again by Torres in 1628, when it was still a principal settlement, as rich in pearls as in De Soto’s time (Brooks MSS, in the archives of the Bureau of American Ethnology).

Somewhere in southern Georgia, De Soto had been told of a rich province called Coça (Coosa, the Creek country) toward the northwest. At Cofitachiqui, he again heard of it and of one of its principal towns called Chiaha (Chehaw) as being twelve days inland. Although on first hearing of it he had kept on in the other direction in order to reach Cofitachiqui, he now determined to go there, and made the queen a prisoner to compel her to accompany him a part of the way as a guide. Coça province was, though he did not know it, almost due west, and he was in haste to reach it in order to obtain corn, as his men and horses were almost worn out from hunger. It is apparent, however, that the unwilling queen, afraid of being carried beyond her own territories, led the Spaniards by a roundabout route in the hope of making her escape, as she finally did, or perhaps of leaving them to starve and die in the mountains—precisely the trick attempted by the Indians upon another Spanish adventurer, Coronado, who was entering the great plains from the Pacific coast in search of golden treasure in the same year.

Instead, therefore, of recrossing the river to the westward, the Spaniards, guided by the captive queen, took the direction of the north (“*la vuelta del norte*”—Biedma), and, after passing through several towns subject to the queen, came in seven days to “*the province of Chalaque*” (Elvas). Elvas, Garcilaso, and Ranjel agree upon the spelling, but the last-named makes the distance only two days from Cofitachiqui. Biedma does not mention the country at all. The trifling difference in statement of five days in seven need not trouble us, as Biedma makes the whole distance from Cofitachiqui to Xuala eight days, and from Guaxule to Chiaha four days, whereas Elvas makes it, respectively, twelve and seven days. Chalaque is, of course, Cherokee, as all writers agree, and De Soto was now probably on the waters of the Keowee River, the eastern headstream of the Savannah River, where the Lower Cherokee had their towns. Finding the country bare of corn, he made no stay.

Proceeding six days farther, they came next to Guaquili, where they were kindly received. This name occurs only in the Ranjel narrative, the other three being entirely silent in regard to such a halting place. The name has a Cherokee sound (Wakili), but if we allow for a dialectic substitution of *l* for *r*, it may be connected with such Catawba names as Congaree, Wateree, and Sugeree. It was probably a village of minor importance.

They came next to the province of Xuala, or Xualla, as the Elvas narrative more often has it. In a French edition, it appears as Chouala. Ranjel makes it three days from Guaquili or five from Chalaque. Elvas also makes it five days from Chalaque, while Biedma makes it eight days from Cofitachiqui, a total discrepancy of four days from the last-named place. Biedma describes it as a rough mountain country, thinly populated, but with a few Indian houses, and thinks that in these mountains the great river of Espiritu Santo (the Mississippi) had its birth. Ranjel describes the town as situated in a plain in the vicinity of rivers and in a country with a greater appearance of gold mines than any they had yet seen. The Portuguese gentleman describes it as having very little corn, and says that they reached it from Cofitachiqui over a hilly country. In his final chapter, he states that the course from Cofitachiqui to this place was from south to north, thus agreeing with Biedma. According to Garcilaso (pp. 136–137), it was fifty leagues by the road along which the Spaniards had come from Cofitachiqui to the first valley of the province of Xuala,

with only a few mountains on the way, and the town itself was situated right at the foot of a mountain ("*a la falda de una sierra*" <gloss>at the slope of a mountain range</gloss>) beside a small but rapid stream which formed the boundary of the territory of Cofitachiqui in this direction. From Ranjel, we learn that on the same day they left this place for the next "province," the Spaniards crossed a very high mountain ridge ("*una sierra muy alta*" <gloss>a very high mountain range</gloss>).

Without mentioning the name, Pickett (1851) refers to Xuala as "a town in the present Habersham County, Georgia," but provides no reason for this opinion. Rye and Irving, writing at the same time and arguing from a slight similarity in name, think it may have been on the site of a former Cherokee town, Qualatchee, at the head of the Chattahoochee River in Georgia. The resemblance, however, is quite far-fetched; moreover, this same name is found on the Keowee River in South Carolina. Jones (*De Soto in Georgia*, 1880) interprets Garcilaso's description as referring to "Nacoochee Valley, Habersham County"—which should be White County—and the neighboring Mount Yonah. He overlooks the fact that the same description of mountain, valley, and swift-flowing stream might apply equally well to any one of twenty other locations in this southern mountain country. In direct contradiction, Garcilaso says that the Spaniards rested here for fifteen days because they found plenty of provisions, while the "Portuguese Gentleman" says that they stopped for only two days because they found so little corn! Ranjel records that they stopped for four days and says they found abundant provisions and assistance.

Regardless of those details, there can be no question about the identity of the name. Just as the province of Chalaque is the country of the Cherokee, so the province of Xuala is the territory of the Suwali or Sara Indians, better known later as the Cheraw. In early times, they lived in the Piedmont region around the head of the Broad River in North Carolina, bordering the Cherokee, who still remember them by the name *Ani'-Suwa'li*. A primary trail to their country from the west led up the Swannanoa River and across the gap which, for this reason, was known to the Cherokee as *Suwa'li-nuñnâ*, or "Suwali trail," which white settlers later corrupted to Swannanoa. Lederer, who found them in the same general region in 1670, calls this gap the "Suala pass" and the neighboring mountains the Sara mountains, "which," he says, "The Spaniards call Suala." They afterward moved to the north and finally returned and were incorporated with the Catawba (see Mooney, *Siouan Tribes of the East*, Bureau of Ethnology bulletin, 1894).

Up to this point, the Spaniards had followed a northern course from Cofitachiqui (according to Biedma and Elvas), but they now turned toward the west (Elvas, final chapter). On the same day they left Xuala, they crossed "a very high mountain ridge" and descended the next day to a wide meadow bottom ("*savana*" <gloss>savanna</gloss>), through which flowed a river they concluded was part of the Espiritu Santo, or the Mississippi (according to Ranjel). Biedma speaks of crossing a mountainous country and mentions the river, which he also states they thought to be a tributary of the Mississippi. Garcilaso says that this part of their route passed through an uninhabited mountain region ("*despoblado*" <gloss>uninhabited</gloss>), and the "Portuguese Gentleman" describes it as being over "very rough and high ridges." After five days of such travel—for here, surprisingly, all the narratives agree—they arrived at Guaxule. This is the form given by Garcilaso and the "Gentleman of Elvas"; Biedma has "Guasula," and Ranjel has "Guasili" or "Guasuli." Translators and commentators have given us various forms such as Guachoule, Quaxule, Quaxulla, and Quexale. According to the Spanish method of transcribing Indian words, the name was pronounced *Washulé* or *Wasuli*, which has a Cherokee sound, although it cannot be translated. Buckingham Smith (*Narratives*, p. 222) suggests that the Spaniards may have changed "Guasili" to "Guasule" because the latter was similar to a town name in southern Spain. Such corruptions of Indian names are frequent. Garcilaso speaks of it as a "province and town," while Biedma and Ranjel call it simply a town ("*pueblo*" <gloss>village</gloss>). # MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19

The Spaniards met with a [friendly] reception here, but the only description of the town itself comes from Garcilaso, who says that it was situated in the midst of many small streams which came down from the mountains round about. He states that it consisted of three hundred houses, which is probably an exaggeration, though it goes to show that the village was of considerable size. He also notes that the chief's house, in which the principal officers were lodged, was upon a high hill ("*un cerro alto*"), around which was a roadway ("*paseadero*") wide enough for six men to walk abreast. By the "chief's house," we are to understand the townhouse, while from various similar references in other parts of the narrative, there can be no doubt that the "hill" upon which it stood was an artificial mound. In modern Spanish writing, such artificial elevations are more often called *lomas*, but these early adventurers may be excused for not noting the distinction. Flowing from the mountains around the town were numerous small streams, which united to form the river which the Spaniards henceforth followed from here down to Chiaha, where it was as large as the Guadalquivir at Seville (Garcilaso).

Deceived by the occurrence, in the Portuguese narrative, of the name Canasagua—which they assumed could belong in but one place—earlier commentators have identified this river with the Coosa. Pickett placed Guaxule somewhere upon its upper waters, while Jones improves upon this by making the site "*identical*", or very nearly so, with Coosawattee Old Town, in the southeastern corner of Murray County, Georgia. As we shall show, however, the name in question was duplicated in several states, and a careful study of the narratives, in the light of present knowledge of the country, makes it evident that the river was not the Coosa, but the Chattahoochee.

Turning our attention once more to Xuala, the most northern point reached by De Soto, we have seen that this was the territory of the Suwala or Sara Indians, in the eastern foothills of the Alleghenies, near the headwaters of the Broad and Catawba rivers in North Carolina. As the Spaniards turned here to the west, they probably did not penetrate far beyond the present South Carolina boundary. The "very high mountain ridge" which they crossed immediately after leaving the town was in all probability the main chain of the Blue Ridge. The river which they found after descending to the savanna on the other side, and which they guessed to be a branch of the Mississippi, was almost certainly the upper part of the French Broad—the first stream flowing in an opposite direction from those which they had previously encountered. They may have struck it in the neighborhood of Hendersonville or Brevard, as there are two gaps, passable for vehicles, in the main ridge eastward from the first-named town. The uninhabited mountains through which they struggled for several days on their way to Chiaha and *Coça* (the Creek country) in the southwest were the broken ridges in which the Savannah and the Little Tennessee have their sources; if they followed an Indian trail, they may have passed through the Rabun Gap, near the present Clayton, Georgia. Guaxule, and not Xuala, as Jones supposes, was in Nacoochee Valley, in the present White County, Georgia. The small streams which united to form the river down which the Spaniards proceeded to Chiaha were the headwaters of the Chattahoochee. The hill upon which the townhouse was built must have been the great Nacoochee mound, the most prominent landmark in the valley, on the east bank of Sautee Creek in White County, about twelve miles northwest of Clarkesville. This is the largest mound in upper Georgia, with the exception of the noted Etowah mound near Cartersville, and is the only one which can fill the requirements of the case. There are but two considerable mounds in western North Carolina—that at Franklin and a smaller one on the Oconaluftee River, on the present East Cherokee reservation—and as both of these are on streams flowing away from the Creek country, this fact alone would bar them from consideration. The only large mounds in upper Georgia are this one at Nacoochee and the group on the Etowah River, near Cartersville. The largest of the Etowah group is some fifty feet in height and is ascended on one side by means of a roadway

About fifty feet wide at the base and narrowing gradually to the top. If this had been the mound described in the narrative, it is unlikely that the chronicler would have failed to notice the two other mounds in the group, or the additional mound on the opposite side of the river. Each of these is twenty to twenty-five feet high, not to mention the great ditch—a quarter of a mile long—that encircles the group. Moreover, Cartersville is some distance from the mountains, and the Etowah River at this point does not match the description of a small, rushing mountain stream. There is no significant mound at Coosawattee or in any of the three surrounding counties.

The Nacoochee mound has been cleared and cultivated for many years and no longer shows any sign of a roadway up its side; however, because of its great height, we can be reasonably sure that some such means of easy ascent existed in ancient times. In other respects, it is the only mound in the entire upper country that meets the described conditions. The valley is one of the most fertile spots in Georgia, and numerous ancient remains provide evidence that it was a favorite center of settlement in early days. At the start of the modern historical period, it was held by the Cherokee, who had a town there called Nacoochee, though their claim was disputed by the Creeks. The Gentleman of Elvas states that Guaxule was subject to the queen of Cofitachiqui, but this may only mean that the people of the two towns or tribes were in a friendly alliance. The modern name is pronounced *Nagu'tsi'* by the Cherokee, who say, however, that it is not from their language. The suffix may be the Creek *udshi*, meaning "small," or it may be connected to the name of the Uchee Indians.

From Guaxule, the Spaniards advanced to Canasoga (according to Ranjel) or Canasagua (according to Elvas), a march of one or two days from Guaxule, depending on the authority. Garcilaso and Biedma do not mention the name. Since Garcilaso states that the march from Guaxule to Chiaha followed the bank of the same river—which we identify as the Chattahoochee—the town may have been near present-day Gainesville. However, as we have seen, it is unsafe to trust estimates of distance. Arguing from the name, Meek infers that the town was near the Conasauga River in Murray County, and that the river they marched down to reach it was "no doubt the Etowah," even though reaching the Conasauga from the Etowah would require another sharp turn to the north. Based on the same coincidence, Pickett places it on the Conasauga "in the modern county of Murray, Georgia," while Jones, following the same theory, locates it "at or near the junction of the Connasauga and Coosawattee rivers, in what was originally Cass, now Gordon County." Here, his modern geography is as flawed as his ancient geography, as the original Cass County is now Bartow; the name was changed because of a local dislike for General Cass. The entire theory of a march down the Coosa River rests on this coincidence of the name. However, the same name, pronounced *Gănsâ'gĭ* by the Cherokee, was applied by them to at least three different locations within their old territory, and the one mentioned in the narrative would make a fourth. The others were (1) on the Oostanaula River, opposite the mouth of the Conasauga, where New Echota was later located in Gordon County, Georgia; (2) on Canasauga Creek in McMinn County, Tennessee; and (3) on the Tuckasegee River, about two miles above Webster in Jackson County, North Carolina. At each of these places, there are remains of ancient settlements. It is possible that the name of Kenesaw Mountain, near Marietta in Cobb County, Georgia, may be a corruption of *Gănsâ'gĭ*; if so, the Canasagua of the narrative may have been somewhere in this vicinity on the Chattahoochee. The meaning of the name is lost.

On leaving Canasagua, they continued down the same river they had followed from Guaxule (according to Garcilaso), and after traveling several days through an uninhabited (*despoblado*) country (according to Elvas), they arrived at Chiaha, which was subject to the great chief of Coça (according to Elvas). The name is spelled Chiaha by Ranjel and the Gentle-

the Gentleman of Elvas, Chiha by Biedma in the *Documentos*, China due to a misprint in an English translation, and Ychiaha by Garcilaso. It appears as Chiha on an English map of 1762 reproduced in Winsor, *Westward Movement*, page 31, 1897. Gallatin spells it Ichiaha, while Williams and Fairbanks, through a misprint, call it Chiapa. According to both Ranjel and Elvas, the army entered it on the 5th of June, although the former states it was four days from Canasagua, while the latter says it was five. Biedma says it was four days from Guaxule, and, finally, Garcilaso says it was six days and thirty leagues from Guaxule and on the same river, which was, here at Chiaha, as large as the Guadalquivir at Seville. As we have seen, there is a great discrepancy in the records of the distance from Cofitachiqui to this point. All four authorities agree that the town was on an island in the river, along which they had been marching for some time (Garcilaso, Ranjel); but while the Elvas narrative describes the island as "two crossbow shots" in length above the town and one league in length below it, Garcilaso calls it a "great island more than five leagues long." On both sides of the island, the stream was very broad and easily waded (Elvas). Finding a welcome and food for men and horses, the Spaniards rested here for nearly a month (June 5–28, Ranjel; twenty-six or twenty-seven days, Biedma; thirty days, Elvas). Despite the danger of attack, De Soto allowed his men to sleep under trees in the open air, "because it was very hot and the people would have suffered great hardship if they had not done so" (Elvas). This in itself is evidence that the place was quite far to the south, as it was still only the first week in June. The town was subject to the chief of the great province of Coosa, farther to the west. From here onward, they began to encounter palisaded towns.

On the theory that the march was down the Coosa river, every commentator until now has located Chiaha at some point upon this stream, either in Alabama or Georgia. Gallatin (1836) says that it "must have been on the Coosa, probably some distance below the site of New Echota." He notes a similarity of sound between Ichiaha and "Echoy" (*Itseyĭ*), a Cherokee town name. Williams (1837) says that it was on the Mobile (i.e., the Alabama or lower Coosa river). Meek (1839) says "there can be little doubt that Chiaha was situated but a short distance above the junction of the Coosa and Chattooga rivers," i.e., not far within the Alabama line. He notes the occurrence of a "Chiaha" (Chehawhaw) creek near Talladega, Alabama. Regarding the island upon which the town was said to have been situated, he says: "There is no such island now in the Coosa. It is probable that the Spaniards either mistook the peninsula formed by the junction of two rivers, the Coosa and Chattooga, for an island, or that those two rivers were originally united so as to form an island near their present confluence. We have heard this latter supposition asserted by persons well acquainted with the country."—*Romantic Passages*, p. 222, 1857. Monette (1846) puts it on the Etowah branch of the Coosa, probably in Floyd county, Georgia. Pickett (1851), followed in turn by Irving, Jones, and Shea, locates it at "the site of the modern Rome." The "island" is interpreted to mean the space between the two streams above the confluence.

Pickett, as has been stated, bases his statements chiefly or entirely upon Indian traditions as obtained from mixed-race individuals or traders. How much information can be gathered from such sources regarding events that occurred three centuries earlier may be estimated by considering how much an illiterate mountaineer of the same region might be able to tell concerning the founding of the Georgia colony. Pickett himself seems to have been entirely unaware of the later Spanish expeditions of Pardo and De Luna through the same country, as he makes no mention of them in his history of Alabama, but attributes everything to De Soto. Concerning Chiaha, he says:

> "The most elderly Cherokee Indians, whose traditions have been handed down to us through old Indian traders, disagree as to the precise place <note>!</note> where De Soto crossed the Oostanaula to reach the town of Chiaha—some asserting that he

passed over that river seven miles above its junction with the Etowah, and that he marched from there down to Chiaha, which, everyone contends, lay immediately at the confluence of the two rivers; while other ancient Indians asserted that he crossed, with his army, immediately opposite the town. But this is not very important. Coupling the Indian traditions with the account by Garcilaso and that by the Portuguese eyewitness, we are inclined to believe the latter tradition that the expedition continued to advance down the western side of the Oostanaula until they halted in view of the mouth of the Etowah. De Soto, having arrived immediately opposite the great town of Chiaha, now the site of Rome, crossed the Oostanaula,” etc. (History of Alabama, p. 23, reprint, 1896). He overlooks the fact that Chiaha was not a Cherokee town, but belonged to the province of Coça—that is, the territory of the Creek Indians.

A careful study of the four original narratives makes it plain that the expedition did not descend either the Oostanaula or the Etowah, and that consequently Chiaha could not have been at their junction, the present site of Rome. On the other hand, the conclusion is irresistible that the march was down the Chattahoochee from its extreme headwaters in the mountains, and that the Chiaha of the narrative was the Lower Creek town of the same name, more commonly known as Chehaw, formerly on this river in the neighborhood of the modern city of Columbus, Georgia, while Coste, the next adjacent town in the narrative, was Kasi'ta, or Cusseta, of the same group of villages. The falls at this point mark the geologic break line where the river changes from a clear, swift current to a broad, slow-moving stream of the lower country. Attracted by the fisheries and the fertile bottom lands, the Lower Creeks established their settlement center here, and here, up to the beginning of the present century, they had within easy distance of each other on both sides of the river some fifteen towns, among which were Chiaha (Chehaw), Chiahudshi (Little Chehaw), and Kasi'ta (Cusseta). Most of these settlements were within what are now Muscogee and Chattahoochee counties, Georgia, and Lee and Russell counties, Alabama (see town list and map in Gatschet, Creek Migration Legend). Large mounds and other earthworks on both sides of the river in the vicinity of Columbus attest to the importance of the site in ancient days, while the general appearance indicates that at times the adjacent low grounds were submerged or cut off by overflows from the main stream. A principal trail crossed here from the Ocmulgee, passing by Tuskegee to the Upper Creek towns about the junction of the Coosa and Tallapoosa in Alabama. At the beginning of the present century, this trail was known to the traders as “De Soto’s trace” (Woodward, Reminiscences, p. 76). As the Indian towns frequently shift their position within a limited range on account of epidemics, floods, or impoverishment of the soil, it is not necessary to assume that they occupied exactly the same sites in 1540 as in 1800, but only that as a group they were in the same general vicinity. Thus Kasi'ta itself was at one period above the falls and at a later period some eight miles below them. Both Kasi'ta and Chiaha were principal towns, with several branch villages.

The time mentioned as occupied on the march from Canasagua to Chiaha would seem too little for the actual distance, but as we have seen, the chroniclers do not agree among themselves. We can easily believe that the Spaniards, encouraged by the certainty of finding food and rest at their next halting place, made better progress along the smooth river trail than while blundering helplessly through the mountains at the direction of a most unwilling guide. If Canasagua was anywhere in the neighborhood of Kenesaw, in Cobb County, the time mentioned in the Elvas or Garcilaso narrative would probably have been sufficient for reaching Chiaha at the falls. The uninhabited country between the two towns was the neutral ground between the two hostile tribes, the Cherokee and the Creeks, and it is worth noting that Kenesaw Mountain was made a point on the boundary line afterward established between the two tribes through the mediation of the United States government.

This conclusion is supported by archaeological evidence, historical trail names like "De Soto's trace," and the geographical distribution of Creek settlements.</summary>

<header>MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 1</header>

There is no large island in either the Coosa or the Chattahoochee, and we are forced to the conclusion that what the chronicle describes as an island was really a portion of the bottom land temporarily cut off by backwater from a flood. In a similar way "The Slue," east of the Flint River in Mitchell County, may have been formed by a shifting of the river channel. Two months later, in Alabama, the Spaniards reached a river so swollen by rains that they were obliged to wait six days before they could cross (*Elvas*). Lederer, while crossing South Carolina in 1670, found his further progress barred by a "great lake," which he puts on his map as "Ushery Lake," although there is no such lake in the state; but the mystery is explained by Lawson, who, in going over the same ground thirty years later, found all the bottom lands underwater from a great flood, the Santee in particular being 36 feet above its normal level. As Lawson was a surveyor, his figures may be considered reliable. The "Ushery Lake" of Lederer was simply an overflow of the Catawba River. Floodwater in the streams of upper Georgia and Alabama would quickly be carried off, but would likely remain for some time on the more level country below the falls.

According to information supplied by Mr. Thomas Robinson, an expert engineering authority familiar with the lower Chattahoochee, there was formerly a large mound—now almost entirely washed away—on the eastern bank of the river, about nine miles below Columbus, while on the western or Alabama bank, a mile or two farther down, another of nearly equal size is still to be seen. "During extreme floods, both of these mounds were partly submerged. To the east of the former, known as the Indian mound, the flood plain is a mile or two wide, and along the eastern side of the plain stretches a series of swamps or wooded sloughs, indicating an old river bed. All the plain between the present river and the sloughs is river-made land. The river bluff along the mound on the Georgia side is from twenty to thirty feet above the present low-water surface of the stream. About a mile above the mound are the remains of what was known as Jennies Island. At ordinary stages of the river, no island is there. The eastern channel was blocked by government works some years ago, and the whole area is filled up and now used as a cornfield. I think the island remains can be traced now for a length of half a mile, with a possible extreme width of 300 feet. . . . This whole country, on both sides of the river, is full of Indian lore. I have mentioned both mounds simply to indicate that this portion of the river was an Indian locality, and have also stated the facts about the remains of Jennies Island in order to give a possible clue to a professional who might study the ground."—Letter, April 22, 1900.

Chiaha was the first town of the "province of Coça," the territory of the Coosa or Creek Indians. The next town mentioned, Coste (*Elvas* and *Ranjel*), Costehe (*Biedma*) or Acoste (*Garcilaso*), was Kasi'ta, or Cusseta, as it was afterward known to the whites. While *Garcilaso* puts it at the lower end of the same island upon which Chiaha was situated, the *Elvas* narrative makes it seven days distant! The modern towns of Chehaw and Cusseta were within a few miles of each other on the Chattahoochee; the former was on the western or Alabama side, while Cusseta, in 1799, was on the east or Georgia side about eight miles below the falls at Columbus, and in Chattahoochee County, which has given its capital the same name, Cusseta. From the general tone of the narrative, it is evident that the two towns were near together in De Soto's time, and it may be that the *Elvas* chronicle confounded Kasi'ta with Koasati, a principal Upper Creek town a short distance below the junction of the Coosa and Tallapoosa. At Coste they crossed the river and continued westward "through many towns subject to the <term>cacique</term> of Coça" (*Elvas*) until they came to the great town of Coça itself. This was Kusa or Coosa, the ancient capital of the Upper Creeks. There were two towns of this name at different periods. One, described by Adair in 1775 as "the great and old beloved town of refuge, Koosah," was on the east bank of the Coosa River, a few miles southwest of the present Talladega, Alabama. The

<summary>The author explains that the "island" of Chiaha was likely a flood-isolated area of land and identifies the historical town of Coste as the Creek village of Kasi'ta (Cusseta) near modern Columbus, Georgia. He also locates the ancient Creek capital of Coosa in present-day Alabama.</summary>

the other, known as "Old Coosa," and probably of more ancient origin, was on the west side of the Alabama River, near the present site of Montgomery (see Gatschet, Creek Migration Legend). It was probably the latter which was visited by De Soto, and later on by De Luna, in 1559. Beyond Coça, they passed through another Creek town, apparently lower down on the Alabama, the name of which is variously spelled Ytaua (Elvas, Force translation), Ytava (Elvas, Hakluyt Society translation), or Itaba (Ranjel), and which may be connected with I'tăwă', Etowah, or "Hightower," the name of a former Cherokee settlement near the head of the Etowah River in Georgia. The Cherokee regard this as a foreign name, and its occurrence in upper Georgia, as well as in central Alabama, may help to support the tradition that the southern Cherokee border was formerly held by the Creeks.

De Soto's route beyond the Cherokee country does not concern us except as it clarifies his previous progress. In the seventeenth chapter, the Elvas narrative summarizes that portion from the landing at Tampa Bay to a point in southern Alabama as follows:

> "From the Port of Spirito Santo to Apalache, which is about a hundred leagues, the governor went from east to west; and from Apalache to Cutifachiqui, which is 430 leagues, from the southwest to the northeast; and from Cutifachiqui to Xualla, which is about 250 leagues, from the south to the north; and from Xualla to Tascaluca, which is another 250 leagues—one hundred and ninety of them he traveled from east to west, namely, to the province of Coça; and the other 60, from Coça to Tascaluca, from the north to the south."

Chisca (Elvas and Ranjel), the mountainous northern region where men were sent from Chiaha to look for copper and gold, was somewhere in the Cherokee country of upper Georgia or Alabama. The precise location is not essential, as it is now known that native copper—in a condition that would have been easily workable by the Indians—occurs throughout the entire southern Allegheny region from about Anniston, Alabama, into Virginia. Notable finds of native copper have been made on the upper Tallapoosa, in Cleburne County, Alabama; around Ducktown, in Polk County, Tennessee; and in southwestern Virginia, where one nugget from Virginia weighed several pounds. From the appearance of ancient soapstone vessels which have been found in the same region, there is even a possibility that the Indians had some knowledge of smelting, as the Spanish explorers suspected (oral information from Mr. W. H. Weed, U.S. Geological Survey). We hear again of this "province" after De Soto had reached the Mississippi, and in one place Garcilaso seems to confuse it with another province called Quizqui (Ranjel) or Quizquiz (Elvas and Biedma). The name has some resemblance to the Cherokee word *tsiskwa*, "bird."

(9) DE LUNA AND ROGEL (p. 27): Jones, in his *De Soto's March through Georgia*, incorrectly attributes certain traces of ancient mining operations in the Cherokee country, particularly on the Valley River in North Carolina, to the followers of De Luna, "who, in 1560 . . . came with 300 Spanish soldiers into this region, and spent the summer in an eager and laborious search for gold." Don Tristan de Luna, with fifteen hundred men, landed somewhere near Mobile Bay in 1559 with the intention of establishing a permanent Spanish settlement in the interior, but owing to a series of unfortunate events, the attempt was abandoned the next year. In the course of his wanderings, he traversed the country of the Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Upper Creeks, as shown by the names and other data in the narrative, but he returned without entering the mountains or doing any digging (see Barcia, *Ensayo Cronologico*, pp. 32-41, 1723; Winsor, *Narrative and Critical History*, **II**, pp. 257-259).

In 1569, the Jesuit Rogel—called Father John Roger by Shea—began mission work among the South Carolina tribes inland from Santa Elena (near Port Royal). The mission, which at first promised well, was abandoned the next year due to the unwillingness of the Indians to give up their old habits and beliefs. Shea, in his "Catholic Missions," supposes that these Indians were probably a part of the
