(10) <term>DAVIES' HISTORY OF THE CARRIBBY ISLANDS</term> (page 29): The fraudulent nature of this work—which is itself an altered translation of a fictional history by Rochefort—is noted by Buckingham Smith (Letter of Hernando de Soto, page 36, 1854), Winsor (Narrative and Critical History, volume II, page 289), and Field (Indian Bibliography, page 95). Field says:
> "This book is an example of the most shameless audacity. The supposed author takes credit for the performance, with only the faintest reference to its previous existence. It is a nearly exact translation of Rochefort's 'Histoire des Antilles.' However, there is a satisfying justice in Davies' treatment of Rochefort, because Rochefort’s own work was fictional in every part that was not stolen from authors whose actual knowledge provided the only true information in his treatise."

(11) <term>ANCIENT SPANISH MINES</term> (pages 29, 31): Since the existence of precious metals in the southern Alleghenies was known to the Spaniards from a very early period, it is likely that a more thorough exploration of that region will reveal many pieces of evidence of their mining operations. In his "Antiquities of the Southern Indians," Jones describes a type of underground village discovered in 1834 on Dukes Creek, White County, Georgia. It consisted of a row of small log cabins extending along the creek, but buried several feet below the surface of the ground, upon which large trees were growing. The conclusion was that the houses had been covered by successive floods. The logs had been notched and shaped, apparently with sharp metal tools. Shafts have been discovered on Valley River, North Carolina; at the bottom of one, in 1854, a well-preserved windlass of carved oak timbers was found, showing signs of once being reinforced with iron. Another shaft, passing through hard rock, showed the marks of sharp tools used for boring. The casing and other timbers were still in good condition (Jones, pages 48, 49). Similar ancient shafts have been found in other places in upper Georgia and western North Carolina, along with some remarkable stone-built fortifications or enclosures, notably at Fort Mountain in Murray County, Georgia, and on Silver Creek, a few miles from Rome, Georgia.

Very recently, the remains of an early white settlement, traditionally credited to the Spaniards, have been reported from Lincolnton, North Carolina, on the edge of the ancient territory of the Sara people, where the Spaniards built a fort in 1566. The works include a dam made of cut stone, a series of low cut-stone pillars arranged in squares as if intended for foundations, a stone-walled well, a quarry where the stone was obtained, a fire pit, and a series of depressions extending along the stream. In these depressions, remains of timbers were found, suggesting underground cabins like those on Dukes Creek. All of these preceded the first modern settlement of that region, which occurred around the year 1750. Indications of ancient mining are also reported from Kings Mountain, about twenty miles away (Reinhardt MS, 1900, in the Bureau of American Ethnology archives). The Spanish miners mentioned by Lederer in 1670 and Moore in 1690 were likely working in this neighborhood.

(12) <term>SIR WILLIAM JOHNSON</term> (page 38): This great soldier, whose history is so closely linked with that of the Six Nations, was born in County Meath, Ireland, in 1715, and died at Johnstown, New York, in 1774. As the younger son of an Irish gentleman, he left his home country in 1738 because of a broken heart and emigrated to America. There, he managed the settlement of a large tract of wilderness belonging to his uncle, located along the south side of the Mohawk River in what was then the New York frontier. This brought him into close contact with the Six Nations, particularly the Mohawks. He became so interested in them that he learned their language and, to some extent, adopted their customs, sometimes even wearing native clothing. This interest, combined with his natural kindness and dignity, completely won the hearts of the Six

->MOONEY] SIR WILLIAM JOHNSON—CAPT. JOHN STUART 203<-

Nations, over whom he acquired a greater influence than has ever been exercised by any other white man before or since. He was formally adopted as a chief by the Mohawk tribe. In 1744, while still a very young man, he was placed in charge of British affairs with the Six Nations, and in 1755, he was regularly commissioned at their own urgent request as superintendent for the Six Nations and their dependent and allied tribes—a position he held for the rest of his life. In 1748, he was also placed in command of the New York colonial forces, and two years later, he was appointed to the governor’s council. At the beginning of the French and Indian War, he was commissioned as a major-general. He defeated Dieskau at the battle of Lake George, where he was severely wounded early in the action, yet refused to leave the field. For this service, he received the thanks of Parliament, a grant of £5,000, and a baronetcy. He also distinguished himself at Ticonderoga and Fort Niagara, capturing the latter after routing the French army sent to its relief. At the head of his Indian and colonial forces, he took part in other actions and expeditions and was present at the surrender of Montreal. For his services throughout the war, he received a grant of 100,000 acres of land north of the Mohawk River. Here he built “*Johnson Hall*,” which still stands near the village of Johnstown; the village itself was laid out by him with stores, a church, and other buildings at his own expense. At *Johnson Hall*, he lived in the style of an old country baron, dividing his attention between Indian affairs and the raising of blooded stock, while providing princely hospitality to all visitors. His influence alone prevented the Six Nations from joining Pontiac’s great confederacy against the English. In 1768, he concluded the Treaty of Fort Stanwix, which established the Ohio River as the boundary between the northern colonies and the western tribes—the same boundary for which the Indians afterward fought against the Americans until 1795. In 1739, he married a German girl from the Mohawk Valley, who died after bearing him three children. Later in life, he formed a connection with the sister of Brant, the Mohawk chief. He died from over-exertion at an Indian council. His son, Sir John Johnson, succeeded to his title and estates; at the outbreak of the Revolution, he supported the British side, leading the Mohawks and a large portion of the other Six Nations to abandon their homes and flee with him to Canada (see W. L. Stone, *Life of Sir William Johnson*).

(13) CAPTAIN JOHN STUART (page 44): This distinguished officer lived during the same period as Sir William Johnson and came from the same adventurous Celtic stock that has produced so many men prominent in our early Indian history. Born in Scotland around the year 1700, he came to America in 1733, was appointed to a subordinate command in the British service, and soon became a favorite among the Indians. When Fort Loudon was taken by the Cherokee in 1760, he was second in command, and his rescue by Ata-kullakulla is one of the romantic episodes of that period. In 1763, he was appointed superintendent for the southern tribes, a position he continued to hold until his death. In 1768, he negotiated the Treaty of Hard Labor with the Cherokee, by which the Kanawha River was established as the western boundary of Virginia; at the same time, Sir William Johnson concluded a treaty with the northern tribes by which the boundary continued northward along the Ohio. At the outbreak of the Revolution, he organized the Cherokee and other southern tribes, along with white loyalists, against the Americans, and he was largely responsible for the Indian raids along the southern border. He planned a general invasion by the southern tribes along the entire frontier in cooperation with a British force to be landed in western Florida, while a British fleet was to occupy the Americans' attention on the coast and the Tories were to rise in the interior. Upon the discovery of the plot and the subsequent defeat of the Cherokee by the Americans, he fled to Florida and soon afterward sailed for England, where he died in 1779.

British officer named Ward and her mother, a sister of Ata-kullakulla, the principal chief of the Nation at the time of the first Cherokee war. She was probably related to Brian Ward, an old-time trader among the Cherokee mentioned elsewhere in connection with the battle of Tali'wă. During the Revolutionary period, she lived at Echota, the national capital, where she held the office of "<term>Beloved Woman</term>," or "<term>Pretty Woman</term>." By virtue of this position, she was entitled to speak in councils and to decide the fate of captives. She distinguished herself through her constant friendship with the Americans, always using her best efforts to bring about peace between them and her own people, and frequently giving timely warnings of planned Indian raids—notably on the occasion of the great invasion of the Watauga and Holston settlements in 1776. A Mrs. Bean, captured during this raid, was saved by her intervention after having been condemned to death and already bound to the stake. In 1780, during another Cherokee outbreak, she assisted a number of traders to escape, and the next year she was sent by the chiefs to make peace with Sevier and Campbell, who were advancing against the Cherokee towns. Campbell speaks of her in his report as "the famous Indian woman, Nancy Ward." Although peace was not granted then, her relatives, when brought in later with other prisoners, were treated with the consideration they deserved in return for her helpful services. Robertson, who visited her around this time, describes her as "queenly and commanding" in appearance and manner, and her house as furnished in accordance with her high dignity. While among the Arkansas Cherokee in 1819, Nuttall was told that she had introduced the first cows into the Nation, and that through her own and her children's influence, the condition of the Cherokee had been greatly improved. He was also told that her advice and counsel were nearly supreme, and that her interference was allowed to be decisive even in matters of life and death. Although he speaks in the present tense, it is unlikely that she was still alive then, and he does not claim to have met her. Her descendants are still found in the Nation. See Haywood, Natural and Aboriginal Tennessee; Ramsey, Tennessee; Nuttall, Travels, p. 130, 1821; Campbell letter, 1781, and Springstone deposition, 1781, in Virginia State Papers I, pp. 435, 436, 447, 1875; Appleton's Cyclopædia of American Biography.

(15) GENERAL JAMES ROBERTSON (p. 48): This distinguished pioneer and founder of Nashville was born in Brunswick County, Virginia, in 1742, and died at the Chickasaw agency in west Tennessee in 1814. Like most of the men prominent in the early history of Tennessee, he was of Scotch-Irish ancestry. After his father moved around 1750 to western North Carolina, the boy grew up without an education but with a strong love for adventure, which he satisfied by making exploring expeditions across the mountains. After his marriage, his wife taught him to read and write. In 1771, he led a colony to the Watauga River and established the settlement which became the heart of the future state of Tennessee. He took a leading part in the organization of the Watauga Association, the earliest organized government within the state, and afterward served in Dunmore's War, participating in the bloody battle of Point Pleasant in 1774. He participated in the earlier Revolutionary campaigns against the Cherokee, and in 1777, he was appointed as an agent to live at their capital, Echota, and act as a liaison for their correspondence with the state governments of North Carolina (including Tennessee) and Virginia. In this capacity, he gave timely warning of a planned invasion by the hostile portion of the tribe early in 1779. Soon after in the same year, he led a preliminary exploration from Watauga to the Cumberland. He brought out a larger party late in the fall, and in the spring of 1780, he built the first stockades on the site which he named Nashborough, now Nashville. Only his force of character was able to hold the young settlement together in the face of hardships and Indian hostilities, but by his tact and firmness, he was finally able to make peace with the surrounding tribes and established the Cumberland settlement upon a secure basis. He afterward held the appointment of Indian commissioner to the Chickasaw and Choctaw. See Ramsey’s *Tennessee*; Roosevelt's *Winning of the West*; and *Appleton's Cyclopædia of American Biography*.

(16) **GENERAL GRIFFITH RUTHERFORD** (p. 48): Although this Revolutionary officer commanded the greatest expedition ever sent against the Cherokee, with such distinguished success that both North Carolina and Tennessee have named counties in his honor, little appears to be definitely known of his history. He was born in Ireland about 1731 and, after emigrating to America, settled near Salisbury, North Carolina. At the start of the Revolutionary struggle, he became a member of the Provincial Congress and Council of Safety. In June 1776, he was commissioned a brigadier-general in the American army, and a few months later led his celebrated expedition against the Cherokee, as told elsewhere in this work. He rendered other important service during the Revolution; in one battle, he was taken prisoner by the British and held by them for nearly a year. He afterward served in the state senate of North Carolina and, subsequently removing to Tennessee, was for some time a member of its territorial council. He died in Tennessee around 1800.

(17) **RUTHERFORD'S ROUTE** (p. 49): The various North Carolina detachments that combined to form Rutherford's expedition against the Cherokee in the autumn of 1776 organized at different points around the upper Catawba and probably concentrated at Davidson's fort, now Old Fort, in McDowell County. From there, advancing westward closely following the line of the present Southern Railroad and its Western North Carolina branch, the army crossed the Blue Ridge over the Swannanoa Gap and went down the Swannanoa to its junction with the French Broad River, crossing the latter at the Warrior Ford, below the present Asheville. From there, they went up Hominy Creek and across the ridge to Pigeon River, crossing it a few miles below the junction of the East and West forks; then to Richland Creek, crossing it just above the present Waynesville; and over the dividing ridge between the present Haywood and Jackson counties to the head of Scott's Creek. Then, they moved down that creek by "a hidden path through a very rugged mountainous way," as Moore's old narrative puts it, to its junction with the Tuckasegee River just below the present Webster. Then, crossing to the west (south) side of the river, the troops followed a main trail down the stream for a few miles until they came to the first Cherokee town, Stekoa, on the site of the farm formerly owned by Colonel William H. Thomas, just above the present railroad village of Whittier in Swain County, North Carolina. After destroying the town, a detachment left the main body and pursued the fugitives northward on the other side of the river to Oconaluftee River and Soco Creek, getting back afterward to the settlements by steering an easterly course across the mountains to Richland Creek (Moore narrative). The main army, under Rutherford, crossed the dividing ridge to the south of Whittier and descended Cowee Creek to the waters of the Little Tennessee, in the present Macon County. After destroying the towns in this vicinity, the army ascended Cartoogaja Creek, west from the present Franklin, and crossed the Nantahala Mountains at Waya Gap—where a fight took place—to the Nantahala River, probably at the town of the same name near the present Jarretts Station. From here, the march went west across the mountain into the present Cherokee County and down Valley River to its junction with the Hiwassee at the present Murphy.

Thomas, Major James Bryson (whose grandfather was with Rutherford), and Cherokee informants.

# MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19]

Who was sometimes incorrectly called Christy, was born in Berkeley County, Virginia, in 1732. Accustomed to frontier warfare almost from his youth, he served in the French and Indian War with the rank of captain. He was afterward in command of the Tennessee and North Carolina forces that participated in the great Battle of Point Pleasant in 1774, although he arrived too late for the actual fight. He organized a regiment at the start of the Revolutionary War, and in 1776 led an expedition from Virginia against the Upper Cherokee and forced them to sue for peace. In 1782, while on an expedition against the Ohio tribes, he was captured and burned at the stake.

(19) THE GREAT INDIAN WAR PATH (p. 50): This famous Indian thoroughfare from Virginia through Kentucky and Tennessee to the Creek country in Alabama and Georgia is frequently mentioned in the early narratives of that region. It is indicated on the maps accompanying Ramsey's *Annals of Tennessee* and Royce's *Cherokee Nation*, found in the *Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology*. Royce's map shows it in more accurate detail. It was the primary trading and war path between the northern and southern tribes. Along this same path, Christian, Sevier, and other early Indian fighters led their men to destroy the towns on the Little Tennessee, Hiwassee, and southward.

According to Ramsey (p. 88), one branch of it ran nearly on the line of the later stagecoach road from Harpers Ferry to Knoxville. It passed the Big Lick in Botetourt County, Virginia, and crossed New River near old Fort Chiswell (which stood on the south bank of Reed Creek of New River, about nine miles east of Wytheville, Virginia). It crossed the Holston at the Seven-mile Ford, then stayed to the left of the stage road near the river to the North Fork of the Holston, "crossing where it does now." From there it went to Big Creek and, crossing the Holston at Dodson's Ford, to the Grassy Springs near the former residence of Micajah Lea. It then went down the Nolichucky to Long Creek, up to its head, and down Dumplin Creek nearly to its mouth, where the path bent to the left and crossed the French Broad River near Buckingham's Island. Here a branch left the main path and went up the West Fork of Little Pigeon River and across the mountains to the Middle Towns on the Tuckasegee and the upper Little Tennessee. The main trail continued up Boyd's Creek to its head and down Ellejoy Creek to the Little River, crossing near Henry's place. From there it passed through the present Maryville to the mouth of the Tellico, and, passing through the Cherokee towns of Tellico, Echota, and Hiwassee, it went down the Coosa River, connecting with the great war path of the Creeks. Near the Wolf Hills (now Abingdon, Virginia), another path came in from Kentucky, passing through the Cumberland Gap. It was along this latter road that the early explorers entered Kentucky, and along it the Shawnee and other Ohio tribes often traveled to raid the Holston and New River settlements.

On Royce's map, the trail is marked from Virginia southward. Starting from the junction of Moccasin Creek with the North Fork of the Holston, just above the Tennessee state line, it crosses the Holston from the east side at its mouth or junction with the South Fork, just below Kingsport or Long Island. It then follows down the west side of the Holston, crossing Big Creek at its mouth, and crossing to the south (east) side of the Holston at Dodson's Creek. From there it goes up along the east side of Dodson's Creek and across Big Gap Creek, following it for a short distance and continuing southwest, just touching the Nolichucky. It passes up the west side of Long Creek of that stream and down the same side of Dumplin Creek, crossing the French Broad River just below the mouth of the creek. Then it goes up along the west side of Boyd's Creek to its head and down the west side of Ellejoy Creek to and across the Little River. From there it goes through the present Maryville to cross the Little Tennessee at the entrance of the Tellico River, where old Fort Loudon was built. Then it turns up along the south side of the Little Tennessee River to Echota, the ancient capital, and then southwest across the Tellico River along the ridge between Chestua and Canasauga Creeks, crossing the latter near its mouth to reach the Hiwassee River at the town of the same name.

# MOONEY] PEACE TOWNS AND TOWNS OF REFUGE

From there the trail goes southwest, crossing the Ocoee River near its mouth, passing south of Cleveland, through present-day Ooltewah, and across Chickamauga Creek into Georgia and Alabama.

According to Timberlake (*Memoirs*, with map, 1765), the trail crossed the Little Tennessee from Echota, northward, in two places—just above and below Four-mile Creek. The first camping place was at the junction of Ellejoy Creek and Little River, at the old town site. It crossed the Holston within a mile of Fort Robinson.

According to Hutchins (*Topographical Description of America*, p. 24, 1778), the road which went through Cumberland Gap was the one taken by the northern Indians in their raids into the "Cuttawa" country. It went from Sandusky, on Lake Erie, by a direct path to the mouth of the Scioto (where Portsmouth now is) and from there across Kentucky to the gap.

**(20) PEACE TOWNS AND TOWNS OF REFUGE (p. 51):** Towns of refuge existed among the Cherokee, the Creeks, and probably other Indian tribes, as well as among the ancient Hebrews. This institution was a merciful provision for softening the harshness of primitive law, which required a life for a life. We learn from Deuteronomy that Moses appointed three cities on the east side of the Jordan 
> "so that the slayer who killed his neighbor accidentally and did not hate him in the past might flee there, and that by fleeing into one of these cities, he might live." 
It was also ordained that as more territory was conquered from the heathen, three additional cities should be set aside as havens of refuge for those who should accidentally take human life, where they would be safe until the matter could be resolved. However, the willful murderer was not to be sheltered, but delivered up to punishment without pity (Deut. iv, 41–43, and xix, 1–11).

Echota, the ancient Cherokee capital near the mouth of the Little Tennessee, was the Cherokee town of refuge, commonly designated as the "white town" or "peace town." According to Adair, the Cherokee in his time, although extremely degenerate in other things, still observed the law so strictly in this regard that even a willful murderer who might succeed in escaping to that town was safe as long as he remained there. However, unless the matter was settled in the meantime, the friends of the slain person would seldom allow him to reach home alive after leaving it. He tells how a trader who had killed an Indian to protect his own property took refuge in Echota. After having been there for some months, he prepared to return to his trading store, which was only a short distance away, but he was assured by the chiefs that he would be killed if he ventured outside the town. He was therefore obliged to stay a longer time until the tears of the bereaved relatives had been wiped away with presents. In another place, the same author tells how a Cherokee, having killed a trader, was pursued and attempted to take refuge in the town, but was driven off into the river as soon as he came in sight by the inhabitants, who feared either to have their town polluted by the shedding of blood or to provoke the English by giving him sanctuary (Adair, *American Indians*, p. 158, 1775). In 1768, Oconostota, speaking on behalf of the Cherokee delegates who had come to Johnson Hall to make peace with the Iroquois, said: "We come from Chotte, where the wise <note>white?</note> house, the house of peace, is erected" (treaty record, 1768, *New York Colonial Documents*, viii, p. 42, 1857). In 1786, the friendly Cherokee made "Chota" the watchword by which the Americans might be able to distinguish them from the hostile Creeks (Ramsey, *Tennessee*, p. 343). From conversation with elderly Cherokee, it seems probable that in cases where no compensation was made by the relatives of the manslayer, he continued to reside strictly within the limits of the town until the next occurrence of the annual Green-corn dance, when a general amnesty was proclaimed.

Among the Creeks, the ancient town of Kusa or Coosa, on the Coosa River in Alabama, was a town of refuge. In Adair’s time, although then almost deserted and in ruins, it was still a place of safety for one who had taken human life unintentionally. Certain

towns were also known as peace towns, due to their prominence in peace ceremonies and treaty making. Regarding this, Adair says: "In almost every Indian nation there are several peaceful towns, which are called 'old beloved, ancient, holy, or white towns.' They seem to have formerly been towns of refuge, for it is not within the memory of their oldest people that human blood was ever shed in them, although they often force persons from there and put them to death elsewhere."—Adair, *American Indians*, 159. A closely parallel institution seems to have existed among the Seneca. "The Seneca nation, always the largest and guarding the western door of the 'long house,' which was threatened alike from the north, west, and south, had traditions uniquely their own, besides those common to the other members of the confederacy. The stronghold or fort, *Gau-stra-yea*, on the mountain ridge four miles east of Lewiston, had a unique character as the residence of a virgin queen known as the 'Peacemaker.' When the Iroquois confederacy was first formed, the main factors were mutual protection and domestic peace, and this fort was designed to provide comfort and relieve the distress caused by war. It was a true 'city of refuge,' to which fugitives from battle, regardless of their nationality, might flee for safety and find generous hospitality. Curtains of deerskin separated the pursuer and the pursued while they were being lodged and fed. At parting, the curtains were withdrawn, and the hostile parties, having shared the hospitality of the queen, could neither renew hostilities nor pursuit without the queen's consent. According to tradition, no virgin had for many generations been considered worthy to fill the place or possessed the genius and gifts to honor the position. In 1878 the Tonawanda band proposed to revive the office and conferred the title upon Caroline Parker."—Carrington, in *Six Nations of New York, Extra Bulletin Eleventh Census*, p. 73, 1892.

**(21) SCALPING BY WHITES (p. 53):** To the student aware of how easily civilized man reverts to his original savagery when brought into close contact with its conditions, it will be no surprise to learn that every barbarous practice of Indian warfare was quickly adopted by the white pioneer and soldier, and frequently legalized and encouraged by local authority. Scalping, while the most common, was probably the least savage and cruel of them all, being usually performed after the victim was already dead, with the primary purpose of securing a trophy of the victory. The tortures, mutilations, and nameless atrocities inflicted upon Indians by their white conquerors in the early days could hardly be matched even in civilized Europe, when burning at the stake was the punishment for holding original opinions and sawing a person in two was the penalty for desertion. Actual torture of Indians by legal sanction was rare within the English colonies, but mutilation was common and scalping was the rule down to the end of the War of 1812, and has been practiced more or less in almost every Indian war down to the latest. Captain Church, who commanded in King Philip’s War in 1676, states that his men received thirty shillings a head for every Indian killed or taken, and Philip’s head, after it was cut off, "sold at the same price." When the chief was killed, one of his hands was cut off and given to his Indian slayer "to show to such gentlemen as would give tips to him, and accordingly he earned many a penny by it." His other hand was chopped off and sent to Boston for exhibition; his head was sent to Plymouth and exposed upon a scaffold there for twenty years, while the rest of his body was quartered and the pieces left hanging upon four trees. Fifty years later, Massachusetts offered a bounty of one hundred pounds for every Indian scalp, and scalp hunting thus became a regular and usually a profitable business. On one occasion, a certain Lovewell, having recruited a company of forty men for this purpose, discovered ten Indians lying asleep by their fire and killed the whole party. After scalping them, they stretched the scalps upon hoops and marched into Boston, where the scalps were paraded and the bounty of one thousand pounds was paid for them. By selling a few other scalps from time to time at the regular market rate, Lovewell was gradually acquiring a fortune when, in May 1725, his company—

They were pursued by the tribesmen of the slain hunter, with the result that only sixteen of them returned home alive. A famous old ballad of the time tells how:

> "Our worthy Captain Lovewell died among them there.
> They killed Lieutenant Robbins and wounded good young Frye,

When the mission village of Norridgewock was attacked by the New England men about the same time, women and children were made to suffer the fate of the warriors. The scholarly missionary, Rasles, author of the *Abnaki Dictionary*, was shot down at the foot of the cross, where he was afterward found with his body riddled with bullets, his skull crushed and scalped, his mouth and eyes filled with earth, his limbs broken, and all his members mutilated—and this was done by white men. The frontiersmen of the Revolutionary period and later invariably scalped slain Indians as often as opportunity permitted, and, as has already been shown, both British and American officials encouraged the practice by offering bounties and rewards—even, in the case of the former, when the scalps were those of white people. Our troubles with the Apache date back to a treacherous massacre of them in 1836 by a party of American scalp hunters employed by the governor of Sonora. The bounty offered was one ounce of gold per scalp. In 1864, the Colorado militia under Colonel Chivington attacked a party of Cheyennes camped under the protection of the United States flag, and killed, mutilated, and scalped 170 men, women, and children, bringing the scalps into Denver, where they were paraded in a public hall. One Lieutenant Richmond killed and scalped three women and five children. Scalps were taken by American troops in the Modoc war of 1873, and there is a woman currently living in the Comanche tribe who was scalped, though not mortally wounded, by white soldiers in one of the later Indian encounters in Texas. *Authorities:* Drake, *Indians* (for New England wars); Roosevelt, *Virginia State Papers*, *etc.* (Revolution, *etc.*); Bancroft, *Pacific States* (Apache); *Official Report on the Condition of the Indian Tribes, 1867* (for Chivington episode); author's personal information.

(22) LOWER CHEROKEE REFUGEES (p. 55): "In every hut I have visited, I find the children extremely alarmed at the sight of white men. Here [at Willstown], a little boy of eight years old was excessively alarmed and could not be kept from screaming until he got out the door, and then he ran and hid himself. But as soon as I can converse with them and they are informed who I am, they carry out any order I give them with eagerness. I inquired specifically of the mothers what the reason for this could be. They said this town was the remains of several towns whose people formerly lived on Tugalo and Keowee and had been much harassed by the whites; that the old people remembered their former situation and suffering and frequently spoke of them; that the children listened to these stories, and they made an impression which showed itself in the way I had observed. The women whom I saw gathering nuts told me that they had feelings about my coming to the camp that were extremely alarming to them; and when I dismounted from my horse, took them by the hand, and spoke to them, they at first could not reply, although one of them understood and spoke English very well."—Hawkins, manuscript journal, 1796, in the library of the Georgia Historical Society.

The future chief was born in the Creek Nation around 1740 and died at Pensacola, Florida, in 1793. He

He was educated in Charleston, studying Latin in addition to the standard subjects, and after leaving school was placed by his father with a merchant firm in Savannah. He remained for only a short time before he returned to the Creek country, where he soon began to attract attention. He became a partner in the firm of Panton, Forbes & Leslie of Pensacola, which held a near-monopoly on the Creek trade. He succeeded to the leadership upon the death of his mother, who came from a ruling family, but he refused to accept the position until called to it by a formal council, at which point he assumed the title of Emperor of the Creek Nation. Since his father's estates had been confiscated by Georgia at the outbreak of the Revolution, he joined the British side with all his warriors and continued to be a leading instigator of border conflicts until 1790. In that year, he visited New York with a large entourage and signed a peace treaty with the United States on behalf of his people. President Washington’s instructions to the treaty commissioners, in anticipation of this visit, stated that McGillivray was said to possess great abilities and unlimited influence over the Creeks and part of the Cherokee, and that it was a goal worthy of considerable effort to secure his strong loyalty to the United States. In following this policy, the Creek chiefs were entertained by the Tammany Society, with all its members wearing full Indian dress; the visitors were much delighted by this and responded with an Indian dance. Meanwhile, McGillivray was persuaded to resign his commission as a colonel in the Spanish service for a higher-ranking commission in the service of the United States. Shortly afterward, due to some opposition stirred up by Bowles, a white renegade, he left his tribe for a time, but he was soon recalled and continued to rule over the Nation until his death.

McGillivray appears to have had a curious mixture of Scottish shrewdness, French love of display, and Indian reserve. He established his residence at Little Talassee, on the Coosa River, a few miles above what is now Wetumpka, Alabama. There he lived in a fine house with extensive quarters for his enslaved Black people, so that his estate had the appearance of a small town. He entertained magnificently and always traveled in state, as was fitting for one who called himself emperor. Throughout the Indian wars, he strove, as much as possible, to prevent unnecessary cruelties and was noted for his kindness to captives; his final years were spent in an effort to bring teachers to his people. On the other hand, he conformed closely to Indian customs, and he managed his negotiations with England, Spain, and the United States with such skill that he was able to play them against each other, holding commissions in turn in the service of all three. Woodward, who knew of him by his later reputation, asserts firmly that McGillivray’s mother was of pure Indian blood and that he himself was uneducated, claiming his letters had been written for him by Leslie, of the trading firm with which he was connected. However, the weight of evidence seems to leave no doubt that he was an educated as well as a capable man, regardless of his origin. Authorities: Drake, *American Indians*; documents in *American State Papers, Indian Affairs*, I, 1832; Pickett, *Alabama*, 1896; *Appleton’s Cyclopædia of American Biography*; Woodward, *Reminiscences*, p. 59 and throughout, 1859.

(24) **GOVERNOR JOHN SEVIER** (p. 57): This famous leader and statesman in the pioneer history of Tennessee was born in Rockingham County, Virginia, in 1745, and died at the Creek town of Tukabatchee, in Alabama, in 1815. His father was a French immigrant of high birth and education; the original family name was Xavier. The son received a good education, and being naturally remarkably handsome, with polished manners, great courage, and a generous temperament, he soon acquired a remarkable influence over the rough frontiersmen with whom his life was set and among whom he was afterward affectionately known as “Chucky Jack.” To the Cherokee, he was known as Tsan-usdi′, or “Little John.” After some service against the Indians on the Virginia frontier, he moved to the new Watauga settlement in Tennessee in 1772 and immediately became prominently involved with its affairs. # MOONEY] HOPEWELL—COL. BENJ. HAWKINS 211

He took part in Dunmore’s War in 1774 and, afterward, from the start of the Revolution in 1775 until the end of the Indian wars in Tennessee—a period spanning nearly twenty years—was the recognized leader or organizer of every significant Indian campaign along the Tennessee border. His services in this regard have already been mentioned. He also commanded one wing of the American forces at the Battle of King’s Mountain in 1780, and in 1783, he led a group of mountain men to assist the patriots under General Marion. During the Revolution, a Loyalist plot to assassinate him was revealed by the wife of the main conspirator. In 1779, he was commissioned as the commander of the militia of Washington County, North Carolina—the core of what is now the state of Tennessee—a position he had already held by general agreement. 

Shortly after the Revolution ended, he briefly held the office of governor of the seceding “State of Franklin.” Because of this, he was arrested and brought to trial by the government of North Carolina, but he escaped, and the matter was eventually dropped. The jurisdictional dispute was finally resolved in 1790 when North Carolina ceded the disputed territory to the federal government. Before this, Sevier had been commissioned as a brigadier general. When Tennessee was admitted as a state in 1796, he was elected its first governor, serving three terms (six years). In 1803, he was re-elected and served three additional terms. In 1811, he was elected to Congress, where he served two terms and was elected to a third. However, he died at the age of seventy before he could take his seat, having contracted a fever while serving as a boundary commissioner among the Creek Indians. For more than forty years, he was continuously in the service of his country; no man in his state was more loved or respected. In the prime of his life, he was considered the handsomest man and the most skilled Indian fighter in Tennessee.

(25) **HOPEWELL, SOUTH CAROLINA** (p. 61): This location, referred to in early treaties and Benjamin Hawkins’s manuscript journal as “Hopewell on the Keowee,” was the plantation home of General Andrew Pickens. He lived there from the end of the Revolution until his death in 1817. It was located on the northern edge of modern-day Anderson County, on the eastern side of the Keowee River, opposite and just below the mouth of the Little River, about three miles from present-day Pendleton. Within sight of it, on the opposite bank of the Keowee, was the old Cherokee town of Seneca, which the Americans destroyed in 1776. Significant treaties were signed here with the Cherokee in 1785 and the Chickasaw in 1786.

(26) **COLONEL BENJAMIN HAWKINS** (p. 61): This distinguished soldier, statesman, and author was born in Warren County, North Carolina, in 1754 and died in Hawkinsville, Georgia, in 1816. His father, Colonel Philemon Hawkins, organized and commanded a regiment during the Revolutionary War and was a member of the convention that ratified the United States Constitution. At the start of the Revolution, young Hawkins was a student at Princeton. He volunteered for the American cause and, because of his proficiency in French and other modern languages, George Washington appointed him as a staff interpreter to communicate with the French officers assisting the American army. He fought in several battles and was later appointed as a commissioner to obtain war supplies from abroad. 

After the war, he was elected to Congress, and in 1785, he served on the commission that negotiated the first federal treaty with the Cherokee at Hopewell. He served a second term in the House of Representatives and another in the Senate. In 1796, he was appointed superintendent for all Indian tribes south of the Ohio River. He then moved to the Creek nation and settled in the wilderness at what is now Hawkinsville, Georgia, where he remained in office until he died. As a senator, he signed the document by which North Carolina ceded Tennessee to the United States in 1790. As Indian superintendent, he helped negotiate seven different treaties with Southern tribes. He possessed extensive knowledge of the customs and language of the Creek people, and his “Sketch of the Creek

(27) **GOVERNOR WILLIAM BLOUNT** (p. 68): William Blount, territorial governor of Tennessee, was born in North Carolina in 1744 and died at Knoxville, Tennessee, in 1800. He held several important offices in his native state, including two terms in the assembly and two others as a delegate to the old Congress; in that latter role, he was one of the signers of the Federal Constitution in 1787. Upon the organization of a territorial government for Tennessee in 1790, he was appointed territorial governor and also superintendent for the southern tribes, establishing his headquarters at Knoxville. In 1791, he negotiated an important treaty with the Cherokee and was heavily involved in directing operations against the Indians until the close of the Indian war. He was president of the convention that organized the state of Tennessee in 1796 and was elected to the national Senate, but he was expelled on the charge of having entered into a treasonable conspiracy to assist the British in conquering Louisiana from Spain. A United States officer was sent to arrest him but returned without fulfilling his mission after being warned by Blount's friends that they would not allow him to be taken from the state. The impeachment proceedings against him were afterward dismissed on technical grounds. In the meantime, the people of his own state had shown their confidence in him by electing him to the state senate, of which he was chosen president. He died at the early age of fifty-three, the most popular man in the state after Sevier. His younger brother, Willie Blount, who had been his secretary, was afterward governor of Tennessee, 1809–1815.

(28) **ST CLAIR'S DEFEAT**, 1791 (p. 72): Early in 1791, Major-General Arthur St. Clair, a veteran officer of two wars and governor of the Northwestern Territory, was appointed to the chief command of the army operating against the Ohio tribes. On November 4 of that year, while advancing upon the Miami villages with an army of 1,400 men, he was surprised by an Indian force of about the same number under Little-turtle, the Miami chief, in what is now southwestern Mercer County, Ohio, adjoining the Indiana line. Due to the cowardly conduct of the militia, he was totally defeated, with the loss of 632 officers and men killed and missing, and 263 wounded, many of whom died later. The artillery was abandoned, as not a single horse was left alive to pull it away, and the panic was so great that the men threw away their weapons and fled for miles, even after the pursuit had stopped. It was later learned that the Indians lost 150 killed, besides many wounded. Two years later, General Wayne built Fort Recovery on the same spot. The detachment sent to do the work found 500 skulls within a space of 350 yards, while for several miles along the path of pursuit, the woods were strewn with skeletons and muskets. The two lost cannons were found in the nearby stream. *Authorities:* St. Clair's report and related documents, 1791; American State Papers, Indian Affairs, I, 1832; Drake, Indians 570, 571, 1880; Appleton's Cyclopædia of American Biography.

(29) **CHEROKEE CLANS**, (p. 74): The Cherokee have seven clans, namely: *Ani′-Wa″ya*, Wolf; *Ani′-Kawi′*, Deer; *Ani′-Tsi′skwa*, Bird; *Ani′-Wâ′dǐ*, Paint; *Ani′-Sahâ′nǐ*; *Ani′-Ga′tâge′wǐ*; *Ani′-Gilâ′hǐ*. The names of the last three cannot be translated with certainty. The Wolf clan is the largest and most important in the tribe. It is probable that, in accordance with the general system in other tribes, each clan formerly had certain hereditary duties and privileges, but no trace of these remains today. Children belong to the clan of the mother, and the law forbidding marriage between persons of the same clan is still enforced among the conservative

(30) **WAYNE'S VICTORY**, 1794 (p. 78): After the successive failures of Harmar and St. Clair in their efforts against the Ohio tribes, the chief command was assigned in 1793 to Major-General Anthony Wayne, who had already distinguished himself by his fighting qualities during the Revolution. After building Fort Recovery on the site of St. Clair's defeat, he made that post his headquarters throughout the winter of 1793–94. In the summer of 1794, he advanced down the Maumee River with an army of 3,000 men, two-thirds of whom were regulars. On August 20, he encountered the allied Indian forces near the head of the Maumee rapids at a point known as Fallen Timbers and defeated them with great loss of life. The pursuit was continued by the cavalry until the Indians took refuge under the guns of the British garrison at Fort Miami, just below the rapids. Wayne's own loss was only 33 killed and 100 wounded, 11 of whom later died from their wounds. The loss of the Indians and their white auxiliaries was believed to be more than double this. The Indian force was estimated to number 2,000, while, because of the forcefulness of Wayne's charge, the number of his troops actually engaged did not exceed 900. Because of this defeat and the subsequent destruction of their towns and fields by the victorious army, the Indians were compelled to ask for peace. This was granted by the treaty concluded at Greenville, Ohio, on August 3, 1795, by which the represented tribes ceded nearly their entire territory in Ohio. *Authorities: Wayne's report and related documents, 1794, American State Papers: Indian Affairs, I, 1832; Drake, Indians, 571–577, 1880; Greenville treaty, in Indian Treaties, 1837; Appleton's Cyclopædia of American Biography.*

(31) **FIRST THINGS OF CIVILIZATION** (p. 83): We usually find that the first things the Indians adopted from their white neighbors were improved weapons and cutting tools, along with trinkets and items for personal decoration. After a regular trade has been established, certain traders marry Indian wives and, taking up permanent residence in the Indian country, engage in farming and stock raising according to civilized methods. In this way, even without intending to, they become practical teachers for the tribe.

From data provided by Haywood, guns appear to have been first introduced among the Cherokee around the year 1700 or 1710, although he himself sets the date much earlier. Horses were probably not owned in any great number before the horse-path for traders from Augusta was marked out around 1740. The Cherokee, however, took a liking to the animal, and before the beginning of the war of 1760, they had an "enormous number." In spite of their great losses at that time, they had recovered so much by 1775 that almost every man then had from two to a dozen horses (Adair, p. 231). In the border wars following the Revolution, companies of hundreds of mounted Cherokee and Creeks sometimes invaded the settlements. The cow is called *wa'ka* by the Cherokee and *waga* by the Creeks, indicating that their first knowledge of it came through the Spaniards. Nuttall states that it was first introduced among the Cherokee by the famous Nancy Ward (*Travels*, p. 130). It was not in such favor as the horse, being valuable chiefly for food, of which there was an abundant supply from wild game at that time. A strong reason for avoiding it was the Indian belief that eating the flesh of a slow-moving animal causes a similar sluggishness in the eater. The same argument applied even more strongly to the hog, and to this day a few of the old conservatives among the East Cherokee will have nothing to do with beef, pork, milk, or butter. Nevertheless, Bartram tells of a trader in the Cherokee country as early as 1775 who had a stock

In 1796, Hawkins mentions meeting two Cherokee women driving ten very fat cattle to market in the white settlements (manuscript journal, 1796). Bees, if not native as the Indians claim, were introduced at such an early period that the Indians have forgotten their foreign origin. The De Soto narrative mentions the finding of a pot of honey in an Indian village in Georgia in 1540. The peach was cultivated in orchards a century before the Revolution, and one variety, known as early as 1700 as the "Indian peach," the Indians claimed as their own, asserting that they had it before the whites came to America (Lawson, Carolina, p. 182, ed. 1860). Potatoes were introduced early and were so highly esteemed that, according to one old informant, the Indians in Georgia, before the Removal, "lived on them." Coffee came later, and the same informant remembered when the full-blooded Indians still considered it poison, in spite of the efforts of the chief, Charles Hicks, to introduce it among them.

Spinning wheels and looms were introduced shortly before the Revolution. According to the Wahnenuahi manuscript, the first among the Cherokee were brought over from England by an Englishman named Edward Graves, who taught his Cherokee wife to spin and weave. The anonymous writer may have confused this early civilizer with a young Englishman who was employed by Agent Hawkins in 1801 to make wheels and looms for the Creeks (Hawkins, 1801, in American State Papers: Indian Affairs, I, p. 647). Wafford, in his boyhood, say about 1815, knew an old man named Tsí'nawí on Young-cane creek of Nottely river, in upper Georgia, who was known as a wheelwright and was reputed to have made the first spinning wheel and loom ever made among the mountain Cherokee, or perhaps in the Nation, long before Wafford’s time, or "about the time the Cherokee began to drop their silver ornaments and go to work." In 1785, the commissioners for the Hopewell treaty reported that some of the Cherokee women had lately learned to spin, and many were very desirous of instruction in the raising, spinning, and weaving of flax, cotton, and wool (Hopewell Commissioners' Report, 1785, American State Papers: Indian Affairs, I, p. 39). In accordance with their recommendation, the next treaty made with the tribe, in 1791, contained a provision for supplying the Cherokee with farming tools (Holston treaty, 1791, Indian Treaties, p. 36, 1837), and this civilizing policy was continued and broadened until, in 1801, their agent reported that at the Cherokee agency the wheel, the loom, and the plow were in fairly general use, and farming, manufacturing, and stock raising were the principal topics of conversation among men and women (Hawkins manuscripts, Treaty Commission of 1801).

(32) **COLONEL RETURN J. MEIGS** (p. 84): Return Jonathan Meigs was born in Middletown, Connecticut, December 17, 1734, and died at the Cherokee agency in Tennessee, January 28, 1823. He was the first-born son of his parents, who gave him the somewhat peculiar name of "Return Jonathan" to commemorate a romantic incident in their own courtship, when his mother, a young Quakeress, called back her lover as he was mounting his horse to leave the house forever after what he had supposed was a final refusal. The name has been handed down through five generations, every one of which has produced some man distinguished in the public service. The subject of this sketch volunteered immediately after the opening engagement of the Revolution at Lexington, and was assigned to duty under Arnold with the rank of major. He accompanied Arnold in the disastrous march through the wilderness against Quebec and was captured in the assault upon the citadel and held until exchanged the next year. In 1777, he raised a regiment and was promoted to the rank of colonel. For a gallant and successful attack upon the enemy at Sag Harbor, Long Island, he received a sword and a vote of thanks from Congress, and by his conduct at the head of his regiment at Stony Point, he won the favorable notice of Washington. After the close of the Revolution, he moved to Ohio, where, as a member of the territorial legislature, he drew up the earliest code of regula-

(33) <term>TECUMTHA</term> (p. 87): This great chief of the <term>Shawano</term> <note>Shawnee</note> and commander of the allied northern tribes in the British service was born near present-day Chillicothe, in western Ohio, about 1770, and fell in the Battle of the Thames, in Ontario, October 5, 1813. His name signifies a "flying panther"—that is, a meteor. He came of fighting stock that was good even in a tribe distinguished for its warlike qualities; his father and elder brother had been killed in battle with the whites. His mother is said to have died among the Cherokee. Tecumtha is first heard of as taking part in an engagement with the Kentuckians when he was about twenty years old, and in a few years, he had secured recognition as the ablest leader among the allied tribes. It is said that he took part in every important engagement with the Americans from the time of Harmar’s defeat in 1790 until the battle in which he lost his life. When about thirty years of age, he conceived the idea of uniting the tribes northwest of the Ohio, as Pontiac had united them before, in a great confederacy to resist the further advance of the Americans. He took the stand that the whole territory between the Ohio and the Mississippi belonged to all these tribes in common and that no single tribe had the right to sell any portion of it without the consent of the others. The refusal of the government to admit this principle led him to take active steps to unite the tribes upon that basis, in which he was supported by his brother, the Prophet, who supplemented Tecumtha’s eloquence with his own claims to supernatural revelation. In the summer of 1810, Tecumtha held a conference with Governor Harrison at Vincennes to protest against a recent treaty cession. Finding after exhausting his arguments that the effort was fruitless, he closed the debate with the words:

> "The President is far off and may sit in his town and drink his wine, but you and I will have to fight it out."

Both sides at once prepared for war. Tecumtha went south to enlist the aid of the Creek, Choctaw, and other southern tribes, while Harrison took advantage of his absence to force the issue by marching against the Prophet’s town on the Tippecanoe River, where the hostile warriors from a dozen tribes had gathered. A battle fought before daybreak on November 6, 1811, resulted in the defeat of the Indians and the scattering of their forces. Tecumtha returned to find his plans brought to nothing for the time, but the opening of the war between the United States and England a few months later enabled him to rally the confederated tribes once more to the support of the British against the Americans. As a commissioned brigadier-general in the British service, he commanded 2,000 warriors in the War of 1812, distinguishing himself no less by his bravery than by his humanity in preventing atrocities and protecting prisoners from massacre. At one time, he saved the lives of four hundred American prisoners who had been taken in an ambush near Fort Meigs and were unable to make further resistance. He was wounded at Maguagua, where nearly four hundred were killed and wounded on both sides. He covered the British retreat after the Battle of Lake Erie and, refusing to retreat further, compelled the British General Proctor to make a stand at the Thames River. Almost the whole force of the American attack fell on Tecumtha’s division. Early in the

(34) **FORT MIMS MASSACRE, 1813** (p. 89): Fort Mims, named after an old Indian trader on whose land it was built, was a stockade fort constructed in the summer of 1813 to protect the settlers in what was known as the Tensaw district. It was located on Tensaw Lake, Alabama, one mile east of the Alabama River and about forty miles above Mobile. It was defended by about 200 volunteer troops under Major Daniel Beasley, along with refugees from the neighboring settlement, totaling 553 men, women, and children at the time of its destruction. Because it was poorly guarded, it was surprised on the morning of August 30 by about 1,000 Creek warriors led by the chief of mixed ancestry <note>mixed-blood</note>, William Weatherford. They rushed in through the open gate, and after a fierce but hopeless resistance by the garrison, they killed everyone inside, with the exception of a few Black people and people of mixed heritage <note>half-breeds</note> whom they spared, and about a dozen white people who managed to escape. The Indian losses are unknown but were very heavy, as the fighting continued at close quarters until the buildings were set on fire over the heads of the defenders. This unfortunate tragedy was caused entirely by the negligence of the commanding officer, who had been warned repeatedly that Indians were in the area. At the very moment of the attack, a Black man <note>negro</note> was tied up, waiting to be whipped for reporting that he had seen a number of painted warriors lurking a short distance outside the stockade the day before. *Authorities:* Pickett, *Alabama*, ed. 1896; Hamilton and Owen, note, p. 170, in *Transactions of the Alabama Historical Society*, II, 1898; Agent Hawkins’s report, 1813, *American State Papers: Indian Affairs*, I, p. 853; Drake, *Indians*, ed. 1880. The figures provided are those of Pickett, which in this instance seem most accurate, while Drake’s are clearly exaggerated.

(35) **GENERAL WILLIAM MCINTOSH** (p. 98): This prominent biracial <note>halfbreed</note> chief of the Lower Creeks was the son of a Scottish officer in the British army and an Indian mother. He was born at the Creek town of Coweta in Alabama, on the lower Chattahoochee, nearly opposite the present city of Columbus, Georgia. He was killed at the same location by order of the Creek National Council on April 30, 1825. Having enough education to maintain official correspondence, he brought himself to public attention and came to be regarded as the primary chief of the Lower Creeks. In the Creek War of 1813–14, he led his warriors in support of the Americans against his fellow tribesmen of the Upper towns and played a leading role in the terrible massacres at Autossee and Horseshoe Bend. In 1817, he again led his warriors on the government’s side against the Seminole and was given the rank of major. His common title of "general" was merely an honorary one. In 1821, he was the main supporter of the Treaty of Indian Springs, through which a large tract of land between the Flint and Chattahoochee rivers was surrendered. The treaty was rejected by the Creek Nation as the work of a small faction. Two other attempts were made to finalize the treaty, during which McIntosh's self-interested motives became so obvious that he was labeled a traitor to his Nation and sentenced to death, along with his main subordinates, in accordance with a Creek law that made death the penalty for attempting to sell land without the consent of the National Council. Around the same time, he was publicly exposed and condemned in the Cherokee Council for trying to bribe John Ross and other Cherokee chiefs in a similar manner. At dawn on April 30, 1825, a hundred or more warriors sent by the Creek National Council surrounded his house. After allowing the women and children to leave, they set fire to the building and shot McIntosh and another chief

(36) WILLIAM WEATHERFORD (p. 89): This leader of the hostile forces in the Creek War was the son of a white father and a woman of mixed ancestry <note>half-breed</note> from Tuskegee town, whose own father had been Scottish. Weatherford was born in the Creek Nation around 1780 and died on Little River, in Monroe County, Alabama, in 1826. He first became prominent by leading the attack on Fort Mims on August 30, 1813, which resulted in the destruction of the fort and the massacre of over five hundred people. It is claimed, with apparent truth, that he did his best to prevent the excesses that followed the victory and left the scene rather than witness the atrocities when he found he could not restrain his followers. The fact that Jackson allowed him to go home unmolested after the final surrender is evidence that he believed Weatherford was innocent of those crimes. At the battle of the Holy Ground, in the following December, he was defeated and narrowly escaped capture by troops under General Claiborne. When the last hope of the Creeks had been destroyed and their power of resistance broken by the bloody battle of Horseshoe Bend on March 27, 1814, Weatherford voluntarily walked into General Jackson’s headquarters and surrendered. He created such an impression with his straightforward and fearless manner that the general, after a friendly interview, allowed him to go back alone to gather his people before arranging peace terms. After the treaty, he retired to a plantation in Monroe County, where he lived in comfort and was highly respected by his white neighbors until his death. As an illustration of his courage, it is told how he once, single-handedly, arrested two murderers immediately after their crime, when the local justice and a large crowd of bystanders were afraid to approach them. Jackson declared him to be as honorable <note>high toned</note> and fearless as any man he had ever met. In person, he was tall, straight, and well-proportioned, with features indicating intelligence, bravery, and initiative. *Sources*: Pickett, *Alabama*, 1896 edition; Drake, *Indians*, 1880 edition; Woodward, *Reminiscences*, 1859.

(37) REVEREND DAVID BRAINERD (p. 104): The pioneer American missionary from whom the famous Cherokee mission took its name was born at Haddam, Connecticut, on April 20, 1718, and died at Northampton, Massachusetts, on October 9, 1747. He entered Yale College in 1739 but was expelled because of his religious opinions. In 1742, he was licensed as a preacher, and the next year he began work as a missionary to the Mahican Indians at the village of Kaunameek, twenty miles from Stockbridge, Massachusetts. He persuaded them to move to Stockbridge, where he placed them in the care of a resident minister, after which he took up work with good results among the Delaware and other tribes on the Delaware and Susquehanna rivers. In 1747, his health failed, and he was forced to retire to Northampton, where he died a few months later. He wrote a journal and an account of his missionary work at Kaunameek. His later mission work was taken up and continued by his brother. *Source*: *Appleton’s Cyclopædia of American Biography*, 1894.

(38) REVEREND SAMUEL AUSTIN WORCESTER (p. 105): This noted missionary and <term>philologist</term>, the son of a Congregational minister who was also a printer, was born at Worcester, Massachusetts, on January 19, 1798, and died at Park Hill, in the Cherokee Nation west, on April 20, 1859. Having moved to Vermont with his father while still a child, he graduated with honors from the state university at Burlington in 1819. After finishing a course at the theological seminary at Andover, he was ordained to the ministry in 1825. A week later, with his new bride, he left Boston to begin mission work among the Cherokee and arrived in October at the mission of the American Board at Brainerd, Tennessee, where he remained until the end of 1827. He then, with his wife, moved to New Echota, Georgia, the capital of the Cherokee Nation, where he was the primary worker in establishing the *Cherokee Phoenix*, the first newspaper printed in the Cherokee

In March 1831, he was arrested by the Georgia authorities for refusing to take a special oath of allegiance to the state. He was released, but was rearrested soon afterward, confined in the state penitentiary, and forced to wear prison clothes until January 1833, despite a decision by the Supreme Court of the United States, nearly a year earlier, that his imprisonment was a violation of the law of the land. After the *Cherokee Phoenix* was suspended and the Cherokee Nation was brought into disorder by the extension of state laws over it, he then returned to Brainerd, which was beyond the limits of Georgia. In 1835, he moved to the Indian Territory, where the Arkansas Cherokee had already gone, and after short stays at Dwight and Union missions, he took up his final residence at Park Hill in December 1836. He had already set up his mission press at Union, printing in both the Cherokee and the Creek languages, and upon establishing himself at Park Hill, he began a regular series of publications in the Cherokee language. In 1843, he stated that "at Park Hill, besides the preaching of the gospel, a leading object of attention is the preparation and publication of books in the Cherokee language" (Letter in Report of Indian Commissioner, p. 356, 1843). The list of his Cherokee publications (first editions) under his own name in Pilling's Bibliography comprises about twenty titles, including the Bible, hymn books, tracts, and almanacs, in addition to the *Phoenix* and a large number of anonymous works. Pilling says: "It is very probable that he was the translator of a number of books for which he is not given credit here, especially those portions of the Scripture which are not assigned to any name here. Indeed, it is safe to say that during the thirty-four years of his connection with the Cherokee, little was done in the way of translating in which he had not a share." He also began a Cherokee geography and had both a grammar and a dictionary of the language under way when his work was interrupted by his arrest. The manuscripts, along with all his personal effects, later sank with a steamer on the Arkansas River. His daughter, Mrs. A. E. W. Robertson, became a missionary among the Creeks and has published a number of works in their language. *Authorities:* Pilling, Bibliography of the Iroquoian languages (articles Worcester, Cherokee Phoenix, etc.), 1888; Drake, Indians, 1880 ed.; Report of Indian Commissioner, 1843 (Worcester letter).

(39) DEATH PENALTY FOR SELLING LANDS (p. 107): In 1820, the Cherokee Nation enacted a law making it treason, punishable by death, to enter into any negotiation for the sale of tribal lands without the consent of the national council. A similar law was enacted by the Creeks at about the same time. It was for violating these laws that McIntosh and Ridge were put to death in their respective tribes. The principal parts of the Cherokee law, as reenacted by the United Nation in the West in 1842, appear as follows in the compilation authorized in 1866:

> "AN ACT AGAINST THE SALE OF LAND, ETC.: *Whereas*, the peace and prosperity of Indian nations are frequently sacrificed or placed in jeopardy by the unrestrained greed of their own individual citizens; *and whereas*, we ourselves are liable to suffer from the same cause, and be subjected to future removal and disturbances: Therefore, . . . 
> "*Be it further enacted*, That any person or persons who shall, contrary to the will and consent of the legislative council of this nation, in general council convened, enter into a treaty with any commissioner or commissioners of the United States, or any officer or officers instructed for the purpose, and agree to cede, exchange, or dispose of in any way any part or portion of the lands belonging to or claimed by the Cherokees, west of the Mississippi, he or they so offending, upon conviction before any judge of the circuit or supreme courts, *shall suffer death*, and any of the aforesaid judges are authorized to call a court for the trial of any person or persons so transgressing."

### (40) THE CHEROKEE SYLLABARY (p. 110):

In the various schemes of symbolic thought representation—from the simple pictograph of primitive man to the finished alphabet of civilized nations—our own system, although not yet perfect, stands at the head of the list, the result of three thousand years of development by Egyptians, Phoenicians, and Greeks. Sequoya's syllabary, the unaided work of an uneducated Indian raised amid semi-savage surroundings, stands second.

Twelve years of his life are said to have been dedicated to his great work. Being entirely without instruction and having no knowledge of the philosophy of language—not even being acquainted with English—his first attempts were naturally enough in the direction of the crude Indian pictograph. He set out to design a symbol for every word in the language, and after several years of experiment, finding this an utterly hopeless task, he threw aside the thousands of characters which he had carved or scratched upon pieces of bark and started anew to study the construction of the language itself. By attentive observation for another long period, he finally discovered that the sounds in the words used by the Cherokee in their daily conversation and their public speeches could be analyzed and classified, and that the thousands of possible words were all formed from varying combinations of hardly more than a hundred distinct syllables. Having thoroughly tested his discovery until satisfied of its correctness, he next proceeded to create a symbol for each syllable. For this purpose, he made use of a number of characters which he found in an old English spelling book, picking out capital letters, lowercase letters, italics, and numbers, and placing them right side up or upside down, without any idea of their sound or significance as used in English (see plate v). Having thus utilized some thirty-five ready-made characters, to which must be added a dozen or more produced by modifying those same originals, he designed from his own imagination as many more as were necessary for his purpose, making eighty-five in all. The complete syllabary, as first developed, would have required about one hundred and fifteen characters, but after much hard study over the hissing sound in its various combinations, he hit upon the strategy of representing the sound by means of a distinct character—the exact equivalent of our letter *s*—whenever it formed the beginning of a syllable. Gallatin says: “It lacked only one more step—to have also given a distinct character to each consonant—to reduce the whole number to sixteen and to have had an alphabet similar to ours. In practice, however, and as applied to his own language, the superiority of Guess's alphabet is manifest and has been fully proved by experience. You must indeed learn and remember eighty-five characters instead of twenty-five <note>The author likely means twenty-six, the standard English alphabet.</note>. But once this is accomplished, the education of the pupil is completed; he can read, and he is perfect in his <term>orthography</term> without making it the subject of a distinct study. The boy learns in a few weeks that which occupies two years of the time of ours.” Phillips says: “In my own observation, Indian children will take one or two, and at times several, years to master the English printed and written language, but in a few days they can read and write in Cherokee. They do the latter, in fact, as soon as they learn to shape letters. As soon as they master the alphabet, they have gotten rid of all the perplexing questions in <term>orthography</term> that puzzle the brains of our children. It is not too much to say that a child will learn in a month, by the same effort, as thoroughly in the language

<summary>This page discusses Cherokee legal statutes regarding outlaws and treaty ratification, followed by a detailed history of how Sequoya created the Cherokee syllabary. It highlights the efficiency of his 85-character system compared to the English alphabet for native learners.</summary>
<keywords>Cherokee Law, Sequoya, George Guess, Cherokee Syllabary, orthography, linguistics, education, Gallatin, Phillips</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Sequoyah’s syllabary, focusing on its phonetic application and dialectal adaptations, before transitioning into a historical overview of gold mining in the southern Appalachian region and its impact on the Cherokee Nation.</meta>

of Sequoyah, a system which children can master in a fraction of the time that our own system consumes—at least two years for our children.”

Although the written Cherokee word theoretically has one letter for each syllable, this rule does not always hold true in practice because vowel sounds are frequently dropped. For example, the word for “soul” is written with four letters as *a-da-nún-ta*, but it is pronounced in three syllables as *adanta*. Similarly, *tsá-lún-i-yu-sti* (meaning “like tobacco,” the cardinal flower) is pronounced *tsáliyusti*. As in other languages, there are also many small variations in sound that are not indicated in the written word; therefore, one must hear the language spoken to read it with the correct pronunciation. The old Upper dialect is the standard to which the alphabet was adapted. There is no specific provision for the *r* sound of the Lower dialect or the *sh* sound of the Middle dialect; instead, each speaker usually makes their own dialectal changes while reading. The letters of a word are not connected, and there is no difference between the handwritten and the printed characters. *Authorities:* Gallatin, *Synopsis of the Indian Tribes*, in Trans. Am. Antiq. Soc., II, 1836; Phillips, *Sequoyah*, in Harper’s Magazine, September, 1870; Pilling, *Bibliography of Iroquoian Languages* (article on Guess and plate of syllabary), 1888; author’s personal information.

### (41) SOUTHERN GOLD FIELDS (p. 116): 

Almost every valuable mineral and crystal known to manufacturers or gemstone cutters is found in the southern Alleghenies, although, based on current knowledge, few of these occur in profitable quantities. It is likely, however, that this assessment may change with improved mining methods and expanded railroad access. Excluding the earlier operations by Spanish, French, and English adventurers, which have already been mentioned, the first reliable account of gold being found in any of the states south of the Mason-Dixon line during the American period appears to be the one given by Thomas Jefferson. Writing in 1781, he described a lump of ore found in Virginia that yielded seventeen pennyweights of gold. This was probably not the earliest discovery, however, as there are questionable references to gold being found in both Carolinas before the Revolution. The first mint returns for gold were made from North Carolina in 1793 and from South Carolina in 1829, though gold is known to have been found in the latter state several years earlier. 

The earliest gold records for the other southern states are approximately: Georgia (near Dahlonega), 1815–1820; Alabama, 1830; Tennessee (Coco Creek, Monroe County), 1831; and Maryland (Montgomery County), 1849. The systematic tracing of gold belts southward from North Carolina began in 1829 and quickly resulted in the forced removal of the Cherokee from the gold-bearing regions. Most of the precious metal was obtained from placers or alluvial deposits <note>surface deposits of minerals found in riverbeds</note> through a simple process of digging and washing. Very little quartz mining has been attempted, and that has usually been done using the crudest methods. In fact, for a long period, gold mining was treated as a side business to farming between growing seasons. In North Carolina, prospectors obtained permission from landowners to wash or dig for a share of the profits, varying from one-fourth to one-half. Owners would also put their enslaved people to work in the creek bottoms after the crops had been safely harvested. “Gold dust became a significant form of currency; miners used to carry quills filled with gold and a pair of small hand scales to weigh out the gold at fixed rates. For instance, 3 1/3 grains of gold was the standard equivalent for a pint of whiskey.” For several years around 1830 and later, a man named Bechtler coined gold privately in North Carolina. These coins, along with Mexican silver, are said to have been the primary currency over a large region. A federal mint was established at Dahlonega in 1838 and operated for several years. From 1804 to 1827, all the gold produced in the United States came from North Carolina, though the total amount was only $110,000. The discovery of rich deposits in California halted mining operations in the South, and the Civil War brought about an almost complete suspen—

### (42) **EXTENSION OF GEORGIA LAWS**, 1830 (p. 117): 
> “It is hereby decreed that all the laws of Georgia are extended over the Cherokee country; that after the first day of June, 1830, all Indians residing in said territory at that time shall be subject to such laws and regulations as the legislature may hereafter prescribe; that all laws, usages, and customs established and enforced in the said territory by the Cherokee Indians are hereby declared null and void on and after June 1, 1830; and no Indian, or descendant of an Indian, residing within the Creek or Cherokee nations of Indians, shall be considered a competent witness or party to any suit in any court where a white man is a defendant.”

—Extract from the act passed by the Georgia legislature on December 20, 1828, “to add the territory within this state and occupied by the Cherokee Indians to the counties of DeKalb et al.; and to extend the laws of this state over the same.” *Sources:* Drake, *Indians*, p. 439, 1880 edition; Royce, *Cherokee Nation of Indians*, in the Fifth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, p. 260, 1888.

### (43) **REMOVAL FORTS**, 1838 (p. 130): 
To gather the Cherokee in preparation for the Removal, the following stockade forts were built: In North Carolina, Fort Lindsay, on the south side of the Tennessee River at the junction of the Nantahala in Swain County; Fort Scott, at Aquone, farther up the Nantahala River in Macon County; Fort Montgomery, at Robbinsville in Graham County; Fort Hembrie, at Hayesville in Clay County; Fort Delaney, at Valleytown in Cherokee County; and Fort Butler, at Murphy in the same county. In Georgia, Fort Scudder, on Frogtown Creek, north of Dahlonega in Lumpkin County; Fort Gilmer, near Ellijay in Gilmer County; Fort Coosawatee in Murray County; Fort Talking-rock, near Jasper in Pickens County; and Fort Buffington, near Canton in Cherokee County. In Tennessee, Fort Cass, at Calhoun on the Hiwassee River in McMinn County. In Alabama, Fort Turkeytown, on the Coosa River at Center in Cherokee County. *Source:* Author’s personal information.
