Just inside the Tennessee line, where the Conasauga River bends back into Georgia, is a stone-walled grave with a slab. It bears an epitaph that tells its own story of the heartbreak of the Removal. McNair was a white man, prominent in the Cherokee Nation, whose wife was a daughter of the chief, Vann—the man who welcomed the Moravian missionaries and gave his own house for their use. (45) **PRESIDENT SAMUEL HOUSTON**, (p. 145): This remarkable man was born in Rockbridge County, Virginia, on March 2, 1793, and died at Huntsville, Texas, on July 25, 1863. A man of strangely versatile but forceful character, he occupies a unique position in American history, combining to a wonderful degree the rugged manhood of the pioneer, the eccentric vanity of the Indian, the stern dignity of the soldier, the genius of the statesman, and the high chivalry of a knight of old. His unpredictable career has been the subject of much sensational storytelling, but the simple facts are interesting enough in themselves without the need for fictional additions. To the Cherokee, whom he loved so well, he was known as <term>Kâ'lanû</term>, "The Raven," an old war title within the tribe.

After his father died when the boy was nine years old, his widowed mother moved with him to Tennessee, opposite the territory of the Cherokee, whose boundary was then the Tennessee River. Here he worked on the farm, attending school at intervals; but, being of an adventurous nature, he left home when he was sixteen years old. Crossing the river, he joined the Cherokee, among whom he soon became a great favorite. He was adopted into the family of Chief Jolly, for whom the island at the mouth of the Hiwassee is named. After three years of this life, during which time he wore Indian clothing and learned the Cherokee language, he returned to civilization and enlisted as a private soldier under Jackson in the Creek War. He soon attracted favorable notice and was promoted to the rank of ensign. Through striking bravery at the bloody Battle of Horseshoe Bend—where he climbed the defensive walls with an arrow in his thigh and led his men into the thick of the enemy—he won the lasting friendship of Jackson. Jackson made him a lieutenant, although he was then barely twenty-one. He continued in the army after the war, serving for a time as a subagent for the Cherokee at Jackson's request, until the summer of 1818, when he resigned because of some criticism by Calhoun, who was then the Secretary of War. An official investigation, held at his demand, resulted in him being cleared of all charges.

Moving to Nashville, he began the study of law, and shortly afterward was admitted to the bar and set up a practice in Lebanon. Within five years, he was successively a district attorney, adjutant general, and major general of state troops. In 1823, he was elected to Congress, serving two terms. At the end of these, in 1827, he was elected Governor of Tennessee by an overwhelming majority, being then thirty-four years of age. Shortly before this time, he had fought and wounded General White in a duel. In January 1829, he married a young lady residing near Nashville, but two months later, without a word of explanation to any outsider, he left her, resigned his governorship and other official positions, and left the state forever to rejoin his old friends, the Cherokee, in the West. For years the reason for this strange conduct was a secret, and Houston himself always refused to talk about it, but it is now understood to have been because his wife admitted to him that she loved another man and had only been persuaded to marry him by the heavy pressure of her parents.

From Tennessee, he went to Indian Territory, where a large part of the Cherokee had already moved, and once more took up his residence near Chief Jolly, who was now the principal chief of the Western Cherokee. The great disappointment which seemed to have ruined his life at its brightest was heavy at his

heart, and he sought to forget his troubles in drinking to such an extent that for a time his character seemed to have failed. Despite this, such was his force of personality and his past reputation that he retained the affection of the Cherokee and his standing with the officers and their families at the neighboring posts of Fort Smith, Fort Gibson, and Fort Coffee. In the meantime, his former wife in Tennessee had obtained a divorce. Being free once more, Houston soon afterward married Talihina, the youngest daughter of a prominent Cherokee of mixed heritage named Rogers, who lived near Fort Gibson. She was the niece of Houston's adopted father, Chief Jolly, and he had known her when he was a boy in the old Nation. Being a beautiful girl and more highly educated than those around her, she became a welcome guest wherever her husband was received. He started a trading store near Webbers Falls, but continued his drinking habits until he was shocked back to his senses by the outcome of a drunken brawl in which he assaulted his adopted father, the old chief, and was himself knocked unconscious. Upon recovering from his injuries, he made a public apology for his conduct and from then on led a sober life.

In 1832, he visited Washington on behalf of the western Cherokee, calling on President Jackson in Indian dress; Jackson received him with their old-time friendship. While there, he was accused of connection with a fraudulent Indian contract, and he responded by severely beating his accuser, a member of Congress. For this, he was fined $500 and reprimanded at the bar of the House, but Jackson canceled the fine. Soon after his return to the West, he moved to Texas to take part in the agitation just starting against Mexican rule. He was a member of the convention that adopted a separate constitution for Texas in 1833, and two years later he aided in forming a provisional government and was elected commander-in-chief to organize the new militia. In 1836, he was a member of the convention that declared the independence of Texas. At the battle of San Jacinto in April of that year, with 750 men, he defeated Santa Ana's army of 1,800, inflicting a terrible loss on the Mexicans of 630 killed and 730 prisoners, among whom was Santa Ana himself. Houston received a severe wound in the engagement. In the autumn of the same year, he was elected the first president of the Republic of Texas, receiving more than four-fifths of the votes cast. He served two years and retired at the end of his term, leaving the country on good terms with both Mexico and the Indian tribes, and with its currency valued at its face value. He was immediately elected to the Texas congress and served in that capacity until 1841, when he was reelected president. It was during these years that he made his steadfast fight on behalf of the Texas Cherokee, as is narrated elsewhere, supporting their cause without wavering, even at the risk of his own popularity and position. He frequently declared that no treaty made and carried out in good faith had ever been violated by Indians. His Cherokee wife having died some time before, he married again in 1840, this time to a lady from Alabama who exercised a restraining and ennobling influence over him through the stormy changes of his eventful life. In June 1842, he vetoed a bill that would have made him a dictator for the purpose of resisting a threatened invasion from Mexico.

On December 29, 1845, Texas was admitted to the Union, and in the following March, Houston was elected to the Senate. He served there continuously until 1859, when he resigned to take his seat as governor, a position to which he had just been elected. From 1852 to 1860, his name was three times presented before national presidential nominating conventions, receiving 57 votes the last time. He had disagreed with the Democratic majority throughout his time in the Senate, and when Texas passed the secession ordinance in February 1861, being a firm Union man, he refused to take the oath of allegiance to the Confederacy. He was accordingly removed from the office of governor, declining the offered aid of federal troops to keep him in his seat. Unwilling either to fight against the Union or to take sides against his friends, he held himself apart from the great struggle and remained in silent retirement until his death two years later. (46) CHIEF JOHN ROSS (p. 151): This great chief of the Cherokee, whose name is inseparable from their history, was himself only one-eighth Indian by blood and showed few Indian features. His father, Daniel Ross, had emigrated from Scotland before the Revolution and married a quarter-blood Cherokee woman whose father, John McDonald, was also from Scotland. He was born at or near the family residence at Rossville, Georgia, just across the line from Chattanooga, Tennessee. As a boy, he was known among the Cherokee as Tsan-usdĭ', “Little John,” but after reaching manhood he was called Guwi'sguwí', the name of a rare migratory bird of large size with white or grayish plumage, said to have appeared in the past at long intervals in the old Cherokee country. It may have been the egret or the swan. He was educated at Kingston, Tennessee, and began his public career when barely nineteen years of age. His first wife, a full-blood Cherokee woman, died as a result of the hardships of the Removal during the march west and was buried at Little Rock, Arkansas. Some years later he married again, this time to a Miss Stapler of Wilmington, Delaware, the marriage taking place in Philadelphia (the author’s personal information from Mr. Allen Ross, son of John Ross; see also Meredith, “The Cherokees,” in the Five Civilized Tribes, Extra Bulletin Eleventh Census, 1894.) Cooweescoowee district of the Cherokee Nation west has been named in his honor. The following biographical facts are taken from the tribute in his honor, passed by the national council of the Cherokee upon hearing of his death, “as a feeble expression of the loss they have sustained.”

John Ross was born October 3, 1790, and died in the city of Washington, August 1, 1866, in the seventy-sixth year of his age. His official career began in 1809, when he was entrusted by Agent Return Meigs with an important mission to the Arkansas Cherokee. From that time until the close of his life, with the exception of two or three years in the earlier part, he was in the constant service of his people, “providing an example of confidence on their part and loyalty on his that has never been surpassed in the records of history.” In the war of 1813–14 against the Creeks, he was adjutant of the Cherokee regiment which cooperated with General Jackson and was present at the Battle of the Horseshoe, where the Cherokee, under Colonel Morgan of Tennessee, performed distinguished service. In 1817, he was elected a member of the national committee of the Cherokee council. The first duty assigned to him was to prepare a reply to the United States commissioners who were present for the purpose of negotiating with the Cherokee for their lands east of the Mississippi. Through his firm resistance to this, he was destined, a few years later, to test the power of truth and to achieve a reputation of extraordinary character. On October 26, 1819, his name first appears in the laws of the Cherokee Nation as president of the national committee, and is attached to an ordinance that aimed at the improvement of the Cherokee people by providing for the introduction of schoolmasters, blacksmiths, mechanics, and others into the Nation. He continued to occupy that position until 1826. In 1827, he was associate chief with William Hicks and president of the convention which adopted the constitution of that year. That constitution is believed to be the first attempt at a regular government, with distinct branches and defined powers, ever created and implemented by any of the North American Indians. From 1828 until the removal west, he was principal chief of the eastern Cherokee, and from 1839 to the time of his death, he was principal chief of the united Cherokee Nation.

The conclusion of this tribute is a magnificent honor to a remarkable man:

> “Blessed with a strong physical build and a sharp mind, John Ross had the physical capability to follow the path of duty wherever it led. No danger terrified him. He never hesitated in supporting what he believed to be right, but held to it with a steady purpose that could only have come from the clearest convictions of integrity. He never sacrificed the interests of his nation for convenience. He never lost sight of the people’s welfare. He worked for them daily throughout a long life, and his last spoken thoughts were dedicated to them. A friend of the law, he obeyed it; a friend of education, he faithfully encouraged schools throughout the country and spent his own money generously to provide it for others. Known for his hospitality, no one ever went hungry at his door. As a follower of the Christian religion, he practiced its teachings. His life's work is inseparable from the history of the Cherokee people for nearly half a century, while his example in daily life will endure in the future, whispering words of hope, moderation, and charity to future generations.”

Resolutions were also passed to bring his body back from Washington at the expense of the Cherokee Nation and to provide for proper funeral ceremonies, so “that his remains should rest among those he served for so long” (Resolutions in honor of John Ross, in *Laws of the Cherokee Nation, 1869*).

(47) THE KETOOWAH SOCIETY (p. 156): This Cherokee secret society, which has recently gained some newspaper fame for its defense of Cherokee self-government, takes its name—properly <term>Kĭtu'hwă</term>, but commonly spelled Ketoowah in English print—from the ancient town in the old Nation. This town formed the center of the tribe's most conservative members and sometimes gave its name to the Nation itself (see *<term>Kĭtu'hwagĭ</term>*, under Tribal Synonyms). A strong bond of fellowship, if not a formal organization, seems to have existed among the warriors and leaders of the various settlements in the Kituhwa district since ancient times. Because of this, the name is even now used in councils to represent authentic Cherokee spirit in its highest patriotic form. When, some years ago, delegates from the Western Nation visited the Eastern Cherokee to invite them to join their more prosperous relatives beyond the Mississippi, the speaker for the delegates expressed their brotherly feelings for their separated kin by saying in his opening speech, “We are all Kituhwa people” (<term>Ani'-Kĭtu'hwagĭ</term>). The Ketoowah Society in the Western Cherokee Nation was organized shortly before the Civil War by John B. Jones—son of the missionary Evan Jones and an adopted citizen of the Nation. It was a secret society with the stated goal of fostering national pride among the full-blooded members, in opposition to the modernizing influences of the mixed-blood element. Its true purpose was to counter the influence of the “Blue Lodge” and other secret secessionist organizations among the wealthier slave-holding classes, which consisted mainly of mixed-bloods and white people. The society spread to the Creeks, and its members in both tribes served the Union cause well throughout the war. They were often known as “Pin Indians” for reasons explained below. Since the end of the great struggle, the society has distinguished itself by its determined opposition

The following account of the society was written shortly after the end of the Civil War:

> "Those Cherokees who remained loyal to the Union combined into a secret organization for self-protection, taking the name of the Ketoowha society; this name was soon merged into that of the 'Pins.' The Pins were named this because of a unique way they chose to wear a pin. The symbol was discovered by their enemies, who used the term mockingly, but this loyal league accepted it, and the name has almost replaced the title its members first took. The Pin organization began among the members of the Baptist congregation at Peavine, in the Going-snake district of the Cherokee nation. In a short time, the society numbered nearly three thousand members and had begun recruiting among the Creeks, until the rebellion—which the society was arming itself against—prevented its further expansion, as the poor Creeks were driven into Kansas by the rebels of the Golden Circle. During the war, the Pins served the Union cause in many bloody encounters, as our generals have acknowledged. It was specifically an anti-slavery organization. The slave-holding Cherokees, who made up the wealthy and more educated class, naturally allied themselves with the South, while the loyal Cherokees became increasingly opposed to slavery. This was shown very clearly when the loyalists first met in a convention in February 1863. They not only abolished slavery unconditionally and forever—before any slave state had moved toward emancipation—but they also made any attempt at enslavement a serious misdemeanor.
> 
> The secret signs of the Pins included a unique way of touching the hat as a greeting, especially when they were too far apart to recognize each other otherwise. They had a specific way of grasping the lapel of the coat, first pulling it away from the body and then making a motion as if wrapping it around the heart. During the war, some of them were forced to join the rebellion but quickly rebelled against General Cooper, who was placed in command over them. When they fought against that general at Bird Creek, they wore strips of corn-husk tied in their hair. At night, when two Pins met and one asked the other, 'Who are you?', the reply or password was, 'Tahlequah—who are you?' The response was, 'I am Ketoowha’s son.'" — Dr. D. J. MacGowan, *Indian Secret Societies*, in *Historical Magazine*, x, 1866.

(48) FAREWELL ADDRESS OF LLOYD WELCH (p. 175): In the sad and eventful history of the Cherokee, their talented leaders—who were often of white ancestry—have frequently spoken to the world with eloquent words of appeal, protest, or acknowledgement. They have never spoken more eloquently, however, than in the final farewell of Chief Lloyd Welch to the Eastern Band, as he felt his life coming to an end (leaflet, MacGowan, Chattanooga [n. d., 1880]):

> *"To the Chairman and Council of the Eastern Band of Cherokees:*
> 
> "My Brothers: It has become my urgent duty to bid you an affectionate farewell and to return to your hands the trust you so generously placed in my care: principal chief of the Eastern Band. I am forced to take this course with great concern and anxiety for your welfare. But the unyielding laws of nature and the rapid decline of my health warn me that very soon I will have passed from this earth. My body will be committed to the grave and my spirit to the God who gave it, in that happy home in the beyond where there is no sickness, sorrow, pain, or death, but only eternal joy and happiness forever.
> 
> "The only regret I feel for being called away from you so soon, in the prime of my manhood when hope is sweet, is my great desire to serve and benefit my people. For this, I have studied and worked for the last ten years of my life: to ensure that my brothers receive equal justice from their brothers in the west and from the United States, and to ensure that you would no longer be hewers of wood and drawers of—"

(49) STATUS OF EASTERN BAND (p. 180): For some reason, all authorities who have until now discussed the status of the Eastern Band of Cherokee seem to have been entirely unaware of the enactment of the supplementary articles to the Treaty of New Echota, by which all preemption and reservation rights granted under the twelfth article were canceled. Thus, in the Cherokee case of “The United States *et al.* against D. T. Boyd *et al.*,” we find the United States circuit judge quoting the twelfth article in its original form as a basis for argument, while his associate judge says: “Their forefathers availed themselves of a provision in the treaty of New Echota and remained in the state of North Carolina,” etc. (Report of Indian Commissioner for 1895, pp. 633-635, 1896). The truth is that the treaty, as ratified with its supplementary articles, canceled the residence right of every Cherokee east of the Mississippi, and it was not until thirty years later that North Carolina finally gave assurance that the Eastern Band would be permitted to remain within her borders.

# III—STORIES AND STORY TELLERS

Cherokee myths may be roughly classified as sacred myths, animal stories, local legends, and historical traditions. To the first class belong the genesis stories, which deal with the creation of the world, the nature of the heavenly bodies and elemental forces, the origin of life and death, the spirit world and invisible beings, ancient monsters, and the hero-gods. It is almost certain that most myths of this class are merely disjointed fragments of an original, complete genesis and migration legend that is now lost. With nearly every tribe that has been studied, we find such a sacred legend, preserved by the priests of the tradition, who alone are privileged to recite and explain it. These legends deal with the origin and wanderings of the people from the beginning of the world to the final settlement of the tribe in its home territory. Among the best examples of such genesis traditions are those recorded in the *Walam Olum* of the Delawares and Matthews’ *Navaho Origin Legend*. Others may be found in Cusick’s *History of the Six Nations*, Gatschet’s *Creek Migration Legend*, and the author’s *Jicarilla Genesis*.¹ The Cheyenne, Arapaho, and other plains tribes are known to have similar genesis myths.

The previous existence of such a national legend among the Cherokee is confirmed by Haywood, writing in 1823. He states, based on information obtained from a leading man in the tribe, that they once had a long oration—which was then nearly forgotten—recounting the history of their wanderings from the time they were first placed upon the earth by some superior power from above. Until about the middle of the nineteenth century, this tradition was still recited at the annual Green-corn dance.² Unlike most Indians, the Cherokee are not conservative; even before the Revolution, they had so far lost their primitive customs from contact with white people that Adair, in 1775, called them a nest of apostate hornets who, for more than thirty years, had been fast degenerating.³ Whatever it may have been, their national legend is now lost forever. The secret organizations that must have formerly existed among the priesthood have also disappeared, and each man now works independently according to his individual gifts and knowledge.

The sacred myths were not for everyone; only those who observed the proper form and ceremony were permitted to hear them. When John Ax and

When other old men were boys, about eighty years ago, the myth-keepers and priests used to meet together at night in the <term>âsǐ</term> (a low-built log sleeping house) to recite traditions and discuss their secret knowledge. At times, those who desired instruction from an expert in the sacred lore of the tribe met him by appointment in the <term>âsǐ</term>, where they sat up all night talking by the light of a small fire burning in the middle of the floor. At daybreak, the entire party went down to the running stream. There, the pupils or listeners of the myths stripped themselves and were scratched on their naked skin with a bone-toothed comb by the priest. After this, they waded out, facing the rising sun, and dipped seven times under the water while the priest recited prayers on the bank. This purification rite, observed more than a century ago by Adair, is also part of the ceremony of the ballplay, the Green-corn dance, and, in fact, every important ritual performance. Before beginning one of the sacred stories, the informant would sometimes jokingly suggest that the author first submit to being scratched and "go to water."

As a special privilege, a boy was sometimes admitted to the <term>âsǐ</term> on such occasions to tend the fire, which gave him the opportunity to listen to the stories and learn something of the secret rites. In this way, John Ax gained much of his knowledge, although he does not claim to be an expert. As he describes it, the fire intended to heat the room—since the nights are cold in the Cherokee mountains—was built on the ground in the center of the small house. The house was not high enough to allow one to stand up, so the occupants sat in a circle around the fire. In front of the fire was placed a large flat rock, and near it a pile of pine knots or splints. When the fire had burned down to a bed of coals, the boy lit one or two of the pine knots and laid them on the rock. There they blazed with a bright light until nearly consumed, at which point others were laid upon them, and so on until daybreak.

Sometimes the pine splints were set up crosswise, like this: xxxx, in a circle around the fire, with a gap at the eastern side. They were then lit from one end and burned gradually around the circle, with fresh splints being set up behind as those in front were consumed. Lawson describes this identical custom as witnessed at a dance among the Waxhaw on the Catawba River in 1701:

> Now, to return to our state house, where we were invited by the dignitaries. As soon as we entered it, they placed our Englishmen near the king; it was my fortune to sit next to him, with his great general or war captain on my other side. The house is as dark as a dungeon and as hot as one of the Dutch stoves in Holland. They had made a circular fire of split canes in the middle of the house; it was one man's job to add more split reeds to one end as they were consumed at the other, leaving a small gap to supply it with fuel. <note>Lawson, Carolina, 67-68, 1860 reprint.</note>

<page-num>231</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] THE MYTHIC ANIMALS</header>

To the second class belong the shorter animal myths, which have lost whatever sacred character they may once have had and are told now merely as humorous explanations of certain animal peculiarities. While the sacred myths have a constant influence on formulaic prayers and observances, it is only in rare instances that any rite or custom is based upon an animal myth. Moreover, the sacred myths are generally known only to the professional priests or conjurers, while the shorter animal stories are more or less familiar to nearly everyone and are found in almost identical form among the Cherokee, Creeks, and other southern tribes.

The animals of the Cherokee myths, like the traditional hero-gods, were larger and more perfect than their present representatives. They had chiefs, councils, and townhouses; they mingled with humankind on terms of perfect equality and spoke the same language. In some unexplained manner, they finally left this lower world and ascended to *Galûñ’lătĭ*, the world above, where they still exist. Their departure was not simultaneous; instead, each animal chose its own time. The animals we know today—small in size and lesser in intellect—came to the earth later. They are not the descendants of the mythic animals but are only weak imitations. In one or two special cases, however, the present creature is the descendant of a former monster. Trees and plants were also alive and could talk in the old days and had their place in the council, but they do not figure prominently in the myths.

Each animal had its appointed station and duty. Thus, the *Walâ'sĭ* frog was the marshal and leader in the council, while the Rabbit was the messenger who carried all public announcements and usually led the dance as well. He was also the great trickster and mischief-maker, a role he plays in Eastern and Southern Indian myths generally, as well as in Southern African American stories. The bear is described as having originally been a man, with human form and nature.

As with other tribes and countries, almost every prominent rock and mountain and every deep bend in the river in the old Cherokee country has an accompanying legend. It may be a short story that can be told in a single paragraph to account for some natural feature, or it may be one chapter of a myth that continues at a mountain a hundred miles away. As is typical when a people has lived for a long time in the same region, nearly every important myth is localized, thus taking on a more definite character.

There is the usual number of anecdotes and stories of personal adventure—some of them irredeemably vulgar—but historical traditions are strangely lacking. The authentic records of non-literate peoples are brief at best, seldom reaching back much further than the memories of their oldest men. Although the Cherokee have been the most important of the southern tribes—engaging in wars and treaties for three centuries with the Spanish, English, French, Americans, and Iroquois,

Shawnee, Catawba, and Creeks, there is little evidence of this in their traditions. This condition may be due in part to the character of the Cherokee mind, which, as has been already stated, is accustomed to look forward to new things rather than to dwell upon the past. The first Cherokee war, with its stories of Âganstâ'ta and Ată-gûl'kălû', is absolutely forgotten. They have hardly a recollection of the long Revolutionary struggle, although they were constantly fighting throughout the whole period and for several years after, and at one time were brought to the verge of ruin by four coordinated expeditions which ravaged their country simultaneously from different directions and destroyed almost every one of their towns. Even the Creek war, in which many of their warriors took a prominent part, was already nearly forgotten some years ago. Beyond a few stories of encounters with the Shawnee and Iroquois, there is hardly anything that can be called history until well within the present century.

With some tribes, the winter season and the night are the times for telling stories, but to the Cherokee, all times are alike. As our grandmothers begin with "Once upon a time," so the Cherokee storyteller introduces his narrative by saying: "This is what the old men told me when I was a boy."

Not all tell the same stories, for in tribal lore, as in all other sorts of knowledge, we find specialists. Some common minds take note only of common things—little stories of the rabbit, the terrapin, and the others, told to emphasize a joke or amuse a child. Others dwell upon the wonderful and supernatural—Tsul'kălû', Tsuwe'năhǐ, and the Thunderers—and those sacred things to be told only with prayer and purification. Then, again, there are still a few old warriors who live in the memory of heroic days when there were wars with the Seneca and the Shawnee, and these men are the historians of the tribe and the guardians of its antiquities.

The question of the origin of myths is one which affords abundant opportunity for ingenious theories in the absence of any possibility of proof. Those of the Cherokee are too far broken down ever to be woven together again into any long-connected origin legend, such as we find with some tribes, although a few still exhibit a certain sequence which indicates that they once formed component parts of a cycle. From the prominence of the rabbit in the animal stories, as well as in those found among the southern Negroes, an effort has been made to establish a Negro origin for them, regardless of the fact that the rabbit—the Great White Rabbit—is the hero-god, trickster, and wonder-worker of all the tribes east of the Mississippi from Hudson Bay to the Gulf. In European folklore also, the rabbit is regarded as something uncanny and half-supernatural, and even in far-off Korea, he is the central figure in the animal myths. Just why this should be so is a question that may be left to the theorist to decide. Among the

<header>MOONEY] CONTACT WITH BLACK PEOPLE</header>
<page-num>233</page-num>

Among the Algonquian tribes, the name *wabos* seems to have been confused with that of the dawn, *waban*, so that the Great White Rabbit is actually the incarnation of the eastern dawn that brings light and life and drives away the dark shadows that have held the world in chains. The animal itself seems to be regarded by the Indians as the fitting type of defenseless weakness protected and made safe by constant alertness, and with a tendency, moreover, for appearing at unexpected moments. The same characteristics would appeal just as strongly to the traditional mind of the Black person. The very expression that Harris puts into the mouth of Uncle Remus, “In dem days Brer Rabbit en his fambly wuz at the head er de gang w’en enny racket wus en hand,”¹ was paraphrased in the Cherokee language by Suyeta when introducing his first rabbit story: “*Tsĭ'stu wuliga'nătûtûn' unĕ'gutsătû' gesĕ'ĭ*—the Rabbit was the leader of them all in mischief.” The expression struck the author so forcibly that the words were recorded exactly as they were spoken.

Regarding the contact between the two races, through which such stories could be borrowed from one by the other, it is not commonly known that in all the southern colonies, Indian slaves were bought and sold, kept in servitude, and worked in the fields side by side with Black people up to the time of the Revolution. Not to go back to the Spanish period, when such things were common, we find the Cherokee as early as 1693 complaining that their people were being kidnapped by slave hunters. Hundreds of captured Tuscarora and nearly the whole tribe of the Appalachee were distributed as slaves among the Carolina colonists in the early part of the eighteenth century, while the Natchez and others shared a similar fate in Louisiana. As late as at least 1776, Cherokee prisoners of war were still sold to the highest bidder for the same purpose. At one time, it was charged against the governor of South Carolina that he was provoking a general Indian war by his encouragement of slave hunts. Furthermore, as the coast tribes dwindled, they were compelled to associate and intermarry with Black people until they finally lost their identity and were classified with that race; thus, a considerable proportion of the ancestry of southern Black people is unquestionably Indian.

The Black person, with a talent for imitation and a love for stories—especially those of the comic variety—must undoubtedly have absorbed much from the Indian in this way. On the other hand, the Indian, with his pride in conservatism and his contempt for a subjugated race, would have taken very little from the Black person, and that little could not easily have found its way back to the free tribes. Some of these animal stories are common to widely separated tribes among whom there can be no suspicion of Black influence. Thus, the famous “tar baby” story has variations, not only among the Cherokee, but also in New

Mexico, Washington, and southern Alaska—wherever, in fact, the piñon or the pine supplies enough gum to be molded into a ball for Indian uses—while the incident of the Rabbit dining with the Bear is found with nearly every tribe from Nova Scotia to the Pacific. The idea that such stories are necessarily of Black origin is due largely to the common but mistaken notion that the Indian has no sense of humor.

In many cases, it is not necessary to assume borrowing from either side, as the myths are such as would naturally spring up in any part of the world among primitive people accustomed to observing the characteristics of animals, which their religious system regarded as differing in no essential way from humankind, save only in outward form. Thus, in Europe and America, the terrapin has been accepted as the type of plodding slowness, while the rabbit, with his sudden dash, or the deer with his bounding stride, is the type of speed. What is more natural than for the storyteller to set one to race against the other, with the victory in favor of the patient striver against the self-confident boaster? The idea of a hungry wolf or other beast of prey luring his victims by the promise of a new song or dance, during which they must close their eyes, is also one that would easily occur among any primitive people whose chief pastime is dancing. <note>For a presentation of the African and European argument, see Harris, *Nights with Uncle Remus*, introduction, 1883; and *Uncle Remus, His Songs and His Sayings*, introduction, 1886; Gerber, *Uncle Remus Traced to the Old World*, in *Journal of American Folklore*, vi, p. 23, October 1893. In regard to tribal dissemination of myths, see Boas, *Dissemination of Tales among the Natives of North America*, in *Journal of American Folklore*, iv, p. 12, January 1891; *The Growth of Indian Mythologies*, in the same journal, ix, p. 32, January 1896; *Northern Elements in the Mythology of the Navaho*, in *American Anthropologist*, x, p. 11, November 1897; introduction to Teit's *Traditions of the Thompson River Indians*, 1898. Dr. Boas has probably devoted more study to the subject than any other anthropologist, and his personal observations include tribes from the Arctic regions to the Columbia.</note>

On the other hand, such a conception as that of Flint and the Rabbit could only be the outgrowth of a special <term>cosmogonic theology</term>, though now indeed broken and degraded, and it is probable that many myths told now only for amusement are really worn-down fragments of ancient sacred traditions. Thus, the story just noted appears in a different dress among the Iroquois as a part of their great creation myth. The Cherokee being a detached tribe of the Iroquois, we may expect to find among the latter—if it is not already too late—the explanation and more perfect statement of some things which are obscure in the Cherokee myths. It must not be forgotten, however, that the Indian, like other men, does some things for simple amusement, and it is useless to look for occult meanings where none exist.

Except as to the local traditions and a few others which are obviously the direct outgrowth of Cherokee conditions, it is impossible to fix a definite starting point for the myths. It would be unwise to assert that even the majority of them originated within the tribe. The Cherokee have strains of Creek, Catawba, Uchee, Natchez, Iroquois, Osage, and Shawnee blood, and such admixture implies contact more or less intimate and continued. <header>MOONEY] ORIGIN OF THE MYTHS</header>
<page-num>235</page-num>

A myth can travel as far as a redstone pipe or a string of wampum. It was customary, as it still is to a limited extent in the West, for large parties—sometimes even a whole band or village—to make long visits to other tribes. They would dance, feast, trade, and exchange stories with their friends for weeks or months at a time, with the expectation that their hosts would return the visit during the next summer. Regular trade routes crossed the continent from east to west and from north to south, and when the subject has been fully investigated, it will be found that this intertribal commerce was as constant and well-recognized a part of Indian life as our own railroad traffic is today. The very existence of a trade jargon or a sign language is proof of intertribal relations over wide areas. Their political alliances also were often far-reaching; for example, Pontiac united all the tribes from the Atlantic border to the head of the Mississippi into a warlike confederacy, while the emissaries of the Shawano <note>Also known as the Shawnee.</note> prophet carried the story of his revelations throughout the whole region from the Florida coast to the Saskatchewan.

In view of these facts, it is as useless to attempt to trace the origin of every myth as it is to claim Cherokee authorship for them all. From what we know of the character of the Shawano, their tendency toward ceremony and mysticism, and their close relations with the Cherokee, it may be inferred that some of the myths originated with that tribe. We should naturally expect also to find close similarities with the myths of the Creeks and other southern tribes within the former area of the Mobilian trade language. The localization of all the more important myths at home indicates a long residence in the country. As the majority of those given here belong to the half-dozen counties still familiar to the East Cherokee, we may guess how many attached to the ancient territory of the tribe are now irrecoverably lost.

Contact with the white race seems to have produced very little impression on the tribal mythology, and not more than three or four stories current among the Cherokee can be assigned to a Caucasian source. These have not been reproduced here, for the reason that they are plainly European, and the author has chosen not to follow the example of some collectors who have assumed that every tale told in an Indian language is necessarily an Indian story. Dozens recorded in collections from the North and West are nothing more than variations of the celebrated *Hausmärchen* <note>German for "folk tales" or "fairy tales."</note>, as told by French trappers and travelers to their Indian campmates and half-breed children. It might perhaps be thought that missionary influence would be evident in the genesis tradition, but such is not the case. The Bible story kills the Indian tradition, and there is no amalgamation. It is hardly necessary to say that stories of a great fish which swallows a man and of a great flood

The supposed Cherokee hero-god, Wâsi—described by one writer as remarkably resembling the great Hebrew lawgiver—is in fact that great teacher himself. Wâsi is the Cherokee approximation of Moses, and the well-meaning missionary who first recorded the story was simply listening to a chapter taken by his convert from the Cherokee Testament. The entire primitive pantheon of the Cherokee is still preserved in their sacred formulas.

Compared with those of some other tribes, Cherokee myths are clean. They rank high for their picturesque imagination and wealth of detail, and some of the wonder stories rival those of Europe and India. The numerous parallels provided will serve to indicate their relationship to the general Indian system. Unless noted otherwise, every myth presented here was obtained directly from the Indians, and in nearly every case has been verified from several sources.

> ->“I do not know what the truth may be,<-
> ->I tell the tale as it was told to me.”<-

First and foremost in the list of storytellers is A'yûñ'inǐ, known as “Swimmer,” from whom nearly three-fourths of the stories were originally obtained, along with nearly as large a proportion of the entire body of Cherokee material now in the author's possession. The collection could not have been made without his help, and now that he is gone, it can never be duplicated. Born about 1835, shortly before the Removal, he grew up under the instruction of masters to be a priest, doctor, and keeper of tradition, so that he was recognized as an authority throughout the tribe and by competent outside judges such as Colonel Thomas. He served through the war as second sergeant of Cherokee Company A, Sixty-ninth North Carolina Confederate Infantry, Thomas Legion. He was prominent in the local affairs of the tribe, and no Green-corn dance, ballplay, or other tribal function was ever considered complete without his presence and active assistance. A genuine native antiquarian and patriot, proud of his people and their ancient ways, he took delight in recording—in his native alphabet—the songs and sacred formulas of priests and dancers, the names of medicinal plants, and the prescriptions with which they were prepared, while his mind was a storehouse of Indian tradition. To a pleasant descriptive style, he added a musical voice for the songs and a unique talent for imitating the characteristic cries of birds or beasts; listening to one of his recitals was often a pleasure in itself, even to someone who did not understand a word of the language. He spoke no English, and until the day of his death, he clung to the moccasin and turban, together with the rattle, his badge of authority. He died in March 1899, aged about sixty-five, and was

<header>MOONEY] STORY-TELLERS</header>

buried like a true <term>Cherokee</term> on the slope of a forest-covered mountain. Peace to his ashes and sorrow for his passing, for with him half the traditions of his people perished.

Next in order comes the name of <term>Ităgû'năhĭ</term>, better known as <term>John Ax</term>, born around 1800 and now, as a result, just reaching the age of one hundred, being the oldest man of the group. He clearly remembers the <term>Creek War</term>, at which time he was about twelve years old, and he was already married and a father when the lands east of <term>Nantahala</term> were sold by the <term>treaty of 1819</term>. Although not a professional priest or doctor, he was recognized—before age had dulled his mind—as an authority on everything relating to tribal custom, and he was an expert in making rattles, wands, and other ceremonial items. Having a poetic and imaginative nature, he cared most for the wonder stories—of the giant <term>Tsul'kălû'</term>, the great <term>Uktena</term>, or the invisible spirit people—but he also had a keen appreciation for humorous animal stories. He speaks no English, and with his upright, lean figure and piercing eyes, he is a fine example of the old-time Indian. Despite his great age, he walked without any help other than his stick to the last ball game, where he watched every run with the closest interest; he would have also attended the dance the night before if not for the intervention of his friends.

<term>Suyeta</term>, "The Chosen One," who preaches regularly as a Baptist minister to an Indian congregation, does not deal much with Indian supernatural beliefs, perhaps out of respect for his duties as a clergyman. However, he has a good memory and a fondness for rabbit stories and others of that class. He served in the Confederate army during the war as a fourth sergeant in Company A of the Sixty-ninth North Carolina regiment and is now an active man of about sixty-two. He speaks no English, but by a clever system of his own, he has learned to use a concordance to verify references in his <term>Cherokee</term> Bible. He is also an excellent carpenter and mason.

Another primary informant was <term>Ta'gwădihi'</term>, "Catawba-killer," of <term>Cheowa</term>, who died a few years ago at about seventy years old. He was a doctor and claimed no special knowledge of myths or ceremonies, but he was able to provide several valuable stories, as well as confirming evidence for many stories obtained from other sources.

Besides these, others among the Eastern <term>Cherokee</term> may be named: the late <term>Chief N. J. Smith</term>; <term>Salâ'lĭ</term>, mentioned elsewhere, who died around 1895; <term>Tsĕsa'nĭ</term> (or Jessan), who also served in the war; <term>Ayâ'sta</term>, one of the primary traditionalists among the women; and James and David Blythe, younger men of mixed heritage with an English education, but who inherited a large share of Indian lore from their father, who was a recognized leader of ceremony.

# MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19

“<term>Worn-out-blanket</term>,” a person of mixed ancestry who spoke and wrote both languages, was born in the old <term>Cherokee</term> Nation near the site of present-day <term>Clarkesville</term>, <term>Georgia</term>, in 1806. He died at about ninety years of age at his home in the eastern part of the <term>Cherokee</term> Nation, next to the <term>Seneca reservation</term>. The name figures prominently in the early history of <term>North Carolina</term> and <term>Georgia</term>. His grandfather, <term>Colonel Wafford</term>, was an officer in the American Revolutionary army, and shortly after the <term>treaty of Hopewell</term> in 1785, he established a colony known as “<term>Wafford’s settlement</term>” in upper <term>Georgia</term>. This was on territory that was afterward found to be within the Indian boundary and was acquired by a special treaty purchase in 1804. His name is added as a witness for the state of <term>Georgia</term> to the <term>treaty of Holston</term> in 1794.<note>See contemporary notice in the Historical Sketch.</note> On his mother’s side, Mr. <term>Wafford</term> was of mixed <term>Cherokee</term>, <term>Natchez</term>, and white blood, as she was a cousin of <term>Sequoya</term>. He was also remotely connected with <term>Cornelius Dougherty</term>, the first trader established among the <term>Cherokee</term>. 

In the course of his long life, he filled many positions of trust and honor among his people. In his youth, he attended the mission school at <term>Valleytown</term> under Reverend <term>Evan Jones</term>, and just before the adoption of the <term>Cherokee</term> alphabet, he finished translating a Sunday school speller—noted in <term>Pilling’s Iroquoian Bibliography</term>—into phonetic <term>Cherokee</term> spelling. In 1824, he was the census enumerator for the district of the <term>Cherokee</term> Nation embracing the upper <term>Hiwassee river</term> in <term>North Carolina</term>, along with <term>Nottely</term> and <term>Toccoa</term> in the adjoining portion of <term>Georgia</term>. The wealth of <term>Cherokee</term> geographic information he acquired this way was found to be invaluable. He was one of the two commanders of the largest detachment of emigrants at the time of the removal, and his name appears as a councilor for the western Nation in the <term>Cherokee Almanac</term> for 1846. When he was employed by the author at <term>Tahlequah</term> in 1891, his mind was still clear and his memory keen. Having a practical nature, he was concerned chiefly with tribal history, geography, linguistics, and everyday life and customs. On all of these subjects, his knowledge was exact and detailed, but there were few myths for which he was not able to furnish supporting testimony. Despite his education, he was a firm believer in the <term>Nûñně'hĭ</term>, and several of the best legends connected with them were obtained from him. His death takes from the <term>Cherokee</term> one of the last connecting links between the present and the past.

It highlights his ancestry, his role in the Cherokee removal, and his contribution to preserving tribal legends and linguistics.</summary>

# IV—THE MYTHS

## COSMOGONIC MYTHS

### 1. HOW THE WORLD WAS MADE

The earth is a great island floating in a sea of water, suspended at each of the four cardinal points by a cord hanging down from the sky vault, which is made of solid rock. When the world grows old and worn out, the people will die and the cords will break, letting the earth sink down into the ocean, and everything will be water again. The Indians are afraid of this.

When all was water, the animals lived above in <term>Gălûn'lătĭ</term>, beyond the arch; but it was very crowded, and they wanted more room. They wondered what was below the water, and at last <term>Dâyuni'sĭ</term>, "Beaver's Grandchild," the little Water-beetle, offered to go and see what it could find out. It darted in every direction over the surface of the water but could find no firm place to rest. Then it dived to the bottom and came up with some soft mud, which began to grow and spread on every side until it became the island which we call the earth. It was afterward fastened to the sky with four cords, but no one remembers who did this.

At first the earth was flat and very soft and wet. The animals were anxious to get down and sent out different birds to see if it was yet dry, but they found no place to alight and came back again to <term>Gălûn'lătĭ</term>. At last it seemed to be time, and they sent out the Buzzard and told him to go and make ready for them. This was the Great Buzzard, the father of all the buzzards we see now. He flew all over the earth, low down near the ground, while it was still soft. When he reached the Cherokee country, he was very tired, and his wings began to flap and strike the ground; wherever they struck the earth there was a valley, and where they turned up again there was a mountain. When the animals above saw this, they were afraid that the whole world would be mountains, so they called him back, but the Cherokee country remains full of mountains to this day.

When the earth was dry and the animals came down, it was still dark. So they got the sun and set it in a track to go every day across the island from east to west, just overhead. It was too hot this way, and <term>Tsiska'gĭlĭ'</term>, the Red Crawfish, had his shell scorched a bright red, so that his meat was spoiled; and the Cherokee do not eat it. The

The conjurers put the sun another handbreadth higher in the air, but it was still too hot. They raised it another time, and another, until it was seven handbreadths high and just under the sky arch. Then it was right, and they left it so. This is why the conjurers call the highest place *Gûlkwâ'gine Di'gălûn'lătiyûñ'*, “the seventh height,” because it is seven handbreadths above the earth. Every day the sun moves along under this arch, and returns at night on the upper side to the starting place.

There is another world under this one, and it is like ours in everything—animals, plants, and people—except that the seasons are different. The streams that come down from the mountains are the trails by which we reach this underworld, and the springs at their heads are the doorways by which we enter it; but to do this one must fast and "go to water" and have one of the underground people for a guide. We know that the seasons in the underworld are different from ours because the water in the springs is always warmer in winter and cooler in summer than the outer air.

When the animals and plants were first made—we do not know by whom—they were told to watch and keep awake for seven nights, just as young men now fast and keep awake when they pray to their medicine. They tried to do this, and nearly all were awake through the first night, but the next night several dropped off to sleep, and the third night others were asleep, and then others, until, on the seventh night, of all the animals only the owl, the panther, and one or two more were still awake. To these were given the power to see and to go about in the dark, and to prey upon the birds and animals which must sleep at night. Of the trees, only the cedar, the pine, the spruce, the holly, and the laurel were awake to the end, and to them it was given to be always green and to be greatest for medicine; but to the others it was said:
> “Because you have not endured to the end, you shall lose your hair every winter.”

<margin>omit</margin>
Men came after the animals and plants. At first there were only a brother and sister, until he struck her with a fish and told her to multiply, and so it was. In seven days a child was born to her, and thereafter every seven days another, and they increased very fast until there was danger that the world could not support them. Then it was decreed that a woman should have only one child in a year, and it has been so ever since.

### 2. THE FIRST FIRE

In the beginning there was no fire, and the world was cold, until the Thunders (*Ani'-Hyûñ'tikwălâ'skĭ*), who lived up in <term>Gălûn'lătĭ</term>, sent their lightning and put fire into the bottom of a hollow sycamore tree which grew on an island. The animals knew it was there because they could see the smoke coming out at the top, but they could not get to it on

# MOONEY] THE FIRST FIRE

On account of the water, they held a council to decide what to do. This was a long time ago.

Every animal that could fly or swim was anxious to go after the fire. The Raven offered, and because he was so large and strong, they thought he could surely do the work, so he was sent first. He flew high and far across the water and landed on the sycamore tree, but while he was wondering what to do next, the heat scorched all his feathers black. He was frightened and came back without the fire. The little Screech-owl (<term>*Wa'huhu'*</term>) volunteered to go and reached the place safely, but while he was looking down into the hollow tree, a blast of hot air came up and nearly burned out his eyes. He managed to fly home as best he could, but it was a long time before he could see well, and his eyes are red to this day. Then the Hooting Owl (<term>*U'guku'*</term>) and the Horned Owl (<term>*Tskĭlĭ'*</term>) went, but by the time they reached the hollow tree, the fire was burning so fiercely that the smoke nearly blinded them. The ashes carried up by the wind made white rings around their eyes. They had to come home again without the fire, and despite all their rubbing, they were never able to get rid of those white rings.

Now, no more of the birds would venture out, and so the little <term>Uksu'hĭ</term> snake, the black racer, said he would go through the water and bring back some fire. He swam across to the island and crawled through the grass to the tree, entering through a small hole at the bottom. The heat and smoke were too much for him as well; after dodging about blindly over the hot ashes until he was almost on fire himself, he managed by good luck to get out again through the same hole. However, his body had been scorched black, and ever since then, he has had the habit of darting and doubling back on his track as if trying to escape from close quarters. He returned, and the great blacksnake, <term>Gûle'gĭ</term>, "The Climber," offered to go for the fire. He swam over to the island and climbed up the tree on the outside, as the blacksnake always does, but when he put his head down into the hole, the smoke choked him so that he fell into the burning stump. Before he could climb out again, he was as black as the <term>Uksu'hĭ</term>.

Now they held another council, for there was still no fire and the world was cold. The birds, snakes, and four-footed animals all had some excuse for not going because they were all afraid to venture near the burning sycamore, until at last <term>Kănăne'skĭ Amai'yěhĭ</term> (the Water Spider) said she would go. This is not the water spider that looks like a mosquito, but the other kind, with black downy hair and red stripes on her body. She can run on top of the water or dive to the bottom, so there would be no trouble getting over to the island. The question was, how could she bring back the fire? "I'll manage that," said the Water Spider. So, she spun a thread from her body and wove it into a <term>*tustĭ* bowl</term>, which she fastened on her back. Then she crossed over to the island and through the grass to where the fire was

### 3. <term>KANA'TĬ</term> AND <term>SELU</term>: THE ORIGIN OF GAME AND CORN

When I was a boy, this is what the old men told me they had heard when they were boys.

Long years ago, shortly after the world was made, a hunter and his wife lived at Pilot Knob with their only child, a little boy. The father’s name was <term>Kana'tĭ</term> (the Lucky Hunter), and his wife was called <term>Selu</term> (Corn). No matter when <term>Kana'tĭ</term> went into the woods, he never failed to bring back a load of game, which his wife would cut up and prepare, washing the blood from the meat in the river near the house. The little boy used to play down by the river every day, and one morning the parents thought they heard laughing and talking in the bushes as though there were two children there. When the boy came home at night, his parents asked him who had been playing with him all day. “He comes out of the water,” said the boy, “and he calls himself my elder brother. He says his mother was cruel to him and threw him into the river.” Then they realized that the strange boy had grown from the blood of the game that <term>Selu</term> had washed off at the river’s edge.

Every day when the little boy went out to play, the other would join him, but since he always went back into the water, the parents never had a chance to see him. At last, one evening <term>Kana'tĭ</term> said to his son, “Tomorrow, when the other boy comes to play, get him to wrestle with you. When you have your arms around him, hold on to him and call for us.” The boy promised to do as he was told. The next day, as soon as his playmate appeared, he challenged him to a wrestling match. The other agreed at once, but as soon as they had their arms around each other, <term>Kana'tĭ</term>'s boy began to scream for his father. The parents immediately came running down. As soon as the Wild Boy saw them, he struggled to free himself and cried out, “Let me go; you threw me away!” but his brother held on until the parents reached the spot, where they seized the Wild Boy and took him home with them. They kept him in the house until they had tamed him, but he was always wild and cunning in his nature, and he led his brother into all sorts of mischief. It was not long before the parents discovered that he had magic powers, and they called him <term>I'năge-utăsûn'hĭ</term> (He-who-grew-up-wild).

Whenever <term>Kana'tĭ</term> went into the mountains, he always brought back a fat buck or doe, or perhaps a couple of turkeys. One day the Wild Boy said to his brother, “I wonder where our father gets all that game; let's follow him next time and find out.” A few days later, <term>Kana'tĭ</term> took a bow and some feathers in his hand and started off

Then the <term>Wild Boy</term> changed himself into a puff of bird's down, which the wind picked up and carried until it landed upon <term>Kana'tĭ</term>'s shoulder just as he entered the swamp; however, <term>Kana'tĭ</term> knew nothing about it. They hurried and reached home before their father, who had the heavy deer to carry, and he never knew that they had followed him.

A few days later, the boys went back to the swamp, cut some reeds, and made seven arrows, and then started up the mountain to where their father kept the game. When they got to the place, they raised the rock and a deer came running out. Just as they drew back to shoot it, another came out, and then another and another, until the boys got confused and forgot what they were doing. In those days, all the deer had their tails hanging down like other animals, but as a buck was running past, the <term>Wild Boy</term> struck its tail with his arrow so that it pointed upward. The boys thought this was good sport, and when the next one ran past, the <term>Wild Boy</term> struck its tail so that it stood straight up, and his brother struck the next one so hard with his arrow that the deer's tail was almost curled over its back. The deer has carried its tail this way ever since. The deer kept running past until the last one had come out of the hole and escaped into the forest. Then came droves of raccoons, rabbits, and all the other four-footed animals—all except the bear, because there was no bear then. Last came great flocks of turkeys, pigeons, and partridges that darkened the air like a cloud and made such a noise with their wings that <term>Kana'tĭ</term>, sitting at home, heard the sound like distant thunder on the mountains and said to himself, "My troublesome boys have gotten into mischief; I must go and see what they are doing."

Without saying a word, he went down into the cave and kicked the covers off four jars in one corner; out swarmed bedbugs, fleas, lice, and gnats, which covered the boys. They screamed with pain and fright and tried to beat off the insects, but thousands of vermin crawled over them and bit and stung them until both boys dropped down nearly dead. Kana'tĭ stood looking on until he thought they had been punished enough; then he knocked off the vermin and spoke to the boys. "Now, you rascals," he said, "you have always had plenty to eat and never had to work for it. Whenever you were hungry, all I had to do was come up here, get a deer or a turkey, and bring it home for your mother to cook. But now you have let out all the animals, and after this, when you want a deer to eat, you will have to hunt all through the woods for it, and then you might not even find one. Go home now to your mother, while I see if I can find something to eat for supper."

When the boys reached home again, they were very tired and hungry and asked their mother for something to eat. "There is no meat," said <term>Selu</term>, "but wait a little while and I'll get you something." So she took a basket and started out to the storehouse. This storehouse was built upon poles high up from the ground to keep it out of the reach of animals, and there was a ladder to climb up and one door, but no other opening. Every day when <term>Selu</term> got ready to cook the dinner, she would go out to the storehouse with a basket and bring it back full of corn and beans. The boys had never been inside the storehouse, so they wondered where all the corn and beans could come from, as the house was not very large. As soon as <term>Selu</term> went out the door, the <term>Wild Boy</term> said to his brother, "Let's go and see what she does." The boys looked at each other and said, "This will never do; our mother is a witch. If we eat any of that, it will poison us. We must kill her."

After <term>Kana'ti</term>’s boys had let the deer out from the cave where their father used to keep them, the hunters tramped about in the woods for a long time without finding any game, so that the people were very hungry. At the first song there was a roaring sound like a strong wind in the northwest, and it grew louder and nearer as the boys sang on, until at the seventh song a whole herd of deer, led by a large buck, came out from the woods. The boys had told the people to be ready with their bows and arrows, and when the song was ended and all the deer were close around the <term>townhouse</term>, the hunters shot into them and killed as many as they needed before the herd could get back into the timber.

Then the <term>Thunder Boys</term> went back to the Darkening Land, but before they left they taught the people the seven songs with which to call up the deer. It all happened so long ago that the songs are now forgotten—all but two, which the hunters still sing whenever they go after deer.

Another story is told of how sin came into the world. A man and a woman reared a large family of children in comfort and plenty, with very little trouble about providing food for them. Accordingly, the next morning the plan was carried out. Those who followed the father saw him stop at a short distance from the cabin and turn over a large stone that appeared to be leaning carelessly against another. On looking closely, they saw an entrance to a large cave, and in it were many different kinds of animals and birds, such as their father had sometimes brought in for food. The man, standing at the entrance, called a deer which was lying at some distance and behind some other animals. It rose immediately as it heard the call and came close up to him. He picked it up, closed the mouth of the cave, and returned, never once seeming to suspect what his sons had done.

When the old man was fairly out of sight, his sons—rejoicing that they had outwitted him—left their hiding place and went to the cave, saying they would show the old folks that they, too, could bring in something. They moved the stone away, though it was very heavy and they were required to use all their combined strength. When the cave was opened, the animals, instead of waiting to be picked up, all made a rush for the entrance; leaping past the frightened and bewildered boys, they scattered in all directions and disappeared in the wilderness, while the guilty offenders could do nothing but gaze in stupefied amazement as they saw them escape. There were animals of all kinds, large and small—buffalo, deer, elk, antelope, raccoons, and squirrels; even <term>catamounts</term> and panthers, wolves and foxes, and many others, all fleeing together. At the same time, birds of every kind were seen emerging from the opening, all in the same wild confusion as the quadrupeds—turkeys, geese, swans, ducks, quails, eagles, hawks, and owls.

Those who followed the mother saw her enter a small cabin, which they had never seen before, and close the door. The culprits found a small crack through which they could peer. They saw the woman place a basket on the ground and, standing over it, shake herself vigorously, jumping up and down—when lo and behold!—large ears of corn began to fall into the basket. When it was well filled, she picked it up and, placing it on her head, came out, fastened the door, and prepared their breakfast as usual. When the meal had been finished in silence, the man spoke to his children, telling them that he was aware of what they had done; that now he must die and they would be required to provide for themselves. He made bows and arrows for them, then sent them to hunt for the animals which they had turned loose.

Then the mother told them that as they had found out her secret, she could do nothing more for them; she said that she would die, and they must drag her body around over the ground; that wherever her body was dragged, corn would come up. From this, they were to make their bread. She told them that they must always save some for seed and plant it every year.

### 4. ORIGIN OF DISEASE AND MEDICINE

In the old days, the animals, birds, fish, insects, and plants could all talk, and they and the people lived together in peace and friendship. But as time went on, the human population increased so rapidly that their settlements spread over the whole earth, and the poor animals found themselves beginning to be cramped for space. This was bad enough, but to make it worse, Man invented bows, knives, blowguns, spears, and hooks, and began to slaughter the larger animals, birds, and fish for their flesh or their skins. Meanwhile, the smaller creatures, such as the frogs and worms, were crushed and stepped on without a thought, out of pure carelessness or contempt. So, the animals resolved to meet and discuss measures for their common safety.

The Bears were the first to meet in council in their townhouse under the <term>Kuwâ'hi</term> mountain, the “Mulberry place,” and the old White Bear chief presided. After each in turn had complained of the way in which Man killed their friends, ate their flesh, and used their skins for his own purposes, it was decided to begin a war against him at once. Someone asked what weapons Man used to destroy them. “Bows and arrows, of course,” cried all the Bears in chorus. “And what are they made of?” was the next question. “The bow is made of wood, and the string is made of our entrails,” replied one of the Bears. It was then proposed that they make a bow and some arrows to see if they could use the same weapons against Man himself. So, one Bear obtained a nice piece of locust wood, and another sacrificed himself for the good of the rest in order to provide a piece of his intestines for the string. But when everything was ready and the first Bear stepped up to try it, it was found that in letting the arrow fly after drawing back the bow, his long claws caught the string and spoiled the shot. This was annoying, but someone suggested that they might trim his claws, which was done; on a second trial, it was found that the arrow went straight to the target. But here the chief, the old White Bear, objected, saying it was necessary for them to have long claws to be able to climb trees. “One of us has already died to provide the bowstring, and if we now cut off our claws, we must all starve together. It is better to trust the teeth and claws that nature gave us, for it is plain that man’s weapons were not intended for us.”

No one could think of any better plan, so the old chief dismissed the council and the Bears scattered to the woods and thickets without having devised any way to prevent the increase of the human race. Had the result of the council been different, we would now be at war with the Bears, but as it is, the hunter does not even ask the Bear’s pardon when he kills one.

The Deer next held a council under their chief, the Little Deer, and after some talk, they decided to send rheumatism to every hunter who should

They sent notice of their decision to the nearest settlement of Indians and told them at the same time what to do when necessity forced them to kill one of the Deer tribe. Now, whenever the hunter shoots a deer, the Little Deer, who is swift as the wind and cannot be wounded, runs quickly up to the spot and, bending over the bloodstains, asks the spirit of the deer if it has heard the hunter's prayer for pardon. If the reply is "Yes," all is well, and the Little Deer goes on his way; but if the reply is "No," he follows the trail of the hunter, guided by the drops of blood on the ground, until he arrives at his cabin in the settlement. When the Little Deer enters invisibly, he strikes the hunter with rheumatism, so that he becomes at once a helpless cripple. No hunter who has regard for his health ever fails to ask pardon of the deer for killing it, although some hunters who have not learned the prayer may try to turn the Little Deer aside from his pursuit by building a fire behind them on the trail.

Next came the fish and reptiles, who had their own complaints against Man. They held their council together and determined to make their victims dream of snakes twining about them in slimy folds and blowing foul breath in their faces, or to make them dream of eating raw or decaying fish, so that they would lose their appetite, sicken, and die. This is why people dream about snakes and fish.

Finally the birds, insects, and smaller animals came together for the same purpose, and the Grubworm was chief of the council. It was decided that each in turn should give an opinion, and then they would vote on the question of whether or not Man was guilty. Seven votes would be enough to condemn him. One after another denounced Man’s cruelty and injustice toward the other animals and voted in favor of his death. The Frog spoke first, saying:

> “We must do something to check the increase of the race, or people will become so numerous that we shall be crowded off the earth. See how they have kicked me about because I am ugly, as they say, until my back is covered with sores;”

and here he showed the spots on his skin. Next came the bird—no one remembers now which one it was—who condemned Man “because he burns my feet off,” meaning the way in which the hunter barbecues birds by impaling them on a stick set over the fire, so that their feathers and tender feet are singed off. Others followed in the same strain. The ground-squirrel alone ventured to say a good word for Man, whom he seldom hurt because he was so small, but this made the others so angry that they fell upon the ground-squirrel and tore him with their claws, and the stripes are on his back to this day.

They began then to devise and name so many new diseases, one after another, that if their invention had not at last failed them, no one of the human race would have been able to survive. The Grubworm grew

He became increasingly pleased as the name of each disease was called out, until at last they reached the end of the list, when someone proposed making menstruation sometimes fatal to women. At this, he rose in his place and cried: “*Wadâñ'!* [Thanks!] I’m glad more of them will die, for they are becoming so numerous that they tread on me.” The thought made him shake so much with joy that he fell over backward and could not get back on his feet, but had to wriggle off on his back, as the Grubworm has done ever since.

When the Plants, who were friendly to Man, heard what had been done by the animals, they determined to defeat the animals' evil designs. Each Tree, Shrub, and Herb, down even to the Grasses and Mosses, agreed to provide a cure for one of the diseases named, and each said: “I shall appear to help Man when he calls upon me in his need.” This is how medicine began; and the plants—every one of which has its use, if only we knew it—provide the remedy to counteract the evil wrought by the revengeful animals. Even weeds were made for some good purpose, which we must find out for ourselves. When the doctor does not know what medicine to use for a sick man, the spirit of the plant tells him.

### 5. THE DAUGHTER OF THE SUN

The Sun lived on the other side of the sky vault, but her daughter lived in the middle of the sky, directly above the earth. Every day, as the Sun was climbing along the sky arch toward the west, she would stop at her daughter’s house for dinner.

Now, the Sun hated the people on the earth because they could never look straight at her without wrinkling their faces. She said to her brother, the Moon, “My grandchildren are ugly; they grin all over their faces when they look at me.” But the Moon said, “I like my younger brothers; I think they are very handsome”—because they always smiled pleasantly when they saw him in the sky at night, for his rays were milder.

The Sun was jealous and planned to kill all the people, so every day when she got near her daughter’s house, she sent down such scorching rays that there was a great fever and the people died by the hundreds, until everyone had lost a friend and there was fear that no one would be left. They went for help to the Little Men, who said the only way to save themselves was to kill the Sun.

The Little Men performed a ceremony and changed two men into snakes, the Spreading-adder and the Copperhead, and sent them to watch near the door of the Sun’s daughter to bite the old Sun when she came the next day. They went together and hid near the house until the Sun arrived, but when the Spreading-adder was about to strike, the bright light blinded him and he could only spit yellow slime, as he does to this day when he tries to bite.
