saying he had been with the mountain people. At last, one man said he believed the story and would go with him to see. They went off together to the woods, where they made a camp, and then Tsuwe'năhĭ went on ahead, saying he would be back soon. The other waited for him, doing a little hunting near the camp, and two nights afterward, Tsuwe'năhĭ was back again. He seemed to be alone, but was talking as he came, and the other hunter heard girls' voices, although he could see no one. When he came up to the fire he said, "I have two friends with me, and they say there is to be a dance in their town in two nights, and if you want to go they will come for you." The hunter agreed at once, and Tsuwe'năhĭ called out, as if to someone close by, "He says he will go." Then he said, "Our sisters have come for some venison." The hunter had killed a deer and had the meat drying over the fire, so he said, "What kind do they want?" The voices answered, "Our mother told us to ask for some of the ribs," but still he could see nothing. He took down some rib pieces and gave them to Tsuwe'năhĭ, who took them and said, "In two days we shall come again for you." Then he started off, and the other heard the voices going through the woods until all was still again.

In two days, Tsuwe'năhĭ came, and this time he had two girls with him. As they stood near the fire, the hunter noticed that their feet were short and round, almost like dogs' paws, but as soon as they saw him looking, they sat down so that he could not see their feet. After supper, the whole party left the camp and went up along the creek to Tsuwa'tel'da. They went in through the cave door until they got to the farther end and could see houses beyond, when all at once the hunter's legs felt as if they were dead and he staggered and fell to the ground. The others lifted him up, but still he could not stand, until the medicine-man brought some "old tobacco" <note>sacred tobacco used in rituals</note> and rubbed it on his legs and made him smell it until he sneezed. Then he was able to stand again and went in with the others. He could not stand at first because he had not prepared himself by fasting before he started.

The dance had not yet begun, and Tsuwe'năhĭ took the hunter into the townhouse and showed him a seat near the fire, but it had long thorns of honey locust sticking out from it and he was afraid to sit down. Tsuwe'năhĭ told him not to be afraid, so he sat down and found that the thorns were as soft as down feathers. Now the drummer came in and the dancers, and the dance began. One man followed at the end of the line, crying *Kû! Kû!* all the time, but not dancing. The hunter wondered, and they told him, "This man was lost in the mountains and had been calling all through the woods for his friends until his voice failed and he was only able to pant *Kû! Kû!* and then we found him and took him in."

### 84. THE MAN WHO MARRIED THE THUNDER'S SISTER

In the old times, the people used to dance often and all night long. Once there was a dance at the old town of Sâkwi'yǐ, at the head of the Chattahoochee River. After it was well started, two young women with beautiful long hair came in, but no one knew who they were or where they had come from. They danced with one partner after another, and in the morning they slipped away before anyone knew they were gone. However, a young warrior had fallen in love with one of the sisters because of her beautiful hair. According to Cherokee tradition, he had already asked her through an old man if she would marry him and let him live with her. To this, the young woman replied that her brother at home must first be consulted. They promised to return for the next dance seven days later with an answer, but in the meantime, if the young man really loved her, he must prove his devotion by a strict fast until then. The eager lover readily agreed and impatiently counted the days.

Seven nights later, there was another dance. The young warrior was there early, and later in the evening, the two sisters appeared as suddenly as before. They told him their brother was willing, and after the dance, they would lead the young man to their home. However, they warned him that if he told anyone where he went or what he saw, he would surely die.

He danced with them again, and around daylight, the three of them left just before the dance closed to avoid being followed, and started off together. The women led the way along a trail through the woods that the young man had never noticed before until they came to a small creek. There, without hesitating, they stepped into the water. The young man paused in surprise on the bank and thought to himself, "They are walking in the water; I don't want to do that." The women knew his thoughts just as though he had spoken, and they turned and said to him, "This is not water; this is the road to our house." He still hesitated, but they urged him on until he stepped into the water and found it was only soft grass that made a fine, level trail.

They continued until the trail came to a large stream which he recognized as the Tallulah River. The women plunged boldly in, but again the warrior hesitated on the bank, thinking to himself, "That water is very

They went only a short distance and came to a rock cave close under Ugûñ'yi (Tallulah Falls). He went inside and stood up close to the entrance. Then the women took off their long hair and hung it up on a rock, and both their heads were as smooth as a pumpkin. The man thought, "It is not hair at all," and he was more frightened than ever.

The younger woman, the one he was about to marry, then sat down and told him to take a seat beside her. He looked, and it was a large turtle, which raised itself up and stretched out its claws as if angry at being disturbed. The young man said it was a turtle and refused to sit down, but the woman insisted that it was a seat. Then there was a louder roll of thunder and the woman said, "Now our brother is nearly home." While they urged him and he still refused to come nearer or sit down, suddenly there was a great thunderclap just behind him, and turning quickly he saw a man standing in the doorway of the cave.

"This is my brother," said the woman, and he came in and sat down upon the turtle, which again rose up and stretched out its claws. The young warrior still refused to come in. The brother then said that he was just about to start for a council, and invited the young man to go with him. The hunter said he was willing to go if only he had a horse; so the young woman was told to bring one. She went out and soon came back leading a great uktena snake, that curled and twisted along the whole length of the cave. Some people say this was a white uktena and that the brother himself rode a red one. The hunter was terribly frightened and said, "That is a snake; I can't ride that." The others insisted that it was not a snake, but their riding horse. The brother grew impatient and said to the woman, "He may like it better if you bring him a saddle and some bracelets for his wrists and arms." So they went out again and brought in a saddle and some armbands, and the saddle was another turtle, which they fastened on the uktena's back, and the bracelets were living slimy snakes, which they got ready to twist around the hunter's wrists.

He was almost dead with fear and said, "What kind of horrible place is this? I can never stay here to live with snakes and creeping things." The brother got very angry and called him a coward, and then it was as if lightning flashed from his eyes and struck the young man, and a terrible crash of thunder knocked him senseless.

### 85. THE HAUNTED WHIRLPOOL

At the mouth of Suck Creek, on the Tennessee River, about 8 miles below Chattanooga, is a series of dangerous whirlpools known as “The Suck.” It is noted among the Cherokee as the place where <term>Ûñtsaiyĭ´</term>, the gambler, lived long ago (see the story). They call it <term>Ûñtiguhi´</term>, “Pot-in-the-water,” because of the appearance of the surging, tumbling water, which suggests a boiling pot. They assert that in the old times the whirlpools were intermittent, and the canoemen attempting to pass the spot used to stay close to the bank, keeping constantly alert for signs of a coming eruption. When they saw the water begin to revolve more rapidly, they would stop and wait until it became quiet again before attempting to proceed.

It once happened that two men, going down the river in a canoe, saw the water circling rapidly ahead of them as they approached this place. They pulled up to the bank to wait until it became smooth again, but the whirlpool seemed to approach with wider and wider circles until they were drawn into the vortex. They were thrown out of the canoe and carried down under the water, where one man was seized by a great fish and was never seen again. The other was taken around and around down to the very lowest center of the whirlpool, until another current caught him and bore him outward and upward. He was finally thrown up again to the surface and floated out into the shallow water, from which he escaped to the shore. He later said that when he reached the narrowest circle of the maelstrom, the water seemed to open below him and he could look down as if through the roof beams of a house. There on the bottom of the river, he had seen a large company of people who looked up and beckoned for him to join them, but as they reached up their hands to seize him, the swift current caught him and took him out of their reach.

Years ago, long before the American Revolution, <term>Yahula</term> was a successful stock trader among the <term>Cherokee</term>, and the tinkling of the bells hanging around the necks of his ponies could be heard on every mountain trail. Once, there was a great hunt and all the warriors were out; but when it was over and they were ready to return to the settlement, <term>Yahula</term> was not with them. They waited and searched for him, but he could not be found, and at last they went back without him. His friends mourned for him as if he were dead.

Some time later, his people were surprised and delighted when he walked in among them and sat down as they were eating supper in the evening. In response to their questions, he told them that he had been lost in the mountains, and that the <term>Nûñnĕ'hĭ</term> (the Immortals) had found him and brought him to their town. He had been kept there ever since with the kindest care and treatment, until his longing to see his old friends brought him back. When his friends invited him to join them for supper, he said that it was now too late—he had tasted the fairy food and could never again eat with humankind. For the same reason, he could not stay with his family but had to return to the <term>Nûñnĕ'hĭ</term>. His wife, children, and brother begged him to stay, but he said that he could not; it was either life with the Immortals or death with his own people. After some further talk, he rose to go. They saw him as he sat talking to them and as he stood up, but the moment he stepped out the doorway, he vanished as if he had never been there.

After that, he came back often to visit his people. They would see him first as he entered the house, and while he sat and talked, he was his old self in every way; but the instant he stepped across the threshold, he was gone, even though a hundred eyes might be watching. He came often, but finally their pleas grew so urgent that the <term>Nûñnĕ'hĭ</term> must have been offended, and he stopped coming. On the mountain at the head of the creek, about ten miles above present-day <term>Dahlonega</term>, is a small square enclosure of uncut stone, without a roof or entrance. It was said that he lived there, so the <term>Cherokee</term> called it <term>Yahulâ'ĭ</term> and called the stream by the same name. Often at night, a traveler caught out late along the trail by the creek would hear the voice of <term>Yahula</term> singing certain favorite old songs that he used to sing as he drove his pack of horses across the mountain. The sound of a voice urging them on, the crack of a whip, and the tinkling of bells accompanied the song, but neither the driver nor the horses could be seen, although the sounds passed close by. The songs and the bells were heard only at night.

There was one man who had been his friend and sang the same songs for a time after <term>Yahula</term> had disappeared, but he died suddenly. Then the <term>Cherokee</term> were afraid to sing these songs any longer until so much time had passed since anyone had heard the sounds on the mountain that they thought <term>Yahula</term> must have gone away—perhaps to the West, where others of the tribe had already gone. ### 87. THE WATER CANNIBALS

Besides the friendly <term>Nûñně'hĭ</term> of the streams and mountains, there is a race of cannibal spirits who live at the bottom of the deep rivers and live upon human flesh, especially that of little children. They come out just after daybreak and go about unseen from house to house until they find someone still asleep, when they shoot him with their invisible arrows and carry the dead body down under the water to feast upon it. So that no one may know what has happened, they leave in place of the body a shade or image of the dead man or little child that wakes up, talks, and goes about just as he did; however, there is no life in it, and in seven days it withers and dies. The people bury it, thinking they are burying their dead friend. It was a long time before the people found out about this, but now they always try to be awake at daylight and wake up the children, telling them, “The hunters are among you.”

This is the way they first knew about the water cannibals: There was a man in <term>Tikwăli'tsĭ</term> town who became sick and grew worse until the doctors said he could not live, and then his friends went away from the house and left him alone to die. They were not as kind to each other in the old times as they are now, because they were afraid of the witches who came to torment dying people.

He was alone for several days, unable to rise from his bed, when one morning an old woman came in through the door. She looked just like the other women of the settlement, but he did not know her. She came over to the bed and said, “You are very sick and your friends seem to have left you. Come with me and I will make you well.” The man was so near death that he could not move, but her words made him feel stronger at once, and he asked her where she wanted him to go. “We live close by; come with me and I will show you,” said the woman, so he got up from his bed and she led the way down to the water. When she came to the water she stepped in and he followed, and there was a road under the water, and another country there just like the one above.

They went on until they came to a settlement with a great many houses, and women going about their work and children playing. They met a party of hunters coming in from a hunt, but instead of deer or bear quarters hanging from their shoulders, they carried the bodies of dead men and children, and the man recognized several of the bodies as those of his own friends in <term>Tikwăli'tsĭ</term>. ### HISTORICAL TRADITIONS

#### 88. FIRST CONTACT WITH WHITES

There are a few stories concerning the first contact of the Cherokee with white people and Black people. They are very modern and have little value as myths, but they throw some light upon the Indian estimate of the different races.

One story relates how the first white people came from the east and tried to enter into friendly relations, but the Indians would have nothing to do with them for a long time. At last the white people left a jug of whisky and a dipper near a spring frequented by the Indians. The Indians came along, tasted the liquor, which they had never known before, and liked it so well that they ended by all getting comfortably drunk. While they were in this happy frame of mind some white men came up, and this time the Indians shook hands with them and they have been friends after a fashion ever since. This may possibly be a Cherokee adaptation of the story of Hudson’s first landing on the island of Manhattan.

When Sequoya, the inventor of the Cherokee alphabet, was trying to introduce it among his people around 1822, some of them opposed it on the grounds that Indians had no business with reading. They said that when the Indian and the white man were created, the Indian, being the elder, was given a book, while the white man received a bow and arrows. Each was instructed to take good care of his gift and make the best use of it, but the Indian was so neglectful of his book that the white man soon stole it from him, leaving the bow in its place. Because of this, books and reading now belong by right to the white man, while the Indian should be satisfied to hunt for a living.—*Cherokee Advocate, October 26, 1844.*

->* * * * * * *<-

The Black man made the first locomotive as a toy and put it on a wooden track. He was having great fun with it when a white man came along and watched until he saw how to run it; he then killed the Black man and took the locomotive for himself. This story, although clearly of very recent origin, was also heard from several informants.

## 89. THE IROQUOIS WARS

Long wars were waged between the Cherokee and their distant northern relatives, the Iroquois. The memory of these wars, though now nearly faded, was a vivid tradition fifty years ago. The (Seneca) Iroquois know the Cherokee as the <term>Oyada'ge'oñnoñ</term>, a name rather freely translated as "cave people." The Cherokee call the Iroquois—or rather their largest and most aggressive tribe, the Seneca—the <term>Nûndăwe'gĭ</term>, <term>Ani'-Nûndăwe'gĭ</term>, or <term>Ani'-Sě'nikă</term>. The first forms are derived from <term>Nûndawa'ga</term> or <term>Nûndawa'-ono</term>, "people of the great hills," which is the name the Seneca use for themselves. According to authorities quoted by Schoolcraft, the Seneca claim to have once had a settlement at Seneca, South Carolina (known historically as one of the principal towns of the Lower Cherokee), from which they were later driven.

The League of the Iroquois was probably founded around the middle of the sixteenth century. Before 1680, they had conquered or exterminated all the tribes on their immediate borders and had turned their weapons against the more distant Illinois, Catawba, and Cherokee. According to Iroquois tradition, the Cherokee were the aggressors, having attacked and plundered a Seneca hunting party somewhere in the west; however, another story claims they violated a peace treaty by murdering Iroquois delegates.

<page-num>352</page-num>
<header>MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19</header>

Whatever the cause, the war was taken up by all the tribes of the league.

From the Iroquois country to the Cherokee frontier was considered a five-day journey for a rapidly traveling war party. As the distance was too great for large expeditions, the war consisted chiefly of a series of individual exploits. A single Cherokee warrior would often travel hundreds of miles to strike a blow, which was sure to be promptly retaliated against by warriors from the north; the primary goal of every Iroquois boy was to go against the Cherokee as soon as he was old enough to take the warpath. Captives were taken on both sides, and likely in roughly equal numbers, as the two parties were too evenly matched for either to gain any permanent advantage. A compromise was finally reached by which the Tennessee River came to be regarded as the boundary between their rival claims. All territory south of that stream was claimed by the Cherokee and acknowledged by the Iroquois as the limit of their own conquests in that direction. This Indian boundary was recognized by the British government until the time of the American Revolution.

Morgan states that a curious agreement was once made between the two tribes, by which this river was also made the limit of pursuit. If a returning Cherokee war party could recross the Tennessee before being overtaken by the pursuing Iroquois, they were as safe from attack as if they were entrenched behind a stockade. The pursuers, if they chose, could still invade the enemy's territory, but they would pass by the camp of the retreating Cherokee without attempting to attack them. A similar agreement existed for a time between the Seneca and the Erie.

The Buffalo dance of the Iroquois is traditionally said to have originated in an expedition against the Cherokee. When the warriors reached the Kentucky salt lick on their way south, they found a herd of buffalo there and heard them, for the first time, “singing their favorite songs”—that is, bellowing and snorting. The music and movements of the dance were derived from the bellowing and actions of the animals.

According to Cherokee tradition, as recounted by Chief Stand Watie, the war was finally ended by the Iroquois, who sent a delegation to the Cherokee to propose a general alliance of the southern and western tribes. The Cherokee accepted the proposal and in turn sent invitations to other tribes. All of them entered into the peace except for the Osage; because of this, it was said that they would henceforth be like wild fruit on the prairie for every bird to pick at. Consequently, the Osage have remained a predatory tribe without friends or allies. This may be the same treaty described in the story of “The Seneca Peacemakers.” A formal and final peace between the two tribes was arranged through the efforts of the British agent, Sir William Johnson, in 1768.

# MOONEY] THE IROQUOIS WARS

In 1847, the grandchildren of Cherokee captives taken in these wars were still living among the Seneca. In 1794, the Seneca pointed out a chief to Colonel Pickering who was a native Cherokee; he had been captured as a boy and adopted by the Seneca, who later made him a chief. This was probably the same man mentioned to Schoolcraft fifty years later. He was a full-blooded Cherokee but had been captured when he was too young to remember the event. Years later, after he had grown to manhood and become a chief in the tribe, he learned of his foreign origin and was immediately filled with an overpowering longing to return to the South to find his people and live and die among them. He traveled to the Cherokee country, but upon arriving there, he found to his great disappointment that the story of his capture had been forgotten by the tribe, and his relatives, if any remained, failed to recognize him. Since he was unable to find his kindred, he stayed for only a short visit and returned again to the Seneca.

From James Wafford of Indian Territory, the author obtained a detailed account of the Iroquois peace embassy mentioned by Stand Watie, as well as the wampum belt that accompanied it. Wafford’s information regarding the proceedings at Echota was obtained directly from two eyewitnesses: Sequoya, the inventor of the alphabet, and Gatûn'wa'lĭ, or "Hard-mush," who later explained the belt at the great council near Tahlequah seventy years afterward. At the time of the Echota conference, Sequoya was a boy living with his mother at Taskigi town a few miles away, while Gatûn'wa'lĭ was already a young man.

The peace treaty between the Cherokee and Iroquois, made at Johnson Hall in New York in 1768, appears from the record to have been initiated by the Cherokee. They sent a delegation of chiefs for this purpose, led by Âgănstâ'ta, also known as "Groundhog-sausage," of Echota, their great leader in the 1760–61 war against the English. After the treaty was concluded, the Cherokee delegates invited some of the Iroquois chiefs to return home with them for a visit, but the Iroquois declined, believing it was not yet safe. In fact, some of their warriors were still out on campaign against the Cherokee at that very time, as they were not yet aware of the peace negotiations. It is probable, therefore, that the Iroquois delegates did not arrive at Echota until a considerable time—perhaps three years—after the formal preliminaries had been concluded in the North.

According to Sequoya’s account, as told to Wafford, there had been a long war between the Cherokee and the northern Indians. The northern tribes were never able to conquer the Cherokee or break their spirit, until at last the Iroquois grew tired of fighting and sent a delegation to make peace. The messengers set out for the South with their wampum belts and peace emblems, but they lost their way after passing Ten-

<header>MOONEY] THE IROQUOIS WARS</header>

The chief and his family were working in their cornfield, and his daughter had just returned to the house for some reason when the Iroquois entered and asked for something to eat. Seeing that he was a stranger, she set out food for him according to the old custom of hospitality. While he was eating, her father, the chief, came in to see what was delaying her and was surprised to find one of the hereditary enemies of his tribe there. By this time, word had gone out that an Iroquois was in the chief’s house, and the men of the town had left their work and seized their guns to kill him. However, the chief heard them coming and, standing in the doorway, kept them back, saying: “This man has come here on a peace mission, and before you kill him, you must first kill me.” They finally listened to him and allowed the messenger to go out and bring his companions to the chief’s house, where they were all cared for.

When they were well rested after their long journey, the chief of Tă'likwă himself went with them to Itsâ'tĭ, the capital, where the great chief Âgănstâ'ta lived, who was then the civil ruler of the Nation. The chiefs of the various towns were summoned and a council was held, at which the speaker for the Iroquois delegation delivered his message and produced the wampum belts and pipes which they had brought as proof of their mission, having carried them the whole way in packs on their backs.

He said that for three years his people had wanted to make peace. There was a spring of dark, cloudy water in their country, and they had covered it over for one year and then looked, but the water was still cloudy. Again they had covered it over, but when they looked at the end of another year, it was still dark and troubled. For a third year they had covered the spring, and this time when they looked, the water was clear and sparkling. Then they knew the time had come, and they left home with their wampum belts to make peace with their enemies.

The Cherokee accepted the friendly message, and the belts and other symbolic peace tokens were delivered into their keeping. Other belts were likely given to the Iroquois in return, and after the usual round of feasting and dancing, the messengers returned to their people in the north, and the long war was at an end.

For nearly a century, these symbolic records of the peace with the Iroquois were preserved by the Cherokee and were carried with them to the western territory when the tribe was finally driven from its old home in 1838. They were then in the keeping of John Ross, the principal chief at the time of the removal, and were solemnly produced at a great intertribal council held near Tahlequah, in the Indian Territory, in June 1843. On that occasion, they were interpreted by the Cherokee speaker, Gatûn'wa'lĭ, or “Hard-mush,” who had seen them delivered to the chiefs of his tribe at old Itsâ'tĭ seventy years before. Wafford was present at this event and describes it.

Holding the belts over his arm while speaking, Hard-mush told of the original treaty with the Iroquois and explained the meaning of each belt in turn. According to the best of Wafford’s recollection, there was one large belt to which the smaller belts were fitted. The beads did not seem to be made of shell and may have been porcelain. There were also red pipes for the warriors, grayish-white pipes for the chiefs who were foremost in making peace, and some fans or other feather ornaments. There were several red pipes, resembling the red-stone pipes of the Sioux, but only one, or perhaps two, of the white peace pipes, which may have been only painted and were much larger than the others. The pipes were passed around the circle at the council so that each delegate might take a puff. The objects together made a considerable package, which was carefully guarded by the Cherokee keeper. It is thought that they were destroyed in the War of the Rebellion when the house of John Ross, located a few miles south of Tahlequah, was burned by the Confederate Cherokee under their general, Stand Watie.

### 90. HIADEONI, THE SENECA

“Hiadeoni was the father of the late chief Young-king. He was a Seneca warrior, a man of great prowess, dexterity, and swiftness of foot, and he had established his reputation for courage and skill on many occasions. He resolved, while the Seneca were still living on the Genesee River, to make an incursion alone into the country of the Cherokee. He took pride in the idea that he could distinguish himself in this daring adventure, and he prepared for it according to the custom of warriors. They never encumber themselves with baggage. He took nothing but his weapons and a small amount of parched and pounded corn meal. The forest provided his meat.

Hiadeoni reached the borders of the Cherokee country safely and alone. He waited for evening before entering the outskirts of a village. He found the people engaged in a dance. He watched for his opportunity, and when one of the dancers left the ring to go into the bushes, he killed him with his hatchet. In this way, he killed two men that night at the edge of the woods without raising an alarm, took their scalps, and retreated. It was late when he came to a lodge standing apart from the others on his way home. Watching there, he saw a young man come out and killed him as he had done the others and took his scalp. Looking into the lodge cautiously, he saw it was empty and ventured in with the hope of finding some tobacco and ammunition to serve him on his way home.

While busy searching the lodge, he heard footsteps at the door and immediately threw himself on the bed from which the young man had risen, covering his face and pretending to sleep. They proved to be the footsteps of his last victim’s mother. Supposing him to be her son, whom she had left lying there a short time before, she said,

He jumped up instantly and fled; but the early dawn had revealed his intrusion, and he was closely pursued. Being light-footed and having a head start, he succeeded in reaching and hiding himself in a remote patch of woods, where he lay until night. He then continued his way toward the Genesee River, which he reached in due time, bringing his three Cherokee scalps as trophies of his victory and bravery."—Schoolcraft, *Notes on the Iroquois*, p. 253, 1847.

### 91. THE TWO MOHAWKS

"In the year 1747, a couple of Mohawk Indians attacked the lower towns of the Cherokee and so cleverly ambushed them through most of the spring and summer that they killed more than twenty people in various attacks before they were discovered by any party of the enraged and dejected residents. They had a thorough knowledge of the most convenient ground for their purpose and were extremely fast and had great endurance. Whenever they killed anyone and took the scalp, they escaped to the nearby mountains and ran over the wide ledges of rocks in different directions, as the situation required, so that the pursuers could not track them at all. Once, when a large company was chasing them, they ran around a steep hill at the head of the main eastern branch of the Savannah River, intercepted, killed, and scalped the last man in the party, and then escaped between them and Keowee. Since this was the town to which the company belonged, they hurried home in a tight group, considering it the only safe place from such enemy wizards. In this manner, those two energetic, brave savages confused and intimidated their enemies for four months in the greatest security, even though they were often forced to kill and barbecue the food they mainly lived on in the midst of their watchful enemies. Having sufficiently avenged their relatives' blood and satisfied their own ambition with an unusual number of scalps, they resolved to take someone captive and run home with him as proof that they had killed only the enemies of their country. Accordingly, they approached very near to Keowee, about half a mile below the former Fort Prince George. Advancing with the usual caution for such an occasion, one crawled along using the best cover available about a hundred yards ahead, while the other moved from tree to tree, looking sharply in every direction. In the evening, however, an old, beloved man <note>A title for a Cherokee official or elder</note> spotted them from the top of a nearby hill and knew them to be enemies by the cut of their hair and their light attire for

running and their postures. He returned to the town and first went to the house of one of our traders and informed him of the affair, urging him not to mention it to anyone, so that the people would not set out against them unsuccessfully before their tracks could be discovered and he be accused of deceiving them. But, contrary to the proper policy for traders among unforgiving savages, that thoughtless member of the Choctaw Sphinx Company busied himself, as usual, outside of his proper sphere, sent for the headmen, and told them the story. Since the Mohawks were allies and were not known to bother any of the traders on the paths or in the woods, he should have maintained a strict neutrality. The youth of the town, by order of their headmen, carried on their noisy public games in their usual manner to prevent their enemies from suspecting any danger, while messengers were sent from the town to their neighbors to come silently and help them capture the prey while they felt secure. They came like silent ghosts, coordinated their plan of operation, crossed the river at the old trading ford opposite the former fort—which lay between two adjacent, commanding hills—and, proceeding downward over a broad creek, formed a large semicircle from the riverbank, while the town seemed to be taking its usual rest. They then closed into a narrower circle and finally discovered the two brave, unfortunate men lying close under the tops of some fallen young pine trees. The group gave the war signal, and the Mohawks, leaping up, bravely echoed it; but because of their sudden jump from under thick cover, their weapons were useless. They made desperate efforts, however, to kill or be killed, as their situation required. One of the Cherokee, the well-known half-breed of Istanare [<gloss>Ustǎna'lĭ</gloss>] town, which was 2 miles from there, was knocked down at the first attack and almost killed with his own cutlass, which was snatched from him, even though he was the strongest man in the whole nation. But they were overpowered by numbers, captured, and subjected to the most intense tortures of fire, amidst a massive crowd of gloating enemies.

One of the current Choctaw traders, who was there, told me that when they were tied to the stake, the younger of the two spotted our traders on a nearby hill, addressed them in English, and begged them to ransom their lives. The elder immediately spoke to him in his own language, telling him to stop. At this, he regained his composure and became calm like a stoic, showing an indifference to life or death, pleasure or pain, according to their standard of military virtue; their behavior while dying did not reflect the slightest dishonor on their former gallant actions. All the pains of fiery torture served only to refine their manly spirits, and since it was beyond the power of the traders to ransom them, they, according to our usual custom, withdrew as soon as the Indians began the diabolical tragedy."—Adair, *American Indians*, p. 383, 1775.

### 92. ESCAPE OF THE SENECA BOYS

Some Seneca warriors were hunting in the woods, and one morning, as they set out for the day, they left two boys behind to take care of the camp. Soon after they had gone, a war party of Cherokee arrived, and finding the boys alone, took them both and started back to the south, traveling at such a speed that when the hunters returned in the evening, they decided there was no use in following them. When the Cherokee reached their own country, they gave the boys to an old man whose sons had been killed by the Seneca. He took the boys and adopted them as his own, and they grew up with him until they were large and strong enough to go hunting for themselves.

But all the time they remembered their own home, and one day the elder one said to his brother, “Let's kill the old man and run away.” “No,” said the other, “we might get lost if we ran away; we are so far from home.” “I remember the way,” said his brother, so they made a plan to escape. A few days later, the old man took the boys with him, and the three set out together for a hunt in the mountains. When they were well away from the settlement, the boys killed the old man, took all the meat and parched corn meal they could easily carry, and started to make their way back to the north, keeping away from the main trail and following the ridge of the mountains. After many days, they came to the end of the mountains and found a trail which the older brother recognized as the one along which they had been taken when they were first captured. They went on bravely now until they came to a wide clearing with houses at the farther end, and the older brother said, “I believe that is where we used to live.” It was so long ago that they were not quite sure, and besides, they were dressed now like Cherokee, so they thought it safer to wait until dark. They saw a river ahead and went down to it and sat behind a large tree to wait. Soon several women came down for water and passed close to the tree without noticing the boys. The older brother said, “I know those women. One of them is our mother.” They waited until the women had filled their buckets and started back to the village, when both boys ran out to meet them with the Seneca hailing-shout, “<term>Gowĕ! Gowĕ!</term>” At first the women were frightened and thought it was a party of Cherokee, but when they heard their own language, they came nearer. Then the mother recognized her two sons and said, “Let us go back and dance for the dead who have come to life,” and they were all very glad and went into the village together.—Arranged from Curtin, Seneca manuscript.

When he thought they were asleep, he went into the house. The fire had burned down low, but the girl was still awake and saw him. She was about to scream when he said, “I am Ganogwioeoñ. She promised to do it and told him where he should wait. Just before daylight, he left the house.

In the morning, the girl went to the chief’s house and said to his daughter, “Let’s go out together for wood.” The chief’s daughter got ready and went with her, and when they came to the place where Ganogwioeoñ was hiding, he sprang out and killed her, but did not hurt the other girl. He pulled off the scalp and gave such a loud scalp yell that all the warriors in the town heard it and came running out after him. He shook the scalp at them and then turned and ran. He killed the first one that came up, but when he tried to shoot the next one, the bow broke and the Cherokee captured him.

They tied him and carried him to the two women of the tribe who had the power to decide what should be done with him. Each of these women had two snakes tattooed on her lips, with their heads opposite each other, in such a way that when she opened her mouth, the two snakes opened their mouths also. They decided to burn the soles of his feet until they were blistered, then to put grains of corn under the skin and to chase him with clubs until they had beaten him to death.

They stripped him and burned his feet. Then they tied a bark rope around his waist, with an old man to hold the other end, and made him run between two lines of people who held clubs in their hands. When they gave the word to start, Ganogwioeoñ pulled the rope away from the old man, broke through the line, and ran until he had left them all out of sight. When night came, he crawled into a hollow log. He was naked and unarmed, with his feet in a pitiful condition, and he thought he could never get away.

He heard footsteps on the leaves outside and thought his enemies were upon him. The footsteps came up to the log and someone said to another, “This is our friend.” Then the stranger said to Ganogwioeoñ, “You think you are as good as dead, but it is not so. We will take care of you. Stick out your feet.” He put out his feet from the log and felt something licking them. After a while, the voice said, “I think we have licked his feet enough. Now we must crawl inside the log and lie on each side of him to keep him warm.” They

Toward evening, he looked around until he found another hollow tree and crawled into it to sleep. At night, he heard the footsteps and voices again. In the morning, after they went out, they licked his feet again and said to him, “At noon you will find food.” Then they went away.

Ganogwioeoñ crawled out of the tree and went on. At noon, he came to a burning log, and near it was a dead bear, which was still warm, as if it had been killed only a short time before. He skinned the bear and found it very fat. He cut up the meat and roasted as much as he could eat or carry. While it was roasting, he scraped the skin and rubbed rotten wood dust on it to clean it until he was tired. When night came, he lay down to sleep. He heard the steps and the voices again, and one said, “Well, our friend is lying down. He has plenty to eat, and it does not seem as if he is going to die. Let us lick his feet again.” When they had finished, they said to him, “You need not worry anymore now. You will get home all right.” Before it was day, they left him.

When morning came, he put the bearskin around him like a shirt, with the hair on the outside, and started on again, taking as much of the meat as he could carry. That night, his friends came to him again. They said, “Your feet are well, but you will be cold,” so they lay again on each side of him. Before daylight, they left, saying, “About noon, you will find something to wear.” He went on, and about midday, he came to two young bears that had just been killed. He skinned them and dressed the skins, then roasted as much meat as he wanted and lay down to sleep. In the morning, he made leggings of the skins, took some of the meat, and started on.

His friends came again the next night and told him that in the morning, he would come upon something else to wear. As they said, about noon he found two fawns that had just been killed. He turned the skins and made himself a pair of moccasins, then cut some of the meat and traveled on until evening, when he made a fire and had supper.

That night again he heard the steps and voices, and one said, “My friend, very soon now you will reach home safely and find your friends all well. Now we will tell you why we have helped you. Whenever you went hunting you always gave the best part of the meat to us and kept only the smallest part for yourself. For that we are thankful and help you. In the morning you will see us and know who we are.”

In the morning when he woke up they were still there—two men as he thought—but after he had said the last words to them and started on, he turned again to look, and one was a white wolf and the other a black wolf. That day he reached home.—Arranged from Curtin, Seneca manuscript.

### 94. HATCINOÑDOÑ’S ESCAPE FROM THE CHEROKEE

Hatcinoñdoñ was a great warrior, the greatest among the Seneca. Once he led a company against the Cherokee. They traveled until they came to the great ridge on the border of the Cherokee country, and then they knew their enemies were on the lookout on the other side. Hatcinoñdoñ told his men to halt where they were while he went ahead to see what was in front. The enemy discovered and chased him, and he ran into a canebrake, where the canes were in two great patches with a narrow strip of open ground between. They saw him go into the canes, so they set fire to the patch and watched at the open place for him to come out, but before they got around to it he had run across into the second patch and escaped. When the canes had burned down the Cherokee looked for his body in the ashes, but could not find any trace of it, so they went home.

When Hatcinoñdoñ got into the second canebrake he was tired out, so he lay down and fell asleep. At night while he was asleep two men came and took him by the arm, saying: “We have come for you. Somebody has sent for you.” They took him a long way, above the sky vault, until they came to a house. Then they said: “This is where the man lives who sent for you.” He looked, but could see no door. Then a voice from the inside said “Come in,” and something like a door opened of itself. He went in and there sat Hawĕñni'o, the Thunder-god.

Hawĕñni'o said, “I have sent for you and you are here. Are you hungry?” Hatcinoñdoñ thought: “That’s a strange way to talk; that’s not the way I do—I give food.” The Thunder knew his thoughts, so he laughed and said, “I said that only in fun.” He rose and brought half a cake of bread, half a wild apple, and half a pigeon. Hatcinoñdoñ said, “This is very little to fill me,” but the Thunder replied, “If you eat that, there is more.” He began eating, but, as he ate, everything became whole again, so that he was not able to finish it.

While he was sitting he heard some one running outside, and directly

The door was thrown open and the Sun came in, so bright that Hatcinoñdoñ had to hold his head down. The two beings talked together, but the Seneca could not understand a word, and soon the visitor went out again. Then the Thunder said: "That is the one you call the Sun, who watches in the world below. It is night down there now, and he is hurrying to the east. He says there has just been a battle. I love both the Seneca and the Cherokee, and when you get back to your warriors you must tell them to stop fighting and go home." Again he brought food, half of each kind, and when Hatcinoñdoñ had eaten, the Thunder said, "Now my messengers will take you to your place."

The door opened again of itself, and Hatcinoñdoñ followed the two Sky People until they brought him to the place where he had slept, and there left him. He found his party and told the warriors what he had seen. They held a council over the matter and decided to strike the enemy once before going home. Hatcinoñdoñ led them. They met the Cherokee and went home with scalps.

He led another party against the Cherokee, but this time he was captured and carried to the Cherokee town. It was the custom among the Cherokee to let two women decide what should be done with captives. They decided that he should be tortured with fire, so he was tied to a tree, and wood was piled around him. Hatcinoñdoñ gave himself up for lost, when a rainstorm came up and the people decided to wait until it was over. They went away and left him tied to the tree.

Soon an old woman came up to him and said, "My grandson, you think you are going to die, but you are not. Try to move your limbs." He struggled and finally got his limbs free. Then she said, "Now you are free. I have come to repay your kindness. You remember that you once found a frog in the middle of a circle of fire and that you picked it up and put it into the water. I was that frog, and now I am helping you. I sent the rainstorm, and now you must go down to the creek and follow the current."

When the rain was over, the people came back, but Hatcinoñdoñ was gone. They tracked him down to the creek, but he had found a hollow tree lying in the water with a hole on the upper side through which he could breathe; so he crawled into it and they could not find him. Once, two of the Cherokee came and sat on the log, and he could hear them talking about him, but they did not know that he was inside. When they were all gone, he came out and continued down the stream. After dark, he came to a place where three hunters had made a fire and gone to sleep for the night. Their hatchets and weapons were hung up on a tree. Hatcinoñdoñ was naked. He listened until he was sure the men were asleep, then he took one of their hatchets and killed all three, one after another. He dressed himself in the clothes of one and put on his belt with the knife and hatchet. Then he washed himself at the creek, sat down by the fire, and cooked his supper.

They went home together. This is their story.—Arranged from Curtin, Seneca manuscript.

### 95. HEMP-CARRIER

On the southern slope of the ridge, along the trail from Robbinsville to Valley River, in Cherokee County, North Carolina, are the remains of a number of stone cairns. The piles are leveled now, but thirty years ago the stones were still heaped up into pyramids, to which every Cherokee who passed added a stone. According to tradition, these piles marked the graves of a number of women and children of the tribe who were surprised and killed on the spot by a raiding party of the Iroquois shortly before the final peace between the two Nations. As soon as the news was brought to the settlements on Hiwassee and Cheowa, a party was formed under Tâle'tanigi'skĭ, "Hemp-carrier," to follow and take vengeance on the enemy. Among others in the party was the father of the noted chief Tsunu'lăhûñ'skĭ, or Junaluska, who died on Cheowa about 1855.

For days they followed the trail of the Iroquois across the Great Smoky Mountains, through forests and over rivers, until they finally tracked them to their very town in the far northern Seneca country. On the way, they met another war party headed for the south, and the Cherokee killed them all and took their scalps. When they came near the Seneca town, it was almost night, and they heard shouts in the townhouse, where the women were dancing over the fresh Cherokee scalps. The avengers hid themselves near the spring, and as the dancers came down to drink, the Cherokee silently killed one after another until they had counted as many scalps as had been taken on Cheowa, and still the dancers in the townhouse never thought that enemies were near. Then the Cherokee leader said, "We have covered the scalps of our women and children. Shall we go home now like cowards, or shall we raise the war whoop and let the Seneca know that we are men?" "Let them come, if they will," said his men; and they raised the scalp yell of the Cherokee. At once there was an answering shout from the townhouse, and the dance came to a sudden stop. The Seneca warriors swarmed out with ready guns and hatchets, but the nimble Cherokee were off and away. There was a hot pursuit in the darkness, but the Cherokee knew the trails and were light and active

### 96. THE SENECA PEACEMAKERS

During the long war with the Cherokee, it happened once that eight Seneca determined to undertake a journey to the south to see if they could make peace with their enemies. On approaching the border of the Cherokee country, they met some hunters of that tribe to whom they explained their purpose. The hunters at once hurried ahead with the news, and when the peacemakers arrived, they found themselves well received by the Cherokee chiefs, who called a council to consider the proposition. All but one of the chiefs favored peace, but he demanded that the eight delegates should first join them in a war party which was just preparing to go against a tribe farther south, probably the Creeks. The Seneca agreed and set out with the war party for the south; but in the resulting fight, the Seneca leader, The Owl, was captured. The other seven escaped with the Cherokee.

A council was held in the enemy’s camp, and it was decided that The Owl should be burned at the stake. The wood was gathered and everything was made ready, but as they were about to tie him, he claimed the warrior’s privilege to sing his death song and strike the post as he recited his warlike deeds. The request pleased his enemies, who put a tomahawk into his hands and told him to begin.

He told first of his exploits in the north, and then in the west, giving times and places and the number of scalps taken, until his enemies were so pleased and interested that they forgot the prisoner in the warrior. It was a long story, but at last he came to the battle in which he was taken. He told how many relatives he had killed of the very men around him, and then, striking the post with his tomahawk, he said, “I have killed so many of your people, and I will kill many more!” With that, he struck down two men, sprang through the circle of warriors, and was away. It was all so sudden that it took several moments before his enemies could recover from their surprise. Then they seized their weapons and pursued him through the woods, but he had a good start and was running for his life, so he outran the chase and finally reached the Cherokee camp in safety and rejoined his seven companions.

On this proof of goodwill, the Cherokee then concluded the treaty, and the peacemakers returned to their own country.—Arranged from *Schoolcraft, Notes on Iroquois*, p. 258.

The Cherokee carried the women with them until they were within one day's journey of the Cherokee towns. The older sister learned this and made up her mind to try to escape. In a little while, they heard an alarm behind them and knew that their escape had been discovered. They found they had come directly back to the enemy's camp, so the older sister said, "This will never do; we must try again. Let us go straight ahead to that big tree in front, and from that straight on to the next, and the next." In this way, they kept on a straight course until morning. When the sun came up, they took another direction toward home, and at night they rested in the woods.

They traveled all the next day, and at night they rested again. During the night, a voice spoke to the younger woman, "Is that where you are resting?" and she answered, "Yes." The voice said again, "Keep going, and you will come out at the spot where you were captured. No harm will come to you. Tomorrow you will find food." She woke her sister and told her what the voice had said.

Nearby they found a burning log, so they roasted some of the meat, had a good meal, and afterward carried away as much of the meat as they could. They kept on, camping every night, and when the meat was nearly gone, they saved the rest for the little boy.

### 98. GA'NA'S ADVENTURES AMONG THE CHEROKEE

Ga'na' was a Seneca war chief. He called a council and said, "We must go to the Cherokee and see if we can agree to be friendly together and live in peace hereafter." The people consented, and the chief said, "We must go to the water first before we start." So they went, a great party of warriors, far away into the deep forest by the riverside. There were no women with them. For ten days, they drank medicine every morning to make them vomit and washed and bathed in the river each day.

Then the chief said, "Now we must get the eagle feathers." They went to the top of a high hill and dug a trench there the length of a man's body. They put a man into it, with boughs over the top so that he could not be seen, and above that, they placed the whole body of a deer. Then the people went off out of sight and said the words to invite <term>Shada'ge'a</term>, the great eagle that lives in the clouds, to come down.

The man under the brushwood heard a noise, and a common eagle came and ate a little and flew away again. Soon it came back, ate a

They had to trap many eagles in this way, and it was two years before they could get enough feathers to make a full tail and were ready to start for the Cherokee country.

They were many days on the road, and when they reached the first Cherokee town, they found a stockade around it so that no enemy could enter. They waited until the gate was open, and then two Seneca dancers went forward, carrying the eagle feathers and shouting the signal yell. When the Cherokee heard the noise, they came out and saw the two men singing and dancing, and the chief said, “These men must have come on some errand.” The Seneca messengers approached and said, “Call a council; we have come to talk about important business.” Everyone turned and went toward the townhouse, with the rest of the Seneca following the two who were dancing. The townhouse was crowded, and the Seneca sang and danced until they were tired before they stopped. The Cherokee did not dance.

After the dance, the Seneca chief said, “Now I will tell you why we have come so far through the forest to see you. We have decided among ourselves that it is time to stop fighting. Your people and ours are always on the lookout to kill each other, and we think it is time for this to stop. Here is a wampum belt to show that I speak the truth. If your people are willing to be friendly, take it,” and he held up the belt. The Cherokee chief stepped forward and said, “I will hold it in my hand, and tomorrow we will tell you what we decide.” He then turned and said to the people, “Go home and bring food.” They went and brought so much food that it made a great pile across the house, and members of both tribes ate together, but they could not finish it all.

The next day they ate together again, and when all were finished, the Cherokee chief said to the Seneca, “We have decided to be friendly and to bury our weapons—these knives and hatchets—so that no man may take them up again.” The Seneca chief replied, “We are glad you have accepted our offer. Now we have all thrown our weapons into a pile, and the white wampum hangs between us. The belt shall be as long as a man and hang down to the ground.”

They began to play, and the Cherokee lost the game. Then the Seneca said, "We will try this time." Both sides bet heavily again and the game began, but after a little running, the Seneca carried the ball to their goal and made a point. Before long, they made all the points and won the game. Then the bets were doubled, and the Seneca won again. When they won a third game as well, the <term>Seoqqwageono</term> said, "Let us try a race," and the Seneca agreed.

The course was level, and the open space was very wide. The Cherokee selected the Seneca runner, and it was agreed that they would run the first race without betting and then make their bets on the second race. They ran the first race, and when they reached the post, the Seneca runner was just a body’s length behind the other. His people asked him if he had done his best, but he said, "No; I have not." So they made their bets, and the second race—the real race—began. When they reached the middle, the Seneca runner said to the other, "Do your best now, for I am going to do mine," and as he said it, he pulled ahead and left the other far behind and won the race. Then the <term>Seoqqwageono</term> said, "There is one more race yet—the long race," and they prepared for it, but the Cherokee chief said to his own men, "We have won everything from these people. I think it will be best to let them have one race, for if they lose all, they may make trouble." They selected a Cherokee to run, and he was beaten, and the <term>Seoqqwageono</term> went home.

In a few days, they sent a messenger to challenge the Cherokee to meet them halfway for a battle. When the Cherokee heard this, they said to the Seneca, "There are so few of you here that we do not want to have you killed. It is better for you to go home." So the Seneca went back to their own country.

Three years later, they came again to visit the Cherokee, who told them that the <term>Seoqqwageono</term> had won the battle, and that the chief of the enemy had said afterward, “I should like to fight the Seneca, for I am a double man.” <note>A "double man" likely refers to a person of supernatural strength or one who is spiritually protected.</note> Before long, the enemy heard that the Seneca were there and sent a challenge to come and fight. The Seneca said, “We must try to satisfy them,” so with Cherokee guides they set out for the country of the <term>Seoqqwageono</term>. They went on until they came to an opening in the woods within one day’s journey of the first village. Then they stopped and prepared to send two messengers to notify the enemy, but the Cherokee said, “You must send them so that they arrive about sundown.” They did this, and when the messengers arrived near the town, they saw all the people out playing ball.

The two Seneca went around to the other side and began throwing sumac darts as they approached, so that the others would think they were some of their own men at play. In this way, they got near enough to kill a man who was standing alone. They scalped him, and then raising the scalp yell, they rushed off through the woods, saying to each other as they ran, “Be strong—Be strong.” Soon they saw the <term>Seoqqwageono</term> coming on horses, but managed to reach a dry creek and hide under the bank, so that the enemy passed by without seeing them.

The next morning they came out and started off, but the enemy was still watching, and before long the two men saw the dust of the horses behind them. The others approached until they were almost upon them and began to shoot arrows at them, but by this time the two Seneca were near the opening where their own friends were hiding, drawn up on each side of the pass. As the pursuers dashed in, the two lines of the Seneca closed in and every man of the <term>Seoqqwageono</term> was either killed or captured.

The Seneca went back to the Cherokee country and after about a month they returned to their own homes. Afterward, the Cherokee told them, “We hear the <term>Seoqqwageono</term> think you are dangerous people. They themselves are conjurers and can tell what other people are going to do, but they cannot tell what the Seneca are going to do. The Seneca medicine is stronger.”—Arranged from Curtin, Seneca manuscript.

### 99. THE SHAWANO WARS

Among the most persistent foes of the Cherokee were the <term>Shawano</term>, known to the Cherokee as <term>Ani′-Sawănu′gĭ</term>, who in ancient times, probably as early as 1680, moved from the Savannah (that is, Shawano) River in South Carolina and occupied the Cumberland River region in middle Tennessee and Kentucky. They were later driven from there by the superior force of the southern tribes and compelled to take refuge north of the Ohio River. On all old maps we find the Cumberland

marked as the "river of the <term>Shawano</term>." Although the two tribes were frequently, and perhaps for long periods, on friendly terms, the ordinary condition was one of chronic warfare, from an early traditional period until the close of the American Revolution. This hostile feeling was intensified by the fact that the <term>Shawano</term> were usually the steady allies of the <term>Creeks</term>, the hereditary southern enemies of the <term>Cherokee</term>. In 1749, however, we find a party of <term>Shawano</term> from the north, accompanied by several <term>Cherokee</term>, making an inroad into the <term>Creek</term> country, and afterward taking refuge among the <term>Cherokee</term>, thus involving the latter in a new war with their southern neighbors <note>Adair, American Indians, 276, 1775</note>. The <term>Shawano</term> made themselves respected for their fighting qualities, gaining a reputation for valor which they maintained in their later wars with the whites; due to their sudden attacks and clever strategies, they came to be regarded as a tribe of magicians. Through capture or intermarriage in the old days, there is a significant amount of <term>Shawano</term> blood among the <term>Cherokee</term>.

According to Haywood, an aged <term>Cherokee</term> chief named the Little Cornplanter (Little Carpenter?) stated in 1772 that the <term>Shawano</term> had moved from the Savannah River a long time before as a result of a disastrous war with several neighboring tribes, and had settled upon the Cumberland River by permission of his people. After a quarrel subsequently arose between the two tribes, a strong body of <term>Cherokee</term> invaded the territory of the <term>Shawano</term> and, attacking them treacherously, killed a great number. The <term>Shawano</term> fortified themselves and a long war followed, which continued until the <term>Chickasaw</term> came to the aid of the <term>Cherokee</term>, at which point the <term>Shawano</term> were gradually forced to withdraw north of the Ohio River.

At the time of their final expulsion, about the year 1710, a boy named Charleville was employed at a French post established for the <term>Shawano</term> trade. This post occupied a mound on the south side of the Cumberland River, where the city of Nashville now stands. For a long time, the <term>Shawano</term> had been so hard-pressed by their enemies that they had been withdrawing to the north in small parties for several years, until only a few remained behind, and these also now determined to leave the country entirely. In March, the trader sent Charleville ahead with several loads of skins, intending to follow with the <term>Shawano</term> himself a few months later. In the meantime, the <term>Chickasaw</term>, learning of the intended move, positioned themselves on both sides of the Cumberland River, above the mouth of the Harpeth, using canoes to cut off any escape by water. They suddenly attacked the retreating <term>Shawano</term>, killing a large number of them, along with the trader, and taking all their skins, trading goods, and other property. Charleville lived to tell the story nearly seventy years later. As the war was never ended by any formal peace treaty, the hostile warriors continued to attack each other whenever they happened to meet on the rich hunting grounds of Kentucky, until finally, from mutual

Due to fear, the region was abandoned by both parties and remained unoccupied until it was settled by white people. <note>Haywood, Natural and Aboriginal History of Tennessee, pages 222-224, 1823.</note>

According to <term>Cherokee</term> tradition, a group of <term>Creeks</term> was already established near the mouth of the <term>Hiwassee</term> while the <term>Cherokee</term> still had their main settlements on the <term>Little Tennessee</term>. The <term>Creeks</term>, being near neighbors, pretended friendship while secretly aiding the <term>Shawano</term>. Having discovered this treachery, the <term>Cherokee</term> took advantage of the <term>Creeks'</term> presence at a great dance at <term>Itsâ'tĭ</term>, or <term>Echota</term>, the ancient <term>Cherokee</term> capital, to launch a sudden attack and kill nearly the entire party. The result was a war, which ended with the <term>Creeks</term> being defeated and forced to abandon all their settlements along the waters of the <term>Tennessee River</term>. <note>Ibid, page 241.</note>

<term>Haywood</term> says that "<term>Little Cornplanter</term>" had seen <term>Shawano</term> scalps brought into the <term>Cherokee</term> towns. When he was a boy, his father, who was also a chief, told him how he had once led a party against the <term>Shawano</term>. While returning with several scalps through a mountain pass, they ran into another party of <term>Cherokee</term> warriors. Mistaking them for enemies, the second party fired on them and killed several before they discovered their mistake. <note>Ibid, page 222.</note>

<term>Schoolcraft</term> also provides the <term>Cherokee</term> tradition of the war with the <term>Shawano</term>, obtained indirectly from white informants, but he incorrectly states it occurred while the latter tribe still lived on the <term>Savannah</term>. "The <term>Cherokees</term> prevailed after a long and bloody contest and drove the <term>Shawnees</term> north. They cherish this event as one of their proudest achievements. 'What!' said an aged <term>Cherokee</term> chief to Mr. <term>Barnwell</term>, who had suggested the eventual preservation of the race through intermarriage with the whites. 'What! Shall the <term>Cherokees</term> perish! Shall the conquerors of the <term>Shawnees</term> perish! Never!'" <note>Schoolcraft, Notes on the Iroquois, page 160, 1847.</note>

Tribal warfare generally consisted of a sporadic succession of small raids, which rarely reached the level of a significant skirmish and were hardly worthy of serious consideration except for their final outcomes. The traditions naturally share this trivial character, being more like anecdotes than historical narratives with specific dates and names. The passage of time also makes them increasingly vague.

On the Carolina side, the <term>Shawano</term> usually approached through the <term>Pigeon River</term> valley to surprise the <term>Cherokee</term> settlements from behind. Small parties were almost constantly lurking about, waiting for a favorable opportunity to take a stray scalp. On one occasion, some <term>Cherokee</term> hunters were lying around a campfire at night when they heard the cry of a flying squirrel in the woods—*tsu-u! tsu-u! tsu-u!* Always alert to danger, they suspected it might be an enemy signal, and all but one hastily left the fire and hid themselves. That one hunter, however, laughed at their fears. Defiantly throwing some heavy logs onto the fire, he stretched himself out on his blanket

and began to sing. Soon he heard a stealthy step coming through the bushes, gradually approaching the fire, until suddenly an enemy sprang out at him from the darkness and knocked him to the ground. But the <term>Cherokee</term> was watchful; putting up his hands, he seized the other by the arms and, with a mighty effort, threw him backward into the fire. The dazed <term>Shawano</term> lay there for a moment squirming on the coals, then jumped to his feet and ran into the woods, howling with pain. There was an answering laugh from his comrades hidden in the bushes, but although the <term>Cherokee</term> kept watch for some time, the enemy made no further attack, probably led by the hunter's very boldness to suspect an ambush.

On another occasion, a small hunting party in the <term>Smoky Mountains</term> heard the gobble of a turkey (in telling the story, <term>Swimmer</term> gives a good imitation). Some eager young hunters wanted to go at once toward the game, but others, who were more cautious, suspected a trick and advised a scouting mission. Accordingly, a hunter went around to the back of the ridge; upon coming up from the other side, he found a man stationed in a large tree, making the gobble call to lure the hunters within reach of a <term>Shawano</term> war party hidden behind some bushes halfway between the tree and the camp. Keeping close to the ground, the <term>Cherokee</term> crept up without being discovered until he was within gunshot; then, springing to his feet, he shot the man in the tree and, shouting "Kill them all," rushed at the enemy. Thinking that a strong force of <term>Cherokee</term> was upon them, the <term>Shawano</term> fled down the mountain without attempting to stand their ground.

Another tradition of these wars concerns <term>Tunâ'ĭ</term>, a great warrior and medicine man of old <term>Itsâ'tĭ</term>, on the <term>Tennessee River</term>. In one hard fight with the <term>Shawano</term> near the town, he overpowered his opponent and stabbed him through both arms. Running cords through the holes, he tied his prisoner's arms and brought him in this condition into <term>Itsâ'tĭ</term>. There, the prisoner was put to death by the women with such tortures that his courage failed him, and he begged them to kill him at once.

After retreating to the upper <term>Ohio River</term>, the <term>Shawano</term> were taken under the protection of the <term>Delawares</term> and their allies. Being strengthened in this way, they felt encouraged to renew the war against the <term>Cherokee</term> with increased vigor. The <term>Cherokee</term>, however, proved to be more than a match for their enemies, pursuing them even to their towns in western <term>Pennsylvania</term> and accidentally killing some <term>Delawares</term> who occupied the country jointly with the <term>Shawano</term>. This involved the <term>Cherokee</term> in a war with the powerful <term>Delawares</term>, which continued until it was brought to an end in 1768 at the request of the <term>Cherokee</term>, who established terms of friendship at the same time with the <term>Iroquois</term>. Since the <term>Shawano</term> were thus left alone and, moreover, were roundly condemned by their friends, the <term>Delawares</term>, as the cause of the entire trouble, they had no heart to continue the war and were forced to make a final peace. <note>Heckewelder, Indian Nations, p. 88, reprint of 1876.</note>

### 100. THE RAID ON TĬKWĂLI'TSĬ

The last famous leader of the <term>Shawano</term> raiding parties was a chief known to the <term>Cherokee</term> as <term>Tawa'lĭ-ukwanûn'tĭ</term>, "Punk-plugged-in," named so because of a red spot on his cheek which looked as though a piece of punk (<term>tawa'lĭ</term> <note>dry wood or tinder used to start fires</note>) had been driven into the flesh.

The people of <term>Tĭkwăli'tsĭ</term> town, on the <term>Tuckasegee</term> River, heard rumors that a war party under this leader had come in from the north and was lurking somewhere in the neighborhood. The <term>Cherokee</term> conjurer, whose name was <term>Ĕtăwa'hă-tsistatla'skĭ</term>, "Dead-wood-lighter," used his magic arts and discovered that the <term>Shawano</term> were in ambush along the trail on the north side of the river, a short distance above the town. On his advice, a party was prepared to go up the south side and come upon the enemy from behind. A few reckless fellows, however, ignored his words and boldly went up the trail on the north side until they reached <term>Deep Creek</term>. There, the <term>Shawano</term>—who were hiding at the ford—caught them "like fish in a trap" and killed nearly all of them.

Their friends on the other side of the river heard the firing. Crossing the river above <term>Deep Creek</term>, they came in behind the <term>Shawano</term> and attacked them, killing several and forcing the others to retreat toward the <term>Smoky Mountains</term> with the <term>Cherokee</term> in pursuit. The invaders had two <term>Cherokee</term> prisoners with them who were not able to keep up with the rapid flight, so their captors took them, bound as they were, and threw them over a cliff. An old conjurer from their own party, finding himself unable to keep up, deliberately sat down against a tree near the same spot to wait for death. The pursuers arrived, split his head with a hatchet, and threw his body over the same cliff, which takes its name from this event. The <term>Shawano</term> continued to retreat with the <term>Cherokee</term> close behind them until they crossed the main ridge at the gap just below <term>Clingman's Dome</term>. Here, the <term>Cherokee</term> ended the pursuit and returned to their homes.

### 101. THE LAST SHAWANO INVASION

Perhaps a year after the raid upon <term>Tĭkwăli'tsĭ</term>, the <term>Shawano</term>—again under the same leader—came down upon the exposed settlement of <term>Kanuga</term>, on the <term>Pigeon River</term>, and carried off a woman and two children whom they found gathering berries near the town. Without waiting to launch an attack, they hastily retreated with their prisoners. The people of <term>Kanuga</term> sent for aid to the other settlements further south, and a strong party was quickly raised to pursue the enemy and recover the captives. By this time, however, the <term>Shawano</term> had a head start of several days, and it was necessary for the <term>Cherokee</term> to take a shorter route across the mountains to overtake them. A noted conjurer named <term>Kâ'lanû</term>, "The Raven," of <term>Hiwassee</term> town, was called upon to discover through his magic arts what direction the <term>Shawano</term> had taken and

They sat down in a circle around the fire and lit the pipe while he went out into the woods. Soon they heard the cry of an owl, and after a short time they heard it again; the next moment, the conjurer walked out from the trees before the first smoke was even finished.

He reported that he had trailed the <term>Shawano</term> to their camp and that they were seven days ahead. The <term>Cherokee</term> immediately followed as <term>The Raven</term> guided them, and they reached the place in seven days. They found all the marks of a camp, but the enemy was already gone. Again and again the conjurer went ahead in his own mysterious fashion to scout the country, and they followed as he pointed the way. On returning the third time, he reported that their enemies had halted beside the great river (the <term>Ohio</term>), and soon afterward he returned with the news that they were crossing it. The <term>Cherokee</term> hurried to the river, but by this time the <term>Shawano</term> were on the other side. The pursuers searched up and down until they found a favorable spot in the stream; then, waiting until it was dark, they prepared to cross, using logs as rafts and navigating with the current. They managed it so well that they were across long before daylight without alerting the enemy.

The trail was now fresh, and following it, they soon came upon the camp. The <term>Shawano</term> were asleep and entirely unguarded, for they thought themselves safe in their own country and had neglected to post sentinels. Rushing in with their knives and tomahawks, the <term>Cherokee</term> fell upon their sleeping enemies and killed many of them before the others could wake and seize their arms to defend themselves. There was a short, desperate encounter, but the <term>Shawano</term> were at a disadvantage; their leader himself was among the first killed, and in a few moments they broke and ran, every man for himself, to escape as best he could. The <term>Cherokee</term> released the captives, whom they found tied to trees, and after taking the scalps from the dead <term>Shawano</term>, along with their guns and other equipment, they returned to their own country.

### 102. THE FALSE WARRIORS OF CHILHOWEE

Some warriors of <term>Chilhowee</term> town, on the <term>Little Tennessee</term>, organized a war party, supposedly to go against the <term>Shawano</term>. They started off north along the great war trail, but when they reached the <term>Pigeon River</term> they changed their course. Instead of continuing toward the <term>Shawano</term> country, they went up the river and approached the back of <term>Cowee</term>, one of the Middle settlements of their own tribe. Here they concealed themselves near the path until a party of three or four unsuspecting townspeople passed by. They then rushed out and killed them, taking their scalps and a gun belonging to a man named <term>Gûñskǎli'skǐ</term>, and then
