They hurriedly made their way home by the same roundabout route to Chilhowee, where they showed the fresh scalps and the gun. They told the people how they had met the Shawano in the north and defeated them without losing a single man.

According to custom, preparations were made at once for a great scalp dance to celebrate the victory over the Shawano. The dance was held in the townhouse, and all the people of the settlement were there to look on. The women danced with the scalps and the gun, while the returned warriors boasted of their deeds. As it happened, among those watching was a visitor from Cowee, a gunstocker, who took particular notice of the gun and recognized it at once as one he had repaired at home for Gûñskăli'skĭ. He said nothing, but wondered greatly how it had come into the possession of the Shawano.

The scalp dance ended, and according to custom, a second dance was appointed to be held seven days later to give the other warriors a chance to boast of their own war deeds. The gunstocker, whose name was Gûlsadihĭ', returned home to Cowee; there, he heard for the first time how a Shawano war party had surprised some of the townspeople, killed several, and taken their scalps and a gun. He understood it all then and told the chief that the mischief had been done, not by a hostile tribe, but by the deceitful men of Chilhowee. It seemed too much to believe, and the chief said it could not be possible, until the gunstocker declared that he had recognized the gun as the one he had himself repaired for the man who had been killed. At last, they were convinced that his story was true, and all of Cowee was eager for revenge.

It was decided to send ten of their bravest warriors, under the leadership of the gunstocker, to the next dance at Chilhowee to take their own method of reprisal. Volunteers offered their service at once. They set out at the proper time and arrived at Chilhowee on the night the dance was to begin. As they crossed the stream below the town, they met a woman coming for water and took their first revenge by killing her. Men, women, and children were gathered in the townhouse, but the Cowee men concealed themselves outside and waited.

In this dance, it was customary for each warrior in turn to tell the story of some deed against the enemy, putting his words into a song which he first whispered to the drummer, who then sang with him while drumming the whole time. Usually, it is a serious business, but occasionally, for a joke, a man will act the clown or sing of some extravagant performance that is so clearly impossible that all the people laugh. One man after another stepped into the ring and sang of what he had done against the enemies of his tribe. At last, one of the recent war party rose from his seat, and after a whisper to the drummer, began to sing of how they had gone to Cowee and taken scalps and the gun, which he carried as he danced. The chief and the people, who knew nothing of the treacherous act, laughed heartily at what they thought was a great joke.

<summary>A gunstocker from Cowee discovers that warriors from Chilhowee committed a treacherous attack on their own people and lied about it. In response, Cowee warriors infiltrate a Chilhowee victory dance to seek revenge while the perpetrators unknowingly mock their victims in song.</summary>

Now the gunstocker, who had been waiting outside with the Cowee men, stripped off his breechcloth and rushed naked into the townhouse. Bending down to the drummer—who was one of the traitors, but failed to recognize Gûlsadihĭ'—he gave him the words. Then, straightening up, he began to sing, “*Hi!* Ask who has done this!” while he danced around the circle, making insulting gestures toward everyone there. The song was quick and the drummer beat very fast.

He made one round and bent down again to the drummer, then straightened up and sang, “*Yu!* I have killed a pregnant woman at the ford and thrown her body into the river!” Several men started with surprise, but the chief said, “He is only joking; continue the dance,” and the drummer beat rapidly.

Another round and he bent down again to the drummer and then began to sing, “We thought our enemies were from the north, but we have followed them and they are here!” Now the drummer knew at last what it all meant and he drummed very slowly, and the people grew uneasy. Then, without waiting for the drummer, Gûlsadihĭ' sang, “Cowee will have a ball play with you!”—and everyone knew this was a challenge to battle—and then fiercely: “But if you want to fight now my men are ready to die here!”

With that he waved his hand and left the townhouse. The dancers looked at each other uneasily and some of them rose to go. The chief, who could not understand it, urged them to continue with the dance, but it was to no avail. They left the townhouse, and as they went out they met the Cowee men standing with their guns ready and their hatchets in their belts. Neither party said anything, because they were still on friendly ground, but everyone knew that trouble was ahead.

The Cowee men returned home and organized a strong party of warriors from their own and all the neighboring Middle settlements to go and take vengeance on Chilhowee and on Kuwâ'hĭ, just below, which had also been involved in the raid. They went down the Tennessee and crossed over the mountains, but when they came to the other side they found that their enemies had abandoned their homes and fled for refuge to the remoter settlements or to the hostile Shawano in the north.

---

### 103. COWEE TOWN

Cowee, properly Kawi'yĭ, abbreviated Kawi'yĭ, was the name of two Cherokee settlements. One existed in 1755 on a branch of the Keowee River in upper South Carolina, while the other and more important one was on the Little Tennessee River at the mouth of Cowee Creek, about 10 miles below the present Franklin, in North Carolina. It was destroyed by the Americans in 1<gloss>7</gloss>76, when it contained about a hundred houses, but was rebuilt and continued to be occupied until the cession of 1819. The name cannot be translated, but may possibly mean “the place of the Deer clan” (Ani'-Kawi'yĭ). It was one

...of the oldest and largest of the Cherokee towns, and when Wafford visited it as a boy, he found the trail leading to it worn so deep in places that, although he was on horseback, he could touch the ground with his feet on each side.

There is a story, told by Wafford as a fact, about a Shawano who had been a prisoner there but had escaped to his people in the north. After the peace between the two tribes, he wandered back into the neighborhood on a hunting trip. While standing on a hill overlooking the valley, he saw several Cherokees on an opposite hill and called out to them, “Do you still own Cowee?” They shouted in reply, “Yes; we still own it.” The answer came back from the Shawano, who wanted to encourage them not to sell any more of their lands, “Well, it’s the best town of the Cherokee. It’s a good country; hold on to it.”

### 104. THE EASTERN TRIBES

Besides the Iroquois and Shawano, the Cherokee also remember the Delawares, Tuscarora, Catawba, and Cheraw as tribes to the east or north with which they formerly had relations.

The Cherokee call the Delawares *Anakwan′kǐ* (in the singular *Akwan′kǐ*), a derivative formed according to the usual Cherokee phonetic modification of *Wapanaq′kǐ*, “Easterners,” which is the generic name by which the Delawares and their nearest kindred call themselves.

In the most ancient tradition of the Delawares, the Cherokee are called *Talega*, *Tallige*, *Tallige-wi*, etc.<note>1. Brinton, *Lenape and Their Legends*, p. 130 and throughout, 1885; Schoolcraft, *Notes on Iroquois*, pp. 147, 305 and throughout, 1847; Heckewelder, *Indian Nations*, pp. 47–50, 1876 edition.</note> In later Delaware tradition they are called *Kǐtu′hwa*, and again we find the two tribes at war, for which their neighbors are held responsible. According to the Delaware account, the Iroquois, during one of their raids to the south, killed a Cherokee in the woods and intentionally left a Delaware war club near the body to make it appear that the work had been done by men of that tribe. The Cherokee found the body and the club, and naturally assuming that the murder had been committed by the Delawares, they suddenly attacked the latter. The result was a long and bloody war between the two tribes.<note>2. Heckewelder, work cited, p. 54.</note> At this time (that is, about the end of the seventeenth century), it appears that at least a part of the Cherokee lived near the waters of the Upper Ohio, where the Delawares made continual raids upon them, finally driving them from the region and seizing it for themselves around the year 1708.<note>3. Loskiel, *History of the [Moravian] Mission*, pp. 124–127; London, 1794.</note> A century ago, the Delawares used to tell how their warriors would sometimes mingle in disguise with the Cherokee at their night dances until the opportunity came to strike a sudden blow and escape before their enemies recovered from the surprise.

Later there seems to have been peace until war was again brought on

<page-num>379</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] THE DELAWARES AND THE TUSCARORA</header>

...due to the actions of the Shawano, who had taken refuge with the Delawares after being driven from their old home on the Cumberland River by the Cherokee. Feeling secure in their new alliance, the Shawano renewed their raids against the Cherokee. The Cherokee retaliated by pursuing them into Delaware territory, where they mistakenly killed several Delawares. This angered the Delawares, who were already agitated by the sight of Cherokee scalps and prisoners being brought through their country by the Iroquois, and another war resulted. This conflict lasted until the Cherokee, tired of fighting so many enemies, voluntarily made peace proposals in 1768, addressing the Delawares as "Grandfather," an honorary title given to them by all the Algonquian tribes. The Delawares then reprimanded the Shawano as the cause of the trouble and advised them to keep quiet; since they were now left to fight their battles alone, the Shawano were glad enough to do so. At the same time, the Cherokee made peace with the Iroquois, and the long war with the northern tribes came to an end. The friendly feeling established in this way was emphasized in 1779, when the Cherokee sent a message of condolence following the death of the Delaware chief, White-eyes. <note>Heckewelder, *Indian Nations*, pages 88-89, 1876.</note>

The Tuscarora, formerly the ruling tribe of eastern North Carolina, are still remembered under the name <term>Ani'-Skălâ'lĭ</term>, and are mentioned in the Feather dance of the Cherokee, in which some of the performers are supposed to be visiting strangers from other tribes.

Since the majority of the Tuscarora fled from North Carolina to the Iroquois country around 1713 as a result of their disastrous war with the whites, they have nearly faded from the memory of the southern Indians. From the limited information that history provides regarding their mutual relations, the two tribes seem to have been almost constantly at war with each other. When the Cherokee, having already made peace with some of their other neighbors, were once urged by the whites to also make peace with the Tuscarora, they refused. They argued that, since they could not live without war, it was better to let matters stand as they were than to make peace with the Tuscarora and be forced to immediately look for new enemies to fight. For some years before the outbreak of the Tuscarora war in 1711, the Cherokee had stopped their raids against this tribe, and it was therefore assumed that they were more busily engaged with some other people west of the mountains—these were probably the Shawano, whom they drove out of Tennessee about this time. <note>See Haywood, *Natural and Aboriginal History of Tennessee*, pages 220, 224, 237, 1823.</note> In the war of 1711–1713, the Cherokee assisted the whites against the Tuscarora. In 1731, the Cherokee again threatened to make war upon the remnant of that tribe still living in North Carolina, and the colonial government was compelled to intervene. <note>*North Carolina Colonial Records*, volume 3, pages 153, 202, 345, 369, 393, 1886.</note>

<page-num>380</page-num>
<header>MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19</header>

The Cheraw or Sara, ranging at various times from upper South Carolina to the southern frontier of Virginia, are also remembered under the name of Ani'-Suwa'lǐ, or Ani'-Suwa'la. This name agrees with the Spanish form *Xuala* from De Soto's chronicle, and *Suala*, or *Sualy*, mentioned by Lederer. The Cherokee remember them as having lived east of the Blue Ridge; the trail to their country led across the gap at the head of the Swannanoa River, east of Asheville. The name of the stream and gap is a corruption of the Cherokee Suwa'lǐ-Nûñnâ'hǐ, meaning "Suwa'lǐ trail." Being a very warlike tribe, they were finally so diminished by conflicts with colonial governments and the Iroquois that they were forced to merge with the Catawba, among whom they still maintained their distinct language as late as 1743.¹

The Catawba are known to the Cherokee as Ani'ta'gwa (singular Ata'gwa, or Ta'gwa), which is the Cherokee attempt at the name by which they are most commonly known. They were the immediate neighbors of the Cherokee to the east and southeast, with their primary settlements located on the river of the same name, just within the borders of South Carolina. They held the leading position among all the tribes east of the Cherokee country, with the exception of the Tuscarora. At the time of the first settlement of South Carolina, the tribe was estimated to have about 7,000 people, but their decline was rapid. Due to war and disease, their number had been reduced by 1775 to barely 500, including the absorbed remnants of the Cheraw and several smaller tribes. There are now, perhaps, 100 still remaining on a small reservation near the site of their ancient towns. Some local names in the old Cherokee territory seem to indicate the former presence of the Catawba, although there is no tradition of any Catawba settlement within those limits. Among such names, Toccoa Creek in northeastern Georgia and Toccoa River in north-central Georgia may be mentioned; both names are derived from the Cherokee Tagwâ'hǐ, "Catawba place." An old Cherokee personal name is Ta'gwădihǐ', meaning "Catawba-killer."

The two tribes were hereditary enemies, and the feeling between them is nearly as bitter today as it was a hundred years ago. Perhaps the only recorded instance of them acting together was during the war of 1711–13, when they cooperated with the colonists against the Tuscarora. The Cherokee, according to the late Colonel Thomas, claim to have formerly occupied all the territory around the head of the Catawba River, down to below present-day Morganton, until game became scarce. At that time, they retired to the west of the Blue Ridge and afterward "loaned" the eastern territory to the Catawba. This aligns fairly well with a Catawba tradition recorded in Schoolcraft, according to which the Catawba—who are incorrectly described as relatively recent immigrants from the north—upon arriving at the Catawba River found

<header>MOONEY] THE CATAWBA</header>

Their progress was disputed by the Cherokee, who claimed original ownership of the country. A battle was fought with incredible loss on both sides, but with no decisive result, although the advantage was with the Catawba because they had guns, while their opponents had only Indian weapons. Preparations were under way to renew the fight when the Cherokee offered to recognize the river as the boundary, allowing the Catawba to settle anywhere to the east. The proposal was accepted and an agreement was finally made by which the Catawba were to occupy the country east of that river and the Cherokee the country west of Broad River, with the region between the two streams to remain as neutral territory. Stone piles were heaped up on the battlefield to commemorate the treaty, and the Broad River was from then on called *Eswau Huppeday* (Line River) by the Catawba, while the country eastward to the Catawba River was left unoccupied. <note>Catawba manuscript from South Carolina official archives. Schoolcraft, Indian Tribes, III, pp. 293-4, 1853.</note> The fact that one party had guns would bring this event within the early historic period.

The Catawba helped the whites against the Cherokee in the war of 1760 and in the later Revolutionary struggle. About 100 warriors, nearly the whole fighting strength of the tribe, took part in the first war mentioned, with several being killed; a smaller number accompanied Williamson's force in 1776. <note>Ibid., p. 294, 1853.</note> At the battle fought under Williamson near the present site of Franklin, North Carolina, the Cherokee—according to the tradition related by Wafford—mistook the Catawba allies of the troops for some of their own warriors. They were fighting for some time under this impression before they noticed that the Catawba wore deer tails in their hair so that the whites would not make the same mistake. In this engagement, which was one of the bloodiest Indian encounters of the Revolution, the Cherokee claim that they had actually defeated the troops and their Catawba allies, until their own ammunition ran out and they were consequently forced to retreat. The Cherokee leader was a noted war chief named Tsanĭ (John).

About 1840, nearly the whole Catawba tribe moved up from South Carolina and joined the eastern band of Cherokee, but because of tribal jealousies they remained only a short time and afterward returned to their former home, as is discussed elsewhere.

Other tribal names (of uncertain authority) are *Ani'-Sa'nı* and *Ani'-Sawahâ'nĭ*, belonging to people said to have lived toward the north; both names are perhaps intended for the Shawano or Shawnee, properly *Ani'-Sawanu'gĭ*. The *Ani'-Gilĭ'* are said to have been neighbors of the Anin'tsĭ or Natchez; the name may possibly be a Cherokee form for Congaree.

### 105. THE SOUTHERN AND WESTERN TRIBES

The nearest neighbors of the Cherokee to the south were the Creeks or Muscogee, who formed a mixed confederacy holding central and southern Georgia and Alabama. They were known to the Cherokee as *Ani'-Ku'sa* or *Ani'-Gu'sa*, from Kusa, the principal town of the Upper Creeks, which was situated on the Coosa River, southwest from the present Talladega, Alabama. The Lower Creeks, residing chiefly on the Chattahoochee River, were formerly always distinguished as *Ani-Kawi'ta*, from Kawita or Coweta, their ancient capital, on the west side of the river in Alabama, nearly opposite the present Columbus, Georgia. In number, the Creeks were nearly equal to the Cherokee, but they differed in being a confederacy of related or incorporated tribes, of which the Muscogee proper was the principal. The Cherokee were called by them *Tsal-gal'gi* or *Tsûlgûl'gi*, a plural derivative from *Tsa'lăgĭ'*, the proper name of the tribe.

The ordinary condition between the two tribes was one of hostility, with occasional intervals of good will. History, tradition, and linguistic evidence combine to show that the Creeks at one time occupied almost the whole of northern Georgia and Alabama, extending a considerable distance into Tennessee and perhaps North Carolina, and were dispossessed by the Cherokee pressing upon them from the north and northeast. This conquest was accomplished chiefly during the first half of the eighteenth century and culminated with the decisive engagement of *Tali'wă* about 1755. In most of their early negotiations with the government, the Creeks demanded that the lands of the various tribes be regarded as common property, and that only the boundary between the Indians and the whites be considered. Failing in that, they claimed as theirs the whole region of the Chattahoochee and Coosa, north to the dividing ridge between those streams and the Tennessee, or even beyond to the Tennessee itself; they asserted that any Cherokee settlements within those limits were only there by their own permission. In 1783, they claimed the Savannah River as the eastern boundary between themselves and the Cherokee, and asserted their own exclusive right of sale over all the territory between that river and the Oconee. On the other hand, the Cherokee as stoutly claimed all land to a point some 70 miles south of the present city of Atlanta, on the grounds of having driven the Creeks out of it in three successive wars, and asserted that their right had been admitted by the Creeks themselves in a council held to decide the question between the two tribes before the Revolution. By mutual agreement, about 1816, members of either tribe were allowed to settle within the territory claimed by the other. The line as finally established through the mediation of the colonial and federal governments ran from the mouth of Broad River on the Savannah nearly due west across Georgia, passing

about 10 miles north of Atlanta, to the Coosa River in Alabama, and from there northwest to hit the west line of Alabama about 20 miles south of the Tennessee River. 1

Among the names which remain to show the former presence of Creeks north of this boundary are the following: Coweeta, a small creek entering the Little Tennessee above Franklin, North Carolina; Tomatola (Cherokee, *Tama'lǐ*), a former town site on the Valley River, near Murphy, North Carolina, the name being that of a former Creek town on the Chattahoochee; Tomotley (Cherokee, *Tama'lǐ*), a ford at another town site on the Little Tennessee, above the mouth of the Tellico, in Tennessee; Coosa (Cherokee, *Kusǎ'*), an upper creek of the Nottely River, in Union County, Georgia; Chattooga (Cherokee, *Tsatu'gǐ*), a river in northwest Georgia; Chattooga (Cherokee, *Tsatu'gǐ*), another river, a head-stream of the Savannah; Chattahoochee River (Creek, *Chatu-huchi*, "pictured rocks"); Coosawatee (Cherokee, *Ku'sǎ-weti'yǐ*, "Old Creek place"), a river in northwestern Georgia; Tali'wǎ, the Cherokee form of a Creek name for a place on an upper branch of the Etowah River in Georgia, probably from the Creek <term>ta'lua</term> or <term>ita'lua</term>, "town"; Euharlee (Cherokee, *Yuha'lǐ*, said by the Cherokee to be from *Yufala* or *Eufaula*, the name of several Creek towns), a creek flowing into the lower Etowah River; Suwanee (Cherokee, *Suwa'nǐ*) a small creek on the upper Chattahoochee, the site of a former Cherokee town with a name which the Cherokee say is Creek. Several other names within the same territory are said by the Cherokee to be of foreign origin, although perhaps not Creek, and may be from the <term>Taskigi</term> language.

According to Cherokee tradition as given to Haywood nearly eighty years ago, the country about the mouth of the Hiwassee River, in Tennessee, was held by the Creeks, while the Cherokee still had their main settlements farther to the north, on the Little Tennessee. In the <term>Shawano war</term>, about the year 1700, the Creeks pretended friendship for the Cherokee while secretly helping their enemies, the <term>Shawano</term>. The Cherokee discovered the treachery and took the opportunity, when a party of Creeks was visiting a dance at <term>Itsâ'ti</term> (Echota), the Cherokee capital, to fall upon them and massacre nearly every man. The consequence was a war between the two tribes, with the final result that the Creeks were forced to abandon all their settlements upon the waters of the Tennessee and to withdraw south to the Coosa and the neighborhood of the "Creek path," an old trading trail from South Carolina. This trail crossed at the junction of the Oostanaula and Etowah rivers, where the city of Rome, Georgia, is now located, and reached the Tennessee at the present Guntersville, Alabama.

The great leader of the Cherokee in this war was a chief named Bullhead, renowned in tradition for his bravery and skill in strategy.<note>¹ Haywood, Natural and Aboriginal History of Tennessee, p. 241, 1823. Bullhead may be intended for Doublehead, an old Cherokee name.</note> At about the same time, according to Wafford, the Cherokee claim to have driven the Creeks and Shawano from a settlement which they occupied jointly near Savannah, Georgia.

There was a tradition among the few old traders still living in upper Georgia in 1890 that a large tract in that part of the State had been won by the Cherokee from the Creeks in a ball game.<note>² Mooney, The Cherokee Ball Game, in The American Anthropologist, III, p. 107, April, 1890.</note> There are no Indians now living in that region to substantiate the story. As originally told, it may have had a veiled meaning, as among the Cherokee the expression “to play a ball game” is frequently used figuratively to denote fighting a battle. There seems to be no good reason for Bartram’s statement that the Cherokee had been driven out by the Creeks from the region between the Savannah and the Ocmulgee, in southwestern Georgia, within the historic period.<note>³ Bartram, Travels, p. 518, 1791.</note> The territory is south of any traditional Cherokee claim, and the statement is at odds with what we know through history. He probably had in mind the Uchee, who did actually occupy that country until they were incorporated with the Creeks.

The victory was not always on one side, however, for Adair states that toward the end of the last war between the two tribes the Creeks, having easily defeated the Cherokee in an engagement, contemptuously sent a number of women and boys against them. According to this writer, the “true and sole cause” of this last war was the killing of some adopted relatives of the Creeks in 1749 by a party of northern Shawano, who had been guided and afterward sheltered by the Cherokee. The war, which he represents as a losing game for the Cherokee, was finally brought to an end through the efforts of the governor of South Carolina, with the unfortunate result to the English that the Creeks encouraged the Cherokee in the war of 1760 and provided them with essential help in the form of men and ammunition.<note>⁴ Adair, History of American Indians, pp. 227, 247, 252–256, 270, 276–279, 1775.</note>

The old trail crossed the river near Long-swamp town. All our information concerning it is traditional, obtained from James Wafford, who heard the story as a boy around the year 1815 from an old trader named Brian Ward, who had witnessed the battle sixty years earlier. According to his account, it was probably the hardest battle ever fought between the two tribes, with about five hundred Cherokee and twice that number of Creek warriors being engaged. The Cherokee were at first overmatched and fell back, but they rallied again and returned to the attack, driving the Creeks from cover so that they broke and ran. The victory was complete and decisive, and the defeated tribe immediately afterward abandoned the entire upper portion of Georgia and the adjacent part of Alabama to the conquerors. Before this battle, the Creeks had been accustomed to shift about a good deal from place to place, but thereafter they confined themselves more closely to fixed home locations. It was in consequence of this defeat that they abandoned their town on the Nottely River, below Coosa Creek, near the present Blairsville, Georgia; their old fields were at once occupied by the Cherokee, who moved over from their settlements at the head of the Savannah River. As has been already stated, a peace was made about 1759, just in time to enable the Creeks to assist the Cherokee in their war with South Carolina. We hear little more concerning the relations of the two tribes until the Creek War of 1813–14, described in detail elsewhere; after this, their histories drift apart.

The Yuchi or Uchee, called *Ani'-Yu'tsĭ* by the Cherokee, were a tribe of distinct linguistic stock and of considerable importance in early days; their territory bordered the Savannah River on both sides immediately below the Cherokee country and extended some distance westward into Georgia, where it adjoined that of the Creeks. They were gradually dispossessed by the whites and were incorporated with the Creeks about the year 1740, but they retain their separate identity and language to this day, their town being now the largest in the Creek Nation in Indian Territory.

According to the testimony of a Cherokee mixed-blood named *Gan-sĕ'tĭ* or Rattling-gourd, who was born on the Hiwassee River in 1820 and came west with his people in 1838, a number of Yuchi lived, before the Removal, scattered among the Cherokee near the present Cleveland, Tennessee, and on Chickamauga, Cohutta, and Pinelog Creeks in the adjacent section of Georgia. They had no separate settlements, but spoke their own language, which he described as “hard and grunting.” Some of them spoke also Cherokee and Creek. They had probably drifted north from the Creek country before a boundary had been fixed between the tribes. When Tahlequah was established as the capital of the Cherokee Nation in the West in 1839, a few Yuchi were found already settled at the spot, being supposed to have removed from the East with some Creeks after the chief McIntosh was killed in

Ramsey states that “a small tribe of Yuchi” once occupied the country near the mouth of the Hiwassee and was nearly wiped out in a desperate battle with the Cherokee at the Yuchi Old Fields, in Rhea (now Meigs) County, Tennessee, with the few survivors retreating to Florida, where they joined the Seminoles.<note>Ramsey, Annals of Tennessee, pp. 81, 84, 1853.</note> There seems to be no other authority for this statement.

Another fragmented tribe incorporated partly with the Creeks and partly with the Cherokee was that of the Na'tsǐ, or Natchez, who originally occupied the territory around the site of the present town of Natchez in southern Mississippi and held a leading influence over all the tribes of the region. Because of a disastrous war with the French in 1729–31, the tribe was broken up; some took refuge with the Chickasaw, others with the Creeks, either then or later, while others, in 1736, applied to the government of South Carolina for permission to settle on the Savannah River. The request was evidently granted, and we find the “Nachee” mentioned as one of the tribes living with the Catawba in 1743, but retaining their distinct language. . . Because they killed some of the Catawba in a drunken fight, they were forced to leave this region and seem to have joined the Cherokee soon afterward, as we find them mentioned twice in connection with that tribe in 1755. This appears to be the last reference to them in the South Carolina records.<note>Mooney, Siouan Tribes of the East (bulletin of the Bureau of Ethnology), p. 83, 1894.</note>

Just here the Cherokee tradition takes them up under the name of Anin'tsǐ, abbreviated from Ani'-Na'tsǐ, the plural of Na'tsǐ. From a chance coincidence with the word for pine tree, *na'tsǐ'*, some English-speaking Indians have translated this name as “Pine Indians.” The Cherokee generally agree that the Natchez came to them from South Carolina, though some say that they came from the Creek country. It is likely that the first refugees were from Carolina and were joined later by others from the Creeks and the Chickasaw. Bienville states, in 1742, that some of them had gone to the Cherokee directly from the Chickasaw when they found the latter were too hard-pressed by the French to be able to care for them.<note>Bienville, quoted in Gayarré, Louisiana.</note> They seem to have been regarded by the Cherokee as a race of wizards and sorcerers, a view which was probably due partly to their peculiar religious rites and partly to the interest that belonged to them as the remnant of a wiped-out tribe. According to the statement of James Wafford, who was born in 1806 near the site of Clarkesville, Georgia, when this region was still Indian country, the “Natchez” had their town on the north bank of the Hiwassee River, just above Peachtree Creek, on the spot where a Baptist mission was established by the Reverend Evan Jones in 1821, a few miles above the present Murphy, Cherokee County, North Carolina. On his mother’s side, Wafford himself had a strain of Natchez blood. His grandmother had told him that when she was a young woman, perhaps about 1755, she once had occasion to go to this town on some business, which she was obliged to transact through an interpreter, as the Natchez had been there so short a time that only one or two spoke any Cherokee. They were all in the one town, which the Cherokee called *Gwal'gâ'hĭ*, “Frog place,” but he was unable to say whether or not it had a town house. In 1824, as one of the census takers for the Cherokee Nation, he went over the same section and found the Natchez then living jointly with the Cherokee in a town called *Gû'lăni'yĭ* at the junction of Brasstown and Gumlog creeks, tributaries to the Hiwassee, some 6 miles southeast of their former location and close to the Georgia line. The removal may have been due to the recent establishment of the mission at the old place. It was a large settlement, made up about equally from the two tribes, but by this time the Natchez were not distinguishable in dress or general appearance from the others, and nearly all spoke broken Cherokee while still retaining their own language. As most of the Indians had come under Christian influences so far as to have quit dancing, there was no town house. Harry Smith, who was born about 1820 and was the father of the late chief of the East Cherokee, also remembers them living on the Hiwassee and calling themselves *Na'tsĭ*.

*Gansĕ''tĭ*, already mentioned, states that when he was a boy the Natchez were scattered among the Cherokee settlements along the upper part of the Hiwassee, extending down into Tennessee. They had then no separate town houses. Some of them, at least, had come up from the Creeks and spoke Creek and Cherokee as well as their own language, which he could not understand, although he was familiar with both of the others. They were great dance leaders, which agrees with their traditional reputation for ceremonial and secret knowledge. They went west with the Cherokee at the final removal of the tribe to Indian Territory in 1838. In 1890 there was a small settlement on the Illinois River a few miles south of Tahlequah, Cherokee Nation, where several persons still spoke their own language. Some of these may have come with the Creeks, as by an agreement between the Creeks and Cherokee about the time of the Removal, it had been arranged that citizens of either tribe living within the boundaries claimed by the other might remain without question if they so elected. Haywood, the historian of Tennessee, states that a remnant of the Natchez lived within the current limits of the state as late as 1750 and were numerous even then. He refers to those with the Cherokee and tells a curious story, which seems somehow to have escaped the notice of other writers. According to his statement, a portion of the Natchez, who had been distributed as slaves among the French near their old homes after the defeat of their tribe, took advantage of the withdrawal of the troops to the north in 1758 to rise up, massacre their masters, and make their escape to the neighboring tribes. Upon the return of the troops after the fall of Fort Du Quesne, they found the settlement at Natchez destroyed and their Indian slaves gone. Sometime afterward, a French deserter seeking asylum among the Cherokee, having made his way to the Great Island town on the Tennessee River, just below the mouth of the Tellico River, was surprised to find there some of the same Natchez whom he had formerly driven as slaves. He lost no time in getting away from the place to find safer quarters among the mountain towns. Notchy Creek, a lower tributary of the Tellico in Monroe County, Tennessee, probably takes its name from these refugees. Haywood also states that, although integrated with the Cherokee, they continued for a long time as a separate people, not marrying or mixing with other tribes, having their own chiefs, and holding their own councils; but by 1823, hardly anything was left of them but the name.<note>Haywood, Natural and Aboriginal History of Tennessee, pp. 105-107, 1823. Another refugee tribe integrated partly with the Cherokee and partly with the Creeks was that of the <term>Taskigi</term>, who at an early period had a large town of the same name on the south side of the Little Tennessee, just above the mouth of the Tellico, in Monroe County, Tennessee. Sequoya, the inventor of the Cherokee alphabet, lived here in his boyhood, around the time of the Revolution. The land was sold in 1819. There was another settlement of the same name, and perhaps once occupied by the same people, on the north bank of the Tennessee River in a bend just below Chattanooga, Tennessee, on land also sold in 1819. Still another may have existed at one time on Tuskegee Creek, on the south bank of the Little Tennessee River, north of Robbinsville, in Graham County, North Carolina, on land which was occupied until the Removal in 1838. Who or what the Taskigi were is uncertain and can probably never be known, but they were neither Cherokee nor Muscogee proper. It seems most likely that they were of Muskhogean affinity, but they may have been an immigrant tribe from another section, or may even have constituted a distinct linguistic stock, representing all that was left of an ancient people whose occupation of the country predated the arrival of the Cherokee and the Creeks. The name may be derived from *taska* or *taska'ya*, meaning "warrior" in several of the Muskhogean dialects. It is not a Cherokee word, and Cherokee informants state positively that the Taskigi were a foreign people, with distinct language and customs. They were not Creeks, Natchez, Uchee, or Shawano, with all of whom the Cherokee were well acquainted under other names. In the townhouse of their settlement at the mouth of Tellico they had an upright pole, from the top of which hung their protecting "medicine," the image of a human figure cut from a cedar log. For this reason the Cherokee in derision sometimes called the place *Atsǐnǎ'-k'taûñ*, "Hanging-cedar place." Before the sale of the land in 1819 they were so nearly extinct that the Cherokee had moved in and occupied the ground.

Adair, in 1775, mentions the Tae-keo-ge <note>This is a double misprint</note> as one of several broken tribes which the Creeks had "artfully decoyed" to incorporate with them in order to strengthen themselves against hostile attempts. Milfort, about 1780, states that the Taskigi on the Coosa River were a foreign people who had been driven by wars to seek refuge among the Creeks, being encouraged to do so by the kind reception given to another fugitive tribe. Their request was granted by the confederacy, and they were given lands upon which they built their town. He dates this event shortly before the incorporation of the Yuchi, which would make it early in the eighteenth century. In 1799, according to Hawkins, the town had only 35 warriors, "had lost its ancient language," and spoke Creek. There is still a "white" or peace town named Taskigi in the Creek Nation in Indian Territory. <note>Adair, History of the American Indians, page 257, 1775. The other statements concerning the Taskigi among the Creeks are taken from Gatschet's valuable study, A Migration Legend of the Creek Indians, volume 1, pages 122, 145, 228, 1884.</note>

The nearest neighbors of the Cherokee on the west, after the expulsion of the Shawano, were the Chickasaw, known to the Cherokee as *Ani'-Tsǐ'ksû*, whose territory lay chiefly between the Mississippi and the Tennessee rivers, in what is now western Kentucky and Tennessee and the extreme northern portion of Mississippi. Although peace was afterward made between the two tribes, their rival claims continued to be a subject of dispute throughout the treaty period.

The Choctaw, a loose confederacy of tribes formerly occupying southern Mississippi and the adjacent coast region, are called Ani'-Tsa''ta by the Cherokee, who appear to have had but little communication with them, probably because the intermediate territory was held by the Creeks, who were generally at war with one or the other. In 1708, we find mention of a powerful expedition by the Cherokee, Creeks, and Catawba against the Choctaw living about Mobile Bay. <note>Margry, quoted in Gatschet, *Creek Migration Legend*, I, pp. 16, 87, 1884.</note>

Of the Indians west of the Mississippi, those best known to the Cherokee were the Ani'-Wasa'si, or Osage, a powerful predatory tribe formerly holding most of the country between the Missouri and Arkansas rivers, and extending from the Mississippi far out into the plains. The Cherokee name is a derivative from Wasash', the name by which the Osage call themselves. <note>Wasash, French Ouasage, corrupted by the Americans into Osage.</note> The relations of the two tribes seem to have been almost constantly hostile from the time when the Osage refused to join in the general Indian peace concluded in 1768 (see "The Iroquois Wars") up to 1822, when the Government interfered to compel an end to the bloodshed. The bitterness was largely due to the fact that ever since the first Cherokee treaty with the United States, made at Hopewell, South Carolina, in 1785, small bodies of Cherokee, resenting the constant encroachments of the whites, had been removing beyond the Mississippi to form new settlements within the territory claimed by the Osage, where in 1817 they already numbered between two and three thousand persons. Other old Cherokee names for western tribes that cannot be identified are Tayûn'ksǐ, the untranslatable name of a tribe described simply as living in the West; Tsuniya'tigă, "Naked people," described as living in the far West; Gûn'-tsuskwa'lǐ, "Short-arrows," who lived in the far West and were small but great fighters; and Yûñ'wini'giskǐ, "Man-eaters," a hostile tribe to the west or north, possibly the cannibal Atakapa or Tonkawa of Louisiana or Texas. Their relations with the tribes they have become acquainted with since their removal to Indian Territory do not fall within the scope of this paper.

### 106. THE GIANTS FROM THE WEST

James Wafford, of the western Cherokee, who was born in Georgia in 1806, says that his grandmother (who must have been born about the middle of the 1700s) told him she had heard from the elders that long before her time, a party of giants had once come to visit the Cherokee. They were nearly twice as tall as ordinary men and had eyes set slanted in their heads. The Cherokee called them Tsunil' kălû', "The Slant-eyed people," because they looked like the giant hunter Tsul'kălû' (see the story). They said these giants lived very far away in the direction where the sun sets. The Cherokee received them as friends, and they stayed for some time before returning to their home in the west. This story may be a distorted historical tradition.

### 107. THE LOST CHEROKEE

When the first lands were sold by the Cherokee in 1721, a part of the tribe bitterly opposed the sale. They argued that if the Indians once consented to give up any of their territory, the whites would never be satisfied but would soon want a little more, and then more again, until at last there would be nothing left for the Indians. Finding that all they could say was not enough to prevent the treaty, they determined to leave their old homes forever and go far into the West, beyond the Great River, where the white men could never follow them. They paid no attention to the pleas of their friends but began preparations for the long march. When the others found they could not prevent them from going, they set to work and did their best to supply them with pack horses loaded with bread, dried venison, and other provisions.

When all was ready, they started out under the direction of their chief. A company of selected men was sent with them to help them cross the Great River, and every night until they reached it, runners were sent back to the tribe, and others from the tribe to the marching band, to carry messages and keep each group informed of how the other was progressing. At last, they came to the Mississippi and crossed it by

Still the white men pressed upon the Cherokee, and one piece of land after another was sold. As years went on, the dispossessed people began to turn their faces toward the west as their final resting place, and small bands of hunters crossed the Mississippi to learn what might be beyond. One of these parties pushed on across the plains, and there at the foot of the great mountains—the Rockies—they found a tribe speaking the old Cherokee language and living just as the Cherokee had lived before they had ever known the white man or his ways.

### 108. THE MASSACRE OF THE ANI'-KUTA'NI

Among other fading traditions is the one relating to the <term>Ani'-Kuta'ni</term> or <term>Ani'-Kwǎta'ni</term>. Modern Cherokee know so little about them that their very identity is now a matter of dispute. A few hold that they were an ancient people who preceded the Cherokee and built the mounds. Others, with more authority, claim that they were a clan or society within the tribe and were destroyed long ago by a plague or other calamity. Fortunately, we are not left to depend entirely upon guesswork in the matter, as the tradition was recorded by Haywood about seventy years ago, and by another writer some forty years later, while the connected story could still be obtained from knowledgeable authorities. From the various accounts, it would seem that the Ani'-Kuta'ni were a priestly clan who had hereditary supervision of all religious ceremonies among the Cherokee. However, because they abused their sacred privileges, they were attacked and completely exterminated by the rest of the tribe. This left the priestly functions to be assumed afterward by individual doctors and conjurers.

Haywood says, without giving names or details, "The Cherokee are given to conjuration to determine whether a sick person will recover. This custom arose after the destruction of their priests. Tradition states that such persons lived among their ancestors and were deemed superior to others, but were wiped out long ago because of the misconduct of one of the priests, who attempted to take the wife of a man who was the brother of the leading chief of the nation."¹

A more detailed statement, on the authority of Chief John Ross and Dr. J. B. Evans, was given in 1866 by a writer who speaks of the massacre as having occurred about a century before, although from the

...from the dimness of the tradition, it is evident that it must have been much earlier:

> "The facts, though few, are interesting. The order was hereditary; in this respect it was peculiar, for among Indians it is rare, and among the Cherokees it never happens, that power belongs to any family as a matter of right. Yet the family of the <term>Nicotani</term>—for it seems to have been a family or clan—enjoyed this privilege. The power they exercised was not, however, political, nor does it appear that chiefs were elected from among them.

> "The <term>Nicotani</term> were a mystical, religious body, of whom the people stood in great awe, and they seem to have been somewhat like the Brahmins of India. By what means they attained their dominance, or how long it was maintained, can never be determined. Their extinction by massacre is nearly all that can be discovered about them. They became haughty, insolent, overbearing, and immoral to an intolerable degree. Relying on their hereditary privileges and the strange awe they inspired, they did not hesitate through fraud or violence to tear apart the tender relationships of husband and wife when a beautiful woman excited their passions. The people long brooded in silence over the oppressions and outrages of this high caste, whom they deeply hated but greatly feared. At length, a daring young man from an influential family organized a conspiracy among the people for the massacre of the priesthood. The immediate provocation was the abduction of the wife of the young leader of the conspiracy. His wife was remarkably beautiful and was forcibly abducted and violated by one of the <term>Nicotani</term> while he was away on a hunt. On his return, he found no difficulty in exciting in others the same resentment he felt himself. So many had suffered in the same way, and so many feared they might be made to suffer, that nothing was needed but a leader. Once a leader appeared in the person of the young warrior we have named, the people rose under his direction and killed every <term>Nicotani</term>, young and old. Thus perished a hereditary secret society, and since that time, no hereditary privileges have been tolerated among the Cherokees."¹

### 109. THE WAR MEDICINE

Some warriors had medicine to change their shape as they pleased so that they could escape from their enemies. Once, one of these medicine warriors who had been away from home returned and found a strong party of the enemy attacking the settlement while nearly all the men were away on a hunt. The town was on the other side of the river, but his grandmother was there, so he decided to save her. Going down the stream a little way, he searched until he found a

Then, climbing a tree, he transformed himself into a swamp woodcock, and with one cry, he spread his wings and flew across to the other side of the river. There, both took their natural forms again and made their way through the woods to another settlement.

There was another great Cherokee warrior named Dasĭ'gĭya'gĭ, or Shoe-boots, as the white people called him, who lived on Hightower Creek in Georgia. He was so strong it was said that he could throw a corn mortar over a house, and with his magic power, he could clear a river in one jump. His war medicine was an <term>uktena</term> scale and a very large turtle shell which he obtained from the Shawano. In the Creek War, he put this scale into water and bathed his body with the water; he also burned a piece of the turtle shell and drew a black line around his men with the charcoal, and he was never wounded and never had a man killed.

Some great warriors had medicine by the aid of which they could dive underground as if under water, surface among the enemy to kill and scalp one, then dive underground again and reappear among their friends.

Some war captains knew how to place their lives in the treetops during a fight, so that even if they were struck by the enemy, they could not be killed. Once, in a battle with the Shawano, the Cherokee leader stood directly in front of the enemy and let the whole party shoot at him, but he was not hurt until the Shawano captain, who knew this war medicine himself, ordered his men to shoot into the branches above the Cherokee leader's head. They did this, and the Cherokee leader fell dead.

### 110. INCIDENTS OF PERSONAL HEROISM

In the Cherokee War of 1760, when small groups of the enemy—according to Haywood—were making their raids eastward almost to Salisbury, a party of six or eight warriors was discovered, watched, and followed until they were seen entering a deserted cabin to spend the night. The alarm was given, and shortly before daylight, the white men surrounded the house, positioning themselves behind the fodder stack and some outbuildings so as to control both the door and the wide chimney top. They then began to throw fire onto the roof to drive out the Indians. As the fire caught the dry shingles and death by either fire or bullet seemed certain, one of the besieged warriors called to his companions that it was better for one to be a sacrifice than for all to die. He told them that if they would follow his directions, he would save them, though he would die himself. He proposed to rush out alone to draw the fire of those surrounding the house, while his friends stood

They were ready to head for the woods as soon as the guns of the white men were empty. They agreed, and the door was opened, when he suddenly rushed out, dodging and running in a zigzag path so that every gun was emptied at him before he fell dead, covered with wounds. While the white men were reloading, the other warriors ran out and succeeded in reaching the woods before the besiegers could recover from their surprise. The historian adds, “How greatly it is to be regretted that the name of this hero is not known to the writer, so that it might be recorded with this specimen of Cherokee bravery and patriotism, firmness, and presence of mind in the hour of danger.”<note>Haywood, Natural and Aboriginal History of Tennessee, p. 239.</note>

More than once, women seem to have shown the courage of warriors when the occasion demanded. At the beginning of the last century, there was still living among the Cherokee a woman who had killed her husband’s slayer in one of the Revolutionary engagements. For this deed, she was treated with so much respect that she was permitted to join the warriors in the war dance, carrying her gun and tomahawk. The Wahnenauhi manuscript has a tradition of an attack upon a Cherokee town and the killing of the chief by a hostile war party. His wife, whose name was Cuhtahlatah (Gatûn’lătĭ, “Wild-hemp”?), on seeing her husband fall, snatched up his tomahawk, shouting, “Kill! Kill!” and rushed upon the enemy with such fury that the retreating Cherokee rallied and renewed the battle with such great courage that they gained a complete victory. This may be a different account of the same incident.

In Rutherford’s expedition against the Cherokee in 1776, the Indians made a stand near Waya Gap in the Nantahala Mountains, and a hard-fought engagement took place, with a loss to the Americans of nineteen men, although the enemy was finally driven from the ground. After the main body had retreated, an Indian was seen looking out from behind a tree and was at once shot and killed by the soldiers. Upon going to the spot, they found that it was a woman, painted and stripped like a warrior and armed with a bow and arrows. She had already been shot through the thigh and had therefore been unable to flee with the rest.

### III. THE MOUNDS AND THE CONSTANT FIRE: THE OLD SACRED THINGS

Some say that the mounds were built by another people. Others say they were built by the ancestors of the old Ani’-Kĭtu’hwagĭ for townhouse foundations, so that the townhouses would be safe when floods came. The townhouse was always built on the level bottom lands by the river so that the people might have smooth ground for their dances and ballplays and might be able to go down to the water during the dance.

When they were ready to build the mound, they began by laying a circle of stones on the surface of the ground. Next, they made a fire in the center of the circle and placed near it the body of some prominent chief or priest who had recently died—some say seven chief men from the different clans—together with an Ulûñsû'tǐ stone, an uktena scale or horn, a feather from the right wing of an eagle or a great tlä'nuwä, which lived in those days, and beads of seven colors: red, white, black, blue, purple, yellow, and gray-blue. The priest then conjured all these with disease so that if an enemy ever invaded the country—even if he should burn and destroy the town and the townhouse—he would never live to return home.

The mound was then built up with earth, which the women brought in baskets. As they piled it above the stones, the bodies of their great men, and the sacred items, they left an open place at the fire in the center and lowered a hollow cedar trunk, with the bark still on, which fitted around the fire and protected it from the earth. This cedar log was cut long enough to reach nearly to the surface inside the townhouse when everything was finished. The earth was piled up around it, and the whole mound was smoothed over; then the townhouse was built upon it. One man, called the fire keeper, always stayed in the townhouse to feed and tend the fire. When there was to be a dance or a council, he pushed long stalks of the *ihyâ'ga* weed, which some call *atsil'-sûñ'ti*, "the fire maker" (*Erigeron canadense* or fleabane), down through the opening in the cedar log to the fire at the bottom. He left the ends of the stalks sticking out and piled lichens and punk around them, after which he prayed; as he prayed, the fire climbed up along the stalks until it caught the punk. Then he added wood, and by the time the dancers were ready, there was a large fire blazing in the townhouse. After the dance, he covered the hole again with ashes, but the fire always remained smoldering below. In the old times, just before the Green-corn dance, every fire in the settlement was extinguished and all the people came to get new fire from the townhouse. This was called *atsï'la gälûñkw'tǐ'yu*, "the honored or sacred fire." Sometimes when the fire in a house went out, the woman came to the fire keeper, who made a new fire by rubbing an *ihyâ'ga* stalk against the underside of a hard, dry fungus that grows upon locust trees.

Some say this everlasting fire was only in the larger mounds at Nikwǎsǐ', Kǐtu'hwa, and a few other towns, and that when the new fire was drawn up for the Green-corn dance, it was distributed from them to the other settlements. The fire still burns at the bottom of these great mounds, and when Cherokee soldiers were camped near Kǐtu'hwa during the Civil War, they saw smoke still rising from the mound.

The Cherokee once had a wooden box, nearly square and wrapped in buckskin, in which they kept the most sacred things of their

...practiced the old religion. On every important expedition, two priests carried it in turn and watched over it in camp so that nothing could come near to disturb it. The Delawares captured it more than a hundred years ago, and after that, the old religion was neglected and trouble came to the Nation. They also had a great peace pipe, carved from white stone, with seven stem holes, so that seven men could sit around and smoke from it at once during their peace councils. In the old town of Keowee, they had a stone drum, cut in the shape of a turtle, which was hung up inside the townhouse and used at all the town dances. The other towns of the Lower Cherokee also used to borrow it for their own dances.

All the old things are gone now, and the Indians are different.

### MISCELLANEOUS MYTHS AND LEGENDS

#### 112. THE IGNORANT HOUSEKEEPER

An old man whose wife had died lived alone with his son. One day he said to the young man, "We need a cook here, so you had better get married." So the young man found a wife and brought her home. Then his father said, "Now we must work together and do all we can to help her. You go hunting and bring in the meat, and I will look after the corn and beans; then she can cook." The young man went into the woods to look for a deer, and his father went out into the field to attend to the corn. When they came home at night, they were hungry, and the young woman set out a bowl of walnut hominy (<term>kanâ'talû'hĭ</term>) before them. It looked strange, somehow, and when the old man examined it, he found that the walnuts had been put in whole. "Why didn't you shell the walnuts and then crush the kernels?" he said to the young woman. "I didn't know they had to be shelled," she replied. Then the old man said, "You think about marrying and you don't even know how to cook," and he sent her away.

#### 113. THE MAN IN THE STUMP

A man who had a field of growing corn went out one day to see how it was ripening and climbed a tall stump to get a better view. The stump was hollow, and a bear had a nest of cubs at the bottom. The man slipped and fell down upon the cubs, which set up such a squealing that the mother bear heard them and came climbing down into the stump tail-first, in the way bears do, to see what was the matter. The man caught hold of her by the hind legs, and the old bear was so frightened that she immediately climbed out again, dragging the man with her. In this way, he got out of the stump, and the bear ran away.

A party of warriors once started out for a long hunting trip in the mountains. They went on until they came to a good game region,

This went on until one of the others began to suspect that something was wrong and made it his business to find out. The next morning he followed him secretly through the woods until he saw him come out into a sunny opening, where he sat down upon a large rock, took off his moccasins, and began rubbing them against the rocks until he had worn holes in them. Then the lazy fellow loosened his belt, lay down beside the rock, and went to sleep. The spy set fire to the dry leaves and watched until the flame crept close to the sleeping man, who never opened his eyes.

The spy went back to camp and told what he had seen. About supper time, the lazy fellow came in with the same old story of a long day’s hunt and no game found. When he had finished, the others all laughed and called him a sleepyhead. He insisted that he had been climbing the ridges all day and showed his moccasins to prove how worn they were, not knowing that they were scorched from the fire, as he had slept until sundown. When they saw the blackened moccasins, they laughed again, and he was too much astonished to say a word in his defense; so the captain said that such a liar was not fit to stay with them, and he was driven from the camp.

There was another lazy fellow who courted a pretty girl, but she would have nothing to do with him, telling him that her husband must be a good hunter or she would remain single all her life. One morning he went into the woods, and by a lucky accident, managed to kill a deer. Lifting it upon his back, he carried it into the settlement, passing right by the door of the house where the girl and her mother lived. As soon as he was out of sight of the house, he went by a roundabout course into the woods again and waited until evening, when he appeared with the deer on his shoulder and came down the trail past the girl’s house as he had in the morning. He did this the next day, and the next, until the girl began to think he must be killing all the deer in the woods. So her mother—since the old women are usually the matchmakers—prepared herself and went to the young man’s mother to talk it over.

### 115. THE TWO OLD MEN

Two old men went hunting. One had an eye that was drawn down and was called Uk-kwûnâgi'ta, "Eye-drawn-down." The other had an arm twisted out of shape and was called Uk-ku'sûntsûtëti', "Bent-bow-shape." They killed a deer and cooked the meat in a pot. The second old man dipped a piece of bread into the soup and smacked his lips as he ate it. "Is it good?" asked the first old man. The other replied, "*Hayû'! uk-kwûnâgi'stĭ*—Yes, sir! It will draw down one's eye."

The first old man thought to himself, "He means me." So he dipped a piece of bread into the pot and smacked his lips as he tasted it. "Do you find it good?" asked the other old man. His comrade replied, "*Hayû'! uk-ku'sûntsûtëti'*—Yes, sir! It will twist up one's arm." The second old man thought, "He means me"; so he became very angry and struck the first old man, and then they fought until they killed each other.

### 116. THE STAR FEATHERS

A long time ago, a warrior with a wandering spirit went down into the white settlements toward the east, where he saw a peacock for the first time. The beautiful long feathers surprised and delighted him. By trading some of his own valuable possessions, he managed to buy a few of them. He took them back to the mountains and hid them in an old beaver lodge under the riverbank until he was ready to use them. To get into the beaver lodge, he had to dive underwater.

Then he set to work secretly and made himself a headdress, with the long peacock feathers in the front trailing out behind and the shorter ones at the sides. At the next dance, he wore the new headdress and claimed that he had been up to the sky and that these were star feathers (see number 9, "What the stars are like"). He also made a long speech, which he pretended was a message he had received from the star spirits to deliver to the people.

Everyone marveled at the beautiful feathers, so different from any they had ever seen before. They did not doubt that he had been up to the sky and spoken with spirits. He became a great prophet and kept himself hidden all day in the beaver hole; whenever there was a night gathering for a dance or a council, he would suddenly appear among them wearing his feather headdress and give

The people listened reverently and promised to do everything he commanded. Then he left them, saying that he must return at once to the sky, but as he left the circle, the spies followed him in the darkness and saw him go down to the river and dive under the water. They waited, but he did not resurface, so they went back and told the people. The next morning, a group went to the spot and discovered a beaver lodge beneath the bank. One man dived and surfaced inside, and there he found the prophet sitting with the peacock feathers by his side.

### 119. WHEN BABIES ARE BORN: THE WREN AND THE CRICKET

The little Wren is the messenger of the birds and pries into everything. She gets up early in the morning and goes around to every house in the settlement to get news for the bird council. When a new baby is born, she finds out whether it is a boy or a girl and reports to the council. If it is a boy, the birds sing in a mournful chorus: "Alas! The whistle of the arrow! My shins will burn," because the birds know that when the boy grows older, he will hunt them with his blowgun and arrows and roast them on a stick.

But if the baby is a girl, they are glad and sing: "Thanks! The sound of the pestle! At her home I shall surely be able to scratch where she sweeps," because they know that after a while they will be able to pick up stray grains where she beats the corn into meal.

When the Cricket hears that a girl is born, it also is glad and says, "Thanks, I shall sing in the house where she lives." But if it is a boy, the Cricket laments: "*Gwe-he!* He will shoot me! He will shoot me! He will shoot me!" because boys make little bows to shoot crickets and grasshoppers.

When inquiring as to the sex of the new arrival, the Cherokee asks, "Is it a bow or a (meal) sifter?" or, "Is it ballsticks or bread?"

---

### 120. THE RAVEN MOCKER

Of all the Cherokee wizards or witches, the most dreaded is the Raven Mocker (*Kâ'lanû Ahyeli'skĭ*), the one that robs the dying man of life. They are of either sex, and there is no sure way to know one, though they usually look withered and old because they have added so many lives to their own.

At night, when someone is sick or dying in the settlement, the Raven Mocker goes to the place to take the life. He flies through the air in a fiery shape, with arms outstretched like wings and sparks trailing behind, and a rushing sound like the noise of a strong wind. Every so often as he flies, he makes a cry like the cry of a raven when it "dives" in the air—not like the common raven cry—and those

Those who hear it are afraid, because they know that some person’s life will soon end. When the <term>Raven Mocker</term> arrives at the house, he finds others of his kind waiting there, and unless there is a doctor on guard who knows how to drive them away, they go inside—completely invisible—and frighten and torment the sick person until they kill him. Sometimes to do this, they even lift him from the bed and throw him on the floor, but his friends who are with him think he is only struggling for breath.

After the witches kill him, they take out his heart and eat it, and so add to their own lives as many days or years as they have taken from his. No one in the room can see them, and there is no scar where they take out the heart, yet there is no heart left in the body. Only someone who has the right medicine can recognize a <term>Raven Mocker</term>, and if such a man stays in the room with the sick person, these witches are afraid to come in and retreat as soon as they see him. This is because when one of them is recognized in his true shape, he must die within seven days. There was once a man named *Gûñskǎli'skǐ*, who had this medicine and used to hunt for <term>Raven Mockers</term>, and he killed several. When the friends of a dying person know that there is no more hope, they always try to have one of these medicine men stay in the house and watch the body until it is buried, because after burial, the witches do not steal the heart.

The other witches are jealous of the <term>Raven Mockers</term> and are afraid to come into the same house with one. Once, a man who had the witch medicine was watching over a sick man and saw these other witches outside trying to get in. All at once, they heard a <term>Raven Mocker</term> cry overhead and the others scattered “like a flock of pigeons when the hawk swoops.” When at last a <term>Raven Mocker</term> dies, these other witches sometimes take revenge by digging up the body and abusing it.

The following is told on the reservation as an actual happening:

A young man had been out on a hunting trip and was on his way home when night fell while he was still a long distance from the settlement. He knew of a house not far off the trail where an old man and his wife lived, so he turned in that direction to look for a place to sleep until morning. When he got to the house, there was nobody in it. He looked into the <term>âsǐ</term> <note>A small Cherokee winter house or sweat house.</note> and found no one there either. He thought maybe they had gone to get water, and so he stretched himself out in the far corner to sleep. Very soon he heard a raven cry outside, and a little while afterward, the old man came into the <term>âsǐ</term> and sat down by the fire without noticing the young man, who kept still in the dark corner. Soon there was another raven cry outside, and the old man said to himself, “Now my wife is coming,” and sure enough, in a little while, the old woman came in and sat down by her husband. Then the young man knew they were <term>Raven Mockers</term>, and he was frightened and kept very quiet.

<vocab>Raven Mocker, Cherokee, Gûñskǎli'skǐ, âsǐ, medicine men, folklore, witches</vocab>

It also shares a traditional account of a hunter who unknowingly shelters in the home of two Raven Mockers.</summary>

<header>MOONEY] THE RAVEN MOCKERS</header>

The old man said to his wife, “Well, what luck did you have?” “None,” said the old woman, “there were too many doctors watching. What luck did you have?” “I got what I went for,” said the old man, “there is no reason to fail, but you never have any luck. Take this and cook it and let’s have something to eat.” She prepared the fire, and then the young man smelled meat roasting and thought it smelled sweeter than any meat he had ever tasted. He peeked out with one eye, and it looked like a man’s heart roasting on a stick.

Suddenly the old woman said to her husband, “Who is over in the corner?” “Nobody,” said the old man. “Yes, there is,” said the old woman, “I hear him snoring,” and she stirred the fire until it blazed and lit up the whole place, and there was the young man lying in the corner. He kept quiet and pretended to be asleep. The old man made a noise at the fire to wake him, but still he pretended to sleep. Then the old man came over and shook him, and he sat up and rubbed his eyes as if he had been asleep the entire time.

Now it was near daylight and the old woman was out in the other house getting breakfast ready, but the hunter could hear her crying to herself. “Why is your wife crying?” he asked the old man. “Oh, she has lost some of her friends lately and feels lonely,” said her husband; but the young man knew that she was crying because he had heard them talking.

When they came out to breakfast the old man put a bowl of corn mush before him and said, “This is all we have—we have had no meat for a long time.” After breakfast the young man started on again, but when he had gone a little way the old man ran after him with a fine piece of beadwork and gave it to him, saying, “Take this, and don’t tell anybody what you heard last night, because my wife and I are always quarreling that way.” The young man took the piece, but when he came to the first creek he threw it into the water and then went on to the settlement. There he told the whole story, and a party of warriors started back with him to kill the <term>Raven Mockers</term>. When they reached the place it was seven days after the first night. They found the old man and his wife lying dead in the house, so they set fire to it and burned it and the witches together.

### 121. HERBERT’S SPRING

> “From the head of the southern branch of the Savannah River it does not exceed half a mile to a head spring of the Mississippi water that runs through the middle and upper parts of the Cherokee nation on a northwest course, and, joining other rivers, they empty themselves into the great Mississippi. The above fountain is called ‘Herbert’s Spring,’ so named after an early commissioner of Indian affairs, and it was natural for strangers to drink from it to quench their thirst, satisfy their curiosity, and be able to say they had drunk of the French waters.

<summary>A hunter escapes a pair of Raven Mockers who are later discovered dead and burned by warriors, followed by a description of Herbert's Spring near the Savannah River.</summary>

<header>MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19</header>

> Some of our people, who went only with the intention of staying a short time, but because of some attraction or another stayed longer than planned, reported upon their return—either out of humor or superstition—that the spring possessed such a natural, bewitching quality that whoever drank from it could not possibly leave the nation during the tedious span of seven years. All the debauchees readily accepted this superstitious notion as an excuse for their poor lifestyle, when they had no real reason to stay in that country; and over time it became as accepted a truth as any ever believed to have been spoken by the Delphic oracle. One cursed it because its enchantment had ruined his good fortune; another condemned his own weakness for drinking down witchcraft, despite his own secret suspicions; one swore he would never taste another such dangerous poison, even if he were forced to go down to the Mississippi for water; and another comforted himself that several of the seven years had already passed, and wished that if he ever tasted it again, even in the greatest necessity, he might be confined to the Stygian waters. Those who were more broad-minded greatly amused themselves at the others' expense, for it was a famous favorite place because of its reputation; and, being a well-situated and good spring, all travelers there commonly drank a bottle of choice liquor. But now most of the pack-horse men, even if they are thirsty and are also peerless followers of Bacchus, would swear to give up sacred liquor for the better part of their lives rather than basely renew or confirm the loss of their liberty, which that cursed fountain causes.”—*Adair, American Indians*, p. 231, 1775.

### 122. LOCAL LEGENDS OF NORTH CAROLINA

Chiefly because the Cherokee still occupy western North Carolina, the existing local legends for that section are more numerous than for all the rest of their ancient territory. For the more important legends, see the stories: Agân-unitsi’s Search for the Uktena, Atagâ'hĭ, Hemp-carrier, Herbert’s Spring, Kăna'sta, The Great Leech of Tlanusi'yĭ, The Great Yellow-jacket, The Nûñně'hĭ, The Raid on Tikwali'tsĭ, The Removed Townhouses, The Spirit Defenders of Nĭkwăsĭ', The Uw'tsûñ'ta, Tsul'kălû', Tsuwe'năhĭ, and The U'tlûñ'ta.

AKWĚTI'YĬ: A spot on the Tuckasegee River in Jackson County, between Dick’s Creek and the upper end of the Cowee tunnel. According to tradition, there was a dangerous water monster in the river there. The meaning of the name is lost.

ATSĬ'LA-WA'Ĭ: “Fire’s relative,” a peak, sometimes called Rattlesnake Knob, east of the Oconaluftee River and about 2 miles northeast of Cherokee or Yellow Hill in Swain County. It is so called from a tradition that a ball of fire was once seen to fly through the air from

**BLACK ROCK**: A very high bald peak toward the head of Scott’s creek, northeast of Webster, on the line of Jackson and Haywood counties. Either this peak or the adjacent Jones knob, which is of equal height, is known to the Cherokee as <term>Ûñ'wădâ-tsu'gilasûñ'</term>, meaning “Where the storehouse was taken off.” This name comes from a large flat rock supported by four other rocks, making it resemble a storehouse (<term>ûñwădâ'lĭ</term>) raised on poles. It was formerly in clear view upon the summit until it was thrown down by lightning some fifty years ago.

**BUFFALO CREEK, WEST**: A tributary of the Cheowa river in Graham county. The Cherokee name is <term>Yûnsâ'ĭ</term>, or “Buffalo place,” based on a tradition that a buffalo formerly lived under the water at its mouth (see <term>Tsuta'tsinasûñ'yĭ</term>).

**CHEOWA MAXIMUM**: A bald mountain at the head of the Cheowa river, on the line between Graham and Macon counties. This and the adjoining peak, Swim bald, are together called <term>Sehwate'yĭ</term>, or “Hornet place.” According to tradition, a monster hornet formerly had its nest there and could be seen flying about the tree tops or sunning itself on the bald spots. It was so fierce that it drove away everyone who came near the mountain, though it finally disappeared.

**DAKWÂ'Ï**: “<term>Dăkwă'</term> place,” located in the French Broad river about 6 miles above Warm Springs in Madison county, and 30 miles below Asheville. A <term>dăkwă'</term>, or monster fish, is said to have lived in the stream at that point.

**DA'NAWA-(A) SA'TSÛÑYĬ**: “War crossing,” a ford in the Cheowa river about 3 miles below Robbinsville in Graham county. A hostile war party from the North, probably Shawano or Iroquois, was pursued and crossed the river at this place after having killed a man on the Cheowa.

**DATLE'YĂSTA'Ĭ**: “Where they fell down,” located on the Tuckasegee river at the bend above Webster in Jackson county. This was formerly the site of the old town of <term>Gănsâ'gĭ</term> (Conasauga). Two large <term>uktenas</term>, twined about each other as if in combat, were once seen to lift themselves from a deep hole in the river there and fall back into the water.

**DÂTSĬ'YĬ**: “<term>Dâtsĭ</term> place,” just above Eagle creek on the Little Tennessee river, between Graham and Swain counties. It is named for a traditional water monster of that name which was said to have lived in a deep hole in the stream.

**DEGAL'GÛÑ'YĬ**: “Where they are piled up,” a series of cairns on both sides of the trail down the south side of the Cheowa river in Graham county. They extend along the trail for several miles, from below Santeetla creek nearly to Slick Rock creek on the Tennessee line (the
