At least one, located nearly opposite Yellow Creek, is said to be the grave of a Cherokee killed by the enemy. Every passing Indian throws an additional stone onto each heap, believing that some misfortune will happen to them should they neglect this duty. Other cairns are on the west side of Slick Rock Creek, about a mile from the Little Tennessee River, and others are south of Robbinsville, near where the trail crosses the ridge to Valleytown in Cherokee County.

**DIDA'SKASTI'YĬ:** "Where they were afraid of each other," a spot on the east side of the Little Tennessee River, near the mouth of Alarka Creek in Swain County. A ball game once scheduled to take place there before the Indian Removal, between rival teams from Qualla and Valleytown, was canceled because of the mutual fear between the two parties.

**DISGÂ'GISTI'YĬ:** "Where they gnaw," a spot where the trail down the south side of the Cheowa River crosses a small branch about halfway between Cockram Creek and Yellow Creek in Graham County. Indians passing by gnaw the twigs from the laurel bushes here, believing that if they fail to do so, they will encounter some misfortune before crossing the next ridge. Nearby is a cairn to which each person also adds a stone (see **Degal'gûn'yĭ**).

**DUDUÑ'LĚKSÛÑ'YĬ:** "Where its legs were broken off," a spot on the east side of the Tuckasegee River, opposite the mouth of the Cullowhee River, a few miles above Webster in Jackson County. The name suggests a tradition that appears to have been lost.

**DULASTÛÑ'YĬ:** "Potsherd place," a former settlement on the Nottely River in Cherokee County, near the Georgia line. A Cherokee ball captain of mixed heritage who formerly lived there, John Butler or *Tsan-uga'sĭtǎ* (Sour John), having been defeated in a ball game, said in contempt of his men that they were of no more use than broken pots.

**DUNIDÛ'LALÛÑYĬ:** "Where they made arrows," on Straight Creek, a headstream of the Oconaluftee River, near Cataluchee Peak in Swain County. A Shawano war party coming against the Cherokee, after having crossed the Smoky Mountains, halted there to prepare arrows.

**FRENCH BROAD RIVER:** A magazine writer states that the Indians called this stream "the racing river." This is only partially correct. The Cherokee have no name for the river as a whole, but the district through which it flows near Asheville is called by them *Un-ta'kiyas-ti'yĭ*, "Where they race." They translate the name of the city as *Kâs-du'yĭ*, "Ashes place."

**GAKATI'YĬ:** "Place of setting free," a south bend in the Tuckasegee River about 3 miles above Bryson City in Swain County. It is sometimes referred to in the plural form, *Diga'katiyĭ*, "Place of setting them free." In one of their old wars, the Cherokee generously released some prisoners there.

**GATUTI'YǏ:** "Town-building place," near the head of Santeetla Creek, southwest from Robbinsville in Graham County. High up on the slopes of the neighboring mountain, Stratton Bald, is a wide "bench" where the people once started to build a settlement but were frightened off by a strange noise, which they thought was made by an *uktena*.

**GI'LI'-DINĚHÛÑ'YǏ:** "Where the dogs live," a deep place in the Oconaluftee River, Swain County, a short distance above Yellow Hill (Cherokee) and just below the mound. It is so named from a tradition that two "red dogs" were once seen there playing on the bank. They were supposed to live under the water.

**GISEHÛÑ'YǏ:** "Where the Female lives," on the Tuckasegee River, about 2 miles above Bryson City, Swain County. There is a tradition that some supernatural "white people" were seen there washing clothes in the river and hanging them out upon the bank to dry. They were probably supposed to be the family of the *Agis'-e'gwa*, or "Great Female," a spirit invoked by the conjurers.

**GREGORY BALD:** A high peak of the Great Smoky Mountains on the western border of Swain County, adjoining Tennessee. The Cherokee call it *Tsistū'yǐ*, "Rabbit place." Here the rabbits had their townhouse and here lived their chief, the Great Rabbit, and in the old times the people could see him. He was as large as a deer, and all the little rabbits were subject to him.

**JOANNA BALD:** A bald mountain near the head of Valley River, on the line between Graham and Cherokee counties. Called *Diyâ'hăli'yǐ*, "Lizard place," from a traditional great lizard with a glistening throat, which used to haunt the place and was frequently seen sunning itself on the rocky slopes.

**JUTACULLA OLD FIELDS:** A bald spot of perhaps a hundred acres on the slope of Tennessee Bald (*Tsul'kǎlû' Tsunegûn'yǐ*), at the extreme head of the Tuckasegee River in Jackson County, on the ridge from which the boundaries of Haywood, Jackson, and Transylvania counties diverge. The giant *Tsul'kǎlû'*, or Jutaculla, as the name is distorted by white settlers, had his residence in the mountain (see story). According to a local legend among the whites, said to be derived from the Indians, this bald spot was a clearing which he made for a farm. Some distance farther to the west, on the north bank of Caney Fork, about 1 mile above Moses Creek and perhaps 10 miles above Webster in the same county, is the Jutaculla Rock—a large soapstone slab covered with crude carvings which, according to the same tradition, are scratches made by the giant while jumping from his farm on the mountain to the creek below.

**JUTACULLA ROCK:** See Jutaculla Old Fields.

**KÂL-DETSI'YÛÑYǏ:** "Where the bones are," a ravine on the north side of the Cheowa River, just above the mouth of East Buffalo Creek in Graham County. In the old time, two Cherokee were killed here by

**NANTAHALA**: A river and ridge of very steep mountains in Macon County; the name is a corruption of *Nûn'dăye''lĭ*, which was applied to a former settlement near the mouth of Briertown Creek. The townhouse was on the west side of the river, near present-day Jarretts. The word means "middle sun" (that is, "midday sun"), from *nûndă'* ("sun") and *aye''lĭ* ("middle"), and refers to the fact that in certain places along the stream, the high cliffs block out the direct light of the sun until nearly noon. Based on the mistaken idea that the name is derived from *unûñtĭ'* ("milk"), it has been fancifully translated as "Center of a woman's breast," "Maiden's bosom," and so on. The valley was the legendary haunt of the <term>Uw'tsûn'ta</term> (see number 45). To illustrate the steepness of the cliffs along the stream, it was said of a famous hunter named <term>Tsasta'wĭ</term>, who lived in the old town, that he used to stand on top of the bluff overlooking the settlement and throw the liver of a freshly killed deer down onto the roof of his house, so that his wife would have it cooked and waiting for him by the time he reached the bottom of the mountain.

**NUGĂTSA'NĬ**: A ridge below Yellow Hill (Cherokee), on the Oconaluftee River in Swain County, said to be a resort of the <term>Nûñně'hĭ</term> fairies. The word is an archaic form denoting a high ridge with a long, gradual slope.

**QUALLA**: A post office and former trading station in Jackson County, on the border of the present East Cherokee reservation; because of this, it is sometimes called the Qualla reservation. The Cherokee form is <term>Kwalĭ</term>, or <term>Kwalûñyĭ</term> in the locative case. According to Captain Terrell, the former trader at that place, it was named after <term>Kwalĭ</term> (that is, Polly), an old Indian woman who lived there about sixty years ago.

**SĂLĬGU'GĬ**: "Turtle place," a deep hole in the Oconaluftee River, about half a mile below Adams Creek near Whittier in Swain County. It is said to be the haunt of a monster turtle.

**SKWAN'-DIGÛ'GÛÑ'YĬ**: From <term>Askwan'-digû'gûñ'yĭ</term>, meaning "Where the Spaniard is in the water," on Soco Creek, just above where Wright’s Creek enters in Jackson County. According to tradition, a party of Spaniards advancing into the mountains was attacked here by the Cherokee, who threw one of them (possibly already dead) into the stream.

**SOCO GAP**: <term>Ăhălu'na</term>, <term>Ă'hălûnûn'yĭ</term>, or <term>Uni'hălu'na</term>, meaning "Ambush" or "Where they ambushed"; located at the head of Soco Creek on the boundary between Swain and Haywood counties. The trail from Pigeon River crosses this gap, and in the old days, the Cherokee used to keep a lookout here for enemies approaching from the north. On the occasion that gave the place its name, they ambushed a large party of invading Shawano just below the gap on the Haywood side, killing all but one. They cut off his ears, after which,

**STANDING INDIAN:** A high bald peak at the extreme head of the Nantahala River, in Macon County. The name is a translation of the Cherokee name <term>Yûñ'wĭ-tsulenûñ'yĭ</term>, "Where the man stood" (originally <term>Yûñ'wĭ-dĭkatâgûn'yĭ</term>, "Where the man stands"), given to it because of a uniquely shaped rock that formerly jutted out from the bald summit, but is now broken off. As the old memory faded, a tradition grew up of a mysterious being once seen standing upon the mountain top.

**STEKOA:** A spot on the Tuckasegee River, just above Whittier, in Swain County, better known as the Thomas farm, because it was the former residence of Colonel W. H. Thomas, who was for a long time the agent of the East Cherokee. The correct form is <term>Stikâ'yĭ</term>, the name of an ancient settlement at the place, as well as another on a creek of the same name in Rabun County, Georgia. The word has been incorrectly translated as "little grease," from <term>usdĭ'ga</term> or <term>usdĭ'</term>, "little," and <term>ka'ĭ</term>, "grease" or "oil," but the true meaning is lost.

**SWANNANOA:** A river joining the French Broad at Asheville, and the gap in the Blue Ridge at its head. A magazine writer has translated this name as "the beautiful." The word, however, is a corruption of <term>Suwa'li-nûñnâ'(-hĭ)</term>, "Suwali trail," which is the Cherokee name not for the stream, but for the trail crossing the gap toward the country of the <term>Ani'-Suwa'li</term> or Cheraw (see number 104, "The Eastern Tribes").

**SWIM BALD OR WOLF CREEK BALD.** See Cheowa Maximum.

**TSI'SKWUNSDI'-ADSISTI'YĬ:** "Where they killed Little-bird," a place near the head of West Buffalo Creek, southwest of Robbinsville, in Graham County. A trail crosses the ridge near this place, which takes its name from a man who was killed here by a hostile war party in the days of the old wars.

**TSU'DINÛNTI'YĬ:** "Throwing down place," the site of a former settlement in a bend on the west side of the Nantahala River, just within the limits of Macon County. It is so called from a tradition that a Cherokee man, pursued by the enemy, threw away his equipment there.

**TSUKILÛNNÛÑ'YĬ:** "Where he alighted," two small bald spots on the side of the mountain at the head of Little Snowbird Creek, southwest of Robbinsville, in Graham County. A mysterious being, having the form of a giant with a head blazing like the sun, was once seen to fly through the air, alight at this place, and stand for some time looking out over the landscape. It then flew away, and when the people afterward went to look, they found the plants burned from the ground where it had stood. They do not know who it was, but some think it may have been the Sun.

**TSULÂ'SINÛÑ'YI:** "Where the footprint is," on the Tuckasegee River, about a mile above Deep Creek, in Swain County. From a rock now

**<term>TSUÑDA'NILTÏ'YÏ</term>:** "Where they demanded the debt from him," a fine camping ground on the north side of Little Santeetla Creek, about halfway up and west from Robbinsville in Graham County. Here a hunter once killed a deer, which the others of the party demanded in payment of a debt owed to them. The Cherokee commonly give the creek the same name.

**<term>TSÛTA'GA UWEYÛÑ'Ï</term>:** "Chicken Creek," an extreme eastern headstream of the Nantahala River, entering about 4 miles above Clear Branch in Macon County. It is so called from a story that some hunters camping there for the night once heard a noise like chickens constantly crowing upon a high rock farther up the stream.

**<term>TSÛTA'TSINÂSÛÑ'YÏ</term>:** "Where it eddies," a deep hole at the mouth of Cockram Creek of the Cheowa River in Graham County. There is an eddy here said to be caused by a buffalo that lives under the water at this spot, and which in ancient times lived at the mouth of West Buffalo Creek, farther up the river.

**<term>TUSQUITTEE BALD</term>:** A bald mountain at the head of Tusquittee Creek, eastward from Hayesville in Clay County. The Cherokee name is <term>Tsuwă'-uniyetsûñ'yï</term>, "Where the water-dogs laughed." The water-dog of the southern Alleghenies—sometimes also called the mud-puppy or hell-bender—is a large amphibious lizard or salamander of the genus *Menopoma* that frequents muddy waters. According to the story, a hunter once crossing over the mountain in a very dry season heard voices. Creeping silently toward the place from which the sound proceeded, he peeped over a rock and saw two water-dogs walking together on their hind legs along the trail and talking as they went. Their pond had dried up and they were on their way over to the Nantahala River. As he listened, one said to the other, "Where is the water? I am so thirsty that my apron (gills) hangs down," and then both water-dogs laughed.

**<term>UKTE'NA-TSUGANÛÑ'TATSÛÑ'YÏ</term>:** "Where the <term>uktena</term> became fastened," a spot on the Tuckasegee River about 2 miles above Deep Creek, near Bryson City in Swain County. There is a tradition that an <term>uktena</term>, trying to make its way upstream, became fastened here; in its struggles, it pried up some large rocks now lying in the bed of the river and left deep scratches upon other rocks along the bank.

**<term>UKTE'NA-UTANSI'NASTÛÑ'YÏ</term>:** "Where the <term>uktena</term> crawled," a large rock on the Hyatt farm on the north bank of the Tuckasegee River, about four miles above Bryson City in Swain County. In the rock bed of the stream and along the rocks on the side are wavy depressions said to have been made by an <term>uktena</term> while going up the river.

**<term>UNTLASGÂSTÏ'YÏ</term>:** "Where they scratched," at the head of Hyatt Creek, of the Valley River in Cherokee County. According to hunting

tradition, every animal, upon arriving at this spot, was accustomed to scratch the ground like a turkey.

**VENGEANCE CREEK:** A southern tributary of the Valley River in Cherokee County. It was named by the first settlers after an old Indian woman who lived there, whom they nicknamed "Vengeance" because of her irritable appearance. The Cherokee call the district <term>Gän̒sa´ti´yi</term>, "Robbing place," because they robbed a trader there during the Revolutionary War.

**WAYA GAP:** A gap in the Nantahala Mountains in Macon County, where the trail crosses from Laurel Creek of the Nantahala River to Cartoogaja Creek of the Little Tennessee River. The Cherokee call it <term>A´tâhi´ta</term>, "Shouting place." For the legend, see story number 13. It was the site of a fierce battle during the Revolutionary War (see page 49). The name Waya seems to come from the Cherokee word <term>wă´ya</term>, meaning "wolf."

**WEBSTER:** The county seat of Jackson County, located on the Tuckasegee River. It is known to the Cherokee as <term>Unadän̒ti´yi</term>, "Where they conjured." The name actually belongs to a gap three miles east of Webster, on the trail leading up Scotts Creek. According to tradition, a war party of <term>Shawano</term> <note>Shawnee</note>, coming from the direction of the Pigeon River, stopped here to "perform rituals" against the Cherokee. While they were doing this, they were surprised by the Cherokee, who attacked from behind and killed several of them, including the conjurer.

**<term>YA´NU-DINEHU͂N´YI</term>:** "Where the bears live," on the Oconaluftee River, about a mile above its junction with the Tuckasegee River in Swain County. A family of "water bears" is said to live at the bottom of the river in a deep hole at this location.

**<term>YA´NU-U´NATAWASTI´YI</term>:** "Where the bears wash," a small pond of very cold, purple water that has no outlet and is now nearly dried up. It is located in a gap of the Great Smoky Mountains, at the very head of the Raven Fork of the Oconaluftee River in Swain County. It was said to be a favorite wallow for bears, and according to some accounts, its waters had the same healing properties attributed to those of <term>Atagâ´hī</term> (see story number 69).

**<term>YAWA´I</term>:** "Yawa place," a spot on the south side of Yellow Creek of the Cheowa River in Graham County, about a mile above the trail crossing near the mouth of the creek. The legend says that a mysterious person, apparently a human being, used to haunt a round hill nearby. This person was sometimes seen walking around the top of the hill crying, "Yawa! Yawa!" while the sound of invisible guns came from the hill, making the people afraid to go near it.

### 123. LOCAL LEGENDS OF SOUTH CAROLINA

Because the Cherokee withdrew from all of South Carolina (except for a small strip in the far west) as early as 1777, the memory of the old legends associated with specific locations in the state has completely faded from the tribe. However, some local names still exist about which the white settlers who

<meta>This page continues the discussion of local legends in South Carolina, specifically addressing the origins of place names near the Keowee River, before transitioning to local legends of Tennessee.</meta>

succeeded to the inheritance have built traditions of more or less doubtful authenticity.

In Pickens and Anderson counties, in the northwest corner of the state, there is a series of creeks joining the Keowee River and named, respectively in order from top to bottom, Mile, Six-mile, Twelve-mile, Eighteen-mile, Twenty-three-mile, and Twenty-six-mile. According to the local story, they were named by a young woman during one of the early Indian wars as she crossed each ford on a rapid horseback flight to the lower settlements to secure help for the besieged garrison of Fort Prince George. The names actually date back almost to the first establishment of the colony and were intended to indicate roughly the distances along the old trading path from Fort Ninety-six, on Henleys Creek of the Saluda River, to Keowee—which was at that time the frontier town of the Cherokee Nation. The two points were considered 96 miles apart as the trail ran. Fort Prince George was on the east bank of the Keowee River, near the entrance of Crow Creek, and directly opposite the Indian town.

**CONNEROSS**: The name of a creek which enters the Keowee (or Seneca) River from the west, in Anderson County; it is a corruption of the Lower Cherokee dialect form, <term>Kăwân'-urâ'sûñyĭ</term> or <term>Kăwân'-tsurâ'sûñyĭ</term>, “Where the duck fell off.” According to surviving Cherokee tradition, a duck once had her nest upon a cliff overlooking the stream in a cave with its mouth positioned so that, when leaving the nest, she appeared to fall from the cliff into the water. There was probably an Indian settlement of the same name.

**TOXAWAY**: The name of a creek and former Cherokee settlement at the extreme head of the Keowee River; it has been incorrectly translated as “Place of shedding tears,” from <term>daksăwa'ihû</term>, “he is shedding tears.” The correct Cherokee form of the name is <term>Dûksa'ĭ</term> or <term>Dûkw'sa'ĭ</term>, a word which cannot be analyzed and whose meaning is now lost.

### 124. LOCAL LEGENDS OF TENNESSEE

For the more important legends localized in Tennessee, see the stories <term>The Hunter in the Dăkwă'</term>, <term>The Nest of the Tlă'nuwă</term>, <term>The Removed Townhouses</term>, <term>The Haunted Whirlpool</term>, <term>Ûñtsaiyĭ'</term>, and <term>U'tlûñ'ta</term>.

**BUFFALO TRACK ROCK**: This rock, whose Indian name is now lost, is vaguely mentioned as being located southwest from Cumberland Gap on the northern border of the state. According to Wafford, it was well known about eighty years ago to the old Cherokee hunters, who described it as being covered with deep impressions made by buffalo running along the rock and then hitting their heads, as if in a mad fury, against a rock wall, leaving the prints of their heads and horns in the stone.

As far as is known, there was no Cherokee settlement at the place, although some prominent men of the tribe lived in the vicinity. The name originally belonged to some location upon the creek. The Cherokee pronounce it *<term>Tsatănu'gĭ</term>*, but say that it is not a Cherokee word and has no meaning in their language. The best informants express the opinion that it was from the Chickasaw (Choctaw) language, which seems possible, as the Chickasaw country formerly extended a considerable distance up the Tennessee River, with the nearest settlement being within 80 miles of the present city. The Cherokee sometimes call the city *<term>A'tlă'nuwă'</term>*, or “*<term>Tlă'nuwă</term>* (Hawk) hole,” which was their old name for a bluff on the south side of the river at the foot of the present Market Street. From this circumstance probably originated the statement by a magazine writer that the name Chattanooga signifies “The crow's nest.”

**CHICKAMAUGA**: The name of two creeks in Hamilton County, entering the Tennessee River from opposite sides a few miles above Chattanooga. A creek of the same name is one of the head-streams of the Chattahoochee River, in White County, Georgia. The Cherokee pronounce it *<term>Tsĭkăma'gĭ</term>*, applying the name in Tennessee to the territory around the mouth of the southern, or principal, stream, where they formerly had a town from which they moved in 1782. They state, however, that it is not a Cherokee word and has no meaning in their language. Filson, in 1793, erroneously states that it is from the Cherokee language and signifies “Boiling pot,” referring to a dangerous whirlpool in the river nearby, and later writers have further expanded upon this by translating it to mean “Whirlpool.” The error arises from confusing this place with "The Suck," a whirlpool in the Tennessee River 15 miles farther down and known to the Cherokee as *<term>Ûñtiguhĭ'</term>*, “Pot in the water” (see number 63, “*<term>Ûñtsaiyĭ'</term>*, the Gambler”). On account of the hard fighting in the neighborhood during the Civil War, the stream was sometimes called, poetically, “The River of Death,” the term being frequently given as a translation of the Indian word. It has been suggested that the name is derived from an Algonquian word referring to a fishing or fish-spearing place, in which case it may have originated with the Shawano, who formerly occupied Middle Tennessee, and some of whom at a later period resided jointly with the Cherokee in the settlements along this part of the river. If not Shawano, it is probably from the Creek or Chickasaw.

Concerning “Chickamauga gulch,” a canyon on the northern stream of that name, a newspaper writer gives the following so-called legend which, it is hardly necessary to say, is not genuine:

**CHILHOWEE:** A mountain and station on the north side of the Little Tennessee River, in Blount County. The correct Cherokee form is <term>Tsû'lûnwĕ'ĭ</term>, applied to the lower part of Abrams Creek, which enters the river from the north just above. The meaning of the word is lost, although it may possibly have a connection with <term>tsû'lû</term>, "kingfisher." It has been incorrectly translated as "fire deer," an interpretation based on the false assumption that the name is a compound of <term>atsĭ'la</term>, "fire," and <term>ă'wĭ'</term>, "deer," hence Chil-howee. For legends located in this vicinity, see the stories noted above. Chilhowee also occurs as the name of a stream in the mountains of southwestern Virginia.

**LENOIR:** On the north bank of the main Tennessee River, at the junction of the Little Tennessee, in Loudon County. The Cherokee name is <term>Wa'gĭnsĭ'</term>, of which the meaning is lost. It was originally applied to an eddy in the stream where, it was said, there lived a large serpent, the sight of which was an omen of evil. On one occasion, a man crossing the river at this point saw the snake in the water and soon afterward lost one of his children.

**MORGANTON:** On a rocky hill on the old Indian trail on the west side of the Little Tennessee River, above and nearly opposite Morganton in Loudon County, there are—or were a few years ago—four trees marked in a peculiar manner. The Indians had several unsatisfactory stories concerning these, the most common opinion being that the marks were very old and had been made by Indians to indicate the position of hidden mines.

**NASHVILLE:** The state capital, in Davidson County. The Cherokee name is <term>Dăgû'năwelâ'hĭ</term>, "Mussel-liver place," which would seem to have originated in some legend that is now forgotten.

**NICKAJACK:** A creek entering the Tennessee River from the south about 15 miles below Chattanooga. Near its mouth is a noted cave of the same name. The Cherokee form is <term>Nĭkutse'gĭ</term>, the name of a former settlement of that tribe at the mouth of the creek; however, the word has no meaning in that language and is probably of foreign, perhaps Chickasaw, origin. The derivation from a certain "Nigger Jack," who was said to have made the cave his headquarters, is purely imaginary.

**SAVANNAH:** A farm on the north bank of the Hiwassee River at a ford of the same name, about 5 miles above Conasauga Creek and Columbus, in Polk County. Here are extensive remains of an ancient settlement, including mounds, a cemetery, and also, some seventy years ago, a small

**TENNESSEE**: The Cherokee form is <term>Tănăsĭ'</term>, and it was applied to several localities within the old territory of the tribe. The most important town of this name was on the south bank of the Little Tennessee River, halfway between Citico and Toco creeks, in Monroe County, Tennessee. Another was on the south side of the Hiwassee, just above the junction of the Ocoee, in Polk County, Tennessee. A third district of the same name was on Tennessee Creek, the extreme easterly head of the Tuckasegee River, in Jackson County, North Carolina. The meaning of the name is lost. It was not the Indian name of the river, and it does not mean "Big spoon," as has been incorrectly asserted.

### 125. LOCAL LEGENDS OF GEORGIA

For more important legends localized in Georgia, see the stories Yahula, The Nûñněhǐ, The Ustû'tlǐ, Âgan-uni'tsǐ's Search for the Uktena, and The Man who Married the Thunder's Sister. White's *Historical Collections of Georgia* is responsible for a number of pseudo-myths.

**CHOPPED OAK**: A noted tree, scarred with hundreds of hatchet marks, formerly in Habersham County, 6 miles east of Clarkesville, on the summit of the Chattahoochee ridge, and on the north side of the road from Clarkesville to Toccoa Creek. The Cherokee name is <term>Digălŭ'yătûn'yǐ</term>, "Where it is gashed with hatchets." It was a favorite assembly place for the Indians, as well as for the early settlers, according to whom the gashes were tally marks by means of which the Indians kept the record of scalps taken in their raids. The tradition is thus given by White (*Historical Collections of Georgia*, p. 489, 1855) on some earlier authority:

> Among the curiosities of this country was the Chopped Oak, a tree famous in Indian history and in the traditions of the early settlers. This tree stood about 6 miles southeast of Clarkesville, and was noted as being the Law Ground, or place of holding company musters and magistrates' courts. According to tradition, the Chopped Oak was a celebrated rendezvous of the Indians in their predatory excursions, it being at a point where a number of trails met. Here their plans of warfare were laid; here the several parties separated; and here, on their return, they awaited each other; and then, in their brief language, the result of their enterprise was stated, and for every scalp taken a gash was cut in the tree. If tradition tells the truth, and every scar on the blasted oak counts for a scalp, the success of their scouting parties must have been great. This tree was alive a few years since when a young man, possessing all the prejudices of his countrymen and caring less for the traditions of the Indians than his own revenge, killed the tree by girdling it, so that it might no longer be a living monument of the cruelties of the savages. The stump is still standing.

**DEAD MAN'S GAP:** One mile below Tallulah Falls, on the west side of the railroad in Habersham County. It is so called from a former reputed Indian grave, which is now almost erased. According to the story, it was the grave of an Indian who was killed here while eloping with a white woman whom he had stolen from her husband.

**FROGTOWN:** A creek at the head of the Chestatee River, north of Dahlonega in Lumpkin County. The Cherokee name is Walâsi'yĭ, "Frog place." The name was originally applied to a mountain to the northeast (perhaps Rock Mountain?), from a tradition that a hunter had once seen a frog there as large as a house. The Indian settlement along the creek bore the same name.

**HIWASSEE:** A river having its source in Towns County, northern Georgia, and flowing northwestward to join the Tennessee River. The correct Cherokee form, applied to two former settlements on the stream, is Ayuhwa'sĭ (meaning "A savanna"). Although there is no specific Cherokee story connected with the name, White (*Historical Collections of Georgia*, p. 660) makes it the subject of a long fabricated myth, in which Hiwassee, translated as "The Pretty Fawn," is the beautiful daughter of a Catawba chief. She is courted and at last won by a young Cherokee warrior named Notley, "The Daring Horseman," who finally becomes the head chief of the Cherokee and succeeds in making a lasting peace between the two tribes. The story sounds very pretty, but it is a complete invention.

**NACOOCHEE:** A village on the site of a former Cherokee settlement, in a beautiful and fertile valley of the same name at the head of the Chattahoochee River in White County. The Cherokee form is Nagu'tsĭ', but the word has no meaning in that language and seems to be of foreign, perhaps Creek, origin. About 2 miles above the village, on the east bank of the river, is a large mound. White (*Historical Collections of Georgia*, p. 486) quotes a fictitious legend according to which Nacoochee, "The Evening Star," was a beautiful Indian princess who unfortunately fell in love with a chieftain of a hostile tribe and was killed, together with her lover, while fleeing from the vengeance of an angry father. The two were buried in the same grave and the mound was raised over the spot. The only grain of truth in the story is that the name has a slight resemblance to <term>năkwĭsĭ'</term>, the Cherokee word for "star."

**NOTTELY:** A river rising in Union County and flowing northwestward into the Hiwassee. The Cherokee form is Na'dû'lĭ', applied to a former settlement on the west side of the river in Cherokee County, North Carolina, about a mile from the Georgia line. Although suggestive of <term>na'tû'lĭ</term>, "spicewood," it is a different word and has no meaning in the Cherokee language, being apparently of foreign, perhaps Creek, origin. For a fabricated myth connected with the name, see the preceding note on Hiwassee.

**TALKING ROCK:** A creek in upper Georgia flowing northward to join the Coosawatee River. The Indian settlements along it were considered part of Sanderstown, located on the lower part of the creek. The townhouse was situated about a mile above the current Talking Rock station on the west side of the railroad. The name is a translation of the Cherokee <term>Nûñyû’-gûñwaniskĭ</term>, meaning “Rock that talks.” According to one informant, this refers to an echo rock somewhere on the stream below the present railroad station. An old-time trader among the Cherokees in Georgia says that the name was applied to a rock where the Indians formerly held their councils, but the word's etymology argues against this origin.

**TALLULAH:** A river in Rabun County, northeastern Georgia, which flows into the Tugaloo and has a beautiful waterfall about two miles above its mouth. The Cherokee form is <term>Tălulǔ’</term> (<term>Tărurǐ’</term> in the lower Cherokee dialect), which was the name of an ancient settlement some distance above the falls, as well as a creek and district at the head of the Cheowa River in Graham County, North Carolina. The name cannot be translated. A magazine writer has rendered it as “The Terrible,” for which there is no authority. Schoolcraft, on the authority of a Cherokee lady, translates it as “There lies your child,” derived from a story of a child being carried over the falls. However, the name was not applied to the falls, but to a district on the stream above them, as well as to another in North Carolina. This error stems from the fact that a word of somewhat similar sound denotes “having children” or “being pregnant” when speaking of a woman. One informant derives it from <term>tălulǔ’</term>, the cry of a certain species of frog known as <term>dulusĭ</term>, which is found in that neighborhood (though not on the reservation) and which was formerly eaten as food. A possible derivation is from <term>a’tălulû’</term>, meaning “unfinished, premature, or unsuccessful.” The waterfall was called <term>Ugûñ’yĭ</term>, a name whose meaning is lost and which was also applied to a locality on the Little Tennessee River near Franklin, North Carolina. For a myth set at Tallulah Falls, see number 84, “The Man who Married the Thunder’s Sister.”

In this connection, Lanman gives the following story which, despite its "white man’s" style, appears to be based on a genuine Cherokee tradition of the <term>Nûñnĕ’hǐ</term>:

> During my stay at the Falls of Tallulah, I made every effort to obtain an Indian legend or two connected with them, and it was my good fortune to hear one that has never yet been printed. It was originally obtained from the Cherokees who lived in the region at the time by the white man who first discovered the falls. It is in substance as follows: Many generations ago, it happened that several famous hunters, who had wandered from the West toward what is now the Savannah River in search of game, never returned to their camps. In time, both the curiosity and the fears of the nation were aroused, and an effort was made to determine the cause of their strange disappearance; consequently, a party of medicine men was sent to make a pilgrimage toward the great river. They were away for a whole month, and, on returning to their friends, they reported that they had dis—

covered a terrifying fissure in an unknown part of the country, through which a mountain torrent flowed with a deafening noise. They said that it was an exceedingly wild place, and that its inhabitants were a species of little men and women who lived in the crevices of the rocks and in grottoes under the waterfalls. They had attempted by every trick in their power to hold a council with the little people, but all in vain; and, from the shrieks they frequently uttered, the medicine men knew that they were the enemies of the Indian race. Therefore, it was concluded by the nation at large that the long-lost hunters had been lured to their deaths in the dreadful gorge, which they called Tallulah. In view of this little legend, it is worth noting that the Cherokee nation, before their departure for the distant West, always avoided the Falls of Tallulah and were seldom found hunting or fishing in their vicinity.<note>Letters from the Alleghany Mountains, pages 41-42.</note>

**Toccoa:** (1) A creek flowing into the Tugaloo River, in Habersham County, with a waterfall upon its upper course near the village of the same name. (2) A river in upper Georgia, flowing northwestward into the Hiwassee. The correct Cherokee form applied to the former settlement on both streams is <term>Tagwâ'hĭ</term>, "Catawba place," implying the former presence of Indians of that tribe. The lands around Toccoa Falls were sold by the Cherokee in 1783 and were owned at one time by Wafford's grandfather. According to Wafford, there was a tradition that when the whites first visited the place they saw, as they thought, an Indian woman walking beneath the surface of the water under the falls; on looking again a moment later, they saw her sitting upon an overhanging rock 200 feet in the air, with her feet dangling over. Wafford said, "She must have been one of the <term>Nûñnĕ'hĭ</term>."

**Track Rock Gap:** A gap about 5 miles east of Blairsville, in Union County, on the ridge separating Brasstown Creek from the waters of the Nottely River. The micaceous soapstone rocks on both sides of the trail are covered with petroglyphs, from which the gap takes its name. The Cherokee call the place <term>Datsu'nalâsgûn'yĭ</term>, "Where there are tracks," or <term>Degayelûn'hă</term>, "Printed (Branded) place." The carvings are of many and various patterns, some of them resembling human or animal footprints, while others are squares, crosses, circles, "bird tracks," etc., arranged without any apparent order. On the authority of a Doctor Stevenson, writing in 1834, White (*Historical Collections of Georgia*, p. 658, 1855), and after him Jones (*Antiquities of the Southern Indians*, 1873), give a misleading and greatly exaggerated account of these carvings without having taken the trouble to investigate for themselves, although the spot is easily accessible. No effort, either state or local, is made to preserve the pictographs from destruction, and many of the finest have been cut out from the rock and carried off by vandals—Stevenson himself being among the number, by his own confession. The illustration (plate xx) is from a rough sketch made by the author in 1890.

...covered a terrifying fissure in an unknown part of the country, through which a mountain torrent flowed with a deafening noise. They said that it was an exceedingly wild place, and that its inhabitants were a species of little men and women who lived in the crevices of the rocks and in grottoes under the waterfalls. They had attempted by every trick in their power to hold a council with the little people, but all in vain; and, from the shrieks they frequently uttered, the medicine men knew that they were the enemies of the Indian race. Therefore, the nation at large concluded that the long-lost hunters had been lured to their deaths in the dreadful gorge, which they called Tallulah. In view of this legend, it is worth noting that the Cherokee nation, before their departure for the distant West, always avoided the Falls of Tallulah and were seldom found hunting or fishing in their vicinity.<note>Letters from the Alleghany Mountains, pages 41-42.</note>

**Toccoa:** (1) A creek flowing into the Tugaloo River in Habersham County, with a waterfall on its upper course near the village of the same name. The lands around Toccoa Falls were sold by the Cherokee in 1783 and were owned at one time by Wafford's grandfather. Another tradition is that they were made while the surface of the newly created earth was still soft by a great army of birds and animals fleeing through the gap to escape some pursuing danger from the west—some say a great “drive hunt” by the Indians. Haywood confuses them with other petroglyphs in North Carolina connected with the story of the giant Tsul` kălû' (see number 81).

The following florid account of the carvings and the ostensible Indian tradition of their origin is from White, on the authority of Stevenson:

> The number visible or defined is 136; some of them are quite natural and perfect, and others are rather crude imitations, and most of them have become more or less obliterated by the effects of time. They include human feet ranging from those 4 inches in length to those of great warriors which measure 17 1/2 inches in length and 7 3/4 inches in breadth across the toes. What is somewhat curious is that all the human feet appear natural except this one, which has 6 toes, proving him to have been a descendant of a Titan. There are 26 of these impressions, all bare except one, which has the appearance of having worn moccasins. A well-formed hand, rather delicate, occupied a place near the great warrior, and was probably the impression of his wife's hand, who no doubt accompanied her husband in all his excursions, sharing his labors and soothing his worries. Many horse tracks are to be seen. One seems to have been shod, some are very small, and one measures 12 1/2 inches by 9 1/2 inches. The Cherokee say this was the footprint of the great war horse which their chieftain rode. The tracks of a great many turkeys, turtles, terrapins, a large bear's paw, a snake's trail, and the footprints of two deer are visible. The tradition respecting these impressions varies. One asserts that the world was once deluged with water, and men along with all living beings were destroyed, except for one family and various animals necessary to replenish the earth; that the Great Spirit, before the floods came, commanded them to embark in a big canoe, which after long sailing was drawn to this spot by a flock of swans and rested there; and here the whole troop of animals disembarked, leaving the impressions as they passed over the rock, which, being softened because of long submersion, kindly received and preserved them.

**WAR WOMAN'S CREEK:** Enters the Chattooga River in Rabun County, northeastern Georgia, in the heart of the old Lower Cherokee country. The name seems to be of Indian origin, although the Cherokee name is lost and the story has perished. A writer quoted by White (*Historical Collections of Georgia*, p. 444) attempts to show its origin from the exploit of a certain Revolutionary "Amazon" in capturing a party of Tories, but the name occurs in Adair (note, p. 185) as early as 1775. There is some reason for believing that it refers to a former female dignitary among the Cherokee, described by Haywood under the title of the “Pretty Woman” as having authority to decide the fate of prisoners of war. Wafford once knew an old woman whose name was Da'nă-gâ'stă, an abbreviated form for Da'năwă-gâsta'yă, “Sharp war,” understood to mean “Sharp (that is, Fierce) warrior.” Several cases of women acting the part of warriors are on record among the Cherokee.

### 126. PLANT LORE

The Cherokee have always been an agricultural people, and their ancestral land is a region of lush flora, with tall trees and tangled undergrowth on the slopes and ridges, and countless bright-tinted blossoms and sweet wild fruits along the running streams. The plant kingdom, consequently, holds a much more important place in the mythology and ceremonies of the tribe than it does among the Indians of the treeless plains and dry sage deserts of the West; most of the beliefs and customs in this connection center around the practice of medicine, as explained by the priests and doctors in every settlement. In general, it is believed that the plant world is friendly to the human species and is constantly at the willing service of the doctors to counteract the jealous hostility of the animals. The sacred formulas contain many curious instructions for the gathering and preparation of medicinal roots and barks, which are selected primarily according to the theory of correspondences.

The Indians are close observers, and some of their plant names are peculiarly apt. Thus the mistletoe, which never grows alone but is always found with its roots fixed in the bark of some supporting tree or shrub from which it draws its nourishment, is called by a name which means "it is married" (*uda'li*). The violet is still called by a plural name, *dinda'skwate'ski*, "they pull each other's heads off," showing that the Cherokee children have discovered a game not unknown among our own. The bear-grass (*Eryngium*), with its long, slender leaves like tiny blades of corn, is called *sălikwâ'yĭ*, "greensnake," and the larger grass known as Job's tears—on account of its glossy, rounded grains which the Indian children use for necklaces—is called *sel-utsĭ'*, "the mother of corn." The black-eyed Susan (*Rudbeckia*) of our children is the "deer-eye" (*a'wĭ'-aktă'*) of the Cherokee, and our lady-slipper (*Cypripedium*) is their "partridge moccasin" (*gŭgwĕ'-ulasu'la*). The May-apple (*Podophyllum*), with its umbrella-shaped top, is called *u'niskwetu'gi*, meaning "it wears a hat," while the white puffball fungus is *năkwĭsĭ'-usdĭ'*, "the little star," and the common rock lichen bears the musical, if rather unpoetic, name of *utsăle'ta*, "pot scrapings." Some plants are named from their real or supposed role in animal life, such as the wild rose, *tsist-unĭ'gistĭ*, "the rabbits eat it"—referring to the seed berries—and the shield fern (*Aspidium*), *yân-utse'stû*, "the bear lies on it." Others, again, are named for their domestic or ceremonial uses, such as the fleabane (*Erigeron canadense*), called *atsil'-sûñ'tĭ*, "fire maker," because its dried stalk was used in ancient times to produce fire by friction, and the bugle weed (*Lycopus virginicus*), known as *aniwanĭ'ski*, "talkers," because the chewed root, given to children to swallow or rubbed upon their lips, is supposed to grant them the gift of eloquence. A few plants, in addition to the ordinary term used by the common people, have a sacred or symbolic name, used

...only by the priests and doctors in the prayer formulas. Thus ginseng, or "sang," as it is more often called by the white mountaineers, is known to the common people as <term>*â'talǐ-gûlǐ'*</term>, "the mountain climber," but is addressed in the formulas as <term>*Yûñwǐ Usdi'*</term>, "Little Man," while <term>*selu*</term> (corn) is invoked under the name of <term>*Agawê'la*</term>, "The Old Woman." One or two plant names have their origin in myths; for instance, *Prosartes lanuginosa* bears the curious name <term>*wâlàs'-unûl'stǐ*</term>, "frogs fight with it," from a story that in the long ago—<term>*hǐlahi'yu*</term>—two quarrelsome frogs once fought a duel, using its stalks as lances. In its locative form, this was the name of a former Cherokee settlement in Georgia, which white settlers called "Fighting-town" due to a misunderstanding of the word's meaning. Regarding white clover, the Cherokee say that "it follows the white man."

The division of trees into evergreen and deciduous is explained by a myth, related elsewhere, according to which the loss of their leaves in winter is a punishment inflicted upon the deciduous trees for their failure to endure a trial to the end. Among the Cherokee, as with nearly all other tribes in both the East and West, the cedar is held more sacred than other trees. The reasons for this reverence are easily found in its evergreen needles, its balsamic fragrance, and the beautiful color of its fine-grained wood, which does not warp and is practically decay-resistant. Small green twigs are thrown onto the fire as incense during certain ceremonies, particularly to counteract the effect of <term>*asgina*</term> dreams, as it is believed that the <term>*anisgi'na*</term>, or malevolent ghosts, cannot endure the smell; however, the wood itself is considered too sacred to be used as fuel. In the war dance, the scalp trophies, stretched on small hoops, were hung upon a cedar sapling trimmed and decorated for the occasion. According to a myth, the red color of the wood comes originally from the blood of a wicked magician whose severed head was hung at the top of a tall cedar. The story is now almost forgotten, but it was probably nearly identical to one still existing among the Yuchi, former neighbors of the Cherokee. According to the Yuchi myth, a malevolent magician disturbed the daily course of the sun until, at last, two brave warriors sought him out and killed him in his cave. They cut off his head and brought it home with them to show the people, but it remained alive. To make it die, they were advised to tie it in the topmost branches of a tree. They did this, trying one tree after another, but each morning the head was found at the foot of the tree, still alive. Finally, they tied it in a cedar, and there the head remained until it died, while the blood slowly trickling down along the trunk gave the wood its red color; from then on, the cedar was a "medicine" tree.<note>1 Gatschet, Some Mythic Stories of the Yuchi Indians, in American Anthropologist, VI, p. 281, July, 1893.</note>

The linn or basswood (*Tilia*) is believed to never be struck by lightning, and the hunter caught in one of the frequent thunderstorms of

# MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19

the southern mountains always seeks its shelter. From its stringy bark are twisted the hunting belts worn about the waist. Sourwood (*Oxydendrum*) is used by the hunters for barbecue sticks to roast meat before the fire, on account of the acid flavor of the wood, which they believe is thus communicated to the meat. Spoons and combs are also carved from the wood, but it is never burned, from an idea that lye made from the ashes will bring sickness to those who use it in preparing their food. It is said also that if one should sleep beside a fire containing sourwood sticks, the sourwood “will barbecue him,” which may possibly mean that he will have hot or feverish pains thereafter.

The laurel, in its two varieties, large and small (*Rhododendron* and *Kalmia*, or “ivy”), is much used for spoons and combs, on account of its close grain, as also in medicine, but is never burned, as it is believed that this would bring on cold weather, and would furthermore destroy the medicinal virtues of the whole species. The reason given is that the leaves, when burning, make a hissing sound suggestive of winter winds and falling snow. When the doctor is making up a compound in which any part of the laurel is an ingredient, great precautions are taken to prevent any of the leaves or twigs from being swept into the fire, as this would render the decoction worthless. Sassafras is tabooed as fuel among the Cherokee, as also among their white neighbors, perhaps for the practical reason that it is apt to pop out of the fire when heated and might thus set the house on fire.

Pounded walnut bark is thrown into small streams to stupefy the fish, so that they may be easily dipped out in baskets as they float on the surface of the water. Should a pregnant woman wade into the stream at the time, its effect is nullified, unless she has first taken the precaution to tie a strip of the bark about her toe. A fire of post-oak and the wood of the <term>telûñ'lătĭ</term> or summer grape (*Vitis æstivalis*) is believed to bring a spell of warm weather even in the coldest winter season.

Mysterious properties attach to the wood of a tree which has been struck by lightning, especially when the tree itself still lives, and such wood enters largely into the secret compounds of the conjurers. An ordinary person among the laity will not touch it, for fear of having cracks come upon his hands and feet, nor is it burned for fuel, for fear that lye made from the ashes will cause consumption. In preparing ballplayers for the contest, the medicine-man sometimes burns splinters of it to coal, which he gives to the players to paint themselves with in order that they may be able to strike their opponents with all the force of a thunderbolt. Bark or wood from a tree struck by lightning, but still green, is beaten up and put into the water in which seeds are soaked before planting, to ensure a good crop, but, on the other hand, any lightning-struck wood thrown into the field will cause the crop to wither, and it is believed to have a bad effect even to go into the field immediately after having been near such a tree.

# MOONEY] PLANT LORE

Among all vegetables, the one that holds the first place in the household economy and ceremonial practices of the tribe is <term>selu</term>, "corn." It is invoked in sacred formulas under the name Agawe'la, "The Old Woman," in reference to its mythical origin from the blood of an old woman killed by her disobedient sons (see number 3, "Kana'ti and Selu"). In former times, the annual thanksgiving ceremony of the Green-corn dance—held before eating the first of the new corn—was the most solemn tribal event. It served as an act of atonement and forgiveness for the sins of the past year, an amnesty for public criminals, and a prayer for happiness and prosperity in the year to come. Only those who had properly prepared themselves through prayer, fasting, and purification were allowed to participate in this ceremony, and no one dared to taste the new corn until it was completed. Seven ears from the previous year’s crop were always carefully set aside to *attract the corn* until the new crop ripened and it was time for the dance, at which point they were eaten with the rest. When eating the first new corn after the Green-corn dance, people were careful not to blow on it to cool it, for fear of causing a windstorm that would beat down the standing crop in the field.

Much ceremony accompanied the planting and tending of the crop. Seven grains, the sacred number, were put into each hill, and these were not thinned out afterward. After the final working of the crop, the priest and an assistant—usually the owner of the field—went into the field and built a small enclosure (*detsânûn'li*) in the center. Entering it, they sat on the ground with their heads bowed. While the assistant remained perfectly silent, the priest, with a rattle in hand, sang songs of invocation to the spirit of the corn. Soon, according to traditional belief, a loud rustling would be heard outside. They would know this was caused by the "Old Woman" bringing the corn into the field, but neither man was allowed to look up until the song was finished. This ceremony was repeated for four consecutive nights, after which no one entered the field for seven more nights. Then the priest himself went in, and if all the sacred regulations had been properly followed, he was rewarded by finding young ears upon the stalks. The corn ceremonies could be performed by the owner of the field himself, provided he was willing to pay a sufficient fee to the priest to learn the songs and ritual. Care was always taken to keep a clean path from the field to the house, so that the corn might be encouraged to stay at home and not wander elsewhere. Most of these customs have now fallen into disuse, except among the elderly, by many of whom they are still religiously observed.

Another curious ceremony, of which even the memory is now almost forgotten, was performed after the first working of the corn. During this, the owner or priest stood at each of the four corners of the field in succession and wept and wailed loudly. Even the priests are now unable to give a reason for this ritual, which may have been a lament—

for the bloody death of Selu, just as the women of Byblos used to weep for Adonis.

Next to corn, the bean (<term>tuya</term>) is the most important food plant of the Cherokee and other southern Indians, for whom it is probably native, but there does not appear to be much special ceremony or folklore in connection with it. Beans that crack open during cooking are sometimes rubbed by mothers on the lips of their children in order to make them look smiling and good-tempered. The association of ideas seems to be the same as the one in Ireland that causes a fat, mealy potato that cracks open while boiling to be called a “laughing” potato. Melons and squashes must not be counted or examined too closely while still growing on the vine, or they will stop thriving; neither must one step over the vine, or it will wither before the fruit ripens. Anyone who has eaten a May-apple must not come near the vines under any circumstances, as this plant withers and dries up very quickly, and its presence would make the melons wither in the same way.

Tobacco was used as a sacred incense or as the guarantee of a solemn oath in nearly every important function—in binding the warrior to take up the hatchet against the enemy, in ratifying peace treaties, in confirming sales or other engagements, in seeking omens for the hunter, in driving away witches or evil spirits, and in regular medical practice. It was either smoked in a pipe or sprinkled upon the fire; it was never rolled into cigarettes, as was done among the tribes of the Southwest, nor was it ever smoked for the mere pleasure of the sensation. In recent years, white neighbors have taught the Indians to chew it, but the habit is not native. It is called <term>tsâlû</term>, a name that has lost its meaning in the Cherokee language but is explained by the related Tuscarora language, in which *charhû'*, “tobacco,” can still be analyzed as “fire to hold in the mouth,” showing that its use is as old as the knowledge of the plant itself. The tobacco originally used by the Cherokee, Iroquois, and other eastern tribes was not the common commercial tobacco (*Nicotiana tabacum*), which was introduced from the West Indies, but the *Nicotiana rustica*, or wild tobacco, now distinguished by the Cherokee as <term>tsâl-agăyûñ'li</term>, “old tobacco,” and by the Iroquois as “real tobacco.” Its various uses in ritual and medicine are better described under other headings. For the myth of its loss and recovery, see number 6, “How They Brought Back the Tobacco.” The cardinal flower (*Lobelia*), mullein (*Verbascum*), and one or two related species are called <term>tsâliyu'stĭ</term>, “like tobacco,” because of their general resemblance to it in appearance, but they were never used in the same way.

The poisonous wild parsnip (*Peucedanum?*) bears an unpleasant reputation because of its frequent use in evil spells, especially those intended to destroy the life of a victim. In one of these conjurations, seven pieces of the root are laid upon one hand and rubbed gently

...with the other, and the omen is taken from the position of the pieces when the hand is removed. It is also said that poisoners secretly mix it with the food of their intended victim; if he eats it, he soon becomes drowsy and, unless kept moving until the effect wears off, falls asleep never to wake again. Suicides are said to eat it to cause death. Before starting a journey, a small piece of the root is sometimes chewed and blown upon the body to prevent sickness, but the remedy is almost as bad as the disease, because snakes are said to resent the offensive smell by biting the person who carries it. Despite its poisonous qualities, a decoction of the root is frequently used for steaming patients in the sweat bath, based on the idea that the smell drives away disease spirits.

Poison oak or poison ivy (*Rhus radicans*), which is very common in the damp eastern forests, is feared as much by the Indians as by white people. When forced to approach it or work near it, the Cherokee attempts to win its favor by addressing it as "My friend" (<term>hi'gĭnaliï'</term>). If poisoned by it, he rubs the beaten flesh of a crawfish onto the affected area.

One variety of brier (*Smilax*) is called <term>dĭ'nû'skĭ</term>, "the breeder," because of a belief that if one of its thorns remains in the flesh, it will breed others within a day or two.

Ginseng, which is sold in large quantities to local traders and used in native medical practices, is called <term>âtalĭ-gûlĭ'</term>, "the mountain climber." However, priests address it as <term>Yûñwĭ Usdi'</term>, "Little Man," or <term>Yûñwĭ Usdi'ga Ada'wehĭ'yu</term>, "Little Man, Most Powerful Magician." This Cherokee sacred term, like the Chinese name, originates from how the root often resembles the shape of a human body. There are numerous beliefs and ceremonies regarding its gathering and preparation. The doctor constantly speaks of it as a sentient being, and it is believed to be able to make itself invisible to those who are unworthy to gather it. When hunting for it, the first three plants found are passed by. The fourth is taken after a preliminary prayer in which the doctor addresses it as the "Great <term>Ada'wehĭ</term>," and humbly asks permission to take a small piece of its flesh. Upon digging it from the ground, he drops a bead into the hole and covers it over, leaving it there as payment to the plant spirit. After that, he takes the plants as he finds them without further ceremony.

The catgut or devil's shoestring (*Tephrosia*) is called <term>distai'yĭ</term>, "they are tough," referring to its stringy roots. Cherokee women prepare a decoction from these roots to wash their hair, intending to give it the strength and toughness of the plant. A preparation of the leaves is also used by ballplayers to wash themselves to toughen their limbs. To allow them to spring quickly to their feet if thrown to the ground, the players also bathe their limbs with

...a decoction of the small rush (*Juncus tenuis*), which they say always returns to its upright position, no matter how often it is trampled down. The white seeds of the viper’s bugloss (*Echium vulgare*) were formerly used in many important ceremonies intended to look into the future, but they have now been replaced by the ordinary glass beads of the traders. The culver root (*Leptandra*) is used in love spells, with the omen being read from the movement of the root when held in the hand. The campion (*Silene stellata*), known locally as “rattlesnake’s master,” is called *ganidawâ'skĭ*, meaning “it disjoints itself,” because the dried stalk is said to break off at the joints, starting from the top. As among the white mountain settlers, the juice is considered an excellent remedy for snake bites, and it is even believed that the deadliest snake will flee from anyone who carries a small piece of the root in their mouth.

Almost all varieties of burs, from the Spanish needle up to the cocklebur and Jimsonweed, are grouped together under the generic name *u'nistilûn'istï*, which may be loosely translated as “stickers.” Because of their habit of clinging fast to whatever object they happen to touch, they are believed to have a mystical power for improving the memory and encouraging a stable character. Very soon after a child is born, one of the smaller species—preferably *Lespedeza repens*—is crushed, and a portion is put into a bowl of water taken from a waterfall or cataract where the stream makes a constant noise. This is given to the child to drink on four successive days, with the intention of making him quick to learn and able to retain in his memory anything heard once. The noise of the waterfall from which the water is taken is believed to be the voice of *Yûñwĭ Gûnahi'ta*, the “Long Man,” or river god, teaching lessons that the child may understand, while the stream itself is respected for its power to seize and hold anything cast upon its surface. A somewhat similar ceremony is sometimes used for adults, but in this case the process is much more difficult, as there are taboos for four or seven days. The mind must be kept fixed upon the purpose of the ritual throughout the entire period; if the person so far forgets himself as to lose his temper during that time, he will remain of a quarrelsome disposition forever after.

A flowering vine known as *nuniyu'stï*, or “potato-like,” which grows in cultivated fields and has a tuberous root somewhat resembling a potato, is used in hunting spells. The crushed root, from which a milky juice oozes, is rubbed upon the deer bleat (*a'wi'-ahyeli'skĭ*)—an instrument with which the hunter imitates the bleating of a fawn. This is done under the idea that the doe, hearing it, will think that her offspring wants to nurse and will therefore come all the sooner. The putty-root (also called Adam-and-Eve, *Aplectrum hiemale*), which is of an oily, sticky nature, is carried by the deer hunter. Upon shooting a deer, he puts a small piece of the chewed root into the wound, expecting as a necessary result to find the animal unusually fat when it is skinned. Infants who seem to waste away...

The root of the rare plant known as Venus' flytrap (*Dionaea*), which has the remarkable property of catching and digesting insects that land on it, is chewed by the fisherman and spat upon the bait so that no fish may escape him, and the plant is tied upon the fish trap for the same purpose.

The root of a plant called <term>unatlûnwe'hitû</term>, <gloss>"having spirals,"</gloss> is used in conjurations designed to make strangers view the subject favorably. The priest <term>"takes it to water"</term>—that is, he says certain prayers over it while standing close to a running stream—then chews a small piece and rubs and blows it upon the body and arms of the patient. This person is usually about to start a journey or take part in a council, with the result that all who meet him or listen to his words are at once pleased with his manner and appearance and are inclined to give every assistance to his projects.

### NOTES AND PARALLELS TO MYTHS

In preparing the following notes and parallels, the goal has been to include every Cherokee variant or pseudo-myth available from any source, and to provide some explanation of tribal customs and beliefs mentioned in the myths, especially those of the Southern tribes. A certain number of parallels have been included, but it is clear that this field is too vast to be treated within the limits of a single volume. Moreover, considering the small number of tribes that have been studied compared to the many still unstudied, it is doubtful whether the time is right for any extensive treatment of Indian mythology. The most complete index of parallels to appear so far is the one accompanying the excellent collection by Dr. Franz Boas, *Indianische Sagen von der nordpacifischen Küste Amerikas.*¹ In setting limits, it was necessary to restrict comparisons—except in a few special cases—to the territory of the United States or the immediate border country, even though this requires omitting several of the best collections, particularly those from the northwest coast and the interior of British America. Enough has been provided to show that our native tribes had their own myths without borrowing from other races. These myths were so widely and constantly spread through trade, travel, and the exchange of ceremonies over large areas that the Indian myth system was as much a single unit in this country as the Aryan myth structure was in Europe and Asia. Every additional tribal study is expected to confirm this result.

A more specialized study of Cherokee myths in connection with the tribe's medical and religious rituals is reserved for a future paper, a preliminary version of which was presented in the author's *Sacred Formulas of the Cherokees*, in the Seventh Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology.

STORIES AND STORYTELLERS (p. 229): *Migration legend*—In Buttrick's Antiquities² we find some mention of this migration legend, which, as presented by the missionary, is unfortunately so entangled with Biblical stories that it is almost impossible to isolate the genuine parts. He begins their story under the leadership of their "greatest prophet," <term>Wâsĭ</term>—who is simply Moses—in search of a distant country where they might be safe from their enemies. Who these enemies are, or where they live, is not stated. Soon after setting out, they come to a great body of water, which

Wâsĭ strikes with his staff; the water divides so that they pass through safely, and then rolls back and prevents pursuit by their enemies. They then enter a wilderness and come to a mountain, and we are treated to the Bible story of Sinai and the tablets of stone. Here they also receive sacred fire from heaven, which they carry with them thereafter until the house in which it is kept is finally destroyed by a hostile invasion. This portion of the myth seems to be genuine Indian (see notes to number 111, “The Mounds and the Constant Fire”).

In this journey, “the tribes marched separately, and also the clans. The clans were distinguished by having feathers of different colors fastened to their ears. They had two great standards, one white and one red. The white standard was under the control of the priests and used for civil purposes; but the red standard was under the direction of the war priests for purposes of war and alarm. These were carried when they journeyed, and the white standard was erected in front of the building mentioned above <note>the ark or palladium</note> when they rested.”

They cross four rivers in all—which accords with the Indian idea of the sacred four—and settle at last beyond the fourth, after having been on the march for many years. “Their whole journey through this wilderness was attended with great distress and danger. At one time they were beset by the most deadly kind of serpents, which destroyed many of the people, but at length their leader shot one with an arrow and drove them away. Again, they were walking along in single file when the ground cracked open and a number of people sank down and were destroyed as the earth closed upon them. At another time they nearly perished for water. Their headmen dug with their staffs in all the low places but could find no water. At length their leader found a most beautiful spring coming out of a rock.” <note>Buttrick, Antiquities of the Cherokee Indians, pp. 9–10.</note>

At one point in this migration, according to a tradition given to Schoolcraft by Stand Watie, they encountered a large river or other great body of water, which they crossed upon a bridge made by tying grapevines together. <note>Schoolcraft, Notes on the Iroquois, p. 359, 1847.</note> This idea of a vine bridge or ladder also occurs in the traditions of the Iroquois, Mandan, and other tribes.

Further on, the missionary already quoted says: “Shield-eater once asked if I had ever heard of houses with flat roofs, saying that his father’s great-grandfather used to say that their people once had a great town with a high wall around it; that on a certain occasion their enemies broke down part of this wall; that the houses in this town had flat roofs—though, he used to say, this was so long ago it is not worth talking about now.” <note>Buttrick, op. cit., p. 10.</note>

*Fire of cane splints*—Bartram thus describes the method as witnessed by him at Attasse (*Autossee*) among the Creeks around 1775. The fire that flared up so mysteriously may have been kept constantly smoldering below, as described in number 111:

This is done under an open shed or pavilion, twenty or thirty yards away, directly opposite the door of the council house. ### 1. HOW THE WORLD WAS MADE (p. 239):

Due to the decay of old traditions and the mixing in of Biblical ideas, the Cherokee creation myth is too broken down to be fully recovered except in disjointed fragments. The extent of this destruction can be seen by studying similar myths of the Iroquois or the Ojibwa. What is preserved here was obtained mainly from Swimmer and John Ax, the two most qualified authorities of the eastern band. The story of the evergreens is from <term>Ta'gwădihi'</term>. The incident of the brother striking his sister with a fish to make her pregnant was provided by <term>Ayâsta</term>, and may have a phallic meaning. John Ax says the pregnancy was caused by the “Little People,” <term>Yuñwĭ Tsunsdi'</term>, who commanded the woman to rub saliva (perhaps from the brother?) upon her back and to lie on her stomach, with her body completely covered, for seven days and nights; at the end of that period the child was born, and another followed every seven days thereafter until the interval was made longer. According to Wafford, the first man was created blind and remained so for some time. The incident of the buzzard shaping the mountains also appears in the creation myths of the Creeks² and Yuchi,³ southern neighbors of the Cherokee, though they say the first earth was brought up from under the water by a crawfish. Among the northern tribes, it is commonly the turtle that supports the earth on its back. The water beetle mentioned is the <term>Gyrinus</term>, known locally as the mellow bug or apple beetle. One version has the <term>dilsta'ya'tĭ</term>, or water-spider (“scissors,” <term>Dolomedes</term>), helping with the work. Nothing is mentioned about where the sun comes from. Some tribes believe it is a gaming wheel stolen from a race of superior beings. See also number 7, “The Journey to the Sunrise.”

The missionaries Buttrick and Washburn provide versions of the Cherokee creation story, both of which are so heavily distorted by Biblical interpretation as to be worthless. No recorded native myth about the origin of the universe goes back to the very first act of creation; instead, they all begin with a world and living creatures already in existence, though not in their final form or condition.

**Hand-breadth**—The Cherokee word is <term>utawá'hilú</term>, from <term>uwâyĭ</term>, hand. This should not be taken literally, but is a symbolic expression frequently used in sacred formulas to indicate a sequence of spaces. The idea of moving the sun several times to reduce extreme heat is found in other tribes. Buttrick, already mentioned, says in his account of Cherokee cosmology: “When God created the world, he made a heaven or firmament about as high as the mountain tops, but this was too warm. He then created a second, which was also too warm. He continued this until he had created seven heavens, and he made his home in the seventh. During some of their prayers, they raise their hands to the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh heavens,” etc.⁴

In Hindu cosmogony, we also find seven heavens or stages that increase in sanctity as they ascend; the Aztecs had nine, as did the ancient Scandinavians.<sup>1</sup> Some Polynesian tribes have ten, each built of azure stone with openings for communication. The lowest originally almost touched the earth and was raised to its present position by successive pushes from the gods Ru and Matti—resting first prostrate upon the ground, then upon their knees, then lifting with their shoulders, their hands, and their fingertips, until a final supreme effort sent it to its current place.<sup>2</sup>

*Seven: The sacred numbers*—In every tribe and cult throughout the world, we find sacred numbers. Christianity and the Christian world have three and seven. The Indian has always had four as the primary sacred number, with another usually only slightly less important. The two sacred numbers of the Cherokee are four and seven. The latter is the actual number of the tribal clans, the ritual number of upper worlds or heavens, and the ceremonial number of paragraphs or repetitions in the main formulas. Thus, in prayers for long life, the priest raises his client through successive stages to the first, second, third, fourth, and finally to the seventh heaven before the purpose is accomplished. The sacred four has a direct relation to the four cardinal points, while seven, in addition to these, includes "above," "below," and "here in the center." In many tribal rituals, color and sometimes sex are assigned to each direction. In the sacred Cherokee formulas, the spirits of the East, South, West, and North are, respectively, Red, White, Black, and Blue; each color also has its own symbolic meaning of Power (War), Peace, Death, and Defeat.

2. *THE FIRST FIRE* (p. 240): This myth was obtained from Swimmer and John Ax. It is also noted in Foster's "Sequoyah"<sup>3</sup> and in the Wahnenauhi manuscript.<sup>4</sup> The <term>uksu'hĭ</term> and the <term>gûle'gĭ</term> are, respectively, the *Coluber obsoletus* and *Bascanion constrictor*. The water-spider is the large hairy species *Argyroneta*.

In the version given in the Wahnenauhi manuscript, the Possum and the Buzzard make the first attempt but return unsuccessful; one loses the hair from his tail, while the other has the feathers scorched from his head and neck. In another version, the Dragon-fly assists the Water-spider by pushing the <term>tusti</term> from behind. In the corresponding Creek myth, as given in the Tuggle manuscript, the Rabbit obtains fire by the trick of touching a cap trimmed with sticks of rosin to the blaze while pretending to bend low in the dance. In the Jicarilla myth, the Fox steals fire by wrapping cedar bark around his tail and thrusting it into the blaze while dancing around the circle.<sup>5</sup>

3. <term>KANA'TĬ AND SELU: ORIGIN OF CORN AND GAME</term> (p. 242): This story was obtained in nearly the same form from Swimmer and John Ax (east) and from Wafford (west), and a version is also given in the Wahnenauhi manuscript. Hagar notes it briefly in his manuscript, "Stellar Legends of the Cherokee." So much of belief and custom depends upon the myth of <term>Kana'tĭ</term> that references to the main incidents are constant in the songs and formulas. It is one of those myths held so sacred that, in the old days, anyone who wished to hear it from the priest of the tradition had to first purify himself by "going to water"—that is, bathing in the running stream before daylight while still fasting—while the priest performed his mystic ceremonies upon the bank.

In his *Letters from the Alleghany Mountains*, written more than fifty years ago, Lanman gives (pages 136, 137) a very fair synopsis of this myth, locating the game
