preserve of Kana'tǐ, whom he portrays as an old Cherokee chief, in a traditional cave on the north side of the Black Mountain—now Mount Mitchell, in Yancey County, North Carolina, the highest peak east of the Rocky Mountains. After his father had disappeared and could not be found despite a long search, 

> "The boy fired an arrow toward the north, but it returned and fell at his feet, so he knew that his father had not traveled in that direction. He also fired one toward the east, the south, and the west, but they all came back in the same way. He then thought to fire one directly above his head, and it happened that this arrow never returned; thus, the boy knew that his father had gone to the spirit land. The Great Spirit was angry with the Cherokee nation, and to punish it for the foolish boy's offense, he tore away the cave from the side of the Black Mountain and left only a large cliff in its place, which is now a prominent feature. He then declared that a time would come when another race of men would possess the mountains where the Cherokees had flourished for many generations."

The story has numerous parallels in Indian myth—so many, in fact, that almost every important concept occurring in it is duplicated in the North, the South, and on the plains. It will probably also be found west of the mountains once enough material from that region has been collected. The Ojibwa story of "The Weendigoes"¹ in particular has many striking points of resemblance; so does the Omaha myth, "Two-faces and the Twin Brothers," as recorded by Dorsey.²

*His wife was Selu, "Corn"*—In Cherokee belief, as in the mythologies of nearly every eastern tribe, the corn spirit is a woman, and the plant itself originally grew from the blood drops or the dead body of the Corn Woman. In the Cherokee sacred formulas, the corn is sometimes invoked as Agawe'la, "The Old Woman," and one myth (number 72, "The Hunter and Selu") tells how a hunter once witnessed the transformation of a growing stalk into a beautiful woman.

In the Creek myth "Origin of Indian Corn," as found in the Tuggle manuscript, the corn plant appears to be the transformed body of an old woman whose only son, gifted with magic powers, developed from a single drop of her (menstrual?) blood.

In Iroquois legend, according to Morgan, the corn plant grew from the bosom of the mother of the Great Spirit <note>The author uses "sic" here to indicate the original phrasing in his source</note> after her burial. The spirits of corn, bean, and squash are represented as three sisters. 

> "They are supposed to have the forms of beautiful women, to be very fond of each other, and to delight in living together. This last belief is illustrated by the natural way the plants themselves grow up together in the same field and perhaps from the same hill."³

*Sprang from blood*—This concept of a child born from blood drops reappears in the Cherokee story of Tsul'kalû' (see number 81). Its occurrence among the Creeks has just been noted. It is also found among the Dakota (Dorsey, "The Blood-clots Boy," in *Contributions to North American Ethnology*, IX, 1893), Omaha (Dorsey, "The Rabbit and the Grizzly Bear," *Cont. to N. A. Eth.*, VI, 1890), Blackfeet ("Kutoyis," in Grinnell, "*Blackfoot Lodge Tales*"; New York, 1892), and other tribes. Usually, the child born this way has a wilder and more mischievous nature than is common.

*Deer shut up in hole*—The Indian belief that game animals were originally shut up in a cave, from which they were later released by accident or trickery, is very widespread. In the Tuggle version of the Creek account of the creation of the earth, we find the deer shut up this way and later set free. The Iroquois "believed that the game animals were not always free, but were enclosed in a cavern..."

where they had been concealed by Tawiskara'; but so that they might increase and fill the forest, Yoskehä' gave them freedom."¹ The same idea occurs in the Omaha story of "Ictinike, the Brothers and Sister" (Dorsey, in Contributions to North American Ethnology, <term>vi</term>, 1890). The Kiowa tell how the buffalo were kept imprisoned this way by the Crow until they were released by Sinti when the people were all starving for want of meat. When the buffalo so suddenly and completely disappeared from the plains about twenty-five years ago, the prairie tribes were unable to realize that they had been exterminated, but for a long time cherished the belief that they had been shut up again by the superior power of the whites in some underground prison, from which the spells of their own medicine men would yet bring them back (see references in the author's Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians, in Seventeenth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, part 1, 1901). The Kiowa tradition is almost exactly paralleled among the Jicarilla (Russell, Myths of the Jicarilla Apaches, in Journal of American Folk-Lore, Oct., 1898).

*Storehouse*—The <term>unwadâ'lĭ</term>, or storehouse for corn, beans, dried pumpkins, and other provisions, was a feature of every Cherokee homestead and was probably common to all the southern tribes. Lawson describes it this way among the Santee in South Carolina about the year 1700:

> "They make themselves cribs in a very ingenious manner, in which they secure their corn from pests, which are more frequent in these warm climates than in countries farther from the sun. These fine structures are commonly supported by eight feet or posts about seven feet high from the ground, well smeared inside and out over laths with loam or clay, which makes them tight and fit to keep out the smallest insect. There is a small door at the gable end, which is made of the same material and is to be removed whenever they like, being no larger than what a slender man may crawl through. They seal the door with the same earth when they take the corn out of the crib and leave home, always finding their granaries in the same condition they left them—theft from one another being completely unpracticed."²

*Rubbed her stomach*—This miraculous gathering of provisions by rubbing the body occurs also in number 76, "The Bear Man."

*Knew their thoughts*—Mind reading is a frequent concept in Indian myth and occurs in more than one Cherokee story.

*Seven times*—The idea of sacred numbers has already been noted, and the constant recurrence of seven in the present myth exemplifies well the importance of that number in Cherokee ritual.

*A tuft of down*—In the Omaha story, "The Corn Woman and the Buffalo Woman" (Dorsey, Contributions to North American Ethnology, <term>vi</term>, 1890), the magician changes himself into a feather and allows himself to be blown about by the wind in order to accomplish his purpose. The wolf does the same in a Thompson River myth.³ The self-transformation of the hero into a tuft of bird's down, a feather, a leaf, or some other light object, which is then carried by the wind wherever he wishes to go, is very common in Indian myth.

*Play ball against them*—This is a Cherokee figurative expression for a contest of any kind, more particularly a battle.

*Left an open space*—When the Cherokee conjurer, by his magic spells, coils the great (invisible) serpent around the house of a sick man to keep off the witches, he is always careful to leave a small space between the head and tail of the snake, so that the members of the family can go down to the spring to get water.

434 MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19

Wolves—The wolf is regarded as the servant and watchdog of Kana'tǐ. See number 15, "The Four-footed Tribes."

*From these all have descended*—In nearly every Indian mythology, we find the idea that certain animal tribes are descended from a single survivor of a great slaughter by an early hero-god or trickster. For example, the Kiowa say that all the prairie dogs on the plains are descended from a single little fellow who was too wary to close his eyes, as his companions did, when the hungry wanderer Sinti was planning to capture them all for his dinner under the pretense of teaching them a new dance.

A gaming wheel—This was the stone wheel or circular disk used in the wheel-and-stick game called *gatayûstǐ* by the Cherokee, which in one form or another was practically universal among the tribes. It was the game played by the great mythical gambler Ûñtsaiyǐ' (see number 63). It has sometimes been known in the north as the "snow-snake," while early southern traders called it *chunki* or *chungkey*, a corruption of the Creek name. Timberlake (page 77) mentions it under the name *nettecawaw*—for which there seems to be no other authority—as he saw it among the Cherokee in 1762.<note>Memoirs, p. 77.</note> It was also noted among the Carolina tribes by Lederer in 1670 and Lawson in 1701. John Ax, the oldest man now living among the East Cherokee, is the only one remaining in the tribe who has ever played the game, having been instructed in it as a small boy by an old man who wished to keep the memory of the ancient traditions alive. The sticks used have long since disappeared, but the stones remain and are frequently picked up in plowed fields, especially in the neighborhood of mounds. The best description of the southern game is given by Adair:

> "Near their council house, they have a square piece of ground that is well cleared, and fine sand is carefully spread over it when necessary to allow for swifter motion for the objects they throw along the surface. Only one or two people on each side play this ancient game. They use a stone about two fingers broad at the edge and two spans around. Each side has a pole about eight feet long, smooth and tapering at each end, with flat points. They start off side-by-side six yards from the end of the playground; then one of them hurls the stone on its edge, in as straight a line as possible, a considerable distance toward the middle of the other end of the square. When they have run a few yards, each person throws his pole—which has been rubbed with bear oil—with the force he estimates is needed to match the motion of the stone, so that the end may lie close to the stone. When this happens, the person scores two points, and one point is awarded based on how close the poles are to the mark, unless both are found to be at an equal distance from the stone upon measurement. In this manner, the players will keep running for most of the day at half-speed under the intense heat of the sun, wagering their silver ornaments, their nose, finger, and earrings, their breast, arm, and wrist plates, and even all their clothing except for what barely covers their midsections. All the American Indians are very fond of this game, which appears to us to be a task of mindless drudgery. It seems, however, to be of early origin, from a time when their forefathers practiced diversions as simple as their customs. The throwing stones they use now have been rubbed smooth on rocks since time immemorial and with immense labor. They are kept with the strictest religious care from one generation to another and are never buried with the dead. They belong to the town where they are used and are carefully preserved."<note>History of the American Indians, p. 401.</note>

In one version of the Kana'tǐ myth, the wheel is an arrow, which the wild boy shoots toward the four cardinal points and finally straight upward, until it no longer returns. When they go above the sky, they find Kana'tǐ and Selu sitting together with the arrow sticking in the ground in front of them. In the Creek story, "The Lion [Panther?] and the Little Girl," from the Tuggle collection, the lion has a wheel "which could find anything that was lost."

435 [MOONEY] NOTES AND PARALLELS

*The twilight land*—Usûñhi'yĭ, "Where it is always growing dark," the spirit land in the west. This is the word constantly used in the sacred formulas to denote the west, instead of the ordinary word Wude'ligûñ'yĭ, "Where it sets." In the same way Nûñdâ'yĭ, or Nûñdâgûñ'yĭ, the "Sun place, or region," is the formal name for the east instead of Digâlûñgûñ'yĭ, "Where it [the sun] comes up," the ordinary term. These archaic expressions give to myths and formulas a peculiar beauty which is lost in translation. As the interpreter once said, "I love to hear these old words."

*Struck by lightning*—Among the American tribes, as in Europe, a mysterious power is attributed to the wood of a tree which has been struck by lightning. The Cherokee conjurers claim to do wonderful things by means of such wood. Splinters of it are frequently buried in the field to make the corn grow. It must not be forgotten that the boys in this myth are Thunder Boys.

*The end of the world*—See notes to number 7, "The Journey to the Sunrise."

*Anisga'ya Tsunsdi'*—Abbreviated from Anisga'ya Tsunsdi'ga, "Little Men." These two sons of Kana'tĭ, who are sometimes called Thunder Boys and who live in Usûñhi'yĭ above the sky vault, must not be confused with the Yûñwĭ Tsunsdi', or "Little People," who are also Thunderers, but who live in caves in the rocks and cause the short, sharp claps of thunder. There is also the Great Thunderer, the thunder of the whirlwind and the hurricane, who seems to be identical to Kana'tĭ himself.

*Deer songs*—The Indian hunters of the olden time had many songs intended to call up the deer and the bear. Most of these have perished, but a few are still remembered. They were sung by the hunter, with some accompanying ceremony, to a sweetly mournful tune, either before starting out or on reaching the hunting ground. One Cherokee deer song, sung with repetition, may be freely translated:

->O Deer, you stand close by the tree,<-
->You sweeten your saliva with acorns,<-
->Now you are standing near,<-
->You have come where your food rests on the ground.<-

Gatschet, in his *Creek Migration Legend* (I, p. 79), gives the following translation of a Hichitee deer hunting song:

->Somewhere (the deer) lies on the ground, I think; I walk about.<-
->Awake, arise, stand up!<-
->It is raising up its head, I believe; I walk about.<-
->Awake, arise, stand up!<-
->It attempts to rise, I believe; I walk about.<-
->Awake, arise, stand up!<-
->Slowly it raises its body, I think; I walk about.<-
->Awake, arise, stand up!<-
->It has now risen on its feet, I presume; I walk about.<-
->Awake, arise, stand up!<-

### 4. ORIGIN OF DISEASE AND MEDICINE (p. 250)

This myth was obtained first from Swimmer, as explaining the theory upon which the medical practice of the Cherokee doctor is based. It was afterward heard, with less detail, from John Ax (east) and James Wafford (west). It was originally published in the author's *Sacred Formulas of the Cherokees*, in the *Seventh Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology*.

In the mythology of most Indian tribes, as well as of primitive peoples generally, disease is caused by animal spirits, ghosts, or witchcraft, and the doctor's efforts are directed chiefly to driving out the malevolent spirit. In Creek belief, according to the Tuggle manuscript, "all disease is caused by the winds, which are born in the air and then descend to the earth." It is doubtful, however, if this statement is

### 5. THE DAUGHTER OF THE SUN: ORIGIN OF DEATH (p. 252): 

This is one of the principal myths of the Cherokee, and like most of its class, has several variants. The sequel has an obvious resemblance to the myth of Pandora. It was obtained in whole or in part from Swimmer, John Ax, James Blythe, and other members of the eastern band. The version mainly followed is that of Swimmer, which differs in important details from that of John Ax.

As told by John Ax, it is the Sun herself, instead of her daughter, who is killed; the daughter was assigned the duty of lighting the earth after the death of her mother, the original Sun. The only snakes mentioned are the Spreading Adder and the Rattlesnake; the first is a transformed man, while the other is a stick, upon which the Little Men cut seven rings before throwing it in the pathway of the Sun, where it becomes a rattlesnake. The seven rods or staves of the Swimmer version are, according to John Ax, seven corncobs, which are thrown at the girl as she passes in the dance (compare with the Hagar variant of number 8 in the notes). The Little Men (see number 3, "Kana'tĭ and Selu," and other stories) belong to the John Ax version. The others have only a conjurer or chief to direct proceedings.

This myth is noted in the Payne manuscript, dated about 1835, and quoted in Squier, Serpent Symbol, page 67:

> "The Cherokees state that a number of beings were engaged in the creation. The Sun was made first. The creators intended for humans to live forever. But the Sun, when he passed over, told them that there was not enough land and that it would be better for people to die. At length the daughter of the Sun, who was with them, was bitten by a snake and died. The Sun, on his return, inquired for her and was told that she was dead. He then consented that human beings might live forever, and told them to take a box and go where the spirit of his daughter was and bring it back to her body. He charged them that when they captured her spirit, they should not open the box until they had arrived where her body was. However, impelled by curiosity, they opened it, contrary to the Sun’s command, and the spirit escaped; and then the fate of all humans was decided—that they must die."

This is copied without credit by Foster, Sequoyah, page 241.

Another version is given by the missionary Buttrick, who died in 1847, in his Antiquities of the Cherokee Indians, page 3:

> "Soon after the creation, one of the family was bitten by a serpent and died. Every possible means was used to bring back life, but in vain. Being defeated in this first instance, the whole race was doomed to follow, not only to death, but to misery afterward, as it was supposed—"

that the person had gone to a place of suffering. Another tradition says that soon after the creation, a young woman was bitten by a snake and died. Her spirit went to a certain place, and the people were told that if they could bring her spirit back to her body, the body would live again, and they would prevent the general mortality of all people. Therefore, some young men set out with a box to catch the spirit. They went to a place and saw it dancing about; eventually, they caught it in the box and shut the lid to trap it, and then they started back. However, the spirit constantly pleaded with them to open the box to let in a little light. They hurried on until they arrived near the place where the body was. Then, because of her intense pleading, they opened the lid just a tiny bit. The spirit flew out and was gone, and with it all their hopes for immortality.

In a version noted by Hagar, the messengers carry four staffs and travel for seven days to the <term>ghost country</term>. "They found her dancing in the land of spirits. They struck her with the first 'stick,' but it had no effect. They struck her with the second, and she stopped dancing. They struck her with the third, and she looked around. They struck her with the fourth, and she came to them. They made a box and placed her in it." One informant told him: "Only one man ever returned from the land of souls. He went there in a dream after a snake had bitten him in the forehead. He, Turkey-head, came back seven days later and described everything. The dead go eastward at first, then westward to the Land of Twilight. It is in the west in the sky, but not among the stars" (Stellar Legends of the Cherokee, MS, 1898).

In a Shawano myth, a girl dies, and after mourning her for a long time, her brother sets out to bring her back from the land of shadows. He travels west until he reaches the place where the earth and sky meet. Then he goes through and climbs up on the other side until he comes to the house of a great, kind spirit who is called "grandfather," according to the Indian system of respect. Upon learning his mission, this helper gives him "medicine" to enable him to enter the spirit world and instructs him on how and in what direction to go to find his sister. "He said she would be at a dance, and when she rose to join the movement, he must seize her and place her in the hollow of a reed he was given, covering the opening with the end of his finger." He follows the instructions, secures his sister, and returns to his teacher's house. The teacher transforms both of them back into physical beings again and, after giving them sacred rituals to take back to their tribe, sends them away by a shorter route through a trapdoor in the sky.<sup>1</sup>

In an Algonquian myth from New Brunswick, a grieving father seeks his son’s soul in the spirit domain of <term>Papkootpawut</term>, the Indian Pluto <note>The ruler of the underworld</note>. The spirit gives the soul to him in the shape of a nut, which he is told to insert into his son's body to bring the boy back to life. He puts it into a pouch and returns with the friends who had accompanied him. Preparations are made for a dance of celebration. "The father, wishing to participate, gave his son's soul to the care of a woman standing nearby. Curious to see it, she opened the bag; the soul escaped immediately and flew back to the realms of Papkootpawut."<sup>2</sup>

In a myth from British Columbia, two brothers go on a similar mission to bring back their mother's soul. After crossing a large lake, they approach the shore of the spirit world and hear the sound of singing and dancing in the distance. However, they are stopped at the landing by a guardian who tells them: "Your mother is here, but you cannot enter while alive to see her, nor can you take her away." One of them said, "I must see her!" Then the guardian took his physical body away from him, and he entered. The other brother returned home.<sup>3</sup>

In the ancient Egyptian legend of Râ and Isis, preserved in a Turin papyrus dating from the twentieth dynasty, the goddess Isis, wishing to force the secret of his power from the great god Râ, the sun, sends a serpent to bite him. Her intention was to demand the secret for herself as the price of her assistance. Taking some of her spittle, "Isis kneaded it together with the earth that was there with her hand. She made from it a sacred serpent to which she gave the form of a spear. She . . . threw it on the path that the great god traversed in his double kingdom whenever he wished. The venerable god advanced, the gods who served him as their Pharaoh followed him, and he went forth as he did every day. Then the sacred serpent bit him. The divine god opened his mouth and his cry reached heaven . . . The poison seized his flesh," etc.¹

*The sky vault*—See other references in story number 1, "How the World was Made;" story number 3, "Kanati and Selu," and story number 7, "The Journey to the Sunrise."

*My grandchildren*—The Sun calls the people <term>tsûñgili'sĭ</term>, "my grandchildren," which is the term used by maternal grandparents; the corresponding term used by paternal grandparents is <term>tsûñgini'sĭ</term>. The Moon calls the people <term>tsûñkina'tlĭ</term>, "my younger brothers," a term used by a male speaker, as the Moon is personified as a man in Cherokee mythology. The corresponding term used by a female is <term>tsûñkitâ'</term>.

*The Little Men*—The Thunder Boys, sons of Kana'tĭ (see story number 3, "Kana'tĭ and Selu"). They are always represented as beneficent wonder workers of great power.

*Changed to snakes*—The Cherokee names for the rattlesnake (*Crotalus*), copperhead (*Trigonocephalus*), and spreading adder (*Heterodon*) are, respectively, <term>utsa'natĭ</term>, "he has a bell" (?); <term>wâ'dige'i askâ'li</term>, "red-brown head"; and <term>da'likstă'</term>, "vomiter," named for its habit of vomiting yellow slime, as described in the story. For more information regarding the Uktena, see story number 50, "The Uktena and the Ulûñsû'tĭ."

*Hand-breadth*—See the note for story number 1, "How the World was Made."

### 6. HOW THEY BROUGHT BACK THE TOBACCO (p. 254):
The first version of this myth as given here was obtained from Swimmer and agrees with the version from John Ax, except that for the hummingbird, John Ax substitutes the <term>wasulû</term>, or large red-brown moth, which flies around the tobacco flower in the evening. He states that it was selected because it could fly so quietly that it would not be noticed. The second version was obtained from Wafford, in the Cherokee Nation West, who heard it from his great-uncle nearly ninety years ago; it differs so much from the other that it seemed best to provide it separately. The incident of the tree that grows taller as the man climbs it has close parallels in the mythology of the Kiowa and other Western tribes, but it has no obvious connection with the story. It is likely either one of a series of adventures originally belonging to the journey or a fragment from a forgotten myth. It should be mentioned that Wafford was a man of a rather practical character with little interest in or memory for stories, and he could only recall details for a few of the many he had heard as a boy.

In his *Letters from the Alleghany Mountains*, pages 119-121, Lanman provides the story as he received it in 1848 from Chief Kâlahû (see p. 173), who is still well-remembered by those who knew him as an authority on tribal traditions and rituals. In the Kâlahû version, the story is connected with Hickorynut Gap, a remarkable pass in the Blue Ridge southeast of Asheville, North Carolina. A comparison with later versions clearly shows how much has been lost over fifty years. The entire body of Cherokee tradition has likely suffered a similar loss.

> "Before visiting this remarkable passage through the mountains <note>Hickorynut Gap</note>, I tried to determine from the Cherokees of Quallatown its original Indian

name, but without success. It was my good fortune, however, to obtain a romantic legend connected with it. I heard it from the lips of a chief who prides himself on the two names of All-bones and Flying-squirrel, and although he took no less than two hours to tell the story, I will try to give it to my readers in about five minutes.

“There was a time when the Cherokees were without the famous *tso-lungh*, or tobacco weed, which they had previously been introduced to by a wandering stranger from the far east. After smoking it in their large stone pipes, they became eager to get it in abundance. They learned that the country where it grew in the greatest quantities was located by the great waters, and that the gateway to that country (a massive gorge among the mountains) was perpetually guarded by a huge number of little people or spirits. A council of the bravest men in the nation was called, and while they were discussing the dangers of visiting the unknown country and bringing back a large knapsack of the fragrant tobacco, a young man stepped forward boldly and said that he would take on the task. The young warrior left on his mission and never returned. The Cherokee nation was now in great distress, and another council was held to decide on a new plan. At this council, a famous magician rose and expressed his willingness to relieve his people of their difficulties; he informed them that he would visit the tobacco country and see what he could achieve. He turned himself into a mole, and in that form appeared east of the mountains; but after being chased by the guardian spirits, he was forced to return without any prize. He next turned himself into a humming-bird and succeeded, to a very limited extent, in getting what he needed. On returning to his country, he found many of his friends at the point of death because of their intense desire for the fragrant weed; then he placed some of it in a pipe, and after blowing the smoke into the nostrils of those who were sick, they all revived and were quite happy. The magician now decided that he would avenge the loss of the young warrior and at the same time become the sole owner of all the tobacco in the unknown land. He therefore turned himself into a whirlwind, and in passing through the Hickorynut gorge, he stripped the mountains of their plants and scattered huge rocks in every part of the narrow valley; because of this, the little people were all frightened away, and he was the only being in the country east of the mountains. In the bed of a stream, he found the bones of the young warrior, and after bringing them back to life and turning himself into a man again, the two returned to their own country heavily loaded with tobacco. Ever since that time, it has been very plentiful throughout the whole land.”

In the Iroquois story of “The Lad and the Chestnuts,” the Cherokee myth is mirrored, substituting a chestnut tree guarded by a white heron for the tobacco plant watched by the *dagûl'kû* geese (see Smith, Myths of the Iroquois, in Second Annual Report Bureau of Ethnology, 1883).

*Tobacco*—Tobacco, as is well known, is of American origin and is sacred among nearly all our tribes, holding an important place in almost every formal or religious ceremony. The tobacco of commerce (*Nicotiana tabacum*) was introduced from the West Indies. The original tobacco of the Cherokee and other eastern tribes was the “wild tobacco” (*Nicotiana rustica*), which they now distinguish as *tsâl-agayûñ'li*, “old tobacco.” Among the Iroquois, the same species is called the “real tobacco.”

*Dagûl'kû geese*—The *dagûl'kû* is the American white-fronted goose (*Anser albifrons gambeli*). It is said to have been of a bluish-white color and to have been common in the low country toward the coast, but very rare in the mountains. Around the end of September, it goes south and can be heard at night flying far overhead and crying *dugalû! dugalû! dugalû!* Swimmer had heard them passing over but had never seen one.

### 7. THE JOURNEY TO THE SUNRISE (p. 255): 
This story, obtained from John Ax, with additional details by Swimmer and Wafford, has parallels in many tribes. Swimmer did not know the burial incident, but said—evidently a more recent addition—that when they came near the sunrise, they found a race of black men at work there. It is somewhat remarkable that the story says nothing about the travelers reaching the ocean, as the Cherokee were well aware of its proximity.

*What the Sun is like*—According to the Payne manuscript, already quoted, the Cherokee anciently believed that the world, the first man and woman, and the sun and moon were all created by a number of beneficent beings who came down for that purpose from an upper world, to which they afterward returned, leaving the sun and moon as their deputies to finish and rule the world created in this way. “Hence, whenever the believers in this system offer a prayer to their creator, they mean by the creator the Sun and Moon. As to which of these two was supreme, there seems to have been a wide difference of opinion. In some of their ancient prayers, they speak of the Sun as male and consider, of course, the Moon as female. In others, however, they invoke the Moon as male and the Sun as female because, as they say, the Moon is vigilant and travels by night. But both Sun and Moon, as we have before said, are adored as the creator. . . . The expression, ‘Sun, my creator,’ occurs frequently in their ancient prayers. Indeed, the Sun was generally considered the superior in their devotions” (quoted in Squier, *Serpent Symbol*, p. 68). Haywood, in 1823, says: “The sun they call the day moon or female, and the night moon the male” (*Natural and Aboriginal History of Tennessee*, p. 266). According to Swimmer, there is also a tradition that the Sun had a cannibalistic habit and was once seen in human form killing and devouring human beings. Sun and Moon are sister and brother. See number 8, “The Moon and the Thunders.”

The Indians of the Thompson River, British Columbia, say of the sun that formerly, “He was a man and a cannibal, killing people on his travels every day. . . . He hung up the people whom he had killed during his day’s travel when he reached home, taking down the bodies of those whom he had hung up the night before and eating them.” He was finally induced to abandon his cannibalistic habit (Teit, *Thompson River Traditions*, p. 53).

*In the same grave*—This reminds us of the adventure in the voyage of Sinbad the Sailor, as narrated in the *Arabian Nights*. The sacrifice of the wife at her husband’s funeral was an ancient custom in the Orient and in parts of Africa, and it still survives in the Hindu suttee. It may once have had a counterpart in America, but so far as is known to the author, the nearest approach to it was found in the region of the lower Columbia and adjacent northwest coast, where a slave was frequently buried alive with the corpse.

*Vault of solid rock*—The sky vault, which is constantly rising and falling at the horizon and crushes those who try to go beyond it, occurs in the mythologies of the Iroquois of New York, the Omaha and the Sioux of the plains, the Tillamook of Oregon, and other widely separated tribes. The Iroquois concept is given by Hewitt, “Rising and Falling of the Sky,” in *Iroquois Legends*, in the *American Anthropologist* for October 1892. In the Omaha story of “The Chief’s Son and the Thunders” (Dorsey, *Contributions to North American Ethnology*, vi, 1890), a party of travelers in search of adventures “came to the end of the sky, and the end of the sky was going down into the ground.” They tried to jump across, and all succeeded except one, who failed to clear the distance, and “the end of the sky carried him away under the ground.” The others go on behind the other world and return the same way. In the Tillamook myth, six men go traveling and reach “the lightning door, which opened and closed with great rapidity and force.” They get through safely, but one is caught on the return journey and has his back cut in half by the descending sky (Boas, *Traditions of the Tillamook Indians*, in *Journal of American Folk-Lore*, Jan. 1898). See also number 1, “How the World was Made” and number 3, “Kana'ti and Selu.”

MOONEY] NOTES AND PARALLELS

**8. THE MOON AND THE THUNDERS (p. 256):** The story of the Sun and the Moon, as given here, was obtained first from Swimmer and afterward from other informants. It is noted by Hagar, in his manuscript *Stellar Legends of the Cherokee*, where one narrator describes the girl blackening her brother's face with seven (charred?) corn cobs (compare with John Ax's version of number 5 in the notes). Exactly the same myth is found among the native tribes of Greenland, Panama, Brazil, and Northern India. Among the Khasias of the Himalaya mountains, "the changes of the moon are accounted for by the theory that this orb, who is a man, monthly falls in love with his mother-in-law, who throws ashes in his face. The Sun is female." On some northern branches of the Amazon, "the Moon is represented as a maiden who fell in love with her brother and visited him at night, but who was finally betrayed by him passing his blackened hand over her face." Among the Greenland Eskimo, the Sun and Moon are sister and brother who were playing in the dark, "when Malina, being teased in a shameful manner by her brother Anninga, smeared her hands with the soot of the lamp and rubbed them over the face and hands of her persecutor, so that she might recognize him by daylight. This is the origin of the spots on the moon" (see Timothy Harley, *Moon Lore*, London, 1885, and the story "The Sun and the Moon," in Henry Rink's *Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo*, London, 1875). In British Columbia, the same incident occurs in the story of a girl and her lover, who was a dog transformed into the likeness of a man (Teit, *Thompson River Traditions*, p. 62). A very similar myth occurs among the Cheyenne, in which the chief personages are human, but the offspring of their connection become the Pleiades (A. L. Kroeber, *Cheyenne Tales*, in *Journal of American Folk-Lore*, July, 1900). In nearly all mythologies, the Sun and Moon are sister and brother, with the Moon generally being masculine while the Sun is feminine (compare with German, *Der Mond, Die Sonne*).

The myth connecting the moon with the ball game is from Haywood (*Natural and Aboriginal History of Tennessee*, p. 285), apparently on the authority of Charles Hicks, a mixed-blood chief.

*Eclipse*—Regarding the myth of the eclipse monster, which may be frightened away by all sorts of horrible noises, it is enough to say that it is universal (see Harley, *Moon Lore*). The Cherokee name for the phenomenon is *núñdă' walá'si u'giskă'*, "the frog is swallowing the sun or moon." Adair says (*History of the American Indians*, p. 65):
> "The first lunar eclipse I saw after I lived with the Indians was among the Cherokee in the year 1736, and during its continuance, their conduct appeared very surprising to one who had not seen the like before. They all ran wild, this way and that way, like lunatics, firing their guns, whooping and shouting, beating kettles, ringing horse bells, and making the most horrible noises that human beings possibly could. This was the result of their natural philosophy and done to assist the suffering moon."

*Sun and moon names*—In probably every tribe, both the sun and moon are called by the same name, accompanied by a distinguishing adjective.

*The Thunders*—The Cherokee name for Thunder, *Ani'-Hyûñ'tĭkwălâ'skĭ*, is an animate plural form and signifies literally, "The Thunderers" or "They who make the Thunder." The great Thunderers are *Kana'tǐ* and his sons (see the story), but inferior thunder spirits inhabit all the cliffs and mountains, and more particularly the great waterfalls, such as Tallulah, whose never-ceasing roar is believed to be the voice of the Thunderers speaking to those who can understand. A similar conception prevailed among the Iroquois and the eastern tribes generally. Adair says (*History of the American Indians*, p. 65), speaking of the southern tribes:
> "I have heard them say, when it rained, thundered, and blew sharply for a considerable time, that the beloved or holy people were at war above the clouds; and they believe that the war at such times is moderate or intense in proportion to the noise and violence of the storm."

In Portuguese West Africa also, the Thunderers are twin brothers who quarreled and went, one to the east and the other to the west, from where each answers the

*Rainbow*—The conception of the rainbow as the beautiful dress of the Thunder god also occurs among the South Sea islanders. In Mangaia, it is the girdle of the god Tangaroa, which he loosens and allows to hang down until the end reaches the earth whenever he wishes to descend (Gill, *Myths and Songs of the South Pacific*, p. 44). For some unexplained reason, the dread of pointing at the rainbow—under the penalty of having the finger wither or become misshapen—is found among most of the tribes even to the Pacific coast. The author first heard of this from a Puyallup boy at Puget Sound, Washington.

9. WHAT THE STARS ARE LIKE (p. 257): This story, told by Swimmer, embodies the old tribal belief. A different informant told Hagar: “Stars are birds. We know this because one once shot from the sky to the ground, and some Cherokee who looked for it found a little bird, about the size of a chicken just hatched, where it fell” (MS *Stellar Legends of the Cherokee*, 1898).

The story closely resembles something heard by Lawson among the Tuscarora in eastern North Carolina around the year 1700. An Indian having been killed by lightning, the people were assembled for the funeral, and the priest gave them a long discourse upon the power of lightning over all men, animals, and plants, except only mice and the black-gum tree.

> “At last, he began to tell the most ridiculous and absurd collection of lies about lightning imaginable. He claimed that an Indian of that nation had once captured lightning in the form of a partridge; that no other lightning could harm him as long as he had it with him; and that after he had kept it for several years, it escaped from him, so that he then became just as likely to be struck by lightning as anyone else. There was an Indian present at the same time who had lived since his youth primarily in an English house, so I called to him and told him what a collection of lies the conjurer was telling, not doubting that he thought so as much as I did. However, I found the opposite to be true, for he replied that I was very mistaken, and that the old man—who, I believe, was over a hundred years old—never told lies; and as for what he said, it was very true, for he himself knew it to be so. Seeing the man's ignorance, I spoke no more about it” (*History of Carolina*, page 346).

According to Hagar, a certain constellation of seven stars, which he identifies as the <term>Hyades</term>, is called “The Arm” by the Cherokee because of its resemblance to a human arm bent at the elbow. They say that it is the broken arm of a man who went up to the sky because, having been crippled in this way, he was of no further use on earth.

A meteor, and probably also a comet, is called <term>Atsil'-Tlûñtû'tsĭ</term>, or “Fire-panther.” The same concept is found among the Shawnee, embodied in the name of their great chief, <term>Tecumtha</term> (see p. 215).

10. ORIGIN OF THE PLEIADES AND THE PINE (p. 258): This myth is well known within the tribe and was told in nearly the same form by Swimmer, <term>Ta'gwadihi'</term>, and Suyeta. The Feather Dance, also called the Eagle Dance, is one of the old favorites and is the same as the ancient Calumet Dance of the northern tribes. For a description of the <term>gatayû'stĭ</term> game, see the note for number 3, “<term>Kana'ti</term> and <term>Selu</term>.” In a variant recorded by Stansbury Hagar (MS *Stellar Legends of the Cherokee*), the boys spend their time shooting at cornstalks.

According to Squier (*Serpent Symbol*, p. 69), probably on the authority of the Payne manuscript: “The Cherokee paid a form of veneration to the morning star, and also to the seven stars, with which they have connected a variety of legends. All of these, no doubt, are allegorical, although their significance is now unknown.”

MOONEY] NOTES AND PARALLELS

The corresponding Iroquois myth below, as given by Mrs. Erminnie Smith in her *Myths of the Iroquois* (Second Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, p. 80), is practically the same as far as it goes, and the myth was probably once common over a wide area in the East:
> “Seven little Indian boys were once accustomed to bringing their corn and beans each evening to a little mound. After their feast, the sweetest of their singers would sit on the top and sing for his companions who danced around the mound. On one occasion, they resolved to have a more lavish feast, and each was to contribute toward a flavorful soup. But their parents refused them the needed supplies, and they met for a feastless dance. Their heads and hearts grew lighter as they flew around the mound, until suddenly the whole company whirled off into the air. The inconsolable parents called in vain for them to return, but it was too late. Higher and higher they rose, whirling around their singer, until, transformed into bright stars, they took their places in the sky, where, as the Pleiades, they are still dancing. The brightness of the singer has been dimmed, however, because of his desire to return to earth.”

In an Eskimo tale, a hunter was pursued by enemies, and as he ran, he gradually rose from the ground and finally reached the sky, where he was turned into a star (Kroeber, *Tales of the Smith Sound Eskimo*, in *Journal of American Folk-Lore*). This transformation of human beings into stars and constellations is one of the most common events in primitive myth.

11. **THE MILKY WAY** (p. 259): This story, in slightly different forms, is well known among the Cherokee in both the east and west. The general word for mill is <term>dista´stĭ</term>, including also the self-acting pound-mill or <term>ûlskwûlte´gĭ</term>. In the original version, the mill was probably a wooden mortar, such as was commonly used by the Cherokee and other eastern and southern tribes.

In a variation recorded in the Hagar Cherokee manuscript, there are two hunters; one lives in the north and hunts big game, while the other lives in the south and hunts small game. The former, discovering the latter’s wife grinding corn, seizes her and carries her far away across the sky to his home in the north. Her dog, after eating what meal is left, follows the pair across the sky; the meal falls from his mouth as he runs, making the Milky Way.

Among the Kiowa, Cheyenne, and other plains tribes, the Milky Way is the dusty track along which the Buffalo and the Horse once ran a race across the sky.

12. **ORIGIN OF STRAWBERRIES** (p. 259): This myth, as given here, was obtained from <term>Ta´gwadihi´</term>, who said that all the fruits mentioned were then for the first time created, and added, “So some good came from the quarrel, anyway.” The Swimmer version has more detail, but seems overly embellished.

13. **THE GREAT YELLOW-JACKET: ORIGIN OF FISH AND FROGS** (p. 260): This story, obtained from Swimmer, is well known in the tribe and has numerous parallels in other Indian mythologies. In nearly every tribal origin story, we find the primitive world infested by ferocious monster animals, which are finally destroyed or rendered harmless, leaving only their descendants, the present small types. Notable examples are provided in Matthew’s *Navaho Legends*¹ and in the author’s story of the Jicarilla origin story in the *American Anthropologist* for July, 1898.

Another version of the Cherokee legend is given by Lanman in his *Letters from the Alleghany Mountains*, pages 73–74:
> “The Cherokees relate that there once existed among those mountains [about Nantahala and Franklin] a very large bird, which resembled a green-winged hornet in appearance, and this creature was in the habit of carrying off the younger children of the nation who happened to wander into the woods. Very many children had mysteriously disappeared in this manner, and the entire people declared a

warfare against the monster. A variety of means were employed for his destruction, but without success. In time, it was decided that the wise men (or medicine men) of the nation should try their skill in the matter. They met in council and agreed that each one should station himself on the summit of a mountain, and that, when the creature was discovered, the man who made the discovery should utter a loud shout, which should be taken up by his neighbor on the next mountain, and so continued to the end of the line, so that all the men might have a shot at the strange bird. This experiment was tried and resulted in finding the hiding place of the monster, which was a deep cavern on the eastern side of the Blue Ridge at the headwaters of the river Too-ge-lah [Tugaloo River, South Carolina]. On arriving at this place, they found the entrance to the cavern entirely inaccessible to mortal feet, and they therefore prayed to the Great Spirit that he would bring the bird out from his den and place him within reach of their weapons. Their petition was granted, for a terrible thunderstorm immediately arose, and a stroke of lightning tore away one half of a large mountain. The Indians were then successful in slaying their enemy. The Great Spirit was pleased with the courage shown by the Cherokees during this dangerous fight, and, with a view of rewarding it, he willed that all the highest mountains in their land should thereafter be bare of trees, so that they might always have an opportunity to watch the movements of their enemies.

As a sequel to this legend, it may be appropriately mentioned that at the head of the Too-ge-lah is one of the most remarkable curiosities of this mountain land. It is a granite cliff with a smooth surface or front, half a mile long and twelve hundred feet high, and is generally spoken of in this part of the country as the *White-side Mountain, or the Devil's Court-house.* To think of it is almost enough to make one dizzy, but to see it fills one with awe. Near the top of one part of this cliff is a small cave, which can be reached only by passing over a strip of rock about two feet wide. Only one man has ever been known to enter it, and when he performed the deed, he met a large bear at the entrance of the cave; the animal, in making its escape, slipped off the rock, fell a distance of nearly a thousand feet, and was, of course, killed. When the man saw this, he became so excited that it was some hours before he could quiet his nerves sufficiently to retrace his dangerous pathway.”

The Cherokee myth has a close parallel in the Iroquois story of the great mosquito, as published by the Tuscarora traditionist, Cusick, in 1825, and quoted by Schoolcraft, Indian Tribes, v, page 638:

> “About this time a great mosquito invaded the Onondaga fort; the mosquito was harmful to the people; it flew about the fort with a long stinger and sucked the blood of many lives. The warriors made several attempts to expel the monster but failed. The country was invaded until the Holder of the Heavens was pleased to visit the people. While he was visiting the king at the Onondaga fort, the mosquito appeared as usual and flew about the fort. The Holder of the Heavens attacked the monster; it flew so rapidly that he could hardly keep it in sight, but after a few days' chase, the monster began to fail. He chased it along the borders of the great lakes toward the sunset and around the great country; at last, he overtook the monster and killed it near the salt lake Onondaga, and its blood became small mosquitoes.”

<term>U'la'gû'</term>—This is not the name of any particular species, but signifies a leader, principal, or informally, “boss,” and in this sense is applied to the large queen yellow jacket seen in spring, or to the leader of a working gang. The insect of the story is described as a monster yellow jacket.

Haywood (*Natural and Aboriginal History of Tennessee*, p. 161) mentions the Cherokee deluge myth and suggests that the petroglyphs at Track Rock Gap in Georgia may have some reference to it. The versions provided by the missionaries Buttrick and Washburn are simply the Bible narrative as told by the Indians. Among the American tribes with which it was found, Brinton lists the Athapascan, Algonquian, Iroquois, Cherokee, Chickasaw, Caddo, Natchez, Dakota, Apache, Navaho, Mandan, Pueblo, Aztec, Mixtec, Zapotec, Tlascalan, Michoacan, Toltec, Maya, Quiche, Haitian, Darien, Popayan, Muysca, Quichua, Tupinamba, Achagua, Auraucanian, “and undoubtedly others.” <note>*The Myths of the New World, A Treatise on the Symbolism and Mythology of the Red Race of America*; 3rd ed., Philadelphia, 1896.</note> It is found also along the Northwest coast, was known around Albemarle Sound, and, as has been said, was probably common to all the tribes.

In one Creek version, the warning is given by wolves; in another, by cranes (see Bouton, cited above).

15. **THE FOUR-FOOTED TRIBES** (p. 261): *No essential difference*—

> “I have often reflected on the curious connection which appears to exist in the mind of an Indian between man and the animal kingdom, and found much matter in it for interesting observation. Although they consider themselves superior to all other animals and are very proud of that superiority; although they believe that the beasts of the forest, the birds of the air, and the fishes of the waters were created by the Almighty Being for the use of man; yet it seems as if they attribute the difference between themselves and the animal kind, and the dominion which they have over them, more to their superior physical strength and skill than to their immortal souls. Since all are endowed by the Creator with the power of will and self-motion, they view them in a manner as a great society of which they are the head—whom they are appointed, indeed, to govern, but between whom and themselves intimate ties of connection and relationship may exist, or at least did exist in the beginning of time. They are, in fact, according to their opinions, only the first among equals, the legitimate hereditary sovereigns of the whole living race, of which they are themselves a constituent part. Hence, in their languages, these forms of their nouns, which we call genders, are not, as with us, descriptive of the masculine and feminine species, but of the *animate* and *inanimate* kinds. Indeed, they go so far as to include trees and plants within the first of these descriptions. All living nature, to whatever degree, is in their eyes a great whole from which they have not yet ventured to separate themselves. They do not exclude other animals from their world of spirits, the place to which they expect to go after death.” <note>Heckewelder, *Indian Nations*, p. 254, 1876 edition.</note>

According to the Ojibwa, the animals formerly had the faculty of speech, until it was taken from them by Nanibojou as a punishment for having conspired against the human race. <note>Henry, *Travels and Adventures in Canada, etc.*, pp. 212–213, New York, 1809.</note>

*Animal chiefs and councils*—In Pawnee belief, according to Grinnell, the animals,

He gives a detailed description of each. The fourth is a mound-shaped hill, on the top of which is a deep well or water hole, into which the Pawnee throw offerings. The same belief is noted by Chatelain in Angola, West Africa: "In African folk tales the animal world, as also the spirit world, is organized and governed just like the human world. In Angola the elephant is the supreme king of all animal creation, and the special chief of the edible tribe of wild animals. Next to him in rank the lion is special chief of the tribe of ferocious beasts and highest vassal of the elephant. Chief of the reptile tribe is the python. Chief of the finny tribe is, in the interior, the <term>di-lenda</term>, the largest river fish. Chief of the feathery tribe is the <term>kakulu ka humbi</term>, largest of the eagles. Among the domestic animals the scepter belongs to the bull; among the locusts to the one called <term>di-ngundu</term>. Even the ants and termites have their kings or queens. Every chief or king has his court, consisting of the <term>ngolambole</term>, <term>tandala</term>, and other officers, his parliament of <term>ma-kota</term> and his plebeian subjects, just like any human African <term>saba</term>" (Folk tales of Angola, p. 22).

*Asking pardon of animals*—For other Cherokee references see remarks upon the Little Deer, the Wolf, and the Rattlesnake; also number 4, "Origin of Disease and Medicine," and number 58, "The Rattlesnake's Vengeance." This custom was no doubt general among the tribes, as it is thoroughly in harmony with Indian ideas. The trader Henry thus relates a characteristic instance among the Ojibwa in 1764 on the occasion of his killing a bear near the winter camp:

> "The bear being dead, all my assistants approached, and all, but more particularly my old mother (as I used to call her), took her head in their hands, stroking and kissing it several times; begging a thousand pardons for taking away her life; calling her their relation and grandmother; and requesting her not to blame them, since it was truly an Englishman who had put her to death.

> "This ceremony was not of long duration; and if it was I who killed their grandmother, they themselves were not falling behind in what remained to be performed. The skin being taken off, we found the fat in several places six inches deep. This, being divided into two parts, loaded two persons; and the meat parts were as much as four persons could carry. In all, the carcass must have exceeded five hundred pounds.

> "As soon as we reached the lodge, the bear's head was adorned with all the trinkets in the possession of the family, such as silver armbands and wristbands, and belts of wampum; and then laid upon a scaffold, set up for its reception, within the lodge. Near the nose was placed a large quantity of tobacco.

> "The next morning had no sooner appeared than preparations were made for a feast to the <term>manes</term> <note>the spirits of the dead</note>. The lodge was cleaned and swept; and the head of the bear lifted up, and a new <term>stroud</term> cloth blanket, which had never been used before, spread under it. The pipes were now lit; and Wawatam blew tobacco smoke into the nostrils of the bear, telling me to do the same, and thus appease the anger of the bear because I had killed her. I tried to persuade my benefactor and friendly adviser that she no longer had any life, and assured him that I was under no fear of her displeasure; but the first suggestion was not believed, and the second gave but little satisfaction.

labored in this way to destroy their *friends*. He explained, however, that the misfortune was unavoidable, since without doing so, they could by no means survive. The speech ended, we all ate heartily of the bear’s meat; and even the head itself, after remaining three days on the scaffold, was put into the kettle.”—Travels, pp. 143–145.

*The Rabbit*—The role played by the Rabbit or Hare and his symbolic character in Indian myth has already been noted (see “Stories and Story Tellers”). In his purely animal character, as an actor among the four-footed creatures, the same attributes of trickery and superior wisdom are assigned to him in other parts of the world. In the folktales of Angola, West Africa, “The Hare seems to surpass the fox in shrewdness,” and “The Hare has the swiftness and shrewdness of the Monkey, but he is never reckless, as the Monkey sometimes appears to be” (Chatelain, Folktales of Angola, pp. 295, 300). In farthest Asia also, “The animals, too, have their stories, and in Korea, as in some other parts of the world, the Rabbit seems to come off best, as a rule” (H. N. Allen, Korean Tales, p. 34; New York and London, 1889).

*The buffalo*—Timberlake repeatedly remarks upon the abundance of the buffalo in the Cherokee country of East Tennessee in 1762. On one occasion, while in camp, they heard rapid firing from their scouts and “in less than a minute, seventeen or eighteen buffaloes ran in amongst us before we discovered them, so that several of us were nearly run over, especially the women, who with some difficulty sheltered themselves behind the trees. Most of the men fired, but since they fired at random, only one was killed, though several more were wounded” (Memoirs, p. 101). According to a writer in the Historical Magazine, volume VIII, page 71, 1864, the last two wild buffalo known in Ohio were killed in Jackson County in 1800.

*The elk*—This animal ranged in eastern Carolina in 1700. “The elk is a massive creature of the deer variety. Its skin is used in almost the same way as the buffalo’s. . . . Its flesh is not as sweet as that of the smaller deer. Its hams exceed in weight all creatures which the New World provides. They will often gather and feed with the buffalo, enjoying the same range as they do” (Lawson, Carolina, p. 203).

*Cuts out the hamstring*—No satisfactory reason has been found for this custom, which has been noted for more than a century. Buttrick says of the Cherokee: “The Indians never used to eat a certain sinew in the thigh. . . . Some say that if they eat the sinew, they will have cramps in it when attempting to run. It is said that once a woman had a cramp in that sinew, and therefore no one must eat it” (Antiquities, p. 12). Adair, speaking of the southern tribes generally, says: “When in the woods, the Indians cut a small piece out of the lower part of the thigh of the deer they kill, lengthwise and quite deep. Among the great number of venison hams they bring to our trading houses, I do not remember to have observed one without it” (History of the American Indians, pp. 137–138).

*White animals sacred*—According to a formula in the Tuggle manuscript for curing “deer sickness,” the “White Deer” is also the chief of his tribe in Creek mythology. A peculiar sacredness always attaches, in the Indian mind, to white and albino animals, partly because of the symbolic meaning attached to the color itself and partly due to the mystery surrounding the phenomenon of albinism. Among the Cherokee, the chiefs of both the Deer and the Bear tribe were white. On the plains, the so-called white buffalo was always sacred. Among the Iroquois, according to Morgan (League of the Iroquois, p. 210), “the white deer, white squirrel, and other chance animals of the albino kind were regarded as consecrated to the Great Spirit.” One of their most solemn sacrifices was that of the White Dog.

*The bear*—A reverence for the bear and a belief that it is half-human is very general among the tribes; this is probably based in part upon the animal's ability to stand upright and the resemblance of its tracks to human footprints. According to Grinnell (Blackfoot Lodge Tales, p. 260), “The Blackfeet believe it to be part brute and part human; portions of its body, particularly the ribs and feet, being like those of a man.” In a note upon a Navajo myth, Matthews says (Navajo Legends,

The Ojibwa idea has been noted in connection with the ceremony of asking pardon of a slain animal. A curious illustration of the other side of this perspective is given by Heckewelder (Indian Nations, p. 255):

> “A Delaware hunter once shot a huge bear and broke its backbone. The animal fell and set up a most plaintive cry, something like that of a panther when it is hungry. Instead of giving him another shot, the hunter stood close to him and addressed him with these words: ‘Listen, bear! You are a coward and no warrior, as you pretend to be. If you were a warrior, you would show it by your firmness, and not cry and whimper like an old woman. You know, bear, that our tribes are at war with each other, and that yours was the aggressor <note>probably alluding to an Indian tradition about a very ferocious kind of bear, called the <term>naked bear</term>, which they say once existed but was totally destroyed by their ancestors</note> . . . You have found the Indians too powerful for you, and you have gone sneaking about in the woods, stealing their hogs; perhaps at this time you have hog’s meat in your belly. If you had conquered me, I would have borne it with courage and died like a brave warrior; but you, bear, sit here and cry, and disgrace your tribe by your cowardly conduct.’ I was present at the delivery of this curious verbal attack. When the hunter had dispatched the bear, I asked him how he thought that poor animal could understand what he said to it? ‘Oh,’ he said in answer, ‘the bear understood me very well; did you not observe how ashamed he looked while I was scolding him?’ ”

**The wolf and wolf killer**—Speaking of the Gulf tribes generally, Adair says: “Indeed, many of them do not care to interfere with the wolf, believing it is unlucky to kill them; this is the only reason that few of the Indians shoot at that creature, due to the belief that it would spoil their guns” (History of the American Indians, p. 16). The author has heard among the East Cherokee an incident involving a man who, while standing one night upon a fish trap, was scented by a wolf that came so near the man was compelled to shoot it. He immediately went home and had the gun exorcised by a conjurer. Wafford, when he was a boy in the old Nation, knew a professional wolf killer. It is always permissible to hire a white man to kill a predatory wolf, as in that case no guilt is attached to the Indian or his tribe.

# 16. **THE RABBIT GOES DUCK HUNTING** (p. 266)

This story was heard from Swimmer, John Ax, and Suyeta in the east, and Wafford in the west. Discussions between animals regarding the kind of food they eat are very common in Indian myths; the method chosen to decide the dispute is usually quite characteristic. The first incident is paralleled in a Creek story of the Rabbit and the Lion (Panther?) in the Tuggle manuscript collection and among the remote Wallawalla of Washington (see Kane, Wanderings of an Artist among the Indians of North America, p. 268; London, 1859). In an Omaha myth, Ictinike and the Buzzard, the latter undertakes to carry the trickster across a stream, but drops him into a hollow tree, from which he is chopped out by some women whom he has persuaded that there are raccoons inside (Dorsey, Contributions to North American Ethnology, vi). In the Iroquois tale, “A Hunter’s Adventures,” a hunter, endeavoring to trap some geese in the water, is carried up into the air and falls into a hollow stump, from which he is released by women (Smith, Myths of the Iroquois, in Second Annual Report of Bureau of Ethnology). In the Uncle Remus story, “Mr. Rabbit Meets His Match Again,” the Buzzard persuades the Rabbit to get upon his back in order to be carried across a river, but lands with him upon a tree overhanging the water and thus compels the Rabbit, through fear of falling, to confess a piece of trickery.¹

17. HOW THE RABBIT STOLE THE OTTER'S COAT (p. 267): This story is well known in the tribe and was heard from several informants, both east and west. Nothing is said as to how the Otter recovered his coat. It has exact parallels in the Creek myths of the Tuggle collection, in one of which the Rabbit tries to impersonate a boy hero by stealing his coat, while in another he plays a trick on the Lion (Panther) by throwing hot coals over him while he is asleep, at a creek which the Rabbit says is called “Throwing-hot-ashes-on-you.”

18. WHY THE POSSUM'S TAIL IS BARE (p. 269): This story was heard from several informants, east and west. In one variant, the hair clipping was done by the Moth, and in another by the spells of the Snail, who is represented as a magician. The version given here is the most common and agrees best with the Cherokee folklore concerning the Cricket (see number 59, “The Smaller Reptiles, Fishes, and Insects”).

In the Creek myth, as given in the Tuggle collection, the Opossum burned the hair from his tail while trying to put rings on it like those of the Raccoon’s tail, and he grins from chewing a bitter oak ball which he mistook for a ripened fruit.

The anatomical peculiarities of the opossum, of both sexes, have caused much speculation among the Indians, many of whom believe that the female produces her young without any help from the male. The Creeks, according to the Tuggle manuscript, believe that the young are born in the pouch from the female breathing against it when curled up; even Lawson and Timberlake assert that they are born at the teat, from which they afterward drop off into the pouch.

*A council and a dance*—In the old days, as is still true today among the remote Western tribes, every great council gathering was made the occasion for a series of dances, accompanied always by feasting and a general good time.

19. HOW THE WILDCAT CAUGHT THE GOBBLER (p. 269): This story was heard from John Ax and David Blythe (east) and from Wafford and Boudinot (west). The version given below, modified to suit the white man’s ideas, appears without a signature in the *Cherokee Advocate* of December 18, 1845:

> “There was once a flock of wild turkeys feeding in a valley. As they fed, they heard a voice singing. They soon discovered that the musician was a hare, and the theme of his song was that he had a secret in his breast which he would not reveal under any circumstances. The curiosity of the turkeys was excited, and they begged the hare to tell them the secret. This he finally consented to do if they would obtain the king’s daughter for him as his wife and go with him and dance around their enemy. They promised to do everything, and the hare led them to where a wildcat lay, apparently dead. The hare convinced them to close their eyes as they danced. The wildcat, meanwhile, silently arose and killed several of them before the rest found out what a snare they had been caught in. Through this trick by the wildcat, aided by the hare, the former had a magnificent feast.”

This, with its variants, is one of the most widespread of the animal myths. The same story told by the Cherokee, identical even to the song, is given in the Creek collection of Tuggle, with the addition that the Rabbit’s tail is afterward bitten off by the enraged Turkeys. In another Creek version, evidently a later invention, the Raccoon plays a similar trick on the Deer for the benefit of the Panther. The Kiowa of the southern plains tell how the hungry trickster, Sinti, entices a number of prairie dogs to come near him under the pretense of teaching them a new dance, and then kills all but one while they are dancing around him, according to instructions, with their eyes shut. Among the Omaha, the Rabbit himself captures the Turkeys while they dance around him with closed eyes to his singing (Dorsey, “The Rabbit and the Turkeys,” and “Ictinike, the Turkeys, Turtle, and Elk,” in Contributions to North American Ethnology, vi). The same strategy, with only a change of names, appears again in another Omaha story, “The Raccoon and the Crabs,” from the same collection, and in a Cheyenne story of White-man (A. L. Kroeber, Cheyenne Tales, in Journal

**20. HOW THE TERRAPIN BEAT THE RABBIT** (p. 270): This story was obtained from John Ax and Suyeta and is well known in the tribe. It is sometimes told with the Deer instead of the Rabbit as the defeated runner, and in this form is given by Lanman, who localizes it this way: “The race was to extend from the Black mountain to the summit of the third pinnacle extending to the eastward” (Letters, p. 37).

In the Creek collection of Tuggle, the same story is given in two versions; in one, the Deer is defeated, and in the other, the Wolf is defeated by the strategy of the Terrapin. The Southern Negro parallel is given by Harris (*Uncle Remus, His Songs and His Sayings*) in the story, “Mr. Rabbit Finds His Match at Last.” It seems almost unnecessary to call attention to the European folklore version, the well-known story of the race between the Hare and the Tortoise.

**21. THE RABBIT AND THE TAR WOLF** (p. 271): This story was obtained in the Indian Territory from James Wafford, who said he had repeatedly heard it in his childhood around Valley River, in the old Nation, from Cherokee who spoke no English.

The second version, from the *Cherokee Advocate*, December 18, 1845, is given together with the story of “How the Wildcat caught the Gobbler,” with this introduction:

> “Indian Fables. Mr. William P. Ross: I have recently come across the following Cherokee fables, and perhaps you may think them worth inserting in the *Advocate* for the benefit of the curious. I am told that the Cherokees have a great many fables. If I understand the following, the intention seems to be to teach cunning and strategy in war. Aesop.”

The newspaper paragraph bears the pencil initials of S[amuel] W[orcester] B[utler].

Other Indian versions are found among the Jicarilla (“Fox and Rabbit,” Myths of the Jicarilla, by Frank Russell, in *Journal of American Folk-Lore*, October, 1898) and Sioux (S. D. Hinman, cited in *Transactions of the Anthropological Society of Washington*, I, p. 103, Washington, 1882). The Southern Negro variant, “The Wonderful Tar-Baby Story,” is the introductory tale in Harris’s *Uncle Remus, His Songs and His Sayings*. A close parallel occurs in the West African story of “Leopard, Monkey, and Hare” (Chatelain, *Folktales of Angola*).

**22. THE RABBIT AND THE POSSUM AFTER A WIFE** (p. 273): This example of Indian humor was obtained at different times from Swimmer, John Ax, Suyeta (east), and Wafford (west), and is well known in the tribe. Wafford, in telling the story, remarked that the Rabbit was the chief’s runner, and according to custom was always well entertained wherever he went.

**23. THE RABBIT DINES THE BEAR** (p. 273): This favorite story with the Cherokee of the east and west is another animal myth of wide distribution, being found among almost every tribe from Maine to the Pacific. Beans and peas of several varieties were native to the agricultural tribes.

In the Creek version, in the Tuggle manuscript, “The Bear invited the Rabbit to dinner. When he came, the Bear called his wife and said, ‘Have peas for dinner: the Rabbit loves peas.’ ‘But there is no grease,’ said the Bear’s wife, ‘to cook them with.’ ‘Oh,’ said the Bear, ‘that’s no trouble; bring me a knife.’ So she brought the knife and the Bear took it and cut between his toes, while the Rabbit looked on in wonder. ‘No grease between my toes! Well, I know where there is some,’ so he cut a gash in his side and the grease ran out. His wife took it and cooked the peas and they had a fine dinner and promised always to be good friends,” etc. The

24. **THE RABBIT ESCAPES FROM THE WOLVES** (p. 274): This story was obtained from James Wafford in Indian Territory. Compare number 19, "How the Wildcat Caught the Gobbler."

25. **FLINT VISITS THE RABBIT** (p. 274): This story was told in a slightly different form by John Ax and Swimmer (east) and was confirmed by Wafford (west). Although among the Cherokee it has declined into simply a humorous tale for the entertainment of a winter evening, it was originally a principal part of the great creation myth common to probably all the Iroquoian and Algonquian tribes, and of which we find traces also in the mythologies of the Aztec and the Maya. Among the northern Algonquian tribes, "the West was personified as a flint stone and the twin brother of Michabo, the Great Rabbit. The feud between them was bitter, and the contest long and dreadful. . . . At last Michabo mastered his fellow twin and broke him into pieces. He scattered the fragments over the earth. . . ." Among the Iroquoian tribes, related to the Cherokee, the name is variously *Tăwiskaroñ*, *Tăwiskărá*, and sometimes *Ohaa*, all of which are names both for flint and for hail or ice. *Tăwiskara* is the evil-working god, in perpetual conflict with his twin brother *Yoskeha*, the benevolent god, who finally overpowers him, at which point the blood that drops from his wounds is changed into flint stones. Brinton sees in the Great Rabbit and the Flint the opposing forces of day and night, light and darkness, locally personified as East and West; meanwhile, in the twin gods of the Iroquois, Hewitt sees the conflicting agents of heat and cold, summer and winter. Both conceptions are identical in the final analysis. Hewitt derives the Iroquois name from a root denoting "hail, ice, glass"; in Cherokee we have *tăwiskalûñ'ĭ*, *tăwĭ'skă'lă*, "flint," *tăwĭ'skă*, "smooth," and *une'stălûñ*, "ice." (See Brinton, *American Hero Myths*, pp. 48, 56, 61; Hewitt, *The Cosmogonic Gods of the Iroquois*, in *Proc. Am. Ass. Adv. Sci.*, XLIV, 1895.)

In one of the Cherokee sacred formulas collected by the author occurs the expression: 

> "The terrible Flint is coming. He has his paths laid down in this direction. He is shaking the red switches threateningly. Let us run toward the Sun land."

*Siyu'*—This word, abbreviated from *ásiyu'*, "good," is the regular Cherokee salutation. With probably all the tribes, the common salutation is simply the word "good," and in the sign language of the plains, the gesture conveying that meaning is used in the same way. The ordinary good-bye is usually some equivalent of "I go now."

26. **HOW THE DEER GOT HIS HORNS** (p. 275): This story was heard from Swimmer, Suyeta, and others, and is well known in the tribe.

In a parallel Pawnee myth, "How the Deer Lost His Gall," the Deer and Antelope wager their galls in a race, which the Antelope wins; however, out of sympathy, he takes off his own dewclaws and gives them to the Deer. In the Blackfoot variant, the Deer and the Antelope run two races. In the first, which is over the prairie, the Antelope wins and takes the Deer's gall; in the second, which the Deer insists shall be run through the timber, the Deer wins and takes the Antelope's dewclaws (Grinnell, *Pawnee Hero Tales*, pp. 204, 205).
