27. **WHY THE DEER'S TEETH ARE BLUNT** (p. 276): This story follows the previous one in regular sequence and was told by the same informants. 
In a Jicarilla myth, the Fox kills a dangerous Bear monster under the pretense of trimming down his legs so that he can run faster (Russell, *Myth of the Jicarilla*, in *Journal of American Folk-Lore*, p. 262, October, 1898).

28. **WHAT BECAME OF THE RABBIT** (p. 277): This version was obtained from Suyeta, who says the Rabbit never went up to the sky world because he was "too mean" to be with the other animals. Swimmer, however, says that he did afterward go up to *Gălûñ'lătĭ*. The belief in a large rabbit still existing beyond a great river may possibly have its origin in indirect reports of the jack-rabbit west of the Missouri River.

The myth has a close parallel in the southern African-American story "The Origin of the Ocean" (Harris, *Nights with Uncle Remus*), in which the Rabbit, by a strategy, persuades the Lion to jump across a creek. The Rabbit then "cut the string that held the banks together. . . . Of course, when Brother Rabbit took and cut the string, the banks of the creek fell back, they did, and Mr. Lion could not jump back. The banks kept on falling back, and the creek kept on getting wider and wider, until eventually Brother Rabbit and Mr. Lion were not in sight of one another, and from that day to this the big waters have been rolling between them."

<term>*Kû!*</term>—A Cherokee exclamation used as a starting signal and for introducing the paragraphs of a speech. It might be translated approximately as, *Now!*

29. **WHY THE MINK SMELLS** (p. 277): Obtained from John Ax.

30. **WHY THE MOLE LIVES UNDERGROUND** (p. 277): This story, from John Ax, not only accounts for the Mole's underground habit but also illustrates a common Cherokee belief regarding witchcraft, which has parallels all over the world.

31. **THE TERRAPIN'S ESCAPE FROM THE WOLVES** (p. 278): This story, of which the version given here from Swimmer and John Ax is admittedly imperfect, is also known among the western Cherokee. It was mentioned by Wafford and others in the Nation, although for some reason none of them seemed able to fill in the details. A somewhat similar story was given as belonging to her own tribe by a Catawba woman married among the East Cherokee. It suggests story number 21, "The Rabbit and the Tar Wolf," and has numerous parallels.

In the Creek version, found in the Tuggle manuscript, the Terrapin ridicules a woman, who retaliates by crushing his shell with a corn pestle. He repairs the injury by singing a medicine song, but the scars remain as the checkered spots on his back. In a variation in the same collection, the ants mend his shell with tar in return for his fat and blood. Other parallels are found among the Omaha, "How the Big Turtle went on the Warpath" (Dorsey, *Contributions to North American Ethnology*, <term>vi</term>, p. 275), and the Cheyenne, "The Turtle, the Grasshopper, and the Skunk" (Kroeber, *Cheyenne Tales*, in *Journal of American Folk-Lore*, July, 1900). The myth is also recorded from West Africa by Chatelain ("The Man and the Turtle," in *Folktales of Angola*, 1894).

<term>*Kanahe'na.*</term>—This is a sour corn gruel, the *tamfuli* or "Tom Fuller" of the Creeks, which is a favorite food among all the southern tribes. A large earthen jar of *kanahe'na*, with a wooden spoon standing upright in it, is always kept on a bench just inside the cabin door so that every visitor may help himself.

32. **ORIGIN OF THE GROUNDHOG DANCE** (p. 279): This story is from Swimmer, with the supplementary part added by John Ax. The Groundhog dance is one of those belonging to the great thanksgiving ceremony, the Green-corn dance. It consists of alternate advances and retreats by the entire line of dancers in obedience to signals by the song leader, who sings to the accompaniment of a rattle. The refrain of the song, which is without a specific meaning, is:

->*Ha'wiye'ĕhi' Yaha'wiye'ĕhi'* [twice] *Yu-u*<-
->*Hi'yagu'wĕ Hahi'yagu'wĕ* [twice] *Yu-yu.*<-

33. **THE MIGRATION OF THE ANIMALS** (p. 280): This little story is shared exactly as related by Ayâsta, the only woman allowed to speak in council among the East Cherokee. A similar incident occurs in number 76, "The Bear Man." According to one Cherokee myth concerning the well-known Track Rock gap, near Blairsville in upper Georgia, the rock carvings there are the footprints of all sorts of birds and animals which once crossed over the gap during a great migration toward the south.

34. **THE WOLF’S REVENGE: THE WOLF AND THE DOG** (p. 280): These short stories from Swimmer illustrate the Cherokee belief that if a wolf is injured, its companions will surely avenge the injury. See also the note to number 15, "The Fourfooted Tribes," and number 3, "Kana'tĭ and Selu."

In a West African tale recorded by Chatelain (*Folktales of Angola, 1894*), the dog and the jackal are relatives who live together in the wilderness until the jackal sends the dog to the village for fire. The dog goes, enters a house, and is fed by a woman; he then decides to stay in the village, where there is always food.

35. **THE BIRD TRIBES** (p. 280): *The eagle killer*—Regarding the Southern tribes in general, Adair says: "They use the feathers of the eagle’s tail in certain friendly and religious dances, but the whole town will contribute goods to the value of 200 deerskins to pay for killing a large eagle—they do not value the bald eagle—and the man also receives an honorable title for the exploit, as if he had brought in the scalp of an enemy."<note>History of the American Indians, p. 30.</note>

Timberlake says that the Cherokee held the tail of an eagle in the highest esteem, as these tails were sometimes given along with wampum during their treaties, and none of their warlike ceremonies could be performed without them (*Memoirs*, p. 81). The metaphorical expression, "a snowbird has been killed," used to avoid offending the eagle tribe, is similar to the expression, "he has been scratched by a brier," used by the Cherokee to mean, "he has been bitten by a snake." Professional eagle killers existed among many tribes, along with a prescribed ceremony for securing the eagle. The most common method was probably that described in a note to number 98, "Gana’s Adventures among the Cherokee." A detailed account of the Blackfoot method is given by Grinnell in his *Blackfoot Lodge Tales*, pp. 236–240. The eagle, being both a bird of prey and a sacred bird, was never eaten.

Shifting the blame for a killing to a substitute victim is a common feature of Native American rituals for seeking pardon, especially for offenses against animal tribes or the spirits of the dead. A remarkable parallel to the Cherokee prayer, from the Quichua of Peru, is provided by Dr. G. A. Dorsey. After arriving with a party of Native laborers and a Spanish gentleman well-acquainted with the native language to examine some cave tombs near the ancient city of Cuzco, they reached the spot. Just as he was about to give the order to begin work, the Indians removed their blankets and hats, knelt down, and recited a prayer in unison in their own language to the spirits of the dead. The following translation is an extract:

> "Chiefs, sons of the sun, you and we are brothers, sons of the great Pachacamac. You alone know this, but we know that three persons exist: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This is the only difference between you and us. . . . Chiefs, sons of the sun, we have not come to disturb your peaceful sleep in this, your home. We come only because we have been forced by our superiors; may you direct your vengeance and your curses toward them."

Then followed sacrifices of coca leaves, <term>aguardiente</term>, and <term>chicha</term>, after which they called upon the snow-capped mountain to witness their affection for their ancestors and were then ready to begin work (Dorsey, *A Ceremony of the Quichuas of Peru*, in *Journal of American Folk-Lore*, October, 1894).

Night birds—Adair says of the Southern tribes (*History of the American Indians*, p. 130, 1775): "They consider all birds of prey and nocturnal birds to be unclean and—"

forbidden to be eaten." The mixed feeling of fear and reverence for all nocturnal birds is universal among the Western tribes. Owls, in particular, are believed to bring prophetic messages to the few great conjurers who can interpret their language.

*The hawk—* Since this is a bird of prey, it was never eaten. Adair relates the following incident, probably from the Chickasaw: "Not long ago, when the Indians were making their winter hunt and the old women were without meat at home, I shot a small fat hawk and asked one of them to take and prepare it. However, although I strongly urged her as a test, she refused just as earnestly for fear of contracting pollution, which she called the 'accursed sickness,' believing that disease would be the inevitable result of such an impurity" (Hist. Am. Indians, p. 130).

*Chickadee and titmouse—* Adair mentions once observing a party of Southern Indians "to be intimidated by the voice of a small, uncommon bird when it landed and chirped on a tree over their camp" (op. cit., p. 26). At a conference with the Six Nations at Albany in 1775, the Oneida speaker said: "We, the Six Nations, have heard the voice of a bird called Tskleleli (*Tsǐkǐlǐlǐ*?), a messenger that came among us. It has told us that the path at the western connection, by Fort Stanwix, would be closed by one party or the other." In reply, the commissioners said: "We suspect the bird Tskleleli has been busy again; he seems to be a mischievous bird and should not be encouraged or entertained" (New York Colonial Documents, <term>viii</term>, pp. 612, 628, 1857). The bird's name is in the Oneida dialect. Bruyas gives *teksereri* as the Mohawk name for the tomtit.

36. **THE BALL GAME OF THE BIRDS AND ANIMALS** (p. 286): This is one of the best-known animal stories and was heard with varying levels of detail from John Ax, Swimmer, Suyeta, and A’wani’ta in the east, and from Wafford in the Territory.

The Creeks and the Seminoles also have stories of ball games played by the birds against the four-footed animals, as we learn from the Tuggle manuscript collection. In one story, the bat is rejected by both sides but is finally accepted by the four-footed animals because he has teeth; he then enables them to win the victory over the birds.

*The ballplay—* The ballplay, <term>a'ne'tsâ</term>, is the great athletic game of the Cherokee and the Gulf tribes, as well as those of the St. Lawrence and Great Lakes regions. It should be noted that this is not our own game of baseball, but rather a variety of tennis; the ball is thrown not by hand, but with a netted racket or a pair of rackets. The goals consist of two sets of upright poles at each end of the ball ground, which is always a level, grassy field beside a small stream. There is much accompanying ceremony and ritual, including a ball dance the night before in which the women participate. This is the same game used by hostile tribes to gain entrance to the British post at Mackinaw in 1763, and under the name of lacrosse, it has become the national game of Canada. It has also been adopted by the French Creoles of Louisiana under the name of raquette. In British Columbia, it is considered the favorite amusement of the people of the underworld (Teit, *Thompson River Traditions*, p. 116). In the Southern states, numerous locations named "Ballplay," "Ball Flat," and "Ball Ground" testify to the Indian fondness for the game. Large sums were wagered on it, and there is even a tradition that the Cherokee won a significant amount of territory in northern Georgia from the Creeks in a ball game. For a detailed description, see the author's article, "The Cherokee Ball Play," in the *American Anthropologist* for April 1890.

*Won the game—* Because of their successful performance on this occasion, the Cherokee ballplayer invokes the aid of the bat and the flying squirrel. He also ties a small piece of a bat's wing to his ball stick or fastens it to the frame where the sticks are hung during the preliminary dance the night before.

*Gave the martin a gourd—* The black house-martin is a favorite bird of the Cherokee, who attract it by fastening hollow gourds to the tops of long poles set up near their houses so the birds can build their nests in them. In South Carolina, as far

As far back as 1700, according to Lawson:
> “The planters put gourds on standing poles <note>the original transcription says "holes"</note> on purpose for these birds to build in, because they are very warlike birds and beat the crows away from the plantations” (*History of Carolina*, p. 238).

**37. HOW THE TURKEY GOT HIS BEARD (p. 287)**: This story is well known in the tribe and was heard from several informants.

According to a Creek myth in the Tuggle collection, the Turkey was once a warrior and still wears his last scalp from his neck. In another story from the same collection, it is a man’s scalp which he seized from the Terrapin and accidentally swallowed as he ran off, so that it grew out from his breast.

**38. WHY THE TURKEY GOBBLES (p. 288)**: This story was first heard from John Ax (east) and afterward from Wafford (west). The grouse is locally called a “partridge” in the southern Alleghenies.

**39. HOW THE KINGFISHER GOT HIS BILL (p. 288)**: The first version is from John Ax, the other from Swimmer.

*<term>Yûñwĭ tsunsdi’</term>*—“Little People,” another name for the <term>Nuñně'hĭ</term> (see number 78). These are not to be confused with the <term>Anisga’ya Tsunsdi’</term>, “Little Men,” or Thunder Boys.

*<term>Tugălû’nă</term>*—A small, slender-bodied spotted fish about four inches in length, which likes to lie upon the rocks at the bottom of the larger streams. The name refers to a gourd, from an imagined resemblance of the long nose to the handle of a gourd.

**40. HOW THE PARTRIDGE GOT HIS WHISTLE (p. 289)**: This short story is well known in the tribe.

Whistles and flutes or flageolets were used among nearly all tribes for ceremonial and entertainment purposes. The whistle, usually made from an eagle bone, was worn suspended from the neck. The flute or flageolet was commonly made from cedar wood.

**41. HOW THE REDBIRD GOT HIS COLOR (p. 289)**: This short story was obtained from Cornelius Boudinot, a prominent mixed-blood person of Tahlequah, and differs from the standard Cherokee myth, according to which the redbird is the transformed daughter of the Sun (see number 5, “The Daughter of the Sun”).

*Red paint*—The Indian mind attaches much sacredness to red paint, the color being symbolic of war, strength, success, and spiritual protection. The word "paint," in any Indian language, is generally understood to mean red paint, unless it is otherwise distinctly noted. The Indian red paint is usually a soft hematite ore found in veins of hard-rock formation, from which it must be dug with much labor and patience. In the western tribes, everyone coming to procure paint in this way offers a prayer beside the rock and hangs a small sacrifice upon a convenient bush or stick before beginning operations.

**42. THE PHEASANT BEATING CORN: THE PHEASANT DANCE (p. 290)**: The first of these short tales is from John Ax, the second from Swimmer. The pheasant (*<term>Bonasa umbella</term>*; Cherokee *<term>tluñti’stĭ</term>*) is also locally called a grouse or partridge.

**43. THE RACE BETWEEN THE CRANE AND THE HUMMINGBIRD (p. 290)**: This story is a favorite in the tribe and was heard from several informants, both East and West. The sequel may surprise those who have supposed that women have no rights in Indian society.

In a Creek story under the same title in the Tuggle collection, the rivals agree to fly from a certain spot on a stream to the spring at its head. The hummingbird is obliged to follow the windings of the stream, but the crane takes a direct course above the trees and thus wins the race.

*Fly around the world*—Not around a globe, but around the circumference of a disk, according to the Indian idea.

44. THE OWL GETS MARRIED (p. 291): Told by Swimmer. The three owls of the Cherokee country are known, respectively, as *tskĭlĭ'* (that is, “witch,” *Bubo virginianus saturatus*, the great dusky-horned owl), *wa'huhu'* (*Megascops asio*, the screech owl), and *uguku'* (*Syrnium nebulosum*, the hooting or barred owl). There is no generic term for "owl." The Cherokee say that there is almost no meat on the body of the hooting owl except on its head.

45. THE HUHU GETS MARRIED (p. 292): This story was heard at various times from Swimmer, John Ax, and Ta'gwadihi'. The first mentioned always gave a very good imitation of the huhu call at the proper point, drawing out the *sau-h* slowly, giving the *hŭ, hŭ, hŭ, hŭ, hŭ, hŭ* in quick, muffled tones, and ending with three chirps and a long whistle. From this and one or two other stories of similar meaning, it seems that the woman is the dominant partner in the Cherokee household. Marriages were generally arranged by the mother and were conditional upon the girl's consent (see the notes to number 84, “The Man who Married the Thunder’s Sister”).

The huhu of the Cherokee, named for its cry, is the yellow-breasted chat (*Icteria virens*), also known as the yellow mockingbird because of its wonderful ability to mimic other sounds.

46. WHY THE BUZZARD'S HEAD IS BARE (p. 293): This story was told by Swimmer and other informants and is well known. It has an exact parallel in the Omaha story of “Ictinike and the Buzzard” (Dorsey, in *Contributions to North American Ethnology*, volume vi).

47. THE EAGLE'S REVENGE (p. 293): This story, told by John Ax, illustrates tribal beliefs and customs regarding the eagle and the eagle dance, as already described in number 35, “The Bird Tribes,” and the accompanying notes.

*Drying pole*—A pole placed horizontally in the forks of two upright stakes, planted firmly in the ground, for the purpose of temporarily hanging up game and fresh meat in a hunting camp. This protected it from wolves and other scavengers or allowed it to dry by the fire.

48. THE HUNTER AND THE BUZZARD (p. 294): Told by Swimmer. The custom of lending or exchanging wives as a sign of hospitality and friendship, on certain ceremonial occasions, or as the price for obtaining secret knowledge, was very common among the tribes. This has been noted by explorers and other observers, in both the East and West, from the earliest periods.

49. THE SNAKE TRIBE (p. 294): *Rattlesnake*—The custom of asking pardon from killed or offended animals has already been noted under number 15, “The Four-footed Tribes,” and number 35, “The Bird Tribes” (regarding the eagle). Reverence for the rattlesnake was universal among the Indians and has been frequently remarked upon by travelers in every part of the country. It is not our purpose here to provide a long discussion on the great subject of serpent worship.

The missionary Washburn recounts how, among the Cherokee of Arkansas, he was once riding along accompanied by an Indian on foot when they discovered a poisonous snake coiled beside the path. “I observed that Blanket turned aside to avoid the serpent but made no sign of attack, and I requested the interpreter to get down and kill it. He did so, and I then inquired of Blanket why he did not kill the serpent. He answered, ‘I never kill snakes, and so the snakes never kill me; but I will tell you about it the next time you come to see me.’” He kept his word soon after by relating a long story as a personal experience (though it was likely an Indian dream) of once being led by a rattlesnake to an underground council of the rattlesnake tribe. There, he found all the snakes mourning over one of their members who had been recently killed by an Indian and debating the method of punishment. This punishment was carried out a day or two later by inflicting a fatal bite upon the offender while he was playing a ball game (*Reminiscences*, pp. 208-212). As told by the missionary,

The story is very much dressed up, but strikingly resembles number 58, "The Rattlesnake's Vengeance."

Adair, evidently confusing several Cherokee snake myths, speaks of some reputed gigantic rattlesnakes in the Cherokee mountains, with beautiful changing colors and great power of fascination, by which they drew into their jaws any living creature coming within their vision, and continues:

> "They call them and all of the rattlesnake kind, kings or chieftains of the snakes, and they allow one such to every different species of the brute creation. An old trader of Cheeowhee told me that for the reward of two pieces of stroud cloth <note>A coarse woolen fabric used in the Indian trade.</note> he engaged a couple of young warriors to show him the place of their resort; but the headmen would not by any means allow it, on account of a superstitious tradition—for they imagine the killing of them would expose them to the danger of being bitten by the other inferior species of the serpentine tribe, who love their chieftains and know by instinct those who maliciously killed them, as they fight only in their own defense and that of their young ones, never biting those who do not disturb them."

He mentions also an instance of a Chickasaw priest who, after having applied to his hands the juice of a certain plant, took up a rattlesnake without damage and laid it carefully in a hollow tree to prevent Adair's killing it (*History of the American Indians*, pp. 237-238).

Of the Carolina tribes generally, Lawson, in 1701, says:

> "As for killing snakes, they avoid it if they lie in their way, because their opinion is that some of the serpents' kindred would kill some of the savage's relations that should destroy him" (*History of Carolina*, p. 341).

Bartram says of the Seminoles, about 1775:

> "These people never kill the rattlesnake or any other serpent, saying, if they do so, the spirit of the killed snake will excite or influence his living kindred or relatives to revenge the injury or violence done to him when alive."

He recounts an amusing incident of his own experience where the Indians sent for him to come and kill a rattlesnake which had invaded their camp ground, and which they were afraid to disturb. Their request having been complied with, the Indians then insisted upon scratching him, according to the Indian custom, in order to let out some of his superabundant blood and courage, but were finally, with some difficulty, dissuaded from their purpose.

> "Thus it seemed that the whole was a ludicrous farce to satisfy their people and appease the manes <note>The spirits of the dead.</note> of the dead rattlesnake" (*Travels*, pp. 258-261).

The trader Henry (*Travels*, pp. 176-179) narrates a most interesting instance from among the Ojibwa of Lake Superior in 1764. While gathering wood near the camp he was startled by a sudden rattle, and looking down discovered a rattlesnake almost at his feet, with body coiled and head raised to strike.

> "I no sooner saw the snake, than I hastened to the canoe, in order to procure my gun; but, the Indians observing what I was doing, inquired the occasion, and being informed, begged me to desist. At the same time, they followed me to the spot, with their pipes and tobacco-pouches in their hands. On returning, I found the snake still coiled.
>
> "The Indians, on their part, surrounded it, all addressing it by turns, and calling it their *grandfather*; but yet keeping at some distance. During this part of the ceremony, they filled their pipes; and now each blew the smoke toward the snake, who, as it appeared to me, really received it with pleasure. In a word, after remaining coiled, and receiving incense, for the space of half an hour, it stretched itself along the ground, in visible good humor. Its length was between four and five feet. Having remained outstretched for some time, at last it moved slowly away, the Indians following it, and still addressing it by the title of grandfather, beseeching it to take care of their families during their absence, and to be pleased to open the heart of Sir William Johnson [the British Indian agent, whom they were about to visit], so that he might show them *charity*, and fill their canoe with rum. One of the chiefs added a petition, that the snake would take notice of the insult which had been offered

him by the Englishman, who would even have put him to death if not for the interference of the Indians, to whom it was hoped the snake would attribute no part of the offense. They further requested that he should remain and inhabit their country, and not return among the English; that is, not go eastward.”

He adds that the appearance of the rattlesnake so far north was regarded as an extraordinary omen, and that very little else was spoken of for the rest of the evening. The next day, while steering across Lake Huron in his canoe, a terrible storm came up.

> “The Indians, becoming alarmed, frequently called on the rattlesnake to come to their assistance. By degrees the waves grew high; and at 11 o’clock a hurricane blew, and we expected to be swallowed up at any moment. From prayers, the Indians now proceeded to sacrifices, both of which were offered to the god-rattlesnake, or *manito-kinibic*. One of the chiefs took a dog, and after tying its forelegs together, threw it overboard, while at the same time calling on the snake to preserve us from drowning and asking him to satisfy his hunger with the carcass of the dog. The snake was not favorable, and the wind increased. Another chief sacrificed another dog, adding some tobacco. In the prayer that accompanied these gifts, he begged the snake, as before, not to avenge the insult he had received from me—when I had planned to put him to death—upon the Indians. He assured the snake that I was completely an Englishman, and related neither to him nor to them. At the conclusion of this speech, an Indian who sat near me observed that if we drowned it would be my fault alone, and that I should be sacrificed myself to appease the angry *manito*. I was not without fears that, in such dire circumstances, this would be my fate; but, happily for me, the storm at length died down, and we reached the island safely.”

The Delawares also, according to Heckewelder, called the rattlesnake "grandfather" and refrained from injuring him. He says: “One day, as I was walking with an elderly Indian on the banks of the Muskingum, I saw a large rattlesnake lying across the path, which I was going to kill. The Indian immediately forbade me from doing so; ‘for,’ said he, ‘the rattlesnake is grandfather to the Indians, and is placed here on purpose to guard us, and to give us notice of upcoming danger by his rattle, which is the same as if he were to tell us, ‘*look about*.’ ‘Now,’ added he, ‘if we were to kill one of those, the others would soon know it, and the whole race would rise up against us and bite us.’ I remarked to him that the white people were not afraid of this, for they killed all the rattlesnakes they met. On this he asked whether any white man had been bitten by these animals, and of course I answered yes. ‘No wonder, then!’ he replied, ‘you have yourselves to blame for that. You have essentially declared war against them, and you will find them in your country, where they will not fail to make frequent raids. They are a very dangerous enemy; take care you do not irritate them in *our* country; they and their grandchildren are on good terms, and neither will hurt the other.’ These ancient notions have, however, largely died away with the last generation, and the Indians today kill their grandfather, the rattlesnake, without ceremony whenever they meet him” (Indian Nations, p. 252).

*Sälikwâyĭ*—“The old Tuscaroras had a custom which they supposed would keep their teeth white and strong throughout life. A man caught a snake and held it by its head and tail. Then he bit it through, all the way from the head to the tail, and this kept the teeth from decay” (W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Notes, in Journal of American Folk-Lore, July, 1892).

*Send torrents of rain*—The belief in a connection between the serpent and the rain-gods is nearly universal among primitive peoples and only needs to be mentioned here.

### 50. THE UKTENA AND THE ULÛÑSÛ'TĬ (p. 297):
The belief in the great Uktena and the magic power of the Ulûñsû'tĭ is firmly implanted in the Cherokee heart. The Uktena has its parallel in the *Gitchi-Kenebig* or Great Horned Serpent of the

northern Algonquian tribes, and is somewhat analogous to the *Zemo'gu'ani* or Great Horned Alligator of the Kiowa. Myths of a jewel in the head of a serpent or of a toad are so common to all Aryan nations as to have become proverbial. Talismanic and prophetic stones, which are carefully guarded and to which prayer and sacrifice are offered, are kept by many tribes (see Dorsey, Teton Folklore, in American Anthropologist, April 1889). The name of the serpent is derived from *akta*, "eye," and may be rendered "strong looker," i.e., "keen-eyed," because nothing within the range of its vision can escape discovery. From the same root is derived *akta'tĭ*, "to look into," "to examine closely," which is the Cherokee name for a field glass or telescope. By the English-speaking Indians, the serpent is sometimes called the diamond rattlesnake. The mythic diamond crest, when in its proper place upon the snake's head, is called *ulstĭtlû'*, literally, "it is on his head," but when detached and in the hands of the conjurer, it becomes the *Ulûñsû'tĭ*, "Transparent," the great talisman of the tribe. On account of its glittering brightness, it is sometimes called *Igăgû'tĭ*, "Daylight." Inferior magic crystals are believed to be the scales from the same serpent and are sometimes also called *ulûñsû'tĭ*.

The earliest notice of the *Ulûñsû'tĭ* is given by the young Virginian officer Timberlake, who was sent upon a peace mission to the Cherokee in 1762, shortly after the close of their first war with the whites. He says (*Memoirs*, pp. 47-49):

> "They have many beautiful stones of different colors, many of which I am inclined to believe are of great value; but their superstition has always prevented them from selling them to the traders, who have made many attempts for that purpose. Since they use them in their conjuring ceremonies, they believe that parting with them or bringing them from home would harm their health or affairs. Among others, there is one in the possession of a conjurer that is remarkable for its brilliance and beauty, but even more so for the extraordinary manner in which it was found. It grew, if we may believe the Indians, on the head of a monstrous serpent whose retreat was discovered by its brilliance. However, a great number of snakes attended him—he being of a superior rank among the serpents, as I suppose by his crown—making it dangerous to attack him. The Indians made many attempts, but all were frustrated until a man more bold than the rest, protecting himself in leather that was impenetrable to the bite of the serpent or its guards and watching for a convenient opportunity, surprised and killed him. He tore the jewel from his head, which the conjurer has kept hidden for many years in a place unknown to everyone except two women. These women have been offered large gifts to betray its location but have steadily refused, lest some severe judgment or misfortune should follow. I believe that such a stone exists, having seen many of great beauty; but I cannot think it would live up to all the praise the Indians bestow upon it. I suppose the conjurer invented the account of its discovery; however, I have given it to the reader as a specimen of an Indian story, many of which are much more surprising."

A few years later Adair gives us an account of the serpent and the stone. According to his statement, the *uktenas* had their home in a deep valley between the heads of the Tuckasegee and the "northern branch of the lower Cherokee river" (i.e., the Little Tennessee), the valley being the deep defile of Nantahala, where, by reason of its gloomy and forbidding aspect, Cherokee tradition locates more than one legendary terror. With pardonable error, he confuses the *Uktena* with the Chief of the Rattlesnakes. The two, however, are distinct, the latter being simply the head of the rattlesnake tribe, without the blazing carbuncle or the immense size attributed to the *Uktena*.

> "Between two high mountains, nearly covered with old mossy rocks, lofty cedars, and pines—in the valleys of which the sun's rays reflect a powerful heat—there are, as the natives affirm, some bright old inhabitants or rattlesnakes of a more enormous size than is mentioned in history. They are so large and unwieldy that they take a circle almost as wide as their length to crawl around in their shortest turn; but bountiful nature compensates for the heavy motion of their bodies, for, as they say,

> “The description the Indians give us of their color is as varied as what we are told of the chameleon, which seems to the spectator to change its color with every different position from which it is viewed. This proceeds from the piercing rays of light that blaze from their foreheads, dazzling the eyes from whatever direction they position themselves—for in each of their heads, there is a large carbuncle <note>A carbuncle is a legendary glowing gemstone, often identified with a deep-red garnet or ruby.</note>, which they claim not only reflects but even outshines the midday beams of the sun. They consider it so dangerous to disturb these creatures that no temptation can induce them to reveal their secret hiding places to the uninitiated. They call them, and all of the rattlesnake kind, kings or chieftains of the snakes, and they assign one such leader to every different species of the animal creation. An old trader from Cheeowhee told me that for a reward of two pieces of stroud cloth <note>Stroud was a type of coarse wool fabric commonly used in the Indian trade.</note>, he hired a couple of young warriors to show him the place where they lived; however, the headmen would not allow it under any circumstances because of a superstitious tradition. They believe that killing them would expose them to the danger of being bitten by the other inferior species of that snake family, who love their chieftains and instinctively know those who maliciously killed them; for they fight only in their own defense and that of their young, never biting those who do not disturb them.”—*History of the American Indians, pp. 237–238.*

In another place (page 87) he tells us of an *ulûñsû'tĭ* owned by a medicine man who resided at Tymahse (Tomassee), a former Cherokee town on the creek of the same name near the present Seneca, South Carolina. “The Cherokee prophet mentioned above had a carbuncle nearly as big as an egg, which they said he found where a great rattlesnake lay dead. It sparkled with such surprising luster that it illuminated his dark winter house like strong flashes of continuous lightning, to the great terror of the weak, who did not dare to approach the dreadful, fire-darting place for any reason, fearing sudden death. When he died, it was buried with him according to custom in the town of Tymahse, under the ‘great beloved cabin’ [seat], which stood in the westernmost part of that old building; those who are willing to run the risk of searching may fortunately find it there.”

Hagar also mentions the “Oolunsade,” and says, on the authority of John Ax: “He who owns a crystal can call one of the Little People to him at any time and make him do his bidding. Sometimes when people are ill, it is because some evil invisible being has taken possession of them. Then the Little Man called up by the crystal can be placed on guard near the ill person to prevent the evil spirit from re-entering after it has been expelled” (MS Stellar Legends of the Cherokee).

The Southern Alleghenies, the old Cherokee country, abound with crystals of various kinds as well as with minerals. The *Ulûñsû'tĭ* is described as a triangular crystal about two inches long, flat on the bottom, with slightly convex sides tapering up to a point. It is perfectly transparent with the exception of a single red streak running through the center from top to bottom. It is evidently a rare and beautiful specimen of rutile quartz; crystals of this type found in the region may be seen in the National Museum at Washington.

Other small stones of various shapes and colors are in common use among Cherokee conjurers to discover lost articles or for other occult purposes. These also are frequently called by the same name and are said to have been originally the scales of the Uktena. However, the *Ulûñsû'tĭ*—the talisman from the forehead of the serpent—is the crystal described here. It is so exceedingly rare that, as far as is known, only one remained among the Eastern Cherokee in 1890. Its owner, a famous hunter, kept it hidden in a cave wrapped in a deerskin. He refused all inducements to show it, much less to part with it, stating that if he should expose it to the gaze of a white man, he could kill no more game, even if he were permitted to live after such a sacrilege.

The possession of the talisman ensures success in hunting, love, rainmaking, and

all other undertakings, but its greatest use is in life divination. When it is invoked for this purpose by its owner, the future is mirrored in the transparent crystal just as a tree is reflected in the quiet stream below.

When consulting it, the conjurer gazes into the crystal and, after a short time, sees in its transparent depths a picture of the person or event in question. By the movement of the specter, or its position near the top or bottom of the crystal, he learns not only about the event itself but also its proximity in time or location.

Many of the Eastern Cherokee who enlisted in the Confederate service during the late war <note>This refers to the American Civil War.</note> consulted the *Ulûñsû'tĭ* before departing, and survivors declare that their experiences verified the predictions. One of these men had gone with two others to consult the fates. The conjurer, placing the three men facing him, took the talisman upon the end of his outstretched finger and told them to look intently into it. After some moments, they saw their own images at the bottom of the crystal. The images gradually ascended along the red line. The images of the other two men rose to the middle and then descended again, but the likeness of the one telling the story continued to ascend until it reached the top before going down again. The conjurer then said that the other two would die in the second year of the war, but the third would survive through hardships and narrow escapes and live to return home. As the prophecy was given, so the event occurred.

When consulted by the friends of a sick man to find out if he will recover, the conjurer shows them the image of the sick man lying at the bottom of the *Ulûñsû'tĭ*. He then tells them to go home and kill some game (or, in these more recent days, any food animal) and to prepare a feast. On the appointed day, the conjurer, at his own home, looks into the crystal and sees a picture of the party at dinner. If the image of the sick man rises and joins them at the feast, the patient will recover; if otherwise, he is doomed.

51. **ÂGAN-UNI'TSÏ'S SEARCH FOR THE UKTENA** (p. 248): This is one of the most important Cherokee traditions because it deals with the mythic monster, the Uktena, and explains the origin of the great talisman, the *Ulûñsû'tĭ*. As presented here, it was obtained from Swimmer (east) with additions and variations from Wafford (west) and others. It is recorded by Ten Kate as obtained by him in the Territory <note>Likely referring to the Indian Territory, modern-day Oklahoma.</note> (*Legends of the Cherokees*, in *Journal of American Folk-Lore*, January 1889), and is mentioned in connection with the *Ulûñsû'tĭ* by Adair in 1775 and by Timberlake as early as 1762 (see notes to number 50, “The Uktena and the *Ulûñsû'tĭ*”). One variation makes the *Ulûñsû'tĭ* a scale from the seventh ring of the serpent.

The Shawano <note>The Shawnee tribe.</note>, who at one time occupied the Cumberland region of Tennessee immediately adjoining the Cherokee, were regarded as wizards by all the southern tribes. Brinton says: “Among the Algonquins, the Shawnee tribe did more than all others combined to introduce and spread religious legends and ceremonies. From the earliest times, they seem to have had a peculiar aptitude for the trances, deceptions, and fantasies that make up the spiritual life of their associates. Their constantly wandering life brought them into contact with the myths of many nations, and it is extremely probable that they first brought the tale of the horned serpent from the Creeks and Cherokees” (*Myths of the New World*, p. 137).

*Localities*—*Utăwagûn'ta* mountain, *Walâsi'yĭ* gap, *Duniskwa'lgûn'yĭ* gap, and *Atagâ'hĭ* (mythic) lake are all points in the Great Smoky range, which forms the dividing line between North Carolina and Tennessee. *Tlanusi'yĭ* is the native name for the site of Murphy, at the junction of the Hiwassee and Valley rivers in North Carolina. *Gahû'tĭ* is Cohutta mountain in Murray County, Georgia. According to Wafford, there are several stone enclosures on the sides of this mountain that were built by Âgan-uni'tsï for shelter before attacking the Uktena (see also *Glossary*).

*Asga'ya Gi'gage'ĭ*—The "Red Man," or lightning spirit, who is frequently invoked in the sacred formulas.

*Struck by lightning*—As has been explained elsewhere, the wood of a tree that has been struck by lightning plays an important part in Cherokee folklore.

*Strong and dangerous*—It is a common Native American belief that the presence of a powerful talisman, no matter how beneficial it may be in itself, is exhausting or positively dangerous to those nearby unless they are strengthened by some ceremonial tonic. For this reason, every great "medicine" is usually kept apart in a hut or tipi built for that purpose, much like we are accustomed to store explosives at a distance from a house or business.

53. **THE HUNTER AND THE UKSU'HĬ** (p. 301): This story was told by Swimmer and John Ax as an actual fact. The *uksu'hĭ* is the mountain blacksnake or black racer (*Coluber obsoletus*). The name seems to refer to some peculiarity of the eye, *aktă* (compare with *uktena*). Hickory-log, properly *Wane'asûñ'tlûñyi*, "Hickory footlog," was a Cherokee settlement on the Hiwassee River, near the present Hayesville, Clay County, North Carolina. Another settlement of the same name was on the Etowah River in Georgia.

*Perspiration*—The Indigenous belief may or may not be based on fact.

54. **THE USTÛ'TLĬ** (p. 302): This story was told by Swimmer and John Ax (from the east) and by Wafford (from the west), and it is a common tradition throughout the tribe. The name *ustû'tlĭ* refers to the sole of the foot and was given to the serpent because of its peculiar feet or "suckers." The same name is given to the common hoop-snake of the south (*Abastor erythrogrammus*), about which such wonderful tales are told by the white mountaineers. Cohutta (*Gahû'tĭ*) Mountain, in Murray County, Georgia, was also the traditional haunt of the Uktena (see number 51, "Âgan-Uni'tsĭ's search for the Uktena," and compare also number 55, "The *Uw'tsûñ'ta*.")

55. **THE UW'TSÛÑ'TA** (p. 303): This story was obtained from James Blythe. *Nûñdaye'lĭ*, from which the name Nantahala is derived, was on the river of that name below the present Jarrett's station.

56. **THE SNAKE BOY** (p. 304): This myth was told by Swimmer.

*Âsĭ*—The Cherokee *âsĭ*, or "hot-house," as it was called by the old traders, is the equivalent of the sweat-house used by western tribes. It is a small hut of logs plastered over with clay, with a shed roof, and just tall enough to permit a person to sit or recline, but not to stand. It is used for sweat-bath purposes, and because it is tight and warm—with a fire usually kept smoldering inside—it is a favorite sleeping place for the elderly in cold weather. It is now nearly obsolete.

57. **THE SNAKE MAN** (p. 304): This myth, obtained from Chief Smith, seems designed to impress upon the people the importance of strictly observing the innumerable *gaktûñ'ta*, or taboos, which affect the daily life of the Cherokee, whether in health or sickness, hunting, war, or the arts of peace (see the author's "Sacred Formulas of the Cherokees," in the Seventh Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology).

Similar transformation myths are found all over the world. One of the most ancient is the story of Cadmus, in Ovid's "Metamorphoses," which describes the despair of his wife as she sees the snaky change overcome her husband. "Cadmus, what does this mean? Where are your feet? Where are both your shoulders and your hands? Where is your color? And, while I speak, where is everything else?"

In a Pawnee story provided by Grinnell, two brothers who are traveling camp for the night. The older brother eats some forbidden food and wakes from his sleep to find that he is changing into a great rattlesnake, with the change beginning at his feet. He rouses his brother and gives him his final instructions:

> "When I have changed into a snake, take me in your arms and carry me over to

...that hole. "That will be my home, for that is the house of the snakes." While still possessing a man's mind, he continues to speak as the transformation moves up his body, until at last his head changes into that of a snake. At that point, his brother picks him up and carries him to the hole. The relatives make frequent trips to the place to visit the snake, who always comes out when they call. The brother brings it a share of his war trophies, including a horse and a woman, and receives the protection of the snake-man in return (*Pawnee Hero Stories*, pp. 171-181). A similar Omaha version is provided by Dorsey ("The warriors who were changed to snakes," in *Contributions to North American Ethnology*, volume VI).

58. **THE RATTLESNAKE'S VENGEANCE** (p. 305): This story, told by Swimmer, exemplifies the Native American reverence for the rattlesnake and the dread of offending it, which was already explained in number 49, "The Snake Tribe," and the accompanying notes.

*Prayer song*—See other references under number 3, "Kana'ti and Selu." Many of the Native American ceremonial prayers and invocations take the form of songs or chants.

59. **THE SMALLER REPTILES, FISHES, AND INSECTS** (p. 306): *Gi'gă-tsuha'lĭ*—This lizard is likely the *Pleistodon erythrocephalus*, which is described in Holbrook's "Herpetology" as being about 11 to 13 inches long, with a bright red head, an olive-brown body and tail, and a yellowish-white throat and abdomen. "The *Pleistodon erythrocephalus* chooses to live in deep forests and is commonly found near hollow trees, often at a height of 30 or 40 feet from the ground. Sometimes it takes up residence in a woodpecker's nest from the previous year, out of which it thrusts its bright red head in a threatening way toward those who would disturb its home. It never makes its home on or near the ground, and in fact, it seldom descends from its height unless searching for food or water. Although shy and timid, it is very fierce when captured and bites severely due to the great strength of its jaws and the size and firmness of its teeth. The bite, however, while sharp and painful, is not venomous as is commonly believed." <note>1</note>

*Large horned beetle*—This beetle, variously called the Cherokee crawfish, deer, or buck because of its branching horns, is probably the "flying stag" mentioned by early travelers. Timberlake says: "Of insects, the flying stag is almost the only one worthy of notice. It is about the shape of a beetle, but has very large, beautiful, branching horns, like those of a stag, which is how it got its name" (Memoirs, p. 46). Lawson, around 1700, also mentions "the flying stags, with horns" among the insects of eastern Carolina.

60. **WHY THE BULLFROG'S HEAD IS STRIPED** (p. 310): The first version is from John Ax; the second is from Swimmer, who had forgotten the details.

61. **THE BULLFROG LOVER** (p. 310): This first amusing little tale was heard from several storytellers. The warning words are sometimes given differently, but always in a deep, gruff, singing tone that provides a very good imitation of a bullfrog's croak. The other stories were told by Tsĕsa'ni (Jessan) and confirmed by Swimmer.

In a Creek version of the first story, found in the Tuggle collection, there is a pretty girl who remains stubborn until her lover, the Rabbit, conceals himself in the same way near the spring. Using a blowgun as a trumpet, he frightens her into consenting by singing out: "The girl who stays single will die, will die, will die."

62. **THE KATYDID'S WARNING** (p. 311): Told by Swimmer and James Blythe.

63. **ÛNTSAIYI', THE GAMBLER** (p. 311): This story was obtained from Swimmer and John Ax (from the east) and confirmed also by James Wafford (from the west), who remembered, however, only the main points of the pursuit and final capture at Kâgûn'yĭ. The two versions matched very closely, except that Ax sends the boy to the Sunset land to play against his brothers, while Swimmer has the brothers come to meet him.

at their father's house. In Ax's version, also, the gambler flees directly to the west, and every time the brothers shoot at him with their arrows, the thunder rolls and the lightning flashes; however, he escapes by sinking into the earth, which opens for him, only to reappear in another form somewhere else. Swimmer says that the Little People helped in the chase. In Cherokee tradition, an invitation to a ball contest is a challenge to battle. Thunder is always personified in the plural, <term>Ani'-Hyûñ'tikwălâ'skĭ</term>, "The Thunderers." The father and the two older sons seem to be <term>Kana'tĭ</term> and the Thunder Boys (see story number 3, "<term>Kana'tĭ</term> and <term>Selu</term>"), although neither informant would positively assert this, while the boy hero—who has no other name—is said to be the lightning. Nothing is told of his later career.

*<term>Ûntsaiyĭ'</term>*—In this name (sometimes written *<term>E'tsaiyĭ'</term>* or *<term>Tsaiyĭ'</term>*), the first syllable is almost silent and the vowels are prolonged to imitate the ringing sound produced by striking a thin sheet of metal. The word is now translated as "brass" and is applied to any object made of that metal. The mythic gambler, who has a counterpart in the mythologies of many tribes, is the traditional inventor of the wheel-and-stick game. This game was very popular among the southern and eastern Indians and is variously known as <term>gatayûstĭ</term>, chenco, or chûnki (see the note under story number 3, "<term>Kana'tĭ</term> and <term>Selu</term>"). He lived on the south side of the Tennessee River, at *<term>Ûn'tiguhi'</term>*.

*<term>Ûn'tiguhi'</term>* or *The Suck*—The noted and dangerous rapid known to white settlers as "The Suck" and to the Cherokee as *<term>Ûn'tiguhi'</term>*, "Pot in the water," is in the Tennessee River near the entrance of Suck Creek. This is about 8 miles below Chattanooga, at a point where the river gathers its whole force into a narrow channel to break through the Cumberland Mountain. The popular name, Whirl or Suck, dates back at least to 1780, with the upper portion being known at the same time as "The boiling pot" (Donelson diary, in Ramsey, *Tennessee*, p. 71),¹ a close translation of the Indian name. In the days of pioneer settlement, it was a most dangerous threat to navigation, but some of the most serious obstacles in the channel have now been removed by blasting and other methods. The Cherokee name and legend were probably suggested by the appearance of the rapids at that spot. According to the Indian account, near where *<term>Ûntsaiyĭ'</term>* lived, one may still see the large flat rock upon which he was accustomed to play the <term>gatayûstĭ</term> game with all who accepted his challenge. The lines and grooves worn by the rolling of the wheels are still plainly marked, and the stone wheels themselves are now firmly attached to the surface of the rock. A similarly grooved or striped rock, where it is said *<term>Ûntsaiyĭ'</term>* also used to roll his wheel, is reported to be on the north side of the Hiwassee River, just below Calhoun, Tennessee.

The Suck is described this way by a traveler in 1818, while the region was still Indian country and Chattanooga was not yet imagined:

> "And here, I cannot help pausing a moment to call your attention to the grand and picturesque scenery that opens to the view of the admiring spectator. The country is still possessed by the Native Americans, and the hand of civilization has done little to soften the wild aspect of nature. The Tennessee River, having concentrated the numerous streams it has received over its course of three or four hundred miles into one mass, glides through an extended valley with a rapid and overwhelming current, half a mile wide. At this place, a group of mountains stands ready to dispute its progress. First, the 'Lookout,' an independent range starting thirty miles below, presents its bold and rocky end of two thousand feet opposite the river's course. Around its brow is a palisade of naked rocks, from seventy to one hundred feet high. The river flows at its base and instantly turns to the right. Passing on for six miles further, it turns again and is met by the side of Raccoon Mountain. Collecting its strength into a channel of seventy yards, it cuts through the mountain and rushes tumultuously through the rocky pass, carrying the trembling navigator at the rate of a mile every two or three minutes. The passage is called 'The

*Suck.*' The summit of Lookout Mountain overlooks the entire region. For those who can find delight in the view of an endless forest, cut through by the windings of a powerful river, dotted with hundreds of green prairies, and broken by many ridges and mountains, it provides a landscape in the month of May that is matched by few others in its scale, variety, or beauty."—Rev. Elias Cornelius, in (Silliman's) American Journal of Science, <term>I</term>, p. 223, 1818.

*Bet even his life*—The American Indian was a passionate gambler, and there was absolutely no limit to the risks he was willing to take, even to the point of losing his freedom, if not his life. Lawson says (History of Carolina, p. 287): "They gamble extensively and often strip one another of everything they own in the world; furthermore, I have known several of them to gamble themselves away, so that they remained the winners' servants until they or their relatives could pay the money to redeem them."

*His skin was clean*—The concept of purification or cleansing through the effectiveness of the sweat bath is very common in Indian myths and ceremonies. In an Omaha story recorded by Dorsey, the hero has been transformed into a mangy dog by witchcraft. He builds a sweat lodge, enters it as a dog, and sweats until, at his command, the people remove the blankets; then, "Behold, he was not a dog; he was a very handsome man" ("Adventures of Hingpe-agce," in Contributions to North American Ethnology, <term>VI</term>, p. 175).

*From the bottom*—Choosing the most distant or most insignificant-looking object from a group, which then proves to be the most valuable, is another common element in these myths.

*Honey-locust tree*—The preference for the honey-locust tree and the seat made of thorns from the same species in the home of the Thunder Man may suggest that in Indian thought, as in Aryan thought, there was a mystical connection between pinnate leaves and lightning, similar to what we see with the European rowan or mountain ash.

*All kinds of snakes*—It should be remembered that the boy's father was a thunder god. The connection between the snake and the rain or thunder spirit has already been noted. This also appears in story number 84, "The Man who Married the Thunder's Sister."

*Elder brother*—My elder brother (spoken by a male), *ûngini'lĭ*; my elder brother (spoken by a female), *ûñgidâ'*; your two elder brothers (spoken by a male), *tsetsăni'lĭ*.

*Sunset land*—The Cherokee word used here is *Wusûhihûñ'yĭ*, "the place where they stay overnight." The usual expression in the sacred formulas is *usûñhi'yĭ*, "the place of darkening or twilight"; the common word is *wude'ligûñ'yĭ*, "where the sun goes down."

*Lightning at every stroke*—In the Omaha myth of "The Chief's Son and the Thunders," recorded by Dorsey, several young men traveling to the end of the world meet a Thunder Man who tells the leader to choose one of four medicine bags. Having been warned beforehand, he chooses the oldest but most powerful bag and is then also given a club that creates thunder whenever it is waved in the air (Contributions to North American Ethnology, <term>VI</term>, p. 185).

*Strike the rock*—This method of obtaining water is at least as old as the Book of Exodus.

*The brass rubbed off*—The beautiful metallic shine on the head of the *Phanæus carnifex* beetle is explained this way. The common roller beetle is called the "dung roller," but this species is distinguished as the "horned brass beetle." It is also sometimes called the dog of the Thunder Boys.

*Beavers gnaw at the grapevine*—A similar concept is found among the Cheyenne: "The earth rests on a large beam or post. Far in the north, there is a beaver as white as snow who is the great father of all mankind. One day, he will gnaw through the support at the bottom. We will be helpless, and the earth will fall. This will happen when he becomes angry. The post is already partly eaten through. For

**64. THE NEST OF THE TLĂ'NUWĂ (p. 315):** This story was obtained first from John Ax and Ta'gwadihi', and was afterward heard of frequently in connection with the cave at Citico. It is mentioned by Ten Kate in "Legends of the Cherokees," obtained in the Indian Territory, in the Journal of American Folk-Lore, January, 1889.

*Tlă'nuwă*—The Tlă'nuwă (*Tsă'nuwă* or *Sû'năwă* in the Middle dialect) is a mythic bird, described as a great hawk, larger than any bird now existing. There is a small hawk called *tlă'nuwă usdĭ'*, "little tlă'nuwă," which is described as its smaller counterpart or image, and which the Cherokee say accompanies flocks of wild pigeons, occasionally when hungry swooping down and killing one by striking it with its sharp breast bone. It is probably the goshawk (*Astur atricapillus*). The great Tlă'nuwă, like the other animals, "went up." According to Adair (History of the American Indians, p. 17) the Cherokee used to compare a miserly person to a "sinnawah." When John Ax first recited the story he insisted that the whites must also believe it, as they had it depicted on their money; holding up a silver coin, he triumphantly pointed out what he claimed was the figure of the Tlă'nuwă, holding arrows in its talons and a serpent in its beak. He was not so far wrong, as it is well known that the Mexican coat of arms, stamped upon the coins of the republic, has its origin in a similar legend handed down from the Aztecs. Myths of dangerous monster serpents destroyed by great birds were common to a number of tribes. The Tuscarora, formerly eastern neighbors of the Cherokee, told "a long tale of a great rattlesnake, which, a long time ago, lived by a creek in that river, which was Neuse, and that it killed many Indians; but at last a bald eagle killed it, and they were relieved of a serpent that used to devour whole canoes full of Indians at a time" (Lawson, Carolina, p. 346).

*Tlă'nuwa'i*—"Tlă'nuwă place," the cliff so called by the Cherokee, with the cave halfway up its face, is on the north bank of the Little Tennessee river, a short distance below the entrance of Citico creek, on land formerly belonging to Colonel John Lowrey, one of the Cherokee officers at the battle of Horseshoe Bend (Wafford). Just above, but on the opposite side of the river, is *U'tlûñti'yĭ*, the former haunt of the cannibal liver eater (see number 66, "U'tlûñta, the Spear-finger").

*Soon after the creation*—As John Ax put it, adopting the Bible expression, *Hĭlahi'yu dĭne'tlănă a'nĭgwa*—"A long time ago, soon after the creation."

*Rope of linn bark*—The old Cherokee still do most of their tying and packing with ropes twisted from the inner bark of trees. In one version of the story the medicine man uses a long *udâ'ĭ* or cohosh (*Actæa?*) vine.

*Holes are still there*—The place which the Cherokee call *Tlă'nuwă-a'tsiyelûñisûñ'yĭ*, "Where the Tlă'nuwă cut it up," is nearly opposite Citico, on the Little Tennessee river, just below Talassee ford, in Blount county, Tennessee. The surface of the rock bears a series of long trench-like depressions, extending some distance, which, according to the Indians, are the marks where the pieces bitten from the body of the great serpent were dropped by the Tlă'nuwă.

**65. THE HUNTER AND THE TLĂ'NUWĂ (p. 316):** This myth was told by Swimmer.

**66. U'TLÛÑ'TA, THE SPEAR-FINGER (p. 316):** This is one of the most noted among the Cherokee myths, being equally well known both east and west. The version here given was obtained from John Ax, with some corrections and additions from Swimmer, Wafford (west) and others. A version of it, "The Stone-shields," in which the titmouse is incorrectly identified as a jay, is given by Ten Kate, in his "Legends of the Cherokees," in the Journal of American Folk-Lore for January, 1889, as obtained from a mixed-blood informant in Tahlequah. # MOONEY] NOTES AND PARALLELS

"Consumption," by Capt. James W. Terrell, formerly a trader among the East Cherokee, appears in the same journal for April 1892. Still another version, apparently condensed from Terrell's information, is given by Zeigler and Grosscup in "Heart of the Alleghanies," page 24 (Raleigh and Cleveland, 1883). In Ten Kate's version, the stone coat of mail broke into pieces as soon as the monster was killed, and the fragments were gathered up and kept as amulets by the people.

There is some confusion between this story of <term>U'tlûn'ta</term> and that of <term>Nûn'yunu'wĭ</term> (number 67). According to some myth-tellers, the two monsters were husband and wife and lived together. They were both dressed in stone, had awl-like fingers, and ate human livers; the only difference was that the husband waylaid hunters, while his female partner focused her attention on children.

This story has a close parallel in the Creek myth of the Tuggle collection, "The Big Rock Man," in which the people finally kill the stony monster by following the Rabbit's advice to shoot him in the ear.

Far away, in British Columbia, the Indians tell how the Coyote transformed himself into an Elk, covering his body with a hard shell. "Now this shell was like armor, for no arrow could pierce it; but being hardly large enough to cover all his body, there was a small hole left underneath his throat." He attacks the people, stabbing them with his antlers and trampling them underfoot, while their arrows glance harmlessly from his body, until "the Meadow-lark, who was a great telltale, appeared and cried out, 'There is just a little hole at his throat!'" A hunter directs his arrow to that spot and the Elk falls dead (Teit, Thompson River Traditions, pp. 33-34).

<term>U'tlûn'ta</term>—The word means literally "he (or she) has it sharp," meaning that they have some sharp part or organ. It might be used for a tooth, a fingernail, or some other attached portion of the body, but here it refers to the awl-like finger. Ten Kate spells the name Uilata. On the Little Tennessee River, nearly opposite the entrance of Citico Creek in Blount County, Tennessee, is a place which the Cherokee call <term>U'tlûn'tûn'yĭ</term>, or "Sharp-finger place," because, they say, <term>U'tlûn'ta</term> used to frequent the spot.

<term>Nûñyû'-tlûgûñ'i</term>—"Tree rock," so called on account of its resemblance to a standing tree trunk; it is a notable monument-shaped rock on the west side of the Hiwassee River, about four miles above Hayesville, North Carolina, and nearly on the Georgia line.

Whiteside Mountain—This noted mountain, known to the Cherokee as <term>Sanigilá'gĭ</term> (a name for which they have no meaning), is one of the prominent peaks of the Blue Ridge. It is situated southeast of Franklin and about four miles from Highlands, near the dividing line between Macon and Jackson counties, North Carolina. It is 4,900 feet high, being the loftiest elevation on the ridge that forms the watershed between the tributaries of the Little Tennessee and the Chattooga branch of the Savannah River. It takes its name from the perpendicular cliff on its western exposure and is also known sometimes as the Devil's Courthouse. The Indians compare the appearance of the cliff to a sheet of ice and say that the western summit was formerly crowned by a projecting rock—since destroyed by lightning—which formed a part of the great bridge that <term>U'tlûn'ta</term> attempted to build across the valley. Lanman's description of this mountain from 1848 has been quoted in the notes to number 13, "The Great Yellow-jacket." The following is a notice by a later writer:

> "About five miles from Highlands is that huge old cliff, Whiteside, which forms the advanced guard of all the mountain ranges trending south. It is no higher than the Righi, but, like it, rising directly from the plain, it overpowers the spectator more than its loftier brethren. Through all the lowlands of upper Georgia and Alabama, this dazzling white pillar of rock, uplifting the sky, is an emphatic and significant landmark. The ascent can be made on horseback, on the rear side of the mountain, to within a quarter of a mile of the summit. When the top is reached, after a short stretch of nearly perpendicular climbing, the traveler finds himself on

*Picking strawberries*—For more than a hundred years, as readers of Bartram will remember, the rich bottom lands of the old Cherokee country have been noted for their abundance of strawberries and other wild fruits.

*My grandchildren*—As in most Indian languages, Cherokee kinship terms are usually specialized, and there is no single term for grandchild. "My son's child" is <term>ûñgini'sĭ</term>, plural <term>tsûñgini'sĭ</term>; "my daughter's child" is <term>ûñgili'sĭ</term>, plural <term>tsûñgili'sĭ</term>. The use of kinship terms to express affection or respect is very common among Indians.

*Taking the appearance*—This corresponds closely with the European folk belief in fairy changelings.

*To burn the leaves*—The burning of fallen leaves in the autumn, in order to get to the nuts on the ground below, is still practiced by the white mountaineers of the southern Alleghenies. The line of fire slowly creeping up the mountain side on a dark night is one of the picturesque sights of that picturesque country.

*The song*—As rendered by Swimmer, the songs seem to be intended as an imitation of the mournful notes of some bird, such as the turtle dove, hidden in the deep forests.

*Pitfall*—The pitfall trap for large game was known among nearly all the tribes, but seems not to have been in frequent use.

*Chickadee and tomtit*—These two little birds closely resemble each other; the Carolina chickadee (<term>Parus carolinensis</term>) or <term>tsĭkĭlilĭ</term> is somewhat smaller than the tufted titmouse (<term>Parus bicolor</term>) or <term>utsu'gĭ</term>, which is also distinguished by a topknot or crest. The belief that the <term>tsĭkĭlilĭ</term> foretells the arrival of an absent friend is general among the Cherokee, and has even extended to their neighbors, the white mountaineers. See also number 35, "The Bird Tribes," and accompanying notes.

*Her heart*—The concept of a giant or other monster whose heart or "life" is in some unusual part of the body, or may even be taken out and laid aside at will—so that it is impossible to kill the monster by ordinary means—is common in Indian as well as in European and Asiatic folklore.

In a Navaho myth we are told that the Coyote "did not, like other beings, keep his vital principle in his chest, where it might easily be destroyed. He kept it in the tip of his nose and in the end of his tail, where no one would expect to find it." He meets several accidents, any one of which would be sufficient to kill an ordinary creature, but as his nose and tail remain intact, he is resurrected each time. Finally, a girl whom he wishes to marry beats him into small pieces with a club, grinds the pieces to powder, and scatters the powder to the four winds. "But again she neglected to crush the point of the nose and the tip of the tail," with the result that the Coyote again comes to life, after which they are married and live happily until the next chapter (Matthews, Navaho Legends, pp. 91-94).

In a tale of the Gaelic highlands, the giant's life is in an egg which he keeps concealed in a distant place, and the giant does not die until the hero finds and crushes the egg. The monster or hero with but one vulnerable spot, as was the case with Achilles, is also a common concept.

It was mentioned by <term>Ayâsta</term> and others (east) and by Wafford (west) as a very old

*Nûñyunu'wĭ*, "Dressed in stone"; *adâ'lanûñstĭ*, a staff or cane; *asûñ'tlĭ*, *asûñ'tlânĭ*, a foot log or bridge; *ada'wehĭ*, a great magician or supernatural wonder-worker; see the glossary.

A very close parallel is found among the Iroquois, who have traditions of an invasion by a race of fierce cannibals known as the Stonish Giants. These giants, who were originally like ordinary humans, had wandered off into the wilderness where they became addicted to eating raw flesh and wallowing in the sand until their bodies grew to a gigantic size and were covered with hard scales like stone, which no arrow could penetrate (see Cusick, in Schoolcraft, Indian Tribes, v, p. 637). One of these, which preyed particularly upon the Onondaga, was at last caught in a pitfall and killed. Another, in tracking his victims, used "something which looked like a finger, but was really a pointer made of bone. With this he could find anything he wished." The pointer was finally snatched from him by a hunter, upon which the giant, unable to find his way without it, begged piteously for its return, promising to eat no more men and to grant the hunter long life and good luck for himself and all his friends. The hunter then restored it, and the giant kept his promises (Beauchamp, W. M., Iroquois Notes, in Journal of American Folk-Lore, Boston, July, 1892). As told by Mrs. Smith ("The Stone Giant's Challenge," Myths of the Iroquois, in Second Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, 1883), the pointer was a human finger. "He placed it upright upon his hand, and it immediately pointed the way for him to go."

*Menstrual woman*—Among all our native tribes, it is believed that there is something dangerous or uncanny in the touch or presence of a menstrual woman. Therefore, the universal institution of the "menstrual lodge" exists, to which the woman retires at such periods—eating, working, and sleeping alone—along with a host of taboos and precautions regarding the same subject. Nearly the same ideas are held in regard to a pregnant woman.

*Sourwood stakes*—Cherokee hunters impale meat upon sourwood (*Oxydendrum*) stakes for roasting, and the wood is also believed to have power against the spells of witches.

*Began to talk*—The revelation of "medicine" secrets by a magician when in his final agony is a common incident in Indian myths.

*Whatever he prayed for*—Swimmer gives a detailed statement of the specific petitions made by several of those who were painted in this way. Painting the face and body, especially with red paint, is always a more or less sacred performance among Indians, usually accompanied by prayers.

### 68. THE HUNTER IN THE DĂKWĂ'

This story was told by Swimmer and Ta'gwadihĭ' and is well known in the tribe. The version from the Wahnenauhi manuscript differs considerably from the one given here. In the Bible translation, the word *dăkwă'* is used as the equivalent of whale. Haywood alludes to the story in this way (Nat. and Aborig. Hist. Tenn., p. 244): "One of the ancient traditions of the Cherokees is that once a whale swallowed a little boy, and after some time spewed him upon the land."

It is fairly certain that the Cherokee formerly had some acquaintance with whales, which, around the year 1700, according to Lawson, were "very numerous" on the coast of North Carolina, being frequently stranded along the shore, so that settlers derived considerable profit from the oil and blubber. He enumerates four species known there and adds a general statement that "some Indians in America" hunted them at sea (History of Carolina, pp. 251-252).

In almost every age and country, we find a myth of a great fish swallowing a man,

For parallels and theories on the origin and meaning of the myth among ancient nations, see chapter IX of Bouton's *Bible Myths*.

In an Ojibwa story, the great Manabozho is swallowed, canoe and all, by the king of the fishes. With his war club, he strikes repeated blows upon the heart of the fish, which attempts to spit him out. Fearing that he might drown in deep water, Manabozho stops the attempt by placing his canoe crosswise in the throat of the fish, and continues striking at the heart until the monster heads for the shore and dies there. Then the hero makes his escape through a hole which gulls have torn in the side of the carcass (Schoolcraft, *Algic Researches*, I, pp. 145-146).

## 69. **ATAGÂ'HI, THE ENCHANTED LAKE** (p. 321)

This story was heard from Swimmer, Ta'gwadihí', and others, and is a matter of common knowledge to every hunter among the East Cherokee. If Indian testimony is believed, there is actually a large bare flat of this name in the difficult recesses of the Great Smoky Mountains on the northern boundary of Swain County, North Carolina, somewhere between the headwaters of Bradley's Fork and Eagle Creek. It appears to be a major resort for bears and ducks, and is perhaps submerged at long intervals, which would account for the legend.

*Prayer, fasting, and vigil*—In Indian ritual, as among Eastern cultures and in all ancient religions, these are essential requirements for obtaining clear spiritual vision. In almost every tribe, the young warrior just entering manhood voluntarily subjected himself to an ordeal of this kind, lasting several days, in order to obtain a vision of the "medicine" which was to be his guide and protector for the rest of his life.

## 70. **THE BRIDE FROM THE SOUTH** (p. 322)

This unique allegory was heard from both Swimmer and Ta'gwadihí' in nearly the same form. Hagar also (MS *Stellar Legends of the Cherokee*) heard something of it from Ayâsta, who, however, confused it with the Hagar variant of number 11, "The Milky Way" (see notes to number 11).

In a myth from British Columbia, "The Hot and the Cold Winds," the cold-wind people of the north wage war with the hot-wind people of the south until the Indians, whose country lay between and who constantly suffer from both sides, bring about a peace to be ratified by a marriage between the two parties. Accordingly, the people of the south send their daughter to marry the son of the north. The two are married and have one child, whom the mother after a time decides to take with her to visit her own people in the north. Her visit ended, she starts on her return, accompanied by her elder brother. "They embarked in a bark canoe for the country of the cold. Her brother paddled. After going a long distance, and while crossing a great lake, the cold became so intense that her brother could not endure it any longer. He took the child from his sister and threw it into the water. Immediately the air turned warm and the child floated on the water as a lump of ice."—Teit, *Traditions of the Thompson River Indians*, pp. 55, 56.

## 71. **THE ICE MAN** (p. 322)

This story, told by Swimmer, may be a disguised tradition of a burning coal mine in the mountains, accidentally ignited while firing the woods in the fall according to the regular Cherokee practice, and finally extinguished by a providential rainstorm. One of Buttrick's Cherokee informants told him that "a long time ago a part of the world was burned, though it is not known now how or by whom, but it is said that other land was formed by washing in from the mountains" (*Antiquities*, p. 7).

When the French built Fort Caroline, near present-day Charleston, South Carolina, in 1562, an Indian village was in the vicinity, but shortly afterward the chief, with all his people, removed to a considerable distance in consequence of a strange
