Volcanic activities, some of very recent date, have left many traces in the Carolina mountains. A mountain in Haywood County, near the head of Fines Creek, has been noted for its noises and quakings for nearly a century; one particular explosion split solid masses of granite as though by a blast of gunpowder. These shocks and noises used to recur at intervals of two or three years, but have not been noticed for some time now. In 1829, a violent earthquake on Valley River split open a mountain, leaving a chasm extending for several hundred yards, which is still to be seen. Satoola Mountain, near Highlands in Macon County, has crevices from which smoke is said to issue at intervals. In Madison County, there is a mountain which has been known to rumble and smoke—a phenomenon with which the Warm Springs in the same county may have some connection. Another peak, known as Shaking or Rumbling Bald in Rutherford County, attracted widespread attention in 1874 by a succession of shocks extending over a period of six months (see Zeigler and Grosscup, *Heart of the Alleghanies*, pp. 228–229).

72. **THE HUNTER AND SELU** (p. 323): The explanation of this story, told by Swimmer, lies in the myth which derives corn from the blood of the old woman Selu (see number 3, "Kana'tï and Selu").

In Iroquois myth, the spirits of Corn, Beans, and Squash are three sisters. Corn was originally much more fertile, but was blighted by the jealousy of an evil spirit. "To this day, when the rustling wind waves the corn leaves with a moaning sound, the pious Indian fancies that he hears the Spirit of Corn, in her compassion for the red man, still bemoaning with unavailing regrets her blighted fruitfulness" (Morgan, *League of the Iroquois*, p. 162). See number 126, "Plant Lore," and accompanying notes.

73. **THE UNDERGROUND PANTHERS** (p. 324): This story was told by John Ax. For an explanation of the Indian idea concerning animals, see number 15, "The Four-footed Tribes," and number 76, "The Bear Man."

*Several days*—The strange lapse of time, by which a period really extending over days or even years seems to the stranger under the spell to be only a matter of a few hours, is one of the most common incidents of European fairy recitals and has been made equally familiar to American readers through Irving's story of Rip Van Winkle.

74. **THE TSUNDIGE'WÏ** (p. 325): This curious story was told by Swimmer and Ta'gwădihí' (east) and Wafford (west). Swimmer says the dwarfs lived in the west, but Ta'gwădihí' and Wafford locate them south of the Cherokee country.

A story which seems to be a variant of the same myth was told to the Spanish adventurer Ayllon by the Indians on the South Carolina coast in 1520, and is thus given in translation from Peter Martyr's *Decades*, in the *Discovery and Conquest of Florida*, ninth volume of the Hakluyt Society's publications, pages xv–xvi, London, 1851.

> "Another of Ayllon's strange stories refers to a country called Inzignanin... The inhabitants, by the report of their ancestors, say that a people as tall as the length of a man's arm, with tails a span long, once arrived there, brought there by sea. This tail was not movable or waving, as in four-footed beasts, but solid, broad above and sharp beneath, as we see in fishes and crocodiles, and it extended into a bony hardness. Therefore, when they desired to sit, they used seats with holes through them; or, lacking them, they dug up the earth a span deep or a little more, and they had to convey their tail into the hole when they rested."

---

¹ Buckingham Smith, *Letter of Hernando de Soto and Memoir of Hernando de Escalante*, translated from the Spanish; Washington, 1854, p. 46.

It is given this way in Barcia, *Ensayo*, page 5:

> "They also reached the Province of Yncignavin, where those Indians told them that, at one time, a group of people had arrived there who had tails... about nine inches long and flexible. These tails bothered them so much that they had to make holes in their seats in order to sit down. Their skin was very rough and scaly, and they ate only raw fish. Once these people died, this nation became extinct, and the truth of the matter died with them."

A close parallel to the Cherokee story is found among the Nisqualli of Washington, in a story of three <note>four?</note> brothers who are captured by a miraculously strong dwarf who ties them and carries them off in his canoe.

> "Having rounded the distant point where they had first spotted him, they came to a village inhabited by a race of people as small as their captor; their houses, boats, and tools were all in proportion to their size. The three brothers were then taken out and thrown, bound as they were, into a lodge, while a council was gathered to decide their fate. During the council's meeting, an immense flock of birds, resembling geese but much larger, pounced down upon the inhabitants and began a violent attack. These birds had the power of throwing their sharp quills like a porcupine, and although the little warriors fought with great bravery, they soon became covered with the piercing darts and all fell unconscious on the ground. When all resistance had ceased, the birds took flight and disappeared. The brothers had witnessed the conflict from their place of confinement and, with much labor, had succeeded in freeing themselves from their bonds. They then went to the battlefield and began pulling the quills from the apparently lifeless bodies; but no sooner had they done this than all of them instantly returned to consciousness" (Kane, *Wanderings of an Artist*, pp. 252-253).

75. **ORIGIN OF THE BEAR** (p. 325): This story was told by Swimmer, from whom the hunting songs were also obtained, and it was frequently mentioned by other informants. The Ani'-Tsâ'gûhĭ are said to have been an actual clan in ancient times. For parallels, see number 76, "The Bear Man."

*Had not taken human food*—The Indian is a thorough believer in the doctrine that "man is what he eats." Adair says (*History of the American Indians*, p. 133):

> "They believe that nature possesses such a quality as to transfer into men and animals the characteristics of either the food they eat or the objects that are presented to their senses. He who feeds on venison is, according to their physical system, swifter and more perceptive than the man who lives on the flesh of the clumsy bear or helpless farm fowls, the slow-footed tame cattle, or the heavy wallowing swine. This is the reason that several of their old men recommend and say that formerly their greatest chieftains followed a constant rule in their diet, and seldom ate of any animal of a coarse quality or heavy motion of body, imagining it conveyed a dullness through the whole system and prevented them from exerting themselves with proper vigor in their military, civil, and religious duties."

A continuous adherence to the diet commonly used by a bear will finally give the eater the bear's nature, and perhaps even the bear's form and appearance. A certain period of eating "white man's food" will give the Indian the white man's nature, so that neither the remedies nor the spells of the Indian doctor will have any effect on him (see the author's "Sacred Formulas of the Cherokees," in the *Seventh Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology*, 1891).

*Shall live always*—For an explanation of the doctrine of animal reincarnation, see number 15, "The Four-footed Tribes."

*The songs*—These are fair specimens of the hunting songs found in every tribe, intended to call up the animals or to win the favor of the lords of the game (see also deer songs in the notes to number 3, "Kana'tĭ and Selu"). As usual, the word forms are slightly changed to suit the requirements of the tune. The second song was first published by the author in the paper on sacred formulas mentioned above. Tsistu'yĭ,

Kuwâ'hĭ, Uya'hye, and Gâte'gwâ (-hĭ) are four mountains, under each of which the bears have a town house in which they hold a dance before retiring to their dens for their winter sleep. At Tsistu'yĭ, "Rabbit place," known to us as Gregory Bald in the Great Smoky range, dwells the Great Rabbit, the chief of the rabbit tribe. At Kuwâ'hĭ, "Mulberry place," farther northeast along the same range, resides the White Bear, the chief of the bear tribe, and nearby is the enchanted lake of Atagâ'hĭ, to which wounded bears go to bathe and be cured (see number 15, "The Four-footed Tribes," and number 69, "Atagâ'hĭ, the Enchanted Lake"). Uyâhye is also a peak of the Great Smokies, while Gâtegwâ'hĭ, "Great swamp or thicket (?)," is southeast of Franklin, North Carolina, and is perhaps identical with Fodderstack Mountain (see also the glossary).

76. **THE BEAR MAN** (p. 327): This story was obtained first from John Ax, and has numerous parallels in other tribes, as well as in European and Oriental folklore. The classic legend of Romulus and Remus and the stories of "wolf boys" in India will immediately suggest themselves. Swimmer makes the bears' trial of the hunter's weapons a part of his story of the origin of disease and medicine (number 4), but says that it may have happened on this occasion (see also number 15, "The Four-footed Tribes," and the notes to number 75, "Origin of the Bear").

In a strikingly similar Creek myth from the Tuggle collection, "Origin of the Bear Clan," a little girl lost in the woods is adopted by a she-bear, with whom she lives for four years, until the bear is killed by a hunter and the girl returns to her people to become the mother of the Bear clan.

The Iroquois have several stories of children adopted by bears. In one, "The Man and His Stepson," a boy cared for in this way is afterward found by a hunter, who tames him and teaches him to speak, until in time he almost forgets that he had lived like a bear. He marries a daughter of the hunter and becomes a hunter himself, but always refrains from harming the bears, until at last, angered by the taunts of his mother-in-law, he shoots one, but is himself killed by an accident while on his return home (Smith, *Myths of the Iroquois*, in the Second Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology). Similar to this is the story of a hunter who had pursued a bear into its den. "When some distance in, he could no longer see the bear, but he saw a fire and around it sat several men. The oldest of the three men looked up and asked, 'Why did you try to shoot one of my men? We sent him out to entice you to us'" (Curtin, Seneca MS in the Bureau of American Ethnology archives).

In a Pawnee myth, "The Bear Man," a boy whose father had put him under the protection of the bears grows up with certain bear traits and frequently prays and sacrifices to these animals. On a war party against the Sioux, he is killed and cut to pieces, when two bears find and recognize the body, gather up and arrange the pieces, and restore him to life; after this, they take him to their den, where they care for him and teach him their secret knowledge until he is strong enough to go home (Grinnell, *Pawnee Hero Stories*, pp. 121-128).

In a Jicarilla myth, "Origin and Destruction of the Bear," a boy playing about in animal fashion runs into a cave in the hillside. "When he came out, his feet and hands had been transformed into bear's paws." This is repeated four times, the change mounting higher each time, until he finally emerges as a terrible bear monster that devours human beings (Russell, *Myths of the Jicarilla*, in the *Journal of American Folk-Lore*, October 1898).

*Read the thoughts*—Thought reading is a very common feature of Indian myths. Certain medicine ceremonies are believed to confer the power upon those who fulfill the ordeal conditions.

*Food was getting scarce*—Several references in the myths indicate that, through the failure of the accustomed wild crops, famine seasons were as common among the animal tribes as among the Indians (see number 33, "The Migration of the Animals").

*Kalâs′-Gûnahí′ta*—See number 15, "The Four-footed Tribes."

*Rubbed his stomach*—This very original method of obtaining food occurs also in number 3, "Kana′tĭ and Selu."

*Topknots and Splitnoses*—*Tsuní′stsăhĭ′*, "Having topknots"—that is, Indians, in reference to the crests of upright hair formerly worn by warriors of the Cherokee and other eastern tribes. Timberlake thus describes the Cherokee warrior's headdress in 1762: "The hair of their head is shaved, though many of the old people have it plucked out by the roots, except a patch on the back part of the head about twice the size of a crown piece, which is ornamented with beads, feathers, wampum, stained deer's hair, and such like trinkets" (Memoirs, p. 49). *Tsunû′liyú′ sûnĕstla′tă*, "they have split noses"—that is, dogs.

*Cover the blood*—The reincarnation of the slain animal from the drops of blood spilled upon the ground or from the bones is a regular part of Cherokee hunting belief, and the same idea occurs in the folklore of many tribes. In the Omaha myth, "Ictinike and the Four Creators," the hero visits the Beaver, who kills and cooks one of his own children to provide the dinner. When the meal was over, "the Beaver gathered the bones and put them into a skin, which he plunged beneath the water. In a moment the youngest beaver came up alive out of the water" (Dorsey, in Contributions to North American Ethnology, <term>vi</term>, p. 557).

*Like a man again*—It is a regular principle of Indian belief, which has its parallels in European fairy lore, that someone who has eaten the food of the spirit people or supernatural beings cannot afterward return to his own people and live, unless he is immediately, and sometimes for a long time, put under a rigid course of treatment intended to erase the longing for the spirit food and thus to restore his complete human nature. See also number 73, "The Underground Panthers." In "A Yankton Legend," recorded by Dorsey, a child falls into the water and is taken by the water people. The father hears the child crying under the water and employs two medicine men to bring it back. After preparing themselves properly, they go down into the deep water, where they find the child sitting beside the water spirit, who, when they declare their message, tells them that if they had come before the child had eaten anything he might have lived, but now if taken away "he will desire the food which I eat; that being the cause of the trouble, he shall die." They return and report: "We have seen your child; the wife of the water deity has him. Although we saw him alive, he had eaten part of the food which the water deity eats; therefore, the water deity says that if we bring the child back with us out of the water he shall die," and so it happened. Some time after, the parents lose another child in a similar manner, but this time "she did not eat any of the food of the water deity and therefore they took her home alive." In each case a white dog is thrown in to satisfy the water spirits for the loss of the child (Contributions to North American Ethnology, <term>vi</term>, p. 357).

### 77. THE GREAT LEECH OF TLANUSI′YI (p. 329):

This legend was first heard from Swimmer and Chief Smith, the latter of whom was born near Murphy; it was confirmed by Wafford (west) and others, being one of the best-known myths in the tribe and embodied in the Cherokee name for Murphy. It is apparently based on a peculiar appearance, as of something alive or moving, at the bottom of a deep hole in the Valley River, just below the old Unicoi turnpike ford at Murphy, in Cherokee County, North Carolina. It is said that a tinsmith of the town once made a tin bomb, which he filled with powder and sank in the stream at this spot with the intention of blowing up the strange object to see what it might be, but the device failed to explode. The hole is caused by a sudden drop or split in the rock bed of the stream, extending across the river. Wafford, who once lived on the Nottely River, adds the incident of the two women and says that the Leech had wings and could fly. He also asserts that he found rich lead ore in the hole, but that the swift current prevented him from mining it. About two miles above the mouth of the Nottely River, a bend of the stream brings it within about the same distance of the Hiwassee at Murphy.

This nearest point of approach on the Nottely River is also known to the Cherokee as <term>Tlanusi'yĭ</term>, “leech place.” From certain phenomena common to both streams, there is a general belief among both Indians and whites that they are connected here by a subterranean waterway. The legend and the popular belief were noted in 1848 by Lanman, who incorrectly identifies the leech as a turtle:

> “The little village of Murphy, where I am writing this letter, lies at the junction of the Owassa <note>Hiwassee</note> and Valley rivers, and in terms of location, it is one of the prettiest places in the world. Its Indian name was Klausuna, or the Large Turtle. It was so called, says a Cherokee legend, because it was the sunning place of an immense turtle that lived in its vicinity in ancient times. The turtle was particularly famous for its repelling power, having been known to not be injured at all by a stroke of lightning. Nothing on earth had the power to annihilate the creature; but, because of the many attempts made to take its life, even though it was known to be a harmless and inoffensive creature, it became disgusted with this world and burrowed its way into the middle of the earth, where it now lives in peace.
>
> “In connection with this legend, I may mention what must be considered a remarkable geological fact. Running directly across the village of Murphy is a belt of marble, composed of black, grey, pure white, and flesh-colored varieties, which also crosses the Owassa River. Just above this marble causeway, the Owassa is said to be over one hundred feet deep for a space of perhaps two hundred feet, and at one point, in fact, a bottom has never been found. All of this is simple truth, but I have heard the opinion expressed that there is a subterranean communication between this immense hole in the Owassa and the Nottely River, which is about two miles away. The evidence offered in proof of this theory is that a certain log was once marked on the Nottely, and that same log was later found floating in the pool of the Deep Hole in the Owassa” (Letters, pp. 63-64).

78. **THE NÛÑNĚ'HĬ AND OTHER SPIRIT FOLK** (p. 330): The belief in fairies and kindred spirits, who frequently appear as tiny beings in human form, is so universal among all races that citing parallels is unnecessary. Every Indian tribe has its own spirits of the woods, the cliffs, and the waters; they are usually benevolent and kind when not disturbed, but often mischievous, and in rare cases, malicious and revengeful. These invisible spirit people are regarded as a type of supernatural human being, entirely distinct from ghosts, animal and plant spirits, and the godlike beings who rule the sun, rain, and thunder. Most of the <term>Nûñně'hĭ</term> stories given here were told by Wafford, who firmly believed them all despite his white heritage and education. The others, except for the story of the offended spirits (Wahnenauhi MS) and the Fire-carrier (Wafford), were heard from various people on the reservation. For other <term>Nûñně'hĭ</term> references, see the stories of <term>Tsuwe'nâhi</term>, <term>Kăna'sta</term>, <term>Yahula</term>, etc.

*Nûñně'hĭ*—This word (*gûñně'hĭ* in a dialect form and *nayě'hĭ* in the singular) may be translated as “dwellers anywhere” or “those who live anywhere,” but it is understood to mean “those who live forever,” that is, Immortals. It is spelled <term>Nanehi</term> by Buttrick and <term>Nuhnayie</term> in the Wahnenauhi manuscript. The singular form, *Nayě'hĭ*, also occurs as a personal name, equivalent to <term>Edâ'hĭ</term>, “One who goes about.”

*Some invisible townhouse*—The ancient Creek town of Okmulgee, where the city of Macon, Georgia, now stands, was destroyed by the people of Carolina around the time of the Yamassee War. Sixty years later, Adair says of the Creeks: “They strenuously claim that when necessity forces them to camp there, they always hear at dawn the usual noise of Indians singing their joyful religious songs and dancing, as if going down to the river to purify themselves, and then returning to the old townhouse; they say much more to the same effect. Whenever I have been there, however, everything has been silent . . . . But they say this was ‘because I am a stubborn infidel in that regard’ ” (Hist. Am. Indians, p. 36).

*Nottely town*—Properly *Na'dû'lĭ*, was on the Nottely River, a short distance above

Raper Creek in Cherokee County, North Carolina. The old town house was situated on a large mound on the west side of the river, about five miles below the Georgia line. The town was practically deserted before the forced Removal in 1838 (see glossary).

Hemptown—Properly <term>Gatûñlti'yĭ</term>, <gloss>Hemp place</gloss>, existed until the Removal on Hemptown Creek, a branch of the Toccoa River, a few miles north of present-day Morganton in Fannin County, Georgia.

Noted circular depression—This may have been a circular earthwork about thirty feet in diameter, described as existing in 1890 a short distance east of the Soquee post office near the head of Soquee Creek, about ten miles northwest of Clarkesville, Habersham County, Georgia. There are other circular stone structures on elevated positions within a few miles of Clarkesville (see the author’s manuscript notes on Cherokee archaeology in the Bureau of American Ethnology archives). The same story about throwing logs and stones into one of these sacred places, only to have them thrown out again by invisible hands, is told by Zeigler and Grosscup in connection with the <term>Jutaculla</term> old fields (see the note under number 81, "<term>Tsul'kălû'</term>").

Bewildered—
> "Crazy people were supposed to be possessed by the devil or afflicted by the Nanehi" (Buttrick, Antiquities, p. 14).

According to Hagar's informant:
> "The little people cause men to lose their minds, run away, and wander in the forests. They wear very long hair, reaching down to their heels" (*MS Stellar Legends of the Cherokee*).

In Creek belief, according to the Tuggle manuscript:
> "Fairies or little people live in hollow trees and on rocky cliffs. They often lure people from their homes and lose them in the woods. When a man's mind becomes bewildered—though not crazy—this is caused by the little people."

Loaves seemed to shrink—The deceptive and unsatisfactory character of all fairy belongings once the spell is lifted is well known to European peasantry.

*Tsăwa'sĭ* and *Tsăga'sĭ*—These sprites are frequently named in hunting prayers and other sacred formulas.

Scratching—This is a preliminary rite for the ballplay and other ceremonies, as well as the doctor's method of hypodermic injection. As performed in connection with the ballplay, it is a painful operation inflicted upon the naked skin with a seven-toothed comb made of turkey bone; the scratches are drawn in parallel lines upon the breast, back, arms, and legs until the sufferer is bleeding from head to foot. In medical practice, so that the external application may take hold more effectively, the scratching is done with a rattlesnake's tooth, a brier, a flint, or a piece of glass. See the author's *Cherokee Ball Play* in *American Anthropologist*, April 1890, and *Sacred Formulas of the Cherokees* in the *Seventh Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology*, 1891. The practice seems to have been general among the southern tribes and was sometimes used as a punishment for certain offenders. According to Adair, the doctor bled patients by scratching them with the teeth of a garfish after the skin had first been well softened by the application of warm water, while any unauthorized person who dared to intrude upon the sacred square during ceremonial performances
> "would be dry-scratched with snakes' teeth, fixed in the middle of a split reed or piece of wood, without the privilege of warm water to soften the stiffened skin" (*Hist. Am. Indians*, pp. 46, 120).

The Fire-carrier—This is probably the gaseous phenomenon known as the "will-of-the-wisp," which has been a thing of mystery and fear to many others besides the Indians.

### 80. THE SPIRIT DEFENDERS OF NÏKWÄSÏ' (p. 336)

This story was obtained from Swimmer. <term>Nïkwäsï'</term> or <term>Nïkw'sï'</term>, one of the most ancient settlements of the Cherokee, was on the west bank of the Little Tennessee River, where the town of Franklin is now located in Macon County, North Carolina. The mound upon which the town house stood, in a field adjoining the river, is probably the largest in western Carolina and has never been explored. The Cherokee believe that it is the home of the <term>Nûñnë'hï</term> or Immortals (see number 78) and that a perpetual fire burns within it. The name, which cannot be translated, appears as Nucassee in old documents. The British agent held a council here with the Cherokee as early as 1730. Although twice destroyed, the town was rebuilt and continued to be occupied probably until the land was sold in 1819.

*Bring the news home*—It was a frequent custom in Indian warfare to spare a captive taken in battle so that he might carry the news of the defeat back to his people. After the disastrous defeat of the French under D'Artaguette by the Chickasaw in upper Mississippi in 1736, D'Artaguette, Lieutenant Vincennes, Father Senac, and fifteen others were burned at the stake by the victors, but "one of the soldiers was spared to carry the news of the triumph of the Chickasaws and the death of these unhappy men to the humiliated Bienville" (Pickett, History of Alabama, p. 298, ed. 1896).

### 81. TSUL'KÄLÛ', THE SLANT-EYED GIANT (p. 337)

The story of <term>Tsul'kälû'</term> is one of the finest and best-known of the Cherokee legends. It is mentioned as early as 1823 by Haywood, who spells the name Tuli-cula, and the memory of it is preserved in the local names of western Carolina. Hagar also alludes briefly to it in his manuscript *Stellar Legends of the Cherokee*. The name literally signifies "he has them slanting," referring to his eyes, although the word for eye (<term>aktă'</term>, plural <term>dïktă'</term>) is not a part of the name. In the plural form, it is also the name of a traditional race of giants in the far west (see number 106, "The Giants from the West"). <term>Tsul'kälû'</term> lives in <term>Tsûnegûn'yï</term> and is the great lord of the game; as such, he is frequently invoked in hunting formulas. The story was obtained from Swimmer and John Ax, with the Swimmer version being the one followed here. For parallels to the incident of the child born from blood, see the notes for number 3, "Kana'tï and Selu."

In John Ax's version, it is the girl's father and mother, instead of her mother and brother, who try to bring her back. They are told they must fast seven days to succeed. They fast four days before starting, and then set out and travel for two days, when they come to the mouth of the cave and hear the sound of the drum and the dance within. They are able to look over the edge of the rock and see their daughter among the dancers, but cannot enter until the seventh day has arrived. Unluckily, the man is very hungry by this time, and after watching nearly all night, he insists that it is so near daylight on the seventh morning that he may safely take a small

bite. His wife begs him to wait until the sun appears, but hunger overcomes him and he takes a bite of food from his pouch. Instantly the cave and the dancers disappear, and the man and his wife find themselves alone on the mountain. John Ax was a very old man at the time of the telling, with his memory rapidly failing, and it is evident that his version is only fragmentary.

Haywood records the story on the authority of Charles Hicks, an educated person of mixed heritage <note>Natural and Aboriginal History of Tennessee, p. 280</note>: “They have a legendary tradition concerning the mounds, which proves that they are older than the events of their history. The mounds, they say, were caused by the shaking of the earth and a great noise that went with it—a ceremony used for the adoption of their people into the family of <term>Tuli-cula</term>, who was an invisible person and had married one of their townspeople. And at the time when his first son was born, the shaking of the earth and the noise had commenced, but had stopped at the alarm shout, which had been raised by two careless young men of the town; as a result, the mounds had been raised by the shaking noise. Thereupon the father took the child and mother and moved near Brasstown, and made the tracks in the rocks which can be seen there.”

From Buttrick we get the following version of the tradition, evidently told for the missionary’s special benefit: “God directed the Indians—that is, the warriors—to climb a certain mountain, and he would send them help there. They started and had climbed far up the mountain when one of the warriors began to talk about women. His companion immediately scolded him, but instantly a voice like thunder came from the side of the mountain and God spoke and told them to return, as he could not help them on account of that sin. They put the man to death, yet the Lord never returned to them afterward” <note>Antiquities, p. 14</note>. On the next page he tells it in a somewhat different form: “It is said that before coming to this continent, while in their own country, they were in great distress from their enemies, and God told them to march to the top of a certain mountain and He would come down and provide them relief. They climbed far up the mountain and thought they saw something coming down from above, which they supposed was for their aid. But just then one of the warriors,” etc.

Zeigler and Grosscup give another version, which, although dressed up for advertising purposes, makes a fairly good story:

> “But there is another legend of the Balsams more significant than any of these. It is the *Paradise Gained* of Cherokee mythology, and bears some distant resemblance to the Christian doctrine of mediation. The Indians believed that they were originally mortal in spirit as well as body, but above the blue vault of heaven there was a forest, inhabited by a heavenly race, into which the highest mountains lifted their dark summits. * * *

> “The mediator, by whom eternal life was secured for the Indian mountaineers, was a maiden of their own tribe. Attracted by the haunting sound and diamond sparkle of a mountain stream, she wandered far up into a lonely glen, where the azalea, the kalmia, and the rhododendron brilliantly decorated the deep, shaded slopes, and filled the air with their delicate perfume. The crystal stream wound its crooked way between moss-covered rocks over which tall ferns bowed their graceful stems. Enchanted by the scene, she seated herself upon the soft moss, and, overcome by exhaustion, was soon asleep. The dream picture of a fairyland was soon broken by the soft touch of a strange hand. The spirit of her dream took a place at her side, and, wooing her, won her for his bride.

> “Her supposed kidnapping caused great excitement among her people, who made a diligent search for her recovery in their own villages. Being unsuccessful, they made war upon the neighboring tribes in the hope of finding the place where she was hidden. Grieved because of so much bloodshed and sorrow, she begged the great chief of the eternal hunting grounds to make amends. She was accordingly

> “At the appointed hour, the headmen of the Cherokees gathered. The high Balsam peaks were shaken by thunder and ablaze with lightning. A cloud, as black as midnight, settled over the valley, then lifted, leaving a group of strange men on a large rock, armed and painted for war. An enraged brother of the kidnapped maiden swung his tomahawk and raised a war cry, but a swift thunderbolt struck him down before the echo had died in the hills. The terror-stricken chiefs fled to their towns.
>
> “The bride, grieved by the death of her brother and the failure of the council, prepared to leave her new home and return to her relatives in the valleys. To comfort her, she was promised that all brave warriors and their faithful women would have an eternal home in the happy hunting ground above after death. The great chief of the forest beyond the clouds became the guardian spirit of the Cherokees. All deaths, whether from wounds in battle or disease, were attributed to his desire to add to the heavenly hunting ground, or, on the other hand, to his anger, which might cause their unfortunate spirits to be handed over to the control of the evil spirit of the mountain tops.” —*Heart of the Alleghanies*, pp. 22–24.

*Kānu'ga*—An ancient Cherokee town on the Pigeon River, in present-day Haywood County, North Carolina. It was abandoned before the beginning of the historical period, but it may have been located near the junction of the two forks of the Pigeon River, a few miles east of Waynesville, where several mounds and ancient cemeteries still extend for some miles down the stream. As it was a frontier town, it was probably abandoned early due to its exposed position. The name, meaning “scratcher,” is applied to a comb used for scratching ballplayers and is connected with *kănugû''lă* or *nugû''lă*, a blackberry bush or brier. There are other mounds on Richland Creek near Waynesville.

*Tsul'kălû' Tsunegûn'yĭ*—Abbreviated as *Tsunegûn'yĭ*; the mountain where the giant is supposed to live is Tennessee Bald in North Carolina, where the Haywood, Jackson, and Transylvania county lines meet on the ridge separating the waters of the Pigeon River from those flowing into Tennessee Creek and the Cany Fork of the Tuckasegee, southeast of Waynesville and Webster. The name seems to mean “at the white place,” from *une'ga* (“white”), and may refer to a bald spot of about a hundred acres on the peak, known locally among white people as Jutaculla Old Fields. This comes from a tradition, said to be derived from the Indians, that it was a clearing made by “Jutaculla” <note>that is, *Tsul'kălû'*</note> for a farm. Further west, on the north side of Cany Fork and about ten miles above Webster in Jackson County, is a rock known as Jutaculla Rock. It is covered with various crude carvings which, according to the same tradition, are scratches made by the giant while jumping from his farm on the mountain down to the creek below. Zeigler and Grosscup refer to the mountain by the name “Old Field Mountain” and mention a tradition among the early settlers that the Indians regarded it as the special home of the Indian Satan!

> “On the top of the mountain, there is a prairie-like tract, almost level, reached by steep slopes covered with thickets of balsam and rhododendron that seem to guard the supposedly sacred domain. The Indians understood it to be forbidden territory, but one day a party allowed their curiosity to tempt them. They forced a way through the tangled thickets and entered the open ground with laughter. Awakened from sleep and enraged by their bold intrusion, the devil, taking the form of a massive snake, attacked the party and swallowed fifty of them before they could reach the thicket. Among the first white people who settled among the Indians and traded with them was a party of hunters who used this superstition...

to escape punishment for their reprehensible conduct. They reported that they were in league with the great spirit of evil, and to prove that they were, they frequented this "old field." They described his bed, under a large overhanging rock, as a model of neatness. They had frequently thrown stones and brushwood into it during the day while the master was out, but the place was always as clean the next morning "as if it had been brushed with a bunch of feathers" (*Heart of the Alleghenies*, p. 22).

*The footprints can still be seen*—Shining Rock or Cold Mountain, between the forks of the Pigeon River in Haywood County, North Carolina, is known to the Cherokee as <term>Datsu'nălâsgûn'yĭ</term>, "where their tracks are this way," because of a rock at its base toward Sonoma and three miles south of the trail. Upon this rock are impressions said to be the footprints made by the giant and his children on their way to <term>Tsunegûn'yĭ</term>. Within the mountain is also the legendary home of invisible spirits. Haywood confuses this with Track Rock Gap, near Blairsville, Georgia, where there are other noted <term>petroglyphs</term> (see number 125, "Minor Legends of Georgia").

The rapid growth of the two children is paralleled in many other tribal mythologies. The sequence of growth as indicated by the footprints reminds us of the concluding incident of the *Arabian Nights*, when Queen Scheherazade stands before the king to make a last request:
> "And the king answered her, 'Ask, and you shall receive, O Scheherazade.' Thereupon she called out to the nurses and the eunuchs and said to them, 'Bring my children.' Accordingly, they brought them to her quickly, and they were three male children; one of them walked, one crawled, and one was at the breast."

*Must not raise the war whoop*—See note under number 79, "The Removed Townhouses."

### 82. KĂNA'STA, THE LOST SETTLEMENT (p. 341):
This story, obtained from Swimmer, bears a resemblance to those of <term>Tsul'kălû'</term>, <term>Tsuwe'năhĭ</term>, "The Removed Townhouses," and others, in which individuals or even whole settlements choose to go with the invisible spirit people in order to escape hardships or coming disaster.

*Kăna'sta*—Abbreviated from <term>Känastûn'yĭ</term>, a name which cannot be translated. It is described as an ancient Cherokee town on the French Broad River where the trail from Tennessee Creek of the Tuckasegee comes in, near the present Brevard in Transylvania County, North Carolina. No mounds are known there, and we find no notice of the town in history, but another of the same name existed on the Hiwassee and was destroyed in 1776.

*Tsuwa'tel'da*—Abbreviated from <term>Tsuwa'teldûn'yĭ</term>, and known to white people as Pilot Knob, is a high mountain in Transylvania County, about eight miles north of Brevard. Because of the peculiar layered appearance of the rocks, the faces of the cliffs are said to frequently present a strange appearance under the sun's rays, like shining walls with doors, windows, and shingled roofs.

*Datsu'nălâsgûn'yĭ*—Shining Rock. See note under number 81, "Tsul'kălû'."

*Fast seven days*—This requirement of a seven-day fast for those who would join the spirit people appears in several Cherokee myths. As we learn from the priests, the idea is to spiritualize human nature and sharpen the spiritual vision by abstaining from earthly food. The doctrine is illustrated in an incident from the legend of <term>Tsuwe'năhĭ</term> (see that entry). In a broader application, the same idea is a foundational principle of every ancient religion. In ordinary Cherokee ceremonies, the fast is kept for one day—that is, from midnight to sunset. On occasions of supreme importance, it continues for four or even seven days. Among the Plains tribes, those who voluntarily enter the <term>Sun Dance</term> to make supplication and sacrifice for their people abstain entirely from food and drink during the four days and nights of the ceremony.

*The Thunders*—See number 3, "Kana'tĭ and Selu" and notes, and number 8, "The Moon and the Thunders," with notes.

The name *Tsuwe'năhĭ* cannot be translated, but it may possibly have a connection with *uwe'năhĭ*, meaning "rich."

*Kanu'ga* and *Tsuwa'tel'da*—See the notes under number 81, "Tsul'kălû'," and number 82, "Kăna'sta."

*Parched corn*—This was the standard food supply of the warrior when on the march among all the tribes east of the Mississippi, and probably among all the corn-growing tribes of America. It is the *pinole* of the Tarahumara and other Mexican tribes. The Cherokee call it *găhăwĭ'sita*. Hawkins describes it this way as seen with his Cherokee guides in 1796:

> "They eat very little, use no salt, and eat only a small amount of bread. They carry their parched corn meal, *wissactaw*, and mix a handful in a pint of water to drink. Although they had plenty of corn and poultry, they made no other preparation for the journey except for a small bag of this for the path. I have plenty of supplies and give them some at every meal. I have several times drunk the *wissactaw*, and I like it when some sugar is added. To make it of the best quality, I am told the corn should first be boiled, then parched in hot ashes, sifted, powdered, and ground into flour."¹

*The seat was a turtle*—This incident also appears in number 84, "The Man who Married the Thunder's Sister." The species referred to is the *săligu'gĭ*, or the common water turtle.

*Like dogs' paws*—No reason is given for this unusual detail, which is mentioned nowhere else as a trait of the mountain spirits.

*Old tobacco*—*Tsâl-agăyûñ'lĭ*, "ancient tobacco," the *Nicotiana rustica*, which is sacred among all the eastern tribes. See number 6, "How they Brought back the Tobacco," and number 126, "Plant Lore."

*Thorns of honey locust*—This incident also appears in number 63, "*Ûñtsaiyĭ'*, The Gambler."

### 84. THE MAN WHO MARRIED THE THUNDER'S SISTER (p. 345):

This story was first heard from John Ax, and later with additions and variations from Swimmer and others. It is also briefly mentioned in Hagar's manuscript, "Stellar Legends of the Cherokee."

As explained elsewhere, the Thunder spirits are believed to have their favorite home under waterfalls, of which Tallulah Falls is probably the greatest in the Cherokee country. The connection of Thunder and Rain spirits with snakes and water animals is a matter of universal primitive belief and has already been noted. One Cherokee informant told Hagar (see above) that "Thunder is a horned snake (?), and lightning is its tongue, and it lives with water and rain." It is hardly necessary to mention that the dance was, and is, among all the tribes, not only the most common form of social entertainment, but also an important part of every major religious or ceremonial event.

*Sâkwi'yĭ*—Abbreviated as *Sâkwi'*, an ancient town located approximately on the site of the current village of Soquee on the creek of the same name near Clarkesville, in Habersham County, Georgia.

*Marry him*—Among nearly all the tribes, with the exception of the Pueblo, the marriage ceremony was simple, consisting mainly of the lover giving certain presents to the parents of the intended bride to compensate them for the loss of their daughter, after she herself had first given her consent to the union. Although this has been described as a purchase, it was actually only a formal confirmation of the agreement, which the girl was free to accept or refuse as she chose. On the other hand, if the presents were not enough to satisfy the parents, they were

refused or returned, and the marriage could not take place, however willing the girl might be. The young man usually selected a friend to act as a go-between with the girl’s family, and in all tribes—as is now the case in the West—the outcome seems to have been largely decided by her brother, who continued to exercise some supervision and claim over her even after her marriage.

Lawson’s statement concerning the eastern Carolina tribes in 1700 remains almost equally accurate today in any part of the West: "As for Indian marriages, I have read and heard of much form and ceremony being used, which I never saw myself; nor could I learn during the time I have been among them anything other than what I shall give an account of here, which is as follows:

> "When any young Indian desires a certain girl to be his wife, he, or someone on his behalf, goes to the young woman's parents, if they are living; if not, to her nearest relatives, where they propose the match between the couple. The relatives reply that they will consider it; this serves as a sufficient answer until there is a second meeting about the marriage, which is generally debated before all the elderly relatives on both sides; sometimes the king and all his leading men give their opinions on the matter. If it is agreed upon and the young woman approves of it—for these people never give their children in marriage without their own consent—the man pays a certain amount for his wife, and the more beautiful she is, the higher the price she commands" (History of Carolina, pp. 302-303).

According to Adair, who describes it as a little more formal among the Gulf tribes, "When an Indian first approaches the young woman he intends to marry, she is required by ancient custom to sit by him until he has finished eating and drinking, whether she likes or dislikes him; but afterward, she is free to choose whether to stay or leave" (Hist. Am. Indians, p. 139).

*Would surely die*—In Cherokee myth and ritual, we frequently encounter the idea that anyone who reveals supernatural secrets will die. Sometimes the idea is reversed, such as when the discovery of the wicked actions of a wizard or conjurer causes his death. This latter belief has a parallel in Europe.

*Smooth as a pumpkin*—This is the translation of the peculiar, repetitive Cherokee expression, *i'ya iya'-tăwi'skage—tăwi'skage i'ya-iyu'stĭ*, literally, "pumpkin, of pumpkin smoothness—smooth like a pumpkin." The translation is similar to the repetition found in children's stories like "The House that Jack Built," but it fails to convey the amusing sound effect of the original.

*A large turtle*—This incident also occurs in number 83, "*Tsuwe'năhĭ.*"

*A horse*—Although the reference to the horse must be considered a more modern addition, it may easily date back two centuries, or possibly even to De Soto's expedition in 1540. Among the Plains tribes, the horse quickly became such an essential part of Indian life that it now features in their entire social and mythological system.

*The bracelets were snakes*—The same concept also appears in number 63, "*Ûñtsaiyĭ'*," when the hero visits his father, the Thunder god.

85. THE HAUNTED WHIRLPOOL (p. 347): This legend was related by an East Cherokee known to the whites as Knotty Tom. For a description of the whirlpool rapids known as The Suck, see the notes under number 63, "*Ûñtsaiyĭ'*, the Gambler."

86. YAHULA (p. 347): This fine myth was obtained in the Territory from Wafford, who heard it from his uncle, William Scott, a half-breed who settled on Yahoola Creek shortly after the end of the Revolution. Scott claimed to have heard the bells and the songs, and regarding the story itself, Wafford said, "I've heard it so often and so much that I'm inclined to believe it." It is explained by the beliefs connected with the *Nûñnĕ'hĭ* (see number 78 and notes), in whom Wafford had firm faith.

*Yahula*—This is a fairly frequent Cherokee personal name, but it seems to be of Creek origin, referring to the song used in the "black drink" or "busk" ceremony of that tribe; the songs that the lost trader used to sing may have been those from that ceremony. See the glossary.

*Tinkling of the bells*—Among the southern tribes in the old days, the approach of a trader's pack train along the trail was always announced by the jingling of bells hung around the necks of the horses, somewhat like our own winter sleigh rides. Among the plains tribes, the children's ponies are always equipped with collars of sleigh bells.

In his description of a trader's pack train before the Revolution, Bartram says (*Travels*, p. 439): 
> "Every horse has a bell on it. When we start in the morning, the bells are silenced with a twist of grass or leaves, but they soon shake loose, and they are never silenced again during the day. The constant ringing and clattering of the bells, the cracking of the whips, the shouting, and the all-too-frequent cursing at these miserable four-legged animals cause an incessant uproar and confusion that is inexpressibly disagreeable."

87. THE WATER CANNIBALS (p. 349): This story was obtained from Swimmer and contains several points of resemblance to other Cherokee myths. The idea of the spirit changeling is common to European fairy lore.

*Tikwăli'tsĭ*—This town, called by the white settlers Tuckalechee, was on the Tuckasegee River at the site of present-day Bryson City, in Swain County, North Carolina, where traces of the mound can still be seen on the south side of the river.

*Afraid of the witches*—See number 120, "The Raven Mocker," and the accompanying notes.

88. FIRST CONTACT WITH WHITES (p. 350): The story of the jug of whiskey left near a spring was first heard from Swimmer; the *ulûñsû'tĭ* story was from Wafford; and the locomotive story was from David Blythe. Each was afterward confirmed from other sources.

The story of the book and the bow, quoted from the *Cherokee Advocate* of October 26, 1844, was not heard on the reservation but is mentioned by other authorities. According to an old Cherokee man quoted by Buttrick, "God gave the red man a book and a paper and told him to write, but he merely made marks on the paper. Because he could not read or write, the Lord gave him a bow and arrows and gave the book to the white man." Boudinot, in "*A Star in the West*,"<note>1</note> quoted by the same author, says: "They have a tradition handed down from their ancestors that the book the white people have was once theirs; that while they had it, they prospered greatly; but the white people bought it from them and learned many things from it, while the Indians lost their status, offended the Great Spirit, and suffered greatly from neighboring nations. They say the Great Spirit took pity on them and directed them to this country," etc. It is simply another version of the common tale told by nations in decline: "We were once as great as you."

89. THE IROQUOIS WARS (p. 351): *The Iroquois league*—The Iroquois League originally consisted of a confederacy of five related tribes: the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca, in what is now the state of New York. To these were added the related Tuscarora after they were driven out of Carolina around 1715. The name Iroquois, by which they were known to the French, is thought to be derived from an Indian term. To the English, they were known as the Five Nations, and later the Six Nations. They called themselves by a name commonly spelled *Hodenosaunee*, which is interpreted as "People of the Long House." In this symbolic long house, the Mohawk guarded the eastern door, while the Seneca protected the western door. Their remarkable governmental and clan system is still well preserved. Each tribe, except for the Mohawk and Oneida, has eight clans arranged into two groups or phratries. The Mohawk and Oneida are said to have only three clans each now, probably because of losses from members moving to French missions. The Seneca clans, which are nearly the same for the other tribes, are the Wolf, Bear, Turtle, Beaver, Deer, Snipe, Heron, and Hawk. The confederacy is thought to have been formed about the middle of the sixteenth century, and by 1680, the Iroquois had conquered and destroyed or incorporated all the surrounding tribes, and had asserted a paramount

They claimed the entire territory from the Cherokee border to Hudson Bay, and from southern New England to the Mississippi River. According to a careful estimate in 1677, the Five Nations then numbered 2,150 warriors, or about 10,750 people. The Tuscarora in Carolina were estimated a few years later at 1,200 warriors, or 5,000 people, but this is probably an exaggeration. The league later suffered heavy losses through wars with the French, and even more through the withdrawal of Christianized Indians to the French Catholic mission colonies at Caughnawaga, Saint Regis, and elsewhere, with the Mohawk being the primary sufferers. The American Revolution caused another separation, when about two-fifths of those remaining—including nearly all of the Mohawk and Cayuga—moved as a group to Canada. A mixed band of Seneca and Cayuga, known as the "Seneca of Sandusky," had previously settled in Ohio, from where they moved to Indian Territory in 1831. Between 1820 and 1826, the majority of the Oneida moved from New York to lands in Wisconsin purchased from the Menomini. Despite wars and removals, however, the Iroquois have held their own with a tenacity and vitality that characterize their entire history. Today, in both this country and in Canada, they are fairly prosperous and are increasing in population, appearing more numerous now than at any previous time. Those in New York and Pennsylvania (except for the Saint Regis) and on the Grand River reservation in Canada—constituting about half of the total number—still maintain the forms and ceremonies of the ancient league.

According to a special bulletin of the 1890 census, the total number of Indians then belonging to the tribes that originally formed the Six Nations was 15,833. Of these, 8,483 were living in Canada and 7,350 were in the United States, excluding 37 resident members of other tribes from the latter count. Those in the United States were on six reservations in the state of New York, one in Pennsylvania, one in Wisconsin, and one in the Indian Territory, and were classified as follows:

Assuming the same rate of increase in Pennsylvania and on the Canadian side, the total number of Iroquois today would be approximately 17,000. For detailed information, see Colden, *History of the Five Nations*; Schoolcraft, *Notes on the Iroquois*; Morgan, *League of the Hodenosaunee or Iroquois*; Parkman's works; reports of the commissioners of Indian Affairs for both the United States and Canada, and the excellent report on "The Six Nations of New York," by Donaldson and Carrington, contained in an extra bulletin of the Eleventh Census of the United States.

*Seneca town, South Carolina*—The statement provided by Schoolcraft (*Notes on Iroquois*, 161), on the authority of Calhoun, that the Seneca once lived at Seneca town in South Carolina, likely has no foundation in fact; the story evidently arose from a perceived similarity of name. The Cherokee call it *I'sû'nigû'*, and do not connect it in any way with *A-Sě'nikă* or *Anǐ'-Sě'nikă*, their name for the northern tribe.

*The Cherokee war*—The Iroquois story of the war between themselves and the Cherokee is from Schoolcraft, *Notes on Iroquois*, pages 252 and 256.

*Five days' journey*—This statement is on Morgan's authority, but the distance was certainly greater, unless we are to understand only the distance that separated their furthest customary hunting ranges, not the distance between the permanent settlements of the two peoples.

*The Tennessee River boundary*—The statement from Morgan (*League of the Iroquois*, p. 337) regarding the truce line established at the Tennessee River appears to be confirmed by incidental references in early documents. Boundaries beyond which war parties might not go, or neutral grounds where hereditary enemies met in peace, were a regular institution in ancient Indian society—the most notable instance being perhaps the famous pipestone quarry in Minnesota. Despite the claim of the Iroquois, backed by Sir William Johnson, to all the country north of the Tennessee River, it is very clear from history and treaties that the Cherokee asserted a more or less valid claim as far north as the Ohio. Their actual settlements, however, were all south of the main Tennessee River.

*The Buffalo dance*—The origin attributed to the Buffalo dance of the Iroquois (Morgan, *League of the Iroquois*, p. 287) agrees with the common Indian idea, according to which dances named after animals are performed in imitation of the peculiar actions and cries of these animals, or in obedience to supposed commands from the ruling spirit animals.

*The peace embassy*—The story of the proposed intertribal alliance, along with the statements regarding Cherokee captives among the Seneca, are from Schoolcraft (*Notes on Iroquois*, pp. 158, 252, 257). The records of the conference at Johnson Hall in 1768 are published in the *New York Colonial Documents*. The account of the Iroquois peace embassy to Echota was given to Wafford by two eyewitnesses, one of whom was his mother's cousin, Sequoya. As the old man said, "Sequoya told me all about it." As stated in the narrative, Wafford himself had also seen the belts brought out and explained in a great intertribal council at Tahlequah. By common tribal custom, ambassadors of peace were secure from harm, whatever the result of the negotiations might be, although this rule was sometimes violated, as it is among more civilized nations. According to tradition, the ancient peace pipe of the Cherokee, and probably of other eastern tribes, was made of white stone—white being the universal color for peace. The red stone pipe of the Sioux was also used in peace ceremonies due to the peculiar sacredness attached to it among the western tribes.

The accuracy of Wafford's 1891 statement from memory is remarkably confirmed by a contemporary account of the great intertribal council at Tahlequah in 1843 by the artist, Stanley, who was present and painted several portraits on that occasion. The council was convened by John Ross in June and remained in session for four weeks, with some ten thousand Indians in attendance, representing seventeen

**Wampum**—The celebrated wampum was a species of bead cut from the shell of the clam, conch, or other shell-bearing mollusk of the coast or the larger streams. The common name is derived from an Algonquian word meaning *white*, and was properly applied only to one variety, the generic term varying by tribe. The beads were cylindrical rather than globular and were of two colors: white and purple or dark. They were assigned specific values. Wampum was manufactured by the coast tribes and traded by them to those of the interior; it was used extensively everywhere east of the Mississippi for necklaces, collars, belts, and other purposes of personal adornment, as well as in connection with the famous wampum belts, by which the memory of treaties and tribal traditions was passed down. These belts were woven with various designs in wampum, either pictographic or symbolic, the meaning of which was preserved and explained on public occasions by an officer appointed to that duty. In ancient times, no treaty or covenant was considered binding, and no tribal embassy was recognized as official without the delivery of a wampum belt as a guarantee and memorial. The colonial documents are full of references to this custom. Up to the end of the last century, the Cherokee still offered such belts in their treaties with the Government, and one was delivered in the same manner as late as the treaty of Prairie des Chiens in 1825. The Iroquois still preserve several ancient belts, of which a good idea is provided by the illustration and accompanying description (figure 2, page 354). Because of the high regard in which these shell beads were held, they were frequently used in the East as a standard of exchange, just as eagle feathers were in the West; among the Cherokee, the same word, *atela*, is used for both bead and money. On the Pacific coast,

*Gowe'!*—This is a long-drawn halloo without meaning except as a signal to grab attention. It strikingly resembles the Australian "bush cry" *Coowee!*, which is used for the same purpose.

93. THE UNSEEN HELPERS (p. 359): The meaning of the Seneca name cannot be given.

*Animal Protectors*—The main incident of this tale is closely paralleled by a Kiowa story, told by the old men as an actual event from about fifty years ago. It concerns a warrior who, having been desperately wounded in a battle with Mexican troops in southern Texas, was abandoned to die by his retreating comrades. At night, while lying upon the ground awaiting death and unable to move, he heard a long howl in the distance. This was repeated nearer and nearer until, at last, he heard the patter of feet in the sand. A wolf came up and licked the warrior's festering wounds with such a soothing effect that he fell asleep. This was repeated several times until the man was able to sit up. At that point, the wolf left him after telling him—not in a dream vision, but as a companion face to face—that he must keep up his courage and that he would return safely to his tribe. Soon afterward, the wounded warrior was found by a party of Comanche, who restored him to his people. At the next Sun Dance, he gave public thanks for his rescue (see the author's *Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians*, in the *Seventeenth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology*, part 1, 1901). The story is not impossible. A wolf may easily have licked the wounded man's sores, as a dog might do, and through the relief provided, if not by the sympathy of companionship, enabled him to hold out until rescued by friends. The rest is easily explained by the imagination of an Indian, who believes there is no essential difference between himself and other animals.

*The War Woman*—The women described as having the power to decide the fate of captives, also mentioned in the next story (number 94), are evidently the female dignitaries among the ancient Cherokee known to early writers as "War Women" or "Pretty Women." Due to the loss of Cherokee tradition and custom, it is now impossible to gather anything definite on the subject from Indian informants. However, from documentary references, it is apparent that a custom existed among the Cherokee similar to that found among the Iroquois and probably other Eastern tribes, by which the decision of important questions relating to peace and war was left to a vote of the women. Among the Iroquois, this privilege was exercised by a council of matrons, the mothers of the tribes. It may have been the same among the Cherokee, with the "Pretty Woman" voicing the decision of the council, or the final judgment may have been made according to the will of the "Pretty Woman" herself. The institution served in a measure to lessen the evils of war and had its origin in the clan system. Under this system, a captive enemy remained an enemy until he had been adopted into the tribe, which could only be done through adoption into a clan and family. Since clan descent was traced through the women, it was up to them

to decide the question of adoption. If they were favorable, all was well, and the captive at once became a member of a family and clan and of the tribe at large. Otherwise, as a public enemy, only death remained for him, unless he was ransomed by friends. The proper Cherokee title of this female arbiter of life and death is unknown. The clan of the Ani'-Gila'hĭ, or "Long-hairs," is sometimes spoken of as the Pretty-woman clan, and the office may have been hereditary in that clan. The Seneca stories imply that there were two of these female officers, but from Haywood's account there would seem to have been but one. An upper tributary of the Savannah River in Georgia bears the name War-woman Creek.

Timberlake says in 1765 (Memoirs, p. 70):
> "These chiefs or headmen likewise compose the assemblies of the nation, into which the war women are admitted, . . . many of the Indian women being as famous in war as they are powerful in the council."

At the Hopewell treaty conference in 1785, the principal chief of Echota, after an opening speech, said: "I have no more to say, but one of our beloved women has, who has borne and raised up warriors." After delivering a string of wampum to emphasize the importance of the occasion, "the war woman of Chota then addressed the commissioners." Having expressed her pleasure at the peace, she continued:
> "I have a pipe and a little tobacco to give to the commissioners to smoke in friendship. I look on you and the red people as my children. Your having determined on peace is most pleasing to me, for I have seen much trouble during the late war. I am old, but I hope yet to bear children, who will grow up and populate our nation, as we are now to be under the protection of Congress and shall have no more disturbance. The talk I have given is from the young warriors I have raised in my town, as well as myself. They rejoice that we have peace, and we hope the chain of friendship will never more be broken."

Two strings of wampum, a pipe, and some tobacco accompanied her words (American State Papers; Indian Affairs, I, p. 41, 1832).

Haywood says in 1823:
> "The Cherokees had the law or custom of assigning to a certain woman the office of declaring what punishment should be inflicted on great offenders; whether, for instance, burning or another form of death, or whether they should be pardoned. This woman they called the pretty woman. Mrs. Ward exercised this office when Mrs. Bean, about the year 1776, was taken from the white settlements on the upper parts of the Holston. Being bound and about to be burned on one of the mounds, the pretty woman interfered and pronounced her pardon" (Nat. and Aborig. Hist. Tenn., p. 278). See also historical note 20, "Peace Towns and Towns of Refuge."

*Between two lines of people*—This custom, known to colonial writers as "running the gauntlet," was very common among the eastern tribes and was intended not so much to punish the captive as to test his courage and endurance, with a view to adoption if he proved worthy. It was practiced only upon warriors, never upon women or children, and although the blows were severe, they were not intended to be fatal. The prisoner was usually unbound and made to run along a cleared space in the center of the village toward a certain goal, and was safe for the time being if he succeeded in reaching it.

### 94. HATCIÑONDOÑ’S ESCAPE FROM THE CHEROKEE (p. 362): The Seneca name is not translatable.

*Canebrake*—The tall cane reed (*Arundinaria*), called *i'hya* by the Cherokee, is common along the southern streams, as such names as Cany Fork, Cut-cane Creek, and Young-cane Creek testify. It was greatly valued among the Indians for fishing rods, blowguns, and baskets, as well as for fodder for livestock. The best canebrakes were famous far and wide and were visited from long distances during the gathering season. Most of the cane now used by the Eastern Cherokee for blowguns and baskets is procured by long journeys on foot to the streams of upper South Carolina, or to points on the French Broad River above Knoxville, Tennessee.

MOONEY] NOTES AND PARALLELS

*Sky vault*—See the notes for story number 1, "How the World was Made."

*Hawĕñni'o*—The Seneca name for the Thunder god is used in the singular form. In the Cherokee language, Thunder and the Thunder spirits are always spoken of in the plural. The messengers in the story may have been Thunder spirits.

*Thought reading*—See the notes for story number 76, "The Bear Man."

*Woman arbiters*—See the preceding story, number 93, and the note on "The War Woman."

*My grandson*—Among all the Eastern and Plains tribes, this is an affectionate term of address for a dependent or inferior, just as "grandfather" is a respectful address for someone occupying a superior position or someone venerable because of age or dignity. Both words are used in this way without any reference to actual kinship. In tribal councils, nearly all the Eastern tribes except the Iroquois addressed the Delaware representatives as "grandfather," and in an Arapaho song of the Ghost Dance, the Whirlwind is addressed this way.

### 95. HEMP-CARRIER (p. 364)
This story of the old wars was obtained from Colonel William H. Thomas, who says that *Tâle'danigi'skĭ* was a chief who formerly lived near Valleytown, in Cherokee County. The name is translated in various ways as "Hemp-carrier," "Nettle-carrier," or "Flax-toter," from *tâle'ta*, the richweed (*Pilea pumila*), a plant with a fibrous stalk from which the Indians wove thread and cordage. The trail along which the Seneca came ran from Valley River across the ridge to Cheowa (Robbinsville) and then northwest to connect with the "great war path" in Tennessee (see historical note 19).

*Cairns*—Stone cairns were once very common along the trails throughout the Cherokee country, but they are now almost gone, having been destroyed by treasure hunters after the land was occupied by white settlers. They were usually burial monuments built of large stones piled loosely together over a body to a height of sometimes 6 feet or more, with a corresponding circumference. This method of interment was used only when there was a desire to commemorate a death, and every passerby would add a stone to the heap. The custom is ancient and worldwide, and it is still practiced in Mexico and in many parts of Europe and Asia. Early references to it among the southern tribes occur in Lederer (1670), *Travels*, page 10, 1891 edition, and Lawson (1700), *History of Carolina*, pages 43 and 78, 1860 edition. The latter mentions meeting one day "seven heaps of stones, being the monuments of seven Indians who were killed in that place by the Sinnagers or Iroquois <note>Seneca or Iroquois</note>. Our Indian guide added a stone to each heap." The common name is the Gaelic term, meaning literally "a pile."

*Seven wives*—Polygamy was common among the Cherokee, as it was among nearly all other tribes, although it was not often practiced to such an extreme degree as in this instance. The noted chief *Yânûgûñskĭ*, who died in 1839, had two wives. Among the Plains tribes, and perhaps with others, a man who marries the eldest of several daughters has a prior claim to her unmarried sisters.

### 96. THE SENECA PEACEMAKERS (p. 365)
This story was told to Schoolcraft by the Seneca more than fifty years ago. A somewhat similar story is related by Adair (*History of the American Indians*, p. 392) regarding a young "*Anantooeah*" (meaning *Nûndăwegĭ* or Seneca) warrior taken by the Shawnee.

*Death song*—It seems to have been a chivalrous custom among the Eastern tribes to give a condemned prisoner who requested it a chance to recite his warlike deeds and to sing his death song before proceeding to the final torture. He was allowed the widest freedom to boast, even at the expense of his captors and their tribe. The death song was a chant belonging to the warrior himself or to the war society of which he was a member, the main theme being a farewell to life and defiance of death. When the great Kiowa war chief, Set-ängya, broke his shackles at Fort Sill and attacked the soldiers surrounding him, with the deliberate purpose of dying rather than remaining a prisoner, he first sang the war song of his order, the

### 97. ORIGIN OF THE YONTOÑWISAS DANCE (p. 365)
This is evidently the one called by Morgan (League of the Iroquois, p. 290) the Untowesus. He describes both this and the Oaskanea as a "shuffle dance" for women only. The spelling of the Seneca names in the story is the same as that given in the manuscript.

*Not to go after*—Morgan, in his work quoted above, asserts that the Iroquois never made any effort to recover those of their people who had been captured by the enemy, choosing to consider them from then on as lost to their tribe and kindred. This, if true, is doubly remarkable, in view of the wholesale adoption of prisoners and subjugated tribes by the Iroquois.

*Blazing pine knots*—Torches of seasoned pine knots are much used among the Cherokee for lighting the way on journeys along the difficult mountain trails at night. Because of the accumulation of resin in the knots, they burn with a bright and lasting flame, far surpassing the cloudy glow of a lantern.

*Wild potatoes*—As is well known, the potato is native to America, and our first knowledge of it came from the Indians. Many other native tubers were used among the tribes, even those that practiced no agriculture but depended almost entirely upon hunting. Favorites among the Cherokee are the *Cynara scolymus* or wild artichoke, and the *Phaseolus* or pig potato; the name of the latter, *nuna*, is now used to designate the cultivated potato.

*Sky people*—These spirit messengers are also mentioned in the story of Hatcinoñdoñ (number 94), another Seneca tradition. Every tribe has its own spirit creation.

*Must do all this*—Every sacred dance and religious rite, as well as almost every important detail of Indian ceremony, is supposed to be in accordance with direct instruction from the spirit world as communicated in a vision.

### 98. GA'NA'S ADVENTURES AMONG THE CHEROKEE (p. 367)
This story, from Curtin's Seneca manuscript, is particularly rich in Indian allusion. The purification rite, the eagle capture, the peace ceremony, the ball game, the foot race, and the battle are all described in a way that gives us a vivid picture of the old tribal life. The name of the Seneca hero, Ga'na', means, according to Hewitt, "Arrow" (compare to the Cherokee *gûñĭ*, "arrow"), while the name of the great eagle, Shada'gea, may, according to the same authority, be translated as "Cloud-dweller." The Seoqgwageono, living east of the Cherokee and near the ocean, cannot be identified. They could not have been the Catawba, who were known to the Iroquois as Toderigh-rono, but they may possibly have been the Congaree, Santee, or Sewee, further down in South Carolina. In the Seneca form, as given here, *ge* (*ge‘*) is a locative, and *ono* (*oñnoñ*) is a tribal suffix qualifying the root of the word; the whole name signifies "people of, or at, Seoqgwa" (compare to *Oyadageono*, etc., meaning Cherokee, p. 186).

*Go to water*—This rite, as practiced among the Cherokee, has been already noted in the chapter on stories and storytellers. Ceremonial purification by water or the sweat bath, accompanied by prayer and fasting, is almost universal among the tribes as a preliminary to every important undertaking. With the Cherokee, it precedes the ball game and the Green-corn dance, and is a part of the ritual for obtaining long life, for winning the affections of a woman, for recovering from a wasting sickness, and for calling down prosperity upon the family at each return of the new moon.

*Get the eagle feathers*—The Cherokee ritual for procuring eagle feathers for ceremonial and decorative purposes has been described in number 35, "The Bird Tribes." The Seneca method, as described here, is practically that used among all the Indians of the plains, although the hunter is not usually satisfied with a single feather at a capture. Among certain western tribes, the eagle was sometimes strangled before being stripped.

The Pueblo people were sometimes accustomed to taking young eagles from the nest and keeping them in cages for their feathers. A full tail contains twelve large feathers of the kind used for war bonnets and on the wands of the Eagle dance.

*Stockade*—Stockaded villages were common to the Iroquois and most of the tribes along the Atlantic coast. They are also mentioned among the Cherokee in the exaggerated narratives of the early Spanish period, but they were entirely unknown within the later colonial period, and it is very doubtful whether the nature of the country would permit such a compact mode of settlement.

*Dancers went forward*—The method of ceremonial approach described here was probably more or less general among the eastern tribes. On the plains, visitors usually dismount in sight of the other camp and advance on foot in a slow procession, chanting the “visiting song,” while the leader holds out the red stone pipe, which is the symbol of truce or friendship. For a good description of such a ceremony, reproduced from Battey, see the author’s *Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians*, in the *Seventeenth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology*. In this instance, the visiting Pawnee carried a flag instead of a pipe.

The Cherokee ceremony is described by Timberlake as he witnessed it at Citico in 1762:

> ‘About 100 yards from the townhouse, we were received by a group of between three and four hundred Indians. Ten or twelve of them were entirely naked, except for a piece of cloth around their waists, and were painted all over in a hideous manner. Six of them held eagles’ tails in their hands, which they shook and flourished as they advanced. They danced in a very unusual way, singing in concert with some drums of their own making, and those of the late unfortunate Captain Damere, along with several other instruments that were strange beyond description. Cheulah, the headman of the town, led the procession. He was painted blood-red, except for his face, which was half black, and he held an old rusty broadsword in his right hand and an eagle’s tail in his left. As they approached, Cheulah stepped out from the rest and performed two or three leaps as a signal to the other eagle-tails, who instantly followed his example. This violent exercise, accompanied by the band of music and a loud yell from the crowd, lasted about a minute. Then the headman, waving his sword over my head, struck it into the ground about two inches from my left foot. Directing himself to me, he then gave a short speech (which my interpreter told me was only to bid me a hearty welcome) and presented me with a string of beads. We then proceeded to the door, where Cheulah and one of the beloved men took me by each arm, led me in, and seated me in one of the primary seats. It was so dark that nothing was visible until a fresh supply of cane was brought; when burned in the middle of the house, it served as both fuel and candle. I then discovered about five hundred faces, and Cheulah, addressing me a second time, made a speech much like the first, congratulating me on my safe arrival through the numerous groups of northern Indians who generally frequent the path I took. He then made some professions of friendship, concluding by giving me another string of beads as a token of it. He had scarcely finished when four of those who had performed in the procession appeared again. They were painted milk-white, with their eagle tails in one hand and small gourds with beads in them in the other, which they rattled in time to the music. During this dance, the peace pipe was prepared.’—Timberlake, *Memoirs*, pp. 36–39.

Adair also makes brief mention of the ceremony among the Gulf tribes (*History of the American Indians*, p. 260), but his account is too heavily distorted by his own theories to have much value.

*Adopt a relative*—This seems to point to a custom which has escaped the notice of earlier writers on the eastern tribes, but which is well known in Africa and other parts of the world. It is closely similar to a ceremony still existing among the Plains Indians by which two young men of the same tribe formally agree to become brothers and ratify the agreement by a public exchange of names and gifts.
