# MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19

*White wampum*—As is well known, white was universally representative of peace. The traditional peace pipe of the Cherokee was made of white stone, and the word itself is symbolic of peace and happiness in their oratory and sacred formulas. For example, the speaker at the Green-corn dance invites the people to travel along the white path and enter the white house of peace to share in the new white food.

*Held up the belt*—As already noted, every paragraph of an ambassador's speech was accompanied by the delivery of a string or belt of wampum to give authority to his words; to accept the belt was to accept the condition or treaty which it represented. On the plains, the red stone pipe took the place of wampum.

*Try a race*—Public foot races were common among many tribes, particularly in the West among the Pueblo, the Apache, and the Wichita, either as simple athletic contests or in connection with religious ceremonies. On the plains, the horse race is more popular and is always an occasion for extensive betting.

*Throwing sumac darts*—The throwing of darts and arrows, either at a target or simply to see who can throw the farthest, is a favorite amusement among young men and boys. The arrows used for this purpose are usually longer and heavier than ordinary ones, having carved wooden heads and being artistically painted. They are sometimes tipped with the end of a buffalo horn.

99. THE SHAWANO WARS (p. 370): The primary authority regarding the expulsion of the Shawano from Tennessee is Haywood (*Natural and Aboriginal History of Tennessee*, pp. 222–224). The Schoolcraft reference is from *Notes on the Iroquois*, p. 160, and the account of the Cherokee-Delaware war is from Loskiel, *Mission of United Brethren*, p. 128, and Heckewelder, *Indian Nations*, p. 88. The Tunâ'ĭ story is from Wafford; the other incidents are from Swimmer.

*Shawano*—The Shawano or Shawnee were one of the most important Algonquian tribes. Their most famous chief was the great Tecumtha. The meaning of the name is uncertain. It is commonly interpreted as "Southerners," from the Algonquian *shawan*, "the south," but it may have come from another Algonquian word meaning "salt" (*siutagan*, *sewetagan*, etc., from *sewan*, "sweet, pungent"). Unlike Southern Indians in general, the Shawano were great users of salt and carried on an extensive salt manufacture by boiling water at the salt springs of southwestern Virginia, supplying the product in trade to other tribes. They have thirteen clans—Wolf, Loon, Bear, Buzzard, Panther, Owl, Turkey, Deer, Raccoon, Turtle, Snake, Horse, and Rabbit (according to Morgan), with the clan of the individual being indicated by his name. They are organized also into four divisions or bands, perhaps originally independent allied tribes: the Piqua, Mequachake, Kiscopocoke, and Chilicothe. The hereditary priesthood belonged to the second of these, but the first was the most prominent and apparently the most numerous. The Shawano were very nomadic and warlike. Their earliest historical territory appears to have been on the middle Savannah River, which takes its name from them, but before the end of the seventeenth century we find a portion of them, apparently the main body, occupying the basin of the Cumberland River in Tennessee and the adjacent region of Kentucky. About the year 1692, most of those remaining in South Carolina moved northward and settled upon the upper Delaware River with their relatives and friends, the Delaware and Mahican. These emigrants appear to have been of the Piqua division. Up to about the year 1730, the Shawano still had a town on the Savannah River near Augusta, from which they were finally driven by the Cherokee. Because of their former close association with the Uchee, who lived in the same neighborhood, some early writers have incorrectly supposed the two tribes to be the same. A part of the Shawano joined the Creek confederacy, and up to the beginning of the nineteenth century—and probably until the final removal to the West—occupied a separate town and retained their distinct language. Those settled upon the Cumberland were afterward expelled by the Cherokee and Chickasaw, and retired to the upper waters of the Ohio under the protection of the Delaware, who had given refuge to the original emigrants from South

With the advance of the white settlements, the two tribes moved westward into Ohio, with the <term>Shawano</term> establishing themselves in the vicinity of the present-day Piqua and Chillicothe around the year 1750. They took a leading part in the French and Indian War, Pontiac's War, the American Revolution, and the War of 1812. In 1793, a considerable band settled in Missouri upon lands granted by the Spanish government. As a result of successive sales and removals, all that remain of the tribe are now established in Indian Territory, with about one-half being incorporated into the <term>Cherokee Nation</term>. In 1900, they numbered about 1,580: namely, 790 in the Cherokee Nation (in 1898); 509 Absentee Shawnee of the Sac and Fox Agency; 184 Absentee Shawnee of Big Jim's band, special agency; and 93 Eastern Shawnee of the Quapaw Agency. There are also a few scattered among other tribes. For detailed information, consult Drake’s *Life of <term>Tecumseh</term>*; Heckewelder’s *Indian Nations*; Brinton’s *<term>Lenâpé</term> and Their Legends*; *American State Papers: Indian Affairs*, volumes i and ii; and the *Annual Reports of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs*.

### 100. THE RAID ON TIKWĂLI'TSĬ (p. 374)

Swimmer, from whom this story was obtained, was of the opinion that the event occurred when his mother was a little girl, say about 1795, but it must have been earlier.

The locations are all in Swain County, North Carolina. <term>Tikwăli'tsĭ</term> town was on the Tuckasegee River, at present-day Bryson City, immediately below and adjoining the more important town of <term>Kituhwa</term>. Deep Creek enters the Tuckasegee from the north, about a mile above Bryson City. The place where the trail crossed is called <term>Uni-ga'yata'ti'yĭ</term>, "Where they made a fish trap," a name which may have suggested the simile used by the storyteller. The place where the Cherokee crossed, above Deep Creek, is called <term>Uniyâ'hitûñ'yĭ</term>, "Where they shot it." The cliff over which the prisoners were thrown is called <term>Kala'ăsûñyĭ</term>, "Where he fell off," near Cold Spring Knob, west of Deep Creek. The Cherokee halted for a night at <term>Agitsta'ti'yĭ</term>, "Where they stayed up all night," a few miles beyond, on the western head fork of Deep Creek. They passed <term>Kûnstûtsi'yĭ</term>, "Sassafras place," a gap around the head of Noland Creek, near Clingman's Dome, and finally gave up the pursuit where the trail crossed into Tennessee, at a gap on the main ridge, just below Clingman's Dome, known as <term>Duniyatâ'lûñ'yĭ</term>, "Where there are shelves," so called from an exposure of flat rock on the top of the ridge (see the glossary).

*Magic arts*—It is almost unnecessary to state that no Indian war party ever started out without a vast deal of conjuring and "making medicine" to discover the location and strength of the enemy and to ensure victory and a safe return for the departing warriors.

*Wait for death*—The Indian usually meets inevitable fate with calmness, and more than once in our Indian wars an aged warrior or helpless woman, unable to escape, has sat down upon the ground, and, with a blanket drawn over the head, calmly awaited the fatal bullet or hatchet stroke.

### 101. THE LAST SHAWANO INVASION (p. 374)

This story also is from Swimmer, whose historical interest in the history of these wars may have been heightened by the fact that he had a slight strain of Shawano blood himself. The descendants of the old chief <term>Sawanu'gi</term> and his brothers, originally of Shawano stock, as the name indicates, have been prominent in the affairs of the East Cherokee for more than half a century, and one of them, bearing the ancestral name, is now second chief of the band and starter of the game at every large ballplay.

*The cry of an owl*—One of the most common claims put forth by the medicine men is that of an ability to understand the language of birds and to obtain supernatural knowledge from them, particularly from the owl, which is regarded with a type of fear by the common people as the embodiment of a human ghost, on account of its nocturnal habits and generally eerie appearance. A medicine man who died a few years ago among the <term>Kiowa</term> claimed to derive his powers from that bird. The body of an owl,

*Rafts*—The Cherokee canoe is carved from a poplar log and is too heavy to be carried like the bark canoes of the northern tribes. As a temporary solution, they sometimes used a bear or buffalo skin, tying the legs together at each end to create a simple boat. Upon this, the baggage was loaded while the owner swam behind, pushing it forward through the water.

### 102. THE FALSE WARRIORS OF CHILHOWEE (p. 375):
This story was told by Swimmer and confirmed by others as an actual incident from the old times. The middle Cherokee (<term>Kituhwa</term>) settlements, on the headwaters of the Little Tennessee River, were separated from the upper settlements (near its junction with the main Tennessee River) by many miles of extremely rugged mountain country. Differences in dialect and local jealousies caused friction, which sometimes brought the two sections into conflict and made an occurrence like the one narrated here possible. Because of this jealousy, according to Adair, the first Cherokee war, which began in 1760, only involved a part of the tribe for some time.

> “According to the well-known temperament of the Cherokee in similar cases, it might have either remained this way or soon changed into a very fierce civil war, had we been wise enough to take advantage of the favorable opportunity. There were seven northern towns, across from the middle parts of the Cherokee country, who from the beginning of these unfortunate grievances firmly disagreed with the hostile intentions of their suffering and angry countrymen. For a considerable time before this, they held little goodwill toward them due to some family disputes which caused each party to favor its own interests more than the other. These people would have readily satisfied their vengeful nature through either neutrality or an offensive alliance with our colonists against them” (History of the American Indians, page 248).

Chilhowee (properly <term>Tsû'lûn'we</term> or <term>Tsû'la'wĭ</term>) was a noted settlement on the south bank of the Little Tennessee River, opposite the current Chilhowee in Monroe County, Tennessee. Cowee (properly <term>Kawi'yĭ</term>, abbreviated <term>Kawi'</term>) was the name of two or more former settlements. The one mentioned here was at the junction of Cowee Creek and the Little Tennessee River, a short distance below present-day Franklin in Macon County, North Carolina. Neither name can be easily analyzed. The gunstocker’s name, <term>Gûlsădi'hĭ</term> or <term>Gûltsădi'hĭ</term>, and that of the original owner of the gun, <term>Gûnskăli'skĭ</term>, are both of uncertain origin.

*Great war trail*—See historical note 19.

*Scalp dance*—This dance, common to every tribe east of the Rocky Mountains, was held to celebrate the taking of new scalps from the enemy. The scalps—painted red on the fleshy side, decorated, and stretched in small hoops attached to the ends of poles—were carried in the dance by the wives and sweethearts of the warriors. During the pauses in the song, each warrior in turn recited his exploits in great detail. Among the Cherokee, it was customary for the warrior, as he stepped into the center of the circle, to suggest an improvised song to the drummer that summarized his own part in the encounter in one or two words. A new “war name” was frequently assumed after the dance (see the sketch of <term>Tsunu'lăhûñ'skĭ</term>, page 164). Dances were held over the same scalps on consecutive nights or sometimes at short intervals for weeks together.

*Coming for water*—Fetching water from the neighboring stream or spring was a daily duty for the women, and accordingly, we find constant allusions in Indian stories to ambushes or lovers’ appointments at such places.

*To have a ballplay*—See the note under number 3, <term>Kana'tĭ</term> and <term>Selu</term>.

### 103. COWEE TOWN: See the preceding note.

### 104. THE EASTERN TRIBES (p. 378):

*Delaware*—The Delawares get their common name from the river where they had their main settlements during the earliest colonial period. They call themselves *Lena'pe* or *Leni-lena'pe*, a name that seems to mean "real or original men," or "men of our kind." All the widespread tribes of the related Algonquian stock, as well as the Winnebago, Wyandot, and Cherokee, addressed them by the respectful title of "grandfather"; only the domineering Iroquois refused to give them any title higher than "nephew."

Their various bands and subtribes seem to have originally occupied the entire Delaware River basin, along with all of New Jersey. Their territory extended north to the Hudson watershed and west and southwest to the ridge separating the waters of the Delaware and Susquehanna. Immediately north of them, along the lower Hudson and extending into Massachusetts and Connecticut, were the closely associated Mahican and Wappinger. To the south were their friends and relatives, the Nanticoke and Conoy; the former lived in Delaware and on the eastern shore of Maryland, while the latter lived between Chesapeake Bay and the lower Potomac. All of these groups, though speaking different languages of the common Algonquian stock, claimed a traditional origin from the Delawares. In their later years of decline, most of them merged with the Delawares again. The Delawares proper were organized into three divisions which, according to Brinton, were subtribes rather than clans, even though each of the three had a totemic animal for which it was commonly named. These three subtribes were: (1) the Minsi or Munsee (meaning "people of the stony country"?), also known as the Wolf tribe, who lived in the hill country near the head of the Delaware; (2) the Unami ("downstream" people), or Turtle tribe, on the middle Delaware; and (3) the Unalachtgo ("people near the ocean"?), or Turkey tribe, in the southern part of their shared territory. Of these, the Turtle tribe held the highest position in the council, while the Wolf tribe was responsible for leadership in war. Each of these three was divided into twelve families, or early clans, which bore female names. In this regard, it is worth noting that the Delawares now living with the Wichita in Oklahoma still use the figure of a turtle as their specific cattle brand.

Only a few words can be said here regarding the history of the Delawares. Their earliest relations with Europeans were with the Dutch and Swedes. In 1682, they made the famous treaty with William Penn, which both sides faithfully observed for sixty years. Gradually forced backward by white settlers, they retired first to the Susquehanna and then to the upper Ohio. When the French and Indian War broke out in 1754, they allied themselves with the French. They fought against the Americans in the Revolution and in the War of 1812, having been driven as far west as Indiana by that time. In 1818, they gave up all their lands in that state and were assigned to a reservation in Kansas. There, they were joined by a large group that had moved to Missouri with a band of Shawano some years earlier with the permission of the Spanish government. Near the end of the Revolution, another part of the tribe—including most of those who had been converted to Christianity by Moravian missionaries—fled Ohio and settled permanently on Canadian soil. In 1867, the main body of those in Kansas moved to Indian Territory and were merged into the Cherokee Nation. A smaller band settled on the Wichita reservation in Oklahoma. The current number of Delawares is approximately 1,600: namely, 475 "Moravians and Munsees of the Thames" in Ontario; 870 merged into the Cherokee Nation (as of 1898); 95 on the Wichita reservation; perhaps 100 Munsee in Kansas and merged with the Stockbridges in Wisconsin; and 50 Delawares and others with the Six Nations in New York.

Of their former allies, the Wappinger and Conoy have long since disappeared.

through absorption into other tribes; the Mahican are represented by a group of about 530 Stockbridge Indians, including a number of Munsee, in Wisconsin, while about 70 people of mixed ancestry still keep up the Nanticoke name in southern Delaware.

*Tuscarora*—The Tuscarora, a southern tribe of the Iroquoian stock, formerly occupied an extensive territory upon the Neuse River and its branches in eastern North Carolina. Like their northern cousins, they seem to have assumed and exercised a certain degree of authority over all the smaller tribes around them. As early as 1670, Lederer described the Tuscarora "emperor" as the proudest Indian he had ever met. Around the year 1700, Lawson estimated them at 1,200 warriors (6,000 people?) in 15 towns. In 1711, they rose against the whites; one of their first acts of hostility was the killing of Lawson himself, who was engaged in surveying lands which they claimed as their own. In a struggle extending over about two years, they were so terribly reduced in number that the greater portion fled from Carolina and took refuge with their relatives and friends, the Iroquois of New York, who were henceforth known as the Six Nations. The so-called "friendly" party, under Chief Blount, was settled upon a small reservation north of the Roanoke River in what is now Bertie County, North Carolina. Here, they gradually decreased due to disease and emigration to the north, until the few who were left sold their last remaining lands in 1804. The history of the tribe after the removal to the north is a part of the history of the Iroquois or Six Nations. They now number about 750, of whom about 380 are on the Tuscarora reservation in New York, and the others are on the Grand River reservation in Ontario.

*Xuala, Suwali, Sara* or *Cheraw*—For the identification and earliest notices of the Sara, see historical note 8, "De Soto's Route." Their later history is one of almost constant hostility to the whites until their final incorporation with the Catawba—with whom they were probably related—around the year 1720. In 1743, they still preserved their distinct language, and they appear to be last mentioned in 1768, when they numbered about 50 people living among the Catawba. See Mooney, *Siouan Tribes of the East*, bulletin of the Bureau of Ethnology, 1894.

*Catawba*—The origin and meaning of this name, which dates back at least two centuries, are unknown. It may possibly come from the Choctaw through the Mobilian trade jargon. They call themselves *Nieye*, which means simply "people" or "Indians." The Iroquois call them and other related tribes in their vicinity *Toderigh-rono*, from which *Tutelo* is derived. In the seventeenth century, they were often known as *Esaw* or *Ushery*, apparently from *iswā′*, meaning river, in their own language. The Cherokee name *Ata′gwa* (plural *Ani′ta′gwa*) is a corruption of the popular form. Their linguistic affinity with the Siouan stock was established by Gatschet in 1881. See Mooney, *Siouan Tribes of the East*.

### 105. THE SOUTHERN AND WESTERN TRIBES (p. 382):

*The Creek confederacy*—Next in importance to the Cherokee among the southern tribes were the Indians of the Creek confederacy, occupying the greater portion of Georgia and Alabama, immediately south of the Cherokee. They are said to have been called "Creeks" by the early traders on account of the abundance of small streams in their country. Before the whites began to press upon them, their tribes held nearly all the territory from the Atlantic westward to about the watershed between the Tombigbee and the Pearl and Pascagoula rivers; they were cut off from the Gulf coast by the Choctaw tribes, and from the Savannah River—except near the mouth—by the Uchee, Shawnee, and Cherokee. Around the year 1800, the confederacy comprised 75 towns; the people of 47 of these were the Upper Creeks, centering around the upper waters of the Alabama, while those of the remaining 28 were the Lower Creeks, on the lower Chattahoochee and its branches (Hawkins). Among them were represented a number of tribes formerly distinct and speaking different languages. The ruling tribe and language was the Muscogee (plural, *Muscogûlgee*), which frequently gave its name to the confederacy. Other languages were the Alabama, Koasati, Hitchitee, Taskigi, Uchee, Natchee, and Sawanugi.

or Shawano. The Muscogee, Alabama, Koasati, Hichitee, and Taskigi (?) belonged to the Muskhogean stock. However, the Alabama and Koasati were linguistically closer to the Choctaw than to the Muscogee. The Hichitee represent the Muskhogean tribes of the Georgia coast region that were conquered or otherwise incorporated. The Appalachi on Appalachee bay in Florida, who were conquered by the English around 1705 and afterward joined the Creeks, spoke a dialect closely related to the Hichitee; the Seminole also were largely an offshoot from this tribe. All that is known of the Taskigi has been told elsewhere (see number 105).

The Uchee, Natchee, and Sawanugi were incorporated tribes whose languages differed radically from each other and from the Muskhogean tribes. The territory of the Uchee included both banks of the middle Savannah river, below the Cherokee, and extended into middle Georgia. They possessed strong racial pride, claiming to be older in the country than the Muscogee, and they are likely the same people as those of Cofitachiqui mentioned in early Spanish narratives. According to Hawkins, their incorporation into the Creeks was brought about through intermarriages around the year 1729. The Natchee or Natchez were an important tribe residing in lower Mississippi, near the present town of that name, until they were driven out by the French around the year 1730. At that time, most of them took refuge with the Creeks, while others joined the Chickasaw and Cherokee. The Sawanugi were Shawano who kept their town on the Savannah river, near present-day Augusta, after the main body of their tribe had moved to the north around 1692. They probably joined the Creeks at about the same time as their friends, the Uchee. The Uchee still form a solid group of about 600 people in the Creek Nation, maintaining their distinct language and tribal character. The Natchee are reduced to only one or two old men, while the Sawanugi have likely lost their distinct identity long ago.

According to Morgan, the Muscogee proper—and perhaps also their incorporated tribes—have 22 clans. Of these, the Wind clan appears to be the leading one, possessing privileges granted to no other clan, including the hereditary guardianship of the ancient metal tablets which serve as the <term>palladium</term> <note>a sacred object providing protection</note> of the tribe. By the treaty of Washington in 1832, the Creeks sold all of their remaining lands in their old country and agreed to move west of the Mississippi to what is now the Creek Nation in the Indian Territory. The removal took place over a period of several years and was not finally completed until 1845. In 1898, the citizen population of the Creek Nation numbered 14,771, of whom 10,014 were of Indian blood and the remainder were Black people, their former slaves. It appears that the Indian population included about 700 from other tribes, chiefly Cherokee. There are also about 300 Alabama, "Cushatta" (Koasati), and Muscogee in Texas. See also Hawkins, *Sketch of the Creek Country*; Gatschet, *Creek Migration Legend*; Adair, *History of the American Indians*; Bartram, *Travels*; *The Five Civilized Tribes*, *Bulletin of the Eleventh Census*; and Wyman in the *Alabama Historical Society Collections*.

**Chickasaw**—This tribe, of Muskhogean stock, formerly occupied northern Mississippi and adjacent portions of Alabama and Tennessee. At an early period, they had also incorporated several smaller tribes on the Yazoo river in central Mississippi, chief among which were the related Chokchuma. The name occurs first in the De Soto narrative. The Chickasaw language was simply a dialect of Choctaw, although the two tribes were traditional enemies and differed widely in character; the former were active and warlike, while the latter were notoriously slow-moving. Throughout the colonial period, the Chickasaw were the constant enemies of the French and friends of the English, but they remained neutral during the Revolution. By the treaty of Pontotoc in 1832, they sold their lands east of the Mississippi and agreed to remove to the Indian Territory, where they are now organized as the Chickasaw Nation. According to Morgan, they have 12 clans grouped into two <term>phratries</term> <note>tribal subdivisions or kinship groups</note>. In 1890, the citizen population of the Nation (under Chickasaw laws) consisted of 3,941 full-blood and mixed-blood Chickasaw, 681 adopted white people, 131 adopted Black people, and 946

adopted Indians from other tribes, primarily Choctaws. See also Gatschet, *Creek Migration Legend*; *The Five Civilized Tribes*, Bulletin of the Eleventh Census.

*The Choctaw confederacy*—This was a loose alliance of tribes, primarily of <term>Muskogean</term> stock, occupying southern Alabama and Mississippi, along with the adjacent Gulf coast of western Florida and eastern Louisiana. The Choctaw proper, of <term>Muskogean</term> stock, occupying south-central Mississippi, was the dominant tribe. Smaller tribes more or less closely affiliated were the Mobilian, Tohome, Mugulasha, Pascagoula, Biloxi, Acolapissa, Bayagoula, and Houma, with others of less importance. It had been assumed that all of these were of <term>Muskogean</term> stock until Gatschet in 1886 established the fact that the Biloxi were of <term>Siouan</term> affinity, and it is quite probable that the Pascagoula were also of the same connection. All the smaller tribes except the Biloxi were practically extinct, or had entirely lost their identity, before the year 1800.

The Choctaw were one of the largest of the eastern tribes, being exceeded in numbers, if at all, only by the Cherokee; but this apparent superiority was neutralized by their unwarlike character and lack of cohesion. According to Morgan, whose statement has, however, been challenged, they had eight clans grouped into two <term>phratries</term>. There was also a geographic division into "Long towns," "Potato-eating towns," and "Six towns," the last named differing considerably in dialect and custom from the others. By treaties in 1820 and 1830, the Choctaw sold all their lands east of the Mississippi and agreed to remove to Indian Territory, where they now constitute the Choctaw Nation. A considerable number of vagrant Choctaw who had drifted into Louisiana and Arkansas at an early period have since joined their kindred in Indian Territory, but from 1,000 to 2,000 are still scattered along the swampy Gulf coast of Mississippi. In 1890, those of pure or mixed Choctaw blood in the Choctaw Nation were officially reported to number 10,211. In 1899, under different conditions of citizenship, the "Choctaw by blood" were put at 14,256, while the adopted whites and negroes numbered 5,150. See also Gatschet, *Creek Migration Legend*; *The Five Civilized Tribes*, Bulletin of the Eleventh Census.

*The Osage*—The popular name is a corruption of *Ouasage*, the French spelling of *Wasash*, the name used by themselves. The Osage were the principal southern <term>Siouan</term> tribe, claiming at one time nearly the whole territory from the Missouri to the Arkansas and from the Mississippi far out into the plains. Their geographic position brought them equally into contact with the agricultural and sedentary tribes of the eastern country and the roving hunters of the prairie, and in tribal habit and custom, they formed a connecting link between the two. Whether or not they deserved the reputation, they were considered by all their neighbors as particularly predatory and faithless in character, and consequently had few friends, but were generally at war with all tribes alike. They made their first treaty with the Government in 1808. In 1825, they ceded all their claims in Missouri and Arkansas, together with considerable territory in what is now Kansas. They have decreased terribly from war and dissipation, and are now, to the number of about 1,780, gathered upon a reservation in Oklahoma just west of the Cherokee and south of the Kansas line.

106. **THE GIANTS FROM THE WEST** (p. 391): This may be an exaggerated account of a visit from some warriors of a taller tribe from the plains, where it is customary to pluck out the eyebrows and to wear the hair in two long side pendants, wrapped around with otter skin and reaching to the knees, thus giving a peculiar expression to the eyes and an appearance of height which is sometimes deceptive. The Osage warriors have, however, long been noted for their height.

...the Cherokee, even though all their woods and waters are inhabited by invisible fairy tribes. This seems to be characteristic of Indian mythologies in general, as giants are relatively few in number while the “little people” are numerous. The Iroquois have a story about an invasion by a race of stony-skinned cannibal giants from the west (Schoolcraft, *Notes on Iroquois*, p. 266). Giant races also appear in the mythologies of the Navaho (Matthews, *Navaho Legends*), Choctaw (Gatschet, *Creek Migration Legend*), and other tribes. According to the old Spanish chroniclers, Ayllon in 1520 met a tribe of Indians on the coast of South Carolina whose chiefs were of gigantic size. He was told this was because of a special diet and massage routine they underwent during infancy.

107. **THE LOST CHEROKEE** (p. 391): This tradition as presented here is taken mostly from the Wahnenauhi manuscript. There is a persistent belief among the Cherokee that a portion of their people once wandered far to the west or southwest, where they were sometimes heard of afterward, but they were never reunited with their tribe. Sequoya hoped to verify this tradition and return his lost kinsmen to their tribe, and this goal led him to undertake the journey on which he died. These traditional lost Cherokee are entirely distinct from the historical emigrants who moved away from the East shortly after the American Revolution.

Similar stories are common to nearly all tribes. For example, the Kiowa tell of a chief who, many years ago, quarreled over the division of game and led his people far away across the Rocky Mountains; they are reportedly still living somewhere near the border with Canada and still speak their original Kiowa language. The Tonkawa tell of a band of their people who were separated from the tribe by a sudden encroachment of the sea on the Texas coast. Unable to return, they gradually worked their way deep into Mexico. The Tuscarora tell how, during their early travels, they came to the Mississippi River and were crossing to the west side using a grapevine. The vine broke, leaving those on the far side to wander off until they eventually became enemies of those on the eastern bank. See Mooney, *Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians*, Seventeenth Annual Report Bureau of American Ethnology, part 1, and *The Last of Our Cannibals*, in *Harper’s Magazine*, August, 1901; Cusick, quoted in Schoolcraft, *Notes on the Iroquois*, p. 478.

108. **THE MASSACRE OF THE ANI’-KUTA’NI** (p. 392): Swimmer, Ta'gwădihǐ', Ayâsta, and Wafford all knew this name, which Ayâsta pronounced *Ani'-Kwăta'ni*, but none of them could provide more specific details than what was mentioned in the first sentence. The hereditary passing down of priestly honors within a certain clan or group is the rule rather than the exception among tribes in both the east and west.

109. **THE WAR MEDICINE** (p. 393): The first two paragraphs come from Wafford, and the rest from Swimmer. The stories are characteristic of Indian beliefs and could be found in any tribe. The great Kiowa chief, Set-ängya, who was already mentioned, was—and still is—believed by his tribe to have possessed a magic knife, which he carried in his stomach and could bring out of his mouth whenever he wanted. The Kiowa claim it was this knife—which the soldiers naturally failed to find when disarming him—that he used to attack the guard in the struggle that resulted in his death.

110. **INCIDENTS OF PERSONAL HEROISM** (p. 394): The incident of the fight at Waya Gap is based on the account of the late Major James Bryson of Dillsboro, North Carolina. Born in 1818, he heard it from his great-uncle, Daniel Bryson, who was a member of Williamson’s expedition.

Speaking of the Cherokee “War Women,” who were admitted to the tribal councils, Timberlake says (*Memoirs*, p. 70): “The reader will be quite surprised to find that the story of Amazons is not as much of a myth as we imagined, as many of the Indian women are as famous in war as they are powerful in the council.”

as a matter of popular belief, shaped by tribal custom and ritual. The question of fact is for the archaeologist to decide. The Indian statement is valuable, however, in showing the supposed requirements for the solemn consecration of an important work.

A note by John Howard Payne upon the sacred square of the Creeks, as observed by him in 1835, just before his visit to the Cherokee, may throw further light on the problem: 

> "In the center of this outer square was a very high circular mound. This, apparently, was formed from the earth accumulated yearly by moving the surface of the sacred square there. At every Green-corn festival, the sacred square is strewn with soil yet untrodden; the soil of the previous year being taken away but preserved as explained above. No stranger’s foot is allowed to step on the new earth of the sacred square until its consecration is complete" (Letter of 1835 in *Continental Monthly*, New York, 1862, p. 19). See note on the sacred fire.

*Conjured with disease*—The practice of conjuring certain favorite spots in order to make them fatal to an invading enemy was common to many, if not all, tribes. One of the most terrible battles of the Creek War was fought upon the "Holy Ground," so called because the Indians believed that, due to the mystic rites performed there for that purpose by their prophets, no white troops could set foot upon it and live.

*The sacred fire*—The method described for producing fire and keeping it constantly smoldering in the townhouse appears to have been the one actually used in ancient times, as indicated by the name given to the plant (<term>atsil'-sûñti'</term>), and supported by the unanimous testimony of the elders. All the older East Cherokee believe that the ancient fire still burns within the mounds at Franklin and Bryson City; those men who were stationed for a time near the latter place while in the Confederate service during the Civil War assert that they frequently saw the smoke rising from the adjacent mound.

The missionary Buttrick, citing old Cherokee authority, says:

> "They were required to make new fire for sacred purposes by rubbing two pieces of dry wood together, with a certain dry weed called goldenrod between them. . . . When their enemies destroyed the house in which this holy fire was kept, it was said the fire settled down into the earth, where it still lives, though unknown to the people. The place where they lost this holy fire is somewhere in one of the Carolinas" (Antiquities, p. 9).

The general accuracy of Swimmer's account is strikingly confirmed by the description of the New-fire ceremony given more than half a century earlier by John Howard Payne, the poet. Payne had gone among the Cherokee to study their ethnology and was engaged in that work when he was arrested, along with John Ross, by the Georgia Guard in 1835. He describes the kindling of the new fire as part of the annual spring festival. At that time, says Payne, "the altar in the center of the national heptagon <note>townhouse</note> was repaired. It was constructed in a conical shape out of fresh earth. A circle was drawn around the top to receive the fire of sacrifice. Upon this was laid, ready for use, the inner bark of seven different kinds of trees. This bark was carefully chosen from the east side of the trees and was clear and free from blemish." After some days of preliminary purification, sacrifice, and other ceremonial performances, the day appointed for lighting the new fire arrived.

> "Early in the morning, the seven persons who were commissioned to kindle the fire began their operations. One was the official fire-maker; the remaining six were his assistants. A hearth was carefully cleared and prepared. After a round hole was made in a block of wood, a small quantity of dry goldenrod weed was placed in it. A stick, the end of which just fitted the opening, was whirled rapidly until the weed caught fire. The flame was then lit on the hearth and taken from there to every house by the women, who waited together for that purpose. The old fires having been extinguished everywhere and the hearths cleansed, new fires were lighted

Similar ceremonies were common to many tribes, particularly the southern tribes and the Pueblos, in connection with the annual kindling of the sacred new fire. See Adair, *History of the American Indians*; Hawkins, *Sketch of the Creek Country*, quoted by Gatschet, *Creek Migration Legend*; Bartram, *Travels*; Fewkes, *The New-fire Ceremony at Walpi*, in *American Anthropologist* for January, 1900; Squier, *Serpent Symbol*. Going beyond our own boundaries, it may be said briefly that fire worship was probably as ancient as ritual itself and nearly as universal.

*Wooden box*—The sacred ark of the Cherokee is described by Adair (*History of the American Indians*, pp. 161–162), and its capture by the Delawares is mentioned by Washburn (*Reminiscences*, pp. 191, 221), who states that the old priests of the tribe ascribed the later degeneracy of their people to its loss. They refused to tell him the contents of the ark. On this subject Adair says:

> “A gentleman who was at the Ohio in the year 1756 assured me he saw a stranger there very insistent to view the inside of the Cherokee ark, which was covered with a dressed deerskin and placed on a couple of short blocks. An Indian sentinel watched it, armed with a hickory bow and brass-pointed barbed arrows; and he was faithful to his trust, for finding the stranger intruding to pollute the supposed sacred vehicle, he drew an arrow to the head and would have shot him through the body had he not suddenly withdrawn. The interpreter, when asked by the gentleman what it contained, told him there was nothing in it but a bundle of conjuring traps. This shows what conjurers our common interpreters are, and how much the learned world has really profited by their information.”

Such tribal palladiums <note>sacred objects that protect a group</note> or “medicines,” upon which the existence and prosperity of the tribe are supposed to depend, are still preserved among the plains Indians, the sacred receptacle in each case being confided to the keeping of a priest appointed for the purpose, who alone is privileged to undo the wrappings or expose the contents. Among these tribal “medicines” may be mentioned the sacred arrows of the Cheyenne, the “flat pipe” of the Arapaho, the great shell of the Omaha, and the *taime* image of the Kiowa (see reference in the author's *Ghost-dance Religion* and *Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians*).

*White peace pipe*—This statement concerning the ancient seven-stem peace pipe carved from white stone is given on the authority of Swimmer, who said that the stone was procured from a quarry near the present town of Knoxville, Tennessee. A certain district of western North Carolina has recently acquired an unenviable reputation for the manufacture of fake “Indian pipes,” supposedly taken from mounds, carved from soapstone and having from three to half a dozen stem-holes encircling the bowl.

*Turtle drum*—This statement is on the authority of Wafford, who had talked with men who claimed to have known those who had seen the drum. He was not positive as to the town, but thought it was Keowee. It is believed that the drum was hidden by the Indians, in anticipation of their quick return, when the country was invaded by Williamson in 1776; but as the country was never recovered by the Cherokee, the drum was lost.

112–115. SHORT HUMOROUS STORIES (pp. 397, 399): These short stories are fairly representative of Cherokee humor. Each was heard repeatedly from several informants, both in the east and west.

116. THE STAR FEATHERS (p. 399): This story was obtained from John Ax, with additional details from Chief Smith and others, to whom it was equally familiar. It is told as an actual happening in the early days, before the Indians had much acquaintance with the whites, and it is thoroughly characteristic of the methods of medicine men.

<header>MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19</header>

The deception was based upon the Cherokee belief that the stars are living creatures with feathers (see number 9, “What the Stars are Like”). 
The Indian has always been noted for his love of feather decorations; more than the feathers of any of his native birds, he prized the beautiful feathers of the peacock whenever it was possible to obtain them from the whites. As far back as 1670, Lederer noted of a South Carolina tribe: “The Ushery delight greatly in feather ornaments, of which they have great variety; but peacocks are held in the highest esteem because they are rare in these parts” (*Travels*, p. 32, ed. 1891).

117. <term>THE MOTHER BEAR’S SONG</term> (p. 400): The first of these songs was obtained from Ayâsta and was unknown to Swimmer. The second song was also obtained from Ayâsta, who knew only the verses, while Swimmer knew both the verses and the story which gives them their setting.
The first has an exact parallel among the Creek, which is thus given in the “Baby Songs” of the Tuggle manuscript:

| | |
|---|---|
| Ah tan | Down the stream |
| Ah yah chokese | if you hear |
| Mah kah cho kofe | the chase going |
| Hoche yoke saw | up the stream |
| Lit kahts chars, | run, |
| Lit kahts chars. | run. |
| | |
| A thle poo | Up the stream |
| Ahyohchokese | if you hear |
| Mah kah cho kofe | the chase going |
| Thorne yoke saw | to the high mountain |
| Lit karts chars, | run, |
| Lit karts chars. | run. |

->*Translation*<-

> If you hear the noise of the chase
> Going down the stream,
> Then run up the stream.
>
> If you hear the noise of the chase
> Going up the stream,
> Then run to the high mountain,
> Then run to the high mountain.

118. <term>BABY SONG, TO PLEASE THE CHILDREN</term> (p. 401): This song is well known to the women and was sung by both Ayâsta and Swimmer.

119. <term>WHEN BABIES ARE BORN: THE WREN AND THE CRICKET</term> (p. 401): These little bits of Indian folklore were obtained from Swimmer, but are common tribal property.

120. <term>THE RAVEN MOCKER</term> (p. 401): The gruesome belief in the “Raven Mocker” is universal among the Cherokee and has close parallels in other tribes. Very near to it is the Iroquois belief in the vampire or cannibal ghost, concerning which Schoolcraft relates some blood-curdling stories. He says: “It is believed that such doomed spirits creep into the lodges of men at night, and during sleep suck their blood and eat their flesh. They are invisible” (*Notes on the Iroquois*, p. 144). On one occasion, while the author was among the Cherokee, a sick man was allowed to die alone because his friends imagined they felt the presence of the Raven Mocker or other invisible witches about the house, and were consequently afraid to stay with him. The description of the flying terror appears to be that of a great meteor. It is a universal principle of folk belief that discovery or recognition while disguised in another form brings disaster to the witch.

<header>MOONEY] NOTES AND PARALLELS 505</header>

The "diving" of the raven while flying high in the air is performed by folding one wing close to its body, at which point the bird falls to a lower level, apparently turning a somersault during the descent. It seems to be done purely for amusement.

121. HERBERT’S SPRING (p. 403): The subject of this old trader's legend must have been one of the headwaters of the Chattooga River, an upper branch of the Savannah, which rises in the southern part of Jackson County, North Carolina. It is located on the eastern slope of the ridge from which other streams flow in the opposite direction to join the waters of the Tennessee River. It was probably in the vicinity of the present-day Highlands in Macon County, where the trail from the Chattooga River and the settlements on Keowee crossed the Blue Ridge, then descended the Cullasagee River to the towns on the Little Tennessee.

126. PLANT LORE (p. 420): For the ceremonies, prayers, and precautions used by doctors in connection with the gathering and preparation of medicinal roots, bark, and herbs, see the author's *Sacred Formulas of the Cherokees*, in the *Seventh Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology*, 1891.

*Violet*—The Onondaga name means "two heads entangled," referring, we are told, to "the common sight where the flower heads are interlocked and pulled apart by their stems" (W. M. Beauchamp, in *Journal of American Folk-Lore*, October, 1888).

*Cedar*—For references to the sacred character of the cedar among the plains tribes, see the author's *Ghost-dance Religion*, in the *Fourteenth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology*, part 2, 1896.

*Linn and basswood*—The ancient Tuscarora believed that no tree except for the black gum was immune to lightning. They claimed that lightning would run around the tree many times, seeking in vain to find a way to strike inside. Lawson, who records this belief, adds: "Now, you must understand that this type of gum tree will not split or crack; therefore, I suppose the story might have originated from that fact" (*Carolina*, pp. 345–346, ed. 1860). The Pawnee claim the same immunity for the cedar and throw sprigs of it as incense into the fire during storms to turn aside a lightning strike (Grinnell, *Pawnee Hero Stories*, p. 126).

*Ginseng*—For more information concerning this plant, see the author's *Sacred Formulas*, mentioned above.

# GLOSSARY OF CHEROKEE WORDS

The Cherokee language uses the continental vowel sounds *a*, *e*, *i*, and *u*, but it lacks the sound *o*, which is replaced by a deep *â*. The obscure or short *û* is often nasalized, though this nasal sound is rarely heard at the end of a word. The only labial sound is *m*, which occurs in likely no more than half a dozen words in the Upper and Middle dialects; it is entirely absent from the Lower dialect, where *w* takes its place. The characteristic *l* of the Upper and Middle dialects becomes *r* in the Lower dialect, but no single dialect contains both sounds. There is also an aspirated *l*. The letters *h* and *t* have their standard sounds, but *g* and *d* are "medial" sounds (semi-voiced), roughly similar to the sounds of *k* and *t*, respectively. A common double consonant is *ts*, which was usually written as *ch* by early traders (see page 188, “Dialects”).

| | |
|---|---|
| a | as in far. |
| ă | as in what, or obscure as in showman. |
| â | as in law, all. |
| d | medial (semi-voiced), approximating t. |
| e | as in they. |
| ĕ | as in net. |
| g | medial (semi-voiced), approximating k. |
| h | as in hat. |
| i | as in pique. |
| ĭ | as in pick. |
| k | as in kick. |
| l | as in lull. |
| ’l | voiceless l (sometimes written hl), nearly the Welsh ll. |
| m | as in man. |
| n | as in not. |
| r | takes the place of l in the Lower dialect. |
| s | as in sin. |
| t | as in top. |
| u | as in rule. |
| û | as in cut. |
| ûñ | û nasalized. |
| w | as in wit. |
| y | as in you. |
| ’ | a slight breath (aspirate), sometimes indicating a missing vowel. |

<header>MOONEY] GLOSSARY</header>

Several English words, along with cross-references, have been added to the glossary. These, as well as altered Cherokee forms, are indicated by CAPITAL LETTERS.

adâ'lănun'stĭ—a staff or cane.
adan'ta—soul.
ada'wehĭ—a magician or supernatural being.
ada'wehĭ'yu—a very great magician; an intensive form of *ada'wehĭ*.
â'gănă—groundhog.
Â'gänstâ'ta—"Groundhog-sausage," from *â'gănă* (groundhog) and *tsistâ'û* ("I am pounding it"). This is understood to refer to pounding meat or other items in a mortar after first crisping them over a fire. A war chief prominent in the Cherokee War of 1760 and active until about the end of the Revolution; known to white people as Oconostota. This is also the Cherokee name for Colonel Gideon Morgan of the War of 1812; for his son, Washington Morgan, of the Civil War; and currently for a full-blood on the reservation known to white people as Morgan Calhoun.
Â'găn-uni'tsĭ—"Groundhogs' mother," from *â'gănă* and *uni'tsĭ* (their mother), which is the plural of *utsĭ'* (his mother); *etsĭ'* and *agitsĭ'* mean "my mother." This is the Cherokee name of a Shawnee captive who, according to tradition, killed the great Uktena serpent and obtained the *Ulûñsû'tĭ*.
Agawe'la—"Old Woman," a formulaic name for corn or the spirit of corn.
agăyûn'lĭ—short for *agăyûn'lige*, meaning old or ancient.
agidâ'tă—see *edâ'tă*.
agidu'tŭ—see *edu'tŭ*.
Agĭ'lĭ—"He is rising," possibly a shortened form of the old personal name *Agĭn'-agĭ'lĭ* ("Rising-fawn"). Major George Lowrey, a cousin of Sequoya and assistant chief of the Cherokee Nation around 1840. Stanley incorrectly translates it as "Keeth-la" or "Dog" (mistaking it for *gĭ'lĭ'*).
aginĭ'sĭ—see *enĭ'sĭ*.
agĭ'sĭ—female, usually referring to four-legged animals.
Agis'-e'gwa—"Great Female," possibly "Great Doe." A being, likely an animal deity, called upon in sacred formulas.
agitsĭ'—see *etsĭ'*.
Agitsta'ti'yĭ—"Where they stayed up all night," from *tsigitsûn'tihû'* ("I stay up all night"). A location in the Great Smoky Mountains near the head of Noland Creek in Swain County, North Carolina. (See the notes for number 100).
AGUAQUIRI—see GUAQUILI.
Ăhălu'na—"Ambush," *Ăhălunûn'yĭ* ("Ambush place"), or *Uni'hălu'na* ("Where they ambushed"), from *ăkălu'ga* ("I am watching"). This refers to Soco Gap at the head of Soco Creek, on the border of Swain and Haywood counties, North Carolina (see number 122). The name also refers to a lookout station for deer hunters.
ahănu'lăhĭ—"he is bearded," from *ahănu'lăhû* (a beard).
Ahu'lude'gĭ—"He throws away the drum" (habitual action), from *ahu'lĭ* (drum) and *akwăde'gû* ("I am throwing away a round object"). This was the Cherokee name of John Jolly, a famous chief and the adoptive father of Sam Houston, around 1800.
ahyelĭ'skĭ—a mocker or mimic.
aktă'—eye; plural, *dĭktă'*.
akta'tĭ—a telescope or field glass. The name refers to something used to examine or look into things closely, derived from *aktă'* (eye).
akwandu'lĭ—a song form of *akwidu'lĭ-hû* ("I want it").
Akwan'kĭ—see *Anakwan'kĭ*.
Akwê'ti'yĭ—a location on the Tuckasegee River in Jackson County, North Carolina; the meaning of the name is lost. See number 122.
ALARKA—see *Yalâgĭ*.

âligă'—the redhorse fish (*Moxostoma*).

Alkinĭ'—the last woman known to be of Natchez descent and traits among the East Cherokee; she died about 1890. The name has no apparent meaning.

ămă'—water; in the Lower dialect, ăwă'; compare a'mă, salt.

amăyĕ'hĭ'—"dwelling in the water," from ămă' (ămă'yĭ, "in the water") and ĕhĭ', "I dwell," or "I live."

Ămăyĕ'l-e'gwa—"Great island," from ămăyĕ'lĭ, island (from ămă', water, and ayĕ'lĭ, "in the middle") and e'gwa, great. A former Cherokee settlement on the Little Tennessee River, at Big Island, a short distance below the mouth of Tellico, in Monroe County, Tennessee. Timberlake wrote it Mialaquô, while Bartram spelled it Nilaque. It is not to be confused with Long-island town below Chattanooga.

Ămăyĕ'lĭ-gûnăhĭ'ta—"Long island," from ămăyĕ'lĭ, island, and gûnăhĭ'ta, long. A former Cherokee settlement, known to white people as Long Island Town, at the Long Island in the Tennessee River, on the Tennessee-Georgia line. It was one of the Chickamauga towns (see *Tsĭkăma'gĭ*).

amă'yĭnĕ'hĭ—"dwellers in the water," the plural of *amăyĕ'hĭ*.

Anăda'dûñtăskĭ—"Roasters," that is, Cannibals; from gûñ'tăskû', "I am putting it (around) into the fire to roast." The regular word for cannibals is *Yûñ'winĭ'giskĭ*, which see. See number 3.

anagâhûñ'ûñskû'—the Green-corn dance; literally, "they are having a Green-corn dance"; anagâhûñ'ûñsgûñ'yĭ, "where they are having the Green-corn dance"; the popular name is not a translation of the Cherokee word, which has no reference either to corn or dancing.

Anakwan'kĭ—the Delaware Indians; singular *Akwan'kĭ*, a Cherokee attempt at *Wapanaqkĭ*, "Easterners," the Algonquian name by which, in various corrupted forms, the Delawares are commonly known to the western tribes.

ANANTOOEAH—see *Ani'-Nûn'dăwe'gĭ*.

a'ne'tsâ, or a'netsâ'gĭ—the ballplay.

a'netsâ'ûñskĭ—a ballplayer; literally, "a lover of the ballplay."

ani'—a tribal and animate prefix.

ani'da'wehĭ—plural of *ada'wehĭ*.

a'niganti'skĭ—see *dăgan'tû*.

Ani'-Gatâge'wĭ—one of the seven Cherokee clans; the name now has no meaning, but has been absurdly translated as "Blind savanna," based on an incorrect idea that it is derived from *igâ'tĭ*, a swamp or savanna, and *dige'wĭ*, blind.

Ani'-Gĭlâ'hĭ—"Long-haired people," one of the seven Cherokee clans; singular, *Agĭlâ'hĭ*. The word comes from *agĭlâ'hĭ* (perhaps connected with *agĭ'lge-nĭ*, "the back of his neck"), an archaic term denoting wearing the hair long or flowing loosely, and usually recognized as applying more specifically to a woman.

Ani'-Gĭlĭ'—a problematic tribe, possibly the Congaree. See page 381. The name is not connected with *gĭ'lĭ'*, dog.

Ani'-Gusă—see *Ani'-Ku'să*.

a'nigwa—soon after; *dine'tlănă a'nigwa*, "soon after the creation."

Ani'-Hyûñ'tĭkwălâ'skĭ—"The Thunderers," that is, thunder, which in Cherokee belief is controlled and caused by a family of supernatural beings. The word refers to making a rolling sound; compare *tĭkwăle'lu*, a wheel, hence a wagon; *ămă'-tĭkwălelûñyĭ*, "rolling water place," applied to a cascade where the water falls along the surface of the rock; *ahyûñ'tĭkwălâ'stihû'*, "it is thundering," applied to the roar of a railroad train or waterfall.

Ani'-Kawĭ'—"Deer people," one of the seven Cherokee clans; the regular form for deer is *a'wĭ'*.

Ani'-Kawĭ'tă—The Lower Creeks, from *Kawĭ'tă* or Coweta, their former principal town on the Chattahoochee River near the present Columbus, Georgia; the Upper

<header>MOONEY] GLOSSARY</header>

Creeks on the headwaters of the Alabama River were distinguished as *Ani'-Ku'să* (see below). A small creek of the Little Tennessee River above Franklin, in Macon County, North Carolina, is now known as Coweeta Creek.

*Ani'-Kitu'hwagĭ*—"Kitu'hwă people," from *Kitu'hwă* (see below), an ancient Cherokee settlement; for an explanation, see page 182.

*Ani'-Ku'să* or *Ani'-Gu'să*—The Creek Indians, particularly the Upper Creeks on the waters of the Alabama River; singular, *A-Ku'să*, from Kusa or Coosa (Spanish: Coça, Cossa), their principal ancient town.

*Ani'-Kuta'nĭ* (also *Ani'-Kwăta'nĭ*, or, incorrectly, *Nicotani*)—a traditional Cherokee priestly society or clan, exterminated in a popular uprising. See number 108.

*aninâ'hilidâ'hĭ*—"creatures that fly about," from *tsina'li*, "I am flying," and *tsinâ'ilidâ'hû*, "I am flying about." This is the generic term for birds and flying insects.

*Ani'-Na'tsĭ*—abbreviated as *Anintsĭ*, singular *A-Na'tsĭ*. The Natchez Indians; due to a coincidence with *na'tsĭ* (pine), the name has been incorrectly translated as "Pine Indians," whereas it is actually a Cherokee plural of the proper name of the Natchez.

*Anin'tsĭ*—see *Ani'-Na'tsĭ*.

*Ani'-Nûn'dăwe'gĭ*—singular, *Nûn'dăwe'gĭ*; the Iroquois, more particularly the Seneca, from *Nûndawao*, the name by which the Seneca call themselves. Adair spells it *Anantooeah*. The tribe was also known as *Ani'-Sĕ'nikă*.

*Ani'-Sahâ'nĭ*—one of the seven Cherokee clans; possibly an archaic form for "Blue people," from *sa'ka'ni* or *sa'ka'nige'ĭ*, blue.

*Ani'-Sa'nĭ*, *Ani'-Sawahâ'nĭ*—see *Ani'-Sawănu'gĭ*.

*Ani'-Sawănu'gĭ* (singular *Sawănu'gĭ*)—the Shawano <note>Shawnee</note> Indians. *Ani'-Sa'nĭ* and *Ani'-Sawahâ'nĭ* (see page 380) may be the same.

*Ani'-Sĕ'nikă*—see *Ani'-Nûn'dăwe'gĭ*.

*anisga'ya*—the plural of *asga'ya*, man.

*Anisga'ya Tsuntsdi'(-ga)*—"The Little Men"; the Thunder Boys in Cherokee mythology. See numbers 3 and 8.

*Ani'sgaya'yĭ*—"Men town" (?), a traditional Cherokee settlement on the Valley River, in Cherokee County, North Carolina.

*anisgi'na*—the plural of *asgi'na* (see below).

*Ani'-Skălâ'lĭ*—the Tuscarora Indians; singular, *Skălâ'lĭ* or *A-Skălâ'lĭ*.

*Ani'skwa'nĭ*—Spaniards; singular, *Askwa'nĭ*.

*Ani'-Suwa'lĭ*, or *Ani'-Suwa'la*—the Suala, Sara, or Cheraw Indians, formerly located around the headwaters of the Broad River, North Carolina; this was the Xuala province of the De Soto chronicle, and Joara or Juada of the later Pardo narrative.

*Ani'ta'gwă*—the Catawba Indians; singular, *Ata'gwă* or *Tagwă*.

*Ani'-Tsâ'gûhĭ*—a traditional Cherokee clan, transformed into bears (see number 75). Swimmer's daughter bears the name *Tsâgûhĭ*, which is not recognized as belonging specifically to either sex.

*Ani'-Tsa'lăgĭ'*—the Cherokee. See "Tribal Synonymy," page 182.

*Ani'-Tsa'ta*—the Choctaw Indians; singular, *Tsa'ta*.

*Ani'-Tsĭ'ksû*—the Chickasaw Indians; singular, *Tsĭ'ksû*.

*Ani'-Tsĭ'skwa*—"Bird people"; one of the seven Cherokee clans.

*Ani'tsu'tsă*—"The Boys," from *atsu'tsă*, boy; the Pleiades. See number 10.

*Ani'-Wâ'dĭ'*—"Paint people"; one of the seven Cherokee clans.

*Ani'-Wâdihĭ'*—"Place of the Paint people or clan"; Paint Town, a Cherokee settlement on lower Soco Creek, within the reservation in Jackson and Swain counties, North Carolina. It takes its name from the *Ani'-Wâ'dĭ* or Paint clan.

*ani'wani'skĭ*—the bugle weed, *Lycopus virginicus*; literally, "they talk" or "talkers," from *tsiwa'nihû*, "I am talking," and *awani'skĭ*, "he talks habitually." See number 26.

*Ani'-Wasa'sĭ*—the Osage Indians; singular, *Wasa'sĭ*.

<header>MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19]</header>

**Ani'-Wa"ya"**—"Wolf people"; the most important of the seven Cherokee clans.
**Ani'-Yu'tsĭ**—the Yuchi or Uchee Indians; singular *Yu'tsĭ*.
**Ani'-Yûn'wiyă'**—Indians, particularly Cherokee Indians; literally "principal or real people," from *yûñwĭ*, person, *yă*, a suffix implying principal or real, and *ani'*, the tribal prefix. See pages 5 and 182.
**ANNIE AX**—see *Sadayĭ'*.
**AQUONE**—a post office on the Nantahala river, in Macon county, North Carolina, site of the former Fort Scott. Probably a corruption of *egwânĭ*, river.
**ARCH, JOHN**—see *Atsĭ*.
**asâ'gwălĭhû'**—a pack or burden; *asâ'gwălĭhû'*, or *asâ'gwĭlĭ'*, "there is a pack on him." Compare *sâ'gwălĭ'*.
**asěhĭ'**—surely.
**Asĕ'nikă**—singular of *Ani'-Sĕ'nikă*. See *Ani'-Nûndăwe'gĭ*.
**asga'ya**—man.
**Asga'ya Gĭ'gageĭ**—the "Red Man"; the Lightning spirit.
**asgi'na**—a ghost, either human or animal; since ghosts are commonly thought to be malevolent, the name is frequently translated as "devil."
**ASHEVILLE**—see *Kâsdu'yĭ* and *Unta'kiyastĭ'yĭ*.
**âsĭ**—the sweat lodge and occasional winter sleeping apartment of the Cherokee and other southern tribes. It was a low-built structure of logs covered with earth, and because it was enclosed and the fire usually kept smoldering within, it was known to the old traders as the "hot house."
**â'siyu'** (abbreviated *siyu'*)—good; the common Cherokee salute; *gâ'siyu'*, "I am good"; *hâ'siyu'*, "you are good"; *â'siyu*, "he (it) is good"; *âstû*, "very good" (intensive).
**Askwa'nĭ**—a Spaniard. See *Ani'skwa'nĭ*.
**âstû'**—very good; *âstû' tsĭkĭ'*, very good, best of all. Compare *â'siyu'*.
**Astu'gatâ'ga**—A Cherokee lieutenant in the Confederate service, killed in 1862. See page 170. The name may be translated as "Standing in the doorway" but implies that the man himself is the door or shutter; it has no first person form; *gatâ'ga*, "he is standing"; *stûtĭ*, a door or shutter; *stuhû'*, a closed door or passage; *stugĭ'stĭ*, a key—that is, something with which to open a door.
**asûn'tlĭ, asûntlûn'yĭ**—a footlog or bridge; literally, "log lying across," from *asĭ'ta*, log.
**ătă'**—wood; *ata'yă*, "principal wood," i.e., oak; compare Muscogee *iti*, wood.
**Atagâ'hĭ**—"Gall place," from *ă'tăgû'*, gall, and *hĭ*, locative; a mythical lake in the Great Smoky mountains. See number 69. The name is also applied to that part of the Great Smoky range centering around Thunderhead mountain and Miry ridge, near the boundary between Swain county, North Carolina, and Blount county, Tennessee.
**ă'tăgû'**—gall.
**Ătă'-gûl'kălû'**—a noted Cherokee chief, recognized by the British government as the head chief or "emperor" of the Nation, around 1760 and later, and commonly known to the whites as the Little Carpenter (Little Cornplanter, by mistake, in Haywood). The name is frequently spelled Atta-kulla-kulla, Ata-kullakulla, or Ata-culculla. It may be translated as "Leaning-wood," from *ătă'*, "wood" and *gûl'kălû*, a verb implying that something long is leaning, without sufficient support, against some other object; it has no first person form. Bartram describes him as
> "a man of remarkably small stature, slender and of a delicate frame, the only instance I saw in the Nation; but he is a man of superior abilities."
**Ata'gwă**—a Catawba Indian. See *Ani'ta'gwă*.
**A'tâhi'ta**—abbreviated from *A'tâhitûn'yĭ*, "Place where they shouted," from *gatâ'hiû'*, "I shout," and *yĭ*, locative. Waya gap, on the ridge west of Franklin,

It details linguistic origins and provides geographic context for various North Carolina and Tennessee locations.</summary>

<header>MOONEY] GLOSSARY</header>

Macon County, North Carolina. See number 13. The map name is probably from the Cherokee *wa'ya*, wolf.
**Ata-kullakulla**—see *Ătă'-gǔl' kălǔ'*.
**â'tălĭ**—mountain; in the Lower dialect *â'tărĭ*, from which comes the "Ottare" or Upper Cherokee of Adair. The form *â'tălĭ* is used only in composition; a mountain in its place is *âtălǔñyĭ* or *gatu'sĭ*.
**â'tălĭ-gǔlĭ'**—"it climbs the mountain," that is, "mountain-climber"; the ginseng plant, *Ginseng quinquefolium*; from *â'tălĭ*, mountain, and *gǔlĭ'*, "it climbs" (habitually); *tsĭlâ'hĭ'* or *tsĭlĭ'*, "I am climbing." Also called in the sacred formulas, *Yǔn'wĭ Usdi'*, "Little Man." See number 126.
**a'tălǔlǔ'**—unfinished, premature, unsuccessful; from which comes *utalu'lĭ*, "it is not yet time."
**Ata'lǔntĭ'skĭ**—a chief of the Arkansas Cherokee about 1818, who had originally emigrated from Tennessee. The name, commonly spelled Tollunteeskee, Taluntiski, Tallotiskee, Tallotuskee, etc., signifies one who throws some living object from a place, such as an enemy from a precipice. See number 100 for an instance.
**â'tărĭ**—see *â'tălĭ*.
**ătăsĭ'** (or *ătăsǔ'*, in a dialect form)—a war club.
**atatsǔñ'skĭ**—stinging; literally, "he stings" (habitually).
**A'tlă'nuwă'**—"Tlă'nuwă hole"; the Cherokee name of Chattanooga, Tennessee (see *Tsatănu'gĭ*), originally applied to a bluff on the south side of the Tennessee River at the foot of the present Market Street. See number 124.
**A'tsĭ**—the Cherokee name of John Arch, one of the earliest native writers in the Sequoya characters. The word is simply an attempt at the English name Arch.
**atsi'la**—fire; in the Lower dialect, *atsi'ra*.
**Atsĭl'-dihye'gĭ**—"Fire Carrier"; apparently the Cherokee name for the will-of-the-wisp. See page 335. As is usually the case in Cherokee compounds, the verb form is plural ("it carries fires"); the singular form is *ahye'gĭ*.
**atsĭl'-sǔñ'tĭ** (abbreviated *tsĭl'-sǔñ'tĭ*)—fleabane (*Erigeron canadense*); the name means "material with which to make fire," from *atsi'la*, fire, and *gasǔñ'tĭ* (*gatsǔñ'tĭ* or *gat-lǔñ'tĭ*), material with which to make something; from *gasǔñ'skǔ* (or *gat-lǔñ'skǔ*), "I make it." The plant is also called *ihyâ'ga*. See number 126.
**Atsĭl'-tlǔñtǔ'tsĭ**—"Fire panther." A meteor or comet. See notes to number 9.
**Atsĭ'la-wa'ǐ'**—"Fire ——"; a mountain, sometimes known as Rattlesnake Knob, about two miles northeast of Cherokee, Swain County, North Carolina. See number 122.
**a'tsĭnă'**—cedar; compare Muscogee, *achena* or *auchenau*.
**A'tsĭnă'-k'ta'ǔñ**—"Hanging cedar place"; from *a'tsĭnă'*, cedar, and *k'taǔñ*, "where it (long) hangs down"; a Cherokee name for the old Taskigi town on the Little Tennessee River in Monroe County, Tennessee. See number 105.
**atsi'ra**—see *atsi'la*.
**Atsǔñ'stă'tĭ'yĭ** (abbreviated *Atsǔñ'stă'tĭ'*)—"Fire-light place" (compare *atsĭl-sǔñ'tĭ*), referring to the "fire-hunting" method of killing deer in the river at night. The proper form for the Chestatee River, near Dahlonega, in Lumpkin County, Georgia.
**Attakullakulla**—see *Ătă'-gǔl' kălǔ'*.
**ăwă'**—see *ămă'*.
**awâ'hĭlĭ**—eagle; particularly *Aquila chrysætus*, known as the "pretty-feathered eagle."
**a'wĭ'**—deer; also sometimes written and pronounced *ăhăwĭ'*; the name is sometimes applied to the large horned beetle, the "flying stag" mentioned by early writers.
**a'wĭ'-ahănu'lăhĭ**—goat; literally, "bearded deer."
**a'wĭ'-aktă'**—"deer eye"; the *Rudbeckia* or black-eyed Susan.
**a'wĭ'-ahyeli'skĭ**—"deer mocker"; the deer bleat, a type of whistle used by hunters to call the doe by imitating the cry of a fawn.

*a'wĭ'-e'gwă* (abbreviated *a'w-e'gwă*)—the elk, literally "great deer."
*a'wĭ'-unăde'na*—sheep; literally "woolly deer."
*A'wĭ' Usdi'*—"Little Deer"; the mythic chief of the Deer tribe. See number 15.
AX, ANNIE—see *Sadayĭ'*.
AX, JOHN—see *Ităgû'năhĭ*.
<term>Ayâ'sta</term>—"The Spoiler," from <term>tsiyâ'stihû</term>, "I spoil it"; compare <term>uyâ'ĭ</term>, bad. A prominent woman and informant on the East Cherokee reservation.
*aye'lĭ*—half, middle, in the middle.
AYRATE—see *e'lădĭ'*.
<term>Ayuhwa'sĭ</term>—the proper form of the name commonly written Hiwassee. It signifies a savanna or meadow and was applied to two (or more) former Cherokee settlements. The more important one, commonly distinguished as <term>Ayuhwa'sĭ Egwâ'hĭ</term> or Great Hiwassee, was on the north bank of the Hiwassee River at the current Savannah ford above Columbus, in Polk County, Tennessee. The other was farther up the same river, at the junction of Peachtree Creek, above Murphy, in Cherokee County, North Carolina. Lanman writes it as Owassa.
*A'yûn'inĭ'*—"Swimmer"; literally, "he is swimming," from *gayûnĭnĭ'*, "I am swimming." A principal priest and informant of the East Cherokee, who died in 1899.
*Ayûlsû'*—see *Dayûlsûn'yĭ*.

# MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19

*<term>dăgan'tû</term>*—“he makes it rain”; from *<term>aga'skă</term>*, “it is raining,” and *<term>aga'nă</term>*, “it has begun to rain”; a small variety of lizard whose cry is said to predict rain. It is also called *<term>a'niganti'skĭ</term>*, “they make it rain” (plural form), or “rain-maker.” See number 59.

*<term>dagûl'kû</term>*—the American white-fronted goose (*Anser albifrons gambeli*). The name may be an onomatopoeia. See number 6.

*<term>dăgû'nă</term>*—the freshwater mussel; also a variety of face pimples.

*<term>Dăgûnâ'hĭ</term>*—“Mussel place,” from *<term>dăgû'nă</term>*, mussel, and *<term>hĭ</term>*, locative suffix. The Muscle Shoals on the Tennessee River, in northwestern Alabama. It was sometimes also called simply *<term>Tsu'stănalûñ'yĭ</term>*, “Shoals place.” Compare *<term>U'stăna'lĭ</term>*.

*<term>Dăgû'năwe'lâhĭ</term>*—“Mussel-liver place,” from *<term>dăgû'nă</term>*, mussel, *<term>uwe'la</term>*, liver, and *<term>hĭ</term>*, locative suffix; the Cherokee name for the site of Nashville, Tennessee. No reason can now be given for the name.

DAHLONEGA—A town in Lumpkin County, Georgia, near which the first gold was mined. A mint was established there in 1838. The name is from the Cherokee *<term>dalâ'nige'i</term>*, yellow, from which comes *<term>ate'lă-dalâ'nige'i</term>*, “yellow money,” i.e., gold.

*<term>daksăwa'ihû</term>*—“he is shedding tears.”

*<term>dăkwă'</term>*—a mythical great fish; also the whale. See number 68.

*<term>Dăkwâ'ĭ</term>*—“*<term>Dăkwă'</term>* place,” from a tradition of a *<term>dăkwă'</term>* in the river at that point. A former Cherokee settlement, known to the traders as Toqua or Toco, on the Little Tennessee River, near the mouth of Toco Creek in Monroe County, Tennessee. See number 68. A similar name and tradition is attached to a spot on the French Broad River, about six miles above the Warm Springs, in Buncombe County, North Carolina. See number 122.

*<term>dakwa'nitlastestĭ</term>*—“I shall have them on my legs for garters”; from *<term>anitla'stĭ</term>* (plural *<term>dinitla'stĭ</term>*), garter; *d-*, initial plural; *<term>akwă</term>*, first-person particle; and *<term>estĭ</term>*, future suffix. See number 77.

*<term>da'likstă'</term>*—“vomiter,” from *<term>dagik'stihû'</term>*, “I am vomiting,” and *<term>dalikstă'</term>*, “he vomits” (habitually); the form is plural. The spreading adder (*Heterodon*), also sometimes called *<term>kwandăya'hû</term>*, a word of uncertain etymology.

*<term>Da'năgâstă</term>*—for *<term>Da'năwă-gâstă'yă</term>*, “Sharp-war,” i.e., “Eager-warrior”; a Cherokee woman’s name.

*<term>Da'nawa-(a)sa'tsûñ'yĭ</term>* “War ford,” from *<term>da'nawa</term>*, war, and *<term>asa'tsûñ'yĭ</term>*, a crossing-place or ford. A ford on the Cheowa River about three miles below Robbinsville, in Graham County, North Carolina. See number 122.

*<term>Danda'gănû'</term>*—“Two looking at each other,” from *<term>detsi'gănû'</term>*, “I am looking at him.” A former Cherokee settlement, commonly known as Lookout Mountain town, on Lookout Mountain Creek, near the present Trenton, Dade County, Georgia. One of the Chickamauga towns (see *<term>Tsĭ'kăma'gi</term>*), so called because of the appearance of the mountains facing each other across the Tennessee River at Chattanooga.

*<term>Da'si'giya'gĭ</term>*—an old masculine personal name of doubtful etymology, but commonly translated by the traders as “Shoe-boots,” possibly referring to some peculiar style of moccasin or legging. A chief known to the whites as Shoe-boots is mentioned in the Revolutionary records. Chief Lloyd Welch, of the eastern band, was known in the tribe as *<term>Da'si'giya'gĭ</term>*, and the same name is now used by the Eastern Cherokee as the equivalent of the name Lloyd.

*<term>Da'skwĭtûñ'yĭ</term>*—“Rafters place,” from *<term>daskwitûñ'ĭ</term>*, “rafters,” and *<term>yĭ</term>*, locative suffix. A former settlement on Tusquittee Creek, near Hayesville, in Clay County, North Carolina.

*<term>dasûñ'tălĭ</term>*—ant; *<term>dasûñ'tălĭ atatsûñ'skĭ</term>*, “stinging ant,” the large red cow-ant (*Myrmica*?), also sometimes called, because of its hard body-case, *<term>nûñ'yunu'wĭ</term>*, “stone-clad,” after the mythical monster. See number 67.

*<term>Datle'yăsta'ĭ</term>*—“Where they fell down,” a point on the Tuckasegee River, a short distance above Webster, in Jackson County, North Carolina. For the tradition, see number 122.

<vocab>dăgan'tû, dagûl'kû, dăgû'nă, Dăgûnâ'hĭ, Dăgû'năwe'lâhĭ, Dahlonega, daksăwa'ihû, dăkwă', Dăkwâ'ĭ, dakwa'nitlastestĭ, da'likstă', Da'năgâstă, Da'nawa-(a)sa'tsûñ'yĭ, Danda'gănû', Da'si'giya'gĭ, Da'skwĭtûñ'yĭ, dasûñ'tălĭ, Datle'yăsta'ĭ</vocab>

<header>MOONEY] GLOSSARY 515</header>

**<term>dâtsĭ</term>**—a traditional water monster. See number 122.

**<term>Dâtsĭ'yĭ</term>**—“Dâtsĭ place”; a location on the Little Tennessee River, near the junction of Eagle Creek, in Swain County, North Carolina. See number 122.

<margin>—</margin>**<term>Datsu'nalâsgûñ'yĭ</term>**—“where there are tracks or footprints,” from *<term>ulâ'sinûñ'yĭ</term>* or *<term>ulâsgûñ'yĭ</term>*, meaning "footprint." Track Rock Gap, near Blairsville, Georgia. It is also sometimes called **<term>De'găyelûñ'hă</term>**, “place of branded marks” (*<term>digăletânûñ'hĭ</term>*, branded or printed). See number 125.

**<term>dâ'yĭ</term>**—beaver.

**<term>Dayûlsûñ'yĭ</term>**—“Place where they cried,” a spot on the ridge at the head of the Tuckasegee River, in Jackson County, North Carolina; so called based on an old tradition. See number 80.

**<term>dâ'yuni'sĭ</term>**—“beaver's grandchild,” from *<term>dâ'yĭ</term>*, beaver, and *<term>uni'sĭ</term>*, a son's child of either sex (a daughter's child of either sex is *<term>uli'sĭ</term>*). This refers to the water beetle or mellow bug (*Dineutes discolor*).

<margin>—</margin>**<term>Degal'gûn'yĭ</term>**—a cairn, literally “where they are piled up”; a series of cairns on the south side of the Cheowa River, in Graham County, North Carolina. See number 122.

**<term>De'gătâ'gă</term>**—The Cherokee name of General Stand Watie and of a prominent early western chief known to white people as Takatoka. The word is derived from *<term>tsitâ'gă</term>*, “I am standing,” and *<term>da'nitâ'gă</term>*, “they are standing together”; it conveys the subtle meaning of two people standing together who are so closely united in sympathy that they form a single human body.

**<term>De'găyelûñ'hă</term>**—see **<term>Datsu'nalâsgûñ'yĭ</term>**.

**<term>detsânûñ'lĭ</term>**—an enclosure or piece of level ground cleared for ceremonial purposes; specifically applied to the Green-corn dance ground. The word has a plural form but cannot be definitely analyzed.

**<term>De'tsătă</term>**—a Cherokee sprite. See number 78.

<margin>—</margin>**<term>detsinu'lâhûñgû'</term>**—“I tried, but failed.”

<margin>—</margin>**<term>Dida'lâskĭ'yĭ</term>**—“Showering place.” In the story (number 17), the name is understood to mean “the place where it rains fire.” However, it literally signifies the place where it showers, or comes down and lodges upon something animate; it has no definite reference to fire (*<term>atsi'la</term>*) or rain (*<term>agăskă</term>*, “it is raining”). The term *<term>degă'lâskû'</term>* means “they are showering down and lodging upon him.”

<margin>—</margin>**<term>Dida'skastĭ'yĭ</term>**—“Where they were afraid of each other.” A spot on the Little Tennessee River, near the mouth of Alarka Creek, in Swain County, North Carolina. See number 122.

**<term>diga'gwănĭ'</term>**—the mud-hen or didapper (*Gallinula galeata*). The name is a plural form and implies being “lame” or “crippled in the legs” (compare *<term>detsi'nigwă'nă</term>*, “I am kneeling”), likely because of the bouncing motion of the bird when it is in the water. It is also the name of a dance.

**<term>Diga'kati'yĭ</term>**—see **<term>Gakati'yĭ</term>**.

**<term>di'gălûñgûñ'yĭ</term>**—“where it rises, or comes up”; the east. The sacred term is **<term>Nûñdâ'yĭ</term>**, see that entry.

**<term>digălûñ'lătiyûñ</term>**—a height, one of a series, from *<term>galûñ'lătĭ</term>*, “above.” See number 1.

**<term>Digălu'yâtûñ'yĭ</term>**—“Where it is gashed (with hatchets)”; from *<term>tsilu'yû</term>*, “I am cutting (with a chopping stroke),” *<term>di</term>*, a plural prefix, and *<term>yĭ</term>*, a locative suffix. The Chopped Oak, formerly located east of Clarkesville, Georgia. See number 125.

**<term>Digăne'skĭ</term>**—“He picks them up” (habitually), from *<term>tsĭne'û</term>*, “I am picking it up.” A Cherokee Union soldier in the Civil War. See page 171.

**<term>digi'găge'i</term>**—the plural of *<term>gi'găge'i</term>*, red.

**<term>digû'lănăhi'ta</term>**—for *<term>digû'lĭ-anăhi'ta</term>*, “having long ears” or “long-eared”; from *<term>gû'lĕ</term>*, “ear,” and *<term>gúnahĭ'ta</term>*, “long.”

**<term>Dihyûñ'dulâ'</term>**—“Sheaths” or “Scabbards”; the singular form is *<term>ahyûñ'dulâ'</term>*, “a gun sheath” or other scabbard. This is likely the correct form of a name that appears in Revolutionary documents as “Untoola” or “Gun Rod.”
