<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Cherokee terms and place names, focusing on entries starting with the letter “D.” This section includes botanical and zoological names, historical figures, and geographic locations in the ancestral Cherokee territories of North Carolina, Georgia, and South Carolina.</meta>

<header>MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19</header>

<term>diktä́'</term>—plural of *aktä́'*, eye.
<term>dĭlâ'</term>—skunk.
<term>dĭlsta'ya'tĭ̄</term>—“scissors”; the water-spider (*Dolomedes*).
<term>dĭnda'skwate'skĭ</term>—the violet; the name means, “they pull each other's heads off.”
<term>dĭne'tlănă</term>—the creation.
<term>dĭ'nûskĭ</term>—“the breeder”; a variety of smilax brier. See number 126.
<term>Disgâ'gĭstĭ'yĭ</term>—“Where they gnaw”; a place on the Cheowa River, in Graham County, North Carolina. See number 122.
<term>diskwa'nĭ</term>—“chestnut bread,” that is, a variety of bread that has chestnuts mixed with it. This is also the Cherokee name of James Blythe, an interpreter and agency clerk.
<term>dĭstai'yĭ</term>—“they are strong,” the plural of *astai'yĭ*, “strong or tough.” The *Tephrosia*, also known as devil's-shoestring. See number 126.
<term>dĭsta'stĭ</term>—a mill (generic term).
<term>dita'stayeskĭ</term>—“a barber,” literally “one who cuts things” (as with scissors), from *tsĭsta'yû*, “I cut” (as with scissors). The cricket (*tăla'tŭ*) is sometimes called by this name. See number 59.
<term>Diwa'lĭ</term>—“Bowl,” a prominent chief of the western Cherokee, known to the white people as The Bowl, or Colonel Bowles; he was killed by the Texans in 1839. The chief mentioned on page 100 may have been another person with the same name.
<term>dĭyâ'hălĭ</term> (or *duyâ'hălĭ*)—the alligator lizard (*Sceloporue undulatus*). See number 59.
<term>Dĭyâ'hălĭ'yĭ</term>—“Lizard place,” from *dĭyâ'hălĭ*, lizard, and *yĭ*, a locative suffix. Joanna Bald, a mountain at the head of the Valley River, on the border between Cherokee and Graham Counties, North Carolina. For the tradition, see number 122; also number 59.
<term>DOUBLE-HEAD</term>—see <term>Tăl-tsu'skă'</term>.
<term>DRAGGING-CANOE</term>—see <term>Tsĭ'yu-gûnsĭ'nĭ</term>.
<term>Dudûñ'leksûñ'yĭ</term>—“Where its legs were broken off”; a place on the Tuckasegee River, a few miles above Webster, in Jackson County, North Carolina. See number 122.
<term>Dugĭlu'yĭ</term> (abbreviated as *Dugĭlu'*, and commonly written as Tugaloo, or sometimes Toogelah or Toogoola)—a name occurring in several places in the old Cherokee country. The best known is the Tugaloo River, named after a former Cherokee settlement of that name situated at the junction of Toccoa Creek and the main stream in Habersham County, Georgia. The word has an uncertain etymology, but seems to refer to a place at the forks of a stream.
<term>Dûksa'ĭ</term>, <term>Dûkw'sa'ĭ</term>—The correct form of the name commonly written as Toxaway, applied to a former Cherokee settlement in South Carolina and the creek upon which it stood. This is an extreme head-stream of the Keowee River, with its source in Jackson County, North Carolina. The meaning of the name has been lost, although it has been wrongly interpreted to mean “Place of shedding tears.” See number 123.
<term>Dulastûñ'yĭ</term>—“Potsherd place.” A former Cherokee settlement on the Nottely River in Cherokee County, North Carolina. See number 122.
<term>dule'tsĭ'</term>—“kernels,” referring to a goitrous swelling on the throat.
<term>dulu'sĭ</term>—a variety of frog found at the headwaters of the Savannah River. See number 125.
<term>Duniya'ta'lûñ'yĭ</term>—“Where there are shelves, or flat places,” from *aya'te'nĭ*, meaning flat, from which *da'ya'tana'lûñ'i'*, meaning a shelf, and *yĭ'*, the locative suffix. This is a gap on the Great Smoky range, near Clingman's Dome, in Swain County, North Carolina. See the notes for number 100.
<term>Dunidû'lalûñ'yĭ</term>—“Where they made arrows”; a place on Straight Creek, a headstream of the Oconaluftee River, in Swain County, North Carolina. See number 122.
<term>Dunĭ'skwa'lgûñ'ĭ</term>—the double peak known as the Chimney Tops in the Great Smoky Mountains, located near the head of Deep Creek in Swain County, North Carolina. On the north side is the pass known as Indian Gap. The name signifies a “forked antler,” from *uskwa'lgû*, antler, but it indicates that the antler is still attached, as if the deer itself were hidden below.

# MOONEY] GLOSSARY 517

<term>Du'stăyalūñ'yĭ</term>—“Where it made a noise like thunder or shooting,” apparently referring to a lightning stroke (<term>detsistăya'hihū</term>, “I make a shooting, or thundering, noise,” might be a first-person form used by the personified Thunder-god); a spot on the Hiwassee River, near the junction of Shooting Creek, near Hayesville, in Clay County, North Carolina. A former settlement along the creek bore the same name. See number 79.
<term>du'stū</term>—a species of frog, appearing very early in spring; the name is intended as an onomatopoeia. It is the correct form of the name of the chief noted by McKenney and Hall as “Tooantuh or Spring Frog.”
<term>DUTCH</term>—see <term>Tătsĭ'</term>.
<term>duwě'gă</term>—the spring lizard. See number 59.

<term>EAGLE DANCE</term>—see <term>Tsugidû'lĭ' Ûlsgĭ'stĭ</term>.
<term>EASTINAULEE</term>—see <term>U'stăna'lĭ</term>.
<term>ECHOEE</term>—see <term>Itsĕ'yĭ</term>.
<term>ECHOTA</term>—see <term>Itsâ'tĭ</term>.
<term>Edâ'hĭ</term>—“He goes about” (habitually); a masculine name.
<term>Echota, New</term>—see <term>Gănsâ'gĭ</term>.
<term>edâ'tă</term>—my father (Upper dialect); the Middle and Lower dialect form is <term>agidâ'tă</term>.
<term>edu'tū</term>—my maternal grandfather (Upper dialect); the Middle and Lower dialect form is <term>agidu'tū</term>; compare <term>eni'sĭ</term>.
<term>e'gwa</term>—great; compare <term>u'tănû</term>.
<term>egwâ'nĭ</term>—river.
<term>Egwânul'tĭ</term>—“By the river,” from <term>egwâ'nĭ</term>, river, and <term>nu'lătĭ</term> or <term>nul'tĭ</term>, near, beside. The proper form of Oconaluftee, the name of the river flowing through the East Cherokee reservation in Swain and Jackson counties, North Carolina. The Cherokee town, “Oconalufte,” mentioned by Bartram as existing about 1775, was probably on the lower course of the river at the present Birdtown, on the reservation, where there was formerly a significant mound.
<term>elă</term>—earth, ground.
<term>e'lădĭ'</term>—low, below; in the Lower dialect <term>e'rădĭ'</term>, from which comes the Ayrate or Lower Cherokee of Adair as distinguished from the Ottare (<term>â'tărĭ</term>, <term>â'tălĭ</term>) or Upper Cherokee.
<term>elanti</term>—a song form for <term>e'lădĭ'</term>, <term>q. v.</term>
<term>Elătse'yĭ</term> (abbreviated <term>Elătse'</term>)—possibly “Green (Verdant) earth,” from <term>elă</term>, earth, and <term>itse'yĭ</term>, green, from fresh-springing vegetation. The name of several former Cherokee settlements, commonly known to the whites as Ellijay, Elejoy, or Allagae. One of these was upon the headwaters of the Keowee River in South Carolina; another was on Ellijay Creek of the Little Tennessee River, near the present Franklin, in Macon County, North Carolina; another was near the present Ellijay in Gilmer County, Georgia; and still another was on Ellejoy Creek of the Little River near the present Maryville, in Blount County, Tennessee.
<term>Elăwâ'diyĭ</term> (abbreviated <term>Elăwâ'dĭ</term>)—“Red-earth place” from <term>elă</term>, earth, <term>wâdĭ</term>, brown-red or red paint, and <term>yĭ</term>, the locative suffix. 1. The Cherokee name of the Yellow-hill settlement, now officially known as Cherokee, the post office and agency headquarters for the East Cherokee, on the Oconaluftee River in Swain County, North Carolina. 2. A former council ground, known in history as Red Clay, at the site of the present village of that name in Whitfield County, Georgia, adjoining the Tennessee line.
<term>ELLIJAY</term>—see <term>Elătse'yĭ</term>.
<term>eni'sĭ</term>—my paternal grandfather (Upper dialect); the Middle and Lower dialect form is <term>agini'sĭ</term>. Compare <term>edu'tū</term>.
<term>ESKAQUA</term>—see <term>ISKAGUA</term>.
<term>ESTANAULA, ESTINAULA</term>—see <term>U'stăna'lĭ</term>.

# MOONEY] GLOSSARY 518

<term>Ĕtăwa'hă-tsistatla'skĭ</term>—“Deadwood-lighter,” a traditional Cherokee conjurer. See entry number 100.
<term>e'tĭ</term>, or <term>etĭ</term>—old, or a long time ago.
<term>Etowah</term>—see <term>I'tăwă'</term>.
<term>Etsaiyĭ'</term>—see <term>Ûñtsaiyĭ'</term>.
<term>etsĭ'</term>—my mother (Upper dialect); the Middle and Lower dialect form is <term>agitsĭ'</term>.
<term>EUHARLEE</term>—see <term>Yuha'lĭ</term>.

**FEATHER DANCE**—see <term>Tsugidû'lĭ</term>, <term>Ûlsgi'stĭ</term>.
**FIGHTING-TOWN**—see <term>Walâs'-unûlsti'yĭ</term>.
**FLAX-TOTER**—see <term>Tâle'danigi'skĭ</term>.
**FLYING-SQUIRREL**—see <term>Kâ'lahû'</term>.
**FRENCH BROAD**—see <term>Unta'kiyasti'yĭ</term>.
**FROGTOWN**—see <term>Walâsi'yĭ</term>.

<term>Gadalu'lû</term>—the proper name of the mountain known to white people as Yonah (from <term>yânû</term>, “bear”), or the upper Chattahoochee River, in White County, Georgia. The name has no connection with Tallulah (see <term>Tâlulû'</term>) and cannot be translated.
<term>Gadalu'tsĭ</term>—in the corrupted form of “Cataluchee,” this appears on the map as the name of a peak, or rather a ridge, on the line between Swain and Haywood counties in North Carolina, and of a creek running down on the Haywood side into Big Pigeon River. It is properly the name of the ridge only and seems to refer to a “fringe standing erect,” apparently because of the appearance of the timber growing in streaks along the side of the mountain; from <term>wadâlu'yătâ</term>, fringe, and <term>gadû'tû</term>, “standing up in a row or series.”
<term>găhăwĭ'sita</term>—parched corn; spelled incorrectly as *wissactaw* by Hawkins. See the note under entry number 83.
<term>Gahûtĭ</term> (<term>Gahû'tâ</term> and <term>Gwahû'tĭ</term> in dialect forms)—Cohutta Mountain, in Murray County, Georgia. The name comes from <term>gahûtâ'yĭ</term>, “a shed roof supported on poles,” and refers to an imagined resemblance in the summit.
<term>Gakătĭ'yĭ</term>—“Place of setting free”; sometimes spoken in the plural form, <term>Diga'kătĭ'yĭ</term>, “Place of setting them free.” A point on the Tuckasegee River about three miles above Bryson City, in Swain County, North Carolina. See entry number 122.
<term>gaktûñ'ta</term>—an injunction, command, or rule, especially a prohibition or ceremonial taboo. <term>Tsiga'te'gû</term>, “I am observing an injunction or taboo”; <term>adakte'gĭ</term>, “he is under taboo regulations.”
<term>Gălăgĭ'na</term>—a male deer (buck) or turkey (gobbler); in the first sense, the name is also sometimes used for the large horned beetle (<term>Dynastes tityus?</term>). This was the Indian name of Elias Boudinot, the first Cherokee editor. See page 111.
<term>gălĭ'sgisidâ'hû</term>—I am dancing about; from <term>gălĭ'sgiâ'</term>, “I am dancing,” and <term>edâ'hû'</term>, “I am going about.”
<term>gălûñkwĭ'ti'yu</term>—honored, sacred; used in the Bible to mean holy or hallowed.
<term>gălûñ'lătĭ</term>—above, or on high.
<term>găne'ga</term>—skin.
<term>ganidawâ'skĭ</term>—the campion, catchfly, or “rattlesnake’s master” (*Silene stellata*); the name means “it disjoints itself,” from <term>ganidawâskû'</term>, “it is unjointing itself,” because of the peculiar way the dried stalk breaks off at the joints.
<term>Gănsâ'gĭ</term> (or <term>Gănsâgiyĭ</term>)—the name of several former settlements in the old Cherokee country; its meaning cannot be analyzed. One town of this name was on the Tuckasegee River, a short distance above the present Webster in Jackson County, North Carolina; another was on the lower part of Canasauga Creek in McMinn County, Tennessee; a third was at the junction of the Conasauga and Coosawatee rivers, where the Cherokee capital, New Echota, was later located in Gordon

# MOONEY] GLOSSARY 519

County, Georgia; a fourth, mentioned in the De Soto narratives as Canasoga or Canasagua, was located in 1540 on the upper Chattahoochee River, possibly in the neighborhood of Kenesaw Mountain, Georgia (see page 197).

**<term>Gänsa'ti'yǐ</term>**—“Robbing place,” from *tsina'sahûñskû'*, “I am robbing him.” Vengeance Creek of Valley River, in Cherokee County, North Carolina. The name Vengeance was originally a white man's nickname for an old Cherokee woman of forbidding appearance who lived there before the Removal. See number 122.

**<term>Gänsĕ'tĭ</term>**—a rattle; as the Cherokee dance rattle is made from a gourd, the masculine name <term>Gänsĕ'tĭ</term> is usually rendered by the whites as “Rattling-gourd.”

**<term>gatayûstĭ</term>**—the wheel-and-stick game of the southern tribes, incorrectly called *net-tecawaw* by Timberlake. See the note under number 3.

**<term>Gâtegwâ'</term>**—for <term>Gâtegwâ'hĭ</term>, possibly a contraction of *Igât(ĭ)-egwâ'hĭ*, “Great-swamp (thicket) place.” A high peak southeast of Franklin, Macon County, North Carolina, and perhaps identical to Fodderstack Mountain. See number 75.

**<term>ga'tsû</term>**—see <term>hatlû'</term>.

**<term>Gatu'gitse'yǐ</term>** (abbreviated **<term>Gatu'gitse'</term>**)—“New-settlement place,” from <term>gatu'gĭ</term> or <term>sgatu'gĭ</term> (town, settlement), *itse'hĭ* (new, especially applied to new vegetation), and *yǐ* (the locative). A former settlement on Cartoogaja Creek of Little Tennessee River, above Franklin, in Macon County, North Carolina.

**<term>Gatutĭ'yĭ</term>**—“Town-building place” or “Settlement place,” from <term>gatu'gĭ</term> (a settlement) and *yǐ* (locative). A place on Santeetla Creek, near Robbinsville, in Graham County, North Carolina. See number 122.

**<term>Gatûñ'lti'yǐ</term>**—“Hemp place,” from <term>gatûñ'lâtĭ</term> (“wild hemp,” *Apocynum cannabinum*), and *yǐ* (locative). A former Cherokee settlement, commonly known as Hemptown, on the creek of the same name, near Morganton, in Fannin County, Georgia.

**<term>Gatûñ'wa'lĭ</term>**—a noted western Cherokee around 1842, known to the whites as “Hard-mush” or “Big-mush.” <term>Gatûñ'wa'lĭ</term>, from *ga'tlû'* (“bread”) and *ûñwa'lĭ* (“made into balls or lumps”), is a sort of mush of parched cornmeal, made very thick so that it can be dipped out in lumps almost of the consistency of bread.

**<term>ge'ǐ</term>**—downstream, down the road, with the current; <term>tsâ'gĭ</term> (upstream).

**<term>gese'ǐ</term>**—was; a separate word which, when used after the verb in the present tense, makes it past tense without a change of form; in the form *hǐ'gese'ǐ*, it usually accompanies an emphatic repetition.

**<term>Ge'yăgu'ga</term>** (for <term>Age'hyă-guga</term>?)—a ritualistic name for the moon (<term>nûñ'dâ'</term>); it cannot be analyzed, but seems to contain the word *age'hyă* (“woman”). See also <term>nûñ'dâ'</term>.

**<term>gigă</term>**—blood; compare <term>gi'găge'ǐ</term> (red).

**<term>gi'gă-danegi'skĭ</term>**—“blood taker,” from <term>gigă</term> (blood) and <term>ada'negi'skĭ</term> (“one who takes liquids”), from *tsi'negiâ'* (“I am taking it [liquid]”). Another name for the <term>tsâne'nĭ</term> or scorpion lizard. See number 59.

**<term>gi'găge'ǐ</term>**—red, bright red, scarlet; the brown-red of certain animals and clays is distinguished as <term>wâ'dige'ǐ</term>.

**<term>gi'gă-tsuha'lĭ</term>**—“bloody-mouth,” literally “having blood on the corners of his mouth”; from <term>gi'ga</term> (blood) and *tsuhânûñsi'yǐ* (the corners of the mouth; *ăha'lĭ*, his mouth). A large lizard, probably the <term>Pleistodon</term>. See number 59.

**<term>gǐ'lǐ'</term>**—dog; in the Lower dialect, *gǐ'rǐ'*.

**<term>Gǐ'lǐ'-dĭnĕhûñ'yĭ</term>**—“Where the dogs live,” from <term>gǐ'lǐ'</term> (dog), *dĭnĕhû'* (“they dwell”; *ĕhû'*, “I dwell”), and *yǐ* (locative). A place on Oconaluftee River, a short distance above Cherokee, in Swain County, North Carolina. See number 122.

**<term>Gǐ'lǐ'-utsûñ'stănûñ'yĭ</term>**—“Where the dog ran,” from <term>gǐ'lǐ'</term> (dog) and *utsûñ'stănûñ'yĭ* (“footprints made by an animal running”); the Milky Way. See number 11.

**<term>ginûntĭ</term>**—a song form for <term>ginû'tĭ'</term>, “to lay him (animate object) upon the ground.” See number 75.

# MOONEY] GLOSSARY 520

*gi ri'*—see *gi li'*.

**<term>Gisehûñ'yĭ</term>**—“Where the female lives,” from *agi'sĭ* (female) and *yĭ* (the locative). A place on the Tuckasegee River, a short distance above Bryson City, Swain County, North Carolina. See number 122.

*gitlû'*—hair (Upper dialect); in the Middle and Lower dialects, *gitsû'*.

*gitsû'*—see *gitlû'*.

**<term>Glass, The</term>**—see *Ta'gwădihi'*.

**<term>Gohoma</term>**—A Lower Cherokee chief in 1684; the form cannot be identified. See page 31.

**<term>Going-snake</term>**—see *I'nădûna'ĭ*.

**<term>Gorhaleke</term>**—A Lower Cherokee chief in 1684; the form cannot be identified. See page 31.

**<term>Great Island</term>**—see *Ămăyĕ'l-e'gwa*.

**<term>Gregory Bald</term>**—see *Tsistu'yĭ*.

**<term>Guachoule</term>**—see **<term>Guaxule</term>**.

**<term>Guaquili</term>** (*Wakili*)—a town in the Cherokee country visited by De Soto in 1540, and again in 1567 by Pardo, who calls it Aguaquiri (see pages 25 and 28). The name may be connected to *wa-guli'* (“whippoorwill”) or to *u-wá'gĭli* (“foam”).

**<term>Guasula</term>**—see **<term>Guaxule</term>**.

**<term>Guasili</term>**—see **<term>Guaxule</term>**.

**<term>Guaxule</term>**—a town in the Cherokee country visited by De Soto in 1540; spelled in various ways in the narratives as Guasili, Guachoule, Guasula, Guaxule, Quaxule, etc. It was probably located near the Nacoochee mound in White County, Georgia. It has been suggested that the Spaniards may have changed the Indian name to resemble that of a town in Spain. See pages 26 and 194.

*gû'daye'wû'*—“I have sewn myself together”; “I am sewing,” *tsiye'wiă'*; “I am sewing myself together,” *gûdayewiû*. See number 31.

*gûgwĕ'* (or *g'gwĕ'*)—the quail or partridge; the name is an onomatopoeia.

*gûgwĕ'-ulasu'la*—“partridge moccasin,” from *gûgwĕ'* or *g'gwĕ'* (partridge) and *ulasula* (moccasin or shoe); the lady’s slipper (*Cypripedium*).

**<term>Gûlâhĭ'yĭ</term>** (abbreviated **<term>Gûlâhĭ'</term>**, or **<term>Gûrâhĭ'</term>** in the Lower dialect)—“Gûlâhĭ place,” so named for an unidentified spring plant eaten as a salad by the Cherokee. The name of two or more places in the old Cherokee country; one near Currahee Mountain in Habersham County, Georgia, and the other on the Cullowhee River, an upper branch of the Tuckasegee in Jackson County, North Carolina. Currahee Dick was a notable chief around the year 1820.

**<term>Gû'lani'yĭ</term>**—a Cherokee and Natchez settlement formerly located near the junction of Brass-town Creek with the Hiwassee River, a short distance above Murphy in Cherokee County, North Carolina. The origin of the word is uncertain.

*gulĕ'*—acorn.

*gulĕ'-diska'nihĭ'*—the turtle-dove; literally, “it cries, or mourns, for acorns,” from *gulĕ'* (acorn) and *diska'nihĭ'* (“it cries for them”) (*di-* is the plural prefix, *-hi* is the habitual suffix). The turtle-dove feeds on acorns, and its cry somewhat resembles the name *gulĕ'*.

*gûlĕ'gĭ*—“climber,” from *tsilahĭ'* (“I climb”; second person, *hĭ'lahĭ'*; third person, *gûlahĭ'*); the blacksnake (*Bascanion constrictor*).

**<term>Gû'kăla'skĭ</term>**—An earlier name for *Tsunu'lăhûñ'skĭ*, which see.

*gûl'kwâ'gĭ*—seven; also the mole-cricket (*Gryllotalpa*). See number 59.

*gûl'kwâ'gine*—(seventh); from *gûl'kwâ'gĭ* (seven).

**<term>Gûlsădihĭ'</term>** (or **<term>Gûltsădihĭ'</term>**?)—a masculine personal name of uncertain origin.

**<term>Gumlog</term>**—see *Tsilalu'hĭ*.

*gûnăhi'ta*—long.

# MOONEY] GLOSSARY 521

**<term>Gû'năhitûn'yĭ</term>**—“Long place” (that is, Long Valley), from *gûnăhita* (long) and *yĭ* (the locative). A former settlement known to white settlers as Valleytown, where the town of the same name now stands on the Valley River in Cherokee County, North Carolina. The various settlements on the Valley River and the adjacent part of the Hiwassee were known collectively as the “Valley towns.”

**<term>Gûn'-dĭ'gaduhûn'yĭ</term>** (abbreviated **<term>Gûn'-dĭgadu'hûn</term>**)—“Turkey settlement” (*gû'nă*, turkey), so named after the chief, Turkey or Little Turkey. A former settlement known to white settlers as Turkeytown, located on the west bank of the Coosa River opposite the present-day Center in Cherokee County, Alabama.

**<term>gû'nĭ'</term>**—arrow. Compare to the Seneca word *ga'na'*.

**<term>gûn'năge'ĭ</term>** (or **<term>gûn'năge</term>**)—black.

**<term>Gûûnĕ'hĭ</term>**—see **<term>Nûnnĕ'hĭ</term>**.

**<term>Gûnškălĭ'skĭ</term>**—a masculine personal name of uncertain etymology.

**GUNTERS LANDING, GUNTERSVILLE**—see **<term>Ku'să-Nûnnâ'hĭ</term>**.

**<term>Gûn-tsuskwa'lĭ</term>**—“Short arrows,” from *gûnĭ'* (arrow) and *tsuskwa'lĭ* (the plural of *uskwa'lĭ*, short); a traditional western tribe. See number 105.

**<term>Gûnûn'da'le'gĭ</term>**—see **<term>Nûnnâ'hĭ-dihĭ'</term>**.

**<term>Gustĭ'</term>**—a traditional Cherokee settlement on the Tennessee River near Kingston, Roane County, Tennessee. See number 79. The name cannot be analyzed. Wafford thought it was a Cherokee attempt at “Kingston,” but it seems instead to be aboriginal.

**<term>Gu'wisguwĭ'</term>**—The Cherokee name for Chief John Ross and for the district named in his honor, commonly spelled Cooweescoowee. It is properly an onomatopoeia for a large bird said to have been seen in the past at rare intervals in the old Cherokee country; it accompanied the migratory wild geese and was described as resembling a large snipe with yellow legs and unwebbed feet. In his boyhood, John Ross was known as *Tsan'-usdĭ'*, “Little John.”

**<term>Gwal'gâ'hĭ</term>**—“Frog place,” from *gwal'gû* (a variety of frog) and *hĭ* (the locative). A place on the Hiwassee River, just above the junction of Peachtree Creek near Murphy in Cherokee County, North Carolina; around 1755, this was the site of a village of refugee Natchez and was later the site of a Baptist mission.

**<term>gwehe'ĭ</term>**—a cricket's cry. See number 119.

**ha!**—an introductory exclamation intended to attract attention or add emphasis; roughly equivalent to *Here!* or *Now!*

**ha'-ma'ma'**—a song term compounded of *ha!* (an introductory exclamation) and *mămă'* (a word which has no analysis but is used when speaking to young children to mean “let me carry you on my back”). See number 117.

**HANGING-MAW**—see **<term>Uskwâ'lĭ-gû'tă</term>**.

**ha'nia-lĭl'-lĭl'**—a meaningless dance refrain. See number 24.

**HARD-MUSH**—see **<term>Gatûn'wâ'lĭ</term>**.

— **ha'suyak'**—a song form for *hasuya'gĭ'* (“[you] pick it out,” imperative); “I pick it out, or select it” is *ga'suyăgiû'*; second person is *ha'suyăgiû'*. See number 19.

— **ha'tlû**—a dialect form of *ga'tsû*, meaning “where?” (interrogative).

**ha'wiye'ĕhĭ', ha'wiye'-hyuwe'**—meaningless dance refrains. See numbers 32 and 118.

**hayû'**—an emphatic affirmative, roughly equivalent to “Yes, sir!” See number 115.

**hayuya'haniwâ'**—a meaningless refrain in one of the bear songs. See number 75.

**he-e!**—a meaningless song introduction.

**HEMP-CARRIER**—see **<term>Tâle'danigĭ'skĭ</term>**.

**HEMPTOWN**—see **<term>Gatûntlĭ'yĭ</term>**.

**hi!**—a meaningless dance exclamation.

— **hi'gina'lĭĭ**—“(you are) my friend”; *agina'lĭĭ* means “(he is) my friend.” In the jargon of white men, this is *canaly*.

**<term>i'hya</term>**—the cane reed (*Arundinaria*) of the Gulf states, used by the Indians for blowguns, fishing rods, and basketry.

**<term>i'nǎdû'</term>**—snake.

**<term>I'nǎdû-na'ĭ</term>**—“Going-snake,” a Cherokee chief prominent about eighty years ago. The name properly signifies that the person is “going along in company with a snake,” the verbal part being from the irregular verb **<term>asta'ĭ</term>**, “I am going along with him.” The name has been given to a district of the present Cherokee Nation.

**<term>i'nǎgě'hĭ</term>**—dwelling in the wilderness, an inhabitant of the wilderness; from **<term>i'nǎgě'ĭ</term>**, “wilderness,” and **<term>ĕhĭ</term>**, the habitual present form of **<term>ĕhû</term>**, “he is dwelling”; **<term>gĕ'û</term>**, “I am dwelling.”

**<term>I'nǎgě-utǎsûñ'hĭ</term>**—“He who grew up in the wilderness,” i.e. “He who grew up wild”; from **<term>i'nǎgě'ĭ</term>**, “wilderness, unoccupied timber land,” and **<term>utǎsûñ'hĭ</term>**, the third person perfect of the irregular verb **<term>ga'tûñskû'</term>**, “I am growing up.”

**<term>Inâ'lĭ</term>**—Black-fox; the common red fox is **<term>tsu'lǎ</term>** (in Muscogee, *chula*). Black-fox was the principal chief of the Cherokee Nation in 1810. See page 86.

**ISKAGUA**—“Iskagua or Clear Sky, formerly Nenetooyah or the Bloody-Fellow.” The name appears this way in a document of 1791 as that of a Cherokee chief frequently mentioned about that period under the name of “the Bloody Fellow.” In one treaty it is given as “Eskaqua or Bloody Fellow.” Both forms and etymologies are doubtful, as neither form seems to have any reference either to “sky” (*gălûñ'lǎhĭ*) or “blood” (*gi'ga*). The first may be intended for **<term>Ik-e'gwa</term>**, “Great-day.” See page 69.

**Istanare**—see **<term>U'stǎna'lĭ</term>**.

**<term>I'sû'nigû</term>**—an important Cherokee settlement, commonly known to the whites as Seneca, formerly on the Keowee River, near the mouth of Conneross Creek, in Oconee County, South Carolina. Hopewell, the country seat of General Pickens, where the famous treaty was made, was near it on the east side of the river. The word cannot be translated, but has no connection with the tribal name, Seneca.

**<term>Itǎgû'nǎhĭ</term>**—the Cherokee name of John Ax.

**<term>I'tǎwă'</term>**—The name of one or more Cherokee settlements. One, which existed until the Removal in 1838, was upon the Etowah River, near the present Hightower, in Forsyth County, Georgia. Another may have been on Hightower Creek of

<header>MOONEY] GLOSSARY</header>

Hiwassee River in Towns County, Georgia. The name, commonly written Etowah and corrupted to Hightower, cannot be translated and seems not to be of Cherokee origin. A town called Itaba, Ytaua, or Ytava in the De Soto chronicles existed in 1540 among the Creeks, apparently on the Alabama River.

**<term>Itsâ'tĭ</term>**—commonly spelled Echota, Chota, Chote, Choquata (a misprint), etc.; a name occurring in several places in the old Cherokee country: the meaning is lost. The most important settlement of this name, frequently distinguished as Great Echota, was on the south side of the Little Tennessee River a short distance below Citico Creek in Monroe County, Tennessee. It was the ancient capital and sacred "peace town" of the Nation. Little Echota was on Sautee (that is, ***<term>Itsâ'tĭ</term>***) Creek, a head stream of the Chattahoochee, west of Clarkesville, Georgia. New Echota, the capital of the Nation for some years before the Removal, was established at a spot originally known as ***<term>Gânsâ'gĭ</term>*** (q. v.) at the junction of the Oostanaula and Conasauga rivers, in Gordon County, Georgia. It was sometimes called Newtown. The old Macedonia mission on Soco Creek, of the North Carolina reservation, is also known as Itsâ'tĭ to the Cherokee, as was also the great Nacoochee mound. See ***<term>Nagu'tsĭ'</term>***.

**<term>Itse'yĭ</term>**—“New green place” or “Place of fresh green,” from *itse'hĭ*, “green or unripe vegetation,” and *yĭ*, the locative; applied more particularly to a tract of ground made green by fresh-springing vegetation, after having been cleared of timber or burned over. A name occurring in several places in the old Cherokee country, variously written as Echia, Echoee, Etchowee, and sometimes also falsely rendered as “Brasstown,” from a confusion of ***<term>Itse'yĭ</term>*** with ***<term>ûntsaiyĭ'</term>***, “brass.” One settlement of this name was upon Brasstown Creek of the Tugaloo River, in Oconee County, South Carolina; another was on the Little Tennessee River near the present Franklin, Macon County, North Carolina, and probably about the junction of Cartoogaja (***<term>Gatug-itse'yĭ</term>***) Creek; a third, known to the whites as Brasstown, was on upper Brasstown Creek of the Hiwassee River, in Towns County, Georgia. In Cherokee, as in most other Indian languages, no clear distinction is made between green and blue (***<term>sa'ka'nige'ĭ</term>***).

**<term>i'ya</term>**—pumpkin.

**<term>iya'-iyu'stĭ</term>**—“like a pumpkin,” from *iya* and *iyu'stĭ*, like.

**<term>iya'-tâwi'skage</term>**—“of pumpkin smoothness,” from ***<term>i'ya</term>***, pumpkin, and ***<term>tâwi'skage</term>***, smooth.

**<term>Kâ'lahû'</term>**—“All-bones,” from *kâ'lû*, bone. A former chief of the East Cherokee, also known in the tribe as ***<term>Sawânu'gĭ</term>*** (Shawano), and to the whites as Sawnook or Flying-squirrel.

<header>MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19]</header>

***<term>Kâ'lănû</term>***—“The Raven”; the name was used as a war title in the tribe and appears in old documents as Corani (Lower dialect, *Kâ'rănû*), Colanneh, Colona, etc. It is the Cherokee name for General Samuel Houston or for any person named Houston.

***<term>Kâ'lănû Ahyeli'skĭ</term>***—the Raven Mocker. See number 120.

***<term>Kâ'lănûñ'yĭ</term>***—“Raven place,” from *kâ'lănû*, raven, and *yĭ*, the locative. The proper name of the Big Cove settlement on the East Cherokee reservation, Swain County, North Carolina, sometimes also called Raventown.

***<term>kalâs'-gŭnăhi'ta</term>***—“long-hams” (*gŭnăhi'ta*, “long”); a variety of bear. See number 15.

***<term>Kâl-detsi'yûñyĭ</term>***—“Where the bones are,” from *kâ'lû*, bone, and *detsĭ'yûñyĭ*, “where (*yĭ*) they (*de*—plural prefix) are lying.” A spot near the junction of East Buffalo Creek with Cheowa River, in Graham County, North Carolina. See number 122.

***<term>kăma'mă</term>***—butterfly.

***<term>kăma'mă u'tanû</term>***—elephant; literally “great butterfly,” from the resemblance of the trunk and ears to the butterfly’s proboscis and wings. See number 15.

***<term>kanahe'na</term>***—a sour corn gruel, commonly used among the Cherokee and other Southern tribes; the *tamfuli* or “Tom Fuller” of the Creeks.

***<term>kănăne'skĭ</term>***—spider; also, from a fancied resemblance in appearance, a watch or clock; *kănăne'skĭ amăyĕ'hĭ*, the water spider.

***<term>Kăna'sta, Kănastûñ'yĭ</term>***—a traditional Cherokee settlement formerly on the headwaters of the French Broad River near the present Brevard, in Transylvania County, North Carolina. The meaning of the name is lost. A settlement called Cannostee or Cannastion is mentioned as existing on the Hiwassee River in 1776. See number 82 and notes.

***<term>kănă'talû'hĭ</term>***—hominy cooked with walnut kernels.

***<term>Kana'tĭ</term>***—“Lucky Hunter”; a masculine name, sometimes abbreviated *Kanat'*. The word cannot be analyzed, but is used as a third person habitual verbal form to mean “he is lucky, or successful, in hunting”; the opposite is *u'kwa'legû'*, “unlucky, or unsuccessful, in hunting.” See number 3.

***<term>kanegwâ'tĭ</term>***—the water-moccasin snake.

***<term>Kănu'ga</term>***—also written Canuga; a Lower Cherokee settlement, apparently on the waters of the Keowee River in South Carolina, destroyed in 1761; also a traditional settlement on the Pigeon River, probably near the present Waynesville, in Haywood County, North Carolina. See number 81 and notes. The name signifies “a scratcher,” a sort of bone-toothed comb with which ball players are scratched on their naked skin before applying the conjured medicine; *de'tsinuga'skû*, “I am scratching it.”

— ***<term>kănugû'lă</term>*** (abbreviated *nugû'lă*)—“scratcher,” a generic term for the blackberry, raspberry, and other brier bushes. See *Kănu'ga*.

***<term>Kănu'gû'lâyĭ</term>***, or ***<term>Kănu'gû'lûñ'yĭ</term>***—“Brier place,” from *kănugû'lă*, brier (see *Kănu'ga*); a Cherokee settlement formerly on the Nantahala River, about the mouth of Brier-town Creek, in Macon County, North Carolina.

***<term>kănûñ'năwû'</term>***—pipe.

***<term>Kâsdu'yĭ</term>***—“Ashes place,” from *kâsdu*, ashes, and *yĭ*, the locative. A modern Cherokee name for the town of Asheville, in Buncombe County, North Carolina. The ancient name for the same site is *Unta'kiyasti'yĭ*, see that entry.

***<term>Katâl'stă</term>***—an East Cherokee woman potter, the daughter of the chief *Yânăgûñ'skĭ*. The name conveys the idea of lending, from *tsiyatâl'stă*, “I lend it”; *agatâl'stă*, “it is lent to him.”

***<term>Kăwân'-urâ'sûñyĭ</term>*** (abbreviated *Kăwân'-urâ'sûn* in the Lower dialect)—“Where the duck fell” from *kăwâ'nă*, duck, *urâ'sâ* (*ulâ'sâ*), “it fell,” and *yĭ*, locative. A

point on Conneross Creek (from *Kāwăn'-urá/sŭñ*), near Seneca, in Oconee County, South Carolina. See number 123.

**Kawi'yĭ** (abbreviated *Kawi'*)—a formerly important Cherokee settlement, commonly known as Cowee, located at the mouth of Cowee Creek on the Little Tennessee River, about 10 miles below Franklin, in Macon County, North Carolina. The name may possibly be a contraction of *Anĭ'-Kawi'yĭ*, meaning “Place of the Deer Clan.”

**KEEOWHEE**—see **KEOWEE**.

**KENESAW**—see *Gănsâ'gĭ*.

**KEOWEE**—the name of two or more former Cherokee settlements. One, sometimes distinguished as “Old Keowee,” was the principal town of the Lower Cherokee settlements and was located on the river of the same name, near present-day Fort George in Oconee County, South Carolina. Another, distinguished as New Keowee, was on the headwaters of Twelve-mile Creek in Pickens County, South Carolina. According to Wafford, the correct form is *Kuwâhi'yĭ*, abbreviated as *Kuwâhi'*, meaning “Mulberry-grove place”; Wafford says, “The whites murdered the name, as they always do.” Compare *Kuwâ'hĭ*.

**Ke'sĭ-ka'gămû**—a woman’s name, a Cherokee corruption of Cassie Cockram; *ka'gămû* is also the Cherokee corruption for “cucumber.”

**KETOOWAH**—see *Kĭtu'hwă*.

**KITTUWA**—see *Kĭtu'hwă*.

**Kĭtu'hwă**—An important ancient Cherokee settlement formerly located upon the Tuckasegee River, extending from above the junction of the Oconaluftee River down nearly to present-day Bryson City, in Swain County, North Carolina. The name, which also appears as Kettooah, Kittoa, Kittowa, etc., has lost its meaning. The people of this and the subordinate settlements on the waters of the Tuckasegee were known as *Anĭ'-Kĭtu'hwagĭ*, and the name was frequently extended to include the entire tribe. For this reason, it was adopted in later times as the name of the Cherokee secret organization, commonly known to the whites as the Ketoowah Society, which is pledged to the defense of Cherokee autonomy. See also historical notes 1 and 47.

**kiyu'ga**—ground squirrel; *te'wa*, flying squirrel; *sălá'lĭ*, gray squirrel.

**KLAUSUNA**—see *Tlanusi'yĭ*.

**KNOXVILLE**—see *Kuwandâ'tă lûñ'yĭ*.

**kú!**—an introductory exclamation used to fix attention, roughly equivalent to “Now!”

**kukû'**—"cymling" (a type of squash); also the "jigger weed," or "pleurisy root" (*Asclepias tuberosa*).
   Coco Creek on the Hiwassee River and the Coker post office in Monroe County, Tennessee, derive their names from this word.

**Kûlsetsi'yĭ** (abbreviated *Kûlse'tsĭ*)—“Honey-locust place,” from *kûlse'tsĭ* (honey locust, *Gleditsia*) and *yĭ* (a locative suffix); as the same word, *kûlse'tsĭ*, is also used for “sugar,” the local name has commonly been translated as Sugartown by traders. This was the name of several former settlements in the old Cherokee territory. One was upon the Keowee River, near present-day Fall Creek in Oconee County, South Carolina; another was on Sugartown or Cullasagee (*Kulse'tsĭ*) Creek, near present-day Franklin in Macon County, North Carolina; a third was on Sugartown Creek, near present-day Morganton in Fannin County, Georgia.

**KUNNESEE**—see *Tsi'yu-gûnsĭ'nĭ*.

**Kûnstûtsi'yĭ**—“Sassafras place,” from *kûnstû'tsĭ* (sassafras) and *yĭ* (a locative suffix). A gap in the Great Smoky range, near the head of Noland Creek, on the border between North Carolina and Sevier County, Tennessee.

**kûnu'nû** (abbreviated *kûnun'*)—the bullfrog; the name is likely an onomatopoeia; the common green frog is *walâ'sĭ*, and there are also names for several other varieties of frogs and toads.

**Kusă'**—Coosa Creek, an upper tributary of the Nottely River, near Blairsville, Union County, Georgia. The change of accent from *Ku'să* (referring to the Creek people, see *Anĭ'-Ku'sa*) makes the word locative. See page 383.

**Ku'să-nûñnâ'hĭ**—“Creek trail,” from *Ku'să*, Creek Indian, and *nûñnâ'hĭ*, path or trail; compare *Suwâ'lĭ-nûñnâ'hĭ*. A former important Cherokee settlement, which also included a number of Creeks and Shawano, located where the trail from the Ohio region to the Creek country crossed the Tennessee River, at present-day Guntersville, in Marshall County, Alabama. It was known to traders as Creek-path, and later as Gunter's Landing, named after a Cherokee of mixed heritage named Gunter.

**Ku'săweti'yĭ** (abbreviated *Ku'săweti'*)—“Old Creek place,” from *Ku'să*, a Creek Indian (plural *Ani'-Ku'sa*), *uwe'tĭ*, old, and *yĭ*, locative. Coosawattee, an important Cherokee settlement formerly on the lower part of the Coosawattee River, in Gordon County, Georgia. In one document the name appears, by error, as Tensawattee. See page 382.

**Kuwâ'hĭ**—“Mulberry place,” from *ku'wă*, mulberry tree, and *hĭ*, locative; Clingman's Dome, near the head of Deep Creek, on the Great Smoky range, between Swain County, North Carolina, and Sevier County, Tennessee. See also **KEOWEE**.

**Kuwandâ'ta'lûñ'yĭ** (abbreviated *Kuwandâ'ta'lûñ*)—“Mulberry grove,” from *ku'wă*, mulberry; the Cherokee name for the present-day site of Knoxville, in Knox County, Tennessee.

**Kwa'lĭ, Kwalûñ'yĭ**—Qualla or Quallatown, the former agency for the East Cherokee and now a post office station, just outside the reservation, on a branch of Soco Creek, in Jackson County, North Carolina. It is the Cherokee form of “Polly,” and the station was so named for an old woman of that name who formerly lived nearby; *Kwa'lĭ*, “Polly,” *Kwalûñ'yĭ*, “Polly's place.” The reservation is locally known as the Qualla Boundary.

**kwandăya'hû**—see *da'lĭkstâ'*.

**lâ'lû**—the jar-fly (*Cicada auletes*). See number 59.

LITTLE CARPENTER, LITTLE CORNPLANTER—see *Ătă'-gûl' kălû'*.

LLOYD—see *Da'sĭ giya'gĭ*.

**LONG-HAIR**—a Cherokee chief living with his band in Ohio in 1795. See page 79. The literal Cherokee translation of “Long-hair” is *Gitlû'-gûñăhĭ'ta*, but it is not certain that the English name is a correct rendering of the Indian form. Compare *Ani'-Gilâ'hĭ*.

LONG ISLAND—see *Ămăye'lĭ-gûnăhĭ'ta*.

LOOKOUT MOUNTAIN TOWN—see *Danda'gănû'*.

LOWREY, MAJOR GEORGE—see *Agĭ'lĭ*.

MAYES, J. B.—see *Tsâ'wă Gak'skĭ*.

MIALAQUO—see *Ămăye'l-e'gwa*.

MORGAN—see *Âganstâ'ta*.

MOSES—see *Wâ'sĭ*.

MOYTOY—a Cherokee chief recognized by the English as “emperor” in 1730. Both the correct form and the meaning of the name are uncertain; the name occurs again as Moyatoy in a document of 1792; a boy on the East Cherokee reservation a few years ago bore the name of Ma'tayĭ', for which no meaning can be given.

MUSCLE SHOALS—see *Dâgû'nâhi*.

NACOOCHEE—see *Na'gu'tsĭ'*.

**Na'dû'lĭ'**—known to the whites as Nottely. A former Cherokee settlement on the Nottely River, close to the Georgia line, in Cherokee County, North Carolina. The name cannot be translated and has no connection with *na'tû'lĭ*, “spicewood.”

**Nagu'tsĭ'**—a former important settlement about the junction of the Soquee and Santee rivers, in Nacoochee Valley, at the head of the Chattahoochee River, in Habersham County, Georgia. The meaning of the word is lost and it is doubtful if it be of

*na'tsĭ*—pine.

NELLAWGITEHI—recorded as the name of a Lower Cherokee chief in 1684. See page 31. The correct form and meaning are both uncertain, but the final part appears to be the common suffix *dihĭ'*, "killer." Compare *Ta'gwǎdihĭ'*.

*Nĭ'kwǎsĭ'* (or *Nĭkw'sĭ'*)—an important ancient settlement on the Little Tennessee River, where the town of Franklin now stands in Macon County, North Carolina. A large mound marks the site of the townhouse. The name appears in old documents as Nequassee, Nucassee, and other variations. Its meaning has been lost.

*Nĭkutse'gĭ* (also *Nūkǎtse'gĭ*, *Nĭkwǎtse'gĭ*, or abbreviated *Nĭkutseg'*)—Nickajack, an important Cherokee settlement around 1790 on the south bank of the Tennessee River at the entrance of Nickajack Creek, in Marion County, Tennessee. It was one of the five Chickamauga towns (see *Tsĭkǎma'gĭ*). The meaning of the word is lost and it is probably not of Cherokee origin, although it also occurs in the tribe as a man's name. In the corrupted form of "Nigger Jack," it also occurs as the name of a creek on the Cullasagee River above Franklin, in Macon County, North Carolina.

NILAQUE—see *Amǎyě'l-e'gwǎ*.

NOLICHUCKY—see *Nâ'nǎ-tlū'gûñ'yĭ*.

NOTCHY—a creek entering the Tellico River in Monroe County, Tennessee. The name evidently refers to Natchez Indian refugees who formerly lived in the vicinity (see *Anĭ'-Na'tsĭ*).

NOTTELY—see *Na'dû'lĭ*.

*nû*—used as a suffix to mean "and" or "also"; *û'lĕ-nû*, "and also"; *na'skĭ-nû'*, "and that," or "that also."

NUCASSEE—see *Nikwăsĭ'*.

*nu'dûñnelû'*—he did so and so; an irregular form apparently connected with the archaic forms *adûñni'ga*, "it has just become so," and *udûñnû'*, "it is matured, or finished." See entry number 118.

*nûñ'dă'*—the sun or moon, distinguished as *nûñ'dă' igĕ'hĭ*, "*nûñ'dă'* dwelling in the day," and *nûñ'dă' sûnnâ'yehĭ*, "*nûñ'dă'* dwelling in the night." In the sacred formulas, the moon is sometimes called *Gĕ'yăgû'ga* (see that entry) or *Su'tălidihi'*, "Six-killer," names which are apparently based on myths that are now lost.

*nûñ'dă'-dikani'*—a rare bird formerly seen occasionally in the old Cherokee country, possibly the little blue heron (*Floridus cerulea*). The name seems to mean "it looks at the sun," that is, "sun-gazer," from *nûñ'dă'*, sun, and *da'ka'nă'* or *detsi'ka'nă*, "I am looking at it." See entry number 35.

*Nûñ'dâgûñ'yĭ, Nûñdâ'yĭ*—the Sun land, or east; from *nûñ'dă'*, sun, and *yĭ*, a location marker. Used in the sacred formulas instead of *dĭ'gălûñgûñ'yĭ*, "where it rises," which is the common word.

*Nûñ'dâye'lĭ*—"Middle (meaning Noonday) sun," from *nûñ'dă'*, sun and *ayé'lĭ*, middle; a former Cherokee settlement on the Nantahala River, near the present Jarrett station in Macon County, North Carolina. It was so called because of the high cliffs that block the view of the sun until nearly noon. The name also appears as Nantahala, Nantiyallee, Nuntialla, etc. It seems to have been applied properly only to the point on the river where the cliffs are most vertical, while the settlement itself was known as *Kanu'gû'lâ'yĭ*, "Briertown" (see that entry). See entry number 122.

*Nugătsa'nĭ*—a ridge sloping down to the Oconaluftee River, below Cherokee in Swain County, North Carolina. The word is an archaic form denoting a high ridge with a long, gradual slope. See entry number 122.

*nûñ'gĭ'*—four. See *hĭ'skĭ*.

*nugû'la*—see *kănugû'la*.

NUHNAYIE—see *Nûñnĕ'hĭ*.

*nu'nă*—potato; the name was originally applied to the wild "pig potato" (*Phaseolus*), now distinguished as *nu'nă igâtĕhĭ*, "swamp-dwelling potato."

*Nûndâwe'gĭ*—see *Anĭ'-Nûndâwe'gĭ*.

*nûñnâ'hĭ* (abbreviated *nûñnâ*)—a path, trail, or road.

*Nûñnâ'hĭ-dihĭ'* (abbreviated *Nûñ'nâ-dihĭ'*)—"Path-killer," literally, "He kills (habitually) in the path," from *nûñ'nâ'hĭ*, path, and *ahihĭ'*, "he kills" (habitually); "I am killing" is *tsĭ'ihû'*. A principal chief around the year 1813. Major John Ridge was originally known by the same name, but he later took the name *Gûnûñ'da'le'gĭ*, "One who follows the ridge," which the white people simplified to "Ridge."

*Nûñnâ'hĭ-tsune'ga* (abbreviated *Nûñnâ-tsune'ga*)—"White-path," from *nûñnâ'hĭ*, path, and *tsune'ga*, the plural of *une'ga*, white; the form is in the plural, as is common in Indian names, and it probably has a symbolic reference to the "white" or peaceful paths mentioned in the opening invocation at the Green Corn Dance. A noted chief who led the conservative party around 1828. See pages 113 and 132.

*Nûñnĕ'hĭ* (also *Gûñnĕ'hĭ*; singular *Nayĕ'hĭ*)—a race of invisible spirit people. The name is derived from the verb *ĕ'hû'*, "I dwell, I live," and *ĕ'hĭ'*, "I dwell habitually," and may be translated as "dwellers anywhere" or "those who live anywhere," but it implies having always been there—that is, "Immortals." It has been spelled Nanehi and Nuhnayie by different writers. The singular form *Nayĕ'hĭ* also occurs as a personal name, roughly equivalent to *Edâ'hĭ*, "One who goes about." See entry number 78.

*nuniyu'stĭ*—"potato-like," from *nu'nă*, potato, and *iyu'stĭ*, like. A flowering vine with a tuberous root that somewhat resembles the potato. See entry number 126.

*nûñyû'*—rock, stone. Compare *nâyû*, sand.
*Nûñyû'-gûñwani'skĭ*—"Rock that talks," from *nûñyû'*, rock, and *tsiwani'hû*, "I am talking." A rock from which Talking-rock creek of the Coosawattee river in Georgia derives its name. See number 125.
*Nûñ'yunu'wĭ*—contracted from *Nûñyû-unu'wĭ*. "Stone-clad," from *nûñyû*, rock, and *agwănu'wû*, "I am clothed or covered." A mythical monster, invulnerable because of his stony skin. See number 67. *Nûñyû'-tâwĭ'skă*—"Slick rock," from *nûñyû'*, rock, and *tâwĭskă*, smooth, slick; the form remains unchanged for the locative [place name]. 1. A place at the extreme head of Brasstown creek of the Hiwassee river, in Towns county, Georgia.

PINELOG—see *Na'ts-asûñ'tlûñyĭ*.

QUALATCHEE—a former Cherokee settlement on the headwaters of the Chattahoochee river in Georgia; another of the same name was upon the waters of the Keowee river in South Carolina. The correct form is unknown.

<term>Sadayĭ′</term>—a feminine name, the proper name of the woman known to white people as Annie Ax; it cannot be translated.

<term>Sâgwâ′hĭ</term>, or <term>Sâgwûn′yĭ</term>—“One place,” from *sâ′gwû*, one, and *hĭ* or *yĭ*, locative. Soco creek of Oconaluftee river, on the East Cherokee reservation, in Jackson county, North Carolina. No satisfactory reason is given for the name, which has its parallel in <term>Tsâskâ′hĭ</term>, “Thirty place,” a local name in Cherokee county, in the same state.

<term>sâ′gwâlĭ</term>, horse; from *asâgwălĭhû*, a pack or burden, *asâgwăl lû′*; “there is a pack on him.”

<term>sâ′gwâlĭ dĭgû′lanâhi′ta</term>—mule; literally “long eared horse,” from <term>sâ′gwâlĭ</term>, horse, and <term>dĭgû′lanâhi′ta</term>, see that entry.

<term>Sâkwi′yĭ</term> (or <term>Suki′yĭ</term>; abbreviated <term>Sâkwi′</term> or <term>Suki′</term>)—a former settlement on Soquee river, a head-stream of Chattahoochee, near Clarkesville, Habersham county, Georgia. Also written Saukee and Sookee. The name has lost its meaning.

<term>sălâ′lĭ</term>—squirrel; the common gray squirrel; other varieties are *kiyû′ga*, the ground squirrel, and *tewa*, the flying squirrel. <term>Sălâ′lĭ</term> was also the name of an East Cherokee inventor who died a few years ago; <term>Sălâ′lăni′ta</term>, “Young-squirrels,” is a masculine personal name on the reservation.

<term>săligu′gĭ</term>—turtle, the common water turtle; soft-shell turtle, *u′lănâ′wâ*; land tortoise or terrapin, *tûksĭ′*.

<term>sălikwâ′yĭ</term>—bear-grass (*Eryngium*); also the greensnake, on account of a perceived resemblance; the name of a former Cherokee settlement on Sallacoa creek of Coosawatee river, in Gordon county, Georgia.

<term>Sa′nigilâ′gĭ</term> (abbreviated <term>San′gilâ′gĭ</term>)—Whiteside mountain, a prominent peak of the Blue ridge, southeast from Franklin, Macon county, North Carolina. It is connected with the tradition of <term>U′tlûñ′ta</term> (see story number 66 and its notes).

<term>SANTEETLA</term>—the present map name of a creek joining Cheowa river in Graham county, North Carolina, and of a smaller tributary (Little Santeetla). The name is not recognized or understood by the Cherokee, who insist that it was given by white people. Little Santeetla is known to the Cherokee as <term>Tsundâ′nilti′yĭ</term>, see that entry; the main Santeetla creek is commonly known as <term>Nâyu′hĭ geyûn′ĭ</term>, “Sand-place stream,” from <term>Nâyu′hĭ</term>, “Sand place” (*nâyû*, sand), a former settlement just above the junction of the two creeks.

<term>SARA</term>—see <term>Ani′-Suwa′lĭ</term>.

<term>sa′sa′</term>—goose; an onomatopoeic word.

<term>SAUTEE</term>—see <term>Itsâ′tĭ</term>.

<header>MOONEY] GLOSSARY</header>

“I kill.” An old masculine personal name, still in use on the East Cherokee reservation. It was the proper name of the chief known to the whites around 1790 as “The Glass,” from a confusion of this name with <term>adake'’ti</term>, glass, or mirror.

**Tagwâ'hi**—“Catawba place,” from <term>Ata'gwa</term> or <term>Ta'gwa</term>, Catawba Indian, and <term>hǐ</term>, a locative. A name occurring in several places in the old Cherokee country. A settlement of this name, known to the whites as Toccoa, was on Toccoa Creek, east of Clarkesville, in Habersham County, Georgia; another was on the Toccoa or Ocoee River, near the present Toccoa, in Fannin County, Georgia; a third may have been on Persimmon Creek, which is known to the Cherokee as <term>Tagwâ'hi</term>, and enters the Hiwassee River some distance below Murphy, in Cherokee County, North Carolina.

**TAHKEYOSTEE**—see <term>Unta'kiyasti'yǐ</term>.

**TAHLEQUAH**—see <term>Tâlikwă'</term>.

**TAHCHEE**—see <term>Tâtsǐ'</term>.

**TAKATOKA**—see <term>De'gâtâ'gă</term>.

**tǎ'lǎdŭ'** (abbreviated <term>tǎldŭ'</term>)—twelve, from <term>tǎ'lǐ</term>, two. Compare <term>tǎla'tŭ</term>, cricket.

**Tǎ'lasǐ'**—a former Cherokee settlement on the Little Tennessee River, near Tallassee Ford, in Blount County, Tennessee. The name has lost its meaning.

**TALASSEE**—see <term>Tǎ'lasǐ'</term>.

**tǎla'tŭ**—cricket; sometimes also called <term>dita'staye'skǐ</term> (which see), “the barber.” Compare <term>tǎ'lǎdŭ'</term>, twelve.

**Tǎle'danigǐ'skǐ** (<term>Utǎle'danigǐ'sǐ</term> in a dialectal form)—variously translated by the whites as “Hemp-carrier,” “Nettle-carrier,” or “Flax-toter,” from <term>tǎle'ta</term> or <term>utǎle'ta</term>, flax (*Linum*) or richweed (*Pilea pumila*), and <term>danigǐ'skǐ</term>, “he carries them (habitually).” A former prominent chief on the Valley River, in Cherokee County, North Carolina. See number 95 and notes.

**TALIHINA**—given as the name of the Cherokee wife of Samuel Houston; the form cannot be identified. See page 223.

**Tâlikwă'** (commonly written Tellico, Telliquo or, in the Indian Territory, Tahlequah)—the name of several Cherokee settlements at different periods, namely: 1. Great Tellico, at Tellico Plains, on the Tellico River, in Monroe County, Tennessee; 2. Little Tellico, on Tellico Creek of the Little Tennessee River, about ten miles below Franklin, in Macon County, North Carolina; 3. a town on the Valley River, about five miles above Murphy, in Cherokee County, North Carolina; 4. Tahlequah, established as the capital of the Cherokee Nation, Indian Territory, in 1839. The meaning of the name is lost.

**Tali'wǎ**—the site of a traditional battle between the Cherokee and the Creeks about 1755, on Mountain (?) Creek of the Etowah River in upper Georgia. Probably not a Cherokee but a Creek name from the Creek <term>ta'lua</term> or <term>ita'lua</term>, town. See pages 38 and 384–385.

**TALKING-ROCK**—see <term>Nûñyû'-gûñwanǐ'skǐ</term>.

**TALLULAH**—see <term>Tǎlulŭ'</term>.

**Tǎl-tsu'skǎ'**—“Two-heads,” from <term>tǎ'lǐ</term>, two, and <term>tsu'skǎ'</term>, the plural of <term>uskǎ'</term>, (his) head. A Cherokee chief around the year 1800, known to the whites as Doublehead.

**talulǐ**—pregnant; from which comes <term>alulǐ'</term>, (she is) a mother, said of a woman.

**Tǎlulŭ'** (commonly written Tallulah, and appearing in old documents, from the Lower dialect, as Taruraw, Toruro, Turoree, etc.)—a name occurring in two or more places in the old Cherokee country, namely: 1. An ancient settlement on the upper part of the Tallulah River, in Rabun County, Georgia; 2. a town on Tallulah Creek of the Cheowa River, in Graham County, North Carolina. The word is of uncertain etymology. The <term>dulu'sǐ</term> frog is said to cry <term>tǎlulŭ'</term>. See number 125. The noted falls on the Tallulah River are known to the Cherokee as <term>Ugûñ'yǐ</term>, which see.

**TALUNTISKI**—see <term>Ata'lûntǐskǐ</term>.

**Tama'li**—a name, commonly written Tomotley or Tomatola, occurring in at least two places in the old Cherokee country, namely: 1. On Valley River, a few miles above Murphy, near the present Tomatola, in Cherokee County, North Carolina; 2. on Little Tennessee River, near Tomotley Ford, a few miles above Tellico River, in Monroe County, Tennessee. The name cannot be translated and may be of Creek origin, as that tribe had a town of the same name on the lower Chattahoochee River.

**Tănăsĭ'**—a name which cannot be analyzed, commonly spelled Tennessee, occurring in several places in the old Cherokee country, namely: 1. On Little Tennessee River, about halfway between Citico and Toco creeks, in Monroe County, Tennessee; 2. "Old Tennessee Town," on Hiwassee River, a short distance above the junction of the Ocoee, in Polk County, Tennessee; 3. on Tennessee Creek, a headstream of Tuckasegee River, in Jackson County, North Carolina. Tanasqui, visited by Pardo in 1567 (see page 29), may have been another place of the same name. See number 124.

**TANASQUI**—see <term>Tănăsĭ'</term>.

**Ta'skĭ'gi** (abbreviated from <term>Ta'skĭgi'yĭ</term> or <term>Da'skĭgi'yĭ</term>, the locative <term>yĭ</term> being commonly omitted)—a name variously written Tae-keo-ge (misprint), Tasquiqui, Teeskege, Tuscagee, Tuskegee, etc., derived from that of a foreign tribe incorporated with the Cherokee, and occurring as a local name both in the Cherokee and in the Creek country. 1. The principal settlement of this name was on Little Tennessee River, just above the junction of Tellico, in Monroe County, Tennessee; 2. another was on the north bank of the Tennessee River, just below Chattanooga, Tennessee; 3. another may have been on Tuskegee Creek of Little Tennessee River, near Robbinsville, Graham County, North Carolina. See page 29 and number 105.

**TASQUIQUI**—see <term>Ta'skĭ'gi</term>.

**TASSEL, OLD**—see <term>Utsĭ'dsată'</term>.

**Tätsĭ'**—“Dutch,” also written Tahchee, a western Cherokee chief about 1830. See page 141.

**tatsu'hwă**—the red bird.

**tawa'li**—punk.

**Tawa'lĭ-ukwanûn'tĭ**—“Punk-plugged-in,” from <term>tawa'li</term>, punk; the Cherokee name of a traditional Shawnee chief. See number 100.

**täwĭ'skă**, **täwĭ'skage**—smooth, slick.

**Täwĭ'skälă**—“Flint”; a Cherokee supernatural, the personification of the rock flint; <term>täwĭ'skălûn'ĭ</term>, <term>täwĭ'skălă</term>, flint, from <term>täwĭ'skă</term>, smooth, slick; compare Iroquois <term>Tāwis-karõñ</term>. See number 25 and notes.

**Tayûnksĭ**—a traditional western tribe; the name cannot be analyzed. See number 105.

**TELLICO**—see <term>Tălikwă'</term>.

**telûn'lătĭ**—the summer grape (*Vitis æstivalis*).

**TENSAWATTEE**—see <term>Ku'săweti'yĭ</term>.

**TERRAPIN**—see <term>Tûksĭ'</term>.

**tewa**—flying squirrel; <term>sălâ'lĭ</term>, gray squirrel; <term>kiyu'ga</term>, ground squirrel.

**THOMAS, W. H.**—see <term>Wil-usdĭ'</term>.

**Tĭkwălĭ'tsĭ**—a name occurring in several places in the old Cherokee country, namely: 1. Tuckalegee Creek, a tributary of War-woman Creek, east of Clayton, in Rabun County, Georgia; 2. the <term>Tĭkwălĭ'tsĭ</term> of the story, an important town on Tuckasegee River at the present Bryson City, in Swain County, North Carolina; 3. Tuckaleechee Cove, on Little River, in Blount County, Tennessee, which probably preserves the aboriginal local name. The name appears in old documents as Tuckarechee (Lower dialect) and Tuckalegee, and must not be confused with <term>Tsĭksĭ'tsĭ</term> or <term>Tuckasegee</term>. It cannot be translated. See number 100 and notes.

**TIMOSSY**—see **TOMASSEE**.

**Tlăge'sĭ**—"Field"; the Cherokee name for Lieutenant-Colonel W. W. Stringfield of Waynesville, North Carolina, one of the officers of the Cherokee contingent in the Thomas Legion. It is an abbreviated version of his proper name.
**tlâge'sitûn'i**—a song form for *tlâge'sĭ a-stûn'ĭ*, "on the edge of the field," from *tlâge'sĭ*, or *tsâge'sĭ*, meaning "field," and *astûn'ĭ*, meaning "edge, border, etc."; *ăma'yăstûn'ĭ* means "the bank of a stream." See number 24.
**tla'mehä**—bat (dialect forms: *tsa'mehä*, *tsa'wehă*). See page 187.
**tlanu'sĭ'**—leech (dialect form: *tsanu'sĭ'*). See page 187.
**Tlanusi'yĭ** (abbreviated *Tlanusi'*)—"Leech place," a formerly important settlement at the junction of the Hiwassee and Valley rivers, the current site of Murphy, in Cherokee County, North Carolina; also a point on the Nottely River, a few miles away in the same county. See number 77 and the accompanying notes. The name also appears as Clennuse, Klausuna, Quoneashee, etc.
**tlă'nuwă'** (dialect forms: *tsă'nuwă'*, *sû'năwă'*, "sinnawah"—according to Adair)—a mythical great hawk. See numbers 35, 64, 65, and page 187.
**tlă'nuwă' usdĭ'**—"little tlă'nuwă'"; probably the goshawk (*Astur atricapillus*). See number 35.
**Tlă'nuwă'-atsiyelûn'isûn'yĭ**—"Where the Tlă'nuwă cut it up," from *tlă'nuwă'* (see above) and *tsiyelûn'iskû'*, an ancient form for *tsigûnĭlûn'iskû'*, "I am cutting it up." A place on the Little Tennessee River, nearly opposite the mouth of Citico Creek, in Blount County, Tennessee. See number 64 and notes.
**Tlă'nuwă'ĭ**—"Tlă'nuwă place," a cave on the north side of the Tennessee River a short distance below the mouth of Citico Creek, in Blount County, Tennessee. See number 64 and notes.
**tlay'kû'**—jay (dialect form: *tsay'kû'*). See page 187.
**tlûntĭ'stĭ**—the pheasant (*Bonasa umbella*), locally called grouse or partridge.
**tlutlû'**—the martin bird (dialect form: *tsutsû'*). See page 187.
**tlûntû'tsĭ**—panther (dialect form: *tsûntû'tsĭ*). See page 187.
**TOCAX**—a place, apparently in the Cherokee country, visited by Pardo in 1567 (see page 29). It may possibly have a connection with Toxaway (see *Dûksa'ĭ*) or Toccoa (see *Tagwâ'hĭ*).
**TOCCOA**—see *Tagwâ'hĭ*.
**Toco**—see *Dăkwâ'ĭ*.
**TOLLUNTEESKEE**—see *Ata'lûntĭ'skĭ*.
**TOMASSEE** (also written *Timossy* and *Tymahse*)—the name of two or more former Cherokee settlements, namely: 1. On Tomassee Creek of the Keowee River, in Oconee County, South Carolina; 2. on the Little Tennessee River near the mouth of Burningtow Creek, in Macon County, South Carolina. The correct form and meaning are unknown.
**TOMATOLA, TOMOTLEY**—see *Tama'lĭ*.
**TOOANTUH**—see *Du'stu'*.
**TOOGELAH**—see *Dugilu'yĭ*.
**TOQUA**—see *Dăkwâ'ĭ*.
**TOXAWAY**—see *Dûksa'ĭ*.
**TRACK ROCK GAP**—see *Datsu'nalâsgûn'yĭ*.
**Tsăga'sĭ**—a Cherokee sprite. See number 78.
**tsă'gĭ**—upstream, up the road; the opposite of *ge'ĭ*. See number 117.
**Tsaiyĭ'**—see *Ûntsaiyĭ'*.
**Tsalădĭhĭ'**—Chief N. J. Smith of the East Cherokee. The name might be translated as "Charley-killer," from *Tsalĭ* ("Charley") and *dihĭ'* ("killer" in compound words), but it is actually a Cherokee version of Jarrett (*Tsalădĭ'*), his middle name, by which he was frequently addressed. Compare with *Tagwâdĭhĭ'*.
**tsâl-agăyûn'lĭ**—"old tobacco," from *tsâlû* (tobacco) and *agăyûn'lĭ* or *agăyûn'lige* (old or ancient); the *Nicotiana rustica* or wild tobacco. See number 126.

***Tsa'lägĭ'*** (***Tsa'rägĭ'*** in the Lower dialect)—the correct form of Cherokee. See page 182, "Tribal Synonymy."

***Tsa'li***—Charley; a Cherokee man shot for resisting troops during the time of the Removal. See page 131.

***tsâliyu'stĭ***—"tobacco-like," from *tsâlû* (tobacco) and *iyu'stĭ* (like); a generic name for the cardinal-flower, mullein, and related species. See number 126.

***tsâlû*** or ***tsâlûn*** (in the Lower dialect, ***tsârû***)—tobacco; by comparison with similar forms in other Iroquoian dialects, the meaning "fire to hold in the mouth" seems to be indicated. Lanman spells it *tso-lungh*. See number 126 and page 187.

***tsa'mehă***—see *tla'mehă*.

***tsă'nadiskâ'***—for *tsăndiskâi'*, meaning "they say."

***tsana'sehâ'ĭ'***—so they say, or they say about him. See number 118.

***tsäne'nĭ***—the scorpion lizard; also called *gĭ'gă-danegi'skĭ*, q. v. See number 59.

***Tsänĭ***—John.

***Tsantäwû'***—a masculine name that cannot be analyzed.

***Tsan-uga'sĭtä***—"Sour John"; John Butler, a half-breed Cherokee ball captain who formerly lived on the Nottely River. See number 122.

***Tsan-usdĭ'***—"Little John"; the Cherokee name for General John Sevier, and also the childhood name of the chief John Ross, afterward known as *Gu'wisguwĭ'*, q. v. *Sikwĭ'yă*, a Cherokee attempt at "Sevier," is a masculine name on the East Cherokee reservation.

***tsanu'sĭ'***—see *tlanu'sĭ'*.

***tsă'nuwä'***—see *tlä'nuwä'*.

***Tsa'rägĭ'***—Cherokee; see page 182, "Tribal Synonymy."

***tsârû***—see *tsâlû*.

***Tsasta'wĭ***—a noted hunter who formerly lived on the Nantahala River in Macon County, North Carolina; the meaning of the name is doubtful. See number 122.

***Tsatănu'gĭ*** (commonly spelled Chattanooga)—the Cherokee name for a specific point on the creek entering the Tennessee River at the city of Chattanooga, in Hamilton County, Tennessee. It has no meaning in the Cherokee language and appears to be of foreign origin. The ancient name for the site of the present city is *A'tlä'nuwä*, q. v. See number 124. Before the establishment of the town, the place was known to the white settlers as Ross's Landing, named after a store kept there by Lewis Ross, brother of the chief John Ross.

***Tsatu'gĭ*** (commonly written Chattooga or Chatuga)—a name occurring in two or more places in the old Cherokee country, but apparently of foreign origin (see page 382). Possible Cherokee derivations are from words signifying respectively "he drank by sips," from *gatu'giä'*, "I sip," or "he has crossed the stream and come out on the other side," from *gatu'gi*, "I have crossed," etc. An ancient settlement of this name was on the Chattooga River, a headwater of the Savannah River, on the boundary between South Carolina and Georgia; another appears to have been on the upper Tellico River in Monroe County, Tennessee; another may have been on the Chattooga River, a tributary of the Coosa in northwestern Georgia.

<margin>x</margin> ***Tsâ'wă Gakskĭ***—Joe Smoker, from *Tsâwă* ("Joe") and *gakskĭ* ("smoker"), from *ga'giskû* ("I am smoking"). This is the Cherokee name for Chief Joel B. Mayes of the Cherokee Nation West.

***Tsăwa'sĭ***—a Cherokee sprite. See number 78.

***tsa'wehä***—see *tla'mehă*.

***tsay'kû'***—see *tlay'kû'*.

***Tsek'sĭnĭ'***—the Cherokee form of the name for General Andrew Jackson.

***Tsësa'nĭ***—Jessan, probably a derivative of Jesse; a masculine name on the East Cherokee reservation.

***Tsë'sĭ-Ska'tsĭ***—"Scotch Jesse"; Jesse Reid, the current chief of the East Cherokee, so called because of his mixed Scotch ancestry.

<header>MOONEY] GLOSSARY</header>

*tsetsäni'lĭ*—"your two older brothers" (male speaking); my older brother (male speaking), *ûngini'lĭ*. See note to number 63.

*Tsgâgûñ'yĭ*—"Insect place," from *tsgâyă*, insect, and *yĭ*, locative. A cave in the ridge east of Franklin, in Macon County, North Carolina. See number 13. *tsgâyă*—insect, worm, etc. See page 308.

*Tsĭkăma'gĭ*—a name, commonly spelled Chickamauga, occurring in at least two places in the old Cherokee country, which has lost any meaning in Cherokee and appears to be of foreign origin. It is applied to a small creek at the head of the Chattahoochee River, in White County, Georgia, and also to the district around the southern (not the northern) Chickamauga Creek, which flows into the Tennessee River a few miles above Chattanooga, in Hamilton County, Tennessee. In 1777, the more hostile part of the Cherokee withdrew from the rest of the tribe and established a large settlement here, from which they moved about five years later to settle further down the Tennessee in what were known as the Chickamauga towns or Five Lower towns. See page 54 and number 124.

*tsĭkĭ'*—a word that makes the preceding word emphatic: such as *á'stû*, "very good," *ástû' tsĭkĭ'*, "best of all." See number 75.

*tsĭkĭkĭ'*—the katydid; the name is an onomatopoeia.

*tsĭ'kĭlĭlĭ'*—the Carolina chickadee (*Parus carolinensis*); the name is an onomatopoeia. See number 35.

*Tsĭksĭ'tsĭ* (*Tûksĭ'tsĭ* in dialect form; commonly written Tuckasegee)—1. A former Cherokee settlement around the junction of the two forks of the Tuckasegee, above Webster, in Jackson County, North Carolina (not to be confused with *Tikwălĭ'tsĭ*, q. v.). 2. A former settlement on a branch of Brasstown Creek of the Hiwassee River, in Towns County, Georgia. The word has lost its meaning.

*Tsĭ'nawĭ*—a Cherokee wheelwright, perhaps the first in the Nation to make a spinning wheel and loom. The name cannot be analyzed. See page 214.

*tsĭne'û*—I am picking it (something long) up; in the Lower and Middle dialects, *tsĭnigĭ'û*.

*tsĭnigĭ'û*—see *tsĭne'û*.

*tsiska'gĭlĭ*—the large red crayfish; the ordinary crayfish is called *tsistû'na*. See number 59.

*tsĭ'skwa*—bird.

*tsiskwa'gwă*—robin, from *tsĭ'skwa*, bird.

*Tsiskwâ'hĭ*—"Bird place," from *tsĭ'skwa*, bird, and *hĭ*, locative. Birdtown settlement on the East Cherokee reservation, in Swain County, North Carolina.

*tsiskwâ'yă*—sparrow, literally "principal bird" (i.e., the most widely distributed), from *tsĭ'skwa*, bird, and *yă*, a suffix meaning principal or real.

*Tsilalu'hĭ*—"Sweet-gum place," from *tsila'lû'*, sweet-gum (*Liquidambar*), and *hĭ*, locative. A former settlement on a small branch of Brasstown Creek of the Hiwassee River, just within the border of Towns County, Georgia. The name is incorrectly translated as Gumlog (Creek).

*Tsiskwunsdi'-adsisti'yĭ*—"Where they killed Little-bird," from *Tsiskw-unsdi'*, "Little-birds" (plural form). A place near the head of West Buffalo Creek, southeast of Robbinsville, in Graham County, North Carolina. See number 122.

*Tsistetsi'yĭ*—"Mouse place," from *tsistetsĭ*, mouse, and *yĭ*, locative; a former settlement on South Mouse Creek, of the Hiwassee River, in Bradley County, Tennessee. The present town of Cleveland, on the same creek, is known to the Cherokee by the same name.

*tsistu*—rabbit.

*tsistû'na*—crayfish; the large horned beetle is also called by this name. The large red crayfish is called *tsiska'gĭlĭ*.

*tsist-uni'gistĭ*—"rabbit foods" (plural), from *tsĭ'stu*, rabbit, and *uni'gistĭ*, plural of *agi'stĭ*, food, from *tsiyĭ'giû* "I am eating" (soft food). The wild rose.

*Tsistu'yĭ*—"Rabbit place," from *tsistu* (rabbit) and *yĭ* (locative). 1. Gregory Bald, a high peak of the Great Smoky range, eastward from the Little Tennessee River, on the boundary between Swain County, North Carolina, and Blount County, Tennessee. See number 75 and notes. 2. A former settlement on the north bank of the Hiwassee River at the entrance of Chestua Creek, in Polk County, Tennessee. The name of Choastea Creek on the Tugaloo River, in Oconee County, South Carolina, is probably also a corruption of the same word.

*Tsiyâ'hĭ*—"Otter place," from *tsiyû* (otter) and *yĭ* (locative); variously spelled Cheowa, Cheeowhee, Chewohe, Chewe, etc. 1. A former settlement on a branch of the Keowee River, near the present Cheohee, Oconee County, South Carolina. 2. A former and still existing Cherokee settlement on the Cheowa River, around Robbinsville, in Graham County, North Carolina. 3. A former settlement in Cades Cove, on Cove Creek, in Blount County, Tennessee.

*Tsi'yu-gûnsi'nĭ*—"He is dragging a canoe," from *tsi'yû* (canoe; compare *tsĭ'yû*, otter) and *gûnsi'nĭ* (he is dragging it). "Dragging-canoe," a prominent leader of the hostile Cherokee during the Revolution. The name appears in documents as Cheucunsene and Kunnesee. See page 54.

*Tskĭl-e'gwâ*—"Big-witch," from *atskĭlĭ'* or *tskĭlĭ'* (witch, owl) and *e'gwâ* (big); an old man of the East Cherokee who died in 1896. See page 179. Although translated as "Big-witch" by the whites, the name is understood by the Indians to mean "Big-owl" (see number 35), having been originally applied to a white man living on the same clearing who was noted for his large, staring eyes.

*tskĭlĭ'* (shortened from *atskĭlĭ'*)—1. witch; 2. the dusky horned owl (*Bubo virginianus saturatus*). See number 35.

TSOLUNGH—see *tsălû*.

*tskwâ'yĭ*—the great white heron or American egret (*Herodias egretta*).

*Tsudâ'tălesûn'yĭ*—"Where pieces fall off," that is, where the banks are caving in; from *adátăle'û* (it is falling off), *ts* (distance prefix, "there"), and *yĭ* (locative). The Cherokee name for the present site of Memphis, Tennessee, overlooking the Mississippi, which was formerly known as the Chickasaw Bluff.

*Tsudâ'ye'lûn'yĭ*—"Isolated place"; an isolated peak near the head of the Cheowa River, northeast of Robbinsville, in Graham County, North Carolina. See number 79 and notes. The root of the word signifies detached or isolated, from which *Uda'ye'lûn'yĭ*, the Cherokee Outlet in the Indian Territory, is derived.

*Tsu'dinûntĭ'yĭ*—"Throwing-down place"; a former settlement on the lower Nantahala River, in Macon County, North Carolina. See number 122.

*Tsugidû'lĭ ûlsgĭ'stĭ* (from *tsugidû'lĭ*, the plural of *ugidû'lĭ*, one of the long wing or tail feathers of a bird, and *ûlsgĭ'stĭ* or *ûlsgĭ'ta*, a dance)—the feather or eagle dance. See number 35.

*tsûngili'sĭ*—plural of *ûngili'sĭ*, which see.

*tsûngini'sĭ*—plural of *ûngini'sĭ*, which see.

*Tsukilûnnûñ'yĭ*—"Where he alighted"; two bald spots on a mountain at the head of Little Snowbird Creek, near Robbinsville, in Graham County, North Carolina. For the tradition, see number 122.

*tsuñkina'tlĭ*—"my younger brothers" (spoken by a male).

*tsuñkită'*—"my younger brothers" (spoken by a female).

*tsu'lă*—fox; compare *tsû'lû* (kingfisher) and *tlutlû'* or *tsutsĭ'* (martin). The black fox is *inâ'lĭ*. The Creek word for fox is *chula*.

*tsula'skĭ*—alligator: the name is of uncertain etymology.

**Tsule'hisanûñ'hĭ**—"Resurrected One," from *di'gwăle'hisanûñ'hĭ*, "I was resurrected," literally, "I was down and have risen." *Tsa'lăgi' Tsule'hisanûñ'hĭ*, the Cherokee title of the newspaper known to white people as the *Cherokee Phoenix*. The Cherokee title was devised by Worcester and Boudinot as suggesting the idea of the phoenix of classic fable. The Indian name of the recent *Cherokee Advocate* is *Tsa'lăgi Asdeli'skĭ*.

**Tsul'kălû' tsunegûñ'yĭ**—see *Tsunegûñ'yĭ*.

**tsulie'na**—the nuthatch (*Sitta carolinensis*); the word signifies literally "deaf" (a plural form referring to the ear, *gûlĕ'*), although no reason is given for such a name.

**tsû'lû**—kingfisher. Compare *tsu'lă*.

**Tsû'lûñwe'ĭ** (abbreviated *Tsû'lûñ'we* or *Tsûla'wĭ*, possibly connected with *tsû'lû*, kingfisher)—Chilhowee Creek, a north tributary of the Little Tennessee River, in Blount County, Tennessee.

**Tsunda'nilti'yĭ**—"Where they demanded the debt from him"; a place on the Little Santeetla River, west of Robbinsville, in Graham County, North Carolina. The creek also is commonly known by the same name. See number 122.

**Tsundige'wĭ**—"Closed anuses," literally "They have them closed," understood to refer to the anus; from *dige'wĭ*, plural of *ge'wĭ*, closed, stopped up, blind; compare *Tsul'kălû'*; also *Gûlisge'wĭ*, "Blind, or closed, ears," an old personal name. See number 74.

**tsun'digwûn'tskĭ** (contracted from *tsun'digwûntsû'gĭ*, "they have them forked," referring to the peculiar forked tail; compare *Tsul'kălû'*)—a migratory bird which once appeared for a short time upon the East Cherokee reservation; apparently, from the description, it is the scissortail or swallow-tailed flycatcher (*Milvulus forficatus*). See number 35.

**Tsunegûñ'yĭ** (sometimes called *Tsul'kălû' Tsunegûñ'yĭ*)—Tennessee Bald, at the extreme head of the Tuckasegee River, on the east line of Jackson County, North Carolina. The name seems to mean, "There where it is white," from *ts*, a prefix indicating distance, *une'gă*, white, and *yĭ*, locative. See number 81 and notes.

**Tsunil'kălû**—the plural form for *Tsul'kălû*, see entry; a traditional giant tribe in the west. See number 106.

**tsunû'liyû' sûnĕstlâ'tă**—"they have split noses," from *agwă'liyû'*, "I have it," and *unĕstlâû'*, "it is cracked" (as a crack made by the sun's heat in a log or in the earth); the initial *s* makes it refer to the nose, *kăyăsâ'*. See number 76 and notes.

**tsunĭs'tsăhĭ**—"(those) having topknots or crests," from *ustsăhû'*, "having a topknot," *ustsăhĭ'*, "he has a topknot" (habitual). See number 76 and notes.

**Tsuniya'tigă**—"Naked People"; literally "They are naked there," from *uya'tigă*, naked (singular), with the prefix *ts*, indicating distance. A traditional western tribe. See number 105.

**tsunsdi'**—contracted from *tsunsdi'ga*, the plural of *usdi'ga* or *usdi'*, small.

**Tsunu'lăhûñ'skĭ**—"He tries, but fails" (habitually), from *detsinu'lăhûñ'gû'* (see entry), "I tried, but failed." A former noted chief among the East Cherokee, commonly known to white people as Junaluska. In early life he was called *Gûlkă-la'skĭ*, a name which denotes something habitually falling from a leaning position (compare *Ătă'-gûl'kălû'* and *Tsul'kălû'*). See page 164.

<insert>X</insert> <term>Tsûsgină'ĭ</term>—"the Ghost country," from *asgi'na*, "ghost," *ĭ*, locative, and *ts*, a prefix denoting distance. The land of the dead; it is situated in *Usûñhi'yĭ*, the Twilight land, in the west. See number 5.

<term>tsuskwa'lĭ</term>—plural of *uskwa'lĭ*, short.

<term>Tsuskwănûñ'năwa'tă</term>—"Worn-out blanket," from *tsuskwănûñ'nĭ*, blanket (the word refers to something having stripes), and *uwa'tă*, "worn out." James D. Wafford, a prominent Cherokee mixed-blood and informant in the Western nation, who died about 1896. See page 236.

<term>Tsûta'ga Uweyûñ'ĭ</term>—"Chicken creek," from *tsûta'ga*, chicken, and *uweyûñ'ĭ*, stream. An extreme eastern head-stream of the Nantahala River, in Macon County, North Carolina. See number 122.

<term>Tsuta'tsinasûñ'yĭ</term>—"Eddy place." A place on the Cheowa River at the mouth of Cockram Creek, in Graham County, North Carolina. For tradition see number 122.

<term>tsutsŭ'</term>—see *tlutlŭ'*.

<term>tsûn̂tû'tsĭ</term>—see *tlûn̂tû'tsĭ*.

<term>tsuwă'</term>—the mud-puppy or water-dog (*Menopoma* or *Protonopsis*). See number 59.

<term>Tsuwa'tel'da</term>—a contraction of *Tsuwa'teldûñ'yĭ*; the name has lost its meaning. Pilot Knob, north from Brevard, in Transylvania County, North Carolina. See number 82 and notes.

<term>Tsuwă'-uniyetsûñ'yĭ</term>—"Where the water-dogs laughed," from *tsuwă'* (*q. v.*), "water-dog," *uniyĕ'tsû*, "they laughed" (*agiyet'skû*, "I am laughing"), and *yĭ*, locative; Tusquittee Bald, near Hayesville, in Clay County, North Carolina. For the story see number 122.

<term>Tsuwe'năhĭ</term>—A traditional hunter, in communication with the invisible people. See number 83. The name seems to mean "He has them in abundance," an irregular or archaic form for *Uwe'năhĭ*, "he has abundance," "he is rich," from *agwe'năhĭ'*, "I am rich." As a masculine name it is used as the equivalent of Richard. See number 83.

<term>TUCKALEECHEE</term>—see *Tikwălĭ'tsĭ*.

<term>TUCKASEGEE</term>—see *Tsĭksĭ'tsĭ*.

<term>TUGALOO</term>—see *Dugilu'yĭ*.

<term>tugalû'!</term>—the cry of the *dagû'l'kû* goose.

<term>tugălû'nă</term>—a variety of small fish, about four inches long, frequenting the larger streams (from *gălû'nă*, a gourd, on account of its long nose). See number 39 and notes.

<term>tûksĭ'</term>—the terrapin or land tortoise; also the name of a Cherokee chief about the close of the Revolution. *Sălĭgu'gĭ*, common turtle; soft-shell turtle, *u'lănă'wă*.

<term>Tûksĭ'tsĭ</term>—see *Tsĭksĭ'tsĭ*.

<term>TULI-CULA</term>—see *Tsul' kălû'*.

<term>tûlsku'wa</term>—"he snaps with his head," from *uskă'*, head; the snapping beetle.

<term>Tunâ'ĭ</term>—a traditional warrior and medicine-man of old Itsâ'tĭ; the name cannot be analyzed. See number 99.

<term>TURKEYTOWN</term>—see *Gûn-dĭ'gaduhûñ'yĭ*.

<term>TURNIPTOWN</term>—see *U'lûñ'yĭ*.

<term>TUSKEGEE</term>—see *Tă'skĭ'gĭ*.

<term>TUSQUITTEE BALD</term>—see *Tsuwă'-uniyetsûñ'yĭ*.

<term>TUSQUITTEE CREEK</term>—see *Daskwitûñ'yĭ*.

<term>tu'stĭ</term>—for *tustĭ'gă*, a small bowl; larger jars are called *diwa'lĭ* and *ûn̂tĭ'yă*.

<term>tûñ'tăwû'</term>—a small yellow night-moth. The name comes from *ahûn'tû*, a word implying that something flits into and out of the blaze. See number 59.

<term>tu'tĭ</term>—snowbird.

<term>Tutĭ'yĭ</term>—"Snowbird place," from *tu'tĭ*, snowbird, and *yĭ*, locative. Little Snowbird Creek of the Cheowa River, in Graham County, North Carolina.

<term>tû'tsahyesĭ'</term>—"he will marry you."
