Uchee—see *Anĭ'-Yu'tsĭ*.
*udâ'hale'yĭ*—"on the sunny side."
*udâ'ĭ*—the baneberry or cohosh vine (*Actæa?*). The name signifies that the plant has something long hanging from it.
*uda'lĭ*—"(it is) married"; the mistletoe, so named because of its parasitic habit.
*U'dăwagûñ'ta*—"Bald." A bald mountain of the Great Smoky range, in Yancey County, North Carolina, not far from Mount Mitchell. See number 51.
*Udsi'skalâ*—a masculine name.
*uga'sĭtă*—sour.
*ûñgidă'*—"your two elder brothers" (male speaking). See notes for number 63.
*ûñgili'sĭ* (plural, *tsûñgili'sĭ*)—"my daughter's child." See the note for number 66, and compare *ûñgini'sĭ*.
*ûñgini'lĭ*—"my elder brother" (female speaking). See notes for number 63.
*ûñgini'sĭ* (plural *tsûñgini'sĭ*)—"my son's child." See the note for number 66, and compare *ûñgili'sĭ*.
*u'gĭskâ'*—"he is swallowing it"; from *tsĭkiû'*, "I am eating." See number 8 and the notes.
*u'guku'*—the hooting or barred owl (*Syrnium nebulosum*); the name is onomatopoeic. See also *tskĭlĭ'* and *wa'huhu'*.
*ugûnste'lĭ* (*ugûnste'lû* in dialectal form)—the hornyhead fish (*Campostoma*, stone roller). The name is said, though on doubtful authority, to refer to its having horns. See number 59.
*Ugûñ'yĭ*—Tallulah Falls, on the river of that name, northeast from Clarkesville, in Habersham County, Georgia; the meaning of the name is lost. See number 84.
UILATA—See *U'tlûn'tă*.
*uk-ku'sûñtsûtëtĭ'*—"it will twist up one's arm." See number 115.
*Uk-ku'sûñtsûtĭ'*—"Bent-bow-shape"; a comic masculine name. Compare *gûltsû'tĭ*, bow. See number 115.
*uk-kwûnâgi'stĭ*—"it will draw down one's eye." See number 115.
*Uk-kwûnâgi'ta*—"Eye-drawn-down"; a comic masculine name. See number 115.
*uksu'hĭ*—the mountain blacksnake or black racer (*Coluber obsoletus*); the name seems to refer to some peculiarity of the eye, *aktâ'*; *uksuhâ'*, "he has something lodged in his eye." See number 53 and the notes.
*Ukte'na*—"Keen-eyed (?)" from *aktâ'*, eye, *akta'ti*, to examine closely. A mythical great horned serpent, with a talismanic diadem. See number 50 and the notes.
*Ukte'na-tsuganûñ'tatsûñ'yĭ*—"Where the Uktena became fastened." A spot on the Tuckasegee River, about two miles above Bryson City, in Swain County, North Carolina. See number 122.
*Uktena-utansi'nastûñ'yĭ*—"Where the Uktena crawled." A rock on the north bank of the Tuckasegee River, about four miles above Bryson City, in Swain County, North Carolina. See number 122.
*Ukwû'nû* (or *Ukwû'nĭ*)—a former Cherokee settlement, commonly known to white people as Oconee, on Seneca Creek, near present-day Walhalla, in Oconee County, South Carolina.
*Ula'gû'*—the mythical original of the yellow-jacket tribe. See number 13. The word signifies "leader," "boss," or "principal one," and is applied to the first yellow-jacket (*dĭska'ĭ*) seen in the spring, to a queen bee, and to the leader of a working squad.
*u'lănă'wă*—the soft-shell turtle; the etymology of the word is uncertain. See also *sâligu'gĭ* and *tûksĭ'*.
*ulasu'la*—moccasin, shoe.

*ûlĕ'*—and; *ûlĕ'-nû'*, and also.

*Ûnlĭ'ta*—"(He is) long-winded," an archaic form of the regular word *gûnlĭ'ta*; an old masculine name. This was the name of a chief around the year 1790, known to white people as "The Breath."

*ûlskwûlte'gĭ*—a "pound-mill," a self-acting water-mill used in the Cherokee mountains. The name signifies that "it butts with its head" (*uskă'*, head), referring to the way the pestle works in the mortar. The general word for mill is *dista'stĭ*.

*ulstĭtlû'*—literally, "it is on his head." This refers to the diamond crest on the head of the mythical Uktena serpent. When detached, it becomes the *Ulûñsû'tĭ*.

*Ultiwâ'ĭ*—a former Cherokee settlement near present-day Ooltewah, on the creek of the same name in James County, Tennessee. The name uses the locative form (the *ĭ* suffix) but cannot be translated.

*ulûñnĭ'ta*—domesticated or tame; this may be used for people as well as animals, but not for plants. For cultivated or domesticated plants, the adjective is *gûnutlûñ'ĭ* (or *gûnusûn'ĭ*).

*Ulûñsû'tĭ*—"Transparent"; the great talismanic crystal of the Cherokee. It is spelled Oolunsade by Hagar. See entry number 50 and its notes.

*ulûñ'ta*—"it has climbed," from *tsilahĭ'*, "I am climbing"; the poison oak (*Rhus radicans*). See entry number 126.

*U'lûn'yĭ*—"Tuber place," from *U'lĭ'*, a variety of edible tuber, and *yĭ*, the locative suffix. A former settlement on Turniptown (named for *U'lûn'yĭ*) Creek, above Ellijay in Gilmer County, Georgia.

UNACALA—see *Une'gădihĭ'*.

*U'nadanti'yĭ*—"Place where they conjured," the name of a gap about three miles east of Webster in Jackson County, North Carolina, and now the name of the town itself. See entry number 122.

*unăde'na*—woolly or downy (when speaking of animals); *uwă'nû* refers to wool, down, or fine fur when detached from the animal.

*u'năhû'*—see *unăhwĭ'*.

*unăhwĭ'*—heart; in the Middle and Lower dialects, it is *u'năhû'*. See page 187.

UNAKA—see *une'gă* and UNICOI.

*unatlûnwe'hitû*—"it has spirals"; an unidentified plant used in conjuring. See entry number 126.

*une'gă*—white.

*une'guhĭ*—"he is (or was) mischievous or bad"; *tsúne'guhĭ'yu*, "you are very mischievous" (said to a child). See entry number 118.

*une'gutsătû'*—"(he is) mischievous"; *a'gĭne'gutsătû'*, "I am mischievous."

*Une'lănûn'hĭ*—"The Apportioner"; "I am apportioning" is *gané laskû'*; "I apportion" (habitually) is *ganélaskĭ*. In the sacred formulas, this is a title for the Sun deity; in the Bible, it is the name for God.

*une'stălûñ*—ice.

UNICOI—the map name of the old Unicoi turnpike (see page 87), of a gap on the watershed between the Chattahoochee and Hiwassee rivers in Georgia, and of a county in eastern Tennessee. It is probably a corruption of *une'gă* (white), which is also the source of Unaka, the current map name for part of the Great Smoky range.

*uni'gistĭ*—foods; the singular form is *agĭ'stĭ*.

*Uniga'yata'ti'yĭ*—"Where they made a fish trap," from *uga'yatûñ'ĭ* (fish trap) and *yĭ* (locative); a place on the Tuckasegee River at the mouth of Deep Creek, near Bryson City in Swain County, North Carolina. See entry number 100 and its notes.

*Uni'hăluna*—see *Ăhălu'na*.

*Unika'wĭ*—the "Townhouse dance," so called because it was danced inside the townhouse. The name does not refer to a townhouse (*gati'yĭ*) and cannot be analyzed, but it may have some connection with the ancient word for deer. Compare with *Ani'-Kawĭ'*.

<margin>X</margin> **Une'ga-dihi'**—"White-man-killer"; from *une'ga*, "white," for *yûn'wune'ga*, "white person," and *dihi'*, a noun suffix denoting a "killer" (specifically, "he kills them" habitually). A Cherokee chief whose name appears in documents from around 1790 as White-man-killer, or, by misprint, Unacala. It is an old masculine name that existed until recently on the reservation. Compare *Ta'gwădihi'*.

**u'niskwetu'gĭ**—"they wear a hat"; *ûlskwe'tăwă'*, hat, from *uskă'*, head. The may-apple (*Podophyllum*). See entry number 126.

**unistilûn'istĭ**—"they stick on along their whole length"; the generic name for "stickers" and burs, including the Spanish needle, cocklebur, jimson weed, etc. See entry number 126.

**uni'tsĭ**—her mother; *agitsĭ'*, my mother.

**Uniyâ'hitûn'yĭ**—"Where they shot it," from *tsiyâ'ihû*, "I shoot," and *yĭ*, locative. A place on the Tuckasegee River a short distance above Bryson City, in Swain County, North Carolina. See entry number 100.

**Untoola**—see *Dihyûn'dulâ'*.

**Unta'kiyastĭ'yĭ**—"Where they race," from *takiya'tă*, a race, and *yĭ*, locative; locally altered to Tahkeyostee. The district on the French Broad River around Asheville, in Buncombe County, North Carolina. The town itself is known to the Cherokee as *Kâsdu'yĭ*, "Ashes place" (from *kâsdu*, ashes, and *yĭ*, locative), which is intended as a translation of its English name. See entry number 122.

**Untlasgâstĭ'yĭ**—"Where they scratched"; a place at the head of Hyatt Creek of the Valley River, in Cherokee County, North Carolina. For the tradition, see entry number 122.

**UNTOOLA**—see *Dihyûn'dulâ'*.

**unûn'tĭ**—milk.

**usdĭ'gă** (abbreviated *usdĭ'*), small; plural *tsunsdĭ'gă*, *tsunsdĭ'*.

**usga'sĕ'ti'yu**—very dangerous, very terrible; the intensive form of *usga'sĕ'tĭ*.

**Uskwăle'na**—"Big-head," from *uskă'*, head; a masculine name, perhaps the original of the "Bull-head" given by Haywood as the name of a former noted Cherokee warrior.

**Uskwă'lĭ-gû'tă**—"His stomach hangs down," from *uskwă'lĭ*, his stomach, and *gû'tă*, "it hangs down." A prominent chief of the Revolutionary period, known to white people as Hanging-maw.

**U'stăna'lĭ** (from *u'stănalâ'hĭ* or *uni'stăna'lâ* [a plural form], denoting a natural barrier of rocks across a stream)—a name occurring in several places in the old Cherokee country and variously spelled Eastinaulee, Eastanora, Estanaula, Eustenauree, Istanare, Oostanaula, Oostinawley, Ustenary, etc. One settlement of this name was on the Keowee River, below the present Fort George in Oconee County, South Carolina; another seems to have been somewhere on the waters of the Tuckasegee River in western North Carolina; a third, prominent during and after the Revolutionary period, was just above the junction of the Coosawatee and Conasauga rivers (which form the Oostanaula) in Gordon County, Georgia, and adjoining New Echota (see *Gănsâ'gĭ*). Other settlements of the same name may have been on Eastanollee Creek of the Tugaloo River in Franklin County, Georgia, and on Eastanaula Creek, which flows into the Hiwassee River in McMinn County, Tennessee. Compare *Tsû'stănalûn'yĭ*, under *Dăgunâ'hĭ*.

**u'stûtĭ**—see *utsû'gĭ*.

**Ustû'tlĭ**—a traditional dangerous serpent. The name signifies having something on the calf of the leg or on the heel, from *ustûtûn'ĭ*, (his) calf of the leg (attached). It is also applied to the southern hoop-snake (*Abastor erythrogrammus*). See entry number 54.

<margin>X</margin> **Usûnhi'yĭ**—the "Darkening land," where it is always getting dark, as at twilight. This name is used for the west in myths and sacred formulas; the common word is *wude'ligûn'yĭ*, "there where it (the sun) goes down." In entry number 63, the word used is *wusûhĭhûn'yĭ*, "there where they stay overnight." See also *Tsûsginâ'i*.

*u'tänû*—great, fully developed. Compare *e'gwa*.

*utawâ'hilû*—"hand-breadth," from *uwâ'yĭ*, hand. A figurative term used in myths and sacred formulas.

*U'tăwagûn'ta*—"Bald place." A high bald peak of the Great Smoky range on the Tennessee-North Carolina line, northeast of Big Pigeon River. See number 51.

*Ûñ'tiguhi'*—"Pot in the water," from *ûñti'yă* or *ûñti'*, pot, and *guhĭ'*, "it is in the water" (or another liquid—habitually). The Suck, a dangerous rapid in the Tennessee River at the entrance of Suck Creek, about eight miles below Chattanooga, Tennessee. See number 63 and notes.

*U'tlûñ'tă*—"He (or she) has it sharp," that is, has some sharp part or organ; it could be used for a tooth, fingernail, or some other attached part of the body, but in the story it is understood to refer to the awl-like finger. Ten Kate spells it *Uilata*. A mythical half-human monster. See number 66 and notes.

*U'tlûñtûñ'yĭ*—"U'tlûñ'tă place;" see *U'tlûñ'tă*. A place on the Little Tennessee River, nearly opposite Citico Creek, in Blount County, Tennessee. See number 66 and notes, and number 124.

*U'tsălă*—"Lichen"; another form of *utsăle'ta*. A Cherokee chief of the Removal period. See page 157.

*utsăle'ta*—lichen, literally "pot scrapings," named because of an imagined resemblance.

*Ûñtsaiyĭ'* (also *Etsaiyĭ'* or *Tsaiyĭ'*, the first syllable is almost silent)—"Brass." A mythical gambler. See number 63 and notes. The current translation, "brass," is probably a modern application of the old mythical name, and is based on the similarity of the sound to that produced by striking a sheet of metal.

*utsa'nătĭ'*—rattlesnake; the name is of uncertain origin, but is said to refer to the rattle.

*Utsa'nătĭ'yĭ*—"Rattlesnake place." Rattlesnake Springs, about two miles south of Charleston, Bradley County, Tennessee. See page 132.

*utset'stĭ*—"he grins" (habitually). See *sĭ'kwă utset'stĭ*.

*utsĭ'*—her (or his) mother; *etsĭ'*, *agitsĭ'*, my mother.

*Utsĭ'dsătă'*—"Corn-tassel," "Thistle-head," etc. It is used as a masculine name and was probably the Cherokee name of the chief known during the Revolutionary period as "Old Tassel."

*utsu''gĭ*—the tufted titmouse (*Parus bicolor*); also called *u'stûtĭ*, "topknot, or tip," because of its crest. See numbers 35 and 66.

*û'tsûtĭ'*—fish. Compare *u'tsûtĭ*, many.

*ûñwădâ'lĭ*—storehouse, provision house. See number 3 and notes.

*Un'wădâ-tsu'gilasûñ'*—"Where the storehouse (*ûñwădâ'lĭ*) was taken off." Either Black Rock or Jones Knob, northeast of Webster, on the east line of Jackson County, North Carolina. See number 122.

*Uwagâ'hĭ* (commonly written Ocoee)—"Apricot place," from *uwa'gă*, the "apricot vine" or "maypop" (*Passiflora incarnata*), and *hĭ*, locative. A former important settlement on the Ocoee River, near its junction with the Hiwassee, near present-day Benton, in Polk County, Tennessee.

*uwâ'yĭ*—hand, paw; generally used with the possessive suffix, as *uwâye'nĭ*, "his hand."

*uwe'la*—liver.

*uwe'năhĭ*—rich; also used as a personal name as the equivalent of Richard. Compare *Tsuwe'năhĭ*.

*Uw'tsûñ'tă*—"Bouncer" (habitual); from *k'tsĭ*, "it is bouncing." A traditional serpent described as moving in jerks like a measuring worm, to which the name is also applied. See number 55.

*Uyâhye'*—a high peak in the Great Smoky range, probably along the border between Swain County, North Carolina, and Sevier or Blount County, Tennessee. See number 75 and notes.

## MOONEY] GLOSSARY

**Uy'gilâ'gĭ**—abbreviated from *Tsuyu'gilâ'gĭ*, "Where there are dams," that is, beaver dams; from *qu' gilû'ûñskû'*, "he is damming it." 1. A former settlement on Oothcaloga (Ougillogy) Creek of the Oostanaula River, near the present Calhoun, in Gordon County, Georgia; 2. Beaverdam Creek, west of Clarkesville, in Habersham County, Georgia.

VALLEYTOWN—see *Gû'nahitûñ'yĭ*.
VENGEANCE CREEK—see *Gănsa'tĭ'yĭ*.

WACHESA—see *Watsi'sŭ*.
**wadâñ'**—thanks!
**wâ'dĭ**—paint, especially red paint.
**wâ'dige-askâ'lĭ**—"his head (is) brown," that is, "brown-head," from *wâdige'ĭ*, brown or brownish-red, and *askâ'lĭ*, possessive of *uskâ'*, head; the copperhead snake.
**Wadĭ'yâhĭ**—A feminine name of doubtful etymology. An expert basket-making woman among the Eastern Cherokee who died in 1895. She was known to the whites as Mrs. Bushyhead. See page 179.
WAFFORD—see *Tsuskwunûn'nâwa'tă*.
**Wa'gĭnsĭ'**—The name of an eddy at the junction of the Little Tennessee and main Tennessee rivers, at Lenoir, in Loudon County, Tennessee. The town is now known to the Cherokee by the same name, the meaning of which is lost. See number 124.
**wagulĭ'**—whippoorwill; the name is an onomatopoeia; the Delaware name is *wekolis* (Heckewelder).
WAHNENAUHI—see *Wanĭ'nâhĭ'*.
**wa'huhu'**—the screech-owl (*Megascops asio*); see also *tskĭlĭ'* and *uguku'*.
**wa'ka**—cow; from the Spanish *vaca*, as is also the Creek *waga* and the Arapaho *wakúch*.
**walâ'sĭ**—the common green frog; there are different names for the bullfrog (*kûnu'nŭ*, which see) and for other varieties; warts are also called *walâ'sĭ*.
**Walâsĭ'yĭ**—"Frog place." 1. A former settlement, known to the whites as Frogtown, upon the creek of the same name, north of Dahlonega, in Lumpkin County, Georgia. 2. Le Conte and Bullhead mountains in the Great Smoky range on the North Carolina-Tennessee line, together with the ridge extending into Sevier County, Tennessee, between the Middle and West forks of the Little Pigeon River. See number 51 and notes.
**walâs'-unûl'stĭ**—"it fights frogs," from *walâ'sĭ*, frog, and *unûl'stĭ*, "it fights" (habitually); *gâ'lĭhû'*, "I am fighting." The *Prosartes lanuginosa* plant. See number 126.
**Walâs'-unûlstĭ'yĭ**—"Place of the plant *walâs'-unûl'stĭ*," commonly known to the whites as Fightingtown, from a translation of the latter part of the name; a former settlement on Fightingtown Creek, near Morganton, in Fannin County, Georgia. See number 125.
**Walinĭ'**—a feminine name, compounded from *Walĭ*, another form of *Kwalĭ*, "Polly," with a suffix added for euphony.
**Wane'-asûñ'tlûñyĭ**—"Hickory footlog place," from *wane'ĭ*, hickory, *asûñtlûñ'ĭ* (which see), footlog or bridge, and *yĭ*, locative. A former settlement, known to the whites as Hickory-log, on the Etowah River, a short distance above Canton, in Cherokee County, Georgia.
**Wanĭ'nâhĭ'**—a feminine name of uncertain etymology; the Wahnenauhi of the Wahnenauhi manuscript.
WASHINGTON—see *Wa'sitû'nâ*.
**Wâ'sĭ**—the Cherokee form for Moses.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Cherokee terms, moving from "Wa'sitû'nă" to "Xuala." It provides definitions for personal names, geographic locations in North Carolina, Tennessee, and Alabama, and translations for natural elements and cardinal directions.</meta>

# 546 MYTHS OF THE CHEROKEE [ETH. ANN. 19]

**Wa'sitû'nă, Wa'sûñtû'nă** (different dialect forms)—a Cherokee known to the white people as Washington, the only survivor of a Removal tragedy. See page 158. The name signifies a hollow log (or another cylindrical object) lying on the ground at a distance; the root of the word is *asi'ita*, log, and the *w* prefix indicates it is at a distance.

**Wa'sulû'**—a large red-brown moth that flies around the blossoming tobacco in the evening.

**Watâ'gĭ** (commonly written Watauga, also Watoga, Wattoogee, Whatoga, etc.)—a name appearing in two or more towns in the old Cherokee territory; one was an important settlement on Watauga Creek of the Little Tennessee River, a few miles below Franklin, in Macon County, Tennessee <note>Franklin is located in Macon County, North Carolina; the author likely misidentified the state.</note>; another was traditionally located at Watauga Old Fields, near the present Elizabethton, on the Watauga River, in Carter County, Tennessee. See page 21. The meaning of the name has been lost.

**WATAUGA**—see *Watâ'gĭ*.

**Watsĭ'să**—a prominent old Cherokee, known to the white people as Wachesa, a name that cannot be translated. He formerly lived on lower Beaverdam Creek of the Hiwassee River, below Murphy, in Cherokee County, North Carolina. Because the Unicoi turnpike passed near his home, it was locally known as the Wachesa trail.

**wa'ya**—wolf; the name is an onomatopoeia, intended to imitate the animal's howl; compare the Creek name, *yähä*.

**Wa'yâ'hĭ**—"Wolf place," meaning the place of the Wolf clan; the form *Anĭ'-Wa'yâ'hĭ* is not used. It refers to the Wolftown settlement on upper Soco Creek, on the East Cherokee reservation, in Jackson County, North Carolina.

**WAYA GAP**—see *Â'tâhĭ'ta*.

**WAYEH**—see *Wâyî*.

**Wâyî**—"Pigeon"; the modern Cherokee name for the Big Pigeon River in western North Carolina; likely a translation of the English name. It also appears as Wayeh.

**WELCH, LLOYD**—see *Da'si'giya'gĭ*.

**wesă**—cat; a corruption of "pussy."

**WHITE-PATH**—see *Nûñnâ'hi-tsunĕ'ga*.

**WILLSTOWN**—a formerly important settlement named after the mixed-heritage chief known to the white people as Red-headed Will, located on Will's Creek below Fort Payne, in Dekalb County, Alabama. The settlement was frequently called *Wilî'yĭ*, "Will's place," after him, but this was not the proper local name.

**Wilsĭnĭ'**—the Cherokee name for H. W. Spray, agent and superintendent for the East Cherokee reservation; an adaptation of his middle name, Wilson.

**Wil-usdĭ'**—"Little Will," from *Wilî'*, Will, and *usdĭ'ga* or *usdĭ'*, little. This was the Cherokee name for Colonel W. H. Thomas, who for many years was the recognized chief of the eastern band.

**WISSACTAW**—see *găhăwĭ'sita*.

**WOLFTOWN**—see *Wa'yâ'hĭ*.

<image-desc>A large right-hand brace groups the following two entries together, pointing to the reference text.</image-desc>

WOOTASSITE } —see OUTACITY.
WROSETASATOW }

**Wude'ligûn'yĭ**—the west; literally "there where it (the sun) goes down" (the *w* prefix implies distance, and *yĭ* is a locative). See also *Usûñhi'yĭ* and *wusûhihûn'yĭ*.

**Wuliga'nătûtûñ**—excelling all others, in either a good or bad sense; it may be used as the equivalent of *wastûñ*, "beyond the limit." See page 232.

<margin>*wusûhihûn'yĭ*—"there where they stay overnight," meaning "the west." This is an archaic term used by the narrator of the story of *Ûñtsaiyĭ'*, number 63. The common word is *wude'ligûn'yĭ* (refer to that entry), while the term used in sacred formulas is *Usûñhi'yĭ* (refer to that entry).</margin>

**XUALA**—see *Anĭ-Suwa'lĭ*.

<vocab>Wa'sitû'nă, Wa'sûñtû'nă, Washington, Wa'sulû', Watâ'gĭ, Watauga, Watsĭ'să, Wachesa, wa'ya, Wa'yâ'hĭ, Wâyî, Welch, wesă, Willstown, Wilsĭnĭ', Wil-usdĭ', Wude'ligûn'yĭ, Wuliga'nătûtûñ, wusûhihûn'yĭ, Xuala</vocab>

It includes linguistic origins for words related to the wolf, the cat, and the cardinal direction of the west.</summary>

# 547 MOONEY] GLOSSARY 547

**-yǎ**—a suffix denoting principal or real, such as *tsiskwa'yă*, "principal bird," the sparrow; *Ani'-Yûnwiya'*, "principal or real people," Indians.

**YAHOOLA**—see *Yahulâ'ǐ*.

**Yahulâ'ǐ**—"Yahu'la place," from *Yahu'la*, a Cherokee trader said to have been taken by the spirit people; *Yahu'la* seems to be from the Creek *yoho'lo*, a name referring to the song (*yoho'lo*) used in the "black drink" ceremony of the Creeks; thus *asi-yoho'lo*, corrupted into Osceola, signified "the black drink song." It may, however, be a true Cherokee word, *yahu'lû* or *yahu'lǐ*, the name for a variety of hickory, and also for the "doodle-bug"; *Ûnyahu'lǎ* is a feminine name, but cannot be translated. Yahoola Creek, near Dahlonega, in Lumpkin County, Georgia. See entry number 86 and the accompanying notes.

**Yalâ'gǐ**—Alarka Creek of the Little Tennessee River, above the junction of the Tuckasegee, in Swain County, North Carolina; the meaning of the name is lost.

**yañdaska'ga**—a faultfinder. See entry number 61.

**Yân-e'gwa**—"Big-bear," from *yánû*, bear, and *egwa*, great or large. A prominent chief around the year 1800; the name occurs in treaties as Yonah, Yohanaqua, and Yonahequah. See page 164.

**yâ'nû**—bear.

**Yâ'nû-diněhûñ'yǐ**—"Where the bears live," from *yánû*, bear, *diněhû'*, "they dwell" (*ě'hû*, "I dwell, I live"), and *yǐ*, the locative suffix. A place on the Oconaluftee River, a short distance above the junction with the Tuckasegee, in Swain County, North Carolina. See entry number 122.

**Yânûgûn'skǐ**—"The bear drowns him" (habitually), from *yánû*, bear, and *tsigûn'iskǎ'*, "I am drowning him." A noted East Cherokee chief, known to the white people as Yonaguska or Drowning-bear. See page 162.

**Yâ'nû-u'nătawastǐ'yǐ**—"Where the bears wash" (from *yánû*, bear, and *yǐ*, the locative suffix); a former pond in the Great Smoky Mountains, near the extreme head of Raven Fork, in Swain County, North Carolina. See entry number 122.

**yân'-utse'stû**—"the bear lies on it"; the shield fern (*Aspidium*). See entry number 126.

**Yawâ'ǐ**—"Yawǎ place"; a place on Yellow Creek of the Cheowa River, in Graham County, North Carolina. See entry number 122.

**YELLOW-HILL**—see *Elǎwâ'diyǐ*.

**YOHANAQUA**—see *Yân-e'gwa*.

**yoho-o!**—a meaningless song refrain. See entry number 75.

**YONAGUSKA**—see *Yâ'nûgûn'skǐ*.

**YONAH**—1. (mountain) see *Gadalû'lû*. 2. An abbreviated treaty form for the name of the chief *Yân-e'gwa*.

**YONAHEQUAH**—see *Yân-e'gwa*.

**YTAUA, YTAVA**—see *I'tǎwǎ'*.

**Yu!**—a meaningless song refrain and interjection.

**Yuha'lǐ**—Euharlee Creek, of the lower Etowah River, in Bartow County, Georgia. The name is said by the Cherokee to be a corruption of Yufala (Eufaula), a well-known Creek local name. See entry number 105.

**yûnsû'**—buffalo; compare the Creek *yěna'sa*, Choctaw *yanash*, and Hichitee *ya'nasi*.

**Yûnsâ'ǐ**—"Buffalo place"; West Buffalo Creek of the Cheowa River in Graham County, North Carolina; the site of a former Cherokee settlement. See entry number 122.

**yu'wě-yuwěhe'**—a meaningless song refrain. See entry number 118.

**yûñ'wǐ**—person, man; compare the Mohawk *oñgwe'*.

**Yûñ'wǐ Amă'yǐně'hǐ**—"Water-dwelling People," from *yûñ'wǐ*, person, and *ămă'yǐně'hǐ*, the plural of *ămǎyě'hǐ* (see *ămǎyě'hǐ*); a race of water fairies. See entry number 78.

**Yûñ'wǐ-dǐkatǎgûñ'yǐ**—see *Yûñ'wi-tsulenûñ'yǐ*.

**Yûñ'wǐ Gûnăhi'ta**—"Long Man"; a formulaic name for the river, personified as a man with his head resting on the mountain and his feet stretching down to the lowlands, who is constantly speaking to those who can understand the message.

<summary>This page concludes the Cherokee glossary, detailing terms beginning with "Y," including names for bears, buffalo, and people, as well as geographic locations and spiritual entities like the "Long Man." It also clarifies the etymology of several prominent chiefs' names and their variants found in historical treaties.</summary>

<margin>X</margin>
**Yûn'wini'giskĭ**—"Man-eaters," literally, "They eat people" (habitually), from *yûn'wĭ*, person, man, and *uni'giskĭ*, "they eat" (habitually), from *tsĭkiu'*, "I am eating"; the Cherokee name for a distant cannibal tribe, possibly the Atakapa or the Tonkawa. See entry number 105. Compare *Anăda'dûñtăskĭ*.

**Yûn'wĭ-tsulenûñ'yĭ**—"Where the man stood," originally *Yûn'wĭ-dĭkatágûñ'yĭ*, "Where the man stands," from *yûn'wĭ*, person, man, *tsĭtâ'gă*, "I am standing," and *yĭ*, locative; Standing Indian, a high bald mountain at the head of the Nantahala River, in Macon County, North Carolina. See entry number 122.

**Yûn'wĭ Tsunsdi'**—"Little People," from *yûn'wĭ*, person, people, and *tsunsdi'gă* or *tsunsdi'*, plural of *usdi'gă* or *usdi'*, little; the Cherokee fairies. See entry number 78.

<margin>/</margin>
**Yûn'wĭ Usdi'**—"Little Man." A formulaic name for the ginseng, *â'tălĭ-gûli'*, see that entry.

<margin>X</margin>
**Yûn'wĭ-usga'sĕ'tĭ**—"Dangerous Man, Terrible Man"; a traditional leader in the westward migration of the Cherokee. See page 99.

**Yûn'wiya'**—"Indian," literally, "principal or real person," from *yûn'wĭ*, person and *yă*, a suffix denoting principal or real. See pages 15 and 181.
